steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean; identity infrastructure integrity restored.

steps.title: Verify backup integrity before restoring
steps.desc: Confirm backups predate the compromise and are free of the ransomware/backdoor before restoring; check for operator tampering with backup systems specifically.
steps.guidance: Human operators frequently target and disable/delete backups before triggering encryption — verify backup system integrity itself.
steps.outcome: Clean, verified backup identified for restore.
steps.abort: If no clean backup exists, escalate rebuild timeline and options to leadership.

steps.title: Do not pay the ransom; coordinate with Legal and law enforcement if demanded
steps.desc: Standard guidance is against payment. Leadership/Legal make the final decision.
steps.outcome: Payment decision made deliberately by Legal/Executive.

steps.title: Document the full incident and reassess privileged-access controls
steps.desc: Record the operator's full activity timeline and remediate the privileged-access and detection gaps that allowed manual, hands-on-keyboard compromise.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31142.def: A targeted ransomware attack in which the deploying group purchased or otherwise received already-established access to the victim environment from a separate initial access broker (IAB), rather than performing their own initial compromise.
ITID-31142.purpose: Captures targeted ransomware attacks where the deploying actor obtained access via a handoff from a separate initial access broker.
scopeIncludes: Ransomware deployment following confirmed handoff of existing footholds (e.g., a pre-planted backdoor or valid credentials) from a distinct access-broker actor
Cases where forensic evidence shows two distinct actor toolsets: an earlier access-establishing intrusion and a later, separate ransomware deployment
scopeExcludes: Ransomware deployed by a single actor who performed their own initial access (ITID-31141 or vector-specific leaves under Encrypting Ransomware)
ITID-31142.severity: Critical; pre-established access often means the ransomware actor has a running start on lateral movement.
ITID-31142.escalation: Escalate immediately; treat any prior unexplained access/backdoor found in the environment as a potential precursor requiring separate investigation of how it was originally established.
indicators: Two distinct sets of tooling/timelines in forensic evidence: an earlier access-establishment phase and a later, separate deployment phase
Backdoor or credential access with no clear link to the ransomware operator's usual initial-access pattern
vectors: Use of access purchased from an initial access broker (compromised credentials, existing backdoor, or web shell) as the entry point for ransomware deployment
rootCauses: Undetected initial compromise that was later resold/handed off before ransomware deployment
Insufficient monitoring to detect dormant unauthorized access prior to its exploitation by a second actor
controls: Regular credential rotation and anomalous-access monitoring
Threat hunting for dormant/unexplained persistence mechanisms
Immutable/offline backups
ITID-31142.detection: Best identified retrospectively through forensic timeline analysis distinguishing two separate actor toolsets; real-time detection relies on catching the original unauthorized access before handoff.
ITID-31142.response: Investigate and remediate the original access-establishment vector in addition to standard ransomware containment, since the same broker may resell access again.
metrics: Time between original access establishment and ransomware deployment
Number of incidents attributed to a broker handoff pattern
ITID-31142.notes: Differentiated by attack characteristic (initial-access broker handoff) rather than the specific technical delivery vector, which may vary.

playbook.name: Response: Targeted Ransomware Following Initial Access Broker Handoff
playbook.description: For a confirmed targeted ransomware incident where access was purchased from or handed off by an initial access broker rather than obtained directly by the ransomware operator.

steps.title: Confirm encryption scope across the environment
steps.desc: Identify every host/share showing signs of encryption.
steps.outcome: Full encryption scope established.

steps.title: Investigate the full access chain, including the original broker compromise
steps.desc: Determine how the initial access broker originally gained access (often weeks/months before the ransomware operator's handoff), separately from the ransomware deployment itself.
steps.guidance: The broker's original access method may be entirely different from the ransomware operator's tradecraft — investigate both as distinct phases.
steps.outcome: Both the broker's original access vector and the ransomware operator's handoff/activity documented.

steps.title: Determine the handoff timeline and any overlap in access
steps.desc: Establish when access was handed off to the ransomware operator and whether the broker retains any separate persistent access.
steps.outcome: Handoff timeline established; broker's continued access (if any) identified.

steps.title: Isolate the entire affected network segment immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect affected systems at a segment level given ransomware's rapid lateral-spread nature.
steps.outcome: Further encryption and lateral movement halted.

steps.title: Close every access point used by both the broker and the ransomware operator
steps.desc: Remediate the broker's original foothold as well as any additional access mechanisms introduced by the ransomware operator, since either could remain independently.
steps.outcome: All identified access points from both actors closed.

steps.title: Engage Legal, Executive leadership, and law enforcement
steps.desc: Notify Legal and executives; consider law-enforcement referral. Do not engage with the extortion demand without Legal involvement.
steps.outcome: Leadership engaged and coordinating the business/legal response track.

steps.title: Remove the ransomware and every persistence/access mechanism from both actors
steps.desc: Clean confirmed-compromised hosts and close the full initial-access chain identified, including any broker-introduced tooling that predates the ransomware.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean of the ransomware and both actors' access.

steps.title: Verify backup integrity before restoring
steps.desc: Confirm backups predate the earliest known compromise (the broker's original access, not just the ransomware deployment) and are free of malware before restoring.
steps.outcome: Clean, verified backup identified for restore.
steps.abort: If no clean backup exists, escalate rebuild timeline to leadership.

steps.title: Do not pay the ransom; coordinate with Legal and law enforcement if demanded
steps.desc: Standard guidance is against payment. Leadership/Legal make the final decision.
steps.outcome: Payment decision made deliberately by Legal/Executive.

steps.title: Document the full access chain and remediate the original entry point
steps.desc: Record the complete timeline from the broker's original access through the ransomware handoff, and remediate the root-cause gap the broker exploited.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31143.def: A targeted ransomware attack in which the adversary deliberately timed encryptor deployment to coincide with a business-critical event (e.g., financial close, a major holiday/weekend, a merger announcement, or peak operational period) to maximize disruption and pressure to pay.
ITID-31143.purpose: Captures targeted ransomware attacks deliberately timed to coincide with a business-critical event to maximize pressure on the victim.
scopeIncludes: Deployment timed to a weekend, holiday, or off-hours window to delay detection/response
Deployment timed to coincide with a known business-critical date (financial close, product launch, seasonal peak)
scopeExcludes: Deployment where timing shows no deliberate correlation to a business-critical event (ITID-31141 or other sibling leaves)
ITID-31143.severity: Critical; deliberate timing is designed to maximize operational and negotiating pressure.
ITID-31143.priority: P1, with heightened urgency given the compounding business impact of the timing.
ITID-31143.escalation: Escalate immediately to executive leadership given the compounded business timing; ensure on-call/holiday IR coverage is adequate to respond as quickly as during business hours.
indicators: Encryptor deployment observed during a weekend, holiday, or known critical business window
Adversary dwell-time patterns showing deliberate waiting for a specific calendar date before deployment
vectors: Adversary monitoring internal calendars/communications to identify a high-pressure deployment window
Deployment deliberately delayed until reduced staffing coverage (nights, weekends, holidays)
rootCauses: Reduced security monitoring/staffing coverage during off-hours and holidays
Lack of an on-call IR process capable of responding as quickly outside business hours
controls: 24/7 SOC monitoring or equivalent on-call coverage including holidays/weekends
Immutable/offline backups
EDR behavioral detection independent of staffing hours
ITID-31143.detection: Technical detection is the same as other targeted ransomware, but response speed is the key risk factor given reduced off-hours staffing.
ITID-31143.response: Activate holiday/weekend IR on-call procedures immediately; do not allow reduced staffing to delay containment relative to a business-hours incident.
metrics: Time to first response by hour-of-week/holiday status
Number of incidents correlated with off-hours or business-critical timing
ITID-31143.notes: Differentiated by attack characteristic (deliberate timing) rather than the specific technical delivery vector, which may vary.

playbook.name: Response: Targeted Ransomware Deployment Timed to Business-Critical Event
playbook.description: For a confirmed targeted ransomware incident where deployment was deliberately timed to a business-critical event (e.g., financial close, major transaction, holiday weekend) to maximize pressure on the victim.

steps.title: Confirm encryption scope across the environment
steps.desc: Identify every host/share showing signs of encryption, prioritizing systems tied to the business-critical event in progress.
steps.outcome: Full encryption scope established, with critical-event-related systems flagged.

steps.title: Assess business impact of the timing specifically
steps.desc: Determine what critical process (close, transaction, event) is impacted and the operational/financial consequences of the timing, to inform prioritization.
steps.outcome: Business-impact assessment completed and shared with leadership.

steps.title: Identify the initial-access vector and attacker dwell time
steps.desc: Determine how and when the attacker gained access, noting whether the timing suggests advance planning around the known business event.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector and timeline established.

steps.title: Isolate the entire affected network segment immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect affected systems at a segment level given ransomware's rapid lateral-spread nature.
steps.outcome: Further encryption and lateral movement halted.

steps.title: Activate business continuity/disaster recovery plan for the affected process
steps.desc: Engage the business continuity plan to keep the time-critical process running via manual or alternate means while IR proceeds.
steps.outcome: Critical business process kept running or minimally disrupted via contingency plan.

steps.title: Engage Legal, Executive leadership, and law enforcement
steps.desc: Notify Legal and executives, emphasizing the deliberate timing pressure; consider law-enforcement referral. Do not engage with the extortion demand without Legal involvement.
steps.guidance: Attackers time deployment for leverage — leadership should be made aware this pressure is deliberate and factored into decision-making, not treated as coincidence.
steps.outcome: Leadership engaged and coordinating the business/legal response track.

steps.title: Remove the ransomware and every persistence/access mechanism found
steps.desc: Clean confirmed-compromised hosts and close the full initial-access chain identified.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean of the ransomware and attacker access.

steps.title: Verify backup integrity before restoring
steps.desc: Confirm backups predate the compromise and are free of the ransomware before restoring, prioritizing systems needed for the business-critical process.
steps.outcome: Clean, verified backup identified for restore.
steps.abort: If no clean backup exists, escalate rebuild timeline and contingency options to leadership.

steps.title: Do not pay the ransom; coordinate with Legal and law enforcement if demanded
steps.desc: Standard guidance is against payment despite the timing pressure. Leadership/Legal make the final decision.
steps.outcome: Payment decision made deliberately by Legal/Executive, resisting the induced urgency.

steps.title: Document the incident and review resilience of business-critical processes
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate whether critical processes need improved contingency plans or additional protection during known high-value windows.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31144.def: A targeted (human-directed, non-commodity) ransomware attack not yet attributable to a specific defining characteristic (human-operated deployment, initial-access-broker handoff, or deliberate business-critical timing).
ITID-31144.purpose: Catch-all for targeted ransomware attacks that do not fit a more specific attack-characteristic leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific targeted-attack characteristic has been confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Targeted Ransomware Attacks
ITID-31144.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Critical by default.
ITID-31144.escalation: Escalate immediately as with any targeted ransomware event; reclassify once the specific characteristic is clarified.
indicators: Confirmed targeted ransomware deployment, specific defining characteristic not yet determined
vectors: Activity of unclear specific targeted-attack characteristic
rootCauses: Insufficient forensic detail captured at time of detection
controls: Immutable/offline backups
ITID-31144.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31144.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31144.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Targeted Ransomware Attack
playbook.description: For a confirmed targeted, human-directed ransomware incident where the specific access-chain characteristics (broker handoff, timing, operator tradecraft) have not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm encryption scope across the environment
steps.desc: Identify every host/share showing signs of encryption, not just the first reported system.
steps.outcome: Full encryption scope established.

steps.title: Reconstruct the attacker's activity and access chain
steps.desc: Review EDR/log telemetry to determine initial access, dwell time, lateral movement, and any evidence of manual/hands-on-keyboard activity.
steps.outcome: Attacker timeline and access chain established.

steps.title: Identify all privileged accounts and systems reached
steps.desc: Determine the full scope of privileged access obtained by the attacker.
steps.outcome: Full scope of compromised privileged access established.

steps.title: Isolate the entire affected network segment immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect affected systems at a segment level given ransomware's rapid lateral-spread nature.
steps.outcome: Further encryption and lateral movement halted.

steps.title: Force reset of all privileged and domain-level credentials
steps.desc: Reset administrative, domain admin, and service-account credentials the attacker may have accessed.
steps.outcome: Attacker's privileged access fully revoked.

steps.title: Engage Legal, Executive leadership, and law enforcement
steps.desc: Notify Legal and executives; consider law-enforcement referral. Do not engage with the extortion demand without Legal involvement.
steps.outcome: Leadership engaged and coordinating the business/legal response track.

steps.title: Remove the ransomware and every persistence/access mechanism found
steps.desc: Clean confirmed-compromised hosts and close the full access chain identified during investigation.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean of the ransomware and attacker access.

steps.title: Verify backup integrity before restoring
steps.desc: Confirm backups predate the compromise and are free of the ransomware/backdoor before restoring; check for tampering with backup systems.
steps.outcome: Clean, verified backup identified for restore.
steps.abort: If no clean backup exists, escalate rebuild timeline and options to leadership.

steps.title: Do not pay the ransom; coordinate with Legal and law enforcement if demanded
steps.desc: Standard guidance is against payment. Leadership/Legal make the final decision.
steps.outcome: Payment decision made deliberately by Legal/Executive.

steps.title: Document the full incident and reassess relevant access controls
steps.desc: Record the attacker's full activity timeline and remediate the access/detection gaps that allowed the targeted compromise.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31211.def: A backdoor trojan implemented as a web shell — a script uploaded to or planted on a web server that provides the adversary an ongoing, browser- or HTTP-reachable command interface into the host.
ITID-31211.purpose: Captures backdoor trojans deployed as a web shell on a compromised web server or application.
scopeIncludes: Malicious script file placed within a web application's directory providing remote command execution over HTTP(S)
Web shell planted following exploitation of a web application vulnerability or insecure file upload function
scopeExcludes: Firmware/bootkit-level backdoors (ITID-31212)
Backdoors introduced via a compromised open-source dependency (ITID-31213) or a compromised software update (ITID-31214)
ITID-31211.severity: High; a web shell provides persistent, often long-lived remote access to a server.
ITID-31211.priority: P1 upon confirmation of an active web shell.
ITID-31211.escalation: Escalate immediately; treat the host as compromised and assess for lateral movement, since a web shell often persists for extended periods before detection.
indicators: Unrecognized script file present in a web application directory
Web server logs showing HTTP requests to an unexpected file path executing commands
File-integrity monitoring alert on an unauthorized new file in the web root
vectors: Exploitation of an insecure file-upload function
Exploitation of a web application vulnerability allowing arbitrary file write
rootCauses: Insecure file upload validation on web applications
Lack of file-integrity monitoring on web server directories
Delayed patching of web application vulnerabilities
mitreTechniques: T1505.003 Server Software Component: Web Shell
controls: File-integrity monitoring on web server directories
Web application firewall
Regular web application vulnerability scanning/patching
ITID-31211.detection: Good with file-integrity monitoring and web-server access-log analysis identifying anomalous file paths and request patterns.
ITID-31211.response: Remove the web shell, patch the vulnerability that allowed its placement, and review web server and application logs for the full duration of its presence to assess actions taken through it.
metrics: Dwell time of the web shell before detection
Number of web shell incidents per quarter
detections: Web server anomalous request pattern alert
ITID-31211.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by the layer/mechanism of the backdoor (web-application layer) rather than the delivery method.

playbook.name: Response: Web Shell Backdoor
playbook.description: For a confirmed web shell discovered on a web application or server, providing an attacker with persistent remote command execution.

steps.title: Locate and confirm all web shell instances
steps.desc: Scan the web root and related directories for known and unknown web shell signatures; confirm each finding manually.
steps.outcome: All web shell files identified and confirmed.
steps.tool: File integrity scanner / web server logs

steps.title: Hunt for additional persistence and re-entry points beyond the found shell
steps.desc: Search for other backdoors, scheduled tasks, added admin accounts, or modified configuration files the attacker may have planted alongside the web shell.
steps.guidance: An attacker who dropped one web shell typically establishes multiple re-entry points — do not assume the one found is the only one.
steps.outcome: Full persistence footprint identified across the environment, not just the initial shell.
steps.tool: EDR / file integrity monitoring / log review

steps.title: Determine the vulnerability that allowed the web shell upload
steps.desc: Identify the vulnerable upload/injection point exploited to place the web shell.
steps.outcome: Root-cause vulnerability identified.

steps.title: Isolate or take the affected web application offline
steps.desc: Remove the affected application from production traffic or isolate the host to prevent further attacker command execution.
steps.outcome: Attacker command-and-control via the shell halted.

steps.title: Preserve forensic evidence before remediation
steps.desc: Preserve the web shell file, web server logs, and any command history before cleanup.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved for investigation.

steps.title: Remove all web shells and every other persistence mechanism found
steps.desc: Delete all confirmed web shell files and remediate every additional re-entry point identified during the persistence hunt.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed free of web shells and related persistence.

steps.title: Patch the vulnerability that allowed the upload
steps.desc: Apply the patch or code fix closing the upload/injection vulnerability.
steps.outcome: Vulnerability closed and verified.

steps.title: Restore the application from a known-clean deployment
steps.desc: Redeploy the application from source control/clean artifact rather than trusting the live filesystem, and verify integrity before returning to production.
steps.outcome: Application restored to service from a verified-clean state.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve web application monitoring
steps.desc: Record the timeline and implement file-integrity monitoring and upload validation to detect/prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31212.def: A backdoor trojan implanted in device firmware (e.g., UEFI/BIOS) or as a bootkit that loads before the operating system, providing persistence that survives OS reinstallation.
ITID-31212.purpose: Captures backdoor trojans implanted at the firmware or bootkit level, persisting below the operating system.
scopeIncludes: Malicious firmware implant persisting across OS reinstallation
Bootkit that loads prior to the OS and injects a backdoor component into the running system
scopeExcludes: Web shell backdoors (ITID-31211)
Backdoors introduced via compromised open-source dependencies or software updates operating at the application/OS level (ITID-31213, ITID-31214)
ITID-31212.severity: Critical; firmware-level persistence survives standard remediation (OS reinstall) and is difficult to detect and remove.
ITID-31212.priority: P1 upon any confirmed or suspected firmware-level implant.
ITID-31212.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR and hardware/vendor support; standard reimaging is insufficient and the device may need firmware reflashing or hardware replacement.
indicators: Backdoor behavior persisting after a full OS reinstall
Firmware integrity verification failure or unexpected firmware version/hash
Anomalous pre-boot network activity
vectors: Exploitation of a firmware update mechanism lacking signature verification
Physical access enabling direct firmware reflashing
rootCauses: Lack of firmware integrity verification (e.g., Secure Boot, measured boot)
Outdated firmware with known vulnerabilities
Insufficient physical security controls over devices
controls: Secure Boot / measured boot with firmware integrity attestation
Firmware update signature verification
Physical security controls over device access
ITID-31212.detection: Weak with standard endpoint tooling; requires specialized firmware integrity/attestation tooling or vendor-provided verification utilities.
ITID-31212.response: Do not rely on OS reinstallation alone; reflash firmware from a verified clean source or replace the affected hardware, and engage the hardware vendor where available.
metrics: Number of confirmed firmware-level implants per year
Time to full remediation (reflash/replace)
ITID-31212.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by persistence layer (firmware/pre-OS) rather than delivery method.

playbook.name: Response: Firmware/Bootkit-Level Backdoor
playbook.description: For a confirmed backdoor implanted at the firmware or bootkit level, surviving OS reinstallation and providing deep, persistent attacker access.

steps.title: Confirm firmware/bootkit compromise
steps.desc: Use firmware-integrity verification tools or vendor attestation to confirm the compromise is at the firmware/bootkit level rather than the OS.
steps.outcome: Firmware/bootkit compromise confirmed with technical evidence.

steps.title: Hunt for additional re-entry points across all potentially affected devices
steps.desc: Given firmware-level implants often affect a specific hardware model/batch, check all devices of the same make/model/firmware version in the fleet.
steps.guidance: A firmware backdoor found on one device suggests a supply-chain or fleet-wide exposure — do not treat it as an isolated case.
steps.outcome: Full scope of potentially affected devices identified.

steps.title: Determine how the firmware/bootkit was implanted
steps.desc: Investigate whether the implant occurred via supply-chain compromise, physical access, or a software-based firmware update mechanism.
steps.outcome: Implant vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate all affected and potentially affected devices from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect confirmed and suspected devices given the depth of access a firmware-level backdoor provides.
steps.outcome: Affected devices isolated.

steps.title: Engage the hardware vendor and preserve evidence
steps.desc: Notify the device vendor for firmware analysis support and preserve the affected hardware/firmware image for investigation.
steps.outcome: Vendor engaged; evidence preserved.

steps.title: Reflash firmware from a verified-clean vendor source or replace the hardware
steps.desc: Reflash affected devices using vendor-verified clean firmware images; if clean reflashing cannot be guaranteed, replace the hardware entirely.
steps.guidance: OS reinstallation alone does not remove a firmware/bootkit-level backdoor — this must be addressed at the firmware layer.
steps.outcome: Devices confirmed running clean, verified firmware.
steps.abort: If clean firmware cannot be verified, escalate to hardware replacement.

steps.title: Rebuild the OS and rotate all credentials used on affected devices
steps.desc: Reinstall the OS on remediated devices and rotate all credentials that were used on them while compromised.
steps.outcome: Devices returned to trusted service; exposed credentials rotated.

steps.title: Document the incident and review hardware supply-chain assurance
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate firmware-integrity monitoring and hardware supply-chain vetting to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31213.def: A backdoor trojan introduced into an environment via an open-source package or dependency (e.g., from a public package registry) that had malicious backdoor functionality inserted, whether through a compromised maintainer account or a deliberately published malicious package.
ITID-31213.purpose: Captures backdoor trojans introduced through a maliciously modified open-source package or software dependency.
scopeIncludes: Malicious code discovered in an open-source library/package pulled in via a dependency manager
Backdoor introduced via a typosquatted or maliciously published package impersonating a legitimate one
scopeExcludes: Backdoors delivered via a compromised vendor software update mechanism for commercial/proprietary software (ITID-31214)
Web shells (ITID-31211) and firmware-level implants (ITID-31212)
ITID-31213.severity: High to Critical, especially where the affected package is widely used across the codebase/environment.
ITID-31213.priority: P1 upon confirmation that a backdoored package is present in a production build or environment.
ITID-31213.escalation: Escalate to application security and development teams immediately; identify every build/deployment that included the affected package version.
indicators: Unexpected outbound network connections from an application shortly after a dependency update
Static/dynamic analysis flagging obfuscated or suspicious code in a dependency
Security advisory identifying a specific compromised package version
vectors: Compromise of a package maintainer's publishing credentials
Deliberate publication of a malicious or typosquatted package to a public registry
rootCauses: Lack of dependency pinning/lockfile integrity verification
Absence of software composition analysis (SCA) scanning in the build pipeline
Automatic acceptance of dependency updates without review
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Software composition analysis (SCA) scanning in CI/CD
Dependency pinning and lockfile integrity verification
Private package registry proxying/allowlisting
ITID-31213.detection: Moderate; SCA tooling and outbound-connection monitoring from application hosts provide the primary detection surface, alongside public vulnerability/advisory feeds.
ITID-31213.response: Identify and rebuild every affected build/deployment with a clean dependency version, rotate any credentials/secrets the backdoored code may have had access to, and add the package to an internal blocklist.
metrics: Number of affected builds/deployments identified
Time from advisory publication to internal remediation
detections: Outbound connection anomaly from application host
ITID-31213.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31214 by supply-chain layer: this leaf is open-source dependency/package compromise, distinct from a compromised commercial vendor update mechanism.

playbook.name: Response: Backdoored Open-Source Package/Dependency
playbook.description: For a confirmed backdoor introduced through a compromised open-source package or dependency pulled into internal software.

steps.title: Identify the compromised package, version, and malicious behavior
steps.desc: Determine the exact package name, version(s), and the specific malicious code/behavior introduced.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference public advisories (e.g., package registry security advisories) where available.
steps.outcome: Compromised package and malicious behavior fully characterized.
steps.tool: Software composition analysis / package registry advisories

steps.title: Enumerate every application/build that depends on the compromised package
steps.desc: Search all repositories, build manifests, and deployed artifacts across the org for use of the compromised package/version, not just the one application where it was found.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected applications, services, and environments.
steps.tool: Software bill of materials (SBOM) / dependency scanning

steps.title: Hunt for additional re-entry points introduced by the backdoor
steps.desc: Investigate whether the backdoor was actually executed/deployed and, if so, hunt for any secondary persistence it may have established.
steps.outcome: Determined whether the backdoor was activated and what additional footholds, if any, resulted.

steps.title: Pin/remove the compromised package version across all affected builds
steps.desc: Block the compromised version at the package-registry/proxy level and remove it from all dependency manifests.
steps.outcome: Compromised package version blocked from further use.

steps.title: Isolate any systems where the backdoor was confirmed to execute
steps.desc: Isolate production systems/services where the malicious code is confirmed to have run.
steps.outcome: Affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild all affected applications with a verified-clean dependency version
steps.desc: Update all affected builds to a clean, verified package version and redeploy.
steps.outcome: All affected applications rebuilt and confirmed clean.

steps.title: Remove any secondary persistence established by the backdoor
steps.desc: Clean any additional footholds identified during the persistence hunt on systems where the backdoor executed.
steps.outcome: All identified persistence mechanisms removed.

steps.title: Rotate credentials/secrets accessible to affected applications
steps.desc: Rotate any secrets, API keys, or credentials the compromised code could have accessed.
steps.outcome: Exposed secrets rotated.

steps.title: Document the incident and strengthen dependency-vetting practices
steps.desc: Record the timeline and implement SBOM tracking, dependency pinning, and package-integrity verification to reduce future supply-chain risk.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31214.def: A backdoor trojan installed via a legitimate commercial/proprietary software vendor's update or distribution mechanism that had been compromised upstream, distinct from an open-source package compromise.
ITID-31214.purpose: Captures backdoor trojans introduced through a compromised commercial or proprietary software update mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Backdoor bundled into a signed vendor update pushed through the vendor's normal update mechanism
Backdoor introduced via compromise of a vendor's build/release infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Backdoored open-source packages/dependencies (ITID-31213)
Ransomware delivered via a compromised software update, which is tracked under Encrypting Ransomware (ITID-31114) rather than here
ITID-31214.severity: Critical; typically affects many downstream customers of the same vendor simultaneously.
ITID-31214.priority: P1 immediately upon suspicion of a compromised trusted vendor update.
ITID-31214.escalation: Escalate to IR and vendor-risk management immediately; halt further rollout of the update and coordinate with the vendor.
indicators: Anomalous outbound connections shortly after installing a routine vendor update
Vendor advisory confirming a compromised release
Unexpected new process/service appearing after an update with no corresponding legitimate feature
vectors: Compromise of a software vendor's build or release pipeline
Compromise of a software distribution/update server
rootCauses: Insufficient code-signing/integrity verification of vendor updates on the customer side
Lack of vendor supply-chain security assessment
No staged/canary rollout of vendor updates
mitreTechniques: T1195.002 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
controls: Code-signing verification for third-party software
Staged/canary rollout of vendor updates
Vendor supply-chain risk assessment program
ITID-31214.detection: Relies heavily on EDR behavioral alerting post-installation and vendor disclosure; pre-installation detection is typically weak.
ITID-31214.response: Halt further rollout, isolate systems that received the compromised update, coordinate with the vendor, and rebuild affected systems from known-clean media.
metrics: Number of hosts receiving the compromised update
Time from vendor advisory to internal containment
ITID-31214.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31213 by supply-chain layer (commercial vendor update vs. open-source dependency); ransomware delivered by the same mechanism is tracked under ITID-31114 to avoid duplicate classification.

playbook.name: Response: Backdoor Installed via Compromised Software Update
playbook.description: For a confirmed backdoor delivered through a compromised vendor software update mechanism to internal systems.

steps.title: Identify the compromised update/vendor product and affected version
steps.desc: Determine which vendor product, update package, and version distributed the backdoor, and the distribution window.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the vendor's security advisory if one has been issued.
steps.outcome: Compromised product/version and distribution window identified.

steps.title: Enumerate every system that installed the compromised update
steps.desc: Cross-reference patch/deployment inventory to find every host that received the update, regardless of whether the backdoor has been observed active on it yet.
steps.outcome: Complete list of exposed systems.

steps.title: Hunt for additional persistence and re-entry points beyond the backdoor itself
steps.desc: Search for any secondary footholds the backdoor may have established once activated, on all confirmed-active systems.
steps.outcome: Full persistence footprint identified.

steps.title: Halt further distribution of the compromised update
steps.desc: Block the update channel/repository so remaining exposed systems cannot install the malicious update.
steps.outcome: No further systems can receive the compromised update.

steps.title: Isolate systems confirmed to have an active backdoor
steps.desc: Disconnect systems where the backdoor is confirmed active from the network.
steps.outcome: Active backdoor communications halted.

steps.title: Remove the backdoor and every additional persistence mechanism found
steps.desc: Clean confirmed-compromised hosts and remediate any secondary footholds identified during the persistence hunt.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean of the backdoor and related persistence.

steps.title: Reinstall a verified-clean version of the affected software
steps.desc: Once the vendor confirms remediation, reinstall a trusted, verified-clean version across all affected systems.
steps.outcome: Affected software restored to a trusted version fleet-wide.

steps.title: Rotate credentials accessible from affected systems
steps.desc: Rotate credentials and secrets that were accessible from systems while the backdoor was active.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials rotated.

steps.title: Document the incident and reassess update-verification controls
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate update-signing verification and staged-rollout practices to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31215.def: A backdoor trojan not yet attributable to a specific mechanism or layer (web shell, firmware/bootkit, backdoored open-source package, or compromised vendor update).
ITID-31215.purpose: Catch-all for backdoor trojan incidents that do not fit a more specific mechanism/layer leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the backdoor's mechanism/layer has been confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Backdoor Trojans
ITID-31215.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High by default.
ITID-31215.priority: P2 by default, escalating to P1 upon confirmation of active remote access.
ITID-31215.escalation: Reclassify once the specific backdoor mechanism is clarified.
indicators: Confirmed unauthorized remote access mechanism, specific type not yet determined
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
controls: EDR detection of unauthorized listening processes
Network egress filtering and monitoring
Application allowlisting
Regular patching of internet-facing services
ITID-31215.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31215.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31215.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Backdoor Trojan
playbook.description: For a confirmed backdoor trojan providing an attacker persistent remote access, where the specific installation mechanism has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm and characterize the backdoor
steps.desc: Identify the backdoor's capabilities, command-and-control communications, and affected host(s).
steps.outcome: Backdoor confirmed and characterized.

steps.title: Hunt for additional re-entry points across all potential vectors
steps.desc: Search for other persistence mechanisms across the environment — a single backdoor found often indicates other footholds exist, whether via web application, firmware, supply chain, or update mechanism.
steps.guidance: Do not assume the found backdoor is the only re-entry point until this hunt is complete.
steps.outcome: Full persistence footprint identified across the environment.
steps.tool: EDR / file integrity monitoring / log review

steps.title: Determine the installation vector
steps.desc: Investigate how the backdoor was installed to guide remediation and closure of the entry point.
steps.outcome: Installation vector identified or narrowed.

steps.title: Isolate affected systems from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect confirmed-compromised systems to halt attacker command-and-control access.
steps.outcome: Attacker access via the backdoor halted.

steps.title: Preserve forensic evidence before remediation
steps.desc: Preserve the backdoor sample, logs, and any command history before cleanup.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved for investigation.

steps.title: Remove the backdoor and every additional persistence mechanism found
steps.desc: Clean confirmed-compromised hosts and remediate every additional re-entry point identified during the persistence hunt.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed free of the backdoor and related persistence.

steps.title: Close the identified installation vector
steps.desc: Patch, reconfigure, or otherwise remediate the vector that allowed the backdoor to be installed.
steps.outcome: Installation vector closed.

steps.title: Rotate credentials accessible from affected systems
steps.desc: Rotate credentials and secrets that were accessible from systems while the backdoor was active.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials rotated.

steps.title: Document the incident and finalize root-cause remediation
steps.desc: Record the full timeline once the installation vector is confirmed and track remediation to completion.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31221.def: A banking trojan running on a desktop endpoint that injects malicious content into banking web pages or captures form-field data as it is submitted, to steal login credentials or transaction details.
ITID-31221.purpose: Captures banking trojans that use browser web-injection or form-grabbing to steal credentials/transaction data from desktop browsers.
scopeIncludes: Malware injecting fake fields or altered content into a legitimate banking website within the browser
Malware capturing form submission data (form-grabbing) from a browser session targeting financial sites
scopeExcludes: Mobile banking trojans using screen overlays (ITID-31222)
Banking trojans that alter transaction details in real time as the defining characteristic (ITID-31223)
ITID-31221.severity: High; direct theft of banking credentials or transaction data.
ITID-31221.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active credential/transaction capture.
ITID-31221.escalation: Escalate to IR and notify affected users/accounts immediately so banking credentials can be reset and accounts monitored for fraud.
indicators: EDR detection of a known banking trojan family (e.g., via browser process injection behavior)
Unusual browser extension or injected script present during banking site visits
User-reported unexpected fields or prompts on a banking website
vectors: Malicious email attachment or drive-by download delivering the trojan
Malicious browser extension performing web injection
rootCauses: Lack of endpoint protection detecting known banking trojan families
Browser extensions installed without vetting/allowlisting
controls: Endpoint protection with banking-trojan signature/behavioral detection
Browser extension allowlisting
Multi-factor authentication on banking/financial applications
ITID-31221.detection: Moderate; EDR behavioral detection of browser process injection is the primary technical signal.
ITID-31221.response: Isolate the host, force credential reset for any accounts accessed from it, and notify the financial institution/account holder to monitor for fraudulent transactions.
metrics: Number of banking trojan detections per quarter
Number of accounts requiring credential reset per incident
detections: EDR browser process injection behavior alert
ITID-31221.notes: Differentiated by platform/technique (desktop browser web-injection/form-grabbing) from mobile overlay and real-time transaction manipulation leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Web Injection/Form-Grabbing Banking Trojan
playbook.description: For a confirmed banking trojan performing web injection or form-grabbing to capture online banking credentials and session data.

steps.title: Confirm the banking trojan and its target institutions
steps.desc: Identify the specific trojan family and the financial institutions/websites targeted by its web-injection configuration.
steps.outcome: Trojan family and targeted institutions identified.

steps.title: Determine what banking sessions/credentials were captured
steps.desc: Establish which accounts, sites, and sessions were accessed from the infected device while the trojan was active.
steps.outcome: Scope of potentially compromised financial credentials/sessions established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to stop any further form-grabbing or live web-injection activity.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; trojan communications halted.

steps.title: Notify the affected financial institution(s) immediately
steps.desc: Contact the bank(s)/financial institution(s) whose credentials or sessions may have been captured, given the direct financial-fraud risk.
steps.guidance: Banking trojans pose immediate financial-fraud risk — do not delay notification pending full investigation.
steps.outcome: Financial institution notified and monitoring account activity.

steps.title: Request transaction monitoring/freeze on affected accounts
steps.desc: Coordinate with the financial institution's fraud team to monitor or temporarily restrict the affected accounts pending review.
steps.outcome: Enhanced transaction monitoring or account restriction in place.

steps.title: Remove the banking trojan and any browser-injected components
steps.desc: Clean the infected device of the trojan, associated browser extensions/injections, and any persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean of the trojan and injected components.

steps.title: Reset banking credentials and re-authenticate via a clean device
steps.desc: Change online banking passwords and re-establish MFA using a confirmed-clean device.
steps.outcome: Banking credentials rotated from a trusted device.

steps.title: Review recent account activity for fraudulent transactions
steps.desc: Work with the financial institution to review transaction history for unauthorized activity during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Fraudulent transactions identified and disputed if found.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce endpoint protections for financial activity
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate browser-isolation or dedicated-device policies for sensitive financial transactions.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31222.def: A mobile banking trojan that displays a fake overlay screen mimicking a legitimate banking app's login interface, capturing credentials entered by the user before passing (or not passing) them to the real app.
ITID-31222.purpose: Captures mobile banking trojans that use a fake overlay screen to steal credentials entered into a banking app.
scopeIncludes: Malicious mobile app that detects a banking app launch and displays an overlay capturing entered credentials
Overlay malware also capturing one-time passcodes/SMS codes to bypass MFA
scopeExcludes: Desktop browser web-injection/form-grabbing banking trojans (ITID-31221)
Mobile device screen-locker ransomware not targeting banking credentials (ITID-31123)
ITID-31222.severity: High; direct theft of banking credentials and potential MFA bypass via SMS interception.
ITID-31222.priority: P1 upon confirmed credential capture via overlay.
ITID-31222.escalation: Escalate immediately; notify the affected user's financial institution and force credential/MFA reset.
indicators: Mobile threat defense detection of overlay-capable malicious app
User report of an unusual login prompt appearing over their banking app
Unauthorized SMS-read/accessibility-service permissions granted to an unrecognized app
vectors: Malicious app sideloaded from outside the official app store
Malicious app abusing accessibility-service permissions to detect app launches and render overlays
rootCauses: Sideloading of apps from untrusted sources
Overly broad accessibility-service permissions granted during installation
Lack of mobile threat defense tooling on corporate/BYOD devices
mitreTechniques: T1417.002 Input Capture: GUI Input Capture
controls: MDM restriction on app installation sources
Mobile threat defense app scanning
MFA methods resistant to SMS interception (e.g., app-based authenticator)
ITID-31222.detection: Moderate via mobile threat defense tooling flagging overlay-capable/accessibility-abusing apps; weaker on unmanaged personal devices.
ITID-31222.response: Remove the malicious app or factory-reset the device, force credential and MFA reset for the affected banking account, and notify the financial institution.
metrics: Number of mobile banking overlay incidents per quarter
Number of affected accounts requiring reset
ITID-31222.notes: Differentiated by platform/technique (mobile overlay attack) from desktop web-injection and real-time transaction manipulation leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Mobile Banking Trojan (Overlay Attack)
playbook.description: For a confirmed mobile banking trojan using screen overlays to trick users into entering banking credentials into a fake login screen.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious app and overlay behavior
steps.desc: Identify the installed malicious app responsible for the overlay attack and the banking app(s) it targets.
steps.outcome: Malicious app and targeted banking app(s) identified.

steps.title: Determine what credentials/one-time-codes were likely captured
steps.desc: Establish the window during which the overlay was active and what banking sessions occurred during that window.
steps.outcome: Scope of potentially compromised credentials/OTPs established.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate/personal accounts
steps.desc: Revoke the device's access to corporate resources if applicable, and advise the user to stop using banking apps on the device immediately.
steps.outcome: Device access to sensitive accounts halted.

steps.title: Notify the affected financial institution(s) immediately
steps.desc: Contact the bank(s) whose credentials or one-time codes may have been captured, given the direct financial-fraud risk.
steps.outcome: Financial institution notified and monitoring account activity.

steps.title: Remove the malicious app or perform a factory reset
steps.desc: Uninstall the malicious app via safe/recovery mode, or factory reset the device if removal cannot be verified clean.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean of the malicious app.

steps.title: Reset banking credentials and MFA from a clean device
steps.desc: Change banking passwords and reissue MFA/authenticator enrollment from a confirmed-clean device.
steps.outcome: Banking credentials and MFA rotated from a trusted device.

steps.title: Review recent account activity for fraudulent transactions
steps.desc: Work with the financial institution to review transaction history for unauthorized activity during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Fraudulent transactions identified and disputed if found.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce mobile app-installation controls
steps.desc: Record how the malicious app was installed (e.g., sideloading, third-party store) and tighten app-installation policy accordingly.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; mobile policy updated.

ITID-31223.def: A banking trojan that intercepts and silently alters transaction details (e.g., destination account number, amount) in real time during a legitimate, user-initiated banking session, so the displayed confirmation differs from what is actually submitted.
ITID-31223.purpose: Captures banking trojans that manipulate transaction details in real time during an active, otherwise legitimate banking session.
scopeIncludes: Real-time modification of transaction destination/amount within an active banking session (man-in-the-browser transaction manipulation)
Malware that displays a falsified confirmation screen while submitting altered transaction data
scopeExcludes: Credential/form-grabbing without real-time transaction alteration (ITID-31221)
Mobile overlay credential-capture attacks (ITID-31222)
ITID-31223.severity: Critical; direct financial theft occurring within a session the user believes is legitimate, often difficult for the user to detect in the moment.
ITID-31223.priority: P1 upon confirmation of transaction manipulation.
ITID-31223.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR and coordinate with the financial institution to attempt to halt or reverse the fraudulent transaction.
indicators: Discrepancy between what the user saw/confirmed and the actual transaction executed
EDR detection of man-in-the-browser injection targeting a banking session
Financial institution fraud alert on an unusual transaction pattern
vectors: Man-in-the-browser malware intercepting and modifying transaction requests before submission
Malicious browser extension or injected script altering transaction form data
rootCauses: Lack of endpoint protection detecting man-in-the-browser behavior
Absence of out-of-band transaction verification (e.g., confirmation via a separate channel/device)
controls: Out-of-band transaction confirmation for financial transfers
Endpoint protection with man-in-the-browser behavioral detection
Transaction anomaly detection at the financial institution
ITID-31223.detection: Difficult from the endpoint alone; strongest detection is at the financial institution via transaction-pattern anomaly monitoring, combined with EDR behavioral alerts on the endpoint.
ITID-31223.response: Contact the financial institution immediately to attempt reversal/hold, isolate the host, and force full credential reset.
metrics: Number of confirmed transaction-manipulation incidents
Value of fraudulent transactions attempted vs. recovered
ITID-31223.notes: Differentiated by technique (real-time transaction manipulation) from credential-capture-only leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Banking Trojan with Real-Time Transaction Manipulation
playbook.description: For a confirmed banking trojan that manipulates transaction details in real time (e.g., web-inject-modified payee/amount) during an active banking session.

steps.title: Confirm the trojan and its transaction-manipulation capability
steps.desc: Identify the specific trojan family and confirm its real-time transaction-manipulation technique (e.g., man-in-the-browser modification of payee/amount fields).
steps.outcome: Trojan family and manipulation technique confirmed.

steps.title: Identify any transactions conducted while the trojan was active
steps.desc: Establish the window of compromise and enumerate all banking transactions conducted from the infected device during that time.
steps.guidance: Given real-time manipulation, any transaction during the active window may have been altered without the user noticing — treat all of them as suspect.
steps.outcome: Full list of transactions during the compromise window established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to stop any further transaction manipulation.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; trojan activity halted.

steps.title: Notify the financial institution and request an urgent transaction review/freeze
steps.desc: Given the risk of already-completed fraudulent transfers, contact the bank immediately to review and potentially reverse or freeze in-flight transactions.
steps.guidance: Real-time manipulation carries the highest immediate financial-fraud risk of the banking-trojan family — treat this notification as time-critical.
steps.outcome: Financial institution engaged; suspect transactions flagged for reversal where possible.

steps.title: Remove the banking trojan and any browser-injected components
steps.desc: Clean the infected device of the trojan, associated browser injections, and any persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean of the trojan and injected components.

steps.title: Reset banking credentials and re-authenticate via a clean, verified device
steps.desc: Change online banking passwords and re-establish MFA using a confirmed-clean device before resuming any banking activity.
steps.outcome: Banking credentials rotated from a trusted device.

steps.title: Reconcile all transactions from the compromise window with the financial institution
steps.desc: Work with the bank to confirm which transactions were legitimate versus manipulated, and dispute/reverse any confirmed fraud.
steps.outcome: All transactions from the compromise window reconciled; fraud disputed.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce out-of-band transaction verification
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate out-of-band confirmation (e.g., separate-channel transaction verification) for high-value transfers.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31224.def: A banking trojan incident not yet attributable to a specific technique or platform (desktop web-injection/form-grabbing, mobile overlay, or real-time transaction manipulation).
ITID-31224.purpose: Catch-all for banking trojan incidents that do not fit a more specific technique/platform leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific technique/platform has been confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Banking Trojans
ITID-31224.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High by default.
ITID-31224.priority: P2 by default, escalating to P1 upon confirmation of active theft.
ITID-31224.escalation: Reclassify once the specific technique/platform is clarified.
indicators: Suspected banking credential/transaction theft, specific technique not yet determined
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Browser isolation/sandboxing
EDR behavioral detection for form-grabbing and code injection
Multi-factor authentication for banking sessions
Email gateway attachment sandboxing
ITID-31224.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31224.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31224.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Banking Trojan
playbook.description: For a confirmed banking trojan incident where the specific technique (web injection, overlay, transaction manipulation) has not yet been fully characterized.

steps.title: Confirm the banking trojan and its capabilities
steps.desc: Identify the trojan family and characterize its specific credential-theft or transaction-manipulation technique.
steps.outcome: Trojan family and technique identified.

steps.title: Determine what financial credentials/sessions were exposed
steps.desc: Establish the compromise window and which banking accounts/sessions were accessed from the infected device during that time.
steps.outcome: Scope of potentially compromised financial credentials/sessions established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to stop any further credential theft or transaction manipulation.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; trojan activity halted.

steps.title: Notify the affected financial institution(s) immediately
steps.desc: Contact the bank(s) given the direct financial-fraud risk inherent to banking trojans, regardless of the specific technique.
steps.outcome: Financial institution notified and monitoring account activity.

steps.title: Remove the banking trojan and any injected/persistence components
steps.desc: Clean the infected device of the trojan and any associated components.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean of the trojan.

steps.title: Reset banking credentials and re-authenticate via a clean device
steps.desc: Change online banking passwords and MFA using a confirmed-clean device.
steps.outcome: Banking credentials rotated from a trusted device.

steps.title: Review recent account activity for fraudulent transactions
steps.desc: Work with the financial institution to review transaction history for unauthorized activity during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Fraudulent transactions identified and disputed if found.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce endpoint protections for financial activity
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate protections for devices used for online banking.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31231.def: An infostealer infection where the malware was bundled within cracked, pirated, or 'keygen' software downloaded by the user from an untrusted source.
ITID-31231.purpose: Captures infostealer infections delivered by bundling the malware with cracked or pirated software downloads.
scopeIncludes: Infostealer payload bundled inside a cracked application or game installer
Infostealer delivered via a fake keygen/license-crack tool
scopeExcludes: Infostealers distributed under a subscription/malware-as-a-service model as the defining characteristic (ITID-31232)
Infostealers whose defining characteristic is advanced anti-analysis/sandbox evasion capability (ITID-31233)
ITID-31231.severity: Medium-High, depending on the sensitivity of credentials/data present on the affected device.
ITID-31231.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if corporate credentials or session tokens are confirmed stolen.
ITID-31231.escalation: Escalate to IR upon confirmation that corporate credentials, session cookies, or sensitive data were harvested; force credential reset and session invalidation.
indicators: EDR/AV detection of an infostealer payload following installation of a cracked application
Unusual outbound connection to a known infostealer exfiltration endpoint shortly after a suspicious download
User report of having downloaded cracked/pirated software shortly before the alert
vectors: User-initiated download and execution of cracked/pirated software from an untrusted site
Infostealer bundled within a fake activation/keygen tool
rootCauses: Users downloading unlicensed/pirated software on corporate or BYOD devices
Lack of application allowlisting or download restrictions on endpoints
controls: Application allowlisting/software restriction policy
User awareness training against pirated software use
Endpoint protection with infostealer signature/behavioral detection
ITID-31231.detection: Good; most infostealer families have known signatures/behavioral patterns detectable by standard endpoint protection.
ITID-31231.response: Isolate the host, identify and reset every credential/session stored on it, and remove the pirated software along with the infostealer payload.
metrics: Number of infostealer incidents traced to pirated software per quarter
Number of credentials/sessions reset per incident
ITID-31231.notes: Differentiated by delivery vector (bundled with cracked/pirated software) from the subscription-model and anti-analysis leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Infostealer Bundled with Cracked/Pirated Software
playbook.description: For a confirmed infostealer infection delivered as a bundled component of cracked or pirated software downloaded by a user.

steps.title: Confirm the infostealer and identify the bundled software source
steps.desc: Identify the specific infostealer family and the cracked/pirated application it was bundled with, including the download source.
steps.outcome: Infostealer family and delivery source identified.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of data harvested by the infostealer
steps.desc: Review the infostealer's known collection behavior and any available exfiltration logs to determine everything it targeted — browser-saved passwords, cookies/sessions, autofill data, crypto wallets, and any other credential stores on the device.
steps.guidance: Infostealers harvest broadly by design — scope the credential-rotation list to everything the device had access to, not just one account.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of harvested credentials/data established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to halt any ongoing exfiltration or command-and-control activity.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Remove the infostealer and the pirated software entirely
steps.desc: Uninstall the cracked application and remove the infostealer and any persistence it established.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If clean removal cannot be verified, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate every credential that was stored or used on the infected device
steps.desc: Reset passwords and re-authenticate for every account with saved credentials or active sessions on the device — email, work systems, banking, social media, and any password manager stored locally — not just the one account first suspected.
steps.guidance: Given infostealers' broad harvesting model, treat every logged-in/saved account as compromised until rotated.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and application tokens
steps.desc: Revoke browser sessions, OAuth tokens, and API keys that may have been harvested alongside passwords.
steps.outcome: Stolen sessions/tokens invalidated.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce software-download policy
steps.desc: Record the timeline and reinforce controls/education against installing unauthorized or pirated software.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; user guidance or controls updated.

ITID-31232.def: An infostealer infection using a known Infostealer-as-a-Service (or broader Malware-as-a-Service) offering, where the malware, panel, and log-distribution infrastructure are operated as a subscription product used by many independent customers/affiliates.
ITID-31232.purpose: Captures infostealer infections attributable to a subscription-based Infostealer-as-a-Service/Malware-as-a-Service offering.
scopeIncludes: Infostealer payload attributable to a known subscription-based stealer family/panel
Stolen credential logs confirmed sold or distributed through a known stealer-log marketplace associated with a MaaS offering
scopeExcludes: Infostealers delivered via bundling with cracked software as the defining characteristic (ITID-31231)
Infostealers whose defining characteristic is advanced anti-analysis capability (ITID-31233)
ITID-31232.severity: High; MaaS stealer logs are frequently resold, increasing the likelihood of follow-on compromise using the harvested data.
ITID-31232.priority: P1 upon confirmation of a known MaaS stealer family and evidence of log exfiltration.
ITID-31232.escalation: Escalate immediately; assume harvested credentials may already be circulating for resale and force broad credential/session resets.
indicators: Payload matching a known subscription stealer family signature
Threat-intel report of the organization's data appearing in a stealer-log marketplace
Outbound connection to known MaaS panel/exfiltration infrastructure
vectors: Delivery via whatever vector the subscribing affiliate chooses (phishing, malvertising, fake software)
Use of a MaaS panel to manage stolen data collection across many victims
rootCauses: Lack of threat-intel-informed detection tuned to known MaaS stealer families
Insufficient monitoring for organizational credentials appearing in external stealer-log marketplaces
controls: Threat-intelligence monitoring of stealer-log marketplaces for organizational exposure
Endpoint protection with MaaS stealer signature/behavioral detection
MFA to reduce impact of stolen credentials
ITID-31232.detection: Good where threat-intel feeds provide known indicators for the MaaS family and where dark-web/stealer-log monitoring is in place.
ITID-31232.response: Force full credential and session-token reset for the affected host's users, monitor for downstream account-takeover attempts using harvested data, and remove the payload.
metrics: Number of incidents attributed per known MaaS family
Number of credentials found exposed in stealer-log marketplaces
detections: Endpoint protection MaaS stealer signature alert
ITID-31232.notes: Differentiated by business model (subscription MaaS offering) rather than delivery vector, which may vary by affiliate.

playbook.name: Response: Infostealer-as-a-Service (Subscription/Malware-as-a-Service Model)
playbook.description: For a confirmed infostealer infection using a subscription-based Malware-as-a-Service platform, where operators may vary but the underlying stealer platform and infrastructure are shared across many campaigns.

steps.title: Confirm the infostealer platform and delivery vector
steps.desc: Identify the specific MaaS infostealer platform/brand and how it was delivered to the device.
steps.outcome: Infostealer platform and delivery vector identified.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of data harvested by the infostealer
steps.desc: Review the platform's known collection capabilities to determine everything targeted on the device — credentials, cookies/sessions, autofill, crypto wallets, and any other local credential stores.
steps.guidance: MaaS platforms are typically full-featured harvesters — scope credential rotation to everything the device had access to, not just one account.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of harvested credentials/data established.

steps.title: Check threat intelligence for stolen-data marketplace listings
steps.desc: Search known stealer-log marketplaces/forums for indicators that this device's data has already surfaced for sale, given the MaaS model's typical monetization via log resale.
steps.outcome: Determined whether harvested data has already appeared in underground marketplaces.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to halt any ongoing exfiltration to the MaaS platform's infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Remove the infostealer and any associated persistence
steps.desc: Clean the device of the infostealer payload and any dropped persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If clean removal cannot be verified, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate every credential that was stored or used on the infected device
steps.desc: Reset passwords and re-authenticate for every account with saved credentials or active sessions on the device.
steps.guidance: Given the broad harvesting model, treat every logged-in/saved account as compromised until rotated.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and application tokens
steps.desc: Revoke browser sessions, OAuth tokens, and API keys that may have been harvested alongside passwords.
steps.outcome: Stolen sessions/tokens invalidated.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce endpoint protection controls
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate detection coverage for known MaaS infostealer indicators.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31233.def: An infostealer infection using a variant with notable anti-analysis or sandbox-evasion capability (e.g., detecting virtualized/analysis environments and altering behavior to avoid detection by automated security tooling).
ITID-31233.purpose: Captures infostealer infections whose defining characteristic is advanced anti-analysis or sandbox-evasion capability.
scopeIncludes: Stealer variant confirmed to check for sandbox/VM artifacts and withhold malicious behavior when detected
Stealer variant using packing/obfuscation specifically noted to evade standard automated analysis
scopeExcludes: Infostealers delivered via cracked software or subscription MaaS as the defining characteristic, without notable evasion capability being the distinguishing factor (ITID-31231, ITID-31232)
ITID-31233.severity: High; evasion capability increases the likelihood of the payload passing undetected through automated security tooling before reaching a real endpoint.
ITID-31233.priority: P1 upon confirmation of an evasive stealer variant reaching a production endpoint.
ITID-31233.escalation: Escalate to IR and threat intelligence; treat automated-tooling misses as a coverage gap requiring detection-engineering follow-up.
indicators: Sample fails detonation in automated sandboxing but exhibits malicious behavior on a real endpoint
Static/dynamic analysis reveals sandbox-detection or anti-debugging logic
Endpoint behavioral detection triggers where sandbox-based detection did not
vectors: Delivery via any vector, with the evasive payload designed to slip past automated detonation/sandboxing specifically
Multi-stage loader that only unpacks the stealer payload once it confirms a non-sandboxed environment
rootCauses: Over-reliance on sandbox-based detonation as the sole detection layer
Insufficient endpoint-level behavioral detection to catch payloads that evade pre-execution analysis
controls: Endpoint behavioral detection independent of sandbox-only analysis
Layered detection combining network, endpoint, and sandbox telemetry
Regular tuning of sandbox environments to reduce fingerprintable artifacts
ITID-31233.detection: Weaker for sandbox-only detection layers; stronger where endpoint behavioral/EDR telemetry is relied upon in addition to sandboxing.
ITID-31233.response: Treat as a detection-engineering finding as well as an incident: remediate the affected endpoint and review why automated tooling missed the sample, adjusting detection layers accordingly.
metrics: Number of evasive-stealer incidents that bypassed automated sandboxing
Time to detect via endpoint-level telemetry after sandbox miss
detections: EDR behavioral detection alert following sandbox-evasion bypass
ITID-31233.notes: Differentiated by capability (anti-analysis/evasion) rather than delivery vector or business model.

playbook.name: Response: Infostealer with Anti-Analysis/Sandbox Evasion Capability
playbook.description: For a confirmed infostealer infection built with anti-analysis and sandbox-evasion techniques, complicating detection and initial triage.

steps.title: Confirm the infostealer despite evasion behavior
steps.desc: Use behavioral/endpoint telemetry rather than sandbox detonation alone to confirm the infostealer's presence and activity, since it may not trigger in automated sandboxes.
steps.guidance: Anti-analysis malware may behave benignly in a sandbox — rely on live endpoint behavior and memory analysis for confirmation.
steps.outcome: Infostealer presence confirmed via endpoint-based evidence.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of data harvested by the infostealer
steps.desc: Review available telemetry to determine everything targeted on the device — credentials, cookies/sessions, autofill, crypto wallets, and other local credential stores.
steps.guidance: Given evasion capability, assume the malware ran undetected for longer than usual — scope credential rotation broadly.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of harvested credentials/data established, accounting for possible extended dwell time.

steps.title: Assess whether other analysis-evading malware exists on the same or similar systems
steps.desc: Given the actor's demonstrated evasion sophistication, check for additional undetected implants on this and similar systems using deeper forensic techniques.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of related compromise beyond the initially detected infostealer.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to halt any ongoing exfiltration.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Remove the infostealer using verified endpoint-based remediation
steps.desc: Clean the device of the infostealer and any persistence, confirming removal via endpoint telemetry rather than a single scan pass given its evasion design.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean through verified, repeated checks.
steps.abort: If clean removal cannot be verified, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate every credential that was stored or used on the infected device
steps.desc: Reset passwords and re-authenticate for every account with saved credentials or active sessions on the device, accounting for the likely extended exposure window.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and application tokens
steps.desc: Revoke browser sessions, OAuth tokens, and API keys that may have been harvested alongside passwords.
steps.outcome: Stolen sessions/tokens invalidated.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve detection for evasive malware
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate detection-engineering improvements (behavioral analytics, memory scanning) to catch sandbox-evading threats sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31234.def: An infostealer incident not yet attributable to a specific delivery vector or capability (bundled with pirated software, subscription MaaS model, or notable anti-analysis capability).
ITID-31234.purpose: Catch-all for infostealer incidents that do not fit a more specific delivery/capability leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific delivery vector/capability has been confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Infostealers
