ITID-31234.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium-High by default.
ITID-31234.priority: P2 by default, escalating to P1 upon confirmed data exfiltration.
ITID-31234.escalation: Reclassify once the specific delivery vector/capability is clarified.
indicators: Suspected credential/data theft, specific stealer family or vector not yet determined
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: EDR detection of credential access and browser data theft
Password manager with anti-keylogging protections
Multi-factor authentication to limit stolen-credential impact
Email gateway attachment sandboxing
ITID-31234.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31234.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31234.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Infostealer Incident
playbook.description: For a confirmed infostealer infection where the specific delivery mechanism (pirated software, MaaS platform, sandbox-evading build) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm the infostealer and its capabilities
steps.desc: Identify the infostealer family and its known data-collection capabilities.
steps.outcome: Infostealer family identified.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of data harvested by the infostealer
steps.desc: Review the infostealer's collection behavior to determine everything targeted on the device — credentials, cookies/sessions, autofill, crypto wallets, and other local credential stores.
steps.guidance: Infostealers harvest broadly by design — scope the credential-rotation list to everything the device had access to, not just one account.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of harvested credentials/data established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to halt any ongoing exfiltration or command-and-control activity.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Remove the infostealer and any persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Clean the device of the infostealer payload and any associated persistence.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If clean removal cannot be verified, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate every credential that was stored or used on the infected device
steps.desc: Reset passwords and re-authenticate for every account with saved credentials or active sessions on the device, not just the one account first suspected.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and application tokens
steps.desc: Revoke browser sessions, OAuth tokens, and API keys that may have been harvested alongside passwords.
steps.outcome: Stolen sessions/tokens invalidated.

steps.title: Document the incident and identify the delivery vector for future prevention
steps.desc: Record the timeline and finalize root-cause remediation once the delivery vector is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31241.def: A Remote Access Trojan infection using a widely available, commodity/off-the-shelf RAT (a publicly sold or freely available RAT family used broadly across many unrelated campaigns), rather than a bespoke tool built for a specific target.
ITID-31241.purpose: Captures RAT infections using a widely available, commodity/off-the-shelf remote access trojan family.
scopeIncludes: Payload matching a well-known, publicly available commodity RAT family
RAT deployment with no indication of custom development specific to this target
scopeExcludes: Custom-built RATs developed specifically for a targeted intrusion (ITID-31242)
RATs delivered via impersonating a legitimate remote-support tool as the defining vector (ITID-31243)
ITID-31241.severity: Medium-High; commodity RATs are generally well-signatured but still grant full remote control.
ITID-31241.priority: P2, escalating to P1 upon confirmed active remote control session.
ITID-31241.escalation: Escalate to IR upon confirmation of an active command-and-control connection; isolate the host and terminate the session.
indicators: EDR/AV detection of a known commodity RAT family signature
Outbound connection to known C2 infrastructure associated with the RAT family
Anomalous process behavior consistent with remote control (e.g., unexpected screen capture or keylogging activity)
vectors: Delivery via phishing attachment or malicious download bundling the RAT
Delivery via a malicious link leading to RAT installation
rootCauses: Lack of endpoint protection signature coverage for the specific commodity RAT variant
User execution of untrusted attachments/downloads
controls: Endpoint protection with commodity RAT signature/behavioral detection
Network detection/blocking of known RAT C2 infrastructure
Email attachment sandboxing
ITID-31241.detection: Good; commodity RAT families are typically well-covered by signature and network-based threat intelligence.
ITID-31241.response: Isolate the host, terminate the C2 connection at the network boundary, and reimage or fully remediate the endpoint.
metrics: Number of commodity RAT detections per quarter
Time from C2 beacon detection to containment
ITID-31241.notes: Differentiated by origin (commodity/off-the-shelf) from custom-built and fake-remote-support-tool leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Commodity/Off-the-Shelf RAT Deployment
playbook.description: For a confirmed infection by a widely available, commodity remote access trojan providing an attacker remote control of the device.

steps.title: Confirm the RAT family and its capabilities
steps.desc: Identify the specific commodity RAT and its documented capability set (file access, keylogging, screen/webcam control, etc.).
steps.outcome: RAT family and capabilities identified.

steps.title: Assess the level of control the operator had over the device
steps.desc: Determine whether the RAT's configuration and observed activity indicate full desktop/screen control versus limited data-collection capability.
steps.guidance: If full desktop control was available to the operator, assume everything on that device — files, credentials, sessions — is potentially compromised.
steps.outcome: Level of attacker control established and documented.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to cut off the operator's remote access.
steps.outcome: Attacker's remote control severed.

steps.title: Remove the RAT and any persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Clean the device of the RAT payload and any dropped persistence.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If full-control access was confirmed, consider a full reimage rather than in-place removal.

steps.title: Rotate credentials scoped to the assessed level of control
steps.desc: If full desktop control was confirmed, rotate every credential and session accessible from the device; if control was limited, scope rotation to the specific data the RAT could access.
steps.outcome: Credential-rotation scope matched to the confirmed level of attacker control.

steps.title: Rebuild the device if full control was confirmed
steps.desc: Where full desktop control was assessed, reimage the device rather than relying on in-place cleanup.
steps.outcome: Device rebuilt from a trusted image where warranted.

steps.title: Document the incident and close the delivery vector
steps.desc: Record the timeline and remediate the identified delivery vector to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31242.def: A Remote Access Trojan infection using a custom-developed tool built specifically for use against this target or a narrow set of targets, rather than a widely available commodity RAT.
ITID-31242.purpose: Captures RAT infections using a custom-built tool developed specifically for a targeted intrusion.
scopeIncludes: RAT payload confirmed via analysis to be unique/custom-built, not matching any known public family
C2 infrastructure and protocol confirmed to be bespoke rather than reused from a public toolkit
scopeExcludes: Commodity/off-the-shelf RAT deployment (ITID-31241)
ITID-31242.severity: Critical; custom tooling typically indicates a more sophisticated, targeted adversary with specific objectives.
ITID-31242.priority: P1 upon confirmation of custom RAT tooling.
ITID-31242.escalation: Escalate to full IR immediately; treat as a sophisticated, likely targeted intrusion requiring broader threat hunting beyond the initially detected host.
indicators: Malware analysis confirming code/infrastructure not matching any known public RAT family
Highly targeted delivery (e.g., spear-phishing crafted specifically for the recipient) preceding the RAT installation
Unique C2 protocol/beaconing pattern not matching known threat-intel signatures
vectors: Highly targeted spear-phishing delivering a custom loader/RAT
Custom RAT deployed following exploitation specific to the target's environment
rootCauses: Advanced, well-resourced adversary specifically targeting the organization
Detection tooling reliant primarily on known-signature matching, with limited behavioral/anomaly-based coverage
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based network and endpoint detection not reliant solely on known signatures
Threat hunting program for advanced/targeted intrusions
ITID-31242.detection: Weak for signature-based tooling since the sample is novel; strongest via behavioral/anomaly detection and proactive threat hunting.
ITID-31242.response: Engage full forensic investigation and threat hunting across the environment, assuming a capable, motivated adversary with objectives beyond the initially detected host.
metrics: Number of custom RAT/targeted intrusion incidents per year
Time from initial detection to full scope determination
ITID-31242.notes: Differentiated by origin (custom-built for this target) from commodity and fake-remote-support-tool leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Custom-Built RAT for Targeted Intrusion
playbook.description: For a confirmed infection by a custom-developed remote access trojan indicating a targeted, likely well-resourced intrusion rather than commodity malware.

steps.title: Confirm the custom RAT and its capabilities via detailed analysis
steps.desc: Perform deeper malware analysis given the custom nature of the tool, since commodity signatures/IOCs will not apply.
steps.outcome: Custom RAT's capabilities and command-and-control infrastructure characterized.

steps.title: Assess the level of control the operator had over the device
steps.desc: Determine whether the RAT provided full desktop/screen control, given custom tooling is often built for more comprehensive access than commodity RATs.
steps.guidance: If full desktop control was available, assume everything on that device is potentially compromised.
steps.outcome: Level of attacker control established and documented.

steps.title: Investigate for broader targeted-intrusion indicators
steps.desc: Given custom tooling suggests a targeted actor, check for additional footholds, reconnaissance, or lateral movement elsewhere in the environment.
steps.outcome: Scope of the broader intrusion, if any, established.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to cut off the operator's remote access.
steps.outcome: Attacker's remote control severed.

steps.title: Preserve forensic evidence given the targeted nature of the intrusion
steps.desc: Image the device and preserve network artifacts for detailed forensic and threat-intelligence analysis.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved for deeper investigation.

steps.title: Remove the RAT and rebuild the device given full-control risk
steps.desc: Given custom tooling and likely full control, reimage the device rather than relying on in-place removal.
steps.outcome: Device rebuilt from a trusted image.

steps.title: Rotate every credential accessible from the compromised device
steps.desc: Given the assessed level of control, treat everything accessible from the device as compromised and rotate accordingly.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Document the incident and share findings for broader threat-hunting
steps.desc: Record the timeline, custom-tool characteristics, and use findings to hunt for related activity elsewhere in the environment.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; broader threat-hunting initiated; remediations tracked.

ITID-31243.def: A Remote Access Trojan infection delivered by convincing the victim to install what they believe is a legitimate remote-support/IT-help tool (e.g., via a fraudulent tech-support call or fake IT notification), when it is actually a RAT or a legitimate remote-access tool repurposed for malicious control.
ITID-31243.purpose: Captures RAT infections where the adversary tricked the victim into installing a fake or impersonated remote-support tool.
scopeIncludes: Victim guided by a fraudulent caller or message to install a remote-access application believed to be legitimate IT support
Malicious use of a legitimate, dual-use remote-access utility installed under false pretenses
scopeExcludes: Commodity RAT delivered via standard phishing attachment (ITID-31241)
Custom-built RAT for a targeted intrusion (ITID-31242)
ITID-31243.severity: High; the victim knowingly grants remote control, often leading directly to fraud or data theft during the live session.
ITID-31243.priority: P1 upon confirmation that a user granted remote access under false pretenses.
ITID-31243.escalation: Escalate immediately; treat any live remote session granted under this pretext as an active compromise requiring immediate session termination and credential reset.
indicators: Installation of a remote-access utility not authorized by IT, shortly following an unsolicited call/message
User report of being instructed to install remote-access software by an unverified caller/technician
Remote-access tool session originating from an unrecognized external IP
vectors: Fraudulent tech-support phone call directing installation of a remote-access tool
Fake pop-up/notification impersonating IT support prompting a remote-access tool download
rootCauses: Lack of user awareness training on tech-support-scam tactics
Absence of policy/technical controls restricting installation of unauthorized remote-access utilities
controls: Application allowlisting restricting unauthorized remote-access tool installation
User awareness training on tech-support-scam recognition
Monitoring/alerting on installation of unauthorized remote-access utilities
ITID-31243.detection: Moderate; software inventory/allowlisting alerts on unauthorized remote-access tool installation provide a reasonably strong signal.
ITID-31243.response: Terminate the remote session immediately, uninstall the remote-access tool, reset any credentials entered or accessible during the session, and educate the affected user.
metrics: Number of fraudulent remote-support incidents per quarter
Time from installation to session termination
ITID-31243.notes: Differentiated by delivery vector (impersonated remote-support pretext) from commodity and custom-built RAT leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: RAT Delivered via Fake Remote Support Tool Installation
playbook.description: For a confirmed RAT infection where the user was socially engineered into installing a fake remote-support/tech-support tool that provided the attacker remote access.

steps.title: Confirm the fake support tool and the social-engineering vector
steps.desc: Identify the specific fake support tool installed and how the user was convinced to install it (phone scam, pop-up, phishing).
steps.outcome: Delivery vector and social-engineering method identified.

steps.title: Assess the level of control the operator had over the device
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker did during the remote session — fake support tools typically grant full desktop control by design.
steps.guidance: Assume full desktop control was available given the nature of remote-support tools, and treat everything on the device as potentially compromised.
steps.outcome: Level of attacker control established and documented.

steps.title: Isolate the affected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to end the attacker's remote session and cut off further access.
steps.outcome: Attacker's remote control severed.

steps.title: Remove the fake support tool and any additional payloads installed
steps.desc: Uninstall the tool and scan for any additional malware the attacker may have installed during the remote session.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If full-control access is confirmed, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate every credential accessible from the device
steps.desc: Given the assumed full desktop control, rotate all credentials and sessions accessible from the device, including any financial accounts if the scam involved a payment pretext.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Check for financial fraud if the scam involved a payment pretext
steps.desc: Fake support scams frequently attempt to extract payment or banking access — check with the user and financial institution if any payment/banking activity occurred during the session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether financial fraud occurred; institution notified if so.

steps.title: Document the incident and reinforce user awareness of support scams
steps.desc: Record the timeline and provide user education on verifying legitimate support requests before granting remote access.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; user guidance updated.

ITID-31244.def: A Remote Access Trojan infection where the malware's capability provides the adversary full, interactive desktop/screen-control access (equivalent to sitting at the keyboard), rather than limited command-execution or data-collection functions.
ITID-31244.purpose: Captures RAT infections whose defining characteristic is providing the adversary full interactive desktop/screen control, as distinct from a lighter command-execution-only RAT.
scopeIncludes: RAT confirmed to provide live screen viewing and interactive mouse/keyboard control to the adversary
RAT with integrated screen-capture/remote-desktop-equivalent functionality actively used during the incident
scopeExcludes: RATs used only for command execution, file transfer, or data collection without confirmed interactive desktop control (classify by origin under ITID-31241/31242/31243 instead)
ITID-31244.severity: Critical; full interactive control is functionally equivalent to physical adversary presence at the keyboard.
ITID-31244.priority: P1 upon confirmation of an active interactive control session.
ITID-31244.escalation: Escalate immediately and treat as an active, hands-on-keyboard adversary presence; disconnect network access to terminate the session rather than relying on in-band commands.
indicators: EDR detection of screen-capture or remote-desktop-equivalent API usage by an unauthorized process
Unexplained mouse/keyboard activity observed by the user while away from the device
Network telemetry showing sustained, interactive (non-beaconing) traffic pattern to a C2 endpoint
vectors: Delivery of a full-featured RAT via any of the vectors described in sibling leaves, with confirmed use of its interactive control feature
Abuse of a legitimate remote-access tool's screen-sharing/control feature for malicious purposes
rootCauses: Lack of behavioral detection for screen-capture/remote-control API abuse
Insufficient network segmentation limiting what an interactively controlled host can reach
controls: EDR behavioral detection for screen-capture/remote-control API abuse
Network segmentation limiting reach from any single compromised host
Out-of-band network isolation capability for rapid session termination
ITID-31244.detection: Moderate; behavioral detection of screen-capture APIs and sustained interactive network traffic patterns are the primary signals.
ITID-31244.response: Physically or network-isolate the host immediately to terminate the interactive session, then conduct a full review of actions taken during the session using available logging.
metrics: Duration of confirmed interactive control sessions
Time from detection to session termination
ITID-31244.notes: Differentiated by capability (confirmed full interactive desktop control) rather than the tool's origin, which is captured by the other sibling leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: RAT Providing Full Desktop/Screen Control Access
playbook.description: For a confirmed RAT infection where the attacker is confirmed to have had full interactive desktop or screen-control access to the device.

steps.title: Confirm the RAT and verify full desktop-control capability
steps.desc: Confirm via malware analysis and telemetry that the RAT provided interactive full desktop/screen control, not just limited data access.
steps.outcome: Full desktop-control capability confirmed.

steps.title: Assume everything on the device was exposed to the operator
steps.desc: Given confirmed full desktop control, treat all files, credentials, sessions, and locally stored data on the device as compromised.
steps.guidance: Full desktop control means the attacker could see and interact with anything the legitimate user could — scope the response accordingly, broader than a typical limited-access malware infection.
steps.outcome: Full compromise scope for the device established.

steps.title: Isolate the device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to terminate the attacker's live control session.
steps.outcome: Attacker's remote control severed.

steps.title: Preserve forensic evidence of the control session
steps.desc: Image the device and preserve command-and-control traffic logs before remediation.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved for investigation.

steps.title: Rebuild the device rather than attempting in-place cleanup
steps.desc: Given confirmed full desktop control, reimage the device from a trusted source rather than relying on malware removal alone.
steps.outcome: Device rebuilt from a trusted image.

steps.title: Rotate every credential and session accessible from the device
steps.desc: Reset all passwords, revoke all active sessions/tokens, and re-authenticate every account that was accessible from the device.
steps.outcome: Full credential-rotation scope completed.

steps.title: Review for signs of data exfiltration or unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Given full control, check for data staged/exfiltrated and any unauthorized configuration changes made during the session.
steps.outcome: Scope of any exfiltration or tampering established.

steps.title: Document the incident and close the delivery vector
steps.desc: Record the timeline and remediate the identified delivery vector to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31245.def: A Remote Access Trojan incident not yet attributable to a specific origin or capability (commodity/off-the-shelf, custom-built, fake remote-support delivery, or confirmed full interactive desktop control).
ITID-31245.purpose: Catch-all for Remote Access Trojan incidents that do not fit a more specific origin/capability leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific origin/capability has been confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Remote Access Trojans (RATs)
ITID-31245.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High by default.
ITID-31245.priority: P2 by default, escalating to P1 upon confirmation of active remote control.
ITID-31245.escalation: Reclassify once the specific origin/capability is clarified.
indicators: Suspected unauthorized remote access, specific RAT origin/capability not yet determined
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: EDR detection of remote access tool anomalies
Network egress filtering and C2 domain blocklisting
Application allowlisting
Webcam/microphone access alerting
ITID-31245.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31245.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31245.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Remote Access Trojan (RAT) Incident
playbook.description: For a confirmed RAT infection where the specific delivery mechanism and level of attacker control have not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm the RAT and its capabilities
steps.desc: Identify the RAT family and its documented capability set.
steps.outcome: RAT family and capabilities identified.

steps.title: Assess the level of control the operator had over the device
steps.desc: Determine whether the RAT's configuration and observed activity indicate full desktop/screen control versus limited data-collection capability.
steps.guidance: If full desktop control was available, assume everything on that device is potentially compromised.
steps.outcome: Level of attacker control established and documented.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device from the network immediately
steps.desc: Disconnect the device to cut off the operator's remote access.
steps.outcome: Attacker's remote control severed.

steps.title: Preserve forensic evidence before remediation
steps.desc: Image the device and preserve command-and-control traffic logs before remediation, particularly if full control cannot yet be ruled out.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved for investigation.

steps.title: Remove the RAT and any persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Clean the device of the RAT payload and any dropped persistence, or reimage if full control was assessed.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.
steps.abort: If full-control access was confirmed, escalate to full reimage.

steps.title: Rotate credentials scoped to the assessed level of control
steps.desc: Rotate credentials and sessions matching the confirmed scope of attacker access — everything on the device if full control was confirmed.
steps.outcome: Credential-rotation scope matched to the confirmed level of attacker control.

steps.title: Review for signs of data exfiltration or unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Check for data staged/exfiltrated and any unauthorized configuration changes made during the period of access.
steps.outcome: Scope of any exfiltration or tampering established.

steps.title: Document the incident and close the delivery vector
steps.desc: Record the timeline and remediate the identified delivery vector once determined.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; concrete remediations tracked to completion.

ITID-31311.def: A worm that gains code execution on new hosts by directly exploiting a vulnerability in a network-facing service (e.g., SMB, RDP, RPC, a web/application server) and then repeats the process from each newly infected host, spreading automatically across reachable network segments.
ITID-31311.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware spreading across the network by exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in a listening network service, with no user interaction required.
scopeIncludes: Worm exploiting an unpatched or misconfigured network service to gain remote code execution
Rapid, automated lateral spread across subnets following initial exploitation of one host
Self-propagation that continues without any user clicking, opening, or approving anything
scopeExcludes: Propagation via weak/default share credentials rather than a software vulnerability (sibling ITID-31312)
Propagation via email or social engineering (sibling ITID-31313)
A one-off exploit used for initial access without ongoing self-replicating spread (belongs under exploitation ITIDs, not Worms)
ITID-31311.severity: High to Critical. Exploit-driven worms can achieve exponential, cross-segment spread within minutes to hours and frequently carry destructive or ransomware payloads.
ITID-31311.priority: P1 on confirmed exploitation-based spread between hosts; P2 while triage is still confirming worm behavior versus an isolated exploit attempt.
ITID-31311.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC leadership and network/infrastructure teams; consider emergency network segmentation or isolation of the affected service/port pending patching.
indicators: Spike in outbound connection attempts on the exploited service port from an infected host to many internal peers
Identical exploit payload or shellcode pattern observed against multiple hosts in sequence
New/unexpected processes spawned by the vulnerable service process immediately after connection
IDS/IPS alerts for a known CVE-associated exploit signature firing across multiple internal hosts
vectors: Exploitation of an unpatched remote code execution vulnerability in a network service (e.g., SMB, RDP, RPC)
Exploitation of an exposed, outdated web or application server component
rootCauses: Missing security patches for known, publicly disclosed vulnerabilities
Vulnerable services exposed to broader network segments than necessary due to inadequate segmentation
Delayed vulnerability management / patch cadence relative to public exploit availability
controls: Timely patch management aligned to critical/exploited-CVE SLAs
Network segmentation limiting service exposure between subnets
IDS/IPS signatures for known exploit chains
Host-based EDR blocking of anomalous child processes from service daemons
ITID-31311.detection: Strong. Network IDS/IPS, EDR process-lineage telemetry, and vulnerability-to-exploit correlation give reliable, near-real-time detection of exploit-driven spread.
ITID-31311.response: Isolate affected hosts, block the exploited port/service at network boundaries between segments, apply the relevant patch or compensating control, and hunt for all hosts showing the same exploit pattern before declaring containment.
metrics: Time from exploit signature alert to host isolation
Number of hosts infected before containment
Mean patch age of the exploited vulnerability at time of infection
ITID-31311.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: exploitation of a software vulnerability, as opposed to credential abuse, email, or cloud-tenant mechanisms.

playbook.name: Worm Propagating via Unpatched Network Service Vulnerability
playbook.description: A self-propagating worm is spreading across the corporate network by exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in a listening network service.

steps.title: Confirm initial detection and scope the exploited service
steps.desc: Validate the EDR/IDS alert that triggered the incident and identify which network service and CVE/vulnerability is being exploited.
steps.guidance: Review IDS/IPS signatures, EDR process-creation telemetry, and firewall logs for the exploited port/service. Identify the vulnerable service (e.g. SMB, RDP, RPC) and correlate against patch/vulnerability management records.
steps.outcome: The exploited service, port, and vulnerability (CVE where known) are documented along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If the alert cannot be corroborated with a second data source, downgrade to monitoring and continue triage before declaring an incident.

steps.title: Run an organization-wide sweep for the propagation indicators
steps.desc: Because this is a self-propagating worm, scope the search beyond the first-found host to the entire estate, not a single endpoint.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM across all hosts for the same exploit traffic pattern, process hashes, or network scanning behavior (e.g. internal port scanning on the vulnerable service's port) to build a full list of infected or exposed hosts.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of infected hosts and a separate list of hosts still exposed (unpatched, service reachable) but not yet compromised.

steps.title: Identify all hosts still vulnerable to the exploited service
steps.desc: Cross-reference vulnerability scan data to find every host exposing the same unpatched service, since these are the worm's next targets.
steps.guidance: Run or review the latest vulnerability scan results filtered on the specific CVE/service; flag any host that is reachable on the vulnerable port from the infected segment.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of at-risk hosts to patch or isolate before the worm reaches them.

steps.title: Isolate confirmed infected hosts
steps.desc: Move all confirmed infected hosts to network isolation via EDR or NAC quarantine.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation or NAC quarantine VLAN to cut infected hosts off from the network while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: All confirmed infected hosts are isolated and can no longer scan or infect other hosts.
steps.abort: If isolation tooling is unavailable, physically disconnect network cabling/Wi-Fi as an interim measure.

steps.title: Segment or block the vulnerable service network-wide
steps.desc: Apply firewall/ACL rules to block traffic to the exploited service port across network segments, not just at the infected host, to stop further propagation.
steps.guidance: Push temporary firewall rules or micro-segmentation policies blocking the vulnerable port between VLANs/subnets until patching is complete.
steps.outcome: Lateral movement via the exploited service is blocked network-wide, containing the worm's spread even to unpatched hosts.
steps.abort: If blocking the service breaks critical business function, coordinate an exception window with the service owner and compensate with enhanced monitoring.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the vulnerable service where feasible
steps.desc: On at-risk but not-yet-infected hosts, disable the vulnerable service or restrict it to trusted sources as a stopgap ahead of patching.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with system owners to stop/disable the service, or apply host-firewall rules restricting access to management subnets only.
steps.outcome: At-risk hosts are no longer reachable via the vulnerable service, removing them as propagation targets.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from infected hosts
steps.desc: Remove the worm's executable, dropped files, and any persistence mechanisms from each infected host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to kill malicious processes, delete dropped binaries, and remove scheduled tasks/services/registry run keys created by the worm. Reimage hosts where clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts are free of worm binaries and persistence artifacts, confirmed via EDR scan.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host from a known-good baseline instead.

steps.title: Patch the underlying vulnerability on all exposed hosts
steps.desc: Apply the vendor patch or mitigating configuration change that closes the exploited vulnerability on every affected and at-risk host, addressing the root cause of propagation.
steps.guidance: Deploy the patch via the patch management system, prioritizing internet-facing and previously-infected hosts first, then the broader at-risk list identified during identification.
steps.outcome: The exploited vulnerability is remediated across the environment; vulnerability re-scan confirms no remaining exposed hosts.

steps.title: Restore isolated hosts to production
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated and patched hosts to the network in a controlled, phased manner with enhanced monitoring.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean and patched before removing isolation; re-enable network access in batches while watching for renewed propagation indicators.
steps.outcome: All hosts are back in normal operation with no recurrence of worm activity observed over a defined monitoring window.
steps.abort: If propagation indicators reappear, re-isolate immediately and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document root cause and patch-management gap
steps.desc: Record how the vulnerability went unpatched, the full timeline, and remediation actions taken.
steps.guidance: Produce an after-action report covering detection time, scope, containment effectiveness, and recommendations for closing the patch-management gap that allowed exploitation.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with actionable recommendations tracked to closure.

ITID-31312.def: A worm that copies itself to new hosts by brute-forcing, guessing, or reusing weak/default administrative or share credentials (e.g., SMB admin shares, default service accounts) to write and execute its payload on the target, then repeats from each newly infected host.
ITID-31312.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware spreading across the network by authenticating to writable shares using weak, default, or reused network credentials rather than exploiting a software flaw.
scopeIncludes: Worm using harvested, default, or brute-forced credentials to write itself to an administrative or network share
Password-spraying or credential-stuffing behavior originating from an infected host against internal share/authentication services
Spread relying on account/credential weakness rather than an unpatched service vulnerability
scopeExcludes: Propagation via exploitation of an unpatched network service vulnerability (sibling ITID-31311)
Propagation via email/address-book harvesting (sibling ITID-31313)
Credential-based lateral movement performed manually by a human operator without self-replicating worm behavior (belongs under lateral movement / credential access ITIDs)
ITID-31312.severity: High. Spread is often as fast as exploit-based worms in environments with widespread credential reuse or default passwords.
ITID-31312.priority: P1 on confirmed multi-host spread via credential abuse; P2 during initial triage of a single suspicious authentication-and-copy event.
ITID-31312.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership and identity/IAM teams immediately; force credential resets for any account observed being used by the worm.
indicators: Rapid sequence of authentication attempts to admin/hidden shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$) from a single source using varying accounts
New executable files written to administrative shares on multiple hosts in a short window
Successful logons using default or well-known service account credentials from an unexpected source host
Repeated failed authentication attempts followed by a success, consistent with brute-force or credential spraying
vectors: Brute-forcing or spraying weak/default local administrator or service account passwords against SMB/network shares
Reuse of harvested credentials to write and remotely trigger execution on administrative shares
rootCauses: Default or unchanged vendor/service account credentials in production
Local administrator password reuse across many hosts (no per-host randomization)
Absence of account lockout or authentication throttling on internal share/authentication services
controls: Unique, randomized local administrator passwords per host (e.g., LAPS-equivalent)
Account lockout / authentication throttling on share and domain authentication services
Disabling or tightly restricting administrative share access where not required
Credential hygiene monitoring for default/vendor account usage
ITID-31312.detection: Moderate-to-strong. Authentication logs and share-write telemetry provide clear signal, though noisy environments with legitimate admin tooling can require tuning to reduce false positives.
ITID-31312.response: Disable or reset compromised/abused accounts, remove worm artifacts from written shares, isolate source and destination hosts, and audit for other hosts sharing the same weak credential pattern.
metrics: Number of accounts identified as abused per incident
Time from anomalous authentication alert to account disablement
Percentage of hosts with unique local admin credentials post-incident
ITID-31312.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: credential weakness/reuse, as opposed to a software vulnerability, email, or cloud-tenant mechanisms.

playbook.name: Worm Propagating via Weak/Default Network Share Credentials
playbook.description: A worm is spreading across the network by brute-forcing or using weak/default credentials against SMB/network shares.

steps.title: Confirm the credential-based propagation vector
steps.desc: Validate the initial alert and confirm the worm is using weak or default credentials to authenticate to network shares.
steps.guidance: Review authentication logs (Windows Security 4624/4625, share access logs) for repeated logon attempts using common/default usernames and passwords, or successful logons from unusual sources.
steps.outcome: Confirmed evidence of credential-based lateral movement, with the account(s) and share(s) involved identified.
steps.abort: If failed-logon volume is inconclusive, expand log collection window before proceeding.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for compromised accounts and infected hosts
steps.desc: Search across the entire environment for the same credential-based access pattern, not just the initially discovered host.
steps.guidance: Query authentication logs domain-wide for the compromised account(s) and identify every host that authenticated or was authenticated to using them.
steps.outcome: A complete list of compromised accounts and every host touched via those accounts.

steps.title: Identify shares and hosts using weak or default credentials
steps.desc: Audit network shares and service accounts for weak, default, or reused passwords that remain exploitable.
steps.guidance: Run a credential-hygiene audit (e.g. password policy compliance scan) against local accounts and shares to find remaining exposure.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of accounts/shares requiring immediate password rotation or lockdown.

steps.title: Disable or reset compromised accounts
steps.desc: Immediately disable or force a password reset on every account confirmed or suspected to be compromised.
steps.guidance: Use Active Directory/IAM tooling to disable accounts and force reset on next logon; prioritize accounts with administrative or wide share access.
steps.outcome: Compromised accounts can no longer be used to authenticate to shares.
steps.abort: If disabling an account breaks a critical service, coordinate with the service owner for an expedited credential rotation instead.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts and restrict share access network-wide
steps.desc: Isolate confirmed infected hosts and apply network-wide restrictions on SMB/share access to slow further spread while credentials are rotated.
steps.guidance: Use EDR/NAC isolation on infected hosts; apply temporary firewall rules restricting SMB (445) and NetBIOS traffic between untrusted segments.
steps.outcome: The worm can no longer reach additional shares using the compromised credentials, and infected hosts are isolated.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from infected hosts
steps.desc: Remove the worm binary, dropped payloads, and persistence mechanisms from each infected host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate malicious processes and delete dropped files, scheduled tasks, and services created by the worm. Reimage where clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts are verified free of worm artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be verified, reimage from a known-good baseline.

steps.title: Enforce strong credential policy on all shares and service accounts
steps.desc: Rotate all weak/default credentials identified during identification and enforce a strong password/MFA policy going forward, addressing the root cause of propagation.
steps.guidance: Reset all flagged accounts to strong, unique passwords; disable default/guest accounts on shares; enable account lockout thresholds and, where possible, MFA for administrative access.
steps.outcome: No remaining accounts or shares use weak/default credentials, verified by re-running the credential audit.

steps.title: Restore hosts and re-enable share access in a controlled manner
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts and re-enable share access in phases, with monitoring for repeat credential abuse.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring, and monitor authentication logs closely for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Normal share access and network connectivity are restored with no recurrence of worm activity.
steps.abort: If suspicious authentication reappears, re-isolate and return to containment.

steps.title: Document credential hygiene gaps and remediation
steps.desc: Record how weak/default credentials existed, the full incident timeline, and steps taken to close the gap.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report with recommendations such as periodic credential audits, disabling default accounts by policy, and MFA rollout.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and remediation items tracked to closure.

ITID-31313.def: A worm that, once running on a host or mailbox, harvests the local address book or contact list and mass-mails copies of itself (as an attachment or link) to those contacts, often spoofing the sender to increase the likelihood recipients open it, propagating one mailbox-to-mailbox hop at a time.
ITID-31313.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware that spreads by harvesting a victim's email contacts or address book and auto-forwarding itself to those contacts, relying on social trust rather than a technical exploit.
scopeIncludes: Worm code that enumerates a local mail client or webmail address book and sends itself to harvested contacts
Auto-forwarding or mass-mailing behavior triggered automatically once a host/mailbox is infected
Spread that depends on a downstream recipient opening/executing the received message or attachment
scopeExcludes: Propagation via direct exploitation of a network service (sibling ITID-31311)
Propagation via weak/default share credentials (sibling ITID-31312)
Traditional phishing campaigns sent by a human operator with no self-replicating worm component (belongs under phishing ITIDs)
ITID-31313.severity: Medium-High. Spread rate depends on recipient behavior rather than automatic exploitation, but reach can be very large due to address-book fan-out.
ITID-31313.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if confirmed active mass-mailing from a compromised internal mailbox to external or high-value recipients.
ITID-31313.escalation: Escalate to SOC and email/messaging administrators immediately to block/quarantine in-flight messages and disable the compromised mailbox's send capability.
indicators: Sudden spike in outbound email volume from a single mailbox/host, often to a broad or unusual recipient list
Identical or near-identical attachment/subject line sent to many recipients from a single sender in a short window
Address book access or export activity coinciding with mass outbound mail
Multiple recipients reporting receipt of the same suspicious attachment/link from a trusted internal sender
vectors: Malicious attachment or embedded link executed by the victim, which then harvests contacts and mass-mails itself
Abuse of mail client auto-forwarding rules or scripting objects to send copies to the harvested address book
rootCauses: Lack of attachment/macro execution restrictions on end-user mail clients
Absence of outbound mail volume/anomaly monitoring per mailbox
Insufficient user awareness leading to execution of unsolicited attachments
controls: Email gateway attachment sandboxing and macro-execution restrictions
Per-mailbox outbound volume anomaly detection
Address book / contact export monitoring on endpoints
User awareness training on unsolicited attachments from known senders
ITID-31313.detection: Moderate. Mail gateway and mailbox audit logs provide good signal for outbound volume anomalies, though attribution to specific worm code may require endpoint or attachment analysis.
ITID-31313.response: Quarantine in-transit and delivered copies across the mail environment, disable/reset the source mailbox, notify affected recipients not to open the attachment, and remove the worm from the originating host.
metrics: Number of recipients that received the propagated message
Time from outbound volume anomaly alert to mailbox disablement
Number of recipients who opened/executed the attachment before containment
ITID-31313.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: email/address-book harvesting relying on recipient action, as opposed to a software vulnerability, credential abuse, or cloud-tenant mechanisms.

playbook.name: Worm Propagating via Email Auto-Forwarding/Address Book Harvesting
playbook.description: A worm is self-propagating by harvesting address books and sending malicious emails from compromised mailboxes to new victims.

steps.title: Confirm the mailbox-based propagation vector
steps.desc: Validate that the worm is spreading via address-book harvesting and auto-forwarding/auto-send from compromised mailboxes.
steps.guidance: Review mail transport logs and mailbox audit logs for unexpected auto-forward rules, mass-send events, or outbound mail matching the worm's known subject/attachment pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed identification of the propagation mechanism and the first known compromised mailbox(es).
steps.abort: If the pattern cannot be confirmed, treat as suspected phishing and continue monitoring before declaring a worm incident.
steps.tool: Email security gateway / mailbox audit logs

steps.title: Sweep all mailboxes for compromise and malicious forwarding rules
steps.desc: Search the entire mail environment, not just the first-found mailbox, for the same indicators of compromise.
steps.guidance: Query the mail platform for all mailboxes with auto-forward rules matching the malicious pattern, and for all recipients of the worm's outbound emails.
steps.outcome: A complete list of compromised mailboxes and every recipient who received a malicious message.
steps.tool: Email security gateway / mail platform admin tools

steps.title: Identify recipients who may have interacted with the malicious content
steps.desc: Determine which recipients opened, clicked, or otherwise interacted with the worm's email content, as those endpoints may also be infected.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference mail delivery logs with proxy/EDR telemetry to see which recipients clicked links or opened attachments.
steps.outcome: A list of endpoints requiring endpoint-level investigation in addition to mailbox remediation.

steps.title: Disable compromised mailboxes and remove malicious forwarding rules
steps.desc: Disable sending on compromised mailboxes and remove any malicious auto-forward/inbox rules across the entire mail tenant.
steps.guidance: Use mail admin tooling to block sending, remove rogue transport/inbox rules, and force password reset and session revocation on affected accounts.
steps.outcome: Compromised mailboxes can no longer send worm emails or forward mail externally.
steps.abort: If disabling send breaks urgent business communication, coordinate an interim compensating control with the mailbox owner.

steps.title: Block the malicious message pattern and sender domains network-wide
steps.desc: Apply mail-flow rules to block or quarantine further messages matching the worm's pattern across the whole organization.
steps.guidance: Add transport rules or threat-intel blocks for the malicious subject lines, attachment hashes, sender domains/IPs at the email security gateway.
steps.outcome: No further propagation emails reach any mailbox in the organization.

steps.title: Purge malicious emails from all mailboxes
steps.desc: Remove the worm's emails from every mailbox they reached, including sent, inbox, and any auto-forwarded copies.
steps.guidance: Use mail admin search-and-purge capability across the tenant to remove matching messages by hash/subject/sender.
steps.outcome: No copies of the malicious email remain accessible in any mailbox.

steps.title: Remediate endpoint infections and revoke compromised credentials
steps.desc: Clean any endpoints infected via clicked links/attachments and rotate credentials for all compromised mailbox accounts, addressing the root cause of the address-book harvesting.
steps.guidance: Run EDR scans and remediation on flagged endpoints; force password resets and re-enable MFA on all compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: All affected endpoints are clean and all compromised credentials have been rotated.
steps.abort: If an endpoint cannot be verified clean, reimage it.

steps.title: Restore mailbox and endpoint access with monitoring
steps.desc: Re-enable sending and endpoint network access in a controlled manner, monitoring for recurrence.
steps.guidance: Restore capabilities in phases and monitor mail-flow logs and EDR alerts for renewed propagation attempts over a defined period.
steps.outcome: Normal mail and endpoint operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If new propagation is observed, re-isolate the affected mailbox/endpoint.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve email security controls
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend controls such as auto-forward restrictions and attachment sandboxing.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report covering root cause, scope, response effectiveness, and specific recommendations (e.g. disabling external auto-forwarding by default, user awareness training).
steps.outcome: After-action report published with tracked remediation items.

ITID-31314.def: A worm that propagates not across a traditional on-premises network but across cloud resources, accounts, or tenants, by abusing over-permissive IAM roles, shared storage/CI-CD resources, exposed cloud service credentials, or cross-tenant trust/federation relationships to replicate itself into additional cloud accounts or subscriptions.
ITID-31314.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware that spreads across cloud environments by abusing shared infrastructure, misconfigured trust relationships, or federated identities to jump between cloud accounts, subscriptions, or tenants.
scopeIncludes: Worm abusing an over-permissive cloud IAM role or service credential to deploy itself into another account/subscription
Self-propagation through shared CI/CD pipelines, container registries, or infrastructure-as-code artifacts across tenants
Exploitation of cross-tenant federation or trust misconfiguration to replicate into a connected organization's cloud environment
scopeExcludes: Traditional on-premises network exploitation or credential-share propagation (sibling ITIDs 31311/31312)
Email-based propagation (sibling ITID-31313)
A single unauthorized cloud access event with no self-replicating spread to additional accounts/tenants (belongs under cloud account compromise ITIDs)
ITID-31314.severity: Critical. Cross-tenant spread can affect multiple organizations or business units simultaneously and often involves highly privileged cloud identities.
ITID-31314.priority: P1 immediately upon any confirmed cross-account or cross-tenant replication.
ITID-31314.escalation: Escalate immediately to cloud platform/security team, affected tenant owners, and executive leadership given the multi-organization blast radius; engage cloud provider support as needed.
indicators: Unexpected creation of new IAM roles, service principals, or automation resources across multiple accounts/subscriptions in quick succession
Anomalous cross-account API calls (e.g., AssumeRole, cross-tenant token requests) from an already-compromised identity
Identical malicious artifact or deployment template appearing in unrelated cloud accounts/tenants
Sudden spikes in cloud resource provisioning consistent with automated self-replication
vectors: Abuse of over-permissive or misconfigured cross-account/cross-tenant IAM trust relationships
Compromise of shared CI/CD pipelines, container registries, or infrastructure-as-code templates used across multiple tenants
rootCauses: Overly broad IAM role trust policies allowing unintended cross-account assumption
Shared secrets or credentials reused across multiple cloud accounts/tenants
Insufficient monitoring of cross-tenant API activity and resource provisioning
controls: Least-privilege IAM role and trust-policy review across accounts/tenants
Cross-account/cross-tenant API activity monitoring and anomaly alerting
Isolation and scoping of CI/CD pipelines and shared registries per tenant
Regular audit of federation/trust relationships between organizations
ITID-31314.detection: Moderate. Cloud provider audit logs (e.g., CloudTrail-equivalent) give strong raw signal, but correlating cross-account/cross-tenant activity into a single worm narrative requires mature cloud security tooling (CSPM/CIEM).
ITID-31314.response: Revoke abused roles/credentials, isolate affected accounts/tenants, notify all affected organizations, and audit every cloud account reachable via the abused trust relationship before declaring containment.
metrics: Number of cloud accounts/tenants affected
Time from first cross-tenant anomaly alert to trust relationship revocation
Number of over-permissive trust policies remediated post-incident
ITID-31314.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: cloud IAM/trust abuse across accounts and tenants, as opposed to on-premises network exploitation, credential abuse, or email.

playbook.name: Cross-Cloud/Cross-Tenant Propagating Worm
playbook.description: A worm is propagating across cloud environments or between tenants by abusing shared credentials, trust relationships, or misconfigured cross-tenant access.

steps.title: Confirm cross-cloud/cross-tenant propagation vector
steps.desc: Validate the alert and identify which cloud trust relationship, shared credential, or misconfiguration is enabling propagation between cloud accounts or tenants.
steps.guidance: Review cloud provider audit logs (e.g. CloudTrail, Azure AD sign-in logs), cross-account role assumption events, and API activity for anomalous cross-tenant access patterns.
steps.outcome: The specific trust relationship, role, or credential enabling cross-tenant spread is identified along with the first affected tenant/account.
steps.abort: If cross-tenant activity cannot be corroborated, escalate to the cloud provider's security team for additional telemetry before proceeding.

steps.title: Sweep all tenants/accounts in the organization for the same indicators
steps.desc: Search across every cloud account and tenant in the organization, not just the first-found one, for the same propagation indicators.
steps.guidance: Query cloud-wide logging (organization-level CloudTrail/Azure AD logs) for the same API call patterns, role assumptions, or resource creation signatures across all subscriptions/accounts.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected tenants/accounts and resources.

steps.title: Enumerate exposed trust relationships and shared credentials
steps.desc: Identify all cross-account roles, federated trust relationships, and shared service credentials that could still be abused for further propagation.
steps.guidance: Review IAM role trust policies, federation configurations, and shared secrets/API keys across accounts for overly permissive cross-tenant access.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of trust relationships/credentials requiring immediate revocation or tightening.

steps.title: Revoke or suspend the abused cross-tenant access
steps.desc: Immediately revoke or suspend the specific roles, trust relationships, or credentials being used for propagation.
steps.guidance: Disable or restrict the cross-account IAM role, rotate the abused API keys/service principal credentials, and suspend affected federation trust if necessary.
steps.outcome: The worm can no longer move between tenants/accounts using the abused access path.
steps.abort: If revocation breaks a critical inter-tenant integration, coordinate an emergency change with the business owner for a scoped alternative.

steps.title: Isolate affected cloud resources and accounts
steps.desc: Quarantine or isolate compromised cloud workloads/accounts network- and permission-wise across all affected tenants.
steps.guidance: Apply security-group/network-ACL restrictions to affected instances, disable compromised service accounts, and quarantine affected workloads via cloud-native isolation tooling.
steps.outcome: All confirmed affected resources are isolated and can no longer be used for further propagation.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from affected cloud resources
steps.desc: Remove malicious code, unauthorized IAM changes, and persistence mechanisms (e.g. rogue functions, scheduled jobs) from every affected resource across all tenants.
steps.guidance: Terminate/rebuild compromised compute instances from known-good images; delete unauthorized IAM roles, policies, and automation (Lambda/Functions, scheduled tasks) created by the worm.
steps.outcome: All affected cloud resources are verified free of worm artifacts and unauthorized IAM changes.
steps.abort: If a resource's integrity cannot be verified, rebuild it from a trusted image/template.

steps.title: Harden cross-tenant trust configuration
steps.desc: Tighten the cross-account trust policies, remove unnecessary federation/shared credentials, and enforce least-privilege access to address the root cause of cross-tenant propagation.
steps.guidance: Rewrite IAM trust policies to scope permissions tightly, require MFA/conditional access for cross-tenant roles, and eliminate long-lived shared credentials in favor of short-lived tokens.
steps.outcome: Cross-tenant access is scoped to least privilege and re-audited as clean by CSPM.

steps.title: Restore cloud services and re-enable trust relationships carefully
steps.desc: Restore affected workloads and, where still required, re-establish cross-tenant trust with tightened scope and enhanced monitoring.
steps.guidance: Bring resources back online in phases, validating each is clean; re-enable only necessary cross-tenant access with new, scoped credentials and monitor for anomalous activity.
steps.outcome: Normal cloud operations resume with no recurrence of cross-tenant propagation observed.
steps.abort: If anomalous cross-tenant activity reappears, revoke the re-established trust immediately.

steps.title: Document the cross-tenant exposure and remediation
steps.desc: Record the full incident timeline and recommend structural changes to cloud trust architecture.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report covering how the trust relationship was exposed, response timeline, and recommendations such as periodic cross-tenant access reviews and least-privilege enforcement.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with remediation items tracked to closure.

ITID-31315.def: A self-propagating worm confirmed to be spreading across the network but whose exact propagation vector (vulnerability exploitation, credential abuse, email harvesting, or cross-cloud/tenant abuse) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.
ITID-31315.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed network-propagating worm whose specific propagation mechanism does not yet match, or cannot be confirmed against, one of the defined network propagation sibling categories.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered or unclassified worm strains observed propagating across the network during initial triage
Worms using a novel or hybrid network propagation technique not yet covered by a dedicated sibling ITID
Cases pending forensic confirmation of the specific propagation mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any case where the propagation vector has been confirmed and matches an existing sibling ITID (31311-31314) — reclassify once confirmed
Non-network propagation such as USB or purely fileless local mechanisms (Tier-4 siblings USB Worms and Fileless Worms)
ITID-31315.severity: High, pending refinement once the specific propagation mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-31315.priority: P1-P2 during initial triage; reassess priority once propagation vector and scope are confirmed.
ITID-31315.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership as with any suspected worm outbreak; reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as the propagation mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Multiple hosts infected with identical malware in a pattern consistent with automated self-replication
Network-wide spread observed before the specific propagation mechanism has been forensically confirmed
vectors: Unconfirmed or mixed network propagation mechanism pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient telemetry at time of detection to determine the specific propagation mechanism
Novel or hybrid worm technique not yet mapped to an existing category
controls: General network segmentation and outbreak containment capability
Endpoint detection and response coverage across all hosts
ITID-31315.detection: Variable; depends on the eventual confirmed mechanism. Treat as high-priority pending investigation.
ITID-31315.response: Contain and isolate as a suspected worm outbreak while forensics determines the specific propagation mechanism, then reclassify the incident to the matching sibling ITID.
metrics: Number of incidents landing in this catch-all category per quarter
Time to reclassification into a specific sibling ITID
ITID-31315.notes: This is the intake/catch-all leaf for the Network Propagation Worms group; incidents here should be actively triaged toward reclassification rather than left permanently unclassified.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Network Propagation Worm
playbook.description: A worm is self-propagating across the network via an unidentified or mixed set of network-based vectors.

steps.title: Confirm worm activity and characterize the propagation behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather enough telemetry to characterize how the worm is moving across the network, even if the exact vector is not yet fully classified.
steps.guidance: Review EDR, IDS/IPS, and network flow data for scanning behavior, repeated connection attempts, or lateral file/process creation patterns consistent with self-propagation.
steps.outcome: Worm activity is confirmed and a working hypothesis of the propagation mechanism is documented, along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If behavior is ambiguous, continue monitoring and gather more telemetry before declaring a worm incident.

steps.title: Run an organization-wide sweep for infected hosts
steps.desc: Search the entire environment, not just the first-found host, for the same indicators of compromise.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM across all endpoints and servers for matching file hashes, process behavior, or network scanning patterns to build a complete infection map.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of infected hosts and their network segments.

steps.title: Determine the specific propagation vector
steps.desc: Analyze captured samples/traffic to pin down the exact mechanism (e.g. exploit, credential abuse, removable media) so containment and eradication can be targeted correctly.
steps.guidance: Perform malware analysis on captured samples and correlate network traffic to determine the specific exploited service, credential, or medium used for spread.
steps.outcome: The specific propagation vector is identified, allowing reclassification and vector-specific remediation if warranted.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all confirmed infected hosts via EDR or NAC quarantine to halt further spread.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation or NAC quarantine to disconnect infected hosts from the network while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: All confirmed infected hosts are isolated and can no longer infect other systems.
steps.abort: If isolation tooling is unavailable, physically disconnect affected hosts.

steps.title: Apply network segmentation to slow or stop spread
steps.desc: Segment the network to contain the worm to affected zones while the exact vector is confirmed, rather than isolating only single hosts.
steps.guidance: Apply temporary firewall/VLAN segmentation between affected and unaffected zones, restricting broad lateral-movement protocols (SMB, RDP, WMI) as a precaution.
steps.outcome: Spread is contained to the currently affected network segment(s).
steps.abort: If segmentation breaks critical business operations, negotiate a scoped exception with monitoring in place.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from infected hosts
steps.desc: Remove the worm's binaries, dropped files, and persistence mechanisms from every infected host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate malicious processes and remove dropped files, scheduled tasks, services, and registry run keys. Reimage where clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts are verified free of worm artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be verified, reimage from a known-good baseline.

steps.title: Close the confirmed propagation vector
steps.desc: Apply the specific fix appropriate to the now-identified vector (patch, credential rotation, media control policy, etc.) to prevent reinfection.
steps.guidance: Based on the vector identified during identification, apply the corresponding root-cause fix (e.g. patch a vulnerable service, rotate weak credentials, disable autorun) across the environment.
steps.outcome: The confirmed propagation vector is closed environment-wide, verified via targeted scanning.

steps.title: Restore hosts and network connectivity in phases
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts and lift segmentation restrictions gradually, with monitoring.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring; monitor network traffic closely for renewed propagation over a defined period before fully lifting segmentation.
steps.outcome: Normal network operations resume with no recurrence of worm activity.
steps.abort: If propagation recurs, re-isolate and return to containment.

steps.title: Document the incident and update detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the full timeline, confirmed vector, and any detection gaps that delayed classification.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and update detection signatures/playbooks to specifically cover the now-identified propagation vector for future incidents.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and detection/playbook updates tracked to completion.

ITID-31321.def: A worm that places an autorun configuration file and payload on a USB or other removable drive so that inserting the drive into a host with Autorun/Autoplay enabled triggers automatic execution of the worm, which then copies itself to any other removable media subsequently connected.
ITID-31321.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware on removable media that relies on Windows Autorun/Autoplay features to execute automatically the moment a USB drive is inserted, with no deliberate user click required.
scopeIncludes: Worm leveraging autorun.inf or equivalent Autoplay configuration to execute automatically on drive insertion
Automatic execution requiring no explicit user file-open action beyond inserting the media
Self-copying to any additional removable drives connected to the infected host
scopeExcludes: Spread relying on a disguised/hidden executable that the user must manually double-click (sibling ITID-31322)
Re-infection specifically of drives that were previously cleaned and reinserted (sibling ITID-31323)
Network-based propagation not involving removable media (Network Propagation Worms group)
ITID-31321.severity: Medium-High. Historically a major vector; modern OS defaults largely disable Autorun for non-optical media, but legacy or misconfigured systems remain highly susceptible.
ITID-31321.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if observed spreading across multiple hosts/departments via shared removable media.
ITID-31321.escalation: Escalate to SOC and endpoint management if Autorun/Autoplay is found enabled on managed hosts; disable the feature organization-wide as an immediate containment step.
indicators: Presence of autorun.inf files referencing an executable on removable media
Automatic process execution immediately following USB device connection events in host logs
Identical worm binary found on multiple USB drives across different users
vectors: Autorun.inf-triggered automatic execution on USB/removable drive insertion
rootCauses: Autorun/Autoplay left enabled on endpoints via policy or configuration gap
Uncontrolled use of personally owned or shared USB drives across the environment
controls: Group Policy / MDM enforcement disabling Autorun and Autoplay for removable media
USB device control (allow-listing, read-only enforcement, or blocking)
Endpoint detection of autorun.inf creation events
ITID-31321.detection: Strong. Autorun.inf file-creation and USB-triggered execution events are reliably logged by modern EDR and device-control tooling.
ITID-31321.response: Disable Autorun/Autoplay if not already enforced, quarantine affected drives, remove the worm and autorun.inf from all connected media, and scan all recently connected removable devices across the environment.
metrics: Number of hosts found with Autorun/Autoplay enabled during sweep
Number of infected removable drives identified and remediated
ITID-31321.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: automatic Autorun/Autoplay-triggered execution, as opposed to a disguised executable requiring a manual click, or re-infection of previously cleaned media.

playbook.name: Autorun/Autoplay-Triggered USB Worm
playbook.description: A worm is spreading between hosts via removable USB media using autorun/autoplay execution.

steps.title: Confirm autorun-based USB propagation
steps.desc: Validate that the worm executes automatically when removable media is inserted via autorun/autoplay.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry for process execution originating from removable-drive letters immediately following USB insertion events, and inspect any autorun.inf files on affected media.
steps.outcome: Confirmed autorun-triggered execution pattern and the first known affected host/device identified.
steps.abort: If autorun cannot be confirmed as the trigger, treat as a general USB worm and broaden investigation.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for infected hosts and removable media
steps.desc: Search across all endpoints, not just the first-found host, for the same worm artifacts and any USB devices that may carry the infection further.
steps.guidance: Query EDR across all endpoints for the worm's file hash/behavior; correlate USB device connection logs to identify every removable drive that has touched an infected host.
steps.outcome: A complete list of infected hosts and a list of potentially-infected removable media devices in circulation.

steps.title: Identify hosts with autorun/autoplay still enabled
steps.desc: Determine which hosts remain vulnerable because autorun/autoplay is still enabled, as these are the worm's next targets.
steps.guidance: Query endpoint configuration management or GPO reporting for autorun/autoplay registry settings across the fleet.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of hosts requiring autorun/autoplay to be disabled immediately.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all confirmed infected hosts to prevent further spread via network or additional USB devices.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected endpoints while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts are isolated and cannot infect further removable media or network peers.

steps.title: Disable autorun/autoplay organization-wide
steps.desc: Push a policy change disabling autorun/autoplay across the entire fleet, not just the affected hosts, to stop further propagation.
steps.guidance: Deploy a GPO or MDM policy disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay for all removable media across all endpoints.
steps.outcome: No host in the organization will auto-execute content from removable media going forward.

steps.title: Quarantine and recall suspect removable media
steps.desc: Identify and physically quarantine USB devices that may carry the infection until they can be scanned and cleaned.
steps.guidance: Notify device owners identified during the sweep to stop using and hand in their devices for scanning.
steps.outcome: All potentially-infected removable media is collected and held pending eradication.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from infected hosts and media
steps.desc: Clean infected hosts and scan/clean or reformat quarantined removable media.
steps.guidance: Use EDR/AV to remove malicious executables and autorun.inf files from hosts; reformat quarantined USB devices after confirming no other recoverable data risk, or scan-and-clean with updated AV signatures.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts and removable media are verified clean.
steps.abort: If a host cannot be verified clean, reimage it.

steps.title: Restore hosts and reissue cleaned media
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts to the network and return cleaned/reformatted removable media to users.
steps.guidance: Validate each host and device is clean before returning to service; monitor for renewed autorun-execution attempts.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence of autorun-triggered infection.
steps.abort: If reinfection is observed, re-isolate and investigate remaining unpatched policy gaps.

steps.title: Document the incident and formalize removable media policy
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend a permanent removable-media control policy.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending organization-wide autorun-disable-by-default policy and, where appropriate, removable media restrictions or device control tooling.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with policy recommendations tracked to closure.

ITID-31322.def: A worm that copies itself onto removable media as a hidden or disguised executable (e.g., using a folder icon, double file extension, or file name mimicking a legitimate document) so that a user, browsing the drive, is tricked into manually double-clicking it, triggering execution and further propagation.
ITID-31322.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware on removable media that relies on social engineering, disguising itself as a legitimate file or folder icon so a user manually double-clicks the malicious executable.
scopeIncludes: Worm using a fake folder/document icon or disguised file name to induce manual execution
Hiding legitimate drive contents (e.g., via hidden attributes) while presenting a malicious lookalike in their place
Propagation requiring an explicit user double-click rather than automatic Autorun execution
scopeExcludes: Automatic execution via Autorun/Autoplay configuration with no user click needed (sibling ITID-31321)
Re-infection specifically of drives that were previously cleaned and reinserted (sibling ITID-31323)
Disguised executables delivered via email or network shares rather than removable media (other Tier-4 groups)
ITID-31322.severity: Medium. Spread rate is slower than autorun-based worms since it depends on user deception, but remains effective in environments with heavy removable-media use.
