ITID-31322.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if multiple users across the organization report or are found to have executed the disguised file.
ITID-31322.escalation: Escalate to SOC and user awareness/communications teams to issue guidance on the specific disguise technique observed.
indicators: Hidden legitimate files/folders on a USB drive alongside a visible executable using a folder or document icon
Execution of a binary from a removable drive path immediately followed by file-hiding attribute changes on that drive
User reports of double-clicking what appeared to be a folder or document on a USB drive
vectors: Disguising the worm executable with a folder/document icon and hiding legitimate files to induce a manual double-click
rootCauses: Lack of user awareness regarding disguised executables on removable media
Endpoints configured to hide known file extensions, making disguises more convincing
Absence of execution controls restricting binaries launched directly from removable media
controls: Endpoint policy blocking or alerting on executable launch directly from removable media
File extension visibility enforcement to reduce masquerading effectiveness
User awareness training on disguised-icon and hidden-file techniques
ITID-31322.detection: Moderate. EDR can detect execution-from-removable-media and file-attribute-hiding behavior, though initial detection often depends on user reporting.
ITID-31322.response: Remove the disguised executable and restore hidden legitimate files, scan and remediate all removable media used by the affected user, and communicate the specific disguise pattern to raise awareness.
metrics: Number of users who executed the disguised file before detection
Number of removable drives found carrying the disguised executable
ITID-31322.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: social-engineering disguise requiring a manual click, as opposed to automatic Autorun execution or re-infection of cleaned media.

playbook.name: USB Worm Spreading via Hidden/Disguised Executable on Removable Media
playbook.description: A worm spreads via removable USB media by disguising its executable as a legitimate file or folder shortcut to trick users into running it.

steps.title: Confirm the disguised-executable propagation technique
steps.desc: Validate that the worm hides its executable (e.g. via folder-icon disguise, hidden attributes, or fake shortcut/.lnk files) on removable media to induce user execution.
steps.guidance: Inspect affected removable media for hidden/disguised executables and malicious .lnk shortcut files; review EDR telemetry for process execution matching the disguised file name shortly after USB insertion.
steps.outcome: Confirmed technique and sample identified, along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If the disguise technique cannot be confirmed, broaden investigation to general USB worm handling.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for infected hosts and affected media
steps.desc: Search across all endpoints, not just the first-found host, and trace all removable media that may carry the disguised executable.
steps.guidance: Query EDR for the worm's hash/behavior across all endpoints; use USB device connection history to trace every drive that touched an infected host.
steps.outcome: A complete list of infected hosts and potentially-infected removable devices.

steps.title: Identify user behavior patterns that enabled execution
steps.desc: Determine how users were induced to run the disguised file, to inform both eradication and user-awareness follow-up.
steps.guidance: Interview affected users and review file system metadata to confirm whether users clicked a disguised shortcut/folder icon.
steps.outcome: A clear understanding of the social-engineering aspect of the infection vector.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all confirmed infected hosts to prevent further spread.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected endpoints while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts are isolated and cannot infect further systems or media.

steps.title: Quarantine suspect removable media and restrict USB use org-wide
steps.desc: Recall potentially-infected removable media and, where feasible, apply temporary device-control restrictions on USB storage across the fleet.
steps.guidance: Notify affected device owners to hand in devices for scanning; deploy a temporary device-control policy blocking or restricting unauthorized USB mass-storage devices.
steps.outcome: No further disguised-executable infections occur via removable media during the response.
steps.abort: If USB restriction breaks essential business function, scope the restriction to affected teams only.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts and disguised files from hosts and media
steps.desc: Clean infected hosts and scan/reformat quarantined removable media, removing all disguised executables and shortcuts.
steps.guidance: Use EDR/AV to remove malicious files and fake shortcuts; reformat quarantined media after evidence collection, or scan-and-clean with current signatures.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts and media are verified clean.
steps.abort: If a host cannot be verified clean, reimage it.

steps.title: Enable visibility of hidden files and file-extension warnings
steps.desc: Adjust endpoint configuration to reduce the effectiveness of file-disguise techniques going forward.
steps.guidance: Push a GPO/MDM policy to show hidden files and known file extensions by default across the fleet.
steps.outcome: Disguised executables are more visible to users organization-wide.

steps.title: Restore hosts and reissue cleaned media
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts and return cleaned media to users in a controlled manner.
steps.guidance: Validate cleanliness before restoring; monitor for renewed activity over a defined period.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If reinfection occurs, re-isolate and re-investigate.

steps.title: Document the incident and conduct user-awareness follow-up
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend user-awareness training on disguised-file social engineering.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and schedule targeted awareness training for affected teams on recognizing disguised executables/shortcuts.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and awareness training scheduled.

ITID-31323.def: A worm that maintains persistence on an infected host (rather than only on the removable media itself) and monitors for USB/removable device insertion events, automatically writing a fresh copy of itself onto any newly connected drive, causing repeated re-infection cycles even after individual drives are cleaned.
ITID-31323.purpose: Captures the specific worm behavior of persisting on an infected host and automatically re-infecting any removable drive newly inserted into that host, even after the drive itself was previously cleaned.
scopeIncludes: Host-resident worm component that monitors for new removable-device insertion and re-infects each one automatically
Drives that test clean being re-infected upon reconnection to a still-compromised host
Persistence mechanisms on the host dedicated to sustaining ongoing removable-media infection
scopeExcludes: Initial infection via Autorun/Autoplay execution on first insertion (sibling ITID-31321)
Initial infection via a disguised executable requiring a manual click (sibling ITID-31322)
Cleanup verification activity with no evidence of host-side re-infection capability
ITID-31323.severity: High. Failure to identify and remove the host-resident component causes repeated reinfection, undermining containment and prolonging the outbreak.
ITID-31323.priority: P1 once a pattern of drives being re-infected after cleaning is confirmed, since it indicates incomplete initial containment.
ITID-31323.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC leadership; treat as a containment failure requiring full host reimaging rather than partial remediation.
indicators: A previously cleaned USB drive found reinfected shortly after reconnection to the same host
Persistent host-side process or scheduled task that activates on USB/device-insertion events
Repeated worm detections on removable media tracing back to the same source host across multiple cleaning cycles
vectors: Host-resident worm persistence mechanism that re-writes itself to any newly inserted removable drive
rootCauses: Incomplete remediation that removed the drive-side payload but left the host-side persistence mechanism intact
Lack of full host reimaging following initial worm detection
Absence of monitoring for device-insertion-triggered write activity on hosts
controls: Full host reimaging as the standard remediation for confirmed re-infection cases, rather than in-place cleanup
EDR monitoring for persistence mechanisms tied to device-insertion events
Verification scanning of removable media both before and after reconnection to a remediated host
ITID-31323.detection: Strong once suspected. EDR persistence and device-event telemetry reliably reveals the host-side re-infection mechanism when specifically hunted for.
ITID-31323.response: Treat any repeat infection of a cleaned drive as evidence of incomplete remediation, isolate and reimage the source host, and re-verify all removable media that had contacted it.
metrics: Number of re-infection cycles observed before host remediation
Number of hosts requiring reimaging due to confirmed re-infection persistence
ITID-31323.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation vector: host-resident persistence driving ongoing re-infection of removable media, as opposed to the initial infection mechanism (Autorun or disguised executable).

playbook.name: USB Worm Re-Infecting Newly Inserted Removable Drives
playbook.description: A worm resident on a host is actively re-infecting every new removable drive that is inserted, creating an ongoing chain of reinfection.

steps.title: Confirm active re-infection behavior on the resident host
steps.desc: Validate that the worm on the infected host is monitoring for and writing itself to every newly inserted removable drive.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry for a persistent process/service that triggers file-write activity to removable-drive letters immediately upon USB insertion.
steps.outcome: Confirmed active re-infection behavior and the resident host(s) responsible identified.
steps.abort: If re-infection behavior cannot be confirmed, treat as a standard USB worm case.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for all resident hosts and downstream infected media
steps.desc: Search across all endpoints for hosts exhibiting the same re-infection behavior, and trace every removable drive that has been inserted into them.
steps.guidance: Query EDR fleet-wide for the same persistent re-infection process; use USB connection history to build a full chain of downstream-infected drives and any hosts those drives were subsequently inserted into.
steps.outcome: A complete map of resident hosts, the drives they infected, and any secondary hosts those drives touched.

steps.title: Identify all currently-inserted and recently-used removable drives fleet-wide
steps.desc: Compile a current inventory of removable media in active use across the organization to prioritize scanning.
steps.guidance: Query endpoint management or device-control logs for currently connected and recently connected USB storage devices.
steps.outcome: A prioritized inventory of drives requiring immediate scanning.

steps.title: Isolate all resident (re-infecting) hosts immediately
steps.desc: Isolate every host confirmed to be actively re-infecting removable media, as these are the ongoing source of reinfection.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on all resident hosts identified; this is higher priority than isolating downstream-infected drives alone since the source keeps re-seeding new media.
steps.outcome: No further removable media can be re-infected once resident hosts are isolated.

steps.title: Block USB mass storage organization-wide until the source is contained
steps.desc: Apply a temporary organization-wide USB mass-storage restriction to break the reinfection chain while resident hosts are being remediated.
steps.guidance: Deploy an emergency device-control policy via MDM/GPO blocking USB mass storage fleet-wide, with exceptions only for critical, verified-clean workflows.
steps.outcome: The reinfection chain is broken; no new drives can pick up the worm.
steps.abort: If blocking USB fleet-wide is operationally infeasible, scope to the affected business units first and expand as needed.

steps.title: Remove the resident worm process from all source hosts
steps.desc: Fully remove the persistent re-infection mechanism (process, service, driver) from every resident host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the resident worm process/service and any persistence (scheduled task, registry run key, driver). Reimage where removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: No host in the environment retains the active re-infection mechanism, confirmed via EDR scan.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Scan and clean all downstream-infected removable media
steps.desc: Scan and clean, or reformat, every removable drive identified in the reinfection chain before returning them to service.
steps.guidance: Use updated AV/EDR removable-media scanning on each identified drive; reformat where infection cannot be fully verified removed.
steps.outcome: All removable media in the reinfection chain is verified clean or reformatted.

steps.title: Lift USB restrictions in phases and restore normal operation
steps.desc: Gradually restore USB mass-storage access as source hosts are confirmed clean, with enhanced monitoring.
steps.guidance: Re-enable device-control policy in stages, prioritizing business-critical teams, while monitoring EDR for any renewed re-infection behavior.
steps.outcome: Normal removable-media operations resume with no recurrence of re-infection.
steps.abort: If re-infection behavior reappears, reapply the fleet-wide USB block and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the reinfection chain and reinforce device-control policy
steps.desc: Record the full reinfection chain, response timeline, and recommend permanent device-control improvements.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report mapping the reinfection chain and recommending stronger baseline device-control policy and periodic removable-media scanning.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with recommendations tracked to closure.

ITID-31324.def: A self-propagating worm confirmed to be spreading via removable media but whose exact mechanism (Autorun/Autoplay execution, disguised executable requiring manual click, or host-side re-infection persistence) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.
ITID-31324.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed USB/removable-media-propagating worm whose specific propagation mechanism does not yet match, or cannot be confirmed against, one of the defined USB worm sibling categories.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered or unclassified USB worm strains observed during initial triage
USB worms using a novel or hybrid technique not yet covered by a dedicated sibling ITID
Cases pending forensic confirmation of the specific propagation mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any case where the mechanism has been confirmed and matches an existing sibling ITID (31321-31323) — reclassify once confirmed
Network-based or fileless propagation not involving removable media (other Tier-4 groups)
ITID-31324.severity: Medium-High, pending refinement once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-31324.priority: P2 during initial triage; reassess once the propagation mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-31324.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership as with any suspected removable-media worm; reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID once confirmed.
indicators: Worm-like self-copying behavior observed on removable media before the specific mechanism has been confirmed
vectors: Unconfirmed or mixed removable-media propagation mechanism pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient telemetry at time of detection to determine the specific propagation mechanism
Novel or hybrid USB worm technique not yet mapped to an existing category
controls: General removable-media device control and USB scanning capability
Endpoint detection and response coverage across all hosts
ITID-31324.detection: Variable; depends on the eventual confirmed mechanism. Treat as elevated priority pending investigation.
ITID-31324.response: Contain and isolate as a suspected removable-media worm outbreak while forensics determines the specific mechanism, then reclassify to the matching sibling ITID.
metrics: Number of incidents landing in this catch-all category per quarter
Time to reclassification into a specific sibling ITID
ITID-31324.notes: This is the intake/catch-all leaf for the USB Worms group; incidents here should be actively triaged toward reclassification rather than left permanently unclassified.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General USB Worm
playbook.description: A worm is propagating via removable USB media through an unidentified or mixed set of mechanisms.

steps.title: Confirm USB-based propagation and characterize the mechanism
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather telemetry to characterize how the worm spreads via removable media, even if the exact mechanism is not yet fully classified.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry around USB insertion events and file execution/write activity on removable drives to build a working hypothesis of the propagation mechanism.
steps.outcome: USB-based worm activity confirmed and a working hypothesis documented, along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If evidence is ambiguous, continue monitoring before declaring a worm incident.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for infected hosts and affected removable media
steps.desc: Search across all endpoints, not just the first-found host, and trace all removable media potentially carrying the infection.
steps.guidance: Query EDR fleet-wide for matching hashes/behavior; use USB connection history to identify every device that touched an infected host.
steps.outcome: A complete list of infected hosts and potentially-infected removable media.

steps.title: Determine the specific USB propagation mechanism
steps.desc: Analyze samples to determine the exact technique used (autorun, disguised executable, active re-infection, etc.) to enable targeted eradication.
steps.guidance: Perform malware analysis on captured samples/media to pin down the exact mechanism.
steps.outcome: The specific mechanism is identified, allowing reclassification and mechanism-specific remediation if warranted.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all confirmed infected hosts to prevent further spread.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected endpoints while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts are isolated and cannot infect further systems or media.

steps.title: Restrict removable media use organization-wide as a precaution
steps.desc: Apply a temporary, broader USB restriction across the fleet while the exact mechanism is confirmed, rather than acting on a single host alone.
steps.guidance: Deploy a temporary device-control policy via MDM/GPO restricting USB mass storage fleet-wide or in affected business units.
steps.outcome: Further spread via removable media is halted while investigation continues.
steps.abort: If restriction is operationally infeasible fleet-wide, scope to affected units and expand as needed.

steps.title: Remove worm artifacts from infected hosts and media
steps.desc: Clean infected hosts and scan/clean or reformat affected removable media.
steps.guidance: Use EDR/AV to remove malicious executables/artifacts from hosts; scan-and-clean or reformat affected removable media.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts and media are verified clean.
steps.abort: If a host cannot be verified clean, reimage it.

steps.title: Apply mechanism-specific root-cause fix
steps.desc: Once the specific propagation mechanism is confirmed, apply the corresponding fix (disable autorun, enforce device control, patch, etc.) to prevent reinfection.
steps.guidance: Based on the mechanism identified during identification, apply the appropriate targeted control across the fleet.
steps.outcome: The confirmed mechanism is closed off environment-wide.

steps.title: Restore hosts and lift removable-media restrictions in phases
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts and gradually lift USB restrictions with monitoring.
steps.guidance: Validate cleanliness before restoring; monitor for renewed activity over a defined period before fully lifting restrictions.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If reinfection occurs, reapply restrictions and return to containment.

steps.title: Document the incident and update detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the full timeline, confirmed mechanism, and any detection gaps that delayed classification.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and update detection signatures/playbooks to specifically cover the now-identified USB propagation mechanism.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and playbook updates tracked to completion.

ITID-31331.def: A worm that uses PowerShell scripts and/or Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute its payload and replicate itself to other hosts entirely through native OS scripting and remote-management interfaces, avoiding disk-resident binaries and thereby evading traditional signature-based antivirus.
ITID-31331.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware that lives entirely in memory or in native scripting engines, using PowerShell and/or WMI to execute and spread without ever writing a traditional malicious executable to disk.
scopeIncludes: Worm logic implemented as PowerShell script blocks executed in memory, including obfuscated/encoded command lines
Use of WMI (e.g., WMI event subscriptions, remote WMI process creation) to execute and propagate the payload to other hosts
Propagation and execution chains that never write a standalone malicious executable to disk
scopeExcludes: Fileless propagation primarily via other native OS binaries/utilities rather than PowerShell/WMI (sibling ITID-31332)
A fileless worm whose distinguishing behavior is registry/scheduled-task-only persistence rather than the propagation mechanism itself (sibling ITID-31333)
Legitimate administrative use of PowerShell/WMI with no malicious payload or self-replication
ITID-31331.severity: High. Fileless, script-based propagation frequently evades signature-based defenses and can spread quickly across hosts with remote management enabled.
ITID-31331.priority: P1 on confirmed multi-host spread via PowerShell/WMI; P2 during initial triage of a single suspicious script execution.
ITID-31331.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership immediately; disable or restrict remote WMI/PowerShell remoting between affected segments pending containment.
indicators: Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell command-line arguments (e.g., -EncodedCommand) executed across multiple hosts in sequence
WMI process-creation events (Win32_Process Create) originating remotely from an already-affected host
PowerShell script block logging capturing identical malicious logic across multiple endpoints
Absence of a corresponding on-disk malicious executable despite clear malicious execution behavior
vectors: Malicious PowerShell script execution and remote invocation to propagate to additional hosts
Remote WMI process creation used to execute and spread the payload without dropping a file
rootCauses: PowerShell script block/module logging and constrained language mode not enabled on endpoints
WMI and PowerShell remoting left broadly enabled/reachable across network segments
Reliance on signature-based antivirus with insufficient behavioral/script-based detection
controls: PowerShell script block and module logging enabled and forwarded to SIEM
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode / execution policy hardening on endpoints
Restriction of WMI and PowerShell remoting to authorized administrative hosts only
EDR behavioral detection for fileless script and WMI-based lateral movement
ITID-31331.detection: Strong where script block logging and EDR are deployed; weak-to-none in environments lacking PowerShell/WMI telemetry, since no file artifact exists for traditional AV to catch.
ITID-31331.response: Terminate malicious script/process activity, restrict PowerShell/WMI remoting between affected segments, hunt for the same script pattern across all hosts, and remediate any in-memory or registry-based persistence left behind.
metrics: Number of hosts with matching malicious script block logged
Time from script execution alert to remoting restriction
Percentage of endpoints with PowerShell script block logging enabled
ITID-31331.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation mechanism: native PowerShell/WMI scripting and remote execution, as opposed to other LOLBins or registry/scheduled-task-only persistence.

playbook.name: Fileless Worm Propagating via PowerShell/WMI
playbook.description: A worm is propagating between hosts entirely in memory using PowerShell remoting and WMI, without dropping a traditional executable to disk.

steps.title: Confirm fileless PowerShell/WMI propagation
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the worm is using PowerShell remoting and/or WMI to execute in-memory on remote hosts.
steps.guidance: Review PowerShell script-block logging (Event ID 4104), WMI activity logs, and EDR memory-scan alerts for remote command execution patterns consistent with self-propagation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed fileless propagation via PowerShell/WMI, with the first known affected host and the specific commands/scripts used identified.
steps.abort: If script-block logging is not enabled, enable it immediately and continue investigation with available EDR telemetry.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for hosts executing the same in-memory indicators
steps.desc: Search across the entire environment, not just the first-found host, for the same PowerShell/WMI execution patterns.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM fleet-wide for matching script-block content, command-line arguments, or WMI event consumers tied to the worm.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of hosts showing the malicious PowerShell/WMI activity.

steps.title: Identify hosts with excessive PowerShell remoting/WMI exposure
steps.desc: Determine which hosts have PowerShell remoting or WMI enabled broadly and are therefore at risk of further propagation.
steps.guidance: Review WinRM/PowerShell remoting configuration and WMI permissions across the fleet to find hosts with overly permissive remote-execution access.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of hosts requiring remoting/WMI access restriction.

steps.title: Isolate confirmed infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all hosts confirmed to be running the fileless worm to stop further remote execution.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut network access on infected hosts while preserving remote memory-forensics capability.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer issue remote PowerShell/WMI commands to other systems.

steps.title: Restrict PowerShell remoting and WMI network-wide
steps.desc: Apply network- and host-level restrictions on WinRM/PowerShell remoting and WMI across the environment, not just on infected hosts, to stop lateral movement.
steps.guidance: Disable or firewall-restrict WinRM (5985/5986) and WMI (135, dynamic RPC) between workstation segments; restrict to management subnets only via GPO and firewall rules.
steps.outcome: Lateral movement via PowerShell/WMI is blocked network-wide.
steps.abort: If restricting remoting breaks legitimate administrative tooling, scope an exception for verified admin jump hosts only.

steps.title: Terminate malicious processes and clear in-memory artifacts
steps.desc: Kill the malicious PowerShell/WMI processes and clear any in-memory payloads on all infected hosts.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate the malicious processes and, given the fileless nature, reboot affected hosts after termination to clear volatile memory-resident components.
steps.outcome: No malicious PowerShell/WMI processes remain running on any host.
steps.abort: If a process cannot be safely terminated, isolate and reboot the host.

steps.title: Remove WMI event subscriptions and scheduled task persistence
steps.desc: Remove any WMI permanent event subscriptions, scheduled tasks, or registry-based persistence the worm used to survive reboot and re-trigger propagation.
steps.guidance: Enumerate and remove malicious WMI event filters/consumers/bindings and scheduled tasks via EDR or PowerShell forensic scripts on every affected host.
steps.outcome: No persistence mechanism remains on any previously infected host, confirmed via EDR/WMI repository audit.
steps.abort: If WMI repository corruption is suspected, rebuild the WMI repository or reimage the host.

steps.title: Harden PowerShell/WMI configuration to close the propagation path
steps.desc: Apply constrained language mode, WinRM authentication hardening, and least-privilege WMI permissions to prevent reinfection via the same path.
steps.guidance: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode where feasible, require Kerberos/NTLM hardening for WinRM, and tighten WMI namespace permissions to required accounts only.
steps.outcome: The PowerShell/WMI propagation path is closed environment-wide.

steps.title: Restore hosts and re-enable remoting in a controlled manner
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts and cautiously re-enable required PowerShell/WMI remoting with enhanced logging.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring; re-enable remoting only where operationally required, with script-block logging enabled and monitored.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence of fileless propagation.
steps.abort: If malicious activity reappears, re-isolate and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve fileless-threat detection
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improvements to PowerShell/WMI logging and detection coverage.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending script-block logging be enabled organization-wide and behavioral detection rules tuned for fileless propagation patterns.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31332.def: A worm that achieves execution and propagation using trusted, natively signed OS utilities (e.g., certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, bitsadmin) to download, execute, or transfer its payload between hosts, deliberately avoiding both malicious standalone executables and the PowerShell/WMI mechanisms covered by a sibling ITID.
ITID-31332.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware that spreads and executes by abusing legitimate, pre-installed operating system binaries (Living-off-the-Land Binaries) other than PowerShell/WMI to blend in with normal administrative activity.
scopeIncludes: Worm using signed, built-in OS utilities to download or execute its payload on a new host
Abuse of LOLBins for payload transfer or execution as part of the self-replication chain
Techniques deliberately chosen to blend malicious activity with legitimate administrative tool usage
scopeExcludes: Propagation primarily through PowerShell or WMI (sibling ITID-31331)
A fileless worm whose distinguishing behavior is registry/scheduled-task-only persistence rather than the propagation mechanism itself (sibling ITID-31333)
Legitimate administrative use of the same utilities with no malicious payload or self-replication
ITID-31332.severity: High. LOLBin abuse is specifically chosen to evade allow-listing and signature-based controls, often delaying detection.
ITID-31332.priority: P1 on confirmed multi-host spread via LOLBin abuse; P2 during initial triage of a single suspicious LOLBin invocation.
ITID-31332.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership immediately; restrict or monitor the specific abused LOLBin's network-capable functions pending containment.
indicators: Unusual command-line arguments to trusted binaries (e.g., certutil -urlcache, mshta with a remote URL, regsvr32 with /i and a remote scriptlet)
Network connections initiated by a normally non-networked system utility
Identical LOLBin invocation pattern observed across multiple hosts in sequence
Application control / allow-listing logs showing an approved binary performing an unapproved action
vectors: Abuse of signed OS utilities to download and execute the worm payload on a new host
Use of trusted binaries to transfer the payload across hosts, bypassing file-reputation controls
rootCauses: Application allow-listing that permits LOLBins without restricting their networking or execution capabilities
Insufficient command-line auditing/logging for trusted system utilities
Reliance on file-reputation-based controls that inherently trust signed OS binaries
controls: Command-line auditing and logging for high-risk system utilities
Application control policies restricting LOLBin network/execution capabilities beyond legitimate use cases
EDR behavioral detection tuned to known LOLBin abuse patterns
Network egress filtering limiting outbound connections from non-browser system processes
ITID-31332.detection: Moderate. Command-line logging and EDR behavioral analytics can catch known LOLBin abuse patterns, but novel utility choices can evade detection until behavioral baselines are updated.
ITID-31332.response: Terminate the abused process chain, block the specific LOLBin invocation pattern at the endpoint/network layer, hunt for identical invocations across the environment, and remediate any persistence established via the abused utility.
metrics: Number of distinct LOLBins observed abused per incident
Number of hosts affected via the same LOLBin pattern
Time from anomalous LOLBin invocation alert to containment
ITID-31332.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation mechanism: abuse of non-PowerShell/WMI living-off-the-land binaries, as opposed to PowerShell/WMI scripting or registry/scheduled-task-only persistence.

playbook.name: Fileless Worm Exploiting Living-off-the-Land Binaries (LOLBins)
playbook.description: A worm propagates using trusted, pre-installed system binaries (LOLBins) to execute and spread without introducing new malicious executables.

steps.title: Confirm LOLBin abuse and identify the specific binaries used
steps.desc: Validate the alert and identify which legitimate system binaries (e.g. certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, bitsadmin) are being abused for propagation.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process-lineage and command-line telemetry for known LOLBin abuse patterns and unusual parent-child process relationships consistent with self-propagation.
steps.outcome: The specific LOLBins and command patterns used are identified, along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If the command patterns are ambiguous, correlate with threat-intel LOLBin abuse signatures before proceeding.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for the same LOLBin execution patterns
steps.desc: Search across the entire environment, not just the first-found host, for the same LOLBin command-line patterns and process lineage.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM fleet-wide for matching command lines, hashes of any staged scripts, and process-lineage patterns tied to the worm.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of affected hosts.

steps.title: Identify legitimate uses of the abused binaries to plan safe restriction
steps.desc: Determine which business processes legitimately rely on the abused LOLBins so restrictions can be applied without breaking operations.
steps.guidance: Review baseline application-control/EDR telemetry for legitimate historical use of the specific binaries before applying blocking rules.
steps.outcome: A documented list of legitimate use cases to account for when restricting the binaries.

steps.title: Isolate confirmed infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all hosts confirmed to be running the LOLBin-based worm activity.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected hosts while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer execute further propagation commands.

steps.title: Restrict the abused LOLBins network-wide via application control
steps.desc: Apply application-control or EDR blocking rules for the specific abused binaries and command-line patterns across the whole environment, not just infected hosts.
steps.guidance: Deploy AppLocker/WDAC or EDR behavioral-blocking rules to restrict the identified LOLBins from being invoked with the malicious argument patterns, informed by the legitimate-use review.
steps.outcome: The specific LOLBin abuse pattern is blocked fleet-wide.
steps.abort: If blocking breaks a legitimate business process, scope an exception for the verified legitimate use case only.

steps.title: Terminate malicious processes and remove staged scripts/payloads
steps.desc: Kill malicious LOLBin-spawned processes and remove any staged scripts or downloaded payloads referenced by the LOLBin commands.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate processes and delete any staging files, scheduled tasks, or registry entries used to trigger the LOLBin chain.
steps.outcome: No malicious LOLBin execution chain remains active on any host.
steps.abort: If cleanup cannot be verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Harden application control to prevent reoccurrence of LOLBin abuse
steps.desc: Implement durable application-control policy restricting the abused binaries' arguments/network access as the root-cause fix.
steps.guidance: Deploy a permanent WDAC/AppLocker policy or EDR behavioral rule restricting the specific LOLBin abuse pattern, validated against the legitimate-use list.
steps.outcome: The LOLBin abuse pattern is permanently blocked, verified by re-running the fleet-wide sweep with no new detections.

steps.title: Restore hosts to normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts to the network in phases, monitoring for recurrence of the LOLBin abuse pattern.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR closely for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If the pattern reappears, re-isolate and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and update LOLBin detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend expanded detection coverage for living-off-the-land techniques.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and update EDR/SIEM detection content to cover the specific LOLBin chain observed, contributing to broader LOLBin abuse detection.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and detection content updated.

ITID-31333.def: A worm that establishes and maintains its foothold purely through registry-stored payloads (e.g., encoded scripts or shellcode in registry values) and/or scheduled tasks that re-trigger execution, propagating between hosts while leaving no traditional executable file and no dependence on PowerShell/WMI-based lateral movement as the distinguishing mechanism.
ITID-31333.purpose: Captures self-propagating malware whose defining fileless trait is that all persistence lives exclusively in the registry and/or scheduled tasks, with no on-disk executable and no reliance on PowerShell/WMI or other LOLBins as the primary propagation mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Worm payload stored/encoded directly in registry keys/values and invoked via a native loader at logon or on a timer
Scheduled tasks created purely to re-trigger in-memory execution of the worm with no dropped executable
Propagation and persistence chains whose defining characteristic is the registry/scheduled-task storage mechanism itself
scopeExcludes: Propagation primarily through PowerShell or WMI as the execution/lateral-movement mechanism (sibling ITID-31331)
Propagation primarily through other LOLBins for download/execution (sibling ITID-31332)
Traditional disk-resident malware that also happens to use a registry Run key for persistence (not fileless; belongs under other malware ITIDs)
ITID-31333.severity: High. Registry/scheduled-task-only persistence is specifically designed to survive reboots and evade disk-based scanning, often persisting undetected for extended periods.
ITID-31333.priority: P1 on confirmed multi-host spread; P2 during initial triage of a single suspicious registry/scheduled-task artifact.
ITID-31333.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership immediately; prioritize registry and scheduled-task hunting across all potentially affected hosts given the difficulty of disk-based detection.
indicators: Encoded script or shellcode stored in an unusual or non-standard registry key/value
Scheduled task with an obfuscated or encoded action that invokes a native interpreter with no corresponding disk file
Persistence surviving reboot with no matching on-disk executable found during forensic file-system review
Identical registry/scheduled-task artifact found across multiple hosts
vectors: Storing the worm payload directly in registry values and invoking it via a native script host or loader
Creating scheduled tasks that re-trigger fileless execution on a recurring basis or at logon
rootCauses: Endpoint monitoring focused on disk/file scanning with insufficient registry and scheduled-task auditing
Absence of baseline/whitelisting for expected scheduled tasks and registry Run/persistence locations
Limited retention or forwarding of registry-modification and task-creation telemetry to central logging
controls: Registry-modification and scheduled-task-creation auditing forwarded to SIEM
Baseline/allow-listing of expected scheduled tasks and registry persistence locations
EDR behavioral detection for fileless persistence and in-memory execution from registry-stored payloads
Regular sweep for anomalous registry Run keys and scheduled tasks across the fleet
ITID-31333.detection: Moderate. Registry and scheduled-task telemetry, where collected, gives strong signal; environments without this specific auditing enabled have a significant detection gap since no file artifact exists.
ITID-31333.response: Remove the malicious registry values and scheduled tasks, verify no in-memory process remains from the persistence trigger, hunt for the identical artifact across all hosts, and confirm the host is clean across reboot cycles.
metrics: Number of hosts found with the matching registry/scheduled-task artifact
Time from artifact discovery to full removal and reboot verification
ITID-31333.notes: The differentiating axis for this leaf versus its siblings is propagation mechanism: persistence living exclusively in the registry and/or scheduled tasks, as opposed to PowerShell/WMI or other LOLBin-driven execution.

playbook.name: Fileless Worm Persisting via Registry/Scheduled Task Only
playbook.description: A worm persists and propagates using only registry run keys and scheduled tasks, without writing an executable file to disk.

steps.title: Confirm registry/scheduled-task-only persistence
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the worm relies solely on registry run keys and/or scheduled tasks for persistence and propagation, without a dropped file.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry and registry/scheduled-task audit logs for newly created run keys or tasks that invoke script interpreters (PowerShell, cscript, mshta) with embedded or remotely-fetched code.
steps.outcome: Confirmed fileless persistence mechanism identified, along with the first known affected host and the exact registry key/task used.
steps.abort: If no registry/task artifact is found, broaden investigation to other fileless techniques.
steps.tool: EDR / registry and scheduled task audit logs

steps.title: Sweep the organization for the same registry/task artifacts
steps.desc: Search across the entire environment, not just the first-found host, for the same registry key or scheduled task signature.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM or run a fleet-wide registry/scheduled-task audit for the specific key path, task name, or command pattern.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of hosts carrying the persistence artifact.

steps.title: Trace the propagation path used to plant the artifact on each host
steps.desc: Determine how the registry key/scheduled task was remotely planted on each affected host (e.g. via WMI, PsExec, remote registry) to fully understand the spread mechanism.
steps.guidance: Review remote-access and authentication logs correlating with the timestamp each artifact was created on each host.
steps.outcome: The remote-planting mechanism is understood, informing targeted containment.

steps.title: Isolate confirmed infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all hosts confirmed to carry the malicious registry key or scheduled task.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected hosts while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer execute the persistence mechanism to reach other systems.

steps.title: Restrict the remote-planting channel network-wide
steps.desc: Restrict the remote administration channel (e.g. remote registry, WMI, PsExec/SMB admin shares) used to plant the artifact, across the whole environment, not just infected hosts.
steps.guidance: Disable remote registry service where not required, and firewall-restrict admin-share/WMI/PsExec-style access between workstation segments.
steps.outcome: The remote-planting channel is blocked fleet-wide, preventing further spread of the persistence artifact.
steps.abort: If restricting the channel breaks legitimate remote administration, scope an exception for verified admin jump hosts only.

steps.title: Remove the malicious registry keys and scheduled tasks fleet-wide
steps.desc: Delete the identified registry run keys and scheduled tasks from every affected host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR or a scripted remediation to remove the specific registry keys/scheduled tasks across all identified hosts, then verify removal with a follow-up scan.
steps.outcome: No affected host retains the malicious registry key or scheduled task.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Reboot and clear in-memory components
steps.desc: Reboot cleaned hosts to clear any volatile in-memory payload that may still be running from the removed persistence mechanism.
steps.guidance: Coordinate a scheduled reboot of all remediated hosts and confirm the malicious process no longer starts.
steps.outcome: No malicious process is running on any remediated host post-reboot.

steps.title: Restore hosts to normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts to the network in phases, monitoring for recurrence of the registry/task artifact.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring; monitor for a defined period post-restoration for reappearance of the artifact.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If the artifact reappears, re-isolate and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve registry/task-based persistence detection
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend detection rules for registry/scheduled-task persistence techniques.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and add or tune SIEM/EDR detection content for the specific registry key path/task pattern observed.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and detection content updated.

ITID-31334.def: A self-propagating worm confirmed to be operating fileless (no on-disk malicious executable) but whose exact mechanism (PowerShell/WMI, other LOLBins, or registry/scheduled-task-only persistence) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.
ITID-31334.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed fileless self-propagating worm whose specific execution/persistence mechanism does not yet match, or cannot be confirmed against, one of the defined fileless worm sibling categories.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered or unclassified fileless worm strains observed during initial triage
Fileless worms using a novel or hybrid technique not yet covered by a dedicated sibling ITID
Cases pending forensic confirmation of the specific fileless mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any case where the mechanism has been confirmed and matches an existing sibling ITID (31331-31333) — reclassify once confirmed
Traditional disk-resident malware, even if it also uses scripting or registry persistence as a secondary technique
ITID-31334.severity: High, pending refinement once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-31334.priority: P2 during initial triage; reassess once the fileless mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-31334.escalation: Escalate to SOC leadership as with any suspected fileless worm; reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID once confirmed.
indicators: Worm-like self-replicating behavior observed with no corresponding on-disk executable, before the specific mechanism has been confirmed
vectors: Unconfirmed or mixed fileless propagation/persistence mechanism pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient telemetry at time of detection to determine the specific fileless mechanism
Novel or hybrid fileless worm technique not yet mapped to an existing category
controls: General fileless-malware behavioral detection capability (EDR)
Registry, scheduled-task, and script-execution logging coverage across all hosts
ITID-31334.detection: Variable; depends on the eventual confirmed mechanism. Treat as elevated priority pending investigation.
ITID-31334.response: Contain and isolate as a suspected fileless worm outbreak while forensics determines the specific mechanism, then reclassify to the matching sibling ITID.
metrics: Number of incidents landing in this catch-all category per quarter
Time to reclassification into a specific sibling ITID
ITID-31334.notes: This is the intake/catch-all leaf for the Fileless Worms group; incidents here should be actively triaged toward reclassification rather than left permanently unclassified.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Fileless Worm
playbook.description: A worm is propagating in-memory or without a dropped executable via an unidentified or mixed set of fileless techniques.

steps.title: Confirm fileless worm activity and characterize the technique
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather telemetry to characterize the fileless propagation technique, even if not yet fully classified.
steps.guidance: Review EDR memory-scan alerts, PowerShell/WMI logs, and registry/scheduled-task audit logs for indicators of in-memory or file-less propagation.
steps.outcome: Fileless worm activity confirmed and a working hypothesis of the technique documented, along with the first known affected host.
steps.abort: If evidence is ambiguous, continue monitoring before declaring a worm incident.

steps.title: Sweep the organization for hosts with the same indicators
steps.desc: Search across the entire environment, not just the first-found host, for the same fileless indicators.
steps.guidance: Query EDR/SIEM fleet-wide for matching process-memory signatures, command-line patterns, or persistence artifacts tied to the worm.
steps.outcome: A complete, organization-wide list of affected hosts.

steps.title: Determine the specific fileless technique in use
steps.desc: Analyze telemetry to pin down the exact technique (PowerShell/WMI, LOLBins, registry/task persistence) to enable targeted eradication.
steps.guidance: Perform deeper forensic/memory analysis to classify the specific fileless mechanism used.
steps.outcome: The specific technique is identified, allowing reclassification and technique-specific remediation if warranted.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Isolate all confirmed infected hosts to prevent further spread.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation on infected hosts while preserving remote forensic access.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer propagate to other systems.

steps.title: Restrict likely fileless propagation channels network-wide
steps.desc: Apply broad network-level restrictions on common fileless propagation channels (PowerShell remoting, WMI, admin shares) across the environment as a precaution while the exact technique is confirmed.
steps.guidance: Firewall-restrict WinRM, WMI, and admin-share traffic between workstation segments pending confirmation of the specific mechanism.
steps.outcome: Further spread is halted while investigation continues.
steps.abort: If restriction breaks critical operations, scope an exception with monitoring.

steps.title: Terminate malicious processes and remove in-memory/persistence artifacts
steps.desc: Kill malicious processes and remove any registry, scheduled-task, or WMI persistence artifacts identified on infected hosts.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate processes and remove all identified persistence mechanisms; reboot hosts to clear volatile memory components.
steps.outcome: All infected hosts are verified free of the fileless worm's active process and persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Apply technique-specific root-cause fix
steps.desc: Once the specific fileless technique is confirmed, apply the corresponding targeted fix (script-block logging/restrictions, LOLBin application control, persistence hardening) fleet-wide.
steps.guidance: Based on the technique identified during identification, apply the appropriate targeted control across the fleet.
steps.outcome: The confirmed fileless propagation technique is closed off environment-wide.

steps.title: Restore hosts to normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Reconnect remediated hosts to the network in phases, monitoring for recurrence.
steps.guidance: Validate each host is clean before restoring; monitor closely for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If recurrence is observed, re-isolate and return to containment.

steps.title: Document the incident and update fileless-threat detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the full timeline, confirmed technique, and any detection gaps that delayed classification.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and update detection signatures/playbooks to specifically cover the now-identified fileless technique.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and playbook updates tracked to completion.

ITID-31411.def: Malware that records keystrokes entered on recognized banking or financial-institution web pages, filtering out other input to focus collection on payment credentials.
ITID-31411.purpose: Classifies keylogging malware specifically configured to target financial or banking website input fields, distinguishing high-value-target keyloggers from general-purpose ones for severity purposes.
scopeIncludes: Malware with a hardcoded or updatable list of targeted banking domains
Input capture scoped to login/payment form fields on financial sites
scopeExcludes: General-purpose keylogging with no financial-site targeting (ITID-31413)
Human-targeted credential-theft classification and downstream fraud response (ITID-12121 series, Attacks Against the Human domain) — this leaf documents the malware artifact itself
ITID-31411.severity: High — direct financial account compromise risk.
ITID-31411.escalation: Escalate to SOC and, once confirmed, notify the affected individual's financial institution and initiate credential rotation.
indicators: EDR detection of a process hooking keyboard input APIs
Unexplained process persistence tied to browser activity on financial-site domains
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection or malicious download
rootCauses: Endpoint without EDR/behavioral monitoring for input-capture APIs
Lack of application allowlisting
controls: EDR behavioral detection for keyboard-hooking processes
Application allowlisting
ITID-31411.detection: EDR input-capture-API hooking detection provides real technical signal here.
ITID-31411.response: Isolate the endpoint, force credential rotation for any financial accounts accessed, and notify the affected institution.
metrics: Count of financial-targeted keylogger detections per quarter
ITID-31411.notes: Scoped to the malware artifact and its endpoint detection/response; downstream credential-theft fraud handling is owned by the Attacks Against the Human credential domain.

playbook.name: Keylogger Targeting Financial/Banking Site Input Fields Specifically
playbook.description: A keylogger is detected on a corporate device that specifically targets keystrokes entered into financial or banking website input fields, indicating credential-theft intent.

steps.title: Confirm keylogger presence and targeting scope
steps.desc: Validate the EDR/behavioral-analytics alert and confirm the keylogger is specifically hooking input on financial/banking site sessions.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process and API-hooking telemetry (e.g. keyboard hook installation, browser injection) and any exfiltrated data samples to confirm targeting of financial site input fields.
steps.outcome: Confirmed keylogger presence, its persistence method, and evidence of targeting financial/banking sessions specifically.
steps.abort: If hooking behavior is inconclusive, escalate for deeper malware analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what financial credentials or data may have been captured
steps.desc: Establish the scope of potentially captured data, including which banking/financial sites were visited during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Review browser history and any accessible exfiltration logs/C2 artifacts to identify affected financial accounts and the infection timeframe.
steps.outcome: A documented list of financial accounts/services potentially exposed and the exposure window.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network immediately to stop further keystroke capture and exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured keystrokes.

steps.title: Notify the user and financial institutions to freeze/monitor affected accounts
steps.desc: Alert the affected user and, where financial accounts are corporate-linked, notify finance/fraud teams and relevant financial institutions to monitor or freeze affected accounts pending credential rotation.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the affected user, Finance, and (if applicable) the bank's fraud department to flag the accounts for enhanced monitoring.
steps.outcome: Financial institutions and internal stakeholders are aware and have taken interim protective action on potentially exposed accounts.

steps.title: Remove the keylogger and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the keylogger process, browser injection artifacts, and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, browser extension) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the keylogger and associated components; remove malicious browser extensions; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the keylogger and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host from a known-good baseline.

steps.title: Rotate all potentially captured credentials
steps.desc: Force a password reset for all financial and other accounts that may have had credentials captured, and enable MFA where not already present.
steps.guidance: Work with the user and account owners (IT, Finance) to rotate passwords and enable/verify MFA on all potentially exposed accounts.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials are rotated and MFA is enabled where possible.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor exposed accounts
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor previously exposed financial accounts for fraudulent activity.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; coordinate with Finance/the user to monitor account statements for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation and no fraudulent activity is observed on monitored accounts.
steps.abort: If fraudulent activity is detected, escalate to Finance/fraud response immediately.

steps.title: Document the incident and evaluate financial-transaction endpoint protections
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved protections for endpoints used for financial transactions.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending measures such as dedicated hardened endpoints for financial transactions, enhanced browser isolation, or transaction-monitoring alerts.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with recommendations tracked to closure.

ITID-31412.def: Keylogging malware whose captured data is exfiltrated using a covert-channel technique (for example, encoding it within otherwise-innocuous network traffic or files) to evade content-inspection controls.
ITID-31412.purpose: Classifies keylogging malware that exfiltrates captured data through a covert or steganographic channel, a defense-evasion variant warranting different detection approaches than plaintext-exfiltration keyloggers.
scopeIncludes: Keylogger output exfiltrated via an encoded or obfuscated channel rather than a plain outbound connection
scopeExcludes: Keylogging with straightforward, unobfuscated exfiltration (ITID-31413)
ITID-31412.severity: High — the evasion mechanism indicates deliberate anti-detection design.
ITID-31412.escalation: Escalate to SOC for full forensic review given the anti-detection sophistication.
indicators: EDR detection of an input-capturing process with unusual outbound traffic patterns
Network traffic anomalies inconsistent with the apparent protocol
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Insufficient network traffic content inspection
No behavioral detection for keyboard-hooking processes
controls: EDR behavioral detection
Network traffic anomaly detection
ITID-31412.detection: Requires behavioral endpoint detection plus network anomaly detection, since content-based network inspection is specifically evaded here.
ITID-31412.response: Isolate the endpoint and conduct full forensic review of network communications for the covert channel's structure.
metrics: Count of covert-channel keylogger detections per quarter
ITID-31412.notes: Differentiated from the general keylogger catch-all specifically by its exfiltration-evasion mechanism.

playbook.name: Keylogger Configured for Exfiltration via Steganographic/Covert Channel
playbook.description: A keylogger is exfiltrating captured keystroke data through a covert or steganographic channel (e.g. embedded in images, DNS tunneling) to evade standard network monitoring.

steps.title: Confirm keylogger presence and identify the covert exfiltration channel
steps.desc: Validate the alert and identify the specific covert channel (e.g. DNS tunneling, image steganography, ICMP tunneling) used for exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry alongside network traffic analysis (DNS query volume/entropy, unusual outbound image/file transfers) to identify the covert channel mechanism and destination.
steps.outcome: Confirmed keylogger presence and the specific covert exfiltration channel and destination identified.
steps.abort: If the channel cannot be pinpointed from available telemetry, engage network forensics/threat intel for deeper traffic analysis.

steps.title: Determine the scope and duration of data exfiltrated
steps.desc: Establish how long the covert channel has been active and estimate the volume/type of keystroke data exfiltrated.
steps.guidance: Review historical network logs for the covert channel's traffic pattern to establish first-seen timing and estimate data volume.
steps.outcome: A documented exfiltration timeline and estimated scope of captured data.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to immediately stop further keystroke capture and covert exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation while preserving forensic and memory-capture access, since covert-channel malware may be more resistant to standard removal.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate data via the covert channel.

steps.title: Block the covert channel destination and technique network-wide
steps.desc: Block the identified exfiltration destination (domain/IP) and, where feasible, apply network controls against the covert-channel technique across the environment.
steps.guidance: Add the C2/exfiltration destination to DNS/firewall blocklists; if DNS tunneling is used, deploy or tune DNS-tunneling detection at the resolver/firewall.
steps.outcome: The covert exfiltration channel is blocked organization-wide, preventing any other infected host from using it.

steps.title: Remove the keylogger and its covert-channel components
steps.desc: Remove the keylogger process, its persistence mechanisms, and any covert-channel communication modules from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the malware and its components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified, given the evasive nature of covert-channel malware.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the keylogger and covert-channel components.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate potentially captured credentials
steps.desc: Force password resets on accounts whose credentials may have been captured and exfiltrated via the covert channel.
steps.guidance: Identify accounts accessed during the infection window and coordinate credential rotation and MFA enforcement with account owners.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host with enhanced network monitoring
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service with enhanced monitoring for recurrence of covert-channel traffic.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor network traffic closely for a defined period for any reappearance of the covert-channel pattern.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence of covert exfiltration.
steps.abort: If covert traffic reappears, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve covert-channel detection
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improvements to network detection for covert exfiltration channels.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending DNS-tunneling detection, egress traffic baselining, or steganography-aware content inspection improvements.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31413.def: Malware that records keystrokes on an infected device, not clearly matching a more specific Keyloggers leaf.
ITID-31413.purpose: Catch-all for keylogging malware incidents that do not fit the financial-targeting or covert-exfiltration leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific targeting or exfiltration method is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Financial-site-targeted keylogging (ITID-31411)
Covert-channel exfiltration keylogging (ITID-31412)
ITID-31413.severity: High by default given the credential-exposure risk; reassess once specifics are known.
ITID-31413.escalation: Escalate to SOC; reclassify once the specific pattern is confirmed.
indicators: EDR detection of a process hooking keyboard input APIs
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without EDR/behavioral monitoring for input-capture APIs
controls: EDR behavioral detection for keyboard-hooking processes
ITID-31413.response: Isolate the endpoint and investigate to reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31413.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Keylogger Incident
playbook.description: A keylogger of unidentified type or targeting scope is detected capturing keystrokes on a corporate device.

steps.title: Confirm keylogger presence and characterize its behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather telemetry to characterize the keylogger's persistence, hooking method, and any exfiltration behavior.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process and behavioral telemetry for keyboard-hook installation, suspicious log-file creation, or outbound data transfer consistent with keystroke logging.
steps.outcome: Confirmed keylogger presence with persistence method and behavior documented.
steps.abort: If behavior is ambiguous, escalate for deeper malware analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine scope of potentially captured data
steps.desc: Establish what applications and data the device was used for during the infection window to assess exposure.
steps.guidance: Review browser/application usage history and any accessible exfiltration artifacts to build a list of potentially exposed accounts/data.
steps.outcome: A documented list of potentially exposed accounts/data and the exposure window.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further keystroke capture and exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured keystrokes.

steps.title: Remove the keylogger and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the keylogger process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, browser extension) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the keylogger and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the keylogger and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate potentially captured credentials
steps.desc: Force password resets on accounts that may have had credentials captured during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Identify accounts accessed during the infection window and coordinate credential rotation and MFA enforcement with account owners.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of keylogging behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If keylogging behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved detection coverage for keylogging behavior.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending tuning of behavioral detection rules for keyboard-hooking and credential-capture techniques.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31421.def: Spyware that periodically captures still screenshots of a device's display and exfiltrates them, without continuous recording.
ITID-31421.purpose: Classifies spyware that captures periodic still-image screenshots of an infected device's display, as distinct from continuous video capture or targeted-window capture.
scopeIncludes: Timer-based or event-triggered screenshot capture at intervals
scopeExcludes: Continuous screen recording/video capture (ITID-31422)
Capture scoped to a specific targeted application window (ITID-31424)
ITID-31421.severity: High — screen content often includes sensitive data not captured by keylogging alone.
ITID-31421.escalation: Escalate to SOC for full forensic review of what sensitive content may have been captured.
indicators: EDR detection of a process invoking screen-capture APIs on an unexpected schedule
Unusual outbound data volume correlated with capture intervals
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without behavioral monitoring for screen-capture API usage
controls: EDR behavioral detection for screen-capture API usage
ITID-31421.detection: EDR behavioral detection of screen-capture API calls provides real technical signal here.
ITID-31421.response: Isolate the endpoint and assess what sensitive content may have been exposed based on capture timing and user activity logs.
metrics: Count of screen-capture spyware detections per quarter
ITID-31421.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by capture cadence (periodic still images vs. continuous video vs. targeted-window).

playbook.name: Periodic Screenshot Capture Spyware
playbook.description: Spyware is detected capturing periodic screenshots of a corporate device's screen and exfiltrating them to an external destination.

steps.title: Confirm periodic screenshot capture behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the malicious process is periodically capturing and exfiltrating screenshots.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry for screen-capture API calls at regular intervals and correlate with outbound network connections carrying image-sized payloads.
steps.outcome: Confirmed screenshot-capture behavior, its interval/trigger, and exfiltration destination identified.
steps.abort: If behavior is inconclusive, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what sensitive information may have been captured
steps.desc: Establish what applications/data were on-screen during the infection window to assess exposure of sensitive information.
steps.guidance: Review application usage logs and screen-lock/active-window history for the infection period to identify potentially exposed sensitive content.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of potentially exposed sensitive information.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further screenshot exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured screenshots.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for accounts potentially exposed via captured screenshots
steps.desc: Force password resets on any accounts whose credentials may have been visible on-screen during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the exposure assessment with account owners and coordinate credential rotation where warranted.
steps.outcome: Any potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of screen-capture behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If capture behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved detection coverage for screen-capture spyware.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending behavioral detection tuning for screen-capture API abuse and periodic image-sized outbound transfers.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31422.def: Spyware that continuously records a device's screen activity as video and exfiltrates the recording.
ITID-31422.purpose: Classifies spyware that continuously records screen activity as video, a higher-fidelity and higher-bandwidth variant than periodic screenshot capture.
scopeIncludes: Continuous or near-continuous video-format screen recording
scopeExcludes: Periodic still-image screenshot capture (ITID-31421)
ITID-31422.severity: High — continuous recording maximizes the scope of exposed activity.
ITID-31422.escalation: Escalate to SOC for full forensic review; the continuous nature suggests deliberate targeted surveillance.
indicators: Sustained high-volume outbound network traffic from a single endpoint
EDR detection of continuous screen-recording API usage
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without behavioral monitoring for screen-recording API usage
Insufficient outbound bandwidth anomaly detection
controls: EDR behavioral detection
Outbound bandwidth anomaly monitoring
ITID-31422.detection: Sustained outbound volume and EDR behavioral detection together provide real technical signal here.
ITID-31422.response: Isolate the endpoint immediately and conduct full forensic review given the scope of exposure.
metrics: Count of video-capture spyware detections per quarter
ITID-31422.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31421 by continuous video vs. periodic still capture.

playbook.name: Continuous Screen Recording/Video Capture Spyware
playbook.description: Spyware is detected continuously recording the corporate device's screen as video and exfiltrating the recording.

steps.title: Confirm continuous screen recording behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the malicious process is continuously recording screen video and exfiltrating it.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry for screen/video-capture API usage sustained over time and correlate with large, sustained outbound network transfers.
steps.outcome: Confirmed continuous screen-recording behavior and exfiltration destination identified.
steps.abort: If behavior is inconclusive, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what sensitive information may have been captured
steps.desc: Establish what applications/data were displayed during the infection window given the likely extensive capture of on-screen activity.
steps.guidance: Review application usage logs and active-window history for the infection period to identify potentially exposed sensitive content, meetings, or credentials.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of potentially exposed sensitive information.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host immediately
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop the ongoing video exfiltration, given the higher sensitivity of continuous capture.
