steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate the screen recording.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry, driver) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials and notify affected meeting/session participants where applicable
steps.desc: Force password resets for potentially exposed accounts, and if video calls or confidential meetings were likely captured, notify relevant stakeholders.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with account owners for credential rotation; if business-sensitive meetings were likely captured, loop in the relevant business unit and Legal as needed.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials are rotated and relevant stakeholders are notified of possible exposure.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of screen-recording behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If recording behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved detection coverage for continuous screen-recording spyware.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending behavioral detection tuning for sustained screen/video capture and large sustained outbound transfers.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31423.def: Spyware that monitors an infected device's clipboard and exfiltrates copied content.
ITID-31423.purpose: Classifies spyware that monitors and exfiltrates clipboard contents, a lightweight collection mechanism distinct from screen or keystroke capture.
scopeIncludes: Clipboard-monitoring malware capturing copied text, and where applicable, copied images
scopeExcludes: Keystroke capture (ITID-31411-31413)
Screen capture (ITID-31421, ITID-31422)
ITID-31423.severity: Medium-High — clipboard content often includes passwords or sensitive data copied for pasting.
ITID-31423.priority: P1 if financial/credential data is confirmed captured, P2 otherwise.
ITID-31423.escalation: Escalate to SOC; assess whether credentials or payment information were copied during the infection window.
indicators: EDR detection of a process polling or hooking clipboard access APIs
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without behavioral monitoring for clipboard-access APIs
controls: EDR behavioral detection for clipboard-access APIs
ITID-31423.detection: EDR behavioral detection of clipboard-access API usage provides real technical signal here.
ITID-31423.response: Isolate the endpoint and assess whether credentials or payment data were copied during the infection window, rotating any exposed credentials.
metrics: Count of clipboard-scraper detections per quarter
ITID-31423.notes: A lightweight, narrowly-scoped collection technique distinct from full screen or keystroke capture.

playbook.name: Clipboard Content Scraper
playbook.description: Spyware is detected monitoring and exfiltrating clipboard contents from a corporate device, potentially capturing copied passwords, financial data, or sensitive text.

steps.title: Confirm clipboard-monitoring behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the malicious process is monitoring clipboard content and exfiltrating it.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry for clipboard API hooking/polling and correlate with outbound network connections following clipboard-change events.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clipboard-scraping behavior and exfiltration destination identified.
steps.abort: If behavior is inconclusive, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what sensitive data may have been copied during the infection window
steps.desc: Establish what type of sensitive data (passwords, financial details, crypto wallet addresses) may have passed through the clipboard while the spyware was active.
steps.guidance: Interview the user and review application usage logs for the infection period to identify likely sensitive clipboard content.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of potentially exposed sensitive data.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further clipboard-data exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured clipboard data.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials that may have been copied to clipboard
steps.desc: Force password resets for any accounts whose credentials may have been copied during the infection window, and flag cryptocurrency wallets if applicable.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the user and account owners to rotate potentially exposed credentials and monitor any flagged financial/crypto accounts.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of clipboard-monitoring behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If clipboard-monitoring behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved detection coverage for clipboard-scraping behavior.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending behavioral detection tuning for clipboard API hooking and encouraging use of password managers with clipboard-clear features.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31424.def: Spyware that monitors for a specific targeted application window (for example, a banking or email client) and captures screen content only while that window is active.
ITID-31424.purpose: Classifies spyware that captures screen content only when a specific targeted application window is in focus, a narrower and more evasive variant than general screen capture.
scopeIncludes: Window-focus-triggered capture scoped to named target applications
scopeExcludes: Unconditional periodic or continuous screen capture (ITID-31421, ITID-31422)
ITID-31424.severity: High — targeted-window capture indicates deliberate focus on high-value applications.
ITID-31424.escalation: Escalate to SOC and identify which applications were targeted to scope the impact assessment.
indicators: EDR detection of a process monitoring window-focus events combined with screen-capture API calls
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without behavioral monitoring for window-focus-triggered capture patterns
controls: EDR behavioral detection for targeted screen-capture patterns
ITID-31424.detection: EDR behavioral detection of window-focus-triggered capture provides real technical signal here.
ITID-31424.response: Isolate the endpoint and determine which applications were targeted to scope the resulting impact assessment.
metrics: Count of targeted-window spyware detections per quarter
ITID-31424.notes: Differentiated from general screen-capture leaves by its conditional, application-targeted trigger.

playbook.name: Targeted Application Window Screen Scraper
playbook.description: Spyware is detected capturing screen content specifically when a targeted application window (e.g. a banking app, HR system, or specific corporate tool) is in focus.

steps.title: Confirm targeted-window capture behavior and identify the targeted application
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the malicious process captures screen content specifically when a particular application window is in focus.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry for window-focus monitoring APIs combined with conditional screen-capture triggers, and identify which application(s) are targeted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed targeted-capture behavior with the specific targeted application(s) identified.
steps.abort: If targeting cannot be confirmed, treat as general screen-capture spyware and broaden investigation.

steps.title: Determine why the specific application was targeted and assess data exposure
steps.desc: Assess the sensitivity of the targeted application's data and determine how much exposure occurred during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Review the targeted application's data sensitivity classification and usage logs for the infection period to assess potential data exposure.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of exposure specific to the targeted application's data.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further targeted-capture exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured screen content.

steps.title: Alert the owner of the targeted application
steps.desc: Notify the business/system owner of the targeted application so they can assess broader risk and consider interim protective measures.
steps.guidance: Loop in the application owner and relevant security stakeholders to assess whether other users of the same application may be targeted.
steps.outcome: The application owner is aware and interim protective measures (e.g. enhanced monitoring, temporary access review) are considered.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for the targeted application
steps.desc: Force a password reset and session revocation for the user's account in the targeted application, and review for unauthorized access using captured data.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the targeted application's owner/IAM team to rotate credentials and review access logs for anomalous activity.
steps.outcome: Credentials for the targeted application are rotated and no unauthorized access is found, or is remediated if found.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of targeted-capture behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If targeted-capture behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend application-specific protections
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved protections for the targeted application.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending measures such as screen-capture-resistant display modes, anti-screen-scraping controls, or enhanced monitoring for the targeted application.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with recommendations tracked to closure.

ITID-31425.def: Spyware that captures a device's screen or clipboard content, not clearly matching a more specific Screen Scrapers leaf.
ITID-31425.purpose: Catch-all for screen-capture spyware incidents that do not fit the periodic-screenshot, continuous-video, clipboard, or targeted-window leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific capture method is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching ITID-31421 through ITID-31424
ITID-31425.severity: High by default; reassess once specifics are known.
ITID-31425.escalation: Escalate to SOC; reclassify once the specific capture method is confirmed.
indicators: EDR detection of a process using screen or clipboard capture APIs
vectors: Delivered as a payload via a prior malware infection
rootCauses: Endpoint without behavioral monitoring for capture-related APIs
controls: EDR behavioral detection
ITID-31425.detection: Same general EDR telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31425.response: Isolate the endpoint and investigate to reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31425.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Screen Scraper
playbook.description: Spyware of unidentified type is detected capturing and exfiltrating screen content from a corporate device.

steps.title: Confirm screen-capture behavior and characterize its scope
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather telemetry to characterize the screen-capture behavior, even if the exact type (screenshot, video, targeted) is not yet fully classified.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process telemetry for screen-capture API usage and correlate with outbound network activity to characterize frequency and destination.
steps.outcome: Confirmed screen-capture behavior with a working characterization documented.
steps.abort: If behavior is ambiguous, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what sensitive information may have been captured
steps.desc: Establish what applications/data were on-screen during the infection window to assess exposure.
steps.guidance: Review application usage logs and active-window history for the infection period to identify potentially exposed sensitive content.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of potentially exposed sensitive information.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further screen-content exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured screen content.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for accounts potentially exposed via captured screen content
steps.desc: Force password resets on any accounts whose credentials may have been visible on-screen during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the exposure assessment with account owners and coordinate credential rotation where warranted.
steps.outcome: Any potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of screen-capture behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If capture behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline, confirmed capture type, and any detection gaps that delayed classification.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report and update detection signatures/playbooks to specifically cover the now-identified screen-capture technique.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and playbook updates tracked to completion.

ITID-31431.def: A consumer monitoring application installed on a device without the device owner's knowledge or consent by a partner, family member, or other individual with physical access, used to covertly track the owner's activity, location, or communications.
ITID-31431.purpose: Classifies consumer-grade monitoring applications installed on a personal device to covertly track a partner or family member, a distinct incident pattern from corporate espionage or credential-theft spyware given its interpersonal-relationship context and potential physical-safety implications.
scopeIncludes: Covertly installed partner/family monitoring apps discovered on a personal or corporate-issued device
Cases where the affected individual is an employee, raising both a personal-safety and a device-security concern
scopeExcludes: Employer-authorized employee monitoring software used beyond its authorized scope (ITID-31432)
Corporate/nation-state espionage spyware (documented elsewhere in this taxonomy)
ITID-31431.severity: High — beyond the technical compromise, this pattern often correlates with real personal-safety risk to the affected individual.
ITID-31431.escalation: Escalate to IT security for device remediation and, given the personal-safety dimension, offer the affected employee a referral to appropriate support resources; involve HR sensitively and only with the individual's consent.
indicators: Unfamiliar application with broad device permissions discovered during a security review
Device battery drain or performance issues reported alongside a request for a security check
Employee self-report of suspected monitoring
vectors: Installed directly by a person with physical access to the unlocked device
rootCauses: No device lock/passcode in use
Device left unattended and accessible to the installer
controls: Device lock/passcode enforcement
Mobile threat defense scanning for known stalkerware signatures
ITID-31431.detection: Mobile threat defense tools with stalkerware-signature detection provide real technical signal; otherwise relies on manual device review.
ITID-31431.response: Remove the application following the affected individual's own informed choice and pace (removal can itself be a safety risk if done without their awareness), and offer support resources; do not treat this as a routine malware-removal ticket.
metrics: Count of consumer monitoring-app discoveries per year
ITID-31431.notes: Handle with particular care for the affected individual's safety and autonomy — removal timing and disclosure should be led by the individual, not assumed to be a routine IT action, since premature or visible removal can itself create risk in an abusive-relationship context.

playbook.name: Consumer Stalkerware (Partner/Family Surveillance App)
playbook.description: Unauthorized device-based monitoring software, installed without the device owner's knowledge, is found on a personal or corporate device and may be linked to interpersonal safety risk.

steps.title: Confirm presence of unauthorized monitoring software
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm an unauthorized monitoring application is installed and actively reporting device activity/location to a third party.
steps.guidance: Review EDR/mobile-device-management telemetry for the specific monitoring app's process, permissions (location, microphone, messages), and outbound reporting connections. Treat this finding as sensitive and restrict access to a small, need-to-know response group.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence of the unauthorized monitoring application and its reporting destination, documented under restricted access.
steps.abort: If the finding is inconclusive, continue quiet investigation without alerting anyone who might be connected to the app's operator.

steps.title: Assess safety risk before taking any visible action
steps.desc: Before doing anything the operator of the monitoring app might notice, assess whether the affected individual may be at personal safety risk (e.g. a domestic-violence context) if removal or notification happens abruptly or visibly.
steps.guidance: Engage the organization's HR, Legal, or employee-assistance/safety resources as appropriate, and — critically — involve the affected individual in this assessment before proceeding; do not act unilaterally on their device. Removal timing and disclosure should be led by their stated safety needs, since premature or visible removal can itself escalate risk.
steps.outcome: A safety-informed decision is made, in coordination with the affected individual and relevant support resources, about if/when/how to proceed with containment and removal.
steps.abort: If the affected individual is not reachable safely or needs more time, pause technical action and maintain confidentiality while safety planning continues.

steps.title: Coordinate a safe containment approach with the affected individual
steps.desc: Work with the affected individual (and HR/Legal/safety resources as appropriate) to agree on the timing and method of isolating the device from the monitoring app's reporting channel.
steps.guidance: Depending on the safety assessment, this may mean quietly blocking the app's network destination first (invisible to the operator) rather than immediately uninstalling the app, to avoid tipping off the operator before the individual is safe to proceed.
steps.outcome: A containment approach is agreed upon and executed in a way that matches the affected individual's safety needs.
steps.abort: If no safe containment method is available immediately, prioritize the individual's physical safety guidance over speed of technical remediation.

steps.title: Block the monitoring app's reporting channel
steps.desc: Once safe to do so, block the network destination the monitoring app reports to, cutting off further data exposure without necessarily alerting the operator.
steps.guidance: Apply a firewall/DNS block on the identified reporting endpoint; this can often be done without the visible symptom of the app being removed.
steps.outcome: The monitoring app can no longer transmit data, reducing ongoing exposure.

steps.title: Remove the monitoring application when it is safe to do so
steps.desc: Uninstall the monitoring application and any associated persistence/profiles from the device, timed according to the individual's safety plan.
steps.guidance: Use MDM/EDR tooling or manual removal per platform-specific guidance to fully remove the application, associated configuration profiles, and any device-administrator privileges it was granted.
steps.outcome: The device is verified free of the monitoring application and its associated access.
steps.abort: If removal must be delayed for safety reasons, keep the containment block in place until removal can proceed.

steps.title: Rotate credentials and review linked accounts
steps.desc: Rotate credentials for accounts that may have been exposed via the monitoring app (email, cloud storage, location-sharing services) and review for any additional access the operator may have set up.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the affected individual to reset passwords, review and revoke any shared-account access, location-sharing permissions, or linked family/partner device management settings the operator controlled.
steps.outcome: All identified account-level access controlled by the operator is revoked and credentials rotated.

steps.title: Confirm the device is fully restored and provide ongoing support resources
steps.desc: Verify the device is clean and provide the affected individual with information on support resources (safety planning, counseling, legal) as appropriate.
steps.guidance: Confirm no residual monitoring capability remains; offer (without pressuring) contact information for domestic-violence or safety support resources and internal HR/EAP support.
steps.outcome: The device is confirmed clean and the individual has been offered appropriate support resources.

steps.title: Document the incident with strict confidentiality controls
steps.desc: Record the incident in a manner that protects the affected individual's privacy and safety, sharing only what is necessary with a limited audience.
steps.guidance: Produce a restricted-access after-action summary; avoid including identifying details in any broadly-shared incident metrics or reporting, and review handling procedures with HR/Legal for future cases.
steps.outcome: Incident is documented with appropriate confidentiality, and response procedures for future cases are reviewed.

ITID-31432.def: An organization's own sanctioned employee-monitoring software used to collect data beyond what was disclosed to and consented to by employees, or beyond its documented authorized purpose.
ITID-31432.purpose: Classifies cases where legitimately deployed, employer-authorized employee monitoring software is used beyond its documented and consented scope, a policy/governance incident distinct from unauthorized spyware installation.
scopeIncludes: Sanctioned monitoring tooling configured to capture more than its disclosed scope (e.g. personal browsing outside work hours, personal device activity)
Monitoring data accessed or used by personnel without a legitimate business need
scopeExcludes: Unauthorized/covert monitoring apps installed without any organizational sanction (ITID-31431)
ITID-31432.severity: Medium-High — a policy and legal-compliance matter as much as a security one.
ITID-31432.escalation: Escalate to legal, HR, and privacy stakeholders given the compliance and employee-relations implications.
indicators: Monitoring tool configuration found to exceed the documented policy scope
Employee complaint about unexpected monitoring
Monitoring data accessed by personnel outside the authorized review group
vectors: Configuration drift or scope creep in an already-deployed sanctioned tool
rootCauses: No periodic audit of monitoring tool configuration against policy
Unclear or unenforced access controls on monitoring data
controls: Periodic configuration audit against documented monitoring policy
Access controls and audit logging on monitoring data
ITID-31432.detection: Relies on configuration audits and policy review rather than technical malware detection, since the tool itself is sanctioned.
ITID-31432.response: Correct the configuration to match the documented policy, review who accessed out-of-scope data, and involve legal/HR on any necessary employee notification.
metrics: Count of monitoring-scope policy violations per year
ITID-31432.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a policy/governance failure involving an already-sanctioned tool, not an adversary technique.

playbook.name: Employee Monitoring Software Misused Beyond Authorized Scope
playbook.description: Legitimately deployed employee monitoring software is found to be collecting data beyond its authorized scope (e.g. off-hours activity, personal device use, or content beyond policy).

steps.title: Confirm the scope of data being collected versus the authorized policy
steps.desc: Validate the alert and compare what the monitoring software is actually collecting against the organization's documented monitoring policy and consent scope.
steps.guidance: Review the monitoring tool's configuration and collected-data logs against the approved monitoring policy (e.g. work-hours-only, corporate-device-only, specific data categories) to identify the specific overreach.
steps.outcome: The specific scope violation is documented (e.g. off-hours capture, personal device inclusion, unauthorized data categories).
steps.abort: If the policy scope is ambiguous, engage Legal/HR to clarify authorized scope before proceeding.

steps.title: Determine the number of employees affected and involve HR/Legal
steps.desc: Assess how many employees' data was collected outside authorized scope and loop in HR and Legal given the compliance and privacy implications.
steps.guidance: Query the monitoring platform for the affected population and time range; engage HR/Legal early since this may have regulatory or labor-relations implications.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of affected employees and legal/HR stakeholders engaged.

steps.title: Restrict monitoring configuration to authorized scope
steps.desc: Immediately reconfigure the monitoring software to stop collecting data outside the authorized policy scope.
steps.guidance: Adjust the monitoring platform's collection rules/schedules/device scope to match the approved policy exactly; disable any collection modules not covered by policy.
steps.outcome: The monitoring software no longer collects data beyond the authorized scope.

steps.title: Restrict access to the over-collected data pending review
steps.desc: Limit access to any data collected outside the authorized scope while HR/Legal determine appropriate handling.
steps.guidance: Apply access restrictions or a legal hold on the affected data set so it is not viewed, used, or further distributed pending review.
steps.outcome: Out-of-scope collected data is secured and access-restricted pending disposition guidance.

steps.title: Purge or properly disposition the out-of-scope data
steps.desc: Delete or otherwise properly disposition the improperly collected data per HR/Legal guidance and any applicable regulatory requirements.
steps.guidance: Follow HR/Legal's determination on retention vs. deletion of the out-of-scope data set, documenting the disposition decision and execution.
steps.outcome: Out-of-scope data is disposed of per approved guidance, with disposition documented.
steps.abort: If a legal hold requires retention, secure the data separately rather than deleting it, per counsel's direction.

steps.title: Correct the underlying configuration or deployment error
steps.desc: Identify and fix the root cause that allowed the monitoring tool to exceed its authorized scope (misconfiguration, policy gap, unauthorized deployment change).
steps.guidance: Review change-management records for how the over-broad configuration was introduced and implement a corrected, approved configuration with sign-off from policy owners.
steps.outcome: The monitoring configuration is corrected and verified to match the authorized policy, with change controls in place to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Notify affected employees per policy/legal guidance and resume compliant monitoring
steps.desc: Resume monitoring within corrected, authorized scope, and notify affected employees if required by policy, law, or Legal's guidance.
steps.guidance: Follow HR/Legal's determination on employee notification obligations; verify ongoing monitoring collection matches policy through a follow-up audit.
steps.outcome: Monitoring operates within authorized scope going forward, and any required notifications have been made.

steps.title: Document the incident and strengthen monitoring governance
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend governance improvements to prevent scope creep in employee monitoring deployments.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending periodic configuration audits of monitoring tools against policy, and stronger change-control requirements for monitoring scope changes.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with governance improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31433.def: Spyware installed on a device that covertly collects and exfiltrates geolocation data.
ITID-31433.purpose: Classifies spyware whose primary collection target is a device's geolocation data, as distinct from general behavioral-activity tracking.
scopeIncludes: Malware or covert apps reading GPS/location APIs and transmitting location history to a remote party
scopeExcludes: General browsing-habit tracking with no location-specific focus (ITID-31434)
Sanctioned employer/family location-sharing used within its disclosed and consented scope
ITID-31433.severity: High — location data exposure can carry physical-safety implications.
ITID-31433.escalation: Escalate to IT security for device remediation; assess personal-safety risk to the affected individual.
indicators: Unfamiliar application with location-permission access discovered during a device review
Mobile threat defense detection of a known location-tracking spyware signature
vectors: Installed via a malicious app, a prior malware infection, or direct physical access to the device
rootCauses: Overly permissive app location-access grants
No mobile threat defense scanning in place
controls: Mobile threat defense scanning
Periodic review of app location-permission grants
ITID-31433.detection: Mobile threat defense tools with location-tracking-signature detection provide real technical signal here.
ITID-31433.response: Remove the tracking capability, review who had access to the collected location history, and assess personal-safety risk before deciding on disclosure/removal timing.
metrics: Count of location-tracking spyware detections per year
detections: Mobile threat defense location-tracking signature scanning
ITID-31433.notes: As with ITID-31431, removal timing should account for the affected individual's own safety and awareness, not be treated as a purely technical cleanup.

playbook.name: Location Tracking Spyware
playbook.description: Unauthorized software is found tracking and exfiltrating a device's geolocation data without the device owner's knowledge or consent, which may carry personal safety implications.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized location-tracking behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm an unauthorized application or process is collecting and transmitting device location data.
steps.guidance: Review EDR/MDM telemetry for location-API access patterns and outbound transmissions to an unrecognized destination. Restrict knowledge of the finding to a small, need-to-know response group given the potential sensitivity.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized location-tracking behavior and its reporting destination, documented under restricted access.
steps.abort: If inconclusive, continue quiet investigation without alerting anyone who might be connected to the tracking's operator.

steps.title: Assess whether personal safety risk is present before acting visibly
steps.desc: Determine whether the tracking may be connected to an interpersonal safety concern (e.g. a partner or family member with intent to locate/harm the device owner), which changes how and when containment should proceed.
steps.guidance: Involve the affected individual directly in this assessment along with HR/Legal/safety resources as appropriate; do not take visible action on the device without their input, since removal timing is safety-sensitive and premature action could itself increase risk.
steps.outcome: A safety-informed plan is agreed with the affected individual for how and when to proceed.
steps.abort: If the individual needs time or cannot be reached safely, pause visible technical action and maintain confidentiality while safety planning continues.

steps.title: Quietly block the location-reporting channel
steps.desc: Once agreed with the affected individual, block the network destination the tracking software reports to, without necessarily uninstalling the software immediately if doing so would tip off the operator prematurely.
steps.guidance: Apply a firewall/DNS block on the identified reporting endpoint to stop location data reaching the operator while the safety-informed removal plan proceeds.
steps.outcome: Location data is no longer being transmitted to the unauthorized destination.

steps.title: Remove the location-tracking software when it is safe to do so
steps.desc: Uninstall the unauthorized tracking application and any associated persistence or device-administrator privileges, timed per the individual's safety plan.
steps.guidance: Use MDM/EDR tooling or platform-specific manual removal steps to fully remove the application and any elevated permissions it holds.
steps.outcome: The device is verified free of the location-tracking software and its associated access.
steps.abort: If removal must be delayed for safety reasons, keep the containment block in place until removal can proceed.

steps.title: Review and revoke linked location-sharing account settings
steps.desc: Check for account-level location-sharing features (family-locator apps, cloud account location sharing) the operator may also be using, independent of the installed software.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the affected individual to review and revoke any account-based location-sharing permissions (e.g. cloud account 'find my device' sharing) granted to the suspected operator.
steps.outcome: All identified account-level location-sharing access is revoked.

steps.title: Confirm the device is clean and offer support resources
steps.desc: Verify no residual location-tracking capability remains and offer the affected individual appropriate safety and support resources.
steps.guidance: Confirm removal is complete via a follow-up scan; offer, without pressuring, contact information for safety planning, counseling, or law-enforcement resources as appropriate.
steps.outcome: The device is confirmed clean and the individual has been offered appropriate support resources.

steps.title: Document the incident with strict confidentiality controls
steps.desc: Record the incident in a manner that protects the affected individual's privacy and safety.
steps.guidance: Produce a restricted-access after-action summary; avoid identifying details in broadly-shared reporting, and review handling procedures with HR/Legal for future similar cases.
steps.outcome: Incident is documented with appropriate confidentiality, and response procedures for future cases are reviewed.

ITID-31434.def: Spyware that covertly collects and exfiltrates a device's browsing history or usage habits.
ITID-31434.purpose: Classifies spyware focused on collecting a device user's general browsing history or habits, as distinct from location-specific or credential-specific collection.
scopeIncludes: Malware or covert apps logging visited URLs or app-usage patterns and transmitting them to a remote party
scopeExcludes: Location-specific tracking (ITID-31433)
Keystroke or clipboard content capture (documented under Keyloggers/Screen Scrapers)
ITID-31434.severity: Medium — generally lower direct financial/safety risk than credential or location capture, though still a real privacy compromise.
ITID-31434.escalation: Escalate to IT security for device remediation.
indicators: Unfamiliar application with browser-history-access permissions discovered during a device review
vectors: Installed via a malicious app or browser extension
rootCauses: Overly permissive browser extension or app permission grants
No mobile/endpoint threat defense scanning in place
controls: Browser extension permission review
Endpoint/mobile threat defense scanning
ITID-31434.detection: Endpoint/mobile threat defense scanning for known browsing-tracker signatures provides real technical signal here.
ITID-31434.response: Remove the tracking capability and review browser extension permissions more broadly.
metrics: Count of browsing-habit spyware detections per year
detections: Endpoint threat defense browsing-tracker signature scanning
ITID-31434.notes: The lowest-severity leaf in this Tier-4 group given the relatively lower sensitivity of browsing-habit data compared to location or credential data.

playbook.name: Browsing History/Habit Tracking Spyware
playbook.description: Spyware is detected monitoring and exfiltrating a device's browsing history and web activity to an external destination.

steps.title: Confirm browsing-history collection behavior
steps.desc: Validate the alert and confirm the malicious process/extension is collecting and transmitting browsing history or web-activity data.
steps.guidance: Review EDR/browser-extension telemetry for history-API access or DOM-monitoring behavior and correlate with outbound network connections carrying browsing data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed browsing-history tracking behavior and exfiltration destination identified.
steps.abort: If behavior is inconclusive, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine what sensitive browsing activity may have been exposed
steps.desc: Assess what categories of sites/services were visited during the infection window that may represent sensitive exposure (financial, health, internal corporate portals).
steps.guidance: Review browser history and proxy logs for the infection period to identify potentially sensitive categories of exposed browsing activity.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of potentially exposed browsing activity.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further browsing-data exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate browsing data.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process/browser extension and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, browser policy) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware; remove malicious browser extensions and any tampered browser policy settings; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for accounts accessed via tracked browsing sessions
steps.desc: Force password resets for accounts where session tokens or credentials may have been exposed alongside browsing activity tracking.
steps.guidance: Identify accounts accessed during the infection window and coordinate credential rotation and session revocation with account owners.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials/sessions are rotated or revoked.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of browsing-tracking behavior.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If tracking behavior recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend improved detection coverage for browsing-tracking spyware and malicious browser extensions.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report recommending browser-extension allowlisting and behavioral detection tuning for history-API abuse.
steps.outcome: After-action report published with detection improvements tracked to closure.

ITID-31435.def: Spyware that covertly tracks a device user's behavior, not clearly matching a more specific Behavioral Trackers leaf.
ITID-31435.purpose: Catch-all for behavioral-tracking spyware incidents that do not fit the personal-monitoring, employee-monitoring-misuse, location, or browsing-habit leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific tracking focus is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching ITID-31431 through ITID-31434
ITID-31435.severity: Medium-High by default; reassess once specifics are known.
ITID-31435.escalation: Escalate to IT security; reclassify once the specific tracking focus is confirmed.
indicators: Unfamiliar application with broad behavioral-data-access permissions discovered during a device review
vectors: Installed via a malicious app or direct physical device access
rootCauses: Overly permissive app permission grants
No mobile/endpoint threat defense scanning in place
controls: Mobile/endpoint threat defense scanning
ITID-31435.detection: Same general mobile/endpoint threat defense telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31435.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the tracking focus is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31435.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Behavioral Tracking Spyware
playbook.description: Spyware of unidentified type is detected collecting and exfiltrating behavioral data (usage patterns, activity, or habits) from a corporate device.

steps.title: Confirm behavioral-tracking activity and characterize its scope
steps.desc: Validate the alert and gather telemetry to characterize what behavioral data is being collected, even if the exact category is not yet fully classified.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process and API-usage telemetry for data-collection patterns (app usage, activity timestamps, input patterns) and correlate with outbound exfiltration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed behavioral-tracking activity with a working characterization documented, along with the exfiltration destination.
steps.abort: If behavior is ambiguous, escalate for deeper behavioral analysis before declaring confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Assess whether the finding may carry personal safety implications
steps.desc: Before proceeding with standard remediation, briefly assess whether the tracked individual may be at elevated personal risk (e.g. if the tracking appears tied to a personal relationship rather than a purely technical infection), since this would call for the safety-first handling used for stalkerware/location-tracking cases.
steps.guidance: If any indicators suggest an interpersonal-surveillance context, pause and follow the safety-first coordination process (involve the affected individual and HR/Legal/safety resources before any visible action) rather than standard IT remediation alone.
steps.outcome: A determination is made on which handling track (standard SOC remediation vs. safety-first coordination) applies, and the incident proceeds accordingly.

steps.title: Determine what data may have been exposed
steps.desc: Establish what type of behavioral data was likely exposed during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Review usage logs and any accessible exfiltration artifacts to build a list of potentially exposed data categories.
steps.outcome: A documented list of potentially exposed data categories and the exposure window.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device from the network to stop further behavioral-data exfiltration.
steps.guidance: Use EDR host-isolation to cut the device off from the network while preserving forensic access.
steps.outcome: The device can no longer exfiltrate captured behavioral data.

steps.title: Remove the spyware and its persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious process and any persistence (registry, scheduled task, startup entry) from the host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR to terminate and delete the spyware and associated components; reimage if clean removal cannot be verified.
steps.outcome: The host is verified free of the spyware and its persistence artifacts.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be fully verified, reimage the host.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for accounts potentially exposed
steps.desc: Force password resets on any accounts that may have had credentials or session data captured during the infection window.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the user and account owners to rotate potentially exposed credentials.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials are rotated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the cleaned device to service and monitor for any recurrence of behavioral-tracking activity.
steps.guidance: Validate the host is clean before restoring; monitor EDR for a defined period post-restoration.
steps.outcome: Device is restored to normal operation with no recurrence observed.
steps.abort: If tracking activity recurs, re-isolate the host and return to eradication.

steps.title: Document the incident and update detection/handling procedures
steps.desc: Record the full timeline, confirmed data category, and whether the safety-first track was invoked, and recommend detection or process improvements.
steps.guidance: Publish an after-action report (with confidentiality controls if the safety-first track was used) and update detection signatures/playbooks and triage criteria for distinguishing standard spyware from personal-safety-sensitive cases.
steps.outcome: After-action report published and playbook/detection updates tracked to completion.

ITID-31511.def: Adware that spawns persistent, un-closeable, or endlessly re-spawning pop-up/pop-under browser or system windows, typically to force ad impressions, drive scareware clicks, or coerce the user into installing further software.
ITID-31511.purpose: Captures adware that renders the device largely unusable by generating pop-up windows the user cannot close through normal means.
scopeIncludes: Pop-ups that reopen immediately after being closed
Full-screen or focus-stealing ad windows that block normal use of the device
Fake system-warning pop-ups used to pressure the user into clicking an ad or installing software
scopeExcludes: Adware bundled with a freeware installer where the ad delivery itself is not persistent/un-closeable (ITID-31512)
Malicious browser extensions that inject ads into page content rather than spawning pop-up windows (ITID-31531/31533)
ITID-31511.severity: Low-Medium. Primarily a nuisance/productivity impact; escalate only if the pop-ups are a vector for further compromise (e.g. fake update prompts).
ITID-31511.priority: P3, escalating to P2 if the pop-up chain leads to secondary payload download attempts.
ITID-31511.escalation: Escalate to endpoint security if pop-up adware persists after standard removal, or if it is observed dropping additional executables.
indicators: Repeated pop-up/pop-under windows the user cannot dismiss
New browser processes spawning at high frequency
User reports of device being unusable due to ad windows
vectors: Bundled software installers with adware components
Malvertising redirect chains that install a persistent pop-up agent
rootCauses: Installation of freeware/shareware without reviewing bundled components
Lack of endpoint controls blocking known adware installers
controls: Endpoint protection with PUP/adware detection enabled
Browser pop-up blocking policy
ITID-31511.detection: EDR/AV signatures for known adware families and user-reported tickets are the primary detection surface; network telemetry adds limited value.
ITID-31511.response: Run a full adware/PUP removal scan, identify and uninstall the bundled source application, and verify no secondary payload was dropped.
metrics: Count of un-closeable pop-up adware incidents per month
Mean time to remediation
ITID-31511.notes: Scoped to the un-closeable/persistent pop-up behavior itself; freeware-bundling delivery is separately tracked under ITID-31512 and in-page ad injection under ITID-31531/31533 to avoid restating the same content across leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Persistent/Un-closeable Pop-up Adware
playbook.description: For adware generating pop-up windows that resist closing, respawn automatically, or block normal browser/desktop use on an affected endpoint.

steps.title: Confirm the adware behavior and scope
steps.desc: Reproduce or review reported symptoms (recurring pop-ups, windows that reopen when closed, spawned browser processes) and confirm this is adware rather than a legitimate application malfunction.
steps.guidance: Check Task Manager/Process Explorer for repeated child processes spawning the pop-ups.
steps.outcome: Adware behavior confirmed and the responsible process/executable identified.

steps.title: Identify the installed program or extension causing the pop-ups
steps.desc: Check installed programs, browser extensions, and startup items for the adware application or a recently added unknown entry.
steps.outcome: Source application/extension identified.

steps.title: Kill the pop-up-spawning process
steps.desc: Terminate the running process(es) generating the pop-ups to stop the immediate disruption before removal.
steps.outcome: Pop-ups stop appearing.

steps.title: Disconnect from network if pop-ups are pulling remote ad content aggressively
steps.desc: If pop-up volume suggests active remote-controlled ad delivery (rather than a static local loop), temporarily isolate the host from the network.
steps.guidance: Most simple pop-up adware does not require this; use judgement based on volume/behavior.
steps.outcome: Ad delivery traffic stopped.
steps.abort: Skip if pop-ups are clearly generated locally with no active network callback.

steps.title: Uninstall the adware application and remove browser extensions
steps.desc: Fully uninstall the identified adware program via installed-programs and remove any associated browser extensions.
steps.outcome: Adware program and extensions removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan to check for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Adware is frequently bundled with additional software by freeware installers; run a full scan to confirm no heavier payload (trojan, credential stealer) was installed alongside it.
steps.guidance: Do not treat the adware removal as complete until this check is done — bundlers commonly carry secondary payloads.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and separately remediated.

steps.title: Remove persistence entries (startup items, scheduled tasks)
steps.desc: Check Run keys, startup folder, and scheduled tasks for any leftover launch entries tied to the adware.
steps.outcome: No adware-related persistence remains.

steps.title: Restore browser settings to defaults
steps.desc: Reset browser homepage, default search engine, and new-tab page; clear cached ad-injected content.
steps.outcome: Browser settings restored to user-approved configuration.

steps.title: Document the source and advise on safer installation practices
steps.desc: Record how the adware was installed (bundled installer, drive-by, deceptive ad) and note user guidance for avoiding bundled freeware installers going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31512.def: Adware components silently installed alongside a freeware application via an opt-out (pre-checked) bundling model in the installer, rather than through a separate malicious download.
ITID-31512.purpose: Captures adware whose primary delivery mechanism is bundling inside a legitimate-looking freeware/shareware installer.
scopeIncludes: Ad-serving components installed via a bundled/opt-out checkbox in a freeware installer
Toolbars or ad agents installed as a side effect of installing an unrelated free application
scopeExcludes: Persistent un-closeable pop-up behavior once installed (ITID-31511, tracked separately by symptom)
Malicious browser extensions installed via the browser's extension store rather than a desktop installer (ITID-31531-31533)
ITID-31512.severity: Low. Typically a policy/hygiene issue rather than an active compromise.
ITID-31512.escalation: Escalate only if the bundled installer is later found to include a non-adware payload (e.g. infostealer) alongside the adware.
indicators: Presence of unrecognized toolbar/ad-agent software with an install timestamp matching a recent freeware install
User reports of new unwanted software after installing a free application
vectors: Freeware/shareware download sites bundling ad-supported installers
Opt-out (pre-checked) bundling in third-party installer wrappers
rootCauses: Lack of application allowlisting/software restriction policy
Users downloading software from unofficial or ad-supported download sites
mitreTechniques: T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
controls: Application allowlisting
Blocking known bundleware installer domains
ITID-31512.detection: Limited native technical detection surface; this is closer to a PUP/policy issue than a genuine intrusion technique, detected mainly via AV/PUP signatures and software inventory review.
ITID-31512.response: Uninstall the bundled adware/toolbar, identify the source installer, and advise the user on vetted software sources.
metrics: Count of bundled-adware installs identified per quarter
ITID-31512.notes: Deliberately treated as closer to a PUP/policy issue than an ATT&CK-mapped technique per the guidance for low-severity bundled adware; no MITRE technique is invented for it.

playbook.name: Response: Pop-up Adware Bundled with Freeware Installer
playbook.description: For adware installed silently or via deceptive opt-out checkboxes alongside a legitimate free software download.

steps.title: Confirm adware presence and identify the freeware installer it arrived with
steps.desc: Correlate pop-up onset with recent software installations to identify the bundling installer.
steps.guidance: Check installed-programs timestamps against user-reported symptom onset date.
steps.outcome: Bundling installer and adware component identified.

steps.title: Enumerate all components installed by the bundler
steps.desc: Freeware bundlers frequently install multiple unwanted programs in one pass; list every program added at the same time.
steps.outcome: Full list of bundled components identified.

steps.title: Kill running adware processes
steps.desc: Terminate the adware process(es) to stop active pop-up generation.
steps.outcome: Pop-ups stop.

steps.title: Isolate the host if any bundled component shows C2-like network behavior
steps.desc: Check outbound connections from bundled components; isolate the endpoint if any component is communicating with a suspicious external host beyond normal ad-serving.
steps.outcome: Confirmed benign ad traffic only, or host isolated pending further analysis.

steps.title: Uninstall every bundled component
steps.desc: Remove the adware and all other unwanted programs identified from the same bundler, not just the most visible one.
steps.outcome: All bundled components removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for a heavier bundled payload
steps.desc: Confirm no secondary trojan, stealer, or PUP loader was included in the bundle beyond the visible adware.
steps.guidance: Bundlers are a common delivery vector for more damaging malware; treat this step as mandatory, not optional.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware identified and remediated.

steps.title: Restore browser and system settings
steps.desc: Reset any browser settings changed by the bundle and confirm normal system operation.
steps.outcome: System restored to normal state.

steps.title: Document the bundler source and consider a software-installation policy reminder
steps.desc: Record which freeware installer carried the bundle and whether organizational policy on approved software sources needs reinforcement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31513.def: Adware (typically a system-level proxy, browser helper object, or man-in-the-browser component) that inserts, overlays, or replaces advertisements within the rendered pages of otherwise-legitimate websites.
ITID-31513.purpose: Captures adware that injects ads into the content of legitimate websites the user visits, rather than displaying its own pop-up windows.
scopeIncludes: Ad injection into legitimate site content via a system-level proxy or LSP/browser helper object
Ad overlays replacing a site's own advertising with attacker-monetized ads
scopeExcludes: Ad injection performed specifically via a browser extension (ITID-31531/31533, tracked under Malicious Browser Extensions)
Un-closeable pop-up windows not tied to injecting into page content (ITID-31511)
ITID-31513.severity: Low-Medium, escalating if the injection mechanism also intercepts/modifies traffic (e.g. TLS interception) rather than purely visual ad insertion.
ITID-31513.escalation: Escalate to the network security team if the injection is achieved via a system-wide proxy or root certificate installation, since that indicates broader traffic interception capability.
indicators: Ads appearing on sites known not to serve them
Unexpected root certificates or proxy configuration changes
Browser helper objects/LSPs not matching any known legitimate software
vectors: Adware-installed system proxy or Layer Service Provider (LSP) intercepting HTTP traffic
Malicious browser helper object rewriting page DOM content
rootCauses: Installation of adware bundled with free system utilities
Lack of monitoring for unauthorized proxy/certificate changes
controls: Monitoring for unauthorized root CA installs and proxy configuration changes
Endpoint protection with adware/PUP detection
ITID-31513.detection: Proxy/certificate configuration monitoring provides a real technical signal; browser DOM injection itself is harder to detect centrally.
ITID-31513.response: Remove the injecting component, revert proxy/certificate changes, and verify no credential interception occurred alongside ad injection.
metrics: Count of ad-injection incidents per quarter
Count involving unauthorized certificate/proxy changes
ITID-31513.notes: Scoped to system-level/proxy-based ad injection into legitimate site content; browser-extension-driven ad injection is tracked separately under ITID-31531/31533 to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Response: Pop-up Adware Injecting Ads into Legitimate Websites
playbook.description: For adware that injects pop-up or overlay advertisements into the content of otherwise legitimate, trusted websites.

steps.title: Confirm ads are being locally injected, not served by the visited site
steps.desc: Compare the affected site's appearance on the endpoint against a known-clean device/browser to confirm injection is local (adware) rather than a compromise of the website itself.
steps.guidance: If ads appear identically on a clean device, escalate as a possible website compromise instead.
steps.outcome: Confirmed local ad-injection adware, not a website-side compromise.
steps.abort: If the site itself appears compromised, escalate as a web application incident rather than continuing this playbook.

steps.title: Identify the injecting component (extension, proxy config, or root certificate)
steps.desc: Inspect browser extensions, proxy settings, and installed root/CA certificates for the mechanism performing the injection.
steps.guidance: Some ad-injectors install a local proxy or root certificate to intercept and modify HTTPS traffic.
steps.outcome: Injection mechanism identified.

steps.title: Disable the injecting extension or proxy immediately
steps.desc: Disable or remove the identified extension, or revert the proxy configuration, to stop further content tampering.
steps.outcome: Injection stopped.

steps.title: Remove the adware and any rogue root certificate it installed
steps.desc: Uninstall the adware program/extension and remove any unauthorized root certificate it added to the trust store.
steps.guidance: A rogue root certificate left in place would allow future traffic interception even after the adware binary is removed.
steps.outcome: Adware and rogue certificate removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware was bundled alongside the ad-injector.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore browser configuration and verify affected sites render normally
steps.desc: Reset browser/proxy settings and re-visit the previously affected sites to confirm ads are no longer injected.
steps.outcome: Sites render without injected content.

steps.title: Document the injection technique
steps.desc: Record the specific injection mechanism used (extension/proxy/certificate) for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31514.def: An incident involving pop-up adware, not clearly matching the un-closeable, bundled-installer, or ad-injection patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31514.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Pop-up Adware.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Pop-up Adware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Pop-up Adware
ITID-31514.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Low by default.
ITID-31514.escalation: Reclassify once the specific pop-up adware pattern is clarified.
indicators: Pop-up adware alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Adware activity of unclear specific delivery vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
controls: Browser pop-up blocking and ad-injection detection
Application allowlisting
Freeware/software installation policy restricting untrusted sources
Endpoint protection scanning of bundled installers
ITID-31514.detection: Same general endpoint/AV telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31514.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Pop-up Adware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31514.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Pop-up Adware
playbook.description: General response for pop-up adware that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm the adware behavior
steps.desc: Review reported symptoms and confirm unwanted pop-up advertising behavior on the endpoint.
steps.outcome: Adware confirmed.

steps.title: Identify the responsible application or extension
steps.desc: Determine which installed program, extension, or component is generating the pop-ups.
steps.outcome: Source identified.

steps.title: Stop the adware process
steps.desc: Terminate the running adware process to halt further pop-ups.
steps.outcome: Pop-ups stop.

steps.title: Uninstall the adware and any related extensions
steps.desc: Remove the identified application and extensions completely.
steps.outcome: Adware removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no heavier malware was bundled with the adware.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore browser settings
steps.desc: Reset browser homepage, search engine, and cached settings to the approved configuration.
steps.outcome: Browser restored.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the adware type and installation vector where known.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31521.def: Adware/browser-hijacker malware that silently changes the browser's homepage, new-tab page, or default search provider to an attacker-monetized search or landing page.
ITID-31521.purpose: Captures malware that hijacks a browser's homepage or default search engine to redirect the user's search traffic for ad revenue.
scopeIncludes: Silent modification of browser homepage/new-tab/search-provider settings
Redirect chains inserted between the user's search bar and the intended search engine
scopeExcludes: Redirect achieved via DNS or system proxy modification rather than browser settings (ITID-31523)
Click injection on ads the user did not interact with (ITID-31522)
ITID-31521.escalation: Escalate if the hijacker also modifies browser security settings (e.g. disables safe browsing) as part of the takeover.
indicators: Browser homepage/search engine changed without user action
New browser extensions or policies enforcing a specific search provider
User reports of searches redirecting to an unfamiliar site
vectors: Bundled installer silently changing browser settings
Malicious browser extension or policy pushing a hijacked homepage
rootCauses: Lack of browser settings lockdown/GPO enforcement
Installation of untrusted freeware
controls: Browser settings management via GPO/MDM
Endpoint PUP detection
ITID-31521.detection: Browser configuration monitoring and PUP signatures give reasonable coverage.
ITID-31521.response: Reset browser homepage/search settings, remove the hijacking component, and verify no further persistence mechanism remains.
metrics: Count of browser hijack incidents per month
ITID-31521.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by mechanism: this leaf is scoped strictly to browser-setting-level hijacking, not DNS/proxy-level (ITID-31523) or click-fraud (ITID-31522) redirection.

playbook.name: Response: Browser Homepage/Search Engine Hijacker
playbook.description: For malware that changes the browser homepage, default search engine, or new-tab page without user consent and resists manual reversion.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized homepage/search engine changes
steps.desc: Check current browser homepage, default search provider, and new-tab settings against the user/organization's approved configuration.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized change confirmed.

steps.title: Identify the hijacking component and confirm it resists manual reset
steps.desc: Attempt to manually revert the settings; identify the extension, policy entry, or shortcut modification that reverts them back (a hallmark of hijacker persistence).
steps.guidance: Check browser shortcut target paths for appended URL arguments, a common hijacker technique.
steps.outcome: Hijacking mechanism identified.

steps.title: Disable the hijacking extension or policy
steps.desc: Disable the identified extension or remove the browser policy/registry entry enforcing the hijacked settings.
steps.outcome: Settings no longer revert automatically.

steps.title: Remove the hijacker program/extension and fix modified shortcuts
steps.desc: Uninstall the hijacking software and correct any browser shortcut targets that were appended with hijack URLs.
steps.outcome: Hijacker removed and shortcuts restored.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware accompanied the hijacker.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore homepage/search settings and verify persistence
steps.desc: Reset homepage/search settings to approved values and confirm they remain after a browser restart and reboot.
steps.outcome: Settings remain correct after restart.

steps.title: Document the hijack mechanism
steps.desc: Record the technique used (extension, shortcut modification, policy entry) to improve future detection.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31522.def: Malware that silently loads advertisements and simulates clicks on them in a hidden browser instance or background process, generating ad revenue for the attacker without the user's knowledge or interaction.
ITID-31522.purpose: Captures malware that generates fraudulent ad clicks in the background without user interaction, for ad-fraud monetization.
scopeIncludes: Hidden/headless browser instances generating simulated ad clicks
Background processes making silent ad-network requests to inflate click revenue
scopeExcludes: Botnet proxy nodes used specifically to relay ad-fraud traffic at scale on behalf of an operator (ITID-31733, tracked under Proxy Botnets)
Visible pop-up/redirect adware requiring user interaction (ITID-31511/31521)
ITID-31522.severity: Low-Medium, with resource/performance impact on affected devices.
ITID-31522.escalation: Escalate if the click-injection process is also observed exfiltrating data or communicating with a broader C2 infrastructure.
indicators: Hidden browser/WebView processes with no visible window
Unusual outbound traffic to ad-network domains with no corresponding user activity
Sustained CPU/network usage from an unrecognized background process
vectors: Trojanized applications bundling a click-fraud module
Malicious SDKs embedded in freeware
rootCauses: Installation of untrusted freeware/mobile apps
Lack of process behavior monitoring on endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: Endpoint behavioral detection for hidden browser/automation processes
Egress filtering to known ad-fraud infrastructure
ITID-31522.detection: Network telemetry showing high-frequency ad-network requests with no user interaction is a strong technical signal.
ITID-31522.response: Terminate and remove the click-injection process, identify the delivery vector, and block associated ad-fraud infrastructure.
metrics: Count of ad-fraud click-injection incidents per month
Volume of blocked ad-fraud traffic
ITID-31522.notes: Scoped to click-fraud generated by malware on a single infected endpoint; large-scale operator-run ad-fraud traffic relay through recruited bot infrastructure is tracked separately under ITID-31733.

playbook.name: Response: Ad-Fraud Click Injection Malware (Silent Background Clicks)
playbook.description: For malware that generates hidden/background ad clicks or impressions on the endpoint for click-fraud purposes.

steps.title: Confirm silent click-fraud activity
steps.desc: Review network traffic and process activity for evidence of automated, hidden ad-click or impression traffic not initiated by the user.
steps.guidance: Look for unusual background browser instances, headless browser processes, or high-frequency ad-network requests with no corresponding user interaction.
steps.outcome: Click-fraud activity confirmed with the responsible process identified.

steps.title: Identify the installed component driving the fraud
steps.desc: Determine which application, extension, or scheduled task is generating the click traffic.
steps.outcome: Responsible component identified.

steps.title: Terminate the click-generating process
steps.desc: Kill the running process to stop further fraudulent click traffic immediately.
steps.outcome: Click traffic stops.

steps.title: Block the ad-network destinations at the firewall if volume is high
steps.desc: If click traffic volume is significant, block the destination ad-network endpoints at the perimeter pending full removal.
steps.outcome: Outbound fraud traffic blocked.

steps.title: Remove the click-fraud application and its persistence
steps.desc: Uninstall the responsible program and remove any scheduled task, service, or startup entry that relaunches it.
steps.outcome: Component and persistence removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware was bundled with the click-fraud component.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Monitor outbound traffic for recurrence
steps.desc: Monitor the endpoint's outbound network traffic for a defined period to confirm the click-fraud activity has fully stopped.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the fraud mechanism and delivery vector for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31523.def: Malware that changes a device's or router's DNS server configuration, or installs a system-level proxy, to redirect web and ad traffic through attacker-controlled infrastructure.
ITID-31523.purpose: Captures malware that redirects browsing/ad traffic by modifying DNS settings or installing a system-wide proxy, rather than editing browser settings directly.
scopeIncludes: DNS resolver settings changed on the host or the local router/gateway
System-wide proxy configuration installed to intercept and redirect web traffic
scopeExcludes: Browser-setting-level homepage/search hijacking (ITID-31521)
Legitimate ad-network click fraud without traffic redirection (ITID-31522)
ITID-31523.severity: Medium, since DNS/proxy-level control can affect all traffic from the device, not just ads.
ITID-31523.priority: P2, given the broader traffic-interception capability.
ITID-31523.escalation: Escalate to network security immediately if router-level DNS settings were changed, as this can affect every device on the network.
indicators: DNS server settings pointing to an unrecognized/attacker-controlled resolver
System proxy configuration set without user action
Router admin login from an unexpected source
vectors: Malware modifying host DNS/proxy settings directly
Router credential compromise used to change DNS settings network-wide
rootCauses: Default/weak router admin credentials
Lack of monitoring for DNS/proxy configuration changes
controls: Monitoring for unauthorized DNS/proxy configuration changes
Router credential hardening
ITID-31523.detection: DNS resolver and proxy configuration monitoring provide a strong technical signal for this leaf.
ITID-31523.response: Revert DNS/proxy settings, rotate router credentials if applicable, and scan for the malware component that made the change.
metrics: Count of DNS/proxy hijack incidents per month
ITID-31523.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by mechanism: DNS/proxy-level redirection, which has a broader blast radius than browser-setting hijacking (ITID-31521).

playbook.name: Response: DNS/Proxy Hijack Ad-Redirect Malware
playbook.description: For malware that modifies DNS settings or installs a rogue proxy configuration to redirect browsing traffic through ad-injection infrastructure.

steps.title: Confirm DNS/proxy settings have been tampered with
steps.desc: Compare the endpoint's configured DNS servers and proxy settings against approved organizational values.
steps.guidance: Check both OS-level network settings and browser-level proxy configuration, and the router/gateway DNS if applicable.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized DNS/proxy configuration confirmed.

steps.title: Identify the malware component setting the configuration
steps.desc: Determine which process or persistence mechanism is enforcing the rogue DNS/proxy settings.
steps.outcome: Responsible component identified.

steps.title: Revert DNS/proxy settings to known-good values
steps.desc: Immediately restore approved DNS servers and disable the rogue proxy configuration.
steps.outcome: Traffic no longer redirected through rogue infrastructure.

steps.title: Check for router/gateway-level DNS tampering
steps.desc: If the endpoint is on a home/small-office network, verify the router's DNS settings have not also been hijacked (a common companion technique).
steps.outcome: Router DNS confirmed clean or corrected.

steps.title: Remove the malware and its persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Uninstall/delete the responsible component and any startup/registry entry re-applying the rogue configuration.
steps.outcome: Malware and persistence removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
