steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware accompanied the DNS/proxy hijacker.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Verify DNS/proxy settings remain correct after reboot
steps.desc: Reboot the endpoint and confirm the DNS/proxy configuration was not re-applied.
steps.outcome: Settings persist correctly.

steps.title: Document the hijack technique
steps.desc: Record the DNS/proxy tampering method for future detection and consider DNS-change alerting.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31524.def: An incident involving ad-redirecting malware, not clearly matching the browser-hijack, click-injection, or DNS/proxy-hijack patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31524.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Ad-Redirecting Malware.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Ad-Redirecting Malware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Ad-Redirecting Malware
ITID-31524.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Low-Medium by default.
ITID-31524.escalation: Reclassify once the specific redirect mechanism is clarified.
indicators: Ad-redirect alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific redirect vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Browser extension allowlisting/management
DNS filtering against known ad-fraud/malvertising domains
EDR detection of browser process injection
Endpoint protection scanning
ITID-31524.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31524.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Ad-Redirecting Malware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31524.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Ad-Redirecting Malware
playbook.description: General response for ad-redirecting malware that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm the redirect behavior
steps.desc: Confirm unauthorized browser redirection to ad or affiliate destinations.
steps.outcome: Redirect behavior confirmed.

steps.title: Identify the responsible component
steps.desc: Determine which application, extension, or configuration change is causing the redirects.
steps.outcome: Source identified.

steps.title: Disable the redirecting component
steps.desc: Disable the identified extension/process to stop the redirects.
steps.outcome: Redirects stop.

steps.title: Remove the malware and any modified settings
steps.desc: Uninstall the responsible program/extension and revert any modified browser or network settings.
steps.outcome: Malware removed and settings restored.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware was bundled with the redirector.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Verify normal browsing behavior is restored
steps.desc: Confirm redirects no longer occur across a range of test sites.
steps.outcome: No redirects observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the redirect mechanism and delivery vector where known.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31531.def: A browser extension that was legitimate at install time but was later updated (via the extension store's auto-update mechanism) to include ad-injection or other adware behavior, usually after its developer account was compromised or the extension was sold to a new owner.
ITID-31531.purpose: Captures previously-legitimate browser extensions that become malicious after an update, typically following developer account compromise or extension resale.
scopeIncludes: Extension update introducing ad-injection code not present at original install
Extension ownership transfer followed by monetization behavior changes
scopeExcludes: Extensions malicious from initial install/publication (ITID-31533)
Ad injection performed by non-extension components (system proxy/LSP, ITID-31513)
ITID-31531.severity: Medium, since the trust relationship established at install time was abused.
ITID-31531.escalation: Escalate to the browser/extension platform vendor and to affected users' security teams once confirmed, given the supply-chain nature of the compromise.
indicators: Extension behavior change correlating with a recent auto-update
New, unexplained permissions requested after an update
Ads appearing on sites only after an extension update
vectors: Compromise of the extension developer's store account
Sale of an extension's ownership to a party that monetizes it via ad injection
rootCauses: Extension auto-update trust model with no re-review of updated code
Lack of extension permission change monitoring
mitreTechniques: T1195.002 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
controls: Browser extension allowlisting
Monitoring for extension permission changes post-update
ITID-31531.detection: Extension inventory and permission-change monitoring provide reasonable coverage; behavioral detection of the ad injection itself adds further signal.
ITID-31531.response: Remove the compromised extension fleet-wide, notify affected users, and report the compromise to the extension platform.
metrics: Count of extension-supply-chain adware incidents per year
ITID-31531.notes: Scoped to the supply-chain angle (legitimate extension turned malicious post-update); extensions malicious from first publication are tracked under ITID-31533.

playbook.name: Response: Ad-Injecting Browser Extension (Legitimate Extension Turned Malicious via Update)
playbook.description: For a previously trusted browser extension that began injecting ads or affiliate content after a compromised or ownership-transferred update.

steps.title: Confirm the extension's behavior changed after an update
steps.desc: Correlate the onset of ad-injection with the extension's update history and version change log if available.
steps.guidance: Check extension version history/changelog and community reports for the same extension turning malicious.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the malicious behavior began with a specific update.

steps.title: Determine scope across the organization
steps.desc: Check whether the same extension is installed on other endpoints, since a compromised update affects every installation, not just this one.
steps.outcome: Full list of affected endpoints identified.

steps.title: Disable/remove the extension on the affected endpoint and organization-wide
steps.desc: Disable the extension immediately and push removal across all identified affected endpoints.
steps.outcome: Extension disabled/removed everywhere it was found.

steps.title: Block the extension via policy to prevent reinstallation
steps.desc: Add the extension ID to a blocklist via browser management policy so it cannot be reinstalled while the issue is unresolved.
steps.outcome: Extension blocked from reinstallation.

steps.title: Verify complete extension removal and clear injected content
steps.desc: Confirm the extension's files/settings are fully removed and clear any cached ad-injected page content.
steps.outcome: Extension fully removed, no residual injection.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm the compromised extension did not also drop additional malware.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore browser settings and confirm normal operation
steps.desc: Reset any browser settings modified by the extension and confirm affected sites render normally.
steps.outcome: Browser restored to normal.

steps.title: Document the supply-chain compromise and review extension vetting policy
steps.desc: Record the extension name, publisher, and update that introduced the malicious behavior; consider whether organizational extension allowlisting needs tightening.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31532.def: A browser extension that silently rewrites e-commerce/affiliate links the user clicks (or inserts its own undisclosed affiliate tag) to redirect commission revenue to the extension operator, without the user's knowledge.
ITID-31532.purpose: Captures browser extensions that monetize by silently hijacking affiliate links rather than injecting visible ads.
scopeIncludes: Silent rewriting of outbound e-commerce links to insert an undisclosed affiliate tag
Cookie-stuffing behavior tied to a browser extension
scopeExcludes: Visible ad injection into page content (ITID-31533)
Extensions that became malicious via a later update rather than being built for affiliate hijacking (ITID-31531)
ITID-31532.severity: Low-Medium, primarily a financial/fraud impact rather than device compromise.
ITID-31532.escalation: Escalate to legal/fraud teams if the extension is discovered operating at scale across the organization's users.
indicators: Outbound e-commerce URLs modified in transit to include an unfamiliar affiliate parameter
Extension network requests to affiliate-tracking domains not disclosed in its store listing
vectors: Extensions published specifically to perform affiliate-link hijacking
Undisclosed SDK embedded in an otherwise-functional extension
rootCauses: Lack of extension network-traffic review prior to allowlisting
Extension store review process not catching undisclosed monetization behavior
controls: Browser extension allowlisting
Network monitoring for undisclosed affiliate-tracking traffic
ITID-31532.detection: Requires network-level inspection of extension traffic; not visible from endpoint AV alone.
ITID-31532.response: Remove the extension, review for financial/fraud impact, and report to the extension platform if policy violation is confirmed.
metrics: Count of affiliate-hijacking extension incidents per year
ITID-31532.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by monetization mechanism: silent affiliate-link rewriting rather than visible ad injection (ITID-31533) or supply-chain takeover (ITID-31531).

playbook.name: Response: Browser Extension Monetized via Undisclosed Affiliate Link Hijacking
playbook.description: For a browser extension that silently rewrites outbound e-commerce/affiliate links to redirect commission credit to the extension operator.

steps.title: Confirm undisclosed affiliate-link rewriting
steps.desc: Inspect outbound link/URL rewriting behavior on shopping or affiliate sites to confirm the extension is substituting its own affiliate identifiers.
steps.guidance: Compare a link's outbound URL before and after the extension processes the page.
steps.outcome: Confirmed affiliate-hijacking behavior and the responsible extension identified.

steps.title: Assess whether the extension also exfiltrates browsing data
steps.desc: Review the extension's network activity to check whether it is also collecting/transmitting browsing history beyond the link substitution.
steps.outcome: Data exposure scope determined.

steps.title: Disable the extension
steps.desc: Disable the extension immediately to stop further link tampering and any data collection.
steps.outcome: Extension disabled.

steps.title: Remove the extension and any related components
steps.desc: Fully uninstall the extension and remove any associated local storage or configuration it created.
steps.outcome: Extension fully removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware was bundled with the extension.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Verify outbound links resolve correctly
steps.desc: Confirm affiliate/outbound links now resolve to their intended, unmodified destinations.
steps.outcome: Links resolve correctly.

steps.title: Document the monetization scheme
steps.desc: Record the extension and its affiliate-hijacking method for detection tuning and awareness.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31533.def: A browser extension that is malicious/adware from its initial publication, embedding a third-party ad-injection SDK that overlays or inserts advertisements into the pages the user visits.
ITID-31533.purpose: Captures browser extensions built from the outset to inject ads into visited pages via a bundled ad-injection SDK.
scopeIncludes: Extensions published with an ad-injection SDK bundled from release
In-page ad overlays/injections attributable to a specific installed extension
scopeExcludes: Legitimate extensions later turned malicious via an update (ITID-31531)
Affiliate-link hijacking without visible ad injection (ITID-31532)
System-level (non-extension) ad injection via proxy/LSP (ITID-31513)
ITID-31533.escalation: Escalate if the ad-injection SDK is also found exfiltrating browsing history or PII alongside ad injection.
indicators: Ads appearing on sites known not to serve them, traceable to a specific extension
Extension code containing a known ad-injection SDK signature
vectors: Extension marketplaces hosting apps built around ad-injection SDKs
Free "utility" extensions monetized through bundled ad SDKs
rootCauses: Lack of extension allowlisting
Extension store vetting not catching bundled ad-injection SDKs at publication
controls: Browser extension allowlisting
Extension SDK/code review prior to approval
ITID-31533.detection: Extension inventory review against known ad-injection SDK signatures provides good coverage.
ITID-31533.response: Remove the extension across affected devices and add its identifier to the extension blocklist.
metrics: Count of ad-injection-SDK extension incidents per year
ITID-31533.notes: Scoped to extensions malicious from initial publication; post-update compromise is tracked under ITID-31531 to avoid overlap.

playbook.name: Response: Browser Extension Bundled with Ad-Injection SDK
playbook.description: For a browser extension distributing a third-party ad-injection SDK that injects advertising into visited pages independently of the extension's stated purpose.

steps.title: Confirm the extension contains a third-party ad-injection SDK
steps.desc: Inspect the extension's network activity and, where feasible, its code/manifest for a known ad-injection SDK bundled alongside its core functionality.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the extension ID/publisher against known ad-SDK abuse reports.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the extension bundles an ad-injection SDK and the injected content is identified.

steps.title: Determine scope across the organization
steps.desc: Check whether the same extension is installed on other endpoints via endpoint management.
steps.outcome: Full list of affected endpoints identified.

steps.title: Disable/remove the extension organization-wide
steps.desc: Disable the extension on the affected endpoint and push removal to all other endpoints where it is installed.
steps.outcome: Extension disabled/removed everywhere found.

steps.title: Block the extension via policy to prevent reinstallation
steps.desc: Add the extension ID to a browser management blocklist policy.
steps.outcome: Extension blocked from reinstallation.

steps.title: Verify complete removal and clear injected content
steps.desc: Confirm the extension and its SDK components are fully removed and clear cached injected ad content.
steps.outcome: Extension and SDK fully removed.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm the SDK did not also drop heavier malware.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Verify normal browsing on affected sites
steps.desc: Confirm previously affected sites render without injected ad content.
steps.outcome: Sites render normally.

steps.title: Document the SDK and review extension vetting policy
steps.desc: Record the SDK identified and consider whether extension allowlisting/review process needs tightening to catch bundled SDKs earlier.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31534.def: An incident involving a malicious/adware browser extension, not clearly matching the supply-chain-compromise, affiliate-hijacking, or bundled-SDK patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31534.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Malicious Browser Extensions.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Malicious Browser Extensions leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Malicious Browser Extensions
ITID-31534.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Low-Medium by default.
ITID-31534.escalation: Reclassify once the specific extension behavior is clarified.
indicators: Malicious extension alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific extension monetization vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Browser extension allowlisting via group policy
Enterprise browser management restricting extension install sources
Web proxy/EDR monitoring for extension-based data exfiltration
User awareness training on extension permissions
ITID-31534.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31534.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Malicious Browser Extensions leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31534.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Malicious Browser Extension (Adware)
playbook.description: General response for an adware-monetized browser extension that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm the extension's malicious/unwanted behavior
steps.desc: Confirm the extension is responsible for unwanted ad content, redirects, or settings changes.
steps.outcome: Behavior confirmed and extension identified.

steps.title: Determine scope across the organization
steps.desc: Check whether the extension is installed on other endpoints.
steps.outcome: Affected endpoints identified.

steps.title: Disable the extension organization-wide
steps.desc: Disable/remove the extension on all affected endpoints.
steps.outcome: Extension disabled everywhere found.

steps.title: Remove the extension and block reinstallation
steps.desc: Fully uninstall the extension and block its ID via management policy.
steps.outcome: Extension removed and blocked.

steps.title: Run a full AV/anti-malware scan for bundled secondary payloads
steps.desc: Confirm no additional malware was bundled with the extension.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, or additional malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore browser settings
steps.desc: Reset any browser settings modified by the extension.
steps.outcome: Browser restored.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the extension identity and behavior for future detection.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31611.def: A fileless attack stage in which PowerShell is used as a downloader/loader to retrieve a subsequent payload (script or in-memory executable) from a remote location and execute it, with no malicious binary persisted to disk.
ITID-31611.purpose: Captures the first-stage use of PowerShell to fetch and load further malicious content without writing an executable to disk.
scopeIncludes: PowerShell one-liners invoking Net.WebClient/Invoke-WebRequest to fetch and execute remote content
Encoded (-EncodedCommand) PowerShell used to stage a downloader
scopeExcludes: The persistent C2 beacon/implant this stage may lead to (ITID-31612)
PowerShell used purely to deploy ransomware payloads (ITID-31613)
ITID-31611.severity: Medium-High, since this stage typically precedes a more damaging payload.
ITID-31611.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if outbound connection to the download source is confirmed successful.
ITID-31611.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response; treat as an active intrusion in progress, not just a detection.
indicators: PowerShell process with -EncodedCommand or -WindowStyle Hidden arguments
PowerShell making outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests immediately after spawning from an Office or script-host parent process
PowerShell script block logging showing download-and-execute cmdlet patterns
vectors: Malicious document macro spawning PowerShell
Phishing link triggering an LNK/HTA file that launches PowerShell
rootCauses: PowerShell execution policy not restricted
Lack of script block logging/AMSI integration
Office macro execution not disabled by policy
mitreTechniques: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
controls: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode
AMSI integration with EDR
Script block logging enabled
ITID-31611.detection: Script block logging and AMSI-integrated EDR provide strong detection coverage for this stage.
ITID-31611.response: Isolate the host, capture PowerShell logs/memory, block the download source, and hunt for the retrieved second-stage payload.
metrics: Count of PowerShell downloader detections per month
Mean time to isolation after detection
detections: PowerShell script block logging alert on download-and-execute pattern
ITID-31611.notes: Scoped to the initial downloader/loader stage; the resident beacon it may install is tracked separately under ITID-31612 to avoid duplicating the full kill chain in one leaf.

playbook.name: Response: PowerShell-Based Downloader/Loader (Stage 1 Dropper)
playbook.description: For a fileless PowerShell script used as a first-stage downloader/loader to retrieve and execute a further payload in memory.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious PowerShell activity via script-block logging
steps.desc: Review PowerShell script-block/module logging and AMSI telemetry to confirm the downloader command sequence and its download target.
steps.guidance: Standard console history alone is often insufficient — enable/review script-block logging specifically.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious PowerShell downloader activity with the download source identified.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the PowerShell command was triggered (phishing macro, scheduled task, exploit, LOLBin chain).
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent the downloader from retrieving its next-stage payload.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Block the download source
steps.desc: Block the identified download domain/IP at the network perimeter.
steps.outcome: Download source blocked.

steps.title: Terminate the malicious process and locate its launch mechanism
steps.desc: Kill the running PowerShell process and identify/remove whatever triggered it (scheduled task, registry run key, macro-laden document, WMI event subscription).
steps.guidance: A fileless dropper leaves no binary but virtually always leaves a launch mechanism somewhere.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify whether the next-stage payload was already retrieved and executed
steps.desc: Check for evidence the downloader succeeded in fetching and running a second-stage payload before containment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no second stage executed, or second-stage payload identified and separately remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review PowerShell execution policy
steps.desc: Record the delivery technique and assess whether Constrained Language Mode or stricter execution policy would reduce future risk.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31612.def: A PowerShell-based command-and-control beacon or implant that runs persistently (in memory or via a scheduled task/registry trigger re-invoking PowerShell) to maintain an ongoing channel for attacker commands.
ITID-31612.purpose: Captures a resident PowerShell-based implant that maintains ongoing command-and-control communication.
scopeIncludes: Recurring PowerShell beacon activity to a C2 endpoint on a fixed or jittered interval
PowerShell-based implant frameworks (e.g. Empire-style agents) running as an in-memory C2 channel
scopeExcludes: One-off download/execute PowerShell used purely as an initial loader (ITID-31611)
PowerShell used specifically to deploy ransomware (ITID-31613)
ITID-31612.severity: High, since this represents established, ongoing attacker access.
ITID-31612.escalation: Escalate immediately as an active compromise; engage incident response for full scope assessment.
indicators: Periodic PowerShell outbound beacon traffic with consistent interval/jitter
PowerShell process with no corresponding user-initiated script execution
Registry/scheduled-task entries re-invoking PowerShell at intervals
vectors: Initial PowerShell downloader (ITID-31611) installing a resident implant
Living-off-the-land persistence via scheduled task or WMI event subscription re-launching PowerShell
rootCauses: Lack of egress filtering/beaconing detection
PowerShell logging not centrally collected and alerted on
mitreTechniques: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: Network beaconing detection
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode
EDR with AMSI integration
ITID-31612.detection: Network beaconing analytics combined with PowerShell script block logging give strong coverage.
ITID-31612.response: Isolate the host, identify and remove the persistence mechanism, block C2 infrastructure, and assess for lateral movement.
metrics: Count of PowerShell C2 implants detected per quarter
Mean dwell time before detection
ITID-31612.notes: Differentiated from the downloader stage (ITID-31611) by persistence and recurring C2 behavior rather than a single fetch-and-execute action.

playbook.name: Response: PowerShell-Based C2 Beacon/Implant
playbook.description: For a confirmed fileless PowerShell-based command-and-control implant running on an endpoint.

steps.title: Confirm the PowerShell C2 activity via script-block logging
steps.desc: Review PowerShell script-block/module logging and AMSI telemetry to confirm the malicious command sequence and beaconing pattern.
steps.guidance: Standard console history alone is often insufficient — enable/review script-block logging specifically.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious PowerShell activity with the beaconing destination identified.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the PowerShell command was triggered (macro, scheduled task, exploit, LOLBin chain).
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further C2 communication.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination
steps.desc: Block the beaconing domain/IP at the network perimeter.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked.

steps.title: Terminate the malicious PowerShell process and its persistence
steps.desc: Kill the running process and locate/remove whatever triggers it to run again (scheduled task, registry run key, WMI event subscription).
steps.guidance: A fileless implant leaves no binary but virtually always leaves a launch mechanism somewhere.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and persistence mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload was staged
steps.desc: Check for any second-stage payload the implant may have already downloaded.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review PowerShell logging/restriction policy
steps.desc: Record the technique and assess whether Constrained Language Mode or stricter execution policy would reduce future risk.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31613.def: A fileless attack stage in which PowerShell is used to deploy, decrypt-in-memory, or directly execute ransomware encryption logic on a host or across multiple hosts, without a standalone ransomware executable being written to disk beforehand.
ITID-31613.purpose: Captures PowerShell used as the deployment/execution mechanism for a ransomware payload, distinct from generic PowerShell C2 activity.
scopeIncludes: PowerShell scripts that perform file enumeration and encryption directly
PowerShell used to push/execute a ransomware payload across multiple hosts (e.g. via WMI/PsExec/GPO)
scopeExcludes: General PowerShell C2 beaconing not tied to ransomware deployment (ITID-31612)
Disk-resident ransomware executables (tracked elsewhere under the ransomware-specific ITID branch, not this fileless-malware branch)
ITID-31613.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response and crisis management; this indicates active, in-progress ransomware deployment.
indicators: PowerShell process performing mass file read/write/rename operations
PowerShell script referencing encryption cmdlets or embedded cryptographic routines
Simultaneous PowerShell execution across multiple hosts via remote administration
vectors: Compromised domain admin credentials used to push a PowerShell ransomware script via GPO/WMI
PowerShell C2 implant (ITID-31612) pivoting to deploy the final encryption payload
rootCauses: Lack of segmentation limiting lateral push of scripts across the domain
PowerShell remoting not restricted to required administrative hosts
mitreTechniques: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
controls: PowerShell remoting restriction to jump hosts
Backup immutability
EDR blocking mass file-encryption behavior
ITID-31613.detection: Behavioral EDR detection of mass file-encryption activity from a PowerShell process is a strong, high-confidence signal.
ITID-31613.response: Immediately isolate all affected hosts, activate the ransomware response plan, and preserve forensic evidence of the PowerShell deployment mechanism.
metrics: Count of PowerShell-deployed ransomware events per year
Hosts affected per event
ITID-31613.notes: Scoped to the fileless/PowerShell delivery mechanism for ransomware; the broader ransomware incident lifecycle itself is owned by the dedicated ransomware ITID branch, referenced here rather than duplicated.

playbook.name: Response: PowerShell-Based Ransomware Deployment Script
playbook.description: For a fileless PowerShell script used to deploy or trigger ransomware encryption across an endpoint or network.

steps.title: Confirm the PowerShell ransomware-deployment activity
steps.desc: Review script-block/module logging, AMSI telemetry, and file-system activity to confirm the script is encrypting or staging encryption of files.
steps.guidance: Treat this as time-critical — encryption may still be in progress.
steps.outcome: Confirmed active or attempted ransomware deployment via PowerShell.

steps.title: Determine scope — single host or lateral spread
steps.desc: Check whether the script has been executed or is executing against other hosts (e.g., via remote PowerShell, PsExec, WMI, or a domain-wide GPO push).
steps.outcome: Full scope of affected/at-risk hosts identified.

steps.title: Immediately isolate all affected/at-risk hosts
steps.desc: Network-isolate the source host and any hosts showing the same activity to stop encryption from spreading.
steps.guidance: Speed matters — every additional minute may mean more encrypted data.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts isolated.

steps.title: Disable compromised credentials/accounts used for lateral movement
steps.desc: Disable or reset any account credentials the script used to reach other hosts.
steps.outcome: Compromised credentials disabled.

steps.title: Terminate the deployment process and remove its persistence
steps.desc: Kill the running PowerShell process and locate/remove the launch mechanism (scheduled task, GPO, login script, registry run key).
steps.outcome: Process terminated and persistence removed.

steps.title: Confirm no encryption completed and no ransom note was dropped
steps.desc: Verify whether files were actually encrypted before containment; if so, escalate to full ransomware incident response.
steps.outcome: Encryption status confirmed for all in-scope hosts.
steps.abort: If encryption occurred, escalate immediately to the organization's ransomware incident response process.

steps.title: Restore hosts and validate backups if any encryption occurred
steps.desc: Return clean hosts to service; for any encrypted data, validate backup integrity before restoring.
steps.outcome: Hosts restored, data recovered from clean backups where needed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review PowerShell restriction/backup policy
steps.desc: Record the deployment technique and assess PowerShell execution restrictions and backup isolation improvements.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31614.def: An incident involving PowerShell-based fileless malware, not clearly matching the downloader, C2 beacon, or ransomware-deployment patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31614.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under PowerShell-Based Malware.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific PowerShell-Based Malware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under PowerShell-Based Malware
ITID-31614.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium by default given the fileless technique's typical severity.
ITID-31614.escalation: Reclassify once the specific PowerShell malware behavior is clarified.
indicators: PowerShell-based malware alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific PowerShell abuse vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
controls: PowerShell constrained language mode and script block logging
EDR behavioral detection of malicious PowerShell execution
Application control restricting execution to signed scripts
Least-privilege administrative access
ITID-31614.detection: Same general PowerShell logging/EDR telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31614.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific PowerShell-Based Malware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31614.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General PowerShell-Based Malware
playbook.description: General response for fileless PowerShell-based malware that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm malicious PowerShell activity via script-block logging
steps.desc: Review PowerShell script-block/module logging and AMSI telemetry to confirm the malicious command sequence.
steps.guidance: Standard console history alone is often insufficient.
steps.outcome: Malicious activity confirmed.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the PowerShell command was triggered.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process and remove its persistence
steps.desc: Kill the running process and locate/remove whatever triggers it to run again.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload was staged
steps.desc: Check for any second-stage payload the script may have already downloaded or executed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review PowerShell logging/restriction policy
steps.desc: Record the technique observed for future detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31621.def: Fileless persistence achieved by writing a command (often invoking a script interpreter) into a registry Run/RunOnce key or equivalent auto-start registry location, so the malicious logic re-executes at logon/startup without a standalone executable being the persistence artifact.
ITID-31621.purpose: Captures malware that establishes persistence purely through registry Run keys or startup-folder-equivalent registry entries, without a resident disk executable being the primary artifact.
scopeIncludes: Run/RunOnce registry key values invoking PowerShell, mshta, wscript, or similar interpreters
Registry-based auto-start entries pointing at a fileless payload
scopeExcludes: The encoded payload itself stored in a separate registry value for later retrieval (ITID-31622)
COM hijacking via registry modification (ITID-31623)
ITID-31621.severity: Medium-High, since this represents an established persistence mechanism.
ITID-31621.escalation: Escalate if the Run key entry is confirmed to be re-launching an active C2 implant.
indicators: New/modified Run or RunOnce registry values invoking a script interpreter
Registry auto-start entries with obfuscated or encoded command arguments
vectors: Initial PowerShell downloader (ITID-31611) writing a Run key for persistence
Malicious document macro adding a registry auto-start entry
rootCauses: Lack of registry auto-start monitoring
Insufficient least-privilege controls allowing user-writable auto-start locations
mitreTechniques: T1547.001 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
controls: Registry auto-start location monitoring (e.g. Autoruns-style baselining)
EDR alerting on new Run key writes
ITID-31621.detection: Registry auto-start monitoring provides strong, well-established detection coverage.
ITID-31621.response: Remove the malicious Run key entry, identify and remediate the underlying payload it launches, and verify no other persistence mechanism remains.
metrics: Count of registry Run-key persistence detections per month
ITID-31621.notes: Scoped to the persistence-trigger mechanism itself; where the payload is also stored inline in a registry value, see ITID-31622.

playbook.name: Response: Registry Run-Key Persistence Malware
playbook.description: For malware persisting via a Windows registry Run/RunOnce key (or equivalent autostart location) with no reliance on a standalone disk file for triggering.

steps.title: Identify the malicious registry run-key entry
steps.desc: Enumerate Run/RunOnce keys (HKLM and HKCU) and equivalent autostart locations to identify the malicious entry and what it launches.
steps.guidance: Use Autoruns or EDR autostart enumeration rather than manual registry review alone — attackers commonly hide entries among legitimate ones.
steps.outcome: Malicious run-key entry identified along with what it executes.

steps.title: Determine what the run-key launches and what it has done since installation
steps.desc: Trace the process launched by the run key and review its activity history (network connections, file access) since it was installed.
steps.outcome: Full behavior and impact of the persisted payload understood.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host pending removal to prevent further malicious activity or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the running malicious process
steps.desc: Kill the currently running process launched by the registry entry.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Remove the malicious registry run-key entry
steps.desc: Delete the specific registry value/key identified in identification. A generic AV scan often misses this — remove it explicitly.
steps.guidance: Document the exact key path and value before deleting, for the incident record.
steps.outcome: Registry persistence entry removed.

steps.title: Remove any referenced payload file or script and re-scan
steps.desc: Delete any file/script referenced by the run key and run a full scan to confirm no other related persistence remains.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, no remaining reference to the payload.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor autostart locations for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring of autostart locations for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Record the exact registry location and value used, for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31622.def: A fileless loader technique in which the malicious payload itself (e.g. Base64-encoded shellcode or a script) is stored as data in a registry value, and a separate small loader (often a Run key entry) reads and executes that value's content directly into memory.
ITID-31622.purpose: Captures fileless malware that stores its actual payload (not just a launch trigger) encoded inside a registry value.
scopeIncludes: Registry values containing encoded/obfuscated payload data read and executed by a loader
Payloads split across multiple registry values to evade size-based detection
scopeExcludes: The Run-key trigger mechanism itself when no payload is stored in the registry (ITID-31621)
COM hijacking, which modifies object-instantiation registry pointers rather than storing payload data (ITID-31623)
ITID-31622.severity: High, since this indicates a more evasion-conscious persistence design.
ITID-31622.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the decoded payload is confirmed to be a C2 implant or ransomware stager.
ITID-31622.escalation: Escalate to incident response for full memory/registry forensic review once a payload-bearing registry value is confirmed.
indicators: Unusually large or high-entropy data stored in a non-standard registry value
Loader process reading a specific registry value into memory immediately before spawning a new process/thread
vectors: Multi-stage PowerShell downloader stashing its next-stage payload in the registry to avoid disk writes
Malware droppers using the registry as a dead-drop for payload storage
rootCauses: Lack of registry value entropy/size monitoring
EDR not inspecting registry value content, only key/value names
controls: Registry value entropy/anomaly monitoring
EDR memory-scanning integration
ITID-31622.detection: Requires registry content inspection beyond key/value naming; moderate coverage depending on EDR capability.
ITID-31622.response: Extract and analyze the stored payload, remove the registry value and its loader trigger, and assess for further compromise based on payload capability.
metrics: Count of payload-bearing registry value detections per quarter
ITID-31622.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31621 by what is stored: here the registry holds the actual payload data, not merely a launch command.

playbook.name: Response: Registry-Stored Encoded Payload (Fileless Loader via Registry Value)
playbook.description: For malware storing an encoded/encrypted payload directly inside a registry value, loaded and decoded entirely in memory by a small launcher with no payload file ever written to disk.

steps.title: Identify the launcher and the registry value holding the encoded payload
steps.desc: Trace the launcher mechanism (script, LOLBin, scheduled task) back to the registry value it reads and decodes at execution time.
steps.guidance: EDR memory-scanning or manual registry review of unusually large/binary-looking values in non-standard keys is often required — a plain AV file scan will not find this.
steps.outcome: Registry value containing the encoded payload identified, along with the launcher that reads it.

steps.title: Decode/analyze the payload to understand its capability
steps.desc: Extract and analyze the encoded payload (in a controlled analysis environment) to understand its function and any C2 destination.
steps.outcome: Payload capability and any C2 destination understood.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further C2 communication or lateral spread.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the launcher process
steps.desc: Kill the running launcher process to stop it reading/executing the encoded payload.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Delete the registry value holding the encoded payload and the launcher's trigger
steps.desc: Remove the specific registry value containing the encoded payload and whatever mechanism triggers the launcher (run key, scheduled task, WMI subscription).
steps.guidance: A generic AV scan almost always misses this — the removal must explicitly target the identified registry value.
steps.outcome: Encoded payload value and launcher trigger both removed.

steps.title: Re-scan to confirm no residual loader or payload remains
steps.desc: Run a full scan and re-check autostart/registry locations to confirm complete removal.
steps.outcome: Scan clean, no remaining launcher or payload reference.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring of the registry area and process activity for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the technique
steps.desc: Record the registry-based storage/loading technique for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31623.def: A persistence technique in which an adversary modifies the registry CLSID/COM object registration for a commonly-invoked component so that legitimate application or system behavior inadvertently loads and executes attacker-controlled code in place of (or alongside) the legitimate COM object.
ITID-31623.purpose: Captures fileless persistence achieved by hijacking COM object registration in the registry, causing legitimate software to unknowingly load a malicious component.
scopeIncludes: Registry modification of CLSID InprocServer32/LocalServer32 keys to point to a malicious payload
Abuse of a COM object routinely instantiated by a trusted process (e.g. Explorer, scheduled tasks) for persistence
scopeExcludes: Simple Run/RunOnce key persistence with no COM object involvement (ITID-31621)
Payload storage in an arbitrary registry value not tied to COM registration (ITID-31622)
ITID-31623.severity: High, since COM hijacking is a stealthier technique that can evade less mature detection tooling.
ITID-31623.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the hijacked COM object is invoked by a privileged/system process.
ITID-31623.escalation: Escalate to incident response given the defense-evasion sophistication implied by this technique.
indicators: Modified CLSID registry entries pointing outside expected system/application directories
Unexpected DLL/script loaded by a trusted process via COM instantiation
vectors: Post-exploitation persistence tooling that rewrites CLSID registration keys
Living-off-the-land frameworks with built-in COM hijacking modules
rootCauses: Lack of baseline monitoring for CLSID/COM registration changes
Excessive write permissions on HKCU/HKLM COM registration hives
mitreTechniques: T1546.015 Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking
controls: CLSID/COM registration baseline monitoring
Restricting write access to COM registration registry hives
ITID-31623.detection: Requires dedicated COM-hijacking-aware EDR detection logic; coverage varies significantly by tooling maturity.
ITID-31623.response: Revert the hijacked CLSID entry to its legitimate value, identify the malicious payload it referenced, and hunt for other COM objects similarly modified.
metrics: Count of COM hijacking detections per year
ITID-31623.notes: Distinct technique from generic Run-key persistence (ITID-31621) and registry payload storage (ITID-31622): here the registry change abuses object-instantiation redirection rather than direct auto-start or payload storage.

playbook.name: Response: COM Hijacking via Registry Modification
playbook.description: For malware achieving persistence by modifying registry COM object class entries (CLSID) so that a legitimate application unknowingly loads a malicious COM object.

steps.title: Identify the hijacked COM object and its associated CLSID registry entry
steps.desc: Compare the CLSID/COM registration in question against a known-good baseline to identify the modified InprocServer32/LocalServer32 path pointing to the malicious component.
steps.guidance: COM hijacking often targets CLSIDs used by commonly-loaded applications or scheduled tasks — check which legitimate process is triggering the hijacked load.
steps.outcome: Hijacked CLSID and the malicious component it loads identified.

steps.title: Determine which legitimate process is unknowingly triggering the hijack
steps.desc: Identify which application or scheduled task instantiates the hijacked COM object, since that process will keep triggering the malware until the hijack is removed.
steps.outcome: Triggering process/task identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Prevent the triggering process from launching, if feasible
steps.desc: Temporarily disable or pause the scheduled task/application that triggers the hijacked COM object while remediation is underway.
steps.outcome: Hijack no longer being triggered.
steps.abort: Skip if disabling the triggering process would cause unacceptable business disruption; proceed directly to eradication instead.

steps.title: Restore the CLSID registry entry to its legitimate value and remove the malicious component
steps.desc: Correct the hijacked CLSID entry back to the legitimate COM server path and delete the malicious DLL/component it had pointed to.
steps.guidance: A simple AV scan often misses COM hijacking since the registry modification itself is the persistence mechanism, not just the dropped file.
steps.outcome: CLSID entry restored and malicious component removed.

steps.title: Scan for additional hijacked CLSIDs
steps.desc: Check for other modified CLSID entries, since attackers using this technique sometimes hijack more than one COM object for redundancy.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no additional hijacked CLSIDs, or additional entries found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and verify the legitimate process functions normally
steps.desc: Confirm the previously hijacked application/task now functions correctly and no longer loads malicious code.
steps.outcome: Legitimate process functions normally with no malicious load.

steps.title: Document the hijacked CLSID and technique
steps.desc: Record the specific CLSID and technique used for detection rule tuning and future baseline comparison.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31624.def: An incident involving registry-resident fileless malware, not clearly matching the Run-key persistence, payload-storage, or COM-hijacking patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31624.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Registry-Resident Malware.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Registry-Resident Malware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Registry-Resident Malware
ITID-31624.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium by default.
ITID-31624.escalation: Reclassify once the specific registry-resident technique is clarified.
indicators: Registry-resident malware alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific registry-abuse vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: EDR detection of unauthorized registry autostart modifications
Registry integrity monitoring
Application allowlisting
Least-privilege administrative access
ITID-31624.detection: Same general registry-monitoring telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31624.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Registry-Resident Malware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31624.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Registry-Resident Malware
playbook.description: General response for fileless malware persisting via registry manipulation that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Identify the malicious registry persistence entry
steps.desc: Enumerate autostart and relevant registry locations to identify the malicious entry and what it launches.
steps.guidance: Use Autoruns or EDR autostart enumeration rather than manual review alone.
steps.outcome: Malicious registry entry identified.

steps.title: Determine what the entry launches and its activity history
steps.desc: Trace the process/behavior triggered by the registry entry since installation.
steps.outcome: Behavior and impact understood.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host pending removal.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malicious registry entry
steps.desc: Delete the specific registry key/value identified in identification.
steps.guidance: A generic AV scan often misses this — remove it explicitly.
steps.outcome: Registry persistence removed.

steps.title: Re-scan to confirm complete removal
steps.desc: Run a full scan and re-check autostart/registry locations to confirm nothing remains.
steps.outcome: Scan clean.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Record the registry location and technique used for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31631.def: A memory-only execution technique in which a malicious DLL is manually mapped and loaded into a target process's memory (reflective DLL injection) so that it runs without being written to disk or registered through the normal Windows loader.
ITID-31631.purpose: Captures malware that loads its DLL payload directly into a process's memory space without it ever existing as a file on disk.
scopeIncludes: Reflective DLL loading into a legitimate or newly-spawned process
In-memory DLL injection frameworks used as an execution/evasion primitive
scopeExcludes: Process hollowing/injection that replaces or redirects execution flow of a target process's main image (ITID-31632)
A memory-resident C2 implant using injection merely as its delivery mechanism, when the primary classification concern is the ongoing C2 channel (ITID-31633)
ITID-31631.severity: High, since this indicates active defense-evasion tradecraft.
ITID-31631.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response; treat as an active, sophisticated intrusion.
indicators: EDR alert on reflective DLL loading / manual module mapping
Process with a loaded module not present in its normal on-disk module list
Suspicious memory regions with executable permissions not backed by a file
vectors: Post-exploitation frameworks (e.g. Cobalt Strike-style loaders) performing reflective DLL injection
Exploit payloads injecting shellcode reflectively into a target process
rootCauses: Lack of memory-scanning EDR capability
Insufficient application control on which processes can be targeted for injection
mitreTechniques: T1055.001 Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
controls: EDR memory-scanning/injection detection
Attack surface reduction rules blocking known injection APIs
ITID-31631.detection: Requires memory-aware EDR; signature-based AV alone provides little coverage for this technique.
ITID-31631.response: Isolate the host, capture a memory image for forensic analysis, and identify the injecting process and its origin.
metrics: Count of reflective DLL injection detections per quarter
ITID-31631.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31632 by mechanism: DLL mapping into a process's address space, rather than hollowing/replacing the process's own executing image.

playbook.name: Response: Reflective DLL Injection Malware
playbook.description: For malware injecting a DLL directly into a process's memory (reflective loading) without writing the DLL to disk, leaving no standalone file artifact.

steps.title: Confirm reflective DLL injection via EDR memory-scanning telemetry
steps.desc: Review EDR memory-scan alerts for unbacked/anomalous memory regions in a legitimate process consistent with reflective DLL loading.
steps.guidance: Standard AV file scanning will not detect this — rely on EDR memory inspection or YARA memory scanning.
steps.outcome: Confirmed reflective DLL injection and the host process identified.

steps.title: Identify the injected process's behavior and any C2 communication
steps.desc: Analyze the behavior of the host process since injection, including any outbound network connections.
steps.outcome: Behavior and C2 destination (if any) identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further C2 communication or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the injected process
steps.desc: Kill the host process to remove the injected code from memory immediately.
steps.guidance: Killing the process is typically required since the injected DLL cannot be selectively unloaded.
steps.outcome: Process terminated, injected code cleared from memory.

steps.title: Identify and remove the launch mechanism that performed the injection
steps.desc: Locate whatever launched the injection (a loader script, scheduled task, or another process) and remove it — a memory-only technique still requires an initial trigger to persist across reboots.
steps.outcome: Launch mechanism identified and removed.

steps.title: Re-scan memory across other running processes for the same injection technique
steps.desc: Check other running processes for similar unbacked memory regions to confirm the injection was not also performed elsewhere.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other processes are affected, or additional instances found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for reinjection
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated EDR memory-scan monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the injection technique
steps.desc: Record the target process and injection method for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31632.def: A memory-only execution technique (process hollowing or general process injection) in which a legitimate process is started in a suspended state (or targeted while running) and its memory/execution flow is replaced or redirected to execute attacker-supplied code, so the malicious activity appears to originate from a trusted process.
ITID-31632.purpose: Captures malware that hollows out or redirects a legitimate process's execution to run a malicious payload under its identity.
scopeIncludes: Process hollowing of a legitimate suspended process followed by malicious image mapping
Thread execution hijacking or APC-based code injection into a running trusted process
scopeExcludes: Reflective DLL injection that adds a module without replacing the target's primary image (ITID-31631)
The downstream C2 channel established after injection, tracked separately (ITID-31633)
ITID-31632.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response given the process-masquerading nature of this technique.
indicators: Mismatch between a process's on-disk image hash and its in-memory executing code
Process created in suspended state followed by unusual memory writes before resume
Parent-child process relationship inconsistent with normal application behavior
vectors: Post-exploitation tooling hollowing a legitimate Windows binary (e.g. svchost.exe) to mask malicious execution
Exploit chains injecting into a browser or Office process for evasion
rootCauses: Lack of process-image integrity verification
Insufficient EDR coverage of process creation/injection APIs
controls: EDR process-image integrity monitoring
Attack surface reduction rules restricting process hollowing APIs
ITID-31632.detection: Behavioral EDR detection of image/memory mismatch provides strong, well-established coverage for this technique.
ITID-31632.response: Isolate the host, capture memory forensics of the hollowed process, and trace back to the initial injection vector.
metrics: Count of process hollowing/injection detections per quarter
ITID-31632.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31631 by scope: this leaf covers hollowing/redirection of a process's own primary execution, not the addition of an extra module.

playbook.name: Response: Process Hollowing/Process Injection Payload
playbook.description: For malware that launches a legitimate process in a suspended state and replaces its memory image with malicious code (process hollowing) or otherwise injects code into a running legitimate process.

steps.title: Confirm process hollowing/injection via EDR telemetry
steps.desc: Review EDR alerts for a legitimate process exhibiting an image mismatch, unexpected memory layout, or a suspended-then-resumed launch pattern consistent with hollowing.
steps.guidance: A file-based AV scan of the hollowed process's on-disk binary will appear clean — the malicious code exists only in memory.
steps.outcome: Confirmed process hollowing/injection with the affected process identified.

steps.title: Identify the parent process that performed the hollowing
steps.desc: Trace the process tree to identify what launched and hollowed the legitimate process.
steps.outcome: Parent/launching process identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the hollowed process
steps.desc: Kill the affected process to clear the malicious in-memory code.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Remove the launcher and its persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Locate and remove the parent process/dropper and whatever launch mechanism it used to establish persistence.
steps.outcome: Launcher and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify no other processes were hollowed or injected
steps.desc: Check other commonly-abused legitimate processes on the host for the same hollowing pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional instances found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the technique
steps.desc: Record the target process and hollowing/injection method for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31633.def: A resident command-and-control implant that operates entirely in process memory, with no corresponding executable or script artifact persisted to disk, maintaining an ongoing channel for attacker commands.
ITID-31633.purpose: Captures a command-and-control implant that lives entirely in memory, with the C2 channel itself as the classification focus, regardless of the specific injection technique used to place it there.
scopeIncludes: Ongoing memory-resident beacon/implant activity where the delivery injection technique is secondary to the sustained C2 channel
In-memory implants that survive process restarts via re-injection rather than disk-based persistence
scopeExcludes: The specific reflective DLL injection delivery mechanism, tracked on its own when injection technique is the primary finding (ITID-31631)
Process hollowing as the primary finding rather than an established, ongoing C2 channel (ITID-31632)
ITID-31633.severity: Critical, since this represents sustained, hard-to-detect attacker access.
ITID-31633.escalation: Escalate immediately; engage full incident response including network-wide threat hunting for related implants.
indicators: Sustained outbound beaconing from a process with no corresponding on-disk malicious artifact
Memory forensics revealing an active implant with no disk-based persistence found
vectors: Advanced post-exploitation frameworks designed for memory-only operation
Combination of process injection (ITID-31631/31632) followed by sustained C2 tasking
rootCauses: Lack of memory-forensic-capable EDR
Insufficient network beaconing detection
controls: EDR with memory-scanning and beaconing detection
Network traffic analysis for C2 patterns
ITID-31633.detection: Requires both memory forensics capability and network beaconing analytics; a genuinely difficult detection surface.
ITID-31633.response: Treat as an active breach: isolate affected hosts, perform full memory forensics, hunt across the environment for related implants, and rebuild affected systems rather than attempting in-place cleanup.
metrics: Count of confirmed memory-only C2 implants per year
Dwell time before detection
ITID-31633.notes: Scoped to the sustained C2 channel as the classification focus; where the specific injection mechanics are the notable finding instead, use ITID-31631/31632.

playbook.name: Response: Memory-Resident C2 Implant (No Disk Artifact)
playbook.description: For a fully memory-resident command-and-control implant that leaves no file on disk at any stage, surviving only in process memory until reboot.

steps.title: Confirm the memory-resident implant via EDR memory-scanning telemetry
steps.desc: Since no disk artifact exists, confirm the implant purely through EDR memory scanning, process behavior anomalies, and network beaconing patterns.
steps.guidance: A standard file-based scan will find nothing — this depends entirely on memory/behavioral telemetry.
steps.outcome: Confirmed memory-resident implant with the host process and C2 destination identified.

steps.title: Identify how the implant was initially loaded
steps.desc: Determine the initial infection/loading vector (exploit, malicious document, prior stage dropper) since the implant itself leaves no disk trace of its own arrival.
steps.outcome: Initial loading vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host immediately to cut off C2 communication.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination
steps.desc: Block the beaconing domain/IP at the network perimeter.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked.

steps.title: Terminate the host process to clear the implant from memory
steps.desc: Kill the process hosting the implant. Because it is purely memory-resident, terminating the process (or rebooting the host) removes the active implant.
steps.guidance: Confirm no other persistence mechanism will simply reload it on reboot before assuming this alone is sufficient.
steps.outcome: Implant cleared from memory.

steps.title: Identify and remove any mechanism that would reload the implant on reboot
steps.desc: Check for a loader, scheduled task, or exploited service configured to re-establish the implant after reboot; remove it if found.
steps.guidance: A purely memory-resident implant with no reload mechanism will not survive a reboot, but confirm this rather than assume it.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no reload mechanism, or mechanism found and removed.

steps.title: Reboot the host and monitor for reinfection
steps.desc: Reboot the endpoint to ensure the memory-resident implant is fully cleared, then monitor for renewed beaconing.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed after reboot.

steps.title: Document the implant and initial vector
steps.desc: Record the implant's behavior, C2 infrastructure, and initial infection vector for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31634.def: An incident involving memory-only fileless malware, not clearly matching the reflective-injection, process-hollowing, or resident-C2-implant patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31634.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Memory-Only Malware.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Memory-Only Malware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Memory-Only Malware
ITID-31634.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High by default given the technique class's typical severity.
ITID-31634.escalation: Reclassify once the specific memory-only technique is clarified.
indicators: Memory-only malware alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific in-memory execution vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: EDR with in-memory/fileless threat detection
Endpoint memory scanning and behavioral analytics
Script execution restrictions (PowerShell/WMI constrained modes)
Network egress filtering for C2 detection
ITID-31634.detection: Same general memory-forensic/EDR telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31634.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Memory-Only Malware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31634.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Memory-Only Malware
playbook.description: General response for memory-only (fileless) malware that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm memory-resident malicious activity via EDR telemetry
steps.desc: Confirm the malicious activity through EDR memory scanning and behavioral telemetry, since no disk file exists to signature-scan.
steps.outcome: Confirmed memory-only malicious activity and host process identified.

steps.title: Identify the initial infection vector
steps.desc: Determine how the malware was loaded into memory.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the host process
steps.desc: Kill the process hosting the malicious in-memory code.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Identify and remove any persistence/reload mechanism
steps.desc: Check for a mechanism that would reload the malware on reboot and remove it if found.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no reload mechanism, or mechanism found and removed.

steps.title: Reboot and monitor the host for recurrence
steps.desc: Reboot the endpoint and monitor for renewed malicious activity for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the technique and infection vector for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31711.def: Malware that scans for and compromises internet-connected IoT/embedded devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, etc.), typically via default credentials or unpatched firmware vulnerabilities, to recruit them into a distributed botnet.
ITID-31711.purpose: Captures botnet malware whose recruitment vector is compromising internet-connected IoT/embedded devices at scale.
scopeIncludes: Mass scanning and default-credential/exploit-based compromise of IoT devices to add them to a botnet
IoT-specific botnet malware families (e.g. Mirai-style) that persist in device memory/flash
scopeExcludes: Botnet recruitment via compromised web servers/CMS rather than IoT devices (ITID-31712)
The downstream DDoS/DoS attacks such botnets carry out, tracked under the DoS/DDoS ITID branch (e.g. ITID-54831, ITID-41241) rather than here
ITID-31711.severity: Medium at the individual-device level; High at the aggregate/infrastructure level given the scale IoT botnets can reach.
ITID-31711.priority: P2 for confirmed recruitment; escalate to P1 if the organization's own IoT fleet is the vector recruiting others.
ITID-31711.escalation: Escalate to network security if organization-owned IoT devices are found compromised and participating in an external botnet.
indicators: IoT device scanning default-credential ports (Telnet/SSH) outbound at high volume
Firmware/process anomalies on IoT devices with no legitimate update history
Device check-in traffic to known IoT botnet C2 infrastructure
vectors: Default/weak IoT device credentials
Unpatched IoT firmware vulnerabilities exposed to the internet
rootCauses: IoT devices deployed with default credentials
Lack of network segmentation isolating IoT devices from the internet
controls: IoT device credential hardening/rotation
Network segmentation isolating IoT devices
Firmware patch management for IoT devices
ITID-31711.detection: Network-level scanning/beaconing detection to known IoT botnet C2 provides reasonable coverage; device-level detection is often limited by IoT platform constraints.
ITID-31711.response: Isolate and re-flash/factory-reset compromised IoT devices, rotate credentials, and block C2 infrastructure at the network egress.
metrics: Count of IoT devices recruited/remediated per quarter
Mean time to detect IoT botnet recruitment
ITID-31711.notes: Scoped to the recruitment/infrastructure-building activity itself; the resulting DDoS/DoS output of an IoT botnet is tracked separately under the DoS/DDoS ITID branch (e.g. ITID-41241, ITID-54831) to avoid duplicating that content here.

playbook.name: Response: IoT Device Botnet Recruitment
playbook.description: For an organization-owned IoT device (camera, router, sensor, embedded appliance) recruited into a distributed botnet.

steps.title: Confirm the IoT device is generating C2 beacon traffic
steps.desc: Review network traffic from the device for periodic outbound connections to a known or suspected botnet C2 destination.
steps.guidance: IoT devices rarely have local security agents — identification relies almost entirely on network-level traffic analysis.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 beaconing from the device and destination identified.

steps.title: Identify the compromise vector (default credentials, unpatched firmware, exposed management interface)
steps.desc: Determine how the device was recruited — commonly default/weak credentials, an exposed management interface, or an unpatched firmware vulnerability.
steps.outcome: Compromise vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect or network-segment the device immediately to stop it participating in botnet activity.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Block the botnet C2 destination at the perimeter
steps.desc: Block the identified C2 domain/IP at the firewall to protect any other similarly-configured devices.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked.

steps.title: Factory-reset the device and apply the latest firmware
steps.desc: Most IoT botnet malware is memory-resident and removed by a factory reset; apply the latest available firmware afterward to close the vulnerability.
steps.guidance: A reboot alone is often insufficient if the device was compromised via a persistent firmware modification — verify firmware integrity, not just reboot.
steps.outcome: Device reset and updated to patched firmware.
steps.abort: If the device cannot be updated to a patched firmware version, replace it rather than returning it to service.

steps.title: Set strong, unique credentials and disable unnecessary exposed services
steps.desc: Change default/weak credentials and disable any unneeded remote-management interfaces exposed to the internet.
steps.outcome: Device hardened against re-recruitment.

steps.title: Return the device to service and monitor for renewed beaconing
steps.desc: Reconnect the device and monitor its network traffic for a defined period to confirm no renewed C2 activity.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT device management policy
steps.desc: Record the compromise vector and assess whether organizational IoT hardening/inventory policy needs improvement (default credential audits, firmware patch cadence).
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31712.def: Malware that compromises internet-facing web servers or content management systems (via exploited plugins, weak credentials, or unpatched vulnerabilities) to install a bot agent, adding the server to a botnet with higher available bandwidth and uptime than typical consumer devices.
ITID-31712.purpose: Captures botnet malware that recruits nodes by compromising internet-facing web servers or CMS installations, rather than consumer IoT devices.
scopeIncludes: Bot agent installed on a compromised web server/CMS via an exploited plugin or vulnerability
Web-server-hosted bots used as high-bandwidth botnet nodes
scopeExcludes: IoT device recruitment (ITID-31711)
A standalone web shell backdoor with no botnet C2 participation (tracked under the Trojan/Backdoor ITID branch)
ITID-31712.severity: High, given the higher bandwidth/availability of compromised servers relative to consumer devices.
ITID-31712.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for organization-owned servers.
ITID-31712.escalation: Escalate immediately if an organization-owned production web server is found compromised and participating in a botnet.
indicators: Unrecognized process/cron job on a web server making outbound C2 connections
CMS plugin/theme files modified outside a normal deployment window
Sustained high-bandwidth outbound traffic inconsistent with the server's normal role
vectors: Exploited CMS plugin/theme vulnerability
Weak or reused web server/CMS admin credentials
rootCauses: Outdated CMS/plugin software
Lack of web application firewall coverage
Insufficient server egress filtering
controls: Web application firewall (WAF)
CMS/plugin patch management
Server egress filtering
ITID-31712.detection: File integrity monitoring and outbound traffic analysis on web servers provide strong detection coverage.
ITID-31712.response: Isolate the server, remove the bot agent, patch the exploited vulnerability, and block associated C2 infrastructure.
metrics: Count of web-server botnet recruitment incidents per quarter
detections: File integrity monitoring on web root
ITID-31712.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31711 by target infrastructure class (web servers/CMS vs. consumer IoT devices); does not duplicate the standalone web shell backdoor leaf since the focus here is botnet C2 participation.

playbook.name: Response: Botnet Recruiting via Compromised Web Servers/CMS
playbook.description: For an organization-operated web server or CMS platform compromised and recruited as a botnet node, potentially used to attack other organizations.

steps.title: Confirm the server is generating C2 beacon or attack traffic
steps.desc: Review outbound network traffic and server logs for periodic C2 beaconing or evidence of attack traffic (e.g., scanning, credential stuffing, DDoS participation) originating from the server.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet participation and C2 destination or attack pattern identified.

steps.title: Identify the CMS/web application vulnerability or exposed credential used for compromise
steps.desc: Review CMS/plugin versions, admin panel access logs, and file-integrity findings to determine the initial compromise vector.
steps.outcome: Compromise vector identified.
steps.tool: CMS admin logs / file integrity monitoring

steps.title: Isolate the server from the network
steps.desc: Take the server offline or network-isolate it to stop it from being used to attack other organizations.
