steps.guidance: Treat this with urgency — an actively-recruited web server attacking external targets carries reputational and potential legal exposure for the organization.
steps.outcome: Server isolated.

steps.title: Preserve logs and notify legal/compliance of potential third-party impact
steps.desc: Preserve web server, CMS, and network logs before further remediation, and notify legal/compliance given the server may have been used to attack external organizations.
steps.outcome: Logs preserved and appropriate stakeholders notified.

steps.title: Remove the malicious web shell/plugin/backdoor and patch the exploited vulnerability
steps.desc: Identify and remove any web shell, malicious plugin, or backdoor account, and patch or upgrade the vulnerable CMS/plugin/software version.
steps.outcome: Backdoor removed and vulnerability patched.
steps.tool: CMS admin console / file system review

steps.title: Rebuild from a known-clean backup if compromise depth is uncertain
steps.desc: If the extent of the compromise cannot be fully confirmed, rebuild the server/CMS instance from a known-clean backup rather than relying solely on cleanup.
steps.outcome: Server confirmed clean or rebuilt from clean backup.

steps.title: Restore service and monitor for renewed compromise
steps.desc: Bring the server back online and monitor closely for renewed unauthorized access or beaconing.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and any external-attack exposure
steps.desc: Record the compromise vector, whether external organizations were attacked from the server, and any resulting notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31713.def: A botnet in which infected nodes communicate directly with each other in a peer-to-peer topology to relay commands and updates, rather than checking in with a single centralized C2 server, making takedown by seizing a single server ineffective.
ITID-31713.purpose: Captures botnets architected without a central C2 server, using peer-to-peer communication among bots instead.
scopeIncludes: Botnet malware using a P2P protocol for command distribution among bots
Decentralized botnet architectures resilient to single-point takedown
scopeExcludes: Fast-flux DNS botnets, which still rely on centralized C2 domains behind a rotating IP pool (ITID-31714)
Centralized botnet C2 panels (tracked under ITID-44731 in the C2 infrastructure branch, referenced rather than duplicated here)
ITID-31713.severity: High, given the resilience of P2P architecture to standard takedown approaches.
ITID-31713.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence for wider tracking given the difficulty of full eradication via infrastructure takedown alone.
indicators: Infected host communicating with a rotating set of peer IPs rather than a fixed C2 server
P2P protocol traffic patterns not matching known legitimate P2P applications
vectors: Malware families purpose-built with P2P C2 modules
Botnet migration from centralized to P2P architecture following prior takedown
rootCauses: Lack of P2P traffic pattern detection capability
Insufficient network segmentation allowing peer-to-peer bot communication
controls: Network traffic analysis for P2P botnet protocol signatures
Egress filtering
ITID-31713.detection: Requires specialized traffic-pattern analytics; harder to detect than centralized C2 due to the absence of a single fixed indicator.
ITID-31713.response: Isolate and remediate infected hosts individually since no single C2 takedown will disrupt the botnet; coordinate with threat intelligence for broader tracking.
metrics: Count of P2P botnet infections identified per quarter
ITID-31713.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by C2 topology (decentralized peer-to-peer); cross-references the centralized botnet C2 panel leaf (ITID-44731) rather than duplicating it.

playbook.name: Response: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Botnet (No Central C2 Server)
playbook.description: For a bot client using peer-to-peer command distribution with no single central C2 server to identify and block.

steps.title: Confirm P2P botnet behavior via peer-communication patterns
steps.desc: Review network traffic for communication with a large, changing set of peer IP addresses rather than a fixed C2 server, consistent with a P2P botnet protocol.
steps.guidance: Do not expect to find a single C2 IP to block — the identification goal is confirming the peer-swarm pattern itself.
steps.outcome: Confirmed P2P botnet client and its peer-communication pattern.

steps.title: Identify the bot client process on the endpoint
steps.desc: Locate the process responsible for the peer-to-peer traffic on the infected host.
steps.outcome: Bot client process identified.

steps.title: Isolate the infected endpoint from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host, since there is no single C2 to block — isolation of the infected node itself is the primary containment action.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Apply network-level blocking of the P2P protocol/port pattern
steps.desc: Because there is no central server to take down, block the observed peer-communication port/protocol pattern at the network level to limit further P2P traffic from any other potentially-infected hosts.
steps.outcome: P2P communication pattern blocked at the network boundary.

steps.title: Remove the bot client and its persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Uninstall/delete the bot client binary or process and remove any startup/registry persistence.
steps.outcome: Bot client and persistence removed.

steps.title: Scan the network for other hosts exhibiting the same peer-communication pattern
steps.desc: Since a P2P botnet often infects multiple hosts within reach of each other, scan for other endpoints showing the same traffic pattern.
steps.outcome: Additional infected hosts identified and remediated, or confirmed isolated incident.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for renewed peer traffic
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated network monitoring for renewed P2P communication patterns.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the P2P botnet family and detection approach
steps.desc: Record the peer-communication signature used for detection, since blocking a single C2 destination will not be effective against this family.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31714.def: Botnet infrastructure that maps a small set of C2 domains to a rapidly-changing pool of bot/proxy IP addresses via short-TTL DNS records, so that blocking or seizing any individual IP has minimal effect on the botnet's availability.
ITID-31714.purpose: Captures botnet infrastructure that uses fast-flux DNS to rapidly rotate the IP addresses behind its C2 domains, evading IP-based blocking.
scopeIncludes: C2 domains resolving to a rapidly rotating pool of IP addresses with short DNS TTLs
Bots acting as front-end proxies in a fast-flux rotation pointing back to a hidden backend
scopeExcludes: P2P botnets with no reliance on DNS-based C2 domains (ITID-31713)
General residential proxy-as-a-service infrastructure not built around fast-flux DNS rotation (ITID-31731)
ITID-31714.severity: High, given the resilience this architecture provides against IP-based blocking.
ITID-31714.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence/DNS providers for domain-level takedown, since IP blocking alone is ineffective.
indicators: DNS records for a suspicious domain with unusually short TTLs and frequently changing IPs
Large number of distinct low-reputation IPs resolving from a single domain over a short window
vectors: Botnet infrastructure purpose-built with fast-flux DNS management
Compromised domain registrar/DNS accounts used to enable fast-flux rotation
rootCauses: Lack of DNS anomaly detection (TTL/IP-churn monitoring)
Reliance on IP-based blocklists alone for C2 defense
mitreTechniques: T1568.001 Dynamic Resolution: Fast Flux DNS
controls: DNS anomaly detection (TTL/IP churn monitoring)
Domain-reputation-based blocking rather than IP-only blocking
ITID-31714.detection: DNS telemetry analysis for TTL/IP-churn patterns provides a strong, well-established detection signal.
ITID-31714.response: Block at the domain level (DNS sinkholing) rather than relying on IP blocklists, and report the domain for takedown.
metrics: Count of fast-flux botnet domains identified/sinkholed per quarter
ITID-31714.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31713 by reliance on DNS-based domain infrastructure rather than pure peer-to-peer communication; differentiated from ITID-31731 by focus on C2 resilience rather than commercialized proxy resale.

playbook.name: Response: Fast-Flux DNS Botnet Infrastructure
playbook.description: For a bot client using fast-flux DNS (rapidly rotating IP addresses behind a single domain) to evade takedown and IP-based blocking.

steps.title: Confirm fast-flux DNS behavior in the C2 domain resolution
steps.desc: Review DNS query history for the suspected C2 domain to confirm an unusually short TTL and rapidly rotating set of resolved IP addresses, consistent with fast-flux infrastructure.
steps.guidance: IP-based blocking alone will not be effective against fast-flux — confirm this pattern early so containment targets the domain, not individual IPs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed fast-flux domain and rotation pattern.

steps.title: Identify the infected endpoint(s) resolving the fast-flux domain
steps.desc: Identify which internal hosts are querying the fast-flux domain.
steps.outcome: Infected endpoints identified.

steps.title: Isolate infected endpoints
steps.desc: Network-isolate the identified hosts to stop further C2 communication.
steps.outcome: Hosts isolated.

steps.title: Block the fast-flux domain at the DNS resolver level rather than by IP
steps.desc: Since the resolved IPs rotate rapidly, block or sinkhole the domain itself at the DNS layer rather than attempting to block individual IPs.
steps.guidance: IP-only blocking will be evaded within minutes to hours as the fast-flux infrastructure rotates.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked/sinkholed at the resolver.

steps.title: Remove the bot client and its persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Uninstall/delete the bot client and remove any startup/registry persistence on the infected hosts.
steps.outcome: Bot client and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify no other hosts are resolving the fast-flux domain
steps.desc: Re-check DNS query logs organization-wide for any other host resolving the fast-flux domain.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other hosts affected, or additional hosts found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor DNS logs for renewed queries
steps.desc: Return hosts to service with continued monitoring of DNS query logs for the sinkholed domain.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the fast-flux domain and detection approach
steps.desc: Record the domain and rotation characteristics for ongoing DNS-based detection.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31715.def: An incident involving distributed botnet infrastructure, not clearly matching the IoT-recruitment, web-server-recruitment, P2P, or fast-flux DNS patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31715.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Distributed Botnets.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Distributed Botnets leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Distributed Botnets
ITID-31715.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium-High by default.
ITID-31715.escalation: Reclassify once the specific botnet architecture/recruitment vector is clarified.
indicators: Botnet-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific recruitment/architecture vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Network egress filtering and C2 domain/IP blocklisting
EDR detection of bot client processes
DDoS scrubbing/rate-limiting for outbound abuse
Threat intelligence feed-driven blocklist automation
ITID-31715.detection: Same general network/C2 telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31715.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Distributed Botnets leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31715.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Distributed Botnet
playbook.description: General response for distributed botnet infection that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm botnet C2 beacon traffic
steps.desc: Review network traffic for periodic outbound connections consistent with botnet C2 communication.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 beaconing and destination identified.

steps.title: Identify the infected endpoint and compromise vector
steps.desc: Determine which device is infected and how it was compromised.
steps.outcome: Endpoint and vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the infected device
steps.desc: Network-isolate the device to stop botnet participation.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination
steps.desc: Block the identified C2 domain/IP at the perimeter.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked.

steps.title: Remove the bot client and any persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the bot software and any startup/registry persistence, or factory reset the device if appropriate.
steps.outcome: Bot client removed.

steps.title: Harden the device against re-recruitment
steps.desc: Update credentials/firmware and close any exposed services that allowed compromise.
steps.outcome: Device hardened.

steps.title: Restore the device and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the device to service and monitor for renewed beaconing.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the compromise vector and botnet characteristics for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31721.def: A botnet whose bot nodes are tasked by their operator to harvest credentials en masse (via phishing page hosting, form-grabbing malware, or fake login pages) across multiple, unrelated victim organizations, with the botnet infrastructure and campaign orchestration as the classification focus.
ITID-31721.purpose: Captures the botnet infrastructure/operator side of a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign spanning multiple victim organizations, distinct from the credential-attack outcome itself.
scopeIncludes: Botnet C2 tasking bots to host or relay credential-phishing infrastructure across many organizations
Botnet-distributed form-grabbing/keylogging malware whose harvested-credential output is aggregated by a central operator
scopeExcludes: The distributed credential-stuffing/password-spraying attacks themselves, which are tracked as their own outcome-level leaves under the credential-attack domain (ITID-12213 Distributed/Botnet-Driven Credential Stuffing, ITID-12223 Distributed/Botnet-Driven Password Spraying) — this leaf covers the malware/botnet infrastructure enabling harvesting, not the downstream credential-testing attack pattern
Botnet nodes used purely as distributed credential-testing infrastructure without a harvesting/phishing role (ITID-31722)
ITID-31721.severity: High, given the multi-organization blast radius of a credential-harvesting botnet campaign.
ITID-31721.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active harvesting affecting the organization.
ITID-31721.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response and to any partner/customer organizations also affected by the same botnet campaign.
indicators: Bot nodes hosting phishing/credential-capture pages tied to a common C2 infrastructure
Form-grabbing malware exfiltrating captured credentials to a botnet aggregation endpoint
Correlated credential-phishing campaigns across multiple unrelated organizations sharing infrastructure
vectors: Botnet-distributed phishing kits hosted on compromised bot nodes
Form-grabbing malware bundled with a botnet's standard payload
rootCauses: Lack of cross-organization threat intelligence sharing on shared botnet infrastructure
Insufficient anti-phishing controls at the email/web gateway
mitreTechniques: T1056.002 Input Capture: GUI Input Capture
controls: Anti-phishing email/web gateway filtering
Threat intelligence sharing on known botnet infrastructure
ITID-31721.detection: Threat intelligence correlation across organizations and form-grabbing malware signatures provide the primary detection surface.
ITID-31721.response: Remediate infected/harvesting nodes, force credential resets for affected accounts, and share indicators with threat intelligence partners.
metrics: Count of credential-harvesting botnet campaigns identified per year
Number of accounts forced to reset following a campaign
ITID-31721.notes: Scope decision: this leaf and its siblings under Credential Harvesting Botnets are scoped strictly to the malware/botnet infrastructure that enables harvesting; the downstream credential-stuffing (ITID-12213) and password-spraying (ITID-12223) attack outcomes are owned by the credential-attack domain and are cross-referenced here rather than re-described.

playbook.name: Response: Botnet-Operated Mass Credential Harvesting Campaign Across Multiple Organizations
playbook.description: For an organization-owned device recruited into a botnet conducting large-scale credential harvesting (phishing relay, credential-stuffing, or keylogging aggregation) that spans multiple victim organizations.

steps.title: Confirm the device's role in the credential-harvesting botnet
steps.desc: Review network traffic and process activity to confirm the device is participating in credential-harvesting operations (phishing page hosting/relay, credential-stuffing traffic, or keylog exfiltration) rather than acting only as a generic bot.
steps.outcome: Confirmed role in the credential-harvesting operation.

steps.title: Determine whether the device is a victim, a relay, or a target of credential theft
steps.desc: Clarify whether this device's own credentials were harvested, or whether it is being used as relay/attack infrastructure against other organizations' credentials — the two require different downstream actions.
steps.guidance: Because this campaign spans multiple organizations, being a source of outbound attack traffic against third parties carries reputational and potential legal exposure that being merely a victim does not.
steps.outcome: Device's role clearly determined.

steps.title: Isolate the device from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the device immediately to stop it participating in the cross-organization campaign.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Notify legal/compliance and preserve evidence given cross-organizational impact
steps.desc: Preserve logs and notify legal/compliance, since this device may have been used to attack or harvest credentials from external organizations.
steps.outcome: Logs preserved and stakeholders notified.

steps.title: Force credential resets for any local accounts potentially exposed
steps.desc: If the device itself was a victim (e.g., its own stored credentials were harvested), force a reset of all affected account credentials.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials reset.
steps.abort: Skip if the device was purely acting as relay infrastructure with no local credential exposure.

steps.title: Remove the bot client and its persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Uninstall/delete the bot client and remove any startup/registry persistence.
steps.outcome: Bot client and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify no credential-harvesting artifacts (keylog data, phishing kit files) remain
steps.desc: Search the device for locally staged harvested-credential data or phishing kit files and securely remove any found.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or artifacts found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the device and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the device to service with elevated monitoring for renewed botnet or credential-harvesting activity.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the campaign scope and any external notification obligations
steps.desc: Record the campaign's scope, the device's role, and whether third-party notification (affected organizations, regulators) is required.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31722.def: A botnet whose nodes are tasked by their operator to serve as distributed source IPs for automated credential-testing (login attempts) against target services, with the botnet infrastructure itself — its scale, distribution, and evasion of IP-based rate limiting — as the classification focus.
ITID-31722.purpose: Captures botnet nodes used purely as distributed infrastructure to test stolen/guessed credentials at scale, distinct from the credential-testing attack pattern itself.
scopeIncludes: Botnet C2 distributing credential lists/testing tasks across bot nodes to evade per-IP rate limiting
Bot node infrastructure instrumented specifically for automated login-attempt distribution
scopeExcludes: The credential stuffing or password spraying attack pattern and its outcome/impact, tracked under ITID-12213 and ITID-12223 respectively in the credential-attack domain — this leaf covers only the botnet infrastructure enabling distributed testing, cross-referencing those leaves for the attack pattern itself
Botnet infrastructure used for harvesting new credentials via phishing rather than testing existing ones (ITID-31721)
ITID-31722.severity: High, given the account-compromise risk enabled by distributed rate-limit evasion.
ITID-31722.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active testing against organization-owned services.
ITID-31722.escalation: Escalate immediately to the identity/access management team to review affected accounts and adjust rate-limiting/anomaly detection thresholds.
indicators: Login attempts against a service originating from a large, geographically dispersed, low-reputation IP pool
Bot node C2 tasking consistent with distributed login-attempt orchestration
vectors: Botnet-as-a-service offerings marketed specifically for credential-testing distribution
Existing botnet infrastructure repurposed by its operator for a credential-testing campaign
rootCauses: Rate limiting implemented only at the per-IP level rather than per-account/behavioral level
Lack of botnet IP reputation intelligence feeds in authentication defenses
controls: Behavioral/per-account rate limiting
Botnet IP reputation feed integration with authentication systems
ITID-31722.detection: Authentication log analysis for distributed, low-per-IP-volume login attempts provides good coverage when combined with IP reputation intelligence.
ITID-31722.response: Block identified bot-node IP ranges, force credential resets/MFA enrollment for targeted accounts, and tune rate-limiting to behavioral patterns.
metrics: Count of distributed credential-testing botnet campaigns identified per year

playbook.name: Response: Botnet Nodes Used as Distributed Credential-Testing Infrastructure

steps.title: Identify the bot client and its task-distribution mechanism

steps.title: Preserve logs and notify legal/compliance

steps.title: Remove the bot client and its persistence mechanism

steps.title: Restore the device and monitor for recurrence

steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and any external notification obligations

ITID-31732.purpose: Captures botnet nodes used directly by an attacker to relay and anonymize their own malicious traffic, rather than resold as a commercial service.
scopeIncludes: Bot nodes relaying an attacker's own C2 or scanning traffic to obscure origin
Multi-hop proxy chains built from botnet infrastructure for operational anonymity
scopeExcludes: Proxy access resold commercially to third-party customers (ITID-31731)
Proxy relay used specifically for ad-fraud traffic (ITID-31733)

Outbound connections forming a proxy chain pattern inconsistent with normal device use

ITID-31733.purpose: Captures botnet proxy nodes used specifically to relay ad-fraud traffic at scale on behalf of an operator, distinguishing the infrastructure layer from single-host ad-fraud malware.
scopeIncludes: Bot nodes tasked by C2 to relay/generate ad-network traffic as part of a coordinated ad-fraud operation
Proxy infrastructure specifically monetized through distributed ad-fraud traffic generation
scopeExcludes: Single-host ad-fraud click-injection malware without a coordinated botnet relay layer (ITID-31522, tracked under Adware)
General-purpose commercial residential proxy resale not specifically tied to ad-fraud (ITID-31731)
Attacker-use relay for non-ad-fraud purposes (ITID-31732)

C2 tasking distributing ad-impression/click generation across many nodes
vectors: Botnet malware with a bundled ad-fraud relay module
Existing botnet infrastructure repurposed for an ad-fraud campaign

Reliance on ad-network-side fraud detection alone rather than endpoint controls
controls: Endpoint detection for coordinated ad-network traffic generation
Threat intelligence sharing with ad-fraud detection groups

ITID-31811.def: Metamorphic malware that rewrites its own underlying code body — instruction sequences, control flow, and logic structure — each time it propagates or replicates, rather than merely re-encrypting a static payload, so that no two generations share a meaningfully similar binary signature.
ITID-31811.purpose: Captures the most extreme form of polymorphism, where malware fully rewrites its own code logic (not just its encryption wrapper) between generations.
scopeIncludes: Malware embedding a code-mutation/rewriting engine that alters its own instruction logic each generation
Malware with no stable decryption stub or consistent static signature across samples
scopeExcludes: Malware using a consistent encryption engine to wrap an unchanged payload (polymorphic encryption, ITID-31812)
Runtime self-modification within a single execution rather than across generations (ITID-31813)
ITID-31811.severity: High, given the significant evasion of signature-based detection this technique achieves.
ITID-31811.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the metamorphic sample is confirmed to be evading the organization's primary AV/EDR signatures.
ITID-31811.escalation: Escalate to the threat intelligence/detection engineering team to develop behavioral (not signature-based) detection.
indicators: Multiple malware samples with the same behavioral fingerprint but no shared static hash/signature
Repeated AV signature misses on functionally identical malware across incidents
vectors: Malware builder kits with an integrated metamorphic engine
Self-propagating worms that rewrite themselves per infection
rootCauses: Reliance on signature-based detection without behavioral analytics
Lack of sandboxing/dynamic analysis in the detection pipeline
mitreTechniques: T1027.005 Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools
controls: Behavioral/EDR-based detection independent of static signatures
Sandboxed dynamic analysis of suspicious binaries
ITID-31811.detection: Weak for signature-based tooling; behavioral/heuristic EDR detection is required for meaningful coverage.
ITID-31811.response: Isolate affected hosts, submit samples for dynamic/behavioral analysis, and update detection rules to behavioral indicators rather than static hashes.
metrics: Count of metamorphic malware incidents per year
AV signature miss rate on confirmed metamorphic samples
detections: Behavioral EDR detection independent of static hash
ITID-31811.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by depth of mutation: full code-logic rewriting (metamorphism) rather than an unchanging payload wrapped in changing encryption (ITID-31812).

playbook.name: Response: Metamorphic Malware (Full Code Rewrite Each Generation)
playbook.description: For malware that fully rewrites its own code structure on each propagation/generation, defeating both signature and simple pattern-based detection.

steps.title: Detect the infection via behavioral/heuristic analysis rather than signature matching
steps.desc: Since each generation's code differs, confirm the infection through behavioral indicators (process behavior, network activity, file system changes) rather than relying on signature-based AV alerts.
steps.guidance: Signature detection is unreliable by design against metamorphic malware — prioritize EDR behavioral/heuristic alerts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed infection via behavior, with the current generation's file/process identified.

steps.title: Identify the propagation mechanism
steps.desc: Determine how the malware spreads/regenerates (self-replication, network share propagation, removable media) to scope containment.
steps.outcome: Propagation mechanism identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further propagation of the current generation.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Check and isolate any hosts showing early-stage behavioral indicators
steps.desc: Scan other hosts for the same behavioral pattern rather than the (unreliable) file signature, since the malware may have already regenerated on other systems.
steps.outcome: Additional affected hosts identified and isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware and confirm the FULL current variant was removed, not just the originally-detected signature
steps.desc: Because the malware may re-obfuscate itself before removal completes, verify via behavioral re-scan that no trace of the current generation remains — do not rely on a single signature-based cleanup pass.
steps.guidance: This is the critical step for metamorphic malware — a cleanup that only removes the initially-detected file can miss a variant that already regenerated.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal of the current generation via behavioral re-scan.
steps.abort: If behavioral indicators persist after removal, assume the malware regenerated and repeat identification/eradication rather than closing the incident.

steps.title: Remove persistence and check propagation targets for the same infection
steps.desc: Remove any persistence mechanism and check network shares/removable media the host had access to for onward propagation.
steps.outcome: Persistence removed and propagation targets checked.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor behaviorally for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated behavioral monitoring, since signature-based detection alone cannot be relied upon for early re-detection.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the behavioral indicators used for detection
steps.desc: Record the behavioral/heuristic indicators that led to detection, since the file signature itself will not be reusable against future generations.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31812.def: Malware in which the core malicious payload is functionally unchanged across samples, but is wrapped each time in a newly-generated encryption or packing layer (with a correspondingly mutated decryption stub), producing a different static file signature per sample while the underlying logic is identical.
ITID-31812.purpose: Captures the classic polymorphic pattern where the malicious payload logic stays constant but is wrapped in a changing encryption/packing layer to alter its signature.
scopeIncludes: Malware using a polymorphic encryption/packing engine to regenerate its wrapper per sample
Samples with a mutating decryption stub but an identical decrypted payload
scopeExcludes: Malware that rewrites its actual code logic between generations (metamorphism, ITID-31811)
Self-modifying code that changes during a single execution rather than between static samples (ITID-31813)
ITID-31812.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering to prioritize unpacking/emulation-based detection over static signatures.
indicators: Multiple samples with distinct file hashes decrypting to an identical payload hash
AV engines reporting varying detection names/generic heuristics for functionally identical malware
vectors: Commodity malware builders with an integrated polymorphic packer
Crypter-as-a-service offerings used to re-pack a known payload per distribution
rootCauses: Reliance on static file-hash-based detection
Lack of automated unpacking/emulation in the detection pipeline
mitreTechniques: T1027.002 Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
controls: Automated unpacking/emulation-based detection
Behavioral EDR detection of the decrypted payload's runtime activity
ITID-31812.detection: Moderate: emulation/unpacking-capable AV/EDR provides good coverage; pure static-hash detection is easily evaded.
ITID-31812.response: Unpack/analyze the decrypted payload, update behavioral detection to the payload's runtime activity rather than the wrapper's signature.
metrics: Count of polymorphic-packer incidents per quarter
Number of distinct wrapper hashes mapped to a single payload family
ITID-31812.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31811 by what changes: only the encryption/packing wrapper mutates here, while the underlying payload logic remains constant.

playbook.name: Response: Polymorphic Encryption Engine Malware (Same Logic, Changing Signature)
playbook.description: For malware using a polymorphic encryption/packing engine to change its file signature on each infection while retaining the same underlying malicious logic.

steps.title: Detect the infection via behavioral/heuristic analysis rather than signature matching
steps.desc: Confirm the infection using behavioral analysis and generic unpacking/decryption-in-memory detection, since the on-disk signature changes on each infection.
steps.guidance: EDR heuristics targeting the decryption stub behavior are typically more reliable than static signatures here.
steps.outcome: Confirmed infection via behavior/heuristics, with the current packed sample identified.

steps.title: Identify the underlying malware family behind the polymorphic wrapper
steps.desc: Where feasible, unpack/analyze the sample in a controlled environment to identify the constant underlying malicious logic beneath the changing encryption layer.
steps.outcome: Underlying malware family identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further activity or propagation.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware and verify the FULL current variant was removed
steps.desc: Confirm via behavioral re-scan that no trace of the current polymorphic variant remains, since the malware may re-encrypt/repack itself before cleanup completes.
steps.guidance: Do not rely solely on removing the originally-flagged file — verify with a behavioral check, not just a repeat signature scan.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal via behavioral re-scan.
steps.abort: If behavioral indicators persist, assume the malware has re-packed itself and repeat eradication.

steps.title: Remove persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Locate and remove any startup, scheduled task, or registry persistence associated with the malware.
steps.outcome: Persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor behaviorally for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated behavioral monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the underlying family and detection approach
steps.desc: Record the underlying malware family (if identified) and the behavioral indicators used for detection, since the packed signature will not recur.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31813.def: Malware that modifies its own executing code in memory during a single run (e.g. rewriting instructions after execution, decrypting/re-encrypting sections on the fly) to defeat memory-scanning and step-through analysis, independent of any variation between separate distributed samples.
ITID-31813.purpose: Captures malware that alters its own code in memory while running, as a within-execution evasion technique distinct from between-sample mutation.
scopeIncludes: Malware that decrypts, executes, and re-encrypts sections of its own code at runtime
Self-patching code designed to defeat live memory scanning or debugging
scopeExcludes: Between-sample code mutation across generations (metamorphism, ITID-31811)
Between-sample wrapper/encryption mutation (ITID-31812)
ITID-31813.severity: High, given the anti-analysis sophistication this technique implies.
ITID-31813.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if paired with an active C2 channel.
ITID-31813.escalation: Escalate to a malware reverse-engineering resource for full capability analysis given the anti-analysis techniques in use.
indicators: Memory scan showing code sections with mismatched executable content between successive snapshots
EDR alert on self-modifying code / runtime code-page permission changes
vectors: Advanced loaders/packers with a self-modifying runtime stage
Malware frameworks designed specifically to defeat memory-forensic tooling
rootCauses: Lack of runtime memory integrity monitoring
Insufficient reverse-engineering capacity to analyze self-modifying samples
controls: EDR runtime memory integrity/permission-change monitoring
Sandboxed dynamic analysis resilient to anti-debugging
ITID-31813.detection: Requires memory-aware EDR with runtime integrity checks; static analysis alone provides essentially no coverage.
ITID-31813.response: Capture a live memory image for forensic analysis, isolate the host, and engage reverse engineering for full capability assessment.
metrics: Count of self-modifying-code detections per year
ITID-31813.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by scope: within-single-execution self-modification, not between-sample mutation across distributed generations.

playbook.name: Response: Self-Modifying Code at Runtime
playbook.description: For malware that modifies its own in-memory code during execution to evade static analysis and signature detection.

steps.title: Detect via runtime behavioral/heuristic and memory-scanning telemetry
steps.desc: Confirm the infection through EDR behavioral alerts and memory-scanning telemetry capable of observing runtime self-modification, rather than static file analysis.
steps.guidance: Static analysis of the on-disk file will often appear benign or inconclusive — the malicious behavior only manifests at runtime.
steps.outcome: Confirmed self-modifying behavior and the affected process identified.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the malware was initially launched.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process to clear the currently-modified in-memory code
steps.desc: Kill the running process, since the self-modified code exists in memory and cannot be selectively cleaned.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Remove the on-disk loader/dropper and verify the FULL current variant was removed
steps.desc: Remove the file that launches the self-modifying code and confirm via behavioral re-scan that no trace of the runtime-modified variant persists.
steps.guidance: Because the malware may have already re-modified itself, confirm removal behaviorally rather than assuming a single cleanup pass is sufficient.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal via behavioral re-scan.
steps.abort: If behavioral indicators persist, repeat eradication.

steps.title: Remove persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Locate and remove any startup/registry/scheduled task persistence.
steps.outcome: Persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor behaviorally for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated behavioral/memory-scan monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the runtime behavior observed
steps.desc: Record the self-modification technique and detection indicators used.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Code-Altering Malware leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Code-Altering Malware
ITID-31814.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium-High by default.
ITID-31814.escalation: Reclassify once the specific code-alteration technique is clarified.
indicators: Code-altering malware alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific mutation vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Behavioral/heuristic EDR detection rather than signature-only scanning
Application allowlisting
Endpoint protection with machine-learning-based malware detection
Network egress filtering for C2 detection
ITID-31814.detection: Same general behavioral/EDR telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31814.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Code-Altering Malware leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31814.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

steps.title: Detect via behavioral/heuristic analysis rather than signature matching

steps.outcome: Confirmed infection via behavior.

steps.desc: Confirm via behavioral re-scan that no trace of the current code-altered variant remains, since the malware may have already changed form again.
steps.guidance: Do not rely on a single signature-based cleanup pass.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal via behavioral re-scan.
steps.abort: If behavioral indicators persist, repeat eradication.

steps.desc: Locate and remove any startup/registry/scheduled task persistence.
steps.outcome: Persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor behaviorally for recurrence

steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

ITID-31821.def: A malicious script whose payload is obfuscated primarily through a single layer of standard encoding (such as Base64), decoded at runtime by the interpreter before execution, to evade simple string/pattern-matching detection.
ITID-31821.purpose: Captures scripts using simple encoding (e.g. Base64) as their primary obfuscation layer to evade static content inspection.
scopeIncludes: Scripts with a Base64 (or similar single-layer) encoded payload decoded and executed at runtime
Simple encoding used as the sole or primary obfuscation technique
scopeExcludes: Scripts using multiple nested layers of obfuscation/encoding (ITID-31822)
Scripts obfuscated via string encryption or junk-code insertion rather than simple encoding (ITID-31823)
ITID-31821.severity: Medium, since this is a relatively unsophisticated and detectable obfuscation technique.
ITID-31821.escalation: Escalate if the decoded payload is confirmed to be a loader for a more capable second-stage tool.
indicators: Script containing a long Base64-like string passed to a decode function immediately before execution
AMSI/script-block logging revealing decoded content matching known malicious patterns
vectors: Phishing-delivered scripts with Base64-encoded payloads
Malicious macros dropping a Base64-encoded PowerShell command
rootCauses: Lack of AMSI/decode-aware script inspection
Insufficient script execution logging
controls: AMSI integration with EDR for decode-aware inspection
Script block logging
ITID-31821.detection: Strong: AMSI-integrated tooling reliably decodes and inspects this class of obfuscation.
ITID-31821.response: Decode and analyze the payload, block the delivery vector, and verify no further-stage payload executed successfully.
metrics: Count of simple-encoded script detections per month
ITID-31821.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by obfuscation depth: a single, simple encoding layer rather than nested multi-layer (ITID-31822) or string-encryption/junk-code techniques (ITID-31823).

playbook.name: Response: Base64/Encoded Payload Obfuscated Script
playbook.description: For a malicious script (PowerShell, JavaScript, VBScript) using Base64 or similar simple encoding to obscure its command content from static/signature detection.

steps.title: Detect and decode the obfuscated script via behavioral/heuristic telemetry
steps.desc: Identify the encoded script execution through EDR/script-block logging and decode the Base64/encoded content to reveal the actual command.
steps.guidance: Script-block logging typically captures the de-obfuscated command even when the on-disk/command-line form is encoded.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious script activity with the decoded command content understood.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the encoded script was delivered and triggered (email attachment, macro, LOLBin chain).
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process and remove its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Kill the running process and remove whatever triggers it (scheduled task, registry run key, malicious document).
steps.outcome: Process terminated and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload referenced by the decoded command was staged
steps.desc: Based on the decoded command content, check whether it downloaded or executed a further payload before containment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the obfuscation technique and delivery vector
steps.desc: Record the encoding scheme and delivery vector for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31822.def: A malicious script obfuscated through several nested layers of encoding, compression, and/or encryption, such that each layer must be decoded in sequence to reveal the next, significantly raising the effort required for static or automated analysis compared to single-layer encoding.
ITID-31822.purpose: Captures scripts using multiple nested layers of obfuscation/encoding, requiring iterative decoding to reach the underlying payload.
scopeIncludes: Scripts requiring iterative/recursive decoding through multiple distinct obfuscation layers
Combination of compression plus encoding plus encryption applied in sequence to a single payload
scopeExcludes: Single-layer simple encoding (ITID-31821)
Obfuscation achieved through string encryption/junk code insertion rather than layered encoding (ITID-31823)
ITID-31822.severity: Medium-High, given the increased evasion effectiveness of layered obfuscation.
ITID-31822.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering/reverse engineering if automated decoding tools fail to fully unwrap the payload.
indicators: Script producing further encoded content upon initial decode, requiring repeated deobfuscation passes
AMSI/EDR flagging content only after multiple decode iterations
vectors: Commercial obfuscation/crypter services applying multiple obfuscation passes
Malware builder kits with layered obfuscation as a default feature
rootCauses: Detection tooling limited to single-pass decoding
Lack of automated iterative deobfuscation in the analysis pipeline
controls: Iterative/recursive deobfuscation capability in EDR or sandbox tooling
Behavioral detection of the fully-decoded payload's runtime activity
ITID-31822.detection: Moderate: requires sandbox/EDR tooling capable of iterative deobfuscation; single-pass tools may miss the final payload.
ITID-31822.response: Fully deobfuscate the payload through all layers, analyze the final content, and block the delivery vector.
metrics: Count of multi-layer obfuscated script detections per quarter
ITID-31822.notes: Differentiated from ITID-31821 by obfuscation depth: multiple nested layers rather than a single encoding pass.

playbook.name: Response: Multi-Layer/Nested Obfuscated Script
playbook.description: For a malicious script using multiple nested layers of encoding/obfuscation (e.g., Base64 wrapped in compression wrapped in string reversal) to resist automated de-obfuscation and detection.

steps.title: Detect via behavioral telemetry and fully de-obfuscate all layers
steps.desc: Identify the script's execution via EDR/script-block logging and work through each obfuscation layer to reveal the final executed command — do not stop at the first decoded layer if further nesting is present.
steps.guidance: Confirm de-obfuscation is complete by checking the final decoded content is directly executable/interpretable, not itself still encoded.
steps.outcome: Fully de-obfuscated command content understood.
steps.tool: PowerShell script-block logging / EDR / manual de-obfuscation

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the script was delivered and triggered.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process and remove its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Kill the running process and remove whatever triggers it.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload from the fully de-obfuscated command was staged
steps.desc: Based on the fully decoded command, check whether a further payload was downloaded or executed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the nested obfuscation technique
steps.desc: Record the full layering scheme observed, since detection tooling may need to be tuned to unwrap multiple layers rather than just one.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31823.def: A malicious script that obfuscates its intent by encrypting embedded strings (function names, URLs, commands) resolved only at runtime, and/or by inserting large amounts of non-functional junk code to defeat readability-based static analysis and pattern matching.
ITID-31823.purpose: Captures scripts obfuscated primarily through string encryption and junk/dead code insertion rather than encoding-based techniques.
scopeIncludes: Scripts with runtime string-decryption routines protecting key indicators (URLs, commands, API names)
Scripts padded with substantial dead/junk code to obscure the functional logic
scopeExcludes: Simple single-layer encoding of the entire payload (ITID-31821)
Multi-layer nested encoding/compression obfuscation (ITID-31822)
ITID-31823.escalation: Escalate to reverse engineering if the string-encryption routine resists automated deobfuscation.
indicators: Script containing a custom string-decryption function called repeatedly at runtime
Unusually high ratio of non-functional to functional code in a flagged script
vectors: Obfuscator toolkits applying string encryption and junk-code insertion as a bundled feature
Malware developers manually obfuscating strings to evade static YARA-style rules
rootCauses: Detection reliant on static string/pattern matching without runtime resolution
Lack of dynamic analysis capability in the detection pipeline
mitreTechniques: T1027.010 Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
controls: Dynamic/sandbox analysis resolving runtime string decryption
Behavioral detection independent of static string matching
ITID-31823.detection: Moderate: static signature detection is largely defeated; sandbox/dynamic analysis is needed to resolve true indicators.
ITID-31823.response: Run the script in a sandbox to resolve decrypted strings/true indicators, then block the resolved infrastructure and update detection rules.
metrics: Count of string-encryption/junk-code obfuscated script detections per quarter
ITID-31823.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by obfuscation technique: string-level encryption and structural junk-code insertion rather than whole-payload encoding (ITID-31821/31822).

playbook.name: Response: String Encryption/Junk Code Obfuscated Script
playbook.description: For a malicious script using string encryption and inserted junk/dead code to defeat static analysis and pattern matching while remaining functionally identical.

steps.title: Detect via behavioral telemetry and isolate the functional command from junk code
steps.desc: Confirm the script's malicious activity via EDR/script-block logging and strip inserted junk/dead code to isolate the actual functional command sequence.
steps.guidance: Junk code is designed to defeat pattern matching, not behavior — rely on what the script actually does at runtime.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious activity with the functional command sequence isolated from junk code.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the script was delivered and triggered.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process and remove its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Kill the running process and remove whatever triggers it.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload was staged
steps.desc: Based on the isolated functional command, check whether a further payload was downloaded or executed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the obfuscation technique
steps.desc: Record the string-encryption/junk-code pattern for detection rule tuning based on behavior rather than static content.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31824.def: An incident involving an obfuscated malicious script, not clearly matching the simple-encoding, multi-layer, or string-encryption/junk-code patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31824.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Obfuscated Scripts.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Obfuscated Scripts leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Obfuscated Scripts
ITID-31824.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium by default.
ITID-31824.escalation: Reclassify once the specific obfuscation technique is clarified.
indicators: Obfuscated script alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific obfuscation vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Script block logging and deobfuscation analysis (PowerShell/JavaScript)
Application control restricting script execution
EDR behavioral detection of obfuscated script execution
Email/web gateway sandboxing
ITID-31824.detection: Same general script-inspection telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-31824.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Obfuscated Scripts leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31824.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Obfuscated Script
playbook.description: General response for an obfuscated malicious script that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Detect and de-obfuscate the script via behavioral telemetry
steps.desc: Confirm the script's malicious activity via EDR/script-block logging and de-obfuscate its content to understand the actual command executed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious activity with de-obfuscated content understood.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution vector
steps.desc: Determine how the script was delivered and triggered.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process and remove its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Kill the running process and remove whatever triggers it.
steps.outcome: Process terminated and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify no additional payload was staged
steps.desc: Check whether the script downloaded or executed a further payload before containment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional payload found and removed.

steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

ITID-31831.def: Malware delivery in which the final payload is dynamically generated on a remote/attacker-controlled server at the moment of each download request, so every retrieved instance is uniquely built and no static signature can match more than one download.
ITID-31831.purpose: Captures malware whose payload is generated fresh on the attacker's server for each retrieval, so no two downloads are ever identical (server-side polymorphism).
scopeIncludes: Payloads built per-request by a remote server (server-side polymorphic engines)
Delivery infrastructure that guarantees each downloaded sample is functionally equivalent but bytewise unique
scopeExcludes: Payload variation driven by client-side sandbox/environment detection rather than server-side generation (ITID-31832)
Payloads decrypted only in memory at execution but identical across downloads (ITID-31833)
ITID-31831.severity: High, since this defeats hash-based threat intelligence sharing between organizations.
ITID-31831.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the downloaded payload executes successfully.
ITID-31831.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence to share the delivery infrastructure indicator (URL/domain) rather than relying on file-hash sharing, which is ineffective here.
indicators: Repeated downloads from the same URL yielding files with different hashes each time
Delivery server responding differently to sequential identical requests
vectors: Malware-as-a-service platforms with server-side polymorphic payload generation
Exploit kits generating a unique payload per victim session
rootCauses: Reliance on file-hash-based threat intelligence and blocklists
Lack of URL/domain-based blocking for known delivery infrastructure
controls: URL/domain-based blocking of delivery infrastructure
Behavioral detection of the downloaded payload's runtime activity
ITID-31831.detection: Weak for hash-based tooling; URL/domain reputation and behavioral detection provide the meaningful coverage here.
ITID-31831.response: Block the delivery URL/domain, analyze the retrieved payload behaviorally, and share the infrastructure indicator rather than a file hash.
metrics: Count of server-side polymorphic delivery incidents per quarter
ITID-31831.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by where the variation is introduced: server-side, at generation time, rather than client-side branching (ITID-31832) or in-memory-only decryption of an otherwise-static payload (ITID-31833).

playbook.name: Response: Runtime-Generated Payload from Remote Server (Server-Side Polymorphism)
playbook.description: For malware whose actual payload is generated uniquely per-request by a remote server (server-side polymorphism), meaning no two downloaded copies are identical.

steps.title: Confirm behaviorally that the payload was retrieved from a payload-generation server
steps.desc: Identify the download/retrieval request and confirm via network telemetry that the payload came from a server known/suspected to generate unique payloads per request.
steps.guidance: Do not expect the retrieved file's hash to match any known-bad hash — identification must rely on the retrieval behavior and destination, not file signature.
steps.outcome: Confirmed retrieval from a payload-generation server and the destination identified.

steps.title: Analyze the retrieved payload's behavior
steps.desc: Analyze the specific retrieved payload's runtime behavior in a controlled environment, since its code content will differ from any other downloaded instance.
steps.outcome: Payload behavior and capability understood.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further payload retrieval or C2 communication.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Block the payload-generation server destination
steps.desc: Block the identified domain/IP at the network perimeter to protect other hosts, even though future payloads from it would also be unique.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked.

steps.title: Remove the retrieved payload and its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Delete the downloaded payload and remove whatever triggered its retrieval and execution.
steps.outcome: Payload and launch mechanism removed.

steps.title: Verify complete removal via behavioral re-scan rather than signature match
steps.desc: Confirm no trace of the specific retrieved variant remains, using behavioral indicators rather than a signature that will not recur.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for renewed retrieval attempts
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring of the blocked destination and related behavior.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the retrieval infrastructure and behavior
steps.desc: Record the payload-generation server and the observed retrieval/behavior pattern for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31832.def: Malware that inspects its execution environment at runtime (checking for sandbox/VM artifacts, analysis tools, or debugger presence) and branches its behavior accordingly — running benign or dormant when analysis is detected, and executing the malicious payload only in what it assesses to be a genuine target environment.
ITID-31832.purpose: Captures malware that selects among multiple payload behaviors at runtime based on detecting whether it is in a sandbox/analysis environment.
scopeIncludes: Malware performing sandbox/VM/analysis-tool fingerprinting before deciding whether to execute its payload
Environment-aware branching logic that suppresses malicious behavior under observed analysis conditions
scopeExcludes: Payload generated fresh per download on the server side (ITID-31831)
Payload encrypted and decrypted only in memory but not conditionally branching on environment (ITID-31833)
ITID-31832.severity: High, since successful evasion of automated sandboxing significantly delays detection.
ITID-31832.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if confirmed to have evaded the organization's sandbox and executed on a production endpoint.
ITID-31832.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering to harden sandbox environments against the specific fingerprinting technique observed.
indicators: Sample behaving benignly in an automated sandbox but flagged malicious via endpoint EDR on real hardware
Code performing checks for known VM artifacts, analysis tool processes, or unusual system characteristics before proceeding
vectors: Malware builder kits with built-in anti-sandbox/anti-analysis modules
Targeted malware designed to evade a specific known analysis environment
rootCauses: Sandbox environments with detectable VM/analysis artifacts
Lack of endpoint-level behavioral detection to catch what the sandbox missed
controls: Sandbox environment hardening against fingerprinting
Endpoint behavioral detection as a backstop to sandbox analysis
ITID-31832.detection: Weak in automated sandboxes vulnerable to fingerprinting; endpoint EDR behavioral detection provides the necessary backstop.
ITID-31832.response: Analyze the evasion technique to harden sandbox detection, and rely on endpoint behavioral detection for hosts where the sample executed.
metrics: Count of sandbox-evasion-confirmed incidents per quarter
detections: Endpoint behavioral detection as sandbox backstop
ITID-31832.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by mechanism: client-side environment-aware branching, rather than server-side per-download generation (ITID-31831) or memory-only decryption without environment branching (ITID-31833).

playbook.name: Response: Environment-Aware Payload Selection (Sandbox/AV-Evasion Branching)
playbook.description: For malware that inspects its execution environment and selectively withholds or alters its malicious behavior when it detects a sandbox, analysis tool, or AV presence.

steps.title: Confirm environment-aware evasion behavior
steps.desc: Identify evidence the malware performed environment checks (VM/sandbox artifact detection, analysis tool/process enumeration, timing checks) before deciding whether to execute its full payload.
steps.guidance: A sandbox detonation report showing benign behavior does not mean the sample is benign — cross-check against endpoint telemetry from the real (non-sandboxed) execution.
steps.outcome: Confirmed environment-aware behavior and the real-environment payload activity identified.

steps.title: Identify what the malware actually did on the real (non-sandboxed) endpoint
steps.desc: Since sandbox analysis may show no malicious activity, rely on endpoint telemetry from the actual affected host to determine the true payload behavior.
steps.outcome: Real-environment behavior identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host based on the confirmed real-environment behavior.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware and its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the responsible process/file and its persistence, based on real-environment findings rather than sandbox results.
steps.outcome: Malware and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify complete removal via endpoint behavioral re-scan
steps.desc: Confirm removal using the real endpoint's telemetry, not a sandbox re-detonation which may again show false-benign results.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal on the actual endpoint.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the evasion technique and note sandbox analysis limitations
steps.desc: Record the environment-detection technique observed, and flag that sandbox-only analysis is unreliable for this family — endpoint telemetry should be the source of truth.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31833.def: Malware that stores its payload encrypted on disk or in a delivery artifact, decrypting it only into memory at the point of execution and never writing the decrypted plaintext payload back to disk, so static analysis of the at-rest artifact reveals no usable indicators.
ITID-31833.purpose: Captures malware whose payload remains encrypted at rest and is decrypted only in memory at the moment of execution, as a distinct technique from environment-branching or server-side generation.
scopeIncludes: Payloads stored encrypted at rest with decryption performed exclusively in memory just before execution
Loaders whose sole function is to decrypt and execute an in-memory payload without ever persisting the decrypted form
scopeExcludes: Environment-aware conditional payload branching (ITID-31832)
Server-side per-download payload generation (ITID-31831)
ITID-31833.severity: High, given the combination of static-analysis evasion and memory-only execution.
ITID-31833.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the decrypted payload is confirmed to be a C2 implant or destructive tool.
ITID-31833.escalation: Escalate to incident response for memory forensics given the payload is unrecoverable from disk alone.
indicators: High-entropy encrypted blob present in a delivered artifact with no corresponding plaintext on disk
Loader process performing an in-memory decrypt-and-execute sequence
vectors: Crypter/loader combinations bundling an encrypted payload with a small decryption stub
Multi-stage droppers retrieving an encrypted blob for local in-memory decryption
rootCauses: Lack of memory-scanning EDR capability
Static-analysis-only detection pipeline unable to recover the decrypted payload
controls: EDR memory-scanning capable of catching the decrypted payload in memory
Sandbox dynamic analysis capturing the in-memory decryption event
ITID-31833.detection: Weak for static/disk-based analysis; requires memory-aware EDR or dynamic sandbox analysis to recover the true payload.
ITID-31833.response: Capture a memory image at the point of decryption/execution for forensic analysis, and identify the loader's delivery vector.
metrics: Count of memory-only-decryption payload incidents per quarter
ITID-31833.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by mechanism: this leaf covers static-at-rest encryption with in-memory-only decryption, distinct from environment-conditional branching (ITID-31832) or server-side per-request generation (ITID-31831).

playbook.name: Response: Encrypted Payload Decrypted Only in Memory at Execution
playbook.description: For malware storing its payload in encrypted form on disk (or in the registry) and decrypting it only in memory at execution time, leaving no plaintext artifact for static scanning.

steps.title: Confirm decryption-at-execution behavior via memory-scanning telemetry
steps.desc: Since the on-disk artifact is encrypted and inert to static scanning, confirm the malicious behavior via EDR memory-scan detection of the decrypted payload at runtime.
steps.guidance: A file-based AV scan of the encrypted artifact will typically return clean — rely on memory/behavioral telemetry.
steps.outcome: Confirmed decryption-at-execution behavior and the decrypted payload's function identified.

steps.title: Locate the encrypted artifact and its decryption launcher
steps.desc: Identify the on-disk/registry-stored encrypted blob and the small launcher/loader responsible for decrypting and executing it.
steps.outcome: Encrypted artifact and launcher identified.
steps.tool: EDR / file system and registry review

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to prevent further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Terminate the process to clear the decrypted in-memory payload
steps.desc: Kill the running process hosting the decrypted payload.
steps.outcome: Process terminated.

steps.title: Remove the encrypted artifact and its decryption launcher
steps.desc: Delete both the encrypted blob (file or registry value) and the launcher that decrypts it — removing only one leaves the other capable of re-establishing the infection.
steps.outcome: Both the encrypted artifact and launcher removed.

steps.title: Remove any persistence mechanism triggering the launcher
steps.desc: Locate and remove any scheduled task, run key, or service that triggers the launcher.
steps.outcome: Persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated memory-scan monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the storage/decryption technique
steps.desc: Record where the encrypted payload was stored and how it was decrypted, for detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-31834.def: An incident involving a dynamically-generated or environment-aware polymorphic payload, not clearly matching the server-side-generation, sandbox-evasion, or memory-only-decryption patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
ITID-31834.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under Dynamic Payloads.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific Dynamic Payloads leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Dynamic Payloads
ITID-31834.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High by default given the technique class's typical severity.
ITID-31834.escalation: Reclassify once the specific dynamic-payload technique is clarified.
indicators: Dynamic payload alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific dynamic-payload vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: EDR with behavioral/heuristic detection for staged payload delivery
Network egress filtering and sandboxing of downloaded payloads
Application allowlisting
Endpoint protection with machine-learning detection

ITID-31834.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific Dynamic Payloads leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-31834.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Dynamic Payload Malware
playbook.description: General response for dynamic-payload (runtime-generated, environment-aware, or memory-decrypted) malware that does not fit a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious activity via behavioral/memory-scanning telemetry
steps.desc: Confirm the infection using EDR behavioral/memory-scan telemetry, since the payload's static form may not be reliably detectable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious activity and affected process identified.

steps.title: Identify the initial execution/delivery vector
steps.desc: Determine how the payload was delivered and triggered.
steps.outcome: Initial vector identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host to stop further malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Host isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware and its persistence/launch mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the responsible artifact/process and its persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Malware and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify complete removal via behavioral re-scan
steps.desc: Confirm no trace of the malicious activity remains, using behavioral rather than purely signature-based verification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed complete removal.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to service with elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the technique observed
