steps.outcome: Message purged; infrastructure blocked; monitoring in place for re-registration.
steps.tool: Email security gateway / web proxy / domain monitoring

steps.title: Review affected accounts for unauthorized activity
steps.desc: Audit affected accounts for unauthorized logins, mail-forwarding rules, or actions taken before containment.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized activity identified and remediated.

steps.title: Restore accounts and apply elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Return accounts to normal use and monitor for further suspicious activity, including new lookalike-domain campaigns.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and share IOCs with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Record the infrastructure pattern and share IOCs to improve detection of related lookalike domains.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32733.def: A phishing attack built by reusing a phishing kit template that has been leaked, open-sourced, or is otherwise freely circulating (e.g., posted on public code-sharing sites or underground forums at no cost), self-hosted by the attacker with no ongoing vendor relationship or purchased bundle.
ITID-32733.purpose: Captures use of a freely available, open-source, or previously leaked phishing kit template reused without any commercial transaction.
scopeIncludes: Reuse of a publicly leaked or open-source phishing kit template with attacker-sourced hosting
Widely recognized 'commodity' free templates found in public repositories
scopeExcludes: Ongoing subscription-model PhaaS (ITID-32731)
One-time purchased bundle with dedicated hosting (ITID-32732)
ITID-32733.severity: Medium — typically less sophisticated and more easily fingerprinted than commercial/maintained kits, but still effective given low attacker cost.
ITID-32733.priority: P2, escalating to P1 upon confirmed successful credential harvest.
ITID-32733.escalation: Escalate to IR upon confirmed credential compromise.
indicators: Phishing page source code matching a publicly known leaked/open-source kit template
Self-hosted infrastructure with no bulletproof-hosting or subscription-service indicators
vectors: Email lure directing victims to a self-hosted page built from a freely available template
Reuse of a widely circulated template with minimal modification, making it easily fingerprinted
rootCauses: Low barrier to entry from freely available phishing templates
Insufficient anti-phishing/MFA coverage on targeted accounts
controls: Known-template fingerprint matching in web/email filtering
Phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-32733.detection: Known public template fingerprint matching provides strong technical signal, as these templates are typically well-documented in threat intelligence.
ITID-32733.response: Reset compromised credentials and report the self-hosted infrastructure for takedown.
metrics: Count of leaked/open-source template phishing incidents per quarter
detections: Known public phishing template fingerprint alerting
ITID-32733.notes: Differentiated from the two commercial siblings by the absence of any purchase or subscription relationship; the template is free and self-hosted.

playbook.name: Response: Open-Source/Leaked Phishing Kit Template Reuse
playbook.description: For a confirmed phishing attack using a freely available, open-source, or leaked phishing kit template, commonly reused with minimal modification by low-resourced or opportunistic attackers.

steps.title: Confirm the kit template and identify reused artifacts
steps.desc: Analyze the phishing page source/behavior to confirm it matches a known publicly available or leaked template, noting any distinctive reused artifacts (comments, file paths, panel URLs) useful for detection.
steps.outcome: Template match confirmed with reusable detection artifacts noted.
steps.abort: If the page was blocked before any credential entry, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all recipients and any who submitted credentials
steps.desc: Search mail logs for all recipients of the phishing message and correlate with web/proxy logs to identify who reached the page and who submitted credentials.
steps.outcome: Full affected-user population identified.

steps.title: Force-reset credentials and sessions for anyone who submitted data
steps.desc: Immediately reset passwords and revoke active sessions/tokens for every user who submitted credentials.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts secured.

steps.title: Purge the message and block the phishing infrastructure
steps.desc: Remove the phishing email from all mailboxes and block the phishing page domain and hosting infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Message purged; phishing infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Review affected accounts for unauthorized activity
steps.desc: Audit affected accounts for unauthorized logins, mail-forwarding rules, or actions taken before containment.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized activity identified and remediated.

steps.title: Restore accounts and apply elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Return accounts to normal use and monitor for further suspicious activity.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and add detection signatures for the reused template
steps.desc: Record the template's distinctive artifacts and add detection signatures, since the same publicly available template is likely to reappear in future campaigns.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and detection signature added.

ITID-32734.def: An incident involving a phishing/social engineering kit, not clearly matching subscription PhaaS, bundled-purchase, or leaked/free template leaves.
ITID-32734.purpose: Catch-all for social engineering kit incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific social engineering kit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32731-32733)
ITID-32734.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32734.escalation: Reclassify once the specific kit commercial model is clarified.
indicators: Phishing-kit-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Phishing kit of unclear specific origin
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Security awareness training against social engineering
Email/web gateway phishing detection
Multi-factor authentication to limit credential-theft impact
Brand/domain monitoring for lookalike phishing kits
ITID-32734.detection: Same general phishing-infrastructure telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32734.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32734.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Social Engineering Kit
playbook.description: For a confirmed phishing-kit-as-a-service attack that does not fit a more specific commercial-subscription, bundled-infrastructure, or open-source-template classification.

steps.title: Confirm the kit and its capabilities
steps.desc: Analyze the phishing page/infrastructure to characterize the kit's capabilities (credential harvesting, MFA relay/bypass, session-token theft); reclassify to a more specific playbook if the kit's provenance becomes clear.
steps.outcome: Kit capability confirmed.
steps.abort: If the page was blocked before any credential entry, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all recipients and any who submitted credentials
steps.desc: Search mail logs for all recipients of the phishing message and correlate with web/proxy logs to identify who reached the page and who submitted credentials.
steps.outcome: Full affected-user population identified.

steps.title: Force-reset credentials and sessions for anyone who submitted data
steps.desc: Immediately reset passwords and revoke active sessions/tokens for every user who submitted credentials.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts secured.

steps.title: Purge the message and block the phishing infrastructure
steps.desc: Remove the phishing email from all mailboxes and block the phishing page domain and hosting infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Message purged; phishing infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Review affected accounts for unauthorized activity
steps.desc: Audit affected accounts for unauthorized logins, mail-forwarding rules, or actions taken before containment.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized activity identified and remediated.

steps.title: Restore accounts and apply elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Return accounts to normal use and monitor for further suspicious activity.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record findings about the kit and campaign for future correlation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32811.def: Exploitation of a documented vulnerability (with an assigned CVE) in the firmware of a consumer-grade IoT device, achieving code execution, privilege escalation, or persistence on the device via a known, previously patched-or-patchable flaw.
ITID-32811.purpose: Captures exploitation of a known, publicly disclosed CVE in the firmware of a consumer IoT device.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a specific, named firmware CVE against an unpatched consumer IoT device
Remote or local firmware vulnerability exploitation with a public exploit or proof-of-concept available
scopeExcludes: Exploitation via unsigned/unverified firmware update mechanisms (ITID-32812)
Firmware downgrade/rollback attacks (ITID-32813)
ITID-32811.severity: High — often grants full device compromise, and unpatched consumer IoT devices frequently lack timely vendor patching.
ITID-32811.priority: P1 for internet-facing/critical devices; P2 for isolated consumer devices on a segmented network.
ITID-32811.escalation: Escalate to IR upon confirmation; escalate to asset owners to patch or replace the affected device class.
indicators: Device exhibiting anomalous outbound traffic consistent with post-exploitation C2
Firmware version confirmed vulnerable to a known CVE via inventory/scanning
Exploit traffic pattern matching a public proof-of-concept for a known IoT CVE
vectors: Direct exploitation of an internet-exposed or internally-reachable vulnerable device
Automated scanning tools targeting known IoT firmware CVEs at scale
rootCauses: Vendor delay or absence of firmware patch availability
Lack of asset inventory/patch tracking for IoT device firmware versions
controls: IoT asset inventory with firmware version tracking
Network segmentation isolating IoT devices from critical infrastructure
Timely firmware patch deployment where available
ITID-32811.detection: Network-based IDS signatures for known exploit traffic and firmware-version inventory scanning provide meaningful technical coverage.
ITID-32811.response: Isolate the affected device, patch or replace it, and assess for lateral movement from the compromised device.
metrics: Count of vulnerable IoT firmware versions identified per scan cycle
Mean time to patch/replace after CVE disclosure
detections: Known IoT exploit traffic signature alerting
ITID-32811.notes: Scoped to exploitation of a known-CVE vulnerability inherent to the firmware code itself, distinct from update-mechanism and downgrade-specific leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Known-CVE Consumer IoT Firmware Vulnerability Exploitation
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation of a known, published CVE in the firmware of a consumer IoT device (camera, router, smart-home hub, etc.) connected to the network.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation via network-level detection
steps.desc: Since IoT devices typically have limited or no local logging, confirm exploitation primarily via network telemetry (IDS/NetFlow, unusual outbound connections, traffic matching the known CVE's exploitation pattern) rather than device-side logs.
steps.outcome: Exploitation confirmed via network evidence and the specific CVE identified.
steps.abort: If network telemetry shows the exploit attempt failed or was blocked, downgrade to a near-miss.
steps.tool: Network IDS / NetFlow / firmware CVE database

steps.title: Identify all devices running the vulnerable firmware version
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same model/firmware version, since one exploited device usually indicates a broader vulnerable population.
steps.outcome: Full population of vulnerable devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device(s)
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device(s) onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect them, since most consumer IoT devices lack an EDR agent for host-based containment.
steps.outcome: Affected device(s) isolated from the network.

steps.title: Segment the broader vulnerable device population
steps.desc: Move all devices running the same vulnerable firmware to a restricted network segment pending patching.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable population segmented.

steps.title: Apply the firmware patch or replace the device
steps.desc: Update affected devices to the patched firmware version; if no patch is available, replace the device or maintain permanent network isolation.
steps.outcome: Devices patched or replaced/permanently isolated.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return patched devices to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Devices restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT patch-management process
steps.desc: Record the CVE and assess whether the organization's IoT asset inventory and firmware patch-management process needs improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32812.def: Exploitation of a device's failure to cryptographically verify the authenticity or integrity of a firmware update before installing it, allowing an attacker to deliver a malicious or backdoored firmware image that the device accepts and flashes as if it were legitimate.
ITID-32812.purpose: Captures exploitation of a device's lack of firmware update signing or integrity verification to install malicious firmware.
scopeIncludes: Delivery of an unsigned or improperly-verified malicious firmware image accepted by the device
Man-in-the-middle interception and replacement of a legitimate firmware update in transit
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a known-CVE bug within otherwise-legitimate firmware (ITID-32811)
Rollback to a known-vulnerable legitimate prior firmware version (ITID-32813)
ITID-32812.severity: Critical — a malicious firmware image can establish persistent, low-level control surviving factory resets in some cases.
ITID-32812.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; treat the device as fully compromised at the firmware level.
indicators: Firmware update delivered over an unencrypted or unauthenticated channel
Installed firmware hash mismatching any known legitimate vendor release
Device behavior change immediately following an update not sourced from the vendor's official distribution channel
vectors: Man-in-the-middle interception of an unencrypted firmware update check-in/download
Social engineering a user into sideloading a malicious firmware image
rootCauses: Device firmware update mechanism lacking cryptographic signature verification
Firmware update delivered over an unencrypted transport channel
controls: Vendor enforcement of cryptographically signed firmware updates
Encrypted, authenticated firmware update transport (TLS with certificate pinning)
Firmware integrity verification/attestation on boot
ITID-32812.detection: Firmware hash verification against known-good vendor releases provides a direct technical signal where baseline hashes are maintained.
ITID-32812.response: Re-flash the device with verified legitimate firmware or replace it, and identify the delivery vector used for the malicious image.
metrics: Count of unsigned/tampered firmware installations detected per quarter
detections: Firmware hash-mismatch alerting against known-good baselines
ITID-32812.notes: Scoped to exploitation of the update-signing/integrity-verification gap itself, distinct from exploiting a bug within legitimate firmware (ITID-32811).

playbook.name: Response: Unsigned/Unverified Firmware Update Exploitation
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation where an attacker delivered a malicious firmware update to an IoT device because the device failed to enforce signature verification on updates.

steps.title: Confirm the unauthorized firmware update via network-level detection
steps.desc: Since the device itself may have limited logging, confirm the unauthorized update primarily via network telemetry (unexpected firmware download source, update-server traffic anomalies) and any device management console logs available.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized firmware update confirmed and its source identified.
steps.abort: If the update was rejected due to a signature check or other control, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all devices of the same model/type on the network
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same model that share the same firmware-verification weakness.
steps.outcome: Full population of at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device(s)
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device(s) onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect them pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Affected device(s) isolated from the network.

steps.title: Block the malicious firmware source
steps.desc: Block the domain/IP that served the malicious firmware at the network layer.
steps.outcome: Malicious firmware source blocked.

steps.title: Restore known-good firmware and verify integrity
steps.desc: Reflash the device with a verified, vendor-signed firmware image and confirm its integrity before returning it to service.
steps.outcome: Device restored to a verified, trusted firmware state.
steps.tool: Vendor firmware image / device management tools

steps.title: Assess whether the device model can be made to enforce signature verification
steps.desc: Determine whether the device supports a firmware update or configuration change that enables signature enforcement; if not, flag it for replacement.
steps.outcome: Device hardened where possible, or flagged for replacement.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return the device to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Device restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT procurement standards
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether procurement standards should require signed-firmware enforcement for future IoT device purchases.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32813.def: Exploitation of a device's lack of anti-rollback protection to force installation of an older firmware version that reintroduces a previously patched vulnerability, which the attacker then exploits.
ITID-32813.purpose: Captures forcing a device to roll back to an older, known-vulnerable firmware version to re-expose a previously patched flaw.
scopeIncludes: Forcing installation of an outdated firmware version to reintroduce a patched vulnerability
Exploitation of missing anti-rollback/version-monotonicity enforcement
scopeExcludes: Installing a wholly malicious/backdoored firmware image (ITID-32812)
Exploiting a bug present in the currently installed firmware without a rollback step (ITID-32811)
ITID-32813.severity: High — effectively re-opens a vulnerability the organization believed was remediated by patching.
ITID-32813.priority: P1 upon confirmation given the deceptive re-exposure of a supposedly-patched flaw.
ITID-32813.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; verify patch status across the full device fleet, not just the affected unit.
indicators: Device firmware version observed reverting to an older release without an authorized change record
Exploitation traffic matching a CVE that was previously remediated via patching on this device
vectors: Physical or remote access forcing acceptance of an older signed firmware image the device still trusts
Exploiting a device that accepts any validly-signed image regardless of version number
rootCauses: Device firmware update mechanism lacking anti-rollback/version-monotonicity checks
Vendor continuing to sign and distribute older firmware versions without revocation
mitreTechniques: T1601.002 Modify System Image: Downgrade System Image
controls: Anti-rollback/version-monotonicity enforcement in the firmware update mechanism
Fleet-wide firmware version monitoring to detect unauthorized downgrades
ITID-32813.detection: Firmware version monitoring against expected fleet baselines provides a direct technical signal for unauthorized downgrades.
ITID-32813.response: Force reinstallation of the current patched firmware, investigate how the downgrade was achieved, and check the full fleet for similar exposure.
metrics: Count of unauthorized firmware downgrade events detected per quarter
detections: Firmware version downgrade alerting against fleet baseline
ITID-32813.notes: Scoped specifically to the rollback/downgrade mechanism as the exploitation vector, distinct from direct exploitation of current firmware (ITID-32811) or malicious image installation (ITID-32812).

playbook.name: Response: Firmware Downgrade Attack Exploitation
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation where an attacker forced an IoT device to downgrade to an older, vulnerable firmware version in order to exploit a since-patched vulnerability.

steps.title: Confirm the downgrade and the resulting exploitation via network-level detection
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry and any available device management logs that the device's firmware version was rolled back and that a since-patched vulnerability was then exploited.
steps.outcome: Downgrade and subsequent exploitation confirmed.
steps.abort: If the downgrade attempt was rejected (e.g. via anti-rollback protection), downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all devices of the same model/type lacking anti-rollback protection
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same model that share the same lack of anti-rollback protection.
steps.outcome: Full population of at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device(s)
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device(s) onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect them pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Affected device(s) isolated from the network.

steps.title: Segment the broader at-risk device population
steps.desc: Move all devices lacking anti-rollback protection to a restricted network segment pending remediation.
steps.outcome: At-risk population segmented.

steps.title: Restore the current patched firmware version
steps.desc: Reflash the device with the latest patched firmware and confirm the vulnerability exploited via the downgrade is no longer present.
steps.outcome: Device restored to a patched, verified firmware state.

steps.title: Enable anti-rollback protection where supported
steps.desc: Where the device/vendor supports it, enable anti-rollback protection to prevent future forced downgrades; flag unsupported devices for eventual replacement.
steps.outcome: Anti-rollback protection enabled where possible, or device flagged.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return the device to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Device restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT procurement standards
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether procurement standards should require anti-rollback protection for future IoT device purchases.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32814.def: An incident involving exploitation of IoT device firmware, not clearly matching known-CVE, unsigned-update, or downgrade-attack leaves.
ITID-32814.purpose: Catch-all for IoT firmware exploitation incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific IoT firmware exploit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32811-32813)
ITID-32814.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32814.escalation: Reclassify once the specific firmware exploitation pattern is clarified.
indicators: Firmware-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Firmware exploit of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Firmware update/patch management program
Network segmentation isolating IoT devices
Vulnerability scanning of IoT firmware
Vendor security advisory monitoring
ITID-32814.detection: Same general IoT firmware telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32814.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32814.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General IoT Firmware Exploit
playbook.description: For a confirmed IoT firmware exploit that does not fit a more specific known-CVE, unsigned-update, or downgrade-attack classification.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation via network-level detection
steps.desc: Since IoT devices typically have limited or no local logging, confirm exploitation primarily via network telemetry; reclassify to a more specific playbook if the exact firmware weakness becomes clear.
steps.outcome: Exploitation confirmed via network evidence.
steps.abort: If network telemetry shows the exploit attempt failed or was blocked, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all devices of the same model/type on the network
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same model/firmware, since one exploited device usually indicates a broader vulnerable population.
steps.outcome: Full population of at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device(s)
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device(s) onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect them, since most consumer IoT devices lack an EDR agent for host-based containment.
steps.outcome: Affected device(s) isolated from the network.

steps.title: Segment the broader at-risk device population
steps.desc: Move all devices sharing the same model/firmware weakness to a restricted network segment pending remediation.
steps.outcome: At-risk population segmented.

steps.title: Apply available firmware remediation or replace the device
steps.desc: Update affected devices to the latest firmware; if no fix is available, replace the device or maintain permanent network isolation.
steps.outcome: Devices remediated or replaced/permanently isolated.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated devices to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Devices restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT patch-management process
steps.desc: Record findings and assess whether the organization's IoT asset inventory and firmware patch-management process needs improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32821.def: Exploitation of a hardcoded, manufacturer-embedded credential (username/password or service account) that is undocumented, not exposed in user-facing configuration, and typically discovered via firmware reverse-engineering rather than default-settings documentation.
ITID-32821.purpose: Captures exploitation of an undocumented credential intentionally embedded by the manufacturer as a hidden backdoor.
scopeIncludes: Hardcoded credentials discovered via firmware binary analysis/reverse engineering
Undocumented service accounts embedded for vendor support/debug purposes
scopeExcludes: Documented, user-facing default admin credentials not changed by the owner (ITID-32822)
Mass exploitation of default credentials via internet-wide scanning (ITID-32823)
ITID-32821.severity: Critical — an undisclosed backdoor credential is unknown to the device owner and cannot be remediated via normal configuration.
ITID-32821.escalation: Escalate to IR and vendor security contact immediately; treat all devices of the same model/firmware as similarly exposed.
indicators: Authentication success using a credential never provisioned or documented by the device owner
Firmware reverse-engineering revealing a hardcoded credential string
Vendor advisory/CVE disclosing an undocumented backdoor account
vectors: Attacker discovering the hardcoded credential via public firmware analysis research
Automated tooling built around a disclosed backdoor credential targeting the same device model at scale
rootCauses: Manufacturer engineering/support backdoor left in production firmware
Lack of secure development lifecycle review catching hardcoded credentials before release
controls: Vendor firmware update to remove the backdoor once disclosed
Network segmentation limiting management-interface exposure of affected device classes
Asset inventory tracking devices with known backdoor advisories
ITID-32821.detection: Authentication logs alone cannot distinguish this from a legitimate account without threat intelligence on the specific backdoor credential; detection relies heavily on vendor/researcher disclosure.
ITID-32821.response: Apply the vendor patch removing the backdoor, or isolate/replace the device if no patch exists, and audit for use of the credential in logs.
metrics: Count of devices identified with disclosed backdoor credentials per scan cycle
detections: Known backdoor credential authentication alerting (once disclosed)
ITID-32821.notes: Differentiated from ITID-32822 by the credential being manufacturer-hidden/undocumented rather than a known, user-changeable default.

playbook.name: Response: Hardcoded/Undocumented Manufacturer Backdoor Credential
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation of an undocumented, hardcoded backdoor credential built into a device by its manufacturer, giving an attacker access that cannot be remediated by a normal password change alone.

steps.title: Confirm the backdoor credential and access gained
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry and any available device logs that access was obtained using an undocumented manufacturer credential, and determine what access/actions the attacker achieved.
steps.outcome: Backdoor credential and resulting access confirmed.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but blocked (e.g. by network ACL), downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all devices of the same model/firmware carrying the same backdoor
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same model/firmware that likely carry the same hardcoded credential.
steps.outcome: Full population of affected devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect all affected devices
steps.desc: Isolate all devices carrying the backdoor onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect them, since the credential cannot simply be changed by an administrator.
steps.outcome: Affected devices isolated from the network.

steps.title: Apply a vendor patch removing the backdoor, or permanently replace the device
steps.desc: Update to a firmware version confirmed to remove the hardcoded credential; if no such fix exists, treat the device as unremediable and plan for replacement rather than return to trusted use.
steps.guidance: A hardcoded backdoor that cannot be disabled means the device can never be considered fully trustworthy on the network again without a vendor fix.
steps.outcome: Backdoor removed via patch, or device flagged for permanent replacement.

steps.title: Notify the manufacturer and check for public disclosure
steps.desc: Report the hardcoded credential to the manufacturer and check public vulnerability databases for related disclosure and guidance.
steps.outcome: Manufacturer notified; public disclosure status checked.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity only for patched devices
steps.desc: Return only devices confirmed to be running a fix to normal network placement, keeping unpatched/unremediable devices isolated or removed; apply elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Only remediated devices restored; unremediable devices remain isolated or removed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT procurement/vetting standards
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether procurement standards should screen for known-backdoor device models before purchase.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32822.def: Exploitation of a consumer device's factory-default administrative credential (e.g., admin/admin, or a printed default password) that is documented in the device manual but was never changed by the end user or installer, granting an attacker straightforward administrative access.
ITID-32822.purpose: Captures exploitation of a documented, user-facing default administrator credential that the device owner never changed.
scopeIncludes: Login using a documented factory-default credential the owner failed to change
Devices with a default credential still active at time of incident
scopeExcludes: Undocumented manufacturer-embedded backdoor credentials (ITID-32821)
Automated mass exploitation via internet-wide scanning as the primary characteristic (ITID-32823)
ITID-32822.severity: Medium-High — trivially exploitable but the underlying weakness (unchanged default) is well understood and directly remediable.
ITID-32822.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the device controls critical or safety-relevant functions.
ITID-32822.escalation: Escalate to the device owner/asset team to change the credential immediately upon discovery.
indicators: Successful authentication using a known, documented factory-default credential
Device configuration audit revealing an unchanged default password
vectors: Manual attempt of a documented default credential against an internet- or network-exposed device
Reference to publicly available device manuals listing default credentials
rootCauses: Device owner/installer never changed the factory-default credential
No forced credential-change prompt on first device setup
controls: Vendor enforcement of mandatory credential change on first setup
Default credential auditing as part of asset onboarding
Network segmentation limiting exposure of unmanaged consumer devices
ITID-32822.detection: Configuration/credential auditing tools directly and reliably detect this condition before exploitation.
ITID-32822.response: Change the credential immediately, audit for unauthorized access already gained, and review the device's exposed configuration.
metrics: Count of devices found with unchanged default credentials per scan cycle
ITID-32822.notes: Differentiated from ITID-32821 by the credential being a documented, user-changeable default rather than a hidden manufacturer backdoor.

playbook.name: Response: Never-Changed Default Admin Credential Exploitation (Consumer Device)
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation where an attacker accessed a consumer IoT device using its factory-default administrative credential that was never changed after deployment.

steps.title: Confirm access via the default credential
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry and any available device logs that access was obtained using the factory-default admin credential, and determine what access/actions the attacker achieved.
steps.outcome: Default-credential access confirmed.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but the credential had already been changed, downgrade to a near-miss/failed attempt.

steps.title: Identify all other devices still using default credentials
steps.desc: Inventory the network for all devices of the same or similar models to check whether their default credentials have also never been changed.
steps.outcome: Full population of at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect it pending remediation.
steps.outcome: Affected device isolated from the network.

steps.title: Immediately change default credentials on the entire at-risk population
steps.desc: Set strong, unique credentials on every device found still using factory defaults.
steps.outcome: Default credentials eliminated across the identified population.

steps.title: Check the device for unauthorized configuration changes or persistence
steps.desc: Review the device's configuration for any changes made by the attacker (new accounts, altered settings, firmware modification) and revert as needed.
steps.outcome: Device configuration confirmed clean or reverted.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return the device to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Device restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and implement a default-credential audit process
steps.desc: Record the finding and establish a recurring audit to ensure default credentials are changed on all newly deployed IoT devices.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and audit process established.

ITID-32823.def: Exploitation of default credentials at scale via automated internet-wide scanning tools (e.g., Mirai-class botnet scanners) that systematically attempt known default credential lists against every reachable device on the target port/service, rather than a manual, single-device credential attempt.
ITID-32823.purpose: Captures automated, at-scale exploitation of default credentials across many internet-exposed devices via mass scanning.
scopeIncludes: Botnet or scanning-tool-driven mass credential-stuffing against exposed IoT device management ports
Devices swept up in an automated, internet-wide default-credential scanning campaign
scopeExcludes: A single, manually attempted default credential login against one specific device (ITID-32822)
Undocumented backdoor credential exploitation (ITID-32821)
ITID-32823.severity: High — mass exploitation often results in immediate botnet recruitment and rapid, wide-scale compromise.
ITID-32823.priority: P1 if the organization's devices are confirmed compromised into a botnet; P2 for detected-but-blocked scanning attempts.
ITID-32823.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately if compromise is confirmed, given the likelihood of onward participation in DDoS or further scanning.
indicators: High volume of credential attempts against a device's management port from many distinct external source IPs in a short window
Device exhibiting anomalous outbound scanning/DDoS traffic consistent with botnet recruitment
Device configuration or process list showing an unrecognized botnet client binary
vectors: Automated scanning tools (e.g., Mirai and its variants) sweeping default credential lists across exposed IoT devices
Compromised devices used to further scan and recruit additional vulnerable devices
rootCauses: Devices exposed directly to the internet with unchanged default credentials
Lack of egress filtering allowing recruited devices to participate in outbound scanning/DDoS
controls: Eliminate direct internet exposure of IoT device management interfaces
Default credential remediation at scale across the device fleet
Egress filtering to prevent recruited devices from participating in outbound attacks
ITID-32823.detection: Network flow analysis showing high-volume, multi-source credential attempts and anomalous outbound device traffic provide strong technical signal.
ITID-32823.response: Isolate compromised devices, remove internet exposure, remediate credentials at scale, and assess participation in any outbound botnet activity.
metrics: Count of devices confirmed recruited into a botnet per quarter
Count of internet-exposed management interfaces identified per scan cycle
ITID-32823.notes: Differentiated from ITID-32822 by the automated, mass-scale nature of the exploitation rather than a single manual attempt against one device.

playbook.name: Response: Default Credential Exploitation via Internet-Wide Scanning (Mass Exploitation)
playbook.description: For a confirmed compromise of an internet-exposed IoT device using default credentials discovered via automated, internet-wide scanning (e.g. botnet recruitment), rather than a targeted attack.

steps.title: Confirm mass-scan-driven compromise and identify the resulting activity
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry that the device was accessed via default credentials following internet-wide scanning traffic patterns, and identify what the compromised device is now being used for (e.g. botnet participation, DDoS, cryptomining, further scanning).
steps.guidance: Mass-exploitation campaigns typically add the device to a botnet immediately — check for outbound C2/beaconing traffic.
steps.outcome: Compromise confirmed and current malicious activity identified.
steps.abort: If the device was not actually exposed to the internet or the scan failed to authenticate, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all other internet-exposed devices with default credentials
steps.desc: Inventory for any other devices exposed directly to the internet with default or weak credentials, since mass-scanning campaigns target the entire exposed population indiscriminately.
steps.outcome: Full population of exposed at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Remove internet exposure and change credentials immediately
steps.desc: Remove the device from direct internet exposure (close the exposed port/disable remote management) and set a strong, unique credential.
steps.outcome: Device no longer internet-exposed with default credentials.

steps.title: Block C2/botnet infrastructure the device was communicating with
steps.desc: Block any C2 or botnet infrastructure the compromised device was observed contacting.
steps.outcome: Malicious infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Factory-reset or reflash the device to remove botnet malware
steps.desc: Perform a factory reset or firmware reflash to remove any malware/implant installed as part of the botnet, since many IoT botnet implants persist only in memory but some achieve firmware-level persistence.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore connectivity without re-exposing the device to the internet
steps.desc: Return the device to service behind proper network controls (no direct internet exposure) and apply elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Device restored securely; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review internet-exposure policy for IoT devices
steps.desc: Record the finding and establish a policy/scan to detect and remediate any IoT device directly exposed to the internet with default credentials.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and policy/scan established.

ITID-32824.def: An incident involving exploitation of a default or hardcoded IoT device credential, not clearly matching backdoor, unchanged-default, or mass-scanning leaves.
ITID-32824.purpose: Catch-all for IoT default credential exploitation incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific default credential exploit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32821-32823)
ITID-32824.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32824.escalation: Reclassify once the specific credential exploitation pattern is clarified.
indicators: Default-credential-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Default credential exploit of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Mandatory default credential rotation at deployment
Network segmentation isolating IoT devices
IoT asset inventory and vulnerability scanning
Account lockout/rate limiting on device management interfaces
ITID-32824.detection: Same general credential-authentication telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32824.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32824.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General IoT Default Credential Exploit
playbook.description: For a confirmed IoT default-credential exploit that does not fit a more specific manufacturer-backdoor, never-changed-default, or mass-scanning classification.

steps.title: Confirm the default-credential access and resulting activity
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry and any available device logs that access was obtained using a default/weak credential; reclassify to a more specific playbook if the exact scenario becomes clear.
steps.outcome: Default-credential access confirmed.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but failed, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Identify all other devices at similar risk
steps.desc: Inventory the network for other devices of the same or similar models that may share the same default-credential exposure.
steps.outcome: Full population of at-risk devices identified.

steps.title: Network-segment or disconnect the affected device
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device onto a quarantine VLAN or physically disconnect it pending remediation.
steps.outcome: Affected device isolated from the network.

steps.title: Change credentials on the affected device and at-risk population
steps.desc: Set strong, unique credentials on the affected device and any others found sharing the same exposure.
steps.outcome: Default/weak credentials eliminated.

steps.title: Check for unauthorized configuration changes or persistence
steps.desc: Review the device's configuration for any changes made by the attacker and revert as needed.
steps.outcome: Device configuration confirmed clean or reverted.

steps.title: Restore network connectivity and monitor
steps.desc: Return the device to normal network placement and apply elevated network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Device restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review credential-management practices for IoT devices
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether a recurring default-credential audit process is needed.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32831.def: Compromise of an IP camera, baby monitor, or similar connected imaging device that grants the attacker unauthorized live video/audio access, exploited specifically for surveillance or voyeuristic purposes rather than as a foothold for broader network access.
ITID-32831.purpose: Captures unauthorized takeover of a connected camera or monitoring device for the purpose of covert surveillance.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized live video/audio stream access to a compromised camera or monitor
Attacker manipulation of camera pan/tilt/zoom or recording functions for surveillance purposes
scopeExcludes: Hijacking of physical-safety-relevant smart home devices such as locks/thermostats/alarms (ITID-32832)
Connected vehicle system hijacking (ITID-32833)
Medical/health IoT device hijacking (ITID-32834)
ITID-32831.severity: High — direct privacy violation with significant harm potential to affected individuals.
ITID-32831.priority: P1 upon confirmation given the immediate privacy/safety impact.
ITID-32831.escalation: Escalate to IR and, where appropriate, law enforcement/privacy office immediately upon confirmation.
indicators: Unrecognized active viewer session on a camera/monitor's management interface
Device log showing access from an unfamiliar external IP or account
Unexpected device behavior (camera movement, indicator light activity) with no legitimate user present
vectors: Exploitation of default/weak credentials on an internet-exposed camera
Exploitation of a known firmware vulnerability granting unauthorized stream access
rootCauses: Camera/monitor exposed directly to the internet without adequate access controls
Weak or default credentials left unchanged
controls: Remove direct internet exposure of camera management interfaces
Strong, unique credentials enforced on all camera/monitor devices
Two-factor authentication on cloud-connected camera accounts where supported
ITID-32831.detection: Device access/session logs provide a direct technical signal where the device or its cloud platform retains such logs.
ITID-32831.response: Terminate the unauthorized session, reset credentials, notify affected individuals per privacy policy, and assess duration/scope of unauthorized access.
metrics: Count of unauthorized camera/monitor access incidents per quarter
ITID-32831.notes: Differentiated from sibling device-hijacking leaves by the surveillance/imaging-specific outcome (as opposed to physical-safety disruption, vehicle, or medical device targeting).

playbook.name: Response: IP Camera/Baby Monitor Hijacking for Surveillance
playbook.description: For a confirmed hijacking of an IP camera or baby monitor by an attacker for unauthorized surveillance purposes, an incident with a direct and serious privacy impact on those observed.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized access and viewing of the camera feed
steps.desc: Confirm via network telemetry, device management console logs, and/or unusual device behavior (unexpected movement, indicator light activity, active viewer sessions) that an unauthorized party accessed and viewed the feed.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized surveillance access confirmed.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but the device rejected it, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine the duration and scope of surveillance and notify affected individuals
steps.desc: Determine how long the unauthorized access persisted and what was observed, and notify the individuals whose privacy was affected given the sensitive nature of camera/baby-monitor footage.
steps.outcome: Exposure window determined; affected individuals notified.

steps.title: Immediately disconnect or power off the device
steps.desc: Physically disconnect or power off the camera/monitor immediately to stop the ongoing surveillance, given the direct and active privacy violation.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized surveillance stopped.

steps.title: Revoke the attacker's access credentials/session
steps.desc: Change device credentials and revoke any cloud-account access or remote-viewing sessions the attacker established.
steps.outcome: Attacker access revoked.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the access vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access (default credentials, exposed port, vulnerable firmware, compromised vendor cloud account) and remediate that specific weakness.
steps.outcome: Access vector remediated.

steps.title: Restore the device only after confirming the access vector is closed
steps.desc: Reconnect the device only once the vulnerability/weak credential is remediated, with network segmentation and monitoring in place.
steps.outcome: Device restored securely; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review privacy-notification obligations
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether any privacy/breach-notification obligations apply given the surveillance of individuals, and review IoT camera security standards.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; notification obligations assessed.

ITID-32832.def: Compromise of a smart home device (smart lock, thermostat, alarm system) granting the attacker unauthorized control over a physical function, exploited to cause physical disruption, unauthorized physical access, or a safety-relevant condition rather than for data theft or surveillance.
ITID-32832.purpose: Captures unauthorized takeover of a smart home device specifically resulting in, or intended to cause, physical disruption or safety impact.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized unlocking of a smart lock enabling physical entry
Unauthorized manipulation of a thermostat or alarm system creating a safety or comfort-disruption condition
scopeExcludes: Camera/monitor surveillance hijacking (ITID-32831)
Connected vehicle hijacking (ITID-32833)
Medical/health IoT device hijacking (ITID-32834)
ITID-32832.severity: High-Critical — carries direct physical safety and security implications for occupants.
ITID-32832.priority: P1 upon confirmation given potential physical safety impact.
ITID-32832.escalation: Escalate to IR and physical security immediately; notify affected occupants without delay.
indicators: Smart lock unlock event with no corresponding legitimate user action
Thermostat/alarm state change originating from an unrecognized account or session
Device log showing command execution from an unfamiliar external source
vectors: Exploitation of default/weak credentials or a firmware vulnerability granting device control
Compromise of the cloud account controlling the smart home device
rootCauses: Weak or default credentials on the smart home device or its controlling cloud account
Lack of physical-action confirmation/two-factor requirement for safety-relevant commands
controls: Strong, unique credentials and MFA on smart home cloud accounts
Physical-action confirmation requirements for safety-relevant remote commands
Vendor firmware patching for known device vulnerabilities
ITID-32832.detection: Device/cloud-account action logs provide a direct technical signal correlating unauthorized commands to unrecognized sessions.
ITID-32832.response: Regain control of the device/account, reset credentials, verify physical safety of occupants, and assess how access was obtained.
metrics: Count of confirmed physical-disruption hijacking incidents per quarter
ITID-32832.notes: Differentiated from ITID-32831 by the physical-disruption/safety outcome rather than surveillance, and from ITID-32833/32834 by the smart home device class (locks/thermostats/alarms) rather than vehicle or medical devices.

playbook.name: Response: Smart Home Device Hijacking for Physical Disruption (Locks/Thermostats/Alarms)
playbook.description: For a confirmed hijacking of a smart-home device (smart lock, thermostat, or alarm system) resulting in or capable of physical disruption or unauthorized physical access, requiring explicit physical-safety escalation given the potential real-world harm.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized control and immediately escalate for physical safety
steps.desc: Confirm via device management logs and network telemetry that an attacker gained unauthorized control of the lock/thermostat/alarm, and immediately escalate to physical security/facilities given the potential for real-world harm (unauthorized building access, environmental hazard, disabled alarm).
steps.guidance: This is a physical-safety escalation, not just a data/privacy issue — notify physical security or facilities without delay, in parallel with the technical response.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized control confirmed; physical security/facilities notified and engaged.
steps.abort: If control was attempted but rejected by the device, downgrade to a near-miss.
steps.tool: Device management console / physical security team

steps.title: Determine current physical state and immediate risk
steps.desc: Determine the device's current state (locked/unlocked, temperature setting, alarm armed/disarmed) and assess immediate physical risk to occupants or the premises.
steps.outcome: Current physical risk assessed.

steps.title: Regain physical control of the device immediately
steps.desc: Take manual/physical control of the device (manually lock/unlock, override thermostat, re-arm alarm) as an immediate priority alongside or ahead of digital remediation.
steps.guidance: Physical safety takes priority over preserving forensic evidence in this scenario.
steps.outcome: Device returned to a safe physical state.

steps.title: Revoke the attacker's access credentials/session
steps.desc: Change device credentials and revoke any cloud-account access or remote-control sessions the attacker established.
steps.outcome: Attacker access revoked.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the access vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access and remediate that specific weakness (credential, firmware vulnerability, exposed hub).
steps.outcome: Access vector remediated.

steps.title: Restore the device only after confirming the access vector is closed
steps.desc: Return the device to normal operation only once the vulnerability/weak credential is remediated, with monitoring in place.
steps.outcome: Device restored securely; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review physical-safety escalation procedures
steps.desc: Record the incident, confirm physical security was appropriately engaged, and review whether smart-home/physical-security device standards need improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32833.def: Compromise of a connected vehicle's telematics, infotainment, or connected control systems granting the attacker unauthorized remote access to vehicle functions, ranging from location tracking to, in severe cases, safety-relevant driving system interference.
ITID-32833.purpose: Captures unauthorized takeover of a connected vehicle's onboard systems.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized remote access to vehicle telematics/infotainment systems
Exploitation of a vehicle's connected app/API granting unauthorized location, unlock, or start/stop control
scopeExcludes: Non-vehicle smart home device hijacking (ITID-32832)
Camera/monitor surveillance hijacking (ITID-32831)
Medical/health IoT device hijacking (ITID-32834)
ITID-32833.severity: Critical — potential for direct physical safety impact to vehicle occupants and others.
ITID-32833.priority: P1 upon confirmation given the safety-critical nature of vehicle systems.
ITID-32833.escalation: Escalate to IR, physical security, and the vehicle manufacturer/fleet safety team immediately.
indicators: Vehicle telematics account showing access/commands from an unrecognized session
Vehicle system state change (unlock, remote start, location report) with no corresponding legitimate driver action
vectors: Compromise of the vehicle owner's connected-vehicle cloud account credentials
Exploitation of a vulnerability in the vehicle's telematics unit or companion mobile app API
rootCauses: Weak or reused credentials on the connected-vehicle cloud account
Vulnerabilities in the manufacturer's telematics API lacking adequate authorization checks
controls: MFA enforcement on connected-vehicle cloud accounts
Manufacturer API authorization hardening and rate limiting
Vehicle fleet telematics access monitoring for enterprise-owned vehicles
ITID-32833.detection: Telematics cloud account access logs provide a direct technical signal correlating unauthorized commands to unrecognized sessions.
ITID-32833.response: Revoke unauthorized access, reset credentials, verify vehicle physical safety and location, and notify the manufacturer/fleet safety team.
metrics: Count of confirmed vehicle system hijacking incidents per quarter
ITID-32833.notes: Differentiated from sibling device-hijacking leaves by the connected-vehicle device class, distinct from smart home, camera, and medical device leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Connected Vehicle System Hijacking
playbook.description: For a confirmed hijacking of a connected vehicle's onboard systems by an attacker, requiring explicit physical-safety escalation given the potential for real-world harm to occupants or others.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized vehicle system access and immediately escalate for physical safety
steps.desc: Confirm via telematics/vehicle management logs that an attacker gained unauthorized access to vehicle systems, and immediately escalate to physical safety/fleet management and, if the vehicle is in use, direct the driver/occupants to a safe course of action without delay.
steps.guidance: This is a physical-safety escalation of the highest priority — if the vehicle is currently occupied or in motion, safety of occupants and others on the road takes precedence over any other response step.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access confirmed; safety-critical parties notified and engaged immediately.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but rejected by the vehicle's systems, downgrade to a near-miss.
steps.tool: Vehicle telematics platform / fleet safety team

steps.title: Determine which vehicle systems were affected and current risk
steps.desc: Determine whether the access affected safety-critical systems (braking, steering, acceleration) versus non-safety systems (infotainment, climate) and assess ongoing risk.
steps.outcome: Affected systems and risk level determined.

steps.title: Take the vehicle out of service and regain physical control
steps.desc: Direct the vehicle to a safe stop and out of service; where possible, disconnect the vehicle's telematics/connectivity module to cut off remote access.
steps.guidance: Physical safety takes priority over preserving forensic evidence in this scenario.
steps.outcome: Vehicle safely stopped and removed from remote attacker control.

steps.title: Revoke the attacker's access credentials/session
steps.desc: Change telematics account credentials and revoke any remote-access sessions the attacker established.
steps.outcome: Attacker access revoked.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the access vector, involving the manufacturer if needed
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access and remediate; engage the vehicle manufacturer/telematics vendor given the safety implications and likely need for a firmware fix.
steps.outcome: Access vector remediated; manufacturer engaged.

steps.title: Return the vehicle to service only after safety-critical systems are verified
steps.desc: Return the vehicle to service only after the manufacturer/vendor confirms safety-critical systems are unaffected or repaired, and the access vector is closed.
steps.outcome: Vehicle restored to service safely; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review connected-vehicle safety escalation procedures
steps.desc: Record the incident, confirm safety escalation was handled appropriately, and review fleet connected-vehicle security standards.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32834.def: Compromise of a connected medical device or health-monitoring wearable (e.g., an infusion pump, insulin pump, cardiac monitor, or personal health tracker) granting the attacker unauthorized access to device function or patient data, with potential direct impact on patient safety.
ITID-32834.purpose: Captures unauthorized takeover of a connected medical or health-monitoring IoT device.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized remote access or command execution against a connected medical device
Exploitation resulting in unauthorized access to protected health data transmitted by the device
scopeExcludes: Camera/monitor surveillance hijacking (ITID-32831)
Smart home device hijacking (ITID-32832)
Connected vehicle hijacking (ITID-32833)
ITID-32834.severity: Critical — direct patient safety impact potential and regulated health data exposure.
ITID-32834.priority: P1 upon confirmation given patient safety and regulatory implications.
ITID-32834.escalation: Escalate to IR, clinical/biomedical engineering, patient safety, and compliance/privacy office immediately.
indicators: Medical device log showing a command or configuration change from an unrecognized source
Anomalous network traffic from a medical device inconsistent with its clinical function
Device firmware/configuration confirmed altered without an authorized clinical engineering change record
vectors: Exploitation of a known vulnerability in the device's wireless/network interface
Compromise of the device's companion cloud platform or management console
rootCauses: Medical device network segmentation insufficient to isolate it from general IT/guest networks
Delayed vendor patching due to regulatory/validation requirements on medical devices
controls: Dedicated network segmentation for medical/health IoT devices
Biomedical engineering asset inventory and vulnerability tracking
Vendor coordination for expedited patching of safety-critical vulnerabilities
ITID-32834.detection: Medical device network segmentation combined with anomaly monitoring on that segment provides meaningful technical detection coverage.
ITID-32834.response: Isolate the device, engage clinical/biomedical engineering to verify patient safety, remediate the vulnerability, and follow regulatory breach-notification requirements if health data was exposed.
metrics: Count of confirmed medical IoT device hijacking incidents per quarter
ITID-32834.notes: Differentiated from sibling device-hijacking leaves by the medical/health device class and its associated patient-safety and regulated-data considerations.

playbook.name: Response: Medical/Health IoT Device Hijacking
playbook.description: For a confirmed hijacking of a connected medical or health IoT device (e.g. infusion pump, insulin pump, cardiac monitor) by an attacker, requiring explicit physical-safety escalation given the direct risk to patient health and life.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized device access and immediately escalate for patient safety
steps.desc: Confirm via device management/clinical engineering logs that an attacker gained unauthorized access to the medical device, and immediately escalate to clinical/patient safety staff without delay given the direct risk to patient health.
steps.guidance: This is the highest-priority physical-safety escalation category — clinical staff must be notified immediately so they can assess and protect the patient, in parallel with any technical response.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access confirmed; clinical/patient safety staff notified and engaged immediately.
steps.abort: If access was attempted but rejected by the device, downgrade to a near-miss.
steps.tool: Clinical engineering / biomedical device management platform

steps.title: Determine what device functions were affected and current patient risk
steps.desc: Determine whether dosing, monitoring thresholds, or other patient-affecting settings were altered, and assess the immediate risk to the patient.
steps.outcome: Affected functions and patient risk determined.

steps.title: Have clinical staff verify and, if needed, take manual control of patient care
steps.desc: Clinical staff verify current device settings against the prescribed treatment plan and take manual control or switch to a backup device if settings were altered or the device cannot be trusted.
steps.guidance: Patient safety takes absolute priority over preserving forensic evidence in this scenario.
steps.outcome: Patient safety secured; device removed from attacker control or taken out of clinical use.

steps.title: Isolate the device from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the device from network connectivity (while maintaining any life-critical local function) to cut off remote attacker access.
steps.outcome: Device isolated from remote access.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the access vector, involving the device manufacturer
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access and engage the device manufacturer given the patient-safety implications and likely need for a regulated firmware fix.
steps.outcome: Access vector identified; manufacturer engaged.

steps.title: Return the device to clinical use only after manufacturer-confirmed remediation
steps.desc: Return the device to patient use only after the manufacturer confirms the vulnerability is remediated and clinical engineering validates safe operation.
steps.outcome: Device restored to safe clinical use; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review medical-device security and regulatory reporting obligations
steps.desc: Record the incident, confirm patient-safety escalation was handled appropriately, and assess any regulatory reporting obligations (e.g. to a medical device safety authority) alongside standard security lessons learned.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; regulatory obligations assessed.

ITID-32835.def: An incident involving unauthorized takeover of an IoT device, not clearly matching camera/surveillance, smart home, vehicle, or medical device leaves.
ITID-32835.purpose: Catch-all for IoT device hijacking incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific device hijacking leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32831-32834)
ITID-32835.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32835.priority: P2 by default given the general safety/privacy risk of device hijacking.
ITID-32835.escalation: Reclassify once the specific device class and impact are clarified.
indicators: Device-hijacking-related alert of unclear specific device class
vectors: IoT device takeover of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Network segmentation isolating IoT devices
Firmware patch management
IoT device behavioral monitoring
Default credential rotation policy
ITID-32835.detection: Same general IoT device telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32835.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32835.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General IoT Device Hijacking
playbook.description: For a confirmed IoT device hijacking that does not fit a more specific camera-surveillance, smart-home, vehicle, or medical-device classification.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized control and assess whether physical safety is implicated
steps.desc: Confirm via device management logs and network telemetry that an attacker gained unauthorized control of the device, and assess whether the device has any safety-relevant function requiring escalation; reclassify to a more specific playbook if one applies.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized control confirmed; safety relevance assessed.
steps.abort: If control was attempted but rejected by the device, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine the scope and duration of the hijacking
steps.desc: Determine how long the unauthorized control persisted and what actions the attacker took.
steps.outcome: Exposure window and attacker actions determined.

steps.title: Regain control of or disconnect the device
steps.desc: Take back control of the device or disconnect/power it off to stop the unauthorized activity.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized control stopped.

steps.title: Revoke the attacker's access credentials/session
steps.desc: Change device credentials and revoke any cloud-account access or remote sessions the attacker established.
steps.outcome: Attacker access revoked.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the access vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access and remediate that specific weakness.
steps.outcome: Access vector remediated.

steps.title: Restore the device only after confirming the access vector is closed
steps.desc: Reconnect the device only once the vulnerability/weak credential is remediated, with monitoring in place.
steps.outcome: Device restored securely; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IoT device security standards
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether broader IoT device security standards need improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32911.def: Exploitation of a stolen or leaked cloud API access key/secret to make authenticated calls against the cloud provider's management console API, granting the attacker control-plane actions (resource creation, configuration change, data access) as the compromised principal.
ITID-32911.purpose: Captures abuse of a cloud provider's management/control-plane API using a stolen access key.
scopeIncludes: Use of a leaked/stolen static access key to call cloud management APIs
API activity originating from an unexpected geography/IP using valid but compromised long-lived credentials
scopeExcludes: Credential theft via SSRF-to-instance-metadata (ITID-32912)
Role-assumption chain abuse where the initial credential was not itself stolen but legitimately obtained then escalated (ITID-32931)
ITID-32911.severity: Critical — control-plane access can enable full account compromise, resource destruction, or data exfiltration.
ITID-32911.escalation: Escalate to IR and cloud platform engineering immediately; revoke the compromised key without delay.
indicators: API calls from an access key originating from an unrecognized geography or ASN
Cloud audit log (e.g., CloudTrail-equivalent) showing anomalous API call patterns for the given principal
New/unexpected resource creation or IAM policy changes attributable to a specific access key
vectors: Access key leaked in a public code repository or CI/CD configuration
Access key harvested from a compromised developer workstation
rootCauses: Long-lived static access keys used instead of short-lived, scoped credentials
Lack of secrets scanning across code repositories and CI/CD pipelines
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Secrets scanning on code repositories and CI/CD pipelines
Prefer short-lived, scoped credentials (STS/workload identity) over long-lived static keys
Cloud audit logging and anomaly detection on API activity
ITID-32911.detection: Cloud audit logs (management-plane API call history) provide a strong, direct technical signal for this leaf.
ITID-32911.response: Revoke the compromised key immediately, audit all actions taken with it, and rotate any credentials or resources it touched.
metrics: Count of stolen-key API abuse incidents per quarter
Mean time to revoke a compromised key after detection
ITID-32911.notes: Scoped to stolen-credential abuse of the management API itself; distinct from the metadata-service credential-theft technique (ITID-32912) and from IAM privilege-escalation-after-initial-access (ITID-32931).

playbook.name: Response: Cloud Management Console API Abused via Stolen Access Key
playbook.description: For a confirmed abuse of a cloud provider's management/API surface using a stolen long-lived access key, enabling an attacker to make API calls with the victim's permissions.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized API activity via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm API calls were made using the compromised key from an unexpected source (IP, region, user-agent) and identify the actions taken.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized API activity confirmed and characterized.
steps.abort: If the key was already disabled/expired at time of use, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of actions and resources touched
steps.desc: Enumerate every API call made with the stolen key across the account, including resource creation, data access, and permission changes.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity mapped.

steps.title: Revoke/deactivate the compromised access key immediately
steps.desc: Disable or delete the compromised access key without delay to cut off further use.
steps.outcome: Compromised key revoked.

steps.title: Review and revert any unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Identify and revert any unauthorized resources created, permissions altered, or data exfiltrated using the key.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes identified and reverted.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials associated with the affected identity
steps.desc: Rotate any other keys, secrets, or credentials associated with the same IAM identity, since a compromised key often indicates broader exposure.
steps.outcome: All associated credentials rotated.

steps.title: Determine how the key was exposed and remediate the leak vector
steps.desc: Determine how the key was leaked (committed to a code repository, exposed in a config file, phished) and remediate that specific exposure.
steps.outcome: Leak vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the account is clean and apply elevated monitoring/alerting on the affected identity for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Account restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review long-lived-key policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether long-lived access keys should be replaced with short-lived, role-based credentials to reduce future exposure.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32912.def: Exploitation of an SSRF vulnerability in an application running on a cloud compute instance to force that application to make a request to the cloud provider's Instance Metadata Service (IMDS), retrieving the instance's temporary IAM/role credentials for use by the attacker.
ITID-32912.purpose: Captures exploitation of a server-side request forgery vulnerability to reach a cloud instance's metadata service and steal its credentials.
scopeIncludes: SSRF vulnerability chained specifically to reach the cloud instance metadata endpoint
Retrieval and reuse of temporary instance-role credentials obtained via SSRF
scopeExcludes: Direct use of a stolen static access key not obtained via SSRF (ITID-32911)
General role-chaining privilege escalation once a credential is already held (ITID-32931)
ITID-32912.severity: Critical — grants the attacker the full IAM permissions of the compute instance's attached role.
ITID-32912.escalation: Escalate to IR and cloud platform engineering immediately; revoke/rotate the instance role's session.
indicators: Application logs showing an outbound request to the cloud metadata IP (e.g., 169.254.169.254) triggered by user-supplied input
Cloud audit log showing API calls using the instance role's temporary credentials from an unexpected source
SSRF vulnerability confirmed in the application's URL-fetching functionality
vectors: Exploiting a web application's server-side URL fetch functionality (e.g., a webhook, PDF generator, or image proxy feature) to reach the metadata endpoint
Chaining an SSRF finding with knowledge of the cloud provider's metadata service address
rootCauses: Application accepting and fetching user-supplied URLs without adequate validation/allowlisting
IMDSv1 (non-session-oriented metadata service) enabled instead of a hardened, token-bound metadata service version
Overly permissive IAM role attached to the compute instance
mitreTechniques: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
controls: Enforce the hardened, session-oriented metadata service version (e.g., IMDSv2-equivalent) requiring a request token
SSRF-resistant input validation/allowlisting on URL-fetching application features
Least-privilege IAM roles attached to compute instances
ITID-32912.detection: Cloud audit logs correlating instance-role credential use with anomalous source context provide a strong technical signal.
ITID-32912.response: Patch the SSRF vulnerability, rotate/revoke the instance role's active session, and audit all actions taken with the stolen credentials.
metrics: Count of SSRF-to-metadata incidents per quarter
Percentage of compute instances enforcing hardened metadata service
detections: SSRF attempt web application firewall alerting
ITID-32912.notes: Scoped specifically to the SSRF-to-metadata credential theft technique, a distinct mechanism from direct stolen-key abuse (ITID-32911).
