playbook.name: Response: Cloud Metadata Service (IMDS) Exploited for Credential Theft (SSRF-to-Metadata)
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation where a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability was used to reach the cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) and retrieve temporary credentials, requiring identification of exactly which credentials were obtained and rotation of every one of them.

steps.title: Confirm the SSRF-to-metadata chain via application and cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review application logs to confirm the SSRF vulnerability was used to reach the metadata service endpoint, and correlate with cloud audit logs to confirm credentials were successfully retrieved.
steps.outcome: SSRF-to-metadata exploitation confirmed.
steps.abort: If IMDSv2 (session-oriented) protections blocked the request, or the request failed, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine exactly which credentials were retrieved via the metadata service
steps.desc: Identify precisely which instance role/credential set the metadata service returned to the attacker, since this determines the full blast radius requiring rotation.
steps.guidance: Do not assume only one credential was taken — check every metadata path the attacker's requests touched.
steps.outcome: Complete, specific list of retrieved credentials established.

steps.title: Determine what actions were taken with the stolen credentials
steps.desc: Review cloud audit logs for all API activity performed using the retrieved credentials before they were rotated.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity with stolen credentials mapped.

steps.title: Rotate every credential retrieved via the metadata service
steps.desc: Rotate each and every credential identified as retrieved via IMDS — not just the first one found — since the instance role may have granted access to multiple downstream credentials/secrets.
steps.guidance: Treat this as a checklist: confirm each retrieved credential is individually rotated and verify none were missed.
steps.outcome: All retrieved credentials rotated and confirmed invalid.

steps.title: Patch or contain the SSRF vulnerability
steps.desc: Contain the vulnerable application (isolate, take offline, or apply a WAF rule) to stop further SSRF exploitation while the root cause is fixed.
steps.outcome: SSRF vector contained.

steps.title: Enforce IMDSv2 and remediate the SSRF vulnerability
steps.desc: Enforce session-oriented IMDSv2 (or equivalent metadata-hardening control) on the instance and fix the underlying SSRF vulnerability in the application code.
steps.outcome: Metadata service hardened; SSRF vulnerability patched.
steps.tool: Cloud instance configuration / application development team

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the application and affected resources are clean and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Service restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IMDS hardening fleet-wide
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm IMDSv2 enforcement (or equivalent) is applied across all instances, not just the affected one.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; fleet-wide hardening confirmed.

ITID-32913.def: Exploitation of a weakness or bypass in a cloud API's rate-limiting/throttling controls (e.g., distributing requests across many source identities or IPs) to enumerate resources, accounts, or configuration at a scale the rate limit was intended to prevent.
ITID-32913.purpose: Captures exploitation of a cloud API's rate-limiting or throttling controls to enable mass enumeration of resources.
scopeIncludes: Distributed or rotated-source API requests bypassing per-identity/per-IP rate limits to enumerate resources at scale
Exploitation of an inconsistency in rate-limit enforcement across API endpoints
scopeExcludes: Use of a single stolen credential for standard API abuse without a rate-limit-bypass element (ITID-32911)
SSRF-based credential theft (ITID-32912)
ITID-32913.severity: Medium-High — primarily an information-disclosure/reconnaissance risk that can precede a more targeted attack.
ITID-32913.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if enumeration reveals exploitable sensitive resources.
ITID-32913.escalation: Escalate to cloud platform engineering to tighten rate-limit enforcement upon confirmation.
indicators: API request volume anomalously high in aggregate despite each individual source appearing within limits
Enumeration pattern spanning a broad range of resource identifiers in a short time window
Requests originating from a large, rotating pool of source IPs or accounts against the same API endpoint
vectors: Distributing enumeration requests across many cloud accounts, API keys, or IP addresses to stay under per-source limits
Exploiting inconsistent rate-limit enforcement between different versions or regions of the same API
rootCauses: Rate limiting enforced per-source rather than in aggregate for a given resource/endpoint
Inconsistent throttling configuration across API gateway regions/versions
controls: Aggregate/behavioral rate limiting rather than per-source-only enforcement
Consistent throttling policy enforcement across all API gateway regions/versions
Anomaly detection on aggregate enumeration-style request patterns
ITID-32913.detection: Requires aggregate/behavioral API analytics rather than simple per-source rate-limit logs, which is a known blind spot for standard throttling controls alone.
ITID-32913.response: Tighten rate-limit enforcement, block the identified source pool, and assess what was enumerated for follow-on risk.
metrics: Count of rate-limit bypass enumeration incidents detected per quarter
ITID-32913.notes: Scoped to the rate-limit/throttling-bypass mechanism enabling mass enumeration, distinct from credential-theft-focused API exploitation leaves in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Cloud API Rate-Limit/Throttling Bypass for Mass Resource Enumeration
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation where an attacker bypassed cloud API rate-limiting/throttling controls to conduct mass, high-volume enumeration of resources (buckets, instances, users, secrets) beyond what normal usage patterns would produce.

steps.title: Confirm the rate-limit bypass and enumeration activity via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm an abnormally high volume of enumeration API calls occurred and identify the specific bypass technique used (e.g. credential rotation, distributed source IPs, parallel accounts).
steps.outcome: Bypass technique and enumeration scope confirmed.
steps.abort: If throttling successfully limited the activity to a negligible scope, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine what resources/data were enumerated or exposed
steps.desc: Identify exactly which resources, buckets, or configuration data the enumeration exposed, since this determines the follow-on risk (e.g. sensitive bucket names or account IDs now known to an attacker).
steps.outcome: Full scope of enumerated resources identified.

steps.title: Revoke or restrict the credential/identity used for enumeration
steps.desc: Disable the compromised credential or identity used to perform the enumeration.
steps.outcome: Enumeration source credential revoked.

steps.title: Block the source IPs/accounts and tighten rate-limiting
steps.desc: Block identified source IPs or accounts at the network/WAF layer and apply stricter rate-limiting/throttling to close the bypass.
steps.outcome: Bypass vector closed; enumeration source blocked.

steps.title: Harden any resources exposed by the enumeration
steps.desc: Review and harden access controls on any resources identified during enumeration that may now be targeted for follow-on attack.
steps.outcome: Exposed resources hardened.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the environment is clean and apply elevated monitoring for follow-on activity targeting the enumerated resources.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; no recurrence or follow-on attack observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review API rate-limiting design
steps.desc: Record the bypass technique and assess whether the API gateway's rate-limiting design needs strengthening to prevent similar bypasses.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32914.def: An incident involving exploitation of a cloud provider API, not clearly matching stolen-key abuse, SSRF-to-metadata, or rate-limit-bypass leaves.
ITID-32914.purpose: Catch-all for cloud API exploitation incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific cloud API exploit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32911-32913)
ITID-32914.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32914.escalation: Reclassify once the specific API exploitation pattern is clarified.
indicators: Cloud API-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Cloud API abuse of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
controls: API gateway rate limiting and authentication enforcement
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) monitoring
Least-privilege IAM policies
API key/secret rotation and monitoring
ITID-32914.detection: Same general cloud API audit telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32914.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32914.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Cloud API Exploit
playbook.description: For a confirmed cloud API exploit that does not fit a more specific stolen-key, IMDS-SSRF, or rate-limit-bypass classification.

steps.title: Confirm the API abuse via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm unauthorized or anomalous API activity and identify the actions taken; reclassify to a more specific playbook if the technique becomes clear.
steps.outcome: API abuse confirmed and characterized.
steps.abort: If the activity was legitimate or already blocked, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of actions and resources touched
steps.desc: Enumerate every API call made as part of the abuse, including resource creation, data access, and permission changes.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity mapped.

steps.title: Revoke the credential/identity used
steps.desc: Disable or revoke the credential or identity used to perform the abuse.
steps.outcome: Abuse source revoked.

steps.title: Review and revert any unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Identify and revert any unauthorized resources created or permissions altered.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes identified and reverted.

steps.title: Remediate the root-cause weakness
steps.desc: Determine the underlying weakness that permitted the abuse and remediate it.
steps.outcome: Root cause remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the environment is clean and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record findings for future correlation and review.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32921.def: Exploitation of a cloud security group, network ACL, or firewall rule configured more permissively than intended (e.g., open to 0.0.0.0/0 on a sensitive port), granting the attacker network-layer reachability to a resource that should have been restricted.
ITID-32921.purpose: Captures exploitation of an overly permissive cloud network security control exposing resources to unintended access.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a security group/NACL rule allowing unintended inbound access from the internet or an untrusted network
Direct network-layer access to a resource that should have been restricted to an internal or bastion-only source
scopeExcludes: Default/unencrypted storage or resource configuration exploitation (ITID-32922)
Exploitation occurring after legitimate network access via stolen API credentials (ITID-32911, ITID-32912)
ITID-32921.severity: High — network-layer misconfiguration is typically the first exploitable step toward broader compromise of the exposed resource.
ITID-32921.priority: P1 upon confirmed exploitation of an internet-exposed sensitive resource; P2 for detected exposure without confirmed exploitation.
ITID-32921.escalation: Escalate to cloud platform engineering immediately to correct the security group/NACL configuration.
indicators: Cloud configuration audit flagging a security group/NACL rule permitting broad inbound access on a sensitive port
Connection logs showing inbound traffic from an unexpected external source reaching a resource intended to be internal-only
vectors: Direct scanning and connection to a resource exposed by an overly permissive security group rule
Automated internet-wide scanning identifying cloud resources with open management ports
rootCauses: Security group/NACL rule created too broadly during initial setup and never tightened
Lack of continuous cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning for overly permissive rules
controls: Continuous CSPM scanning for overly permissive security group/NACL rules
Default-deny network policy with explicit, minimal allow rules
Bastion/jump-host architecture for administrative access instead of direct internet exposure
ITID-32921.detection: CSPM configuration scanning directly and reliably flags this condition; network flow logs confirm actual exploitation.
ITID-32921.response: Tighten the security group/NACL rule immediately, assess what access occurred during the exposure window, and audit the resource for compromise.
metrics: Count of overly permissive security group rules identified per scan cycle
Mean time to remediate after detection
ITID-32921.notes: Scoped to network-layer (security group/NACL) misconfiguration specifically, distinct from data-at-rest/default-configuration misconfiguration (ITID-32922).

playbook.name: Response: Overly Permissive Cloud Security Group/Network ACL Exploited
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation of an overly permissive cloud security group or network ACL (e.g. open to 0.0.0.0/0 on a sensitive port) that allowed unauthorized network access to a cloud resource.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation via cloud audit and network flow logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs and network flow logs (e.g. VPC flow logs) to confirm unauthorized access occurred through the overly permissive rule and identify what was accessed.
steps.outcome: Exploitation confirmed and access scope identified.
steps.abort: If no unauthorized access actually occurred despite the exposure, treat as a misconfiguration finding rather than an incident.
steps.tool: Cloud audit logs / VPC flow logs

steps.title: Identify all other resources sharing the same overly permissive rule
steps.desc: Search the cloud environment for other security groups/ACLs with the same or similarly overly permissive configuration.
steps.outcome: Full population of similarly misconfigured resources identified.
steps.tool: Cloud security posture management / configuration scanning

steps.title: Tighten the security group/ACL immediately
steps.desc: Restrict the security group/ACL rule to only the necessary source ranges and ports without delay.
steps.outcome: Overly permissive rule closed.

steps.title: Remediate the same misconfiguration across all identified resources
steps.desc: Apply the same tightening fix to every other resource found sharing the overly permissive configuration.
steps.outcome: All similarly misconfigured resources remediated.

steps.title: Assess and remediate the resource for compromise
steps.desc: Determine whether the resource itself was compromised as a result of the exposure (malware installed, data accessed, credentials stolen) and remediate accordingly.
steps.outcome: Resource confirmed clean or remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the resource is clean and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Resource restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and implement automated misconfiguration detection
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether automated cloud security posture management/guardrails should be implemented to catch similar overly permissive rules before exploitation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32922.def: Exploitation of a cloud storage bucket, database, or other resource left in its default configuration (e.g., public read access, no encryption at rest, default access policy) rather than hardened per organizational policy, resulting in unauthorized data access.
ITID-32922.purpose: Captures exploitation of a cloud resource left in its default or unencrypted configuration state, exposing data.
scopeIncludes: Public read/write access to a cloud storage bucket left at default/permissive settings
Database or data store left unencrypted or with a default access policy allowing unauthorized reads
scopeExcludes: Network-layer security group/NACL misconfiguration (ITID-32921)
Exploitation via stolen API credentials rather than a resource-level default configuration gap (ITID-32911)
ITID-32922.severity: Critical if sensitive/regulated data is exposed; High otherwise.
ITID-32922.priority: P1 upon confirmed unauthorized access to exposed data.
ITID-32922.escalation: Escalate to IR, data owners, and compliance/privacy office immediately upon confirmed data exposure.
indicators: CSPM/cloud configuration audit flagging a storage resource with public or overly broad access
Access logs showing reads from unrecognized external principals against a data store
Data discovered indexed by internet scanning tools/search engines due to default public exposure
vectors: Direct access to a publicly-readable storage bucket or database discovered via scanning
Exploitation of a resource never moved off its default (often permissive) access policy after creation
rootCauses: Resource left at default (often permissive) access configuration at time of creation
Lack of encryption-at-rest enforcement policy
Lack of continuous CSPM scanning for public data exposure
controls: Default-deny/private-by-default policy enforcement on all new cloud storage resources
Mandatory encryption-at-rest policy
Continuous CSPM scanning for public data exposure
ITID-32922.detection: CSPM configuration scanning directly and reliably flags this condition; access logs confirm actual unauthorized reads.
ITID-32922.response: Restrict the resource's access policy immediately, assess the scope of data exposed and accessed, and follow regulatory breach-notification requirements if applicable.
metrics: Count of publicly exposed data resources identified per scan cycle
Mean time to remediate after detection
ITID-32922.notes: Scoped to resource-level default configuration/encryption gaps, distinct from network-layer misconfiguration (ITID-32921).

playbook.name: Response: Default/Unencrypted Cloud Resource Configuration Exploited
playbook.description: For a confirmed exploitation of a cloud resource left in a default or unencrypted configuration (e.g. a publicly readable storage bucket, unencrypted database, default-open service) resulting in unauthorized data access.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized access via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm unauthorized access occurred to the default/unencrypted resource and identify what data was accessed.
steps.outcome: Exploitation confirmed and accessed data identified.
steps.abort: If no unauthorized access actually occurred despite the exposure, treat as a misconfiguration finding rather than an incident.

steps.title: Determine the sensitivity of the exposed data
steps.desc: Classify the data that was exposed/accessed to determine whether breach-notification obligations may apply.
steps.outcome: Data sensitivity and potential notification obligations assessed.

steps.title: Close the exposure immediately
steps.desc: Restrict access to the resource (remove public access, enable required authentication) without delay.
steps.outcome: Exposure closed.

steps.title: Identify and remediate other resources with the same default configuration
steps.desc: Search the environment for other resources left in the same default/unencrypted state and remediate them.
steps.outcome: All similarly misconfigured resources remediated.

steps.title: Enable encryption and enforce secure defaults on the resource
steps.desc: Enable encryption at rest/in transit and enforce a secure baseline configuration on the resource going forward.
steps.outcome: Resource brought to a secure configuration baseline.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the resource is secure and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Resource restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and assess breach-notification obligations
steps.desc: Record the finding, confirm whether data-breach notification obligations apply given the sensitivity of exposed data, and implement automated guardrails to enforce secure defaults on resource creation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; notification obligations assessed.

ITID-32923.def: An incident involving exploitation of a cloud misconfiguration, not clearly matching network security group/NACL or default resource configuration leaves.
ITID-32923.purpose: Catch-all for cloud misconfiguration exploitation incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific cloud misconfiguration exploit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32921-32922)
ITID-32923.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32923.escalation: Reclassify once the specific misconfiguration pattern is clarified.
indicators: Cloud misconfiguration-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Cloud misconfiguration exploit of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) monitoring
Automated misconfiguration remediation guardrails
Cloud storage public-access blocking policies
Regular cloud configuration audits
ITID-32923.detection: Same general CSPM telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32923.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32923.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Cloud Misconfiguration Exploit
playbook.description: For a confirmed cloud misconfiguration exploit that does not fit a more specific overly-permissive-network or default/unencrypted-resource classification.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm unauthorized access occurred as a result of the misconfiguration and identify what was accessed; reclassify to a more specific playbook if the misconfiguration type becomes clear.
steps.outcome: Exploitation confirmed and access scope identified.
steps.abort: If no unauthorized access actually occurred, treat as a misconfiguration finding rather than an incident.

steps.title: Identify other resources sharing the same misconfiguration
steps.desc: Search the cloud environment for other resources with the same or similar misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: Full population of similarly misconfigured resources identified.

steps.title: Remediate the misconfiguration immediately
steps.desc: Correct the misconfiguration on the affected resource without delay.
steps.outcome: Misconfiguration corrected.

steps.title: Remediate the same misconfiguration across all identified resources
steps.desc: Apply the same fix to every other resource found sharing the misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: All similarly misconfigured resources remediated.

steps.title: Assess and remediate the resource for compromise
steps.desc: Determine whether the resource was compromised as a result of the exposure and remediate accordingly.
steps.outcome: Resource confirmed clean or remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the resource is clean and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Resource restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and implement automated misconfiguration detection
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether automated cloud security posture management/guardrails should be implemented.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32931.def: Exploitation of a chain of overly permissive IAM role-assumption ('trust') relationships, where an attacker starting from a low-privilege identity assumes a sequence of roles — each individually appearing reasonable — to arrive at a highly privileged role that the original identity should never have been able to reach.
ITID-32931.purpose: Captures privilege escalation achieved by chaining a sequence of cloud IAM role assumptions beyond what any single role should permit.
scopeIncludes: Multi-hop role assumption chains exploited to reach a privilege level unreachable directly
Exploitation of an overly permissive role trust policy allowing unintended cross-account or cross-role assumption
scopeExcludes: Direct abuse of a stolen static access key with no role-chaining element (ITID-32911)
Service principal/managed identity token theft (ITID-32932)
ITID-32931.severity: Critical — represents a full privilege-escalation path to high-value access.
ITID-32931.escalation: Escalate to IR and cloud IAM engineering immediately; treat the final assumed role's access scope as compromised.
indicators: Cloud audit log showing a sequence of AssumeRole (or equivalent) calls chaining from a low-privilege identity to a high-privilege role
IAM policy analysis revealing an unintended trust-chain path between roles
Privileged actions performed shortly after an unusual multi-hop role assumption sequence
vectors: Discovery of an overly permissive role trust policy via IAM enumeration, then chaining assumptions to reach privileged access
Exploiting a role intended for a narrow automation purpose that also trusts a broader set of principals than necessary
rootCauses: IAM role trust policies scoped too broadly (wildcard principals or overly broad conditions)
Lack of periodic IAM policy review/least-privilege auditing to detect unintended role-chaining paths
controls: Least-privilege IAM role trust policies with explicit, narrowly-scoped principals
Periodic automated IAM policy analysis to detect unintended role-chaining paths
Cloud audit logging and alerting on multi-hop role assumption sequences
ITID-32931.detection: Cloud audit logs of role-assumption call chains provide a strong technical signal when correlated across the full sequence, though this requires dedicated chain-analysis tooling rather than single-event alerting.
ITID-32931.response: Revoke access from the compromised chain, tighten the trust policies that enabled it, and audit all actions taken with the final privileged role.
metrics: Count of confirmed role-chaining privilege escalation incidents per quarter
Count of unintended role-chaining paths identified per IAM audit cycle
ITID-32931.notes: Scoped to privilege escalation via IAM trust-policy chaining specifically, distinct from initial credential theft (ITID-32911, ITID-32912) which may be the starting point of such a chain but is classified separately.

playbook.name: Response: Cloud IAM Role Assumption Chain Abuse (Privilege Escalation via Role-Chaining)
playbook.description: For a confirmed privilege-escalation attack where an attacker chained multiple IAM role assumptions to escalate from an initial low-privilege foothold to a much higher level of access, requiring a full review of the entire privilege-escalation path, not just the entry point.

steps.title: Confirm the role-chaining activity via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm the sequence of role assumptions (AssumeRole or equivalent) and reconstruct the full chain from the initial identity to the final escalated privilege level.
steps.outcome: Full role-assumption chain reconstructed from entry point to final privilege level.
steps.abort: If the final assumption was denied by policy, downgrade to a near-miss and assess only the entry point.

steps.title: Identify the initial entry point and every intermediate role in the chain
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker obtained the initial low-privilege credential and identify every intermediate IAM role used in the escalation chain, not just the starting and ending points.
steps.guidance: A role-chaining attack succeeds because multiple roles trust each other in sequence — reviewing only the entry point or only the final privilege leaves the intermediate trust relationships unaddressed.
steps.outcome: Complete chain of identities and trust relationships documented.

steps.title: Determine what actions were taken at the escalated privilege level
steps.desc: Review cloud audit logs for all actions taken once the attacker reached the highest privilege level in the chain.
steps.outcome: Full scope of high-privilege attacker activity mapped.

steps.title: Revoke the initial compromised credential and every assumed role session
steps.desc: Revoke the initial compromised identity's credentials and terminate/invalidate active sessions for every role in the assumption chain.
steps.outcome: Entire chain of access revoked.

steps.title: Review and revert any unauthorized changes made at each privilege level
steps.desc: Identify and revert unauthorized changes made at every stage of the escalation, since privilege was held at multiple levels along the chain.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes at every stage identified and reverted.

steps.title: Review and remediate every trust relationship in the escalation path
steps.desc: Conduct a full review of the IAM trust policies that permitted each assumption in the chain, tightening or removing overly permissive trust relationships end to end — not just at the original entry point.
steps.guidance: This is the core corrective action: the vulnerability is the chain of trust, not any single role.
steps.outcome: Entire privilege-escalation path reviewed and each unnecessary trust relationship removed or tightened.

steps.title: Remediate the initial compromise vector
steps.desc: Determine how the initial low-privilege credential was compromised and remediate that root cause.
steps.outcome: Initial compromise vector remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring across the entire chain
steps.desc: Confirm the environment is clean and apply elevated monitoring/alerting on all identities and roles that were part of the escalation chain.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; no recurrence observed across the full chain.

steps.title: Document the full escalation path and review IAM design principles
steps.desc: Record the complete role-chaining path as a reference and assess whether the organization's IAM design (least privilege, permission boundaries) needs broader review to prevent similar chains elsewhere.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with full chain documented for future reference.

ITID-32932.def: Theft of a short-lived or long-lived authentication token issued to a cloud service principal, managed identity, or workload identity (as opposed to a human user account), typically extracted from a compromised host, container, or CI/CD pipeline where the identity's token is cached or accessible.
ITID-32932.purpose: Captures theft of an authentication token belonging to a cloud service principal or managed/workload identity.
scopeIncludes: Extraction of a service principal/managed identity token from a compromised compute resource, container, or CI/CD runner
Reuse of a stolen workload identity token to authenticate as that identity from an attacker-controlled location
scopeExcludes: Theft of a human user's static access key (ITID-32911)

Credential theft via SSRF-to-instance-metadata as the specific technique (ITID-32912, though a service principal token may be the object retrieved via that technique — classify by the retrieval mechanism when known)
Privilege escalation via role-chaining once a credential is already held (ITID-32931)
ITID-32932.severity: Critical — service principal/managed identities frequently hold broad automation-scoped permissions.
ITID-32932.escalation: Escalate to IR and cloud platform engineering immediately; revoke the token and rotate the identity's credentials.
indicators: Cloud audit log showing the service principal/managed identity's token used from an unexpected source location
Evidence of token extraction from a compromised host's local credential cache or CI/CD secrets store
Anomalous API activity pattern for an identity normally used only by automation
vectors: Extraction of a cached managed identity token from a compromised container or VM
Exfiltration of a CI/CD pipeline's stored service principal credentials
rootCauses: Insufficient isolation of the token cache/credential store on the compromised host or pipeline
Service principal/managed identity granted broader permissions than the automation task requires
mitreTechniques: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
controls: Least-privilege scoping of service principal/managed identity permissions to the specific automation task
CI/CD secrets store hardening and access auditing
Short-lived, frequently-rotated tokens for workload identities
ITID-32932.detection: Cloud audit logs correlating identity token use with anomalous source context provide a strong technical signal.
ITID-32932.response: Revoke the stolen token, rotate the identity's credentials, and audit all actions taken with the compromised identity.
metrics: Count of confirmed service principal/managed identity token theft incidents per quarter
ITID-32932.notes: Scoped to theft of non-human (service principal/workload) identity tokens specifically; overlaps with ITID-32912 when the retrieval mechanism is SSRF-to-metadata, in which case classify by the retrieval technique and cross-reference this leaf for the identity-type context.

playbook.name: Response: Cloud Service Principal/Managed Identity Token Theft
playbook.description: For a confirmed theft of a token belonging to a cloud service principal or managed identity, enabling an attacker to act with that identity's permissions without needing a traditional user credential.

steps.title: Confirm token theft and use via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm the service principal/managed identity token was used from an unexpected source and identify the actions taken with it.
steps.outcome: Token theft and use confirmed and characterized.
steps.abort: If the token had already expired or was rejected, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine what permissions the identity held and what was accessed
steps.desc: Review the service principal/managed identity's assigned permissions and determine what resources/data were accessed using the stolen token.
steps.outcome: Full scope of identity's permissions and accessed resources determined.

steps.title: Revoke/rotate the compromised token or identity credential immediately
steps.desc: Invalidate the stolen token and rotate the underlying credential/certificate for the service principal or managed identity.
steps.outcome: Compromised token/credential revoked.

steps.title: Review and revert any unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Identify and revert any unauthorized resources created, data accessed, or permissions altered using the stolen token.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes identified and reverted.

steps.title: Determine how the token was stolen and remediate the exposure vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker obtained the token (compromised host running under the identity, leaked in logs/config, SSRF to a token endpoint) and remediate that specific weakness.
steps.outcome: Exposure vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the environment is clean and apply elevated monitoring on the affected identity for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review managed-identity scoping
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether the service principal/managed identity's permissions should be scoped more narrowly to reduce the blast radius of any future token theft.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-32933.def: An incident involving exploitation of a cloud identity mechanism, not clearly matching IAM role-chaining privilege escalation or service principal/managed identity token theft leaves.
ITID-32933.purpose: Catch-all for cloud identity exploitation incidents that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific cloud identity exploit leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (32931-32932)
ITID-32933.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-32933.escalation: Reclassify once the specific identity exploitation pattern is clarified.
indicators: Cloud identity-related alert of unclear specific pattern
vectors: Cloud identity exploit of unclear specific mechanism
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1550.001 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
controls: Multi-factor authentication enforcement for cloud identities
Conditional access policies and anomalous sign-in detection
Least-privilege IAM policies
Cloud identity/token monitoring and rotation
ITID-32933.detection: Same general cloud identity/audit telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-32933.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-32933.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Cloud Identity Exploit
playbook.description: For a confirmed cloud identity exploit that does not fit a more specific role-chaining or service-principal/managed-identity-token-theft classification.

steps.title: Confirm the identity exploit via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit/CloudTrail-style logs to confirm unauthorized use of a cloud identity and identify the actions taken; reclassify to a more specific playbook if the technique becomes clear.
steps.outcome: Identity exploit confirmed and characterized.
steps.abort: If the activity was legitimate or already blocked, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of actions and resources touched
steps.desc: Enumerate every action taken using the compromised identity, including resource creation, data access, and permission changes.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity mapped.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised identity's credentials/sessions
steps.desc: Disable or revoke the compromised credential, token, or active session.
steps.outcome: Compromised identity access revoked.

steps.title: Review and revert any unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Identify and revert any unauthorized resources created or permissions altered.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes identified and reverted.

steps.title: Determine and remediate the compromise vector
steps.desc: Determine how the identity was compromised and remediate that specific weakness.
steps.outcome: Compromise vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Restore normal operation with monitoring
steps.desc: Confirm the environment is clean and apply elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review IAM design principles
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether the organization's IAM design needs broader review.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-33111.def: The automated, high-volume use of credential pairs harvested from unrelated prior breaches against this organization's login surfaces, exploiting password reuse across sites to gain unauthorized access.
ITID-33111.purpose: Captures the general/comprehensive form of credential stuffing where a large set of previously breached username/password pairs is used to obtain unauthorized access to an account or system, in cases not covered by a more specific technique-based ITID.
scopeIncludes: Automated login attempts using breached credential lists against corporate/customer login pages
Successful account takeover resulting from credential-stuffing traffic
Bot/tooling patterns (e.g., Sentry MBA-style tools) targeting authentication endpoints
scopeExcludes: Interactive, low-volume guessing of a single account's password (see Brute Force Attacks, ITID-33121)

Detailed credential-stuffing campaign classification against human/end-user credential handling, tracked under the Attacks Against the Human credential domain (ITID-12210 series) — this ITID covers the device/application-side access outcome only
ITID-33111.severity: Medium, escalating to High if the stuffing campaign results in one or more confirmed account takeovers or targets privileged accounts.
ITID-33111.priority: P3 for detected-but-blocked stuffing traffic; P2 if any account is confirmed compromised; P1 if a privileged or high-value account is affected.
ITID-33111.escalation: Escalate to SOC and IAM/identity team on confirmation of any successful login from a known-bad credential list; escalate to incident response if account takeover leads to data access or lateral movement.
indicators: High-volume login failures from distributed/rotating IPs against the same endpoint
Login success rate anomalies consistent with credential-list testing
Logins matching credentials found in known breach dumps
Unusual user-agent or headless-browser patterns on auth endpoints
vectors: Automated login bots using breach-sourced credential lists
Residential proxy networks to evade IP-based rate limiting
Credential-stuffing-as-a-service tooling
rootCauses: Lack of MFA on externally facing logins
No bot/behavioral detection on authentication endpoints
Absence of breached-credential screening at registration/login
Weak or absent account lockout and rate limiting
controls: MFA enforcement on all external logins
Rate limiting and progressive lockout on authentication endpoints
Breached-password screening (e.g., HaveIBeenPwned API) at login/registration
Bot management / WAF credential-stuffing rulesets
ITID-33111.detection: Strong technical signal available via authentication logs, WAF, and bot-management telemetry; distributed-source stuffing is detectable through velocity and failure-pattern analysis even without device fingerprinting.
ITID-33111.response: Block offending source ranges/bot signatures, force password resets and MFA re-enrollment for affected accounts, and review for downstream account activity.
metrics: Volume of credential-stuffing attempts blocked per month
Number of accounts compromised via stuffing
Mean time to detect and force reset
ITID-33111.notes: This leaf is the sole Tier-5 child of the Credential Stuffing Tier-4 group and is scoped as the general/comprehensive definition of the technique's access outcome. Detailed human-factor credential-stuffing campaign analysis (phishing-sourced credential harvesting, victim behavior) is tracked under ITID-12210 series in the Attacks Against the Human domain to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Credential Stuffing Attack (Unauthorized Access)
playbook.description: Automated login attempts using previously breached username/password pairs successfully authenticate to one or more accounts.

steps.title: Identify credential-stuffing signature in auth logs
steps.desc: Query the identity provider / WAF logs for a burst of login attempts from distributed IPs, high failure-to-success ratio, and non-human request timing (headless browser or scripted user-agents) against the login endpoint.
steps.guidance: Filter authentication logs by endpoint over the last 24-72 hours; look for many distinct source IPs each attempting a small number of usernames, or a single IP cycling through many usernames — both patterns indicate stuffing/list validation.
steps.outcome: A confirmed set of source IPs and a list of usernames/accounts that produced successful logins amid the failed attempts.
steps.abort: If the pattern is a single IP with normal login cadence, this is not credential stuffing — reclassify and stop this playbook.
steps.tool: SIEM / IdP audit log / WAF console

steps.title: Enumerate accounts with successful logins from stuffing traffic
steps.desc: Cross-reference the malicious IP/user-agent set against successful authentication events to build the definitive list of compromised accounts.
steps.guidance: Include MFA-bypassed and MFA-prompted-but-approved (MFA fatigue) sessions in the successful set, not just password-only successes.
steps.outcome: Finalized list of compromised account IDs with timestamps of first unauthorized access.

steps.title: Determine post-login activity scope
steps.desc: Review each compromised account's post-authentication activity (data access, mailbox rules, downloads, financial actions) to size the blast radius.
steps.guidance: Pay special attention to sensitive-data access, new forwarding rules, and lateral use of the session token.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of impact per account.

steps.title: Force password reset and session revocation on affected accounts
steps.desc: Immediately expire all active sessions/tokens and force a password reset for every account confirmed compromised.
steps.guidance: Use the IdP's bulk session-revocation and forced-reset capability rather than manual per-user resets to avoid delay.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts logged out and unable to authenticate with the old password.

steps.title: Block malicious source IPs / rate-limit login endpoint
steps.desc: Apply WAF/CDN block rules against the identified stuffing IP ranges and enable or tighten rate limiting and bot-detection on the login endpoint.
steps.guidance: Prefer a bot-management challenge (CAPTCHA/device fingerprint) over a hard IP block if the ranges are shared/cloud-hosted to avoid over-blocking legitimate users.
steps.outcome: Stuffing traffic volume drops to near zero within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Escalate to account/identity owner and notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify impacted users of the compromise and required password change, and loop in the identity/security team lead for accounts with elevated privileges.
steps.guidance: Prioritize notification for accounts with admin, finance, or data-access privileges.
steps.outcome: Affected users and stakeholders informed and cooperating with remediation.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and breached-password screening
steps.desc: Mandate MFA for all affected accounts if not already enforced, and enable a breached-password check (e.g., HaveIBeenPwned list) at password-reset time.
steps.guidance: Where MFA cannot be enforced org-wide immediately, prioritize it for the compromised account set first.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have MFA enabled and are prevented from reusing a breached password.

steps.title: Remove any persistence established during the compromise window
steps.desc: Search for and remove any mailbox rules, OAuth grants, API keys, or forwarding addresses created during the unauthorized session window.
steps.guidance: Check inbox rules, connected apps, and API token lists for each affected account.
steps.outcome: No attacker-created persistence artifacts remain.

steps.title: Restore account access and verify normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm each affected user can authenticate normally with new credentials and MFA, and validate no residual attacker sessions remain active.
steps.guidance: Check active-session lists post-remediation for each account.
steps.outcome: All accounts fully restored to legitimate-user-only access.

steps.title: Deploy proactive breached-credential monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement continuous monitoring against breach-data feeds to proactively force resets before attackers can exploit reused credentials.
steps.guidance: Consider a managed dark-web/breach-corpus monitoring feed integrated with the IdP.
steps.outcome: A follow-up control ticket is created and assigned.

ITID-33121.def: The systematic, repeated attempt of password guesses (dictionary-based or exhaustive) against a specific account or authentication endpoint to gain unauthorized access, distinct from credential-stuffing's use of pre-breached credential pairs.
ITID-33121.purpose: Captures the general/comprehensive form of brute-force password guessing against an account or system, where an attacker systematically tries many password values against one or a small number of usernames.
scopeIncludes: Dictionary or exhaustive password-guessing attacks against a known username
Repeated login attempts against a single account exceeding normal failure thresholds
Brute-force attacks against remote services (RDP, SSH, VPN) using guessed passwords
scopeExcludes: Use of previously breached credential pairs at scale (see Credential Stuffing, ITID-33111)
Password reuse exploitation where the correct password was already known from another compromise (see ITID-33621)
ITID-33121.severity: Medium, escalating to High if directed at privileged/admin accounts or if successful.
ITID-33121.priority: P3 for blocked/failed attempts; P2 if lockout thresholds are repeatedly probed; P1 on confirmed successful compromise of a privileged account.
ITID-33121.escalation: Escalate to SOC when brute-force volume exceeds baseline against any single account, and immediately to IR on any successful authentication following such an attempt pattern.
indicators: Repeated authentication failures against one username from one or few sources
Account lockout events
Sequential or dictionary-pattern password attempts in logs
vectors: Automated brute-force tools against web login forms, RDP, SSH, or VPN endpoints
Password-spraying variants using common passwords across many accounts
rootCauses: No account lockout or rate limiting on authentication endpoints
Weak minimum password complexity requirements
Externally exposed authentication services without MFA
controls: Account lockout / progressive delay policies
MFA on all externally facing authentication
Geo/IP-based anomaly alerting on login attempts
ITID-33121.detection: Strong; authentication failure logs and lockout events provide a direct, reliable technical signal.
ITID-33121.response: Lock or reset the targeted account, block the source, and review for successful authentication in the surrounding window.
metrics: Number of brute-force attempts detected per month
Accounts locked out due to brute-force activity
Successful compromises resulting from brute force
ITID-33121.notes: Sole Tier-5 child of the Brute Force Attacks Tier-4 group; written as the general/comprehensive definition. Differentiated from Credential Stuffing (ITID-33111) by guess-based vs breach-list-based methodology.

playbook.name: Brute Force Attack (Unauthorized Access)
playbook.description: Repeated, systematic password guessing against a single account or small set of accounts results in unauthorized authentication.

steps.title: Identify brute-force pattern in authentication logs
steps.desc: Query auth logs for a high volume of failed login attempts against a specific account/username, typically from one or a small number of source IPs, followed by a success.
steps.guidance: Distinguish from credential stuffing by the narrow username set and sequential/incremental password attempts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed source IP(s), targeted account(s), and time of successful breach.
steps.abort: If failures never resulted in a success, this is an attempted-only event — handle as a lower-severity alert, not a confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Determine account privilege and post-compromise actions
steps.desc: Establish what the compromised account can access and what actions were taken after successful login.
steps.guidance: Check for privileged account status (admin, service, domain account) which changes containment urgency.
steps.outcome: Documented privilege level and activity timeline.

steps.title: Lock the targeted account and reset credentials
steps.desc: Immediately disable or force-reset the compromised account and terminate active sessions.
steps.guidance: Use out-of-band verification to communicate the new credential to the legitimate owner.
steps.outcome: Account no longer accessible with the brute-forced password.

steps.title: Block source IP and enable account lockout / rate limiting
steps.desc: Block the attacking IP(s) at the firewall/WAF and enforce or tighten account lockout thresholds and login rate limiting.
steps.guidance: Verify lockout thresholds are low enough to stop brute forcing without causing excessive legitimate-user lockouts.
steps.outcome: No further brute-force attempts succeed from the identified sources.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and strong password policy on the account
steps.desc: Require MFA and a stronger, policy-compliant password for the affected account going forward.
steps.outcome: Account protected against future single-factor brute-force attempts.

steps.title: Audit for any changes made during compromised session
steps.desc: Review and revert any unauthorized configuration or data changes made while the account was compromised.
steps.outcome: System state confirmed clean of attacker changes.

steps.title: Restore legitimate access and verify controls
steps.desc: Confirm the legitimate user can log in with new credentials/MFA and that lockout/rate-limit controls remain in place.
steps.outcome: Account fully operational under hardened controls.

steps.title: Review account-lockout and rate-limit baseline org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and assess whether lockout thresholds and rate limiting need to be tightened across all authentication endpoints, not just this account.
steps.outcome: Follow-up hardening ticket created.

ITID-33131.def: Unauthorized access to an account achieved using credentials that were harvested from the victim via a phishing attack, where this ITID records the resulting access event rather than the phishing delivery itself.
ITID-33131.purpose: Captures the general/comprehensive case of an adversary using credentials obtained through phishing to gain unauthorized access to an account, as the device/application-side access outcome.
scopeIncludes: Login/access using credentials obtained via a credential-harvesting phishing page
Access via an OAuth consent-phishing flow that yields a valid session (unless scoped to ITID-33141-series token abuse)
Post-phish account access observed shortly after a known phishing click
scopeExcludes: The phishing email/message delivery and lure itself, which is tracked under the Attacks Against the Human phishing ITIDs
Persistent OAuth token abuse following the initial phished access (see OAuth Token Abuse, ITID-33141 series)
ITID-33131.severity: High, given a phished account represents a fully authenticated adversary foothold.
ITID-33131.priority: P1-P2 depending on account privilege and whether the session is still active.
ITID-33131.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC/IR upon confirmation of a successful login following a known phishing event; treat as active compromise pending scope assessment.
indicators: Successful login shortly after a user reports or is confirmed to have clicked a phishing link
Login from anomalous geography/device following a phishing campaign
Mailbox rule creation or data access consistent with account takeover post-phish
vectors: Credential-harvesting phishing pages mimicking legitimate login portals
Consent-phishing pages capturing session tokens
Adversary-in-the-middle phishing proxies (e.g., Evilginx-style) capturing live sessions
rootCauses: Lack of phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO2)
Insufficient user awareness/training
No conditional access policies limiting anomalous logins
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn)
Conditional access / impossible-travel blocking
Rapid credential revocation and session invalidation workflow
ITID-33131.detection: Good; correlation of phishing reports with subsequent authentication events and anomaly detection provides strong signal.
ITID-33131.response: Force password reset, revoke all active sessions/tokens, review mailbox rules and data access, and notify the affected user.
metrics: Number of phished accounts resulting in confirmed access
Mean time from phishing report to session revocation
ITID-33131.notes: Sole Tier-5 child of Phished Account Access; scoped to the access outcome only. The phishing delivery mechanism itself is tracked in the Attacks Against the Human domain to avoid duplication; if the phish yields a persistent OAuth token rather than a session, classify under ITID-33141 series instead.

playbook.name: Phished Account Access
playbook.description: A user's credentials were harvested via a phishing lure and used by an attacker to log into the account.

steps.title: Confirm the phishing lure and credential harvest
steps.desc: Review the reported phishing email/page and confirm the user actually submitted credentials to it (via email gateway logs, proxy logs, or user interview).
steps.guidance: Check for the phishing kit URL in proxy/DNS logs at the time the user reports clicking.
steps.outcome: Confirmed timeline of credential submission.
steps.abort: If the user did not submit credentials (only opened the email or clicked but did not enter data), downgrade to a phishing-exposure-only response.

steps.title: Correlate harvested credentials with actual account logins
steps.desc: Search authentication logs for logins to the affected account from anomalous geolocation/IP/device following the phishing timestamp.
steps.guidance: Impossible-travel and new-device alerts are strong indicators here.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized login(s) tied to the phishing event, with source IP and timestamp.

steps.title: Scope post-access activity
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker did after logging in — mailbox access, data exfiltration, further phishing sent from the account, OAuth consent grants.
steps.guidance: Check Sent Items, mailbox rules, and OAuth app consents specifically.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of attacker activity.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and reset the account credential
steps.desc: Terminate all active sessions/refresh tokens and force a password reset for the affected account.
steps.guidance: Also revoke any OAuth app tokens issued during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has valid session or token access.

steps.title: Block the phishing infrastructure and quarantine related emails
steps.desc: Block the phishing domain/URL at the email gateway and web proxy, and search-and-quarantine the lure from other mailboxes it was sent to.
steps.outcome: No other users can reach the phishing page; lure removed org-wide.

steps.title: Remove attacker persistence (mailbox rules, OAuth grants, forwarding)
steps.desc: Delete any malicious inbox rules, forwarding addresses, or third-party OAuth app grants created by the attacker.
steps.outcome: No attacker persistence remains on the account.

steps.title: Enable/verify MFA on the account
steps.desc: Ensure phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkey preferred over SMS/OTP) is enabled on the account.
steps.outcome: Account protected against reuse of the same harvested credential.

steps.title: Restore access and confirm clean state
steps.desc: Verify the user regains normal access and that no unauthorized emails or actions remain outstanding (e.g., recall any attacker-sent phishing from the compromised mailbox).
steps.outcome: Account fully restored and verified clean.

steps.title: Reinforce phishing awareness training and reporting workflow
steps.desc: Document the incident, including how the lure bypassed email filtering, and feed it into targeted user awareness training and detection-rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Training/detection follow-up ticket created.

ITID-33141.def: Unauthorized persistent access to a user's account or data maintained through an OAuth refresh token issued during an earlier compromise or malicious consent grant, which continues to mint new access tokens after the initiating credential compromise has been remediated.
ITID-33141.purpose: Captures cases where an adversary retains long-term account access via an OAuth refresh token that was never revoked, even after the original password or session was changed.
scopeIncludes: Refresh-token-based access continuing after a password reset or MFA re-enrollment
Long-lived OAuth grants from a malicious or compromised third-party app still minting tokens
Failure to revoke app-level OAuth grants during account remediation
scopeExcludes: Initial theft of the token itself via phishing or malware (tracked as the delivery method under relevant human/device ITIDs)
Malicious app abuse focused on excessive scope at consent time (see ITID-33143)
ITID-33141.severity: High — this represents access that survives standard remediation steps like password reset.
ITID-33141.priority: P1 once identified, since it indicates incomplete incident closure and ongoing exposure.
ITID-33141.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity and IR immediately; treat as an active, unresolved compromise until all app consents and refresh tokens for the account are revoked.
indicators: API/data access continuing after password reset with no new interactive login
OAuth app token usage from unfamiliar IPs after remediation
Refresh token issuance logs showing activity long after the original grant
vectors: Malicious OAuth app consent granted during a phishing campaign
Compromised device that captured a refresh token
Incomplete offboarding/remediation that revokes password but not app grants
rootCauses: Remediation playbooks that reset passwords without revoking OAuth grants/refresh tokens
No inventory or periodic review of third-party app authorizations
Overly long refresh-token lifetimes with no re-consent requirement
controls: Mandatory revocation of all OAuth grants/refresh tokens as part of account compromise remediation
Periodic third-party app consent review and cleanup
Shortened refresh token lifetimes with re-authentication requirements
ITID-33141.detection: Moderate; requires correlating token-issuance and API-access logs with prior incident timelines, which many organizations do not do by default.
ITID-33141.response: Revoke all refresh tokens and app consents for the account, audit API access made under the token, and update remediation SOP to include token revocation.
metrics: Number of incidents with token persistence found post-remediation
Time from remediation to full token revocation
ITID-33141.notes: Differentiated from siblings by its defining trait: access surviving standard remediation via an unrevoked refresh token, regardless of how the token was originally obtained.

playbook.name: Persistent Access via Unrevoked OAuth Refresh Token
playbook.description: An attacker retains long-term account access using an OAuth refresh token that survives a password reset because it was never explicitly revoked.

steps.title: Identify anomalous token-refresh activity post-remediation
steps.desc: Review OAuth/IdP token logs for continued API access or token-refresh events on an account after a password reset was believed to have remediated a prior compromise.
steps.guidance: Look specifically for refresh_token grant type usage continuing after the reset timestamp.
steps.outcome: Confirmed active refresh token being used by an unauthorized party.
steps.abort: If all token activity stopped at the reset time, there is no persistence issue — close this playbook.

steps.title: Identify the specific application and token grant involved
steps.desc: Determine which OAuth client/app the surviving refresh token belongs to and what scopes it holds.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the client_id against the app registry/consent list.
steps.outcome: Identified app, scope, and issuance date of the offending token.

steps.title: Revoke all refresh and access tokens for the account
steps.desc: Perform a full token revocation for the account across all OAuth clients, not just the app implicated, since the attacker may hold others.
steps.guidance: Use the IdP's "revoke all sessions and tokens" function, which differs from a plain password reset.
steps.outcome: All previously issued tokens for the account are invalidated.

steps.title: Escalate to app owner if a first-party integration is implicated
steps.desc: If the token belonged to a business-critical integration, notify the integration owner before hard-revoking to avoid unplanned outage, while still prioritizing security.
steps.outcome: Coordinated revocation with awareness of downstream impact.

steps.title: Fix the password-reset workflow to include token revocation
steps.desc: Update the account-remediation/reset procedure (manual or automated) so that a password reset always also revokes all outstanding refresh tokens.
steps.guidance: This is the root cause — a reset that does not invalidate refresh tokens leaves persistent access.
steps.outcome: Reset procedure updated and validated with a test account.

steps.title: Verify no active tokens remain and restore legitimate app access
steps.desc: Confirm zero active refresh tokens for the account, then re-authorize legitimate applications/integrations from scratch.
steps.outcome: Only freshly-consented, legitimate tokens are active.

steps.title: Codify token revocation into standard compromise-response procedure
steps.desc: Update the incident-response runbook and any automation so every account-compromise remediation includes explicit OAuth token revocation as a mandatory step.
steps.outcome: Runbook/automation updated and reviewed.

ITID-33142.def: Unauthorized silent access to a mailbox, file store, or other data resource via a valid OAuth access/refresh token, without any password entry, MFA prompt, or interactive sign-in event visible to the victim.
ITID-33142.purpose: Captures OAuth-based access to mailbox or data resources that requires no password at all, distinguishing token-only compromise from password-based account takeover.
scopeIncludes: Mail/data API access using a token obtained without the victim ever seeing an authentication prompt
Malicious apps polling mailbox content via Graph/Gmail APIs using a granted token
Silent enumeration or exfiltration of mail/files via token-authenticated API calls
scopeExcludes: Access following a visible consent-phishing prompt where the grant itself is the attack focus (see ITID-33143)
Long-term refresh-token persistence after remediation (see ITID-33141)
ITID-33142.severity: High — silent, credential-less access to mailbox/data content often enables business email compromise or intelligence gathering with no user-visible trace.
ITID-33142.priority: P1, since victims typically have no indication of compromise and dwell time is often long.
ITID-33142.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately on discovery; assume mailbox/data content has been read and assess for downstream BEC or data-exposure impact.
indicators: API access logs showing mailbox reads with no corresponding interactive sign-in
Unusual application IDs in mail audit logs
Data access patterns inconsistent with the user's normal client applications
vectors: Malicious OAuth apps with mail/read scopes
Token theft via malware without triggering a new sign-in
Compromised app secrets used to mint tokens directly
rootCauses: No monitoring of API-only access distinct from interactive sign-ins
Overly broad mail/data scopes granted to third-party apps
No baseline of expected application access patterns per mailbox
controls: Mail/data API access auditing and alerting
OAuth app allowlisting
Scope-limiting for third-party mail access
ITID-33142.detection: Moderate; requires mail/API audit logging capable of distinguishing token-based access from interactive logins, which not all tenants enable by default.
ITID-33142.response: Revoke the offending token/app, notify the user, and conduct a mailbox/data access review to scope what was read or exfiltrated.
metrics: Number of silent token-based access incidents detected
Mean dwell time before detection
ITID-33142.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the defining trait of zero interactive authentication signal — pure API/token access.

playbook.name: OAuth Token Abuse for Silent Mailbox/Data Access
playbook.description: An attacker uses a valid OAuth access/refresh token to read mailbox or data content without ever needing the account password.

steps.title: Detect anomalous API access via OAuth token
steps.desc: Review Graph/API access logs for mailbox or data-read calls from an unfamiliar client application, IP, or unusual access pattern (e.g., bulk mail enumeration) using OAuth tokens rather than interactive sign-in.
steps.guidance: Interactive sign-in logs will show nothing anomalous since no password login occurred — focus on API/token usage logs instead.
steps.outcome: Identified the specific token/app and the data accessed.

steps.title: Determine how the token was obtained
steps.desc: Investigate whether the token originated from a malicious OAuth app consent, a stolen token/session, or a leaked client secret.
steps.guidance: Check the app's consent grant history and client type (public vs confidential).
steps.outcome: Root cause of token acquisition identified.

steps.title: Revoke the offending token and app consent
steps.desc: Revoke the specific access/refresh token and remove the app's consent grant for the affected user(s).
steps.guidance: If the app was granted tenant-wide admin consent, revoke at the tenant level.
steps.outcome: App can no longer access mailbox/data via the token.

steps.title: Block the malicious application at the tenant level
steps.desc: Disable the OAuth application registration or add it to a blocked-apps list to prevent re-consent.
steps.outcome: Application cannot be re-authorized by any user in the tenant.

steps.title: Rotate any secrets exposed via the mailbox/data access
steps.desc: Identify and rotate any credentials, API keys, or sensitive data that were exposed to the attacker via the accessed mailbox/files.
steps.guidance: Search accessed emails for password resets, API keys, or financial data.
steps.outcome: Any exposed secrets invalidated.

steps.title: Tighten tenant OAuth consent policy
steps.desc: Restrict user consent for third-party apps to admin-approved only, closing the gap that allowed the malicious app to be granted access.
steps.outcome: Consent policy updated to require admin review.

steps.title: Verify mailbox integrity and notify affected users
steps.desc: Confirm no residual unauthorized access remains and notify users whose data was exposed, per data-handling policy.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean state and stakeholders informed.

steps.title: Deploy continuous OAuth app risk monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement ongoing monitoring/alerting for newly consented OAuth apps requesting mail/data scopes.
steps.outcome: Monitoring control implemented.

ITID-33143.def: Unauthorized access resulting from a user granting OAuth consent to a malicious or overly permissive third-party application — often via a consent-phishing lure — after which the app abuses its granted scope beyond what the user reasonably expected.
ITID-33143.purpose: Captures cases where a user knowingly (or under deception) grants consent to a malicious OAuth application requesting excessive permissions, which the app later abuses.
scopeIncludes: Consent-phishing campaigns that lead to a completed OAuth grant
Legitimate-looking apps requesting broad scopes (mail, files, directory) later found to be malicious
Post-consent abuse such as mass data exfiltration or persistent mailbox access enabled by the over-broad grant
scopeExcludes: Silent, no-prompt access via an already-issued token (see ITID-33142)
Long-term persistence after the initiating grant is revoked elsewhere (see ITID-33141)
ITID-33143.severity: High, particularly when the granted scope includes mail, file, or directory read/write access.
ITID-33143.priority: P1-P2 depending on scope breadth and evidence of data access following the grant.
ITID-33143.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity and IR upon discovery of a malicious app consent; revoke immediately and assess org-wide exposure to the same app.
indicators: New third-party app consent event followed by unusual data access
App requesting scopes disproportionate to its stated function
Multiple users granting consent to the same suspicious app in a short window
vectors: Consent-phishing emails linking to a malicious app registration
Look-alike apps impersonating trusted vendors in the app consent screen
Compromised legitimate app later modified to request broader scopes
rootCauses: Users permitted to consent to third-party apps without admin review
No scope-risk tiering or admin approval workflow for high-risk permissions
Lack of continuous monitoring of the app consent inventory
controls: Admin consent workflow for high-risk OAuth scopes
Third-party app risk scoring and allowlisting
User awareness training on consent-phishing
ITID-33143.detection: Moderate; depends on app-consent audit logging and a defined risk baseline for acceptable scopes, which requires deliberate configuration.
ITID-33143.response: Revoke the app's consent org-wide if malicious, notify all affected users, and audit data accessed under the grant.
metrics: Number of malicious app consents identified and revoked
Users affected per malicious app incident
ITID-33143.notes: Differentiated from siblings by focus on the consent-grant moment and excessive-scope abuse pattern, rather than silent access or long-term persistence.

playbook.name: Malicious OAuth App Granted Excessive Scope Abused Post-Consent
playbook.description: A user or admin consented to a third-party OAuth application requesting overly broad permissions, which the app (or its operator) later abused.

steps.title: Identify the over-scoped application and consent event
steps.desc: Review the OAuth app consent log to find the application, the scopes granted, who consented, and when.
steps.guidance: Flag apps with scopes such as full mailbox read/write, directory read, or files read/write that exceed the app's stated purpose.
steps.outcome: Identified application, granted scopes, and consenting user(s).

steps.title: Determine what data/actions the app actually accessed
steps.desc: Review API call logs made by the application's service principal to determine actual usage versus granted scope, confirming abuse rather than dormant over-provisioning.
steps.outcome: Evidence of abusive or unexpected data access/exfiltration by the app.
steps.abort: If the app has never used the excessive scope, treat as a lower-severity misconfiguration finding rather than an active incident.

steps.title: Revoke the application's consent and tokens tenant-wide
steps.desc: Remove the service principal / app consent grant for all users and revoke any active tokens it holds.
steps.outcome: Application no longer has any active access to tenant data.

steps.title: Escalate to legal/vendor-risk if a third-party vendor app is implicated
steps.desc: If the app is a known commercial vendor, notify legal/vendor management to pursue breach notification and contract review.
steps.outcome: Appropriate business stakeholders engaged.

steps.title: Rotate secrets/data exposed to the app
steps.desc: Rotate any credentials or sensitive data the app had access to during its consented period.
steps.outcome: Exposure window closed with no reusable secrets remaining.

steps.title: Implement admin consent workflow and scope allowlisting
steps.desc: Restrict future consent so only admin-reviewed apps can request high-risk scopes; add the offending app to a blocklist.
steps.outcome: Consent policy prevents recurrence for this and similarly-scoped apps.

steps.title: Verify tenant data integrity and re-evaluate legitimate app needs
steps.desc: Confirm no lingering access remains and work with the business to find/approve a properly-scoped replacement if the app was providing a legitimate function.
steps.outcome: Business function restored with a properly-scoped, reviewed integration.

steps.title: Audit all existing OAuth app grants for excessive scope
steps.desc: Document the incident and perform a tenant-wide review of existing third-party app consents to identify other over-scoped grants before they are abused.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and remediation tickets filed for other findings.

ITID-33144.def: Unauthorized access occurring when an OAuth token issued for one sanctioned application or integration is reused, replayed, or shared to authenticate a different, unauthorized third-party integration or service.
ITID-33144.purpose: Captures reuse of a legitimately issued OAuth token by an unauthorized third-party integration beyond its intended application boundary.
scopeIncludes: Token replay against an integration other than the one it was issued for
Sharing of a valid application token across unsanctioned tooling or scripts
An integration partner reusing a customer's token beyond agreed scope/purpose
scopeExcludes: The original malicious-app consent event itself (see ITID-33143)
Silent single-app token access with no reuse across integrations (see ITID-33142)
ITID-33144.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of the data/systems the reused token can reach.
ITID-33144.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the reused token grants access to sensitive systems or a large blast radius.
ITID-33144.escalation: Escalate to the application/integration owner and IAM team upon detection; suspend the token and audit all integrations bound to it.
indicators: Same token or client ID used from multiple distinct integration endpoints/IPs
API calls from an integration not on the token's approved allowlist
Contractual/partner audit findings of out-of-scope token use
vectors: Insecure storage of tokens shared between internal teams or scripts
Third-party partner misuse of an API token outside its contracted purpose
Token leakage via source code or config repositories reused elsewhere
rootCauses: No per-integration token scoping or binding
Tokens stored in shared/insecure locations accessible to multiple systems
Lack of monitoring for token use across unexpected client IDs or endpoints
controls: Token binding to a single client/integration
Secrets management for API tokens (vault-based storage)
Anomaly detection on token usage across unexpected integrations
ITID-33144.detection: Moderate; requires client-ID/IP correlation on token use, feasible with API gateway or IdP logging.
ITID-33144.response: Revoke and reissue the token, identify all systems that held a copy, and remediate the storage/sharing practice that allowed reuse.
