metrics: Number of token-reuse incidents detected
Tokens rotated as a result of reuse findings
ITID-33144.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the specific pattern of a validly issued token being reused outside its intended integration boundary, rather than stolen, silently abused, or persisted post-remediation.

playbook.name: OAuth Token Reuse Across Unauthorized Third-Party Integration
playbook.description: A valid OAuth token issued for one integration is replayed or reused to authenticate against a different, unauthorized third-party service.

steps.title: Detect token use against an unexpected audience/service
steps.desc: Review token audience (aud) claims and API gateway logs to identify a token being presented to a service it was not issued for.
steps.guidance: Compare the token's intended audience/client_id against the service that accepted it — a mismatch indicates reuse or a validation flaw.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized service and the reused token's origin.

steps.title: Determine whether this is a token-validation flaw or a leaked token
steps.desc: Assess if the receiving service failed to validate the audience/issuer claim (a bug) or if the token itself was stolen/leaked and replayed intentionally.
steps.outcome: Root cause classified as validation defect vs. stolen token.

steps.title: Revoke the reused token and any related tokens
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the specific token and any others issued in the same session/grant.
steps.outcome: Token no longer valid anywhere.

steps.title: Disable the unauthorized integration's access
steps.desc: Block or disable the third-party service's access at the network/API gateway level until the issue is resolved.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized service can no longer reach the API.

steps.title: Fix audience/issuer validation on the receiving service
steps.desc: Patch the vulnerable service to strictly validate the token's audience, issuer, and scope claims before granting access.
steps.guidance: This is the root-cause fix if a validation flaw was identified in identification step 2.
steps.outcome: Service rejects tokens not explicitly issued for it.

steps.title: Re-issue properly scoped tokens and verify integrations
steps.desc: Issue new, correctly-scoped tokens to legitimate integrations and confirm each service now properly validates and rejects out-of-audience tokens via a test.
steps.outcome: All legitimate integrations restored and validation confirmed working.

steps.title: Add automated token-audience validation testing to CI/CD
steps.desc: Document the incident and add a security test that verifies every new/updated service correctly enforces token audience validation before deployment.
steps.outcome: Test added to pipeline.

ITID-33145.def: Unauthorized access achieved through misuse of an OAuth token or grant that has not yet been further classified into persistence, silent access, malicious consent, or cross-integration reuse.
ITID-33145.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for OAuth token abuse cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered OAuth abuse patterns pending triage
Cases where evidence is insufficient to distinguish among the more specific OAuth Token Abuse siblings
scopeExcludes: Any case that can be classified into ITID-33141 through ITID-33144 once sufficient evidence is gathered
ITID-33145.severity: Assess per incident; default to Medium-High pending clarification given the general sensitivity of OAuth-based access.
ITID-33145.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust priority once root cause is determined.
ITID-33145.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity team for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID as soon as the abuse pattern is clear.
indicators: Any anomalous OAuth token or app-consent activity not yet attributable to a specific pattern
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific OAuth abuse mechanism
controls: OAuth app consent auditing
Token usage monitoring
ITID-33145.detection: Varies by case; this bucket exists precisely because initial detection lacks the fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33145.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into ITID-33141 through ITID-33144 once the specific abuse mechanism is confirmed; apply standard token revocation in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
Average time to reclassify
ITID-33145.notes: This is an intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification. Analysts should reclassify into a specific OAuth Token Abuse sibling as soon as evidence supports it.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General OAuth Token Abuse
playbook.description: OAuth access or refresh tokens are abused to obtain unauthorized account or data access in a manner not otherwise classified.

steps.title: Identify the anomalous OAuth token usage
steps.desc: Review OAuth/token issuance and API access logs for anomalous grants, unexpected client applications, or access patterns inconsistent with the account owner's normal behavior.
steps.guidance: Correlate token issuance timestamps with IP/geolocation and device fingerprint anomalies.
steps.outcome: Identified token(s), issuing client, and scope of unauthorized use.
steps.abort: If no anomaly is confirmed after investigation, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Scope the impact of the token abuse
steps.desc: Determine what data or actions were accessed/performed using the abused token.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke the implicated token(s) and consent grants
steps.desc: Revoke all tokens and consent grants associated with the abused OAuth client for the affected account(s).
steps.outcome: Attacker's token-based access is terminated.

steps.title: Restrict or disable the offending OAuth client
steps.desc: Disable the client application registration or add it to a deny list pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Client cannot issue or use further tokens.

steps.title: Determine and close the root-cause gap
steps.desc: Identify how the token was abused (leak, weak client secret, missing validation, over-broad consent) and remediate that specific gap.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Restore legitimate token issuance and verify controls
steps.desc: Re-issue legitimate tokens where needed and confirm normal, authorized OAuth flows function correctly under the remediated controls.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored; abuse vector closed.

steps.title: Improve OAuth token monitoring and lifecycle controls
steps.desc: Document the incident and identify a durable monitoring or policy improvement (token lifetime limits, anomaly detection, consent governance) to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Follow-up control ticket created.

ITID-33211.def: Unauthorized horizontal access in which a user or tenant in a multi-tenant system gains access to another, unrelated customer's or tenant's data or resources due to a failure of tenant-boundary enforcement.
ITID-33211.purpose: Captures failures of multi-tenant isolation that allow one customer/tenant to access another tenant's data or resources within a shared application or platform.
scopeIncludes: Cross-tenant data leakage due to shared database queries missing tenant-scoping filters
Tenant ID manipulation in requests granting access to another tenant's records
Shared infrastructure misconfiguration exposing one customer's data to another
scopeExcludes: Access to another individual user's data within the same tenant (see IDOR, ITID-33212)
Vertical escalation from user to admin role within one's own tenant (see Vertical Privilege Escalation group)
ITID-33211.severity: High to Critical, since a single flaw can expose many customers' data simultaneously.
ITID-33211.priority: P1, given the multiplicative blast radius across tenants.
ITID-33211.escalation: Escalate immediately to engineering leadership, security, and legal/privacy given likely multi-customer breach notification obligations.
indicators: A user's session returning records tagged with a different tenant/customer ID
Application logs showing tenant-ID parameter tampering
Customer reports of seeing another organization's data
vectors: Manipulating tenant/customer ID parameters in API requests
Exploiting shared caching layers that fail to key by tenant
Race conditions in tenant-provisioning logic
rootCauses: Missing tenant-scoping in database queries or ORM layers
Shared caches/queues without tenant partitioning
Insufficient automated multi-tenancy isolation testing
controls: Mandatory tenant-scoping middleware/ORM enforcement
Automated cross-tenant isolation testing in CI/CD
Row-level security at the database layer
ITID-33211.detection: Weak-to-moderate; often discovered via customer report or security testing rather than real-time detection, since the request itself may look syntactically valid.
ITID-33211.response: Immediately patch the isolation flaw, identify all affected tenants and data exposed, and initiate breach-notification assessment.
metrics: Number of cross-tenant isolation incidents
Tenants affected per incident
Time to patch upon discovery
ITID-33211.notes: Differentiated from IDOR (ITID-33212) by operating at the tenant/customer boundary rather than the individual-object/user boundary.

playbook.name: Multi-Tenant Isolation Bypass (Cross-Customer/Cross-Tenant Data Access)
playbook.description: A flaw in tenant-scoping logic allows a user or process from one customer/tenant to access another tenant's data.

steps.title: Confirm the cross-tenant data access and identify the vulnerable code path
steps.desc: Review application logs, error reports, or the reporting party's evidence to confirm which tenant accessed which other tenant's data and via which endpoint/query.
steps.guidance: Reproduce in a non-production environment if possible using the reported request pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed vulnerable endpoint(s) and the specific missing tenant-scoping check.
steps.abort: If reproduction fails and the report cannot be substantiated, downgrade and continue monitoring rather than declaring a confirmed breach.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of tenants and records exposed
steps.desc: Query database/access logs to identify every instance where the flaw was exploited, intentionally or incidentally, and which tenants/records were exposed.
steps.guidance: Search for the vulnerable query/endpoint pattern across the full log retention window, not just the reported instance.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected tenants and exposed record counts.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the vulnerable endpoint/feature immediately
steps.desc: Take the vulnerable API endpoint or feature offline, or add an emergency WAF rule/feature flag to block the exploitable request pattern.
steps.guidance: Balance availability impact against the severity of ongoing cross-tenant exposure — a full feature disable is often warranted for this class of issue.
steps.outcome: No further cross-tenant access is possible through the flaw.
steps.tool: Feature flag system / WAF / API gateway

steps.title: Escalate to leadership and legal/compliance
steps.desc: Immediately escalate a confirmed multi-tenant isolation breach to engineering leadership, legal, and compliance given likely breach-notification obligations.
steps.guidance: Cross-tenant exposure typically triggers contractual and regulatory notification requirements.
steps.outcome: Executive, legal, and compliance stakeholders engaged with a documented timeline.

steps.title: Patch the tenant-scoping logic and add defense-in-depth checks
steps.desc: Fix the root-cause query/authorization code to enforce tenant ID scoping at every data-access layer (application, ORM, and database row-level security if available).
steps.guidance: Prefer adding a database-level tenant isolation control (e.g., row-level security) in addition to the application fix.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified to block the previously exploitable request pattern.

steps.title: Regression-test tenant isolation across all related endpoints
steps.desc: Test all endpoints sharing the same data-access pattern for similar isolation gaps, not just the originally reported one.
steps.outcome: No other endpoints found with the same class of flaw, or all are remediated.

steps.title: Re-enable the feature and notify affected customers
steps.desc: Restore the feature/endpoint to service after fix verification, and issue required customer/regulatory breach notifications.
steps.outcome: Feature restored; notifications sent per legal guidance.

steps.title: Mandate tenant-isolation testing in the SDLC
steps.desc: Document the incident and require automated multi-tenant isolation tests for all new data-access code as part of the standard development and code-review process.
steps.outcome: SDLC/testing policy updated.

ITID-33212.def: Unauthorized horizontal access achieved by manipulating a direct object reference (such as a record ID, file path, or account number) in a request to retrieve or modify another user's data without proper authorization checks.
ITID-33212.purpose: Captures classic Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerabilities exploited to access another peer user's account or records within the same tenant.
scopeIncludes: Incrementing/guessing record IDs in URLs or API calls to access another user's data
Modifying request parameters to view another user's orders, profile, files, or messages
IDOR in exported or downloadable file references
scopeExcludes: Cross-tenant/customer boundary failures (see Multi-Tenant Isolation Bypass, ITID-33211)
Session or object ID manipulation specifically targeting session tokens rather than data object references (see ITID-33213)
ITID-33212.severity: Medium-High, depending on data sensitivity and whether write access (not just read) is possible.
ITID-33212.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the IDOR allows bulk enumeration or exposes highly sensitive data.
ITID-33212.escalation: Escalate to the application owner and security engineering upon confirmation; assess for evidence of enumeration/scraping.
indicators: Sequential or patterned object-ID requests from a single user/session
Authorization check absent or failing in access logs for object-level requests
Customer/user reports of viewing another user's data
vectors: Manual or automated ID enumeration against object-referencing endpoints
Parameter tampering in API requests (record ID, account number, file path)
rootCauses: Missing object-level authorization checks (Broken Object Level Authorization)
Predictable, sequential object identifiers
Reliance on client-side authorization enforcement
controls: Server-side object-level authorization checks on every request
Use of non-sequential/opaque object identifiers (UUIDs)
Automated IDOR testing in the SDLC (SAST/DAST/API security testing)
ITID-33212.detection: Moderate; sequential-ID enumeration is detectable via rate/pattern analysis, but low-volume single-record IDOR often evades detection until reported.
ITID-33212.response: Patch the missing authorization check, determine scope of records accessed, and notify affected users if sensitive data was exposed.
metrics: Number of IDOR findings/incidents per period
Time to remediate confirmed IDOR vulnerabilities
ITID-33212.notes: Differentiated from Multi-Tenant Isolation Bypass by scope: this leaf covers peer-to-peer object access within the same tenant/organization boundary.

playbook.name: IDOR Exploited for Peer-Account Access
playbook.description: An Insecure Direct Object Reference vulnerability allows a user to access another peer user's account data by manipulating an object identifier.

steps.title: Confirm the IDOR and identify the vulnerable parameter
steps.desc: Review the reported request(s) to confirm that changing an ID parameter (URL, body, or API field) returned another user's data without an authorization check.
steps.guidance: Reproduce with a test account against a non-production or carefully-scoped production test to confirm the exact parameter and endpoint.
steps.outcome: Confirmed vulnerable endpoint(s) and parameter.
steps.abort: If the endpoint correctly denies access when retested, treat as a false report.

steps.title: Determine exploitation scope via log review
steps.desc: Search access logs for the vulnerable endpoint for sequential or out-of-range ID values being requested by any single user, indicating enumeration.
steps.guidance: Look for rapid sequential ID access patterns as a strong enumeration signal.
steps.outcome: List of accounts/records accessed and by whom.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the vulnerable endpoint
steps.desc: Temporarily disable the endpoint or add a gateway-level authorization check as a stopgap until the code fix ships.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized peer-account access possible.

steps.title: Disable/monitor the exploiting account
steps.desc: If a specific user account was identified performing the enumeration, suspend it pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Exploiting account contained.

steps.title: Patch the authorization check on the object reference
steps.desc: Fix the code to verify the requesting user owns or is authorized for the referenced object before returning data, using indirect references or server-side ownership checks.
steps.guidance: Prefer indirect object references (opaque, per-user mapped IDs) over sequential IDs where feasible.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified to block cross-account access attempts.

steps.title: Re-enable the endpoint and notify affected users
steps.desc: Restore the endpoint after fix verification and notify any users whose data was confirmed accessed by another peer account.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored; affected users notified per policy.

steps.title: Add IDOR testing to the security testing checklist
steps.desc: Document the incident and add automated/manual IDOR test cases to the standard pre-release security review for all object-reference endpoints.
steps.outcome: Testing checklist updated.

ITID-33213.def: Unauthorized access to another user's account or context achieved by manipulating, predicting, or substituting a session identifier or session-bound object reference, rather than exploiting a data object reference directly.
ITID-33213.purpose: Captures horizontal privilege escalation achieved by manipulating session identifiers or object-scoped session state to assume another user's identity or context.
scopeIncludes: Predictable or guessable session token values exploited to assume another session
Manipulating a session-scoped parameter (e.g., user context switch parameter) to act as another user
Session fixation leading to peer-account access
scopeExcludes: Theft of an intact session cookie via network/browser attack (see Session Hijacking category, ITID-33511/33521/33531)
Manipulation of a data record reference rather than session/identity context (see IDOR, ITID-33212)
ITID-33213.severity: High, since successful exploitation grants full session-equivalent access to another account.
ITID-33213.priority: P1-P2 depending on the privilege of the impersonated account.
ITID-33213.escalation: Escalate to application security and IR immediately upon confirmation, and force session invalidation platform-wide if the token scheme itself is predictable.
indicators: Session tokens observed to follow a predictable/sequential pattern
A single session token used concurrently from materially different contexts/identities
Application logs showing user-context switching without corresponding re-authentication
vectors: Predictable session token generation algorithms
Session fixation attacks setting a known token before authentication
Parameter-based user-context switching without server-side verification
rootCauses: Weak/predictable session token entropy
Session tokens not regenerated on privilege change or login
Trusting client-supplied user-context parameters
controls: Cryptographically strong, high-entropy session tokens
Session regeneration on authentication/privilege change
Server-side enforcement of user context, never trusting client-supplied identity parameters
ITID-33213.detection: Moderate; requires session-token entropy monitoring and concurrent-session anomaly detection, which is not universally instrumented.
ITID-33213.response: Invalidate the affected session scheme, force re-authentication platform-wide if systemic, and audit access performed under manipulated sessions.
metrics: Number of session/object-ID manipulation incidents
Time to remediate weak session token generation
ITID-33213.notes: Scope decision: session cookie theft via network interception or malware is tracked under the Session Hijacking Tier-3 category, not here; this leaf is reserved for exploitation of weaknesses in session/identity mechanics themselves.

playbook.name: Session/Object ID Manipulation for Cross-Account Access
playbook.description: An attacker manipulates a session token or object identifier value to assume or view another user's session/account context.

steps.title: Confirm session/ID manipulation and identify the affected mechanism
steps.desc: Review the reported incident to confirm whether a session cookie, JWT claim, or object ID was altered to gain another user's context, and identify the exact mechanism (predictable session IDs, unsigned tokens, client-trusted ID parameters).
steps.guidance: Check if session IDs are sequential/predictable or if JWTs are unsigned/weakly signed and accept client-supplied claims.
steps.outcome: Confirmed manipulation vector and affected accounts.
steps.abort: If session tokens are cryptographically random and properly validated, this is not viable — re-investigate the report.

steps.title: Scope accounts and sessions affected
steps.desc: Search logs for other instances of the same manipulation technique being used, and enumerate all impacted user sessions/accounts.
steps.outcome: Full list of affected sessions/accounts.

steps.title: Invalidate all active sessions for affected accounts
steps.desc: Force logout / invalidate session tokens for all affected accounts to eliminate the hijacked session state.
steps.outcome: No hijacked sessions remain active.

steps.title: Disable the vulnerable feature/endpoint if actively exploitable
steps.desc: Temporarily disable or gate the endpoint that trusts client-supplied session/object identifiers until a fix ships.
steps.outcome: No further cross-account access possible via the flaw.

steps.title: Fix session/ID generation and validation
steps.desc: Replace predictable identifiers with cryptographically random, server-validated tokens and ensure session/object ownership is checked server-side rather than trusted from client input.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified against the previous manipulation technique.

steps.title: Re-issue sessions and verify normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm affected users can log in and obtain a properly validated session, and that manipulated identifiers are now rejected.
steps.outcome: All accounts restored under hardened session handling.

steps.title: Add session-integrity testing to the security checklist
steps.desc: Document the incident and require session/object ID unpredictability and server-side ownership validation as a standard security test for future releases.
steps.outcome: Checklist updated.

ITID-33214.def: Unauthorized access by one user to another peer user's or tenant's account, data, or context, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific horizontal privilege escalation sibling.
ITID-33214.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for horizontal privilege escalation cases that do not clearly fit multi-tenant bypass, IDOR, or session/object-ID manipulation.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered horizontal escalation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33211, ITID-33212, or ITID-33213 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33214.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33214.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33214.escalation: Escalate to application security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed peer-to-peer or cross-tenant unauthorized access not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific escalation mechanism
controls: Application-layer access control auditing
ITID-33214.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33214.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33214.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Horizontal Privilege Escalation
playbook.description: A user gains unauthorized access to another peer user's resources or data at the same privilege level through an unspecified access-control gap.

steps.title: Confirm the horizontal access-control gap
steps.desc: Review the reported access and confirm a same-privilege-level user accessed another peer's data or resources without authorization.
steps.guidance: Reproduce the access path in a controlled manner to confirm the specific gap.
steps.outcome: Confirmed vulnerable path and affected accounts.
steps.abort: If access was actually authorized (e.g., shared resource by design), close as a false positive.

steps.title: Scope the extent of exploitation
steps.desc: Determine how many peer accounts were affected and what data/actions were exposed.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Restrict or disable the affected access path
steps.desc: Add an emergency access-control check or disable the feature/endpoint enabling the horizontal escalation.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized peer access possible.

steps.title: Suspend the exploiting account if malicious intent suspected
steps.desc: If evidence indicates deliberate exploitation rather than accidental exposure, suspend the responsible account pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Malicious actor's access contained.

steps.title: Fix the underlying authorization check
steps.desc: Patch the code/config to enforce proper ownership/authorization checks for the affected resource type.
steps.outcome: Fix verified to block the previously exploitable path.

steps.title: Restore service and notify affected users
steps.desc: Re-enable the feature after fix verification and notify any users whose data was accessed without authorization.
steps.outcome: Service restored; users notified per policy.

steps.title: Broaden access-control review to similar resource types
steps.desc: Document the incident and review other resource types sharing similar authorization logic for the same class of gap.
steps.outcome: Review completed and any additional findings ticketed.

ITID-33221.def: Unauthorized vertical access achieved by bypassing or exploiting a flaw in an application's role- or permission-checking logic, rather than by exploiting a missing check on a specific API endpoint or a bad default role assignment.
ITID-33221.purpose: Captures cases where an application's role or permission-check logic itself is flawed or bypassable (broken access control), allowing a lower-privileged user to perform higher-privileged actions.
scopeIncludes: Client-side-only role checks bypassed by direct request manipulation
Logic flaws in role-hierarchy evaluation allowing privilege inheritance abuse
Manipulating a role/permission claim within a token or session to elevate privilege
scopeExcludes: A specific API endpoint entirely missing an authorization check (see ITID-33222)
Privilege gained purely because of an insecure default role at account creation (see ITID-33223)
ITID-33221.severity: High, since broken access control at the role-check level often grants broad administrative capability.
ITID-33221.priority: P1-P2 depending on the scope of functions reachable through the bypassed check.
ITID-33221.escalation: Escalate to application security engineering immediately; treat as a critical vulnerability requiring emergency patching if actively exploited.
indicators: A standard user account performing actions logged as admin-only
Token/session claims showing role values inconsistent with the account's provisioned role
Application errors/logs indicating a role check was skipped or failed open
vectors: Modifying client-side role flags or hidden form fields
Tampering with JWT/session claims where signature verification is weak or absent
Exploiting logic flaws in role-hierarchy inheritance
rootCauses: Authorization enforced client-side rather than server-side
Inconsistent or duplicated role-check logic across code paths
Token signature validation not enforced consistently
controls: Centralized, server-side authorization enforcement (e.g., policy engine)
Mandatory JWT/token signature verification on every request
Regular access-control penetration testing
ITID-33221.detection: Moderate; requires application-layer audit logging capable of flagging role-inconsistent actions.
ITID-33221.response: Patch the broken access-control logic, audit all actions taken under the elevated context, and review for similar flaws elsewhere in the codebase.
metrics: Number of broken access-control findings/incidents
Mean time to patch confirmed vertical escalation vulnerabilities
ITID-33221.notes: Differentiated from siblings by focus on the general role/permission-check logic flaw itself, distinct from a specific missing endpoint check or a bad default assignment.

playbook.name: Application Role/Permission Check Bypass (Broken Access Control)
playbook.description: A standard user bypasses a role or permission check to perform actions reserved for a higher-privileged role within the application.

steps.title: Confirm the role-check bypass and identify the technique
steps.desc: Review logs/reports to confirm a lower-privileged user performed an action gated to a higher role, and identify the bypass technique (e.g., hidden UI element still calling the backend API, client-side-only role check, parameter tampering of a role field).
steps.guidance: Check whether the authorization check exists only in the frontend/UI and is missing server-side.
steps.outcome: Confirmed bypass technique and affected function(s).
steps.abort: If the action was actually within the user's legitimate role, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine actions taken with the escalated privilege
steps.desc: Audit what privileged actions were actually performed using the bypass.
steps.outcome: Documented list of unauthorized privileged actions.

steps.title: Revoke/roll back unauthorized privileged actions
steps.desc: Reverse any configuration changes, data modifications, or grants made via the bypass.
steps.outcome: System state restored to pre-incident condition where possible.

steps.title: Disable the vulnerable function pending a fix
steps.desc: Temporarily disable the affected admin function or gate it behind an additional server-side check.
steps.outcome: No further bypass possible.

steps.title: Implement server-side authorization enforcement
steps.desc: Add or fix server-side role/permission checks for every privileged endpoint, independent of any client-side UI restriction.
steps.guidance: Apply a centralized authorization middleware/policy rather than per-endpoint ad hoc checks where feasible.
steps.outcome: Fix verified to reject the previously successful bypass request.

steps.title: Re-enable the function and verify correct enforcement
steps.desc: Restore the function to service and confirm both authorized and unauthorized roles receive the correct access outcome.
steps.outcome: Function restored with verified access control.

steps.title: Audit all privileged endpoints for missing server-side checks
steps.desc: Document the incident and conduct a broader audit of privileged endpoints to find and fix any others relying solely on client-side role checks.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated or ticketed.

ITID-33222.def: Unauthorized vertical access achieved by directly invoking an API endpoint that performs a privileged/administrative function but has no authorization check implemented, in contrast to a broader role-logic flaw.
ITID-33222.purpose: Captures cases where a specific API endpoint lacks any authorization check at all, allowing direct access to administrative or privileged functionality.
scopeIncludes: Admin-function API endpoints callable by any authenticated (or unauthenticated) user due to a missing authorization decorator/middleware
Undocumented or 'hidden' admin endpoints discovered and invoked directly
API endpoints where authorization was removed or forgotten during development/refactoring
scopeExcludes: Broader flaws in the role-evaluation logic itself where a check exists but is bypassable (see ITID-33221)
Endpoints exposed to the public internet due to network/gateway misconfiguration rather than missing app-level authorization (see Exposed APIs, ITID-33731 series)
ITID-33222.severity: High-Critical, since this typically grants direct administrative capability with minimal effort.
ITID-33222.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the low complexity and high impact of exploitation.
ITID-33222.escalation: Escalate to application security engineering immediately for emergency patching; treat any evidence of exploitation as an active incident.
indicators: Successful invocation of an admin-function endpoint by a non-admin account
API gateway/WAF logs showing direct calls to undocumented admin paths
Absence of authorization middleware in code review for a privileged route
vectors: API endpoint discovery via directory brute-forcing, client-side code review, or documentation leakage
Direct crafted requests to known admin API paths bypassing UI-level restrictions
rootCauses: Authorization middleware/decorator omitted on a new or refactored endpoint
Reliance on 'security through obscurity' (hidden but unauthenticated endpoints)
Insufficient API security testing prior to release
controls: Mandatory authorization middleware enforced by default (deny-by-default API framework configuration)
API security testing (DAST/API fuzzing) in CI/CD covering all discovered endpoints
API inventory/catalog to prevent undocumented endpoints
ITID-33222.detection: Moderate; API gateway and application logs can reveal the calls, but only if endpoint-level monitoring and baselining are in place.
ITID-33222.response: Add the missing authorization check immediately, audit all actions performed via the endpoint, and review the broader API surface for similar gaps.
metrics: Number of missing-authorization API findings
Time to patch upon discovery
ITID-33222.notes: Scope decision: network/gateway-level API exposure without an app-level authorization defect is tracked under Exposed APIs (ITID-33731 series) to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: API Endpoint Missing Authorization Check Exploited for Admin Function Access
playbook.description: An API endpoint lacking any authorization check is called directly to perform an administrative function without proper privileges.

steps.title: Confirm the missing authorization check on the endpoint
steps.desc: Review the request/response evidence to confirm the endpoint executed an admin function for a caller lacking admin privileges, with no authorization error returned.
steps.guidance: Test the endpoint directly (outside the normal UI) with a low-privileged token to confirm the gap.
steps.outcome: Confirmed vulnerable endpoint and missing check.

steps.title: Identify caller and actions performed
steps.desc: Determine the identity/source of the caller and every admin action executed via the endpoint.
steps.outcome: Full action log for the exploitation window.

steps.title: Disable the endpoint immediately
steps.desc: Take the vulnerable endpoint offline or block it at the API gateway pending a fix.
steps.outcome: No further calls to the endpoint succeed.

steps.title: Roll back unauthorized administrative changes
steps.desc: Revert any configuration, data, or account changes made through the exploited endpoint.
steps.outcome: System restored to a known-good state.

steps.title: Add authorization middleware to the endpoint and audit siblings
steps.desc: Implement the missing authorization check on the endpoint, and audit all sibling admin endpoints for the same gap (often an entire route group misses a shared middleware).
steps.guidance: Root cause is frequently a missing middleware registration for a specific route group — check the routing configuration broadly.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed to the endpoint and any siblings found lacking the check.

steps.title: Re-enable the endpoint and verify enforcement
steps.desc: Restore the endpoint to service and confirm unauthorized callers now receive a proper 401/403 response.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored with verified enforcement.

steps.title: Require default-deny authorization middleware on all new routes
steps.desc: Document the incident and adopt a default-deny routing pattern so new endpoints require an explicit authorization annotation rather than opting in.
steps.outcome: Routing standard updated and enforced via code review/lint rule.

ITID-33223.def: Unauthorized vertical access obtained because an application or system's default role assignment for new or unconfigured accounts grants more privilege than intended, and an adversary (or insider) leverages that default rather than bypassing any check.
ITID-33223.purpose: Captures privilege escalation that occurs simply because a system assigns an overly permissive default role to new accounts, requiring no exploitation technique at all.
scopeIncludes: New user accounts provisioned with administrative or elevated default roles
Service/integration accounts defaulting to broad permissions when none were explicitly configured
Self-service sign-up flows that grant elevated privileges by default (e.g., first registered user becomes admin without safeguards)
scopeExcludes: Escalation achieved by actively bypassing a role check (see ITID-33221)
Exploiting a missing authorization check on a specific endpoint (see ITID-33222)
ITID-33223.severity: Medium-High depending on how broadly the default role is provisioned across the account base.
ITID-33223.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the overly permissive default is discovered to be actively exploited or affects many accounts.
ITID-33223.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity governance upon discovery; treat as a systemic configuration issue requiring org-wide remediation, not just a single-account fix.
indicators: Newly created accounts observed with elevated privileges immediately post-provisioning
Access reviews revealing many accounts holding admin-equivalent default roles
Service accounts with broad permissions never explicitly scoped down
vectors: Self-registration exploiting a permissive default role
Insider or low-effort adversary simply using a newly created account's excessive default access
Automated provisioning templates that default to broad roles
rootCauses: Least-privilege principle not applied to default role templates
No periodic access review/certification process
Provisioning automation using overly broad default IAM policies
controls: Least-privilege default role templates
Periodic access certification/review
Automated policy-as-code review of provisioning templates
ITID-33223.detection: Weak-to-moderate; typically found through access reviews or audits rather than real-time alerting, since the access itself is technically 'authorized' by misconfiguration.
ITID-33223.response: Correct the default role template, review and downgrade any accounts that inherited excessive privilege, and re-provision affected accounts under least privilege.
metrics: Number of accounts remediated for excessive default privilege
Time between provisioning and default-role correction
ITID-33223.notes: Differentiated from siblings by requiring no active bypass technique — the excessive privilege is simply the system's configured default.

playbook.name: Privilege Escalation via Insecure Default Role Assignment
playbook.description: New accounts or resources are assigned an overly permissive default role, allowing unintended privileged access without any explicit grant.

steps.title: Identify the insecure default role and affected accounts
steps.desc: Review role-assignment configuration to confirm the default role granted to new users/resources includes unintended privileged permissions, and enumerate all accounts currently holding it.
steps.guidance: Check IAM/role provisioning templates and any recently changed default-role configuration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed default role definition and full list of affected accounts.

steps.title: Determine if the excess privilege was exploited
steps.desc: Review audit logs for evidence that any account used the unintended privileges beyond their intended scope.
steps.outcome: Documented evidence of exploitation, or confirmation none occurred.
steps.abort: If no account has used the excess privilege, this can be treated as a lower-urgency misconfiguration remediation rather than an active incident.

steps.title: Correct the default role definition
steps.desc: Immediately update the default role/template to remove the unintended privileges for all future account provisioning.
steps.outcome: New accounts no longer receive the excess privilege.

steps.title: Remove excess privilege from existing affected accounts
steps.desc: Apply the corrected role to all existing accounts holding the insecure default, removing the unintended permissions.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with account owners if removal may disrupt legitimate, approved use of the extra permission.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts now hold only intended permissions.

steps.title: Review and remediate any actions taken with the excess privilege
steps.desc: If exploitation was confirmed, reverse or validate any actions/changes made using the unintended privilege.
steps.outcome: System state confirmed clean.

steps.title: Verify least-privilege posture restored
steps.desc: Confirm via IAM policy simulation or review that all accounts now hold only their intended, least-privilege permission set.
steps.outcome: Least-privilege posture verified.

steps.title: Add default-role review to IAM change-management process
steps.desc: Document the incident and require security review/approval for any change to default role templates going forward.
steps.outcome: Change-management process updated.

ITID-33224.def: Unauthorized elevation from a lower-privileged to a higher-privileged role or capability, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific vertical privilege escalation sibling.
ITID-33224.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for vertical privilege escalation cases that do not clearly fit broken role-check logic, missing endpoint authorization, or insecure default role assignment.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered vertical escalation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33221, ITID-33222, or ITID-33223 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33224.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33224.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33224.escalation: Escalate to application security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed privilege elevation not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific escalation mechanism
controls: Application-layer access control auditing
ITID-33224.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33224.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33224.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Vertical Privilege Escalation
playbook.description: A user or process obtains privileges higher than their assigned level through an unspecified control gap.

steps.title: Confirm the vertical escalation and identify the mechanism
steps.desc: Review the evidence to confirm a lower-privileged identity obtained higher-privilege access, and identify how (misconfiguration, code flaw, credential theft of a privileged account, etc.).
steps.outcome: Confirmed escalation mechanism and affected identity.
steps.abort: If the access was actually authorized, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Scope actions taken at the elevated privilege level
steps.desc: Determine all actions performed while operating with the escalated privilege.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke the escalated privilege immediately
steps.desc: Remove the unauthorized elevated access/role from the identity and terminate any active privileged sessions.
steps.outcome: Identity restored to its original, intended privilege level.

steps.title: Contain the exploited access path
steps.desc: Disable or restrict the specific mechanism (endpoint, misconfiguration, or credential) that enabled the escalation.
steps.outcome: No further escalation via the same path possible.

steps.title: Fix the root-cause control gap
steps.desc: Remediate the underlying flaw (code fix, IAM policy correction, credential rotation) that allowed the escalation.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Verify least-privilege posture and restore normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm the identity and related systems now operate under correct, least-privilege controls.
steps.outcome: Verified least-privilege state restored.

steps.title: Strengthen privilege-boundary monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement or tune detection for privilege-level anomalies (e.g., a standard account suddenly performing admin actions).
steps.outcome: Detection improvement implemented.

ITID-33231.def: Unauthorized privilege escalation achieved by compromising or abusing a non-human service account (application, automation, or system account) that holds broader or more persistent privileges than typical human accounts, and using it to perform actions beyond the intended scope.
ITID-33231.purpose: Provides the general/comprehensive definition of privilege escalation achieved through exploitation of a service account, since this Tier-4 group has only one Tier-5 leaf.
scopeIncludes: Compromise of a service account's credentials/keys and use to access privileged resources
Abuse of a service account's excessive standing permissions (e.g., broad database or cloud-resource access)
Lateral use of a service account to reach systems not accessible to the compromising actor's own identity
scopeExcludes: Vertical escalation of a human user account via role/endpoint/default-assignment flaws (see ITID-33221 through ITID-33224)

Kerberos/NTLM credential-material abuse (Pass-the-Hash/Pass-the-Ticket) once lateral movement is underway, tracked under ITID-33331 and the Attacks Against the Human credential domain (ITID-12720 series)
ITID-33231.severity: High, since service accounts commonly hold broad, rarely-rotated, and poorly monitored privileges.
ITID-33231.priority: P1-P2 depending on the breadth of access the compromised service account holds.
ITID-33231.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity and infrastructure teams immediately; treat service-account compromise as high severity by default given typical over-privileging.
indicators: Service account authentication from an unusual host, time, or location
Service account performing actions outside its documented automation purpose
Unrotated service account credentials found in exposed configuration or code
vectors: Credentials/keys for a service account leaked in source code, config files, or CI/CD pipelines
Exploiting an application vulnerability to extract a service account's stored credentials
Abuse of an overly broad cloud IAM role attached to a service identity
rootCauses: Service accounts provisioned with far more privilege than their function requires
No credential rotation or vaulting for service account secrets
Lack of behavioral monitoring/baselining for non-human identities
controls: Least-privilege scoping for all service accounts
Secrets management/vaulting with automated rotation
Behavioral anomaly detection for non-human identities (NHI monitoring)
ITID-33231.detection: Moderate; improving with dedicated non-human-identity (NHI) monitoring tools, but historically under-instrumented compared to human identity monitoring.
ITID-33231.response: Rotate the compromised service account's credentials immediately, review all actions taken under the identity, and reduce its standing privilege to least-privilege scope.
metrics: Number of service-account compromise incidents
Percentage of service accounts under vaulted/rotated credential management
ITID-33231.notes: Sole Tier-5 child of Service Account Exploitation; written as the general/comprehensive definition of the Tier-4 concept. Kerberos-specific credential-material replay techniques are tracked under Pass-the-Hash (ITID-33331) and the Attacks Against the Human credential domain (ITID-12720 series) to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Service Account Exploitation (Unauthorized Access Context)
playbook.description: A service/machine account's credentials or excessive permissions are exploited to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Identify anomalous service account activity
steps.desc: Review logs for the service account performing actions outside its normal automated pattern (interactive login, access from an unexpected host/IP, unusual API calls, off-hours activity).
steps.guidance: Service accounts typically have highly predictable, scripted behavior — any deviation is a strong signal.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous activity, source, and time window.
steps.abort: If the activity is explained by a known, approved change (e.g., a new automation job), close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine how the service account credential/permission was obtained or abused
steps.desc: Investigate whether the service account's key/secret was leaked (e.g., in code repo, config file, log) or whether its permissions were simply excessive and abused via a compromised caller.
steps.guidance: Search code repositories and CI/CD logs for exposed service account secrets.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the exploitation identified.

steps.title: Disable or rotate the service account credential
steps.desc: Immediately rotate the service account's key/secret/certificate and disable the compromised credential.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with dependent system owners to avoid breaking legitimate automation during rotation.
steps.outcome: Old credential no longer usable.

steps.title: Restrict the service account to least-privilege scope temporarily
steps.desc: Reduce the account's permissions to the minimum required while investigation continues.
steps.outcome: Blast radius of any further misuse minimized.

steps.title: Remove exposed secrets and remediate the leak source
steps.desc: Purge the exposed credential from any code repository, config file, or log where it was found, and fix the practice that caused the leak (e.g., move to a secrets manager).
steps.outcome: No further copies of the credential remain accessible.

steps.title: Right-size the service account's permanent permission set
steps.desc: Apply a permanent least-privilege policy to the service account based on its actual required operations.
steps.outcome: Service account permissions reduced to only what automation requires.

steps.title: Verify dependent automation functions with new credential
steps.desc: Confirm all legitimate automated processes using the service account operate correctly with the rotated credential and reduced permissions.
steps.outcome: All dependent systems confirmed functioning normally.

steps.title: Implement automated service-account secret scanning and rotation policy
steps.desc: Document the incident and put in place continuous secret-scanning and a mandatory rotation cadence for all service accounts.
steps.outcome: Ongoing control implemented.

ITID-33311.def: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary uses a compromised local administrator account and password (frequently identical across multiple endpoints) to establish RDP sessions to other machines within the environment.
ITID-33311.purpose: Captures lateral movement performed via RDP using stolen local administrator credentials, typically reused identically across many endpoints.
scopeIncludes: RDP logins using a local (non-domain) administrator account to a different host than where it was harvested
Reuse of an identical local admin password across many endpoints enabling multi-host RDP access
RDP-based lateral movement following local credential dumping (e.g., SAM/LSASS extraction)
scopeExcludes: RDP lateral movement using a compromised domain account (see ITID-33312)
Hijacking an already-established RDP session rather than authenticating fresh (see ITID-33313)
ITID-33311.severity: High, since local admin lateral movement often indicates a compromised credential pattern spanning many hosts.
ITID-33311.priority: P1, given the potential for rapid, broad lateral spread.
ITID-33311.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; treat as an active intrusion requiring host isolation and credential rotation across all hosts sharing the local admin password.
indicators: Successful RDP logins using local (non-domain) admin accounts to hosts the user does not normally access
Identical local admin credential used to authenticate to multiple distinct hosts in a short window
RDP logon events (Event ID 4624/Type 10) from source hosts inconsistent with normal admin workflow
vectors: Credential dumping (SAM database, LSASS memory) followed by RDP reuse across hosts sharing the same local admin password
Off-the-shelf lateral movement tooling automating RDP connection attempts with harvested credentials
rootCauses: Identical local administrator password reused across the fleet (no LAPS or equivalent)
RDP enabled and reachable between workstations/servers with no network segmentation
Insufficient monitoring of local account RDP logons
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or equivalent to randomize local admin passwords per host
Network segmentation restricting RDP between workstation tiers
RDP logon monitoring and alerting for local account use
ITID-33311.detection: Strong; RDP logon events and credential-dumping precursors are well covered by endpoint and Windows event log telemetry.
ITID-33311.response: Isolate affected hosts, rotate the shared local admin credential fleet-wide, and hunt for further lateral movement from the same credential.
metrics: Number of RDP lateral-movement incidents using local admin credentials
Percentage of fleet covered by unique local admin passwords (LAPS coverage)
ITID-33311.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33312 by the account type used (local vs domain) and from ITID-33313 by requiring fresh authentication rather than session takeover.

playbook.name: Internal RDP Lateral Movement Using Stolen Local Admin Credentials
playbook.description: An attacker reuses a stolen local administrator credential to RDP into additional internal hosts, moving laterally across the network.

steps.title: Identify RDP logins using the local admin credential across multiple hosts
steps.desc: Query Windows Security event logs (4624/4625 with logon type 10, and 4778/4779) and network flow data for the local admin account authenticating to multiple hosts in a short window.
steps.guidance: Look for the same local admin username/hash authenticating to hosts it has never accessed before, especially from a single originating host.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of hosts accessed via the stolen local admin credential and the source/pivot host.

steps.title: Determine patient-zero host and credential source
steps.desc: Trace back to identify the originally compromised host from which the local admin credential was harvested (e.g., via LSASS dump, cached credentials).
steps.outcome: Identified patient-zero host and credential theft method.

steps.title: Assess whether the local admin password is shared across the fleet
steps.desc: Determine if the same local admin password/hash is reused across multiple machines (a common root-cause enabler of this technique).
steps.guidance: Check for LAPS deployment status.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of password reuse across the environment.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the patient-zero host and every host confirmed accessed via the stolen credential to stop further lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts quarantined; attacker cannot pivot further using them.

steps.title: Disable the compromised local admin account and block RDP where unneeded
steps.desc: Disable or reset the local admin credential fleet-wide and restrict RDP access via firewall/NLA policy to only jump hosts, pending full remediation.
steps.outcome: Stolen credential no longer usable; RDP attack surface reduced.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) fleet-wide
steps.desc: Roll out unique, randomized, automatically-rotated local admin passwords per host to eliminate credential reuse.
steps.guidance: This is the primary root-cause fix for pass-the-shared-local-admin-hash-style movement.
steps.outcome: Every host has a unique local admin password.

steps.title: Remove attacker persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Scan and remediate all touched hosts for backdoors, scheduled tasks, or additional accounts created during lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production and verify RDP restrictions
steps.desc: Bring remediated hosts back online and confirm RDP is restricted per the new policy and that unique local admin passwords are in effect.
steps.outcome: Environment restored under hardened controls.

steps.title: Mandate LAPS and RDP network segmentation as standing controls
steps.desc: Document the incident and formalize LAPS deployment and RDP segmentation (jump-host only) as a required baseline control.
steps.outcome: Baseline control policy updated.

ITID-33312.def: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary authenticates via RDP to additional hosts using a compromised domain user or domain admin account, leveraging Active Directory trust to reach systems the account is entitled to.
ITID-33312.purpose: Captures lateral movement performed via RDP using a compromised domain account, which typically grants broader reach across the environment than a local account.
scopeIncludes: RDP logins to multiple hosts using a single compromised domain account
Domain admin account RDP use to reach domain controllers or servers
RDP access enabled by Kerberos/NTLM authentication of a stolen domain credential
scopeExcludes: RDP lateral movement using a local (non-domain) administrator account (see ITID-33311)
Takeover of an existing RDP session without fresh domain authentication (see ITID-33313)
ITID-33312.severity: High-Critical, especially if the compromised domain account has administrative privileges.
ITID-33312.priority: P1, given domain accounts typically provide the broadest lateral reach.
ITID-33312.escalation: Escalate to IR and Active Directory/identity teams immediately; assume domain-wide exposure until scoped, especially if a privileged domain account is involved.
indicators: A single domain account authenticating via RDP to an unusual number of distinct hosts in a short period
RDP logons from a domain account outside its normal working hours/locations
Domain admin account used for interactive RDP logon to non-administrative workstations
vectors: Credential theft (phishing, keylogging, or dumping) followed by RDP authentication using the domain account
Kerberoasting or NTLM relay yielding a usable domain credential for RDP
rootCauses: Domain admin accounts permitted to RDP into standard workstations/servers
No tiered administration model (e.g., Microsoft's Enterprise Access Model) separating admin credentials by tier
Insufficient monitoring of domain account logon patterns across hosts
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Tiered administration model restricting where privileged domain accounts can log on
Restricted RDP group policies (deny domain admin interactive logon to lower-tier hosts)
Domain logon pattern anomaly detection (e.g., UEBA)
ITID-33312.detection: Strong; domain controller and endpoint logon telemetry provide clear visibility into cross-host domain-account RDP activity.
ITID-33312.response: Disable/reset the compromised domain account, isolate affected hosts, and review Kerberos ticket activity for further compromise indicators.
metrics: Number of domain-account RDP lateral-movement incidents
Mean hosts reached per compromised domain account before containment
detections: Cross-host domain account logon anomaly alerting
ITID-33312.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33311 by account type (domain vs local).

playbook.name: RDP Lateral Movement via Compromised Domain Account
playbook.description: An attacker uses a compromised Active Directory domain account to RDP into multiple hosts across the domain.

steps.title: Identify RDP logons for the compromised domain account across hosts
steps.desc: Query domain controller and endpoint logs (event 4624 logon type 10, and Kerberos TGT/TGS requests) for the account authenticating to multiple hosts atypical of its normal usage.
steps.guidance: Compare against the account's historical login pattern/baseline to flag anomalous hosts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of hosts accessed and login timeline.

steps.title: Determine the account's privilege scope in AD
steps.desc: Check whether the compromised account holds elevated group membership (e.g., Domain Admins) which would materially increase severity.
steps.outcome: Documented privilege level and group memberships.

steps.title: Disable the compromised domain account and revoke Kerberos tickets
steps.desc: Disable the account and force Kerberos ticket invalidation (e.g., double password reset via krbtgt-aware process) to prevent continued use of existing tickets.
steps.guidance: A simple password reset alone does not invalidate already-issued Kerberos tickets — ensure ticket revocation is performed.
steps.outcome: Account and its tickets no longer usable for authentication.

steps.title: Isolate all hosts accessed via the compromised account
steps.desc: Network-isolate every host the account RDP'd into during the compromise window pending forensic review.
steps.outcome: Lateral movement contained to known hosts.

steps.title: Reset the account credential and review its group memberships
steps.desc: Force a permanent password reset and review/remove any unnecessary elevated AD group memberships from the account.
steps.outcome: Account secured with minimal necessary privileges.

steps.title: Sweep affected hosts for attacker persistence
steps.desc: Scan all touched hosts for backdoors, new scheduled tasks, or additional compromised accounts created during the lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts and account to service with monitoring
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production and re-enable the account with heightened monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Environment restored with enhanced monitoring in place.

steps.title: Implement RDP restriction via Restricted Admin/tiered administration model
steps.desc: Document the incident and adopt a tiered administration model (e.g., Microsoft's tiering) restricting which accounts may RDP to which tiers of hosts.
steps.outcome: Tiering model adopted or its adoption tracked as a project.

ITID-33313.def: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary takes over an existing, already-authenticated RDP session (e.g., via session shadowing or disconnected-session reconnection abuse) instead of presenting credentials to establish a new session.
ITID-33313.purpose: Captures lateral movement achieved by hijacking an already-established RDP session rather than authenticating with stolen credentials.
scopeIncludes: Abuse of RDP session shadowing/remote assistance features to take control of another user's active session
Reconnecting to a disconnected RDP session belonging to another user without re-authentication
Exploiting terminal services session-management flaws to hijack a session ID
scopeExcludes: Fresh RDP authentication using stolen local or domain credentials (see ITID-33311/ITID-33312)
ITID-33313.severity: High, since session hijacking bypasses authentication entirely and inherits the victim's full active context.
ITID-33313.priority: P1, given the immediate and complete access this technique grants.
ITID-33313.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; terminate the hijacked session and isolate the host pending investigation.
indicators: RDP session shadowing initiated without documented help-desk/remote-support justification
A disconnected session reconnected from a source host different from the original
Terminal Services event logs showing session ID reuse/takeover
vectors: Abuse of built-in RDP shadowing (mstsc /shadow) with administrative rights on the RDP host
Exploiting terminal services session broker misconfigurations
rootCauses: RDP session shadowing enabled without requiring user consent
Excessive local admin rights allowing shadowing of any session on a host
Insufficient logging/alerting on session shadow/reconnect events
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
T1563.002 Remote Service Session Hijacking: RDP Hijacking
controls: Require explicit user consent for RDP shadowing
Restrict shadowing/administrative RDP rights to authorized support tiers
Monitor and alert on session shadow/reconnect events
ITID-33313.detection: Moderate; requires specific logging of shadowing and session-reconnect events, which is not always enabled by default.
ITID-33313.response: Terminate the hijacked session immediately, isolate the host, and investigate how the adversary obtained the local rights needed to shadow the session.
metrics: Number of RDP session hijacking incidents detected
ITID-33313.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33311/33312 by not requiring fresh credential-based authentication at all — it is a session-takeover technique.

playbook.name: RDP Session Hijacking for Lateral Movement (Existing Session Takeover)
playbook.description: An attacker takes over an existing, disconnected RDP session on a host (e.g., via tscon.exe session-shadowing) to move laterally without needing new credentials.

steps.title: Identify session-hijacking technique usage
steps.desc: Review EDR/process logs for use of tscon.exe, query user, or session-hijack tooling used to attach to another user's disconnected RDP session, typically requiring SYSTEM-level access first.
steps.guidance: Look for tscon.exe execution with a /dest parameter or unusual use of the Terminal Services API.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hijacking technique, source host, and hijacked session owner.

steps.title: Determine how SYSTEM-level access was obtained to enable hijacking
steps.desc: This technique requires prior SYSTEM privilege on the host — trace back the initial compromise/privilege escalation that enabled it.
steps.outcome: Root-cause privilege escalation identified.

steps.title: Isolate the host and terminate all RDP sessions
steps.desc: Network-isolate the affected host and forcibly terminate the hijacked and any other active RDP sessions on it.
steps.outcome: No further session hijacking possible on the host.

steps.title: Reset credentials for the hijacked session's user and any SYSTEM-level footholds
steps.desc: Force credential reset for the user whose session was hijacked, and remove any attacker-established SYSTEM-level persistence.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has session or SYSTEM-level access.

steps.title: Close the privilege-escalation vulnerability that enabled hijacking
steps.desc: Patch or reconfigure the root-cause flaw that allowed the attacker to obtain SYSTEM privilege on the host in the first place.
steps.outcome: Escalation path closed and verified.

steps.title: Rebuild or restore the host and verify integrity
steps.desc: Given SYSTEM-level compromise, prefer rebuilding the host from a known-good image rather than in-place cleanup, then verify integrity before returning to production.
steps.outcome: Host restored to a verified clean state.

steps.title: Restrict local admin rights and monitor for tscon.exe/session-hijack indicators
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement detection rules for session-hijacking tooling plus reduce the population of users with local admin rights.
steps.outcome: Detection rule and admin-rights review completed.

ITID-33314.def: Unauthorized lateral movement via RDP achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific RDP Access sibling.
ITID-33314.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for RDP-based lateral movement cases that do not clearly fit local-credential, domain-credential, or session-hijacking classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered RDP lateral-movement patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33311, ITID-33312, or ITID-33313 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33314.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification given the general severity of RDP lateral movement.
ITID-33314.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33314.escalation: Escalate to IR for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed unauthorized RDP-based lateral movement not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific lateral movement mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: RDP logon monitoring and alerting
ITID-33314.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33314.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed; isolate affected hosts in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33314.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General RDP Lateral Movement
playbook.description: An attacker uses RDP to move between internal hosts through an unspecified credential or session-abuse method.

steps.title: Identify the RDP lateral-movement pattern
steps.desc: Review Windows Security event logs and network flow data for RDP connections between internal hosts inconsistent with normal administrative patterns.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of hosts and accounts involved.

steps.title: Determine the credential/access method used
steps.desc: Investigate whether the movement used a stolen credential, hash, ticket, or hijacked session.
steps.outcome: Identified access method to inform containment.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts
steps.desc: Network-isolate every host confirmed accessed during the lateral-movement window.
steps.outcome: Movement contained to known hosts.

steps.title: Disable/reset the credential(s) used
steps.desc: Disable or reset the account(s)/credential(s) identified as enabling the movement.
steps.outcome: Credential no longer usable.

steps.title: Remove persistence and close the access path
steps.desc: Remediate the underlying gap (RDP exposure, credential reuse, missing NLA/MFA) and remove any attacker persistence from affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Access path closed and hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production with monitoring
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to service with enhanced monitoring for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Environment restored and monitored.

steps.title: Restrict and segment RDP access org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement RDP network segmentation, MFA, and jump-host-only access as standing controls.
steps.outcome: Segmentation policy implemented or tracked.

ITID-33321.def: Unauthorized lateral movement achieved by mounting or accessing a remote host's hidden administrative share (C$, ADMIN$, or similar) using valid or stolen credentials, typically to stage files, read data, or prepare for remote execution.
ITID-33321.purpose: Captures lateral movement performed by connecting to a host's hidden administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) using compromised credentials.
scopeIncludes: Mounting C$/ADMIN$ on a remote host using stolen or valid admin credentials
Copying tools, payloads, or scripts to a remote host via an admin share ahead of execution
Reading or exfiltrating data directly from a remote host's admin share
scopeExcludes: Using the admin share connection specifically to create a remote service for code execution (see ITID-33322)
Anonymous/null-session access to IPC$ specifically for enumeration (see ITID-33323)
ITID-33321.severity: High, since admin share access typically requires (and thus indicates) administrative credential compromise.
ITID-33321.priority: P1, given this is a common precursor to further compromise (ransomware staging, data theft).
ITID-33321.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately upon detection; treat as active lateral movement requiring host isolation and credential rotation.
indicators: SMB connections to C$/ADMIN$ from hosts with no administrative relationship to the target
File write/copy events on a remote host's admin share from an unexpected source
Windows Security Event ID 5140/5145 showing admin share access anomalies
vectors: Stolen local or domain admin credentials used to mount admin shares for staging tools
Automated lateral-movement frameworks (e.g., Impacket-based tooling) leveraging SMB admin shares
rootCauses: SMB/admin shares reachable across broad network segments with no restriction
Excessive credential reuse or shared admin credentials across hosts
Insufficient SMB access logging/monitoring
mitreTechniques: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
controls: Network segmentation restricting SMB traffic between host tiers
Disabling default administrative shares where not operationally required
SMB access logging and anomaly alerting
ITID-33321.detection: Strong; SMB access to administrative shares is a well-documented, high-fidelity detection opportunity via Windows event logs and network monitoring.
ITID-33321.response: Isolate the source and target hosts, rotate the credential used, and hunt for staged tooling or exfiltrated data on the admin share.
metrics: Number of unauthorized admin share access incidents
Mean time to detect anomalous SMB admin share activity
detections: SMB admin share access anomaly alerting
ITID-33321.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33322 by scope: this leaf covers the share access/staging itself, not the subsequent remote execution step.

playbook.name: Lateral Movement via C$/ADMIN$ Hidden Share
playbook.description: An attacker uses stolen administrative credentials to access hidden C$/ADMIN$ shares on remote Windows hosts, moving laterally and staging tools.

steps.title: Identify hidden-share access events
steps.desc: Review Windows Security event logs (5140/5145 share access, 4624 logon type 3) for connections to C$ or ADMIN$ from hosts/accounts that do not normally perform remote administration.
steps.guidance: Correlate share-access events with the account and source host to build the movement timeline.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of hosts and accounts involved in the C$/ADMIN$ access.

steps.title: Check for file staging or tool drop via the share
steps.desc: Inspect the target hosts for files copied via the share (e.g., malware binaries, scripts) around the access timestamps.
steps.outcome: Identified any staged files/tools for eradication.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts and disable the compromised admin credential
steps.desc: Network-isolate all hosts accessed via the shares and disable/reset the credential used.
steps.outcome: No further share access possible via the compromised account.

steps.title: Restrict administrative share access via firewall/GPO
steps.desc: Apply a temporary firewall rule or Group Policy restricting SMB/admin-share access to only approved management hosts.
steps.outcome: Admin shares reachable only from designated jump hosts.

steps.title: Remove staged tools/persistence from all touched hosts
steps.desc: Delete any attacker-staged files, scheduled tasks, or services created via the admin-share access.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS and least-privilege admin model
steps.desc: Roll out unique local admin passwords (LAPS) and reduce the number of accounts with domain/local admin rights to reduce future admin-share exploitation risk.
steps.outcome: Credential reuse across the fleet eliminated.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production with restricted share access
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to service and confirm admin-share access is now restricted per the new firewall/GPO policy.
steps.outcome: Environment restored under hardened controls.

steps.title: Add admin-share access monitoring as a standing detection
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement continuous monitoring/alerting on C$/ADMIN$ access from non-management hosts.
steps.outcome: Detection rule implemented.

ITID-33322.def: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary uses an administrative share (typically ADMIN$) to stage an executable and then remotely creates and starts a Windows service (or scheduled task) to execute code on the target host, mirroring classic PsExec-style tooling.
ITID-33322.purpose: Captures lateral movement where an admin share connection is used specifically to create a remote service for code execution, PsExec-style.
scopeIncludes: Remote service creation via the Service Control Manager following file staging over ADMIN$
PsExec, PsExec-alternatives, or Impacket psexec.py-style remote execution
Remote scheduled task creation used as the execution trigger following admin share staging
scopeExcludes: Admin share access used only for file staging/reading without a subsequent remote-execution step (see ITID-33321)
IPC$ null-session enumeration without any file staging or execution (see ITID-33323)
ITID-33322.severity: Critical, since this technique achieves arbitrary remote code execution on the target host.
ITID-33322.priority: P1, treated as an active intrusion requiring immediate containment.
ITID-33322.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; isolate both source and target hosts and initiate full incident response given confirmed remote code execution.
