indicators: New service creation events (Event ID 7045) shortly after an ADMIN$ file-write from a remote host
Executables staged in ADMIN$/Windows/Temp paths matching known lateral-movement tool signatures
Service Control Manager remote API calls from unexpected source hosts
vectors: PsExec and PsExec-alternative tools using stolen admin credentials
Impacket-based remote execution frameworks
WMI/Service Control Manager abuse combined with SMB staging
rootCauses: Unrestricted SMB and RPC/DCE (Service Control Manager) access between hosts
Excessive or shared local/domain admin credentials across the environment
Endpoint detection not tuned to flag remote service creation patterns
mitreTechniques: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
controls: Network segmentation limiting SMB/RPC between host tiers
EDR detection rules for remote service creation and PsExec-style tooling
Restriction of local admin rights and credential reuse across hosts
ITID-33322.detection: Strong; remote service creation is a well-known, high-fidelity EDR and Windows event log detection point.
ITID-33322.response: Isolate affected hosts immediately, remove the malicious service/scheduled task, rotate credentials used, and hunt for further lateral spread from the same tooling.
metrics: Number of PsExec-style remote execution incidents detected
Mean time to isolate hosts following detection
ITID-33322.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33321 specifically by the additional remote code-execution step via service/task creation.

playbook.name: Remote Service Creation via Admin Share for Code Execution (PsExec-Style)
playbook.description: An attacker uses an admin share to remotely install and start a Windows service (PsExec-style) to execute arbitrary code on a target host.

steps.title: Identify remote service creation events
steps.desc: Review event logs (7045 new service installed, 4697) and EDR telemetry for a remotely-created, short-lived, unusually-named service correlating with an admin-share connection.
steps.guidance: PsExec-style services typically have randomized or generic names and are deleted shortly after execution — check for the associated PSEXESVC or similar artifact.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious service, host, and executing account.

steps.title: Determine payload executed and further spread
steps.desc: Identify what the remotely-created service executed and whether it was used to pivot to additional hosts.
steps.outcome: Full scope of hosts and payload identified.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts
steps.desc: Network-isolate the source and target hosts involved in the remote service creation.
steps.outcome: Further remote execution/spread halted.

steps.title: Disable the compromised administrative credential
steps.desc: Disable/reset the account used to authenticate to the admin share and create the remote service.
steps.outcome: Credential no longer usable for remote service creation.

steps.title: Remove the malicious service and any dropped binaries
steps.desc: Delete the attacker-created service and any associated executable/DLL from all affected hosts.
steps.outcome: No malicious service or binary remains.

steps.title: Restrict remote service creation and SMB admin-share access
steps.desc: Apply Group Policy/firewall restrictions limiting which accounts/hosts can remotely create services or reach admin shares.
steps.outcome: Attack technique blocked going forward.

steps.title: Rebuild or verify integrity of affected hosts, then restore to production
steps.desc: Given remote code execution occurred, verify host integrity thoroughly (or rebuild from image) before returning to service.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean and restored.

steps.title: Deploy detection for remote service creation via admin shares
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement a detection rule for PsExec-style remote service creation patterns.
steps.outcome: Detection rule implemented.

ITID-33323.def: Unauthorized access in which an adversary connects to a target host's IPC$ share using an anonymous or null session (no valid credentials) to enumerate users, shares, policies, or other system information as a precursor to further lateral movement.
ITID-33323.purpose: Captures reconnaissance or limited lateral movement achieved via anonymous/null-session access to a host's IPC$ share.
scopeIncludes: Null-session connections to IPC$ used to enumerate SAM accounts, shares, or domain policy
Anonymous SMB enumeration of a host preceding a credentialed lateral-movement attempt
Tools such as enum4linux or similar leveraging null sessions against IPC$
scopeExcludes: Credentialed access to C$/ADMIN$ for staging or execution (see ITID-33321/ITID-33322)
ITID-33323.severity: Low-Medium on its own (reconnaissance), escalating to High if followed by credentialed lateral movement.
ITID-33323.priority: P3 for isolated enumeration; P1-P2 if correlated with subsequent credentialed access attempts.
ITID-33323.escalation: Escalate to SOC for correlation with subsequent activity; null-session enumeration alone rarely warrants IR escalation but should be tracked as a precursor indicator.
indicators: Anonymous/null-session SMB connections to IPC$
SAM/LSA enumeration activity from an unauthenticated session
Use of known enumeration tools (enum4linux, rpcclient) against internal hosts
vectors: Null-session SMB enumeration tools run from a foothold host
Misconfigured hosts allowing anonymous IPC$ access (legacy SMB1/NTLM settings)
rootCauses: Legacy SMB configuration permitting null/anonymous sessions
SMB1 or weak NTLM settings still enabled on internal hosts
Insufficient internal network segmentation limiting SMB reachability
mitreTechniques: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
controls: Disable null-session/anonymous SMB access (RestrictAnonymous settings)
Disable legacy SMB1 protocol
Network segmentation restricting SMB reachability
ITID-33323.detection: Moderate; null-session activity is loggable via SMB/security event logs but often deprioritized as low-severity noise.
ITID-33323.response: Harden the host against anonymous access, and correlate the enumeration event with any subsequent authenticated access attempts.
metrics: Number of null-session enumeration events detected
Hosts remediated for anonymous SMB access
ITID-33323.notes: This leaf covers reconnaissance-level, uncredentialed IPC$ activity; any credentialed follow-on lateral movement should additionally be logged under ITID-33321 or ITID-33322.

playbook.name: IPC$ Null Session Abuse for Reconnaissance/Lateral Movement
playbook.description: An attacker connects to a host's IPC$ share using a null (unauthenticated) session to enumerate users, shares, and policies for further lateral movement.

steps.title: Identify null-session IPC$ connection attempts
steps.desc: Review event logs and network captures for anonymous/null-session logons (event 4624 logon type 3 with anonymous SID) connecting to IPC$ for enumeration.
steps.guidance: Look for SAMR/LSA enumeration calls immediately following the null session establishment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed source and target hosts of the null-session activity.

steps.title: Determine what information was enumerated
steps.desc: Assess what was disclosed via the null session (user list, share list, password policy) to gauge follow-on risk.
steps.outcome: Documented enumeration scope.

steps.title: Block the source of the null-session connections
steps.desc: Block the source IP/host at the firewall and isolate it if it is an already-compromised internal host.
steps.outcome: No further null-session enumeration from the source.

steps.title: Disable null-session/anonymous access to IPC$ and SAM
steps.desc: Apply the RestrictAnonymous (and RestrictAnonymousSAM) Group Policy settings to disable anonymous enumeration of users and shares.
steps.guidance: This is the standard root-cause hardening for this technique.
steps.outcome: Null-session enumeration no longer possible on affected hosts.

steps.title: Verify hardening applied fleet-wide and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm the anonymous-access restriction is deployed across the domain and set up monitoring for further null-session attempts.
steps.outcome: Fleet-wide hardening confirmed.

steps.title: Baseline and audit legacy SMB/NetBIOS exposure
steps.desc: Document the incident and perform a broader audit for legacy SMBv1/NetBIOS exposure that facilitates null-session and similar reconnaissance techniques.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33324.def: Unauthorized lateral movement via administrative SMB shares achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Admin Shares Abuse sibling.
ITID-33324.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for admin-share-based lateral movement cases that do not clearly fit staging, remote execution, or null-session enumeration classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered admin-share abuse patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33321, ITID-33322, or ITID-33323 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33324.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33324.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33324.escalation: Escalate to IR for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed unauthorized admin share activity not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
controls: SMB access logging and anomaly alerting
ITID-33324.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33324.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33324.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Admin Shares Abuse
playbook.description: An attacker abuses Windows administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) in a manner not otherwise classified to move laterally or execute code.

steps.title: Identify the admin-share abuse pattern
steps.desc: Review event logs and EDR telemetry for anomalous access to administrative shares across the environment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts, accounts, and access pattern involved.

steps.title: Determine the intent and impact of the access
steps.desc: Assess whether the access was used for reconnaissance, file staging, remote execution, or data theft.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts and disable the credential used
steps.desc: Network-isolate hosts involved and disable/reset the account used for the admin-share access.
steps.outcome: No further abuse of the admin shares possible.

steps.title: Restrict admin-share access via firewall/GPO
steps.desc: Limit SMB/admin-share connectivity to approved management hosts only.
steps.outcome: Attack surface reduced.

steps.title: Remove any persistence and close the root-cause gap
steps.desc: Remove attacker artifacts from affected hosts and remediate the specific weakness (credential reuse, missing restriction) that enabled the abuse.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean and gap closed.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production under hardened controls
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to service and confirm the new access restrictions are in effect.
steps.outcome: Environment restored and verified.

steps.title: Implement admin-share access monitoring org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement continuous monitoring/alerting for anomalous administrative share access.
steps.outcome: Detection rule implemented.

ITID-33331.def: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary authenticates to a remote system using a captured NTLM password hash directly, without ever knowing or cracking the underlying plaintext password.
ITID-33331.purpose: Provides the general/comprehensive definition of lateral movement via Pass-the-Hash, since this Tier-4 group has only one Tier-5 leaf.
scopeIncludes: Extraction of NTLM hashes from LSASS memory, SAM database, or NTDS.dit and reuse via pass-the-hash tooling (e.g., Mimikatz, Impacket)
Lateral movement to additional hosts using a reused NTLM hash from an initially compromised host
Pass-the-hash used to authenticate to SMB, RDP (restricted admin mode), or WMI on a remote host
scopeExcludes: Kerberos ticket-based replay (Pass-the-Ticket / Golden/Silver Ticket) and the broader detailed credential-material replay technique breakdown, which is tracked under ITID-12720 series in the Attacks Against the Human credential domain to avoid duplication
Fresh RDP authentication using a stolen plaintext credential (see ITID-33311/ITID-33312)
ITID-33331.severity: Critical, since pass-the-hash typically indicates deep endpoint compromise and enables rapid, credential-less lateral spread.
ITID-33331.priority: P1, treated as an active intrusion requiring immediate containment.
ITID-33331.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; isolate affected hosts and force a full NTLM hash reset (including krbtgt/service accounts if domain-wide) given the difficulty of fully remediating hash-based compromise.
indicators: Authentication events showing NTLM logon without a corresponding interactive/console logon on the source host
LSASS memory access indicative of credential dumping tools
A single account authenticating to many hosts in rapid succession via NTLM
vectors: Mimikatz or similar tools extracting NTLM hashes from LSASS memory
Impacket-based pass-the-hash tooling (wmiexec.py, psexec.py with -hashes)
RDP Restricted Admin mode combined with a stolen hash
rootCauses: NTLM authentication still enabled/permitted where Kerberos could be enforced
Local admin credential reuse across the fleet enabling hash reuse
Lack of Credential Guard or LSASS protection on endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
controls: Windows Defender Credential Guard / LSASS protection
Disabling NTLM where feasible in favor of Kerberos
Unique local admin passwords (LAPS) to prevent hash-reuse lateral spread
ITID-33331.detection: Strong; NTLM logon anomalies and LSASS access are well-covered by modern EDR and Windows event logging.
ITID-33331.response: Isolate affected hosts, force password/hash resets for all potentially exposed accounts, and enable Credential Guard where not already deployed.
metrics: Number of pass-the-hash incidents detected
Percentage of fleet with Credential Guard/LSASS protection enabled
ITID-33331.notes: Sole Tier-5 child of Pass-the-Hash; written as the general/comprehensive definition of the technique. Kerberos ticket-based replay (Pass-the-Ticket, Golden/Silver Ticket) is tracked under ITID-12720 series in the Attacks Against the Human credential domain to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Pass-the-Hash Attack (Lateral Movement Context)
playbook.description: An attacker extracts an NTLM password hash from a compromised host and reuses it to authenticate to other hosts without knowing the plaintext password.

steps.title: Identify pass-the-hash indicators in authentication logs
steps.desc: Review Windows Security logs (4624 logon type 3, NTLM authentication package) and EDR telemetry for NTLM authentications to multiple hosts using an account with no corresponding interactive logon, and for LSASS memory access indicative of hash dumping.
steps.guidance: Look for a Domain Admin or privileged account authenticating via NTLM to unusual hosts, and for tools like Mimikatz accessing LSASS.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts and account(s) involved in the pass-the-hash chain, and the patient-zero host where the hash was dumped.

steps.title: Scope full extent of hosts reached via the reused hash
steps.desc: Trace every host the compromised hash was used to authenticate to, since pass-the-hash chains often span many systems quickly.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected hosts.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the patient-zero host and every host reached via the pass-the-hash chain.
steps.outcome: Lateral movement halted.

steps.title: Force a double password reset for the compromised account(s)
steps.desc: Reset the account's password twice in succession (or otherwise force NTLM hash invalidation) to invalidate the stolen hash immediately.
steps.guidance: A single reset can still leave the old hash valid briefly in some caching scenarios — follow domain-specific guidance for full invalidation.
steps.outcome: Stolen hash no longer usable for authentication.

steps.title: Remove attacker tooling and persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Scan and clean all touched hosts for credential-dumping tools, backdoors, or scheduled tasks left behind.
steps.outcome: All hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Deploy Credential Guard / restrict NTLM and local admin reuse
steps.desc: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard where supported, restrict/disable NTLM in favor of Kerberos, and deploy LAPS to eliminate local admin password reuse.
steps.guidance: This is the primary root-cause hardening against future pass-the-hash attacks.
steps.outcome: Environment hardened against hash-dumping and reuse.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production and verify hardening
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to service and confirm Credential Guard/LAPS and NTLM restrictions are active.
steps.outcome: Environment restored under hardened controls.

steps.title: Implement tiered administration and privileged access workstations
steps.desc: Document the incident and formalize a tiered admin model with privileged access workstations to prevent hash exposure of high-value credentials on lower-tier hosts.
steps.outcome: Tiering/PAW initiative tracked or implemented.

ITID-33411.def: Unauthorized device access in which a maliciously programmed USB device (e.g., a BadUSB-style flash drive or Rubber Ducky-style tool) emulates a Human Interface Device to automatically inject keystrokes and execute commands on the host the moment it is connected.
ITID-33411.purpose: Captures attacks using a malicious USB device that emulates a keyboard/HID input device to inject keystrokes and execute commands automatically upon connection.
scopeIncludes: USB devices programmed to auto-type malicious commands/scripts upon connection
HID-emulating attack tools (e.g., Rubber Ducky, O.MG cable) deployed against corporate endpoints
Firmware-level BadUSB attacks reprogramming a legitimate-looking device's controller
scopeExcludes: Use of a USB storage device purely for data exfiltration with no keystroke injection (see ITID-33412)
USB device used specifically to bypass a lock screen via other mechanisms (see ITID-33413)
ITID-33411.severity: High, since HID emulation can execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the logged-in user almost instantly.
ITID-33411.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the speed and stealth of the attack.
ITID-33411.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; isolate the affected endpoint and treat as a confirmed compromise requiring full endpoint investigation.
indicators: Unusually fast, non-human-pattern keystroke input immediately following a new USB HID device connection
New HID device enumeration events with no corresponding user-reported peripheral
Command execution/process creation immediately following USB device connection
vectors: Deliberately dropped 'lost' USB drives in parking lots/lobbies (USB drop attack) containing BadUSB firmware
Malicious USB devices delivered via mail or supply-chain tampering
Compromised legitimate-looking peripherals (cables, chargers) with embedded HID attack hardware
rootCauses: No USB device control/allowlisting policy on endpoints
Lack of endpoint detection for anomalous HID input patterns
Insufficient user awareness regarding unknown USB devices
controls: USB device control policy (allowlisting approved device classes/IDs)
Endpoint detection rules for anomalous HID keystroke timing
User awareness training on unknown USB device risks
ITID-33411.detection: Moderate; requires specific endpoint telemetry on USB device class and keystroke-timing anomalies, not enabled by default on most EDR.
ITID-33411.response: Isolate the endpoint, physically remove the device, and conduct forensic review of all commands executed since connection.
metrics: Number of BadUSB/HID injection incidents detected
Percentage of endpoints with USB device control enforced
ITID-33411.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33412 by the defining trait of keystroke/command injection via HID emulation, rather than passive data exfiltration.

playbook.name: BadUSB/HID Emulation Attack (Keystroke Injection Device)
playbook.description: A malicious USB device emulates a keyboard/HID to automatically inject commands and execute unauthorized actions on a host the moment it is plugged in.

steps.title: Identify the rogue HID device and injected activity
steps.desc: Review EDR/USB device logs for a newly connected HID (keyboard) device followed immediately by rapid, scripted keystroke/command activity inconsistent with human typing speed.
steps.guidance: Check the device's USB vendor/product ID against known-good keyboard hardware for the affected user.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious device and the commands/actions it executed.
steps.abort: If typing speed and device ID are consistent with a legitimate keyboard, this is likely a false positive.

steps.title: Determine what payload or command was executed
steps.desc: Analyze the injected command sequence/process execution to determine the attacker's objective (e.g., reverse shell, credential harvesting, malware download).
steps.outcome: Documented payload and its impact.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host and physically remove the device
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host immediately and have IT/security physically disconnect the malicious USB device.
steps.outcome: Device disconnected and host isolated from further compromise spread.

steps.title: Kill malicious processes and block C2 if a payload executed
steps.desc: Terminate any malicious process spawned by the injected commands and block associated command-and-control indicators at the firewall/proxy.
steps.outcome: Active payload execution stopped.

steps.title: Remove malware/persistence installed by the injected commands
steps.desc: Fully remediate the host of any malware, scheduled tasks, or accounts created by the injected payload.
steps.guidance: Prefer full reimage if the payload achieved persistence or privilege escalation.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Enforce USB device control policy
steps.desc: Implement or tighten USB device control (allowlisting known HID vendor/product IDs, disabling unauthorized HID enumeration) to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized HID devices are blocked from being recognized.

steps.title: Restore the host to service and verify controls
steps.desc: Return the remediated/reimaged host to production and confirm USB device control policy is enforced.
steps.outcome: Host restored under verified controls.

steps.title: Train staff on physical USB device risks and enforce device-control policy org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and roll out awareness training plus organization-wide USB device control enforcement.
steps.outcome: Training and policy rollout tracked.

ITID-33412.def: Unauthorized access to and removal of data via a USB mass-storage device connected to a corporate endpoint, used to copy files off the network without going through sanctioned data-transfer channels.
ITID-33412.purpose: Captures unauthorized copying of sensitive data from corporate systems onto a USB storage device.
scopeIncludes: Copying sensitive files to a USB flash drive or external hard disk without authorization
Use of personal USB storage media to remove corporate data ahead of departure (e.g., insider/departing-employee exfiltration)
Bulk file transfer to removable media detected by DLP tooling
scopeExcludes: USB devices used for keystroke/command injection rather than storage-based exfiltration (see ITID-33411)
ITID-33412.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity and volume of data copied.
ITID-33412.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the data involved is highly sensitive (e.g., regulated, IP, credentials) or the actor is a departing/hostile insider.
ITID-33412.escalation: Escalate to security/HR/legal for suspected insider exfiltration; escalate to IR if the USB storage device is linked to a broader external compromise.
indicators: DLP alerts for large or sensitive file transfers to removable media
USB storage device connection events immediately preceding resignation/termination
File access logs showing bulk copy operations to an external drive letter
vectors: Unrestricted USB port access allowing any storage device to be mounted
Departing employees copying files before their last day
Malicious insiders or compromised accounts using USB media to bypass network-based DLP
rootCauses: No USB storage restriction/DLP policy enforced on endpoints
Lack of file-activity monitoring for removable media transfers
Insufficient offboarding controls restricting data access ahead of departure
controls: USB storage device control/DLP policy restricting or logging removable-media use
Endpoint DLP monitoring for sensitive file transfers to removable media
Enhanced monitoring/restriction during employee offboarding windows
ITID-33412.detection: Strong; endpoint DLP and USB device logging provide direct, reliable evidence of file transfer to removable media.
ITID-33412.response: Identify and recover/destroy the copied data where possible, interview the individual if insider-related, and assess the scope of data exposure.
metrics: Number of USB exfiltration incidents detected
Volume/sensitivity of data involved per incident
sops: Data Loss Prevention Incident Response SOP
ITID-33412.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33411 by the mechanism: passive bulk data copy to storage media, not active keystroke/command injection.

playbook.name: Unauthorized Data Exfiltration via USB Storage Device
playbook.description: A user or attacker copies sensitive data to a USB storage device without authorization, exfiltrating it from the network.

steps.title: Identify the USB storage exfiltration event
steps.desc: Review DLP/USB device control logs for a large or sensitive-data file transfer to a removable storage device from the host.
steps.guidance: Check file names/classifications and transfer volume against the user's normal data-handling baseline.
steps.outcome: Confirmed device, user, host, and files transferred.
steps.abort: If the transfer is confirmed as an approved, authorized activity, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Classify the sensitivity and scope of exfiltrated data
steps.desc: Determine the classification (PII, IP, financial, etc.) and volume of data copied to assess breach-notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Documented data classification and volume.

steps.title: Disable the user's removable-media access and recover the device if possible
steps.desc: Immediately disable removable storage permissions for the user's account/host and attempt to physically recover the USB device.
steps.outcome: No further data can be copied to removable media; device recovered where possible.

steps.title: Escalate to HR/legal if insider exfiltration is suspected
steps.desc: If the activity indicates deliberate insider data theft, escalate to HR, legal, and management per the insider-threat process.
steps.outcome: Appropriate stakeholders engaged for personnel action and legal review.

steps.title: Enforce DLP/device-control policy to block unauthorized removable media
steps.desc: Tighten DLP rules and device-control policy to block or require encryption/approval for sensitive-data transfers to removable media org-wide.
steps.outcome: Policy updated and enforced.

steps.title: Confirm data disposition and notify affected parties if required
steps.desc: Determine whether the exfiltrated data was destroyed/returned and issue any required breach notifications.
steps.outcome: Data disposition confirmed and notifications sent per policy.

steps.title: Review DLP coverage and removable-media policy org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and assess whether DLP coverage and removable-media restrictions need broadening across the organization.
steps.outcome: Policy review completed.

ITID-33413.def: Unauthorized device access achieved by connecting a specialized USB device or tool to a locked endpoint to bypass its lock-screen authentication, gaining an unlocked, logged-in session without valid credentials.
ITID-33413.purpose: Captures the use of a USB-connected device or tool to bypass an endpoint's lock screen and gain unauthorized local access.
scopeIncludes: Use of DMA-attack tools (e.g., PCILeech-style devices over Thunderbolt/USB-C) to bypass lock-screen memory protections
USB-connected exploitation tools targeting lock-screen authentication bypass vulnerabilities
Physical USB-based attacks against kiosk or unattended locked devices to gain a live session
scopeExcludes: USB devices used for keystroke injection to execute commands post-unlock (see ITID-33411)
USB devices used purely for data exfiltration from an already-unlocked session (see ITID-33412)
ITID-33413.severity: High-Critical, since a successful lock-screen bypass grants a fully authenticated, live user session.
ITID-33413.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the direct access to an active session this technique grants.
ITID-33413.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; treat the endpoint as compromised and isolate it pending forensic review.
indicators: Unexpected unlock events with no corresponding valid authentication log entry
Physical evidence of an unfamiliar device connected to a locked endpoint
DMA/Thunderbolt device enumeration events immediately preceding an unlock
vectors: DMA attack tools exploiting Thunderbolt/USB-C direct memory access to patch lock-screen authentication in memory
Exploitation of unpatched lock-screen vulnerabilities via a connected USB device
rootCauses: DMA protection (Kernel DMA Protection/IOMMU) not enabled on endpoints
Thunderbolt/USB-C ports not restricted or disabled where not needed
Endpoints left unattended and physically accessible in low-security areas
controls: Kernel DMA Protection / IOMMU enforcement on all endpoints
Physical security controls for unattended devices
Port control policies restricting Thunderbolt/USB-C access where feasible
ITID-33413.detection: Weak-to-moderate; DMA-based lock-screen bypass often leaves minimal log evidence unless DMA protection telemetry or physical monitoring is in place.
ITID-33413.response: Isolate and forensically image the affected endpoint, and assess whether DMA protection was enabled and functioning.
metrics: Number of lock-screen bypass incidents detected
Percentage of fleet with Kernel DMA Protection enabled
ITID-33413.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the specific outcome of bypassing lock-screen authentication itself, rather than post-unlock keystroke injection or data exfiltration.

playbook.name: USB-Connected Device Used to Bypass Endpoint Lock Screen
playbook.description: An attacker uses a specially-crafted USB device (e.g., exploiting a driver or PnP flaw) to bypass a locked workstation's authentication screen.

steps.title: Identify the lock-screen bypass event
steps.desc: Review EDR and Windows event logs for a USB device connection immediately followed by an unlock or session-access event without a corresponding valid authentication event.
steps.guidance: Check for unusual PnP driver installation events at the same timestamp.
steps.outcome: Confirmed bypass method, device, and host affected.

steps.title: Determine what was accessed after the bypass
steps.desc: Review post-bypass activity on the host to determine what data or systems the attacker accessed.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host and remove the device
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host and physically remove the malicious USB device.
steps.outcome: Attack halted and device secured for forensics.

steps.title: Force logout and credential reset for the affected user
steps.desc: Terminate the session and reset the affected user's credentials since the session was accessed without authentication.
steps.outcome: No lingering unauthorized session access.

steps.title: Patch the underlying driver/PnP vulnerability
steps.desc: Apply the vendor patch or OS update addressing the specific driver/PnP flaw exploited, or disable the vulnerable driver/device class if no patch exists.
steps.outcome: Bypass technique no longer functional on the host.

steps.title: Enforce USB device control policy fleet-wide
steps.desc: Implement device allowlisting or disable USB port auto-mounting for untrusted device classes to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized devices blocked from being recognized.

steps.title: Restore the host to service and verify patch/policy applied
steps.desc: Return the host to production after confirming the patch and device-control policy are in effect.
steps.outcome: Host restored under verified controls.

steps.title: Audit fleet for the same vulnerable driver/PnP configuration
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit other endpoints for the same vulnerable driver/configuration to prevent similar bypasses elsewhere.
steps.outcome: Fleet-wide audit completed and remediated.

ITID-33414.def: Unauthorized device access via a USB-connected device achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific USB Exploitation sibling.
ITID-33414.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for USB-based unauthorized device access cases that do not clearly fit HID injection, storage exfiltration, or lock-screen bypass classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered USB exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33411, ITID-33412, or ITID-33413 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33414.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33414.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33414.escalation: Escalate to SOC for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed unauthorized USB device activity not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: USB device control policy
ITID-33414.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33414.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33414.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General USB Exploitation
playbook.description: A USB-connected device is used in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access or compromise a host.

steps.title: Identify the USB exploitation event
steps.desc: Review EDR/USB device logs for the anomalous device connection and resulting activity on the host.
steps.outcome: Confirmed device and host involved, and the nature of the exploitation.

steps.title: Determine impact and scope
steps.desc: Assess what data, credentials, or system state was affected by the USB-based exploitation.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host and remove the device
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host and physically remove the offending USB device.
steps.outcome: Further exploitation halted.

steps.title: Remediate the host and close the exploitation vector
steps.desc: Remove any malware/persistence and apply the appropriate fix (patch, policy, device control) for the specific exploitation method used.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean and vector closed.

steps.title: Enforce or tighten USB device control policy
steps.desc: Implement device allowlisting/control appropriate to the exploitation method observed.
steps.outcome: Similar devices blocked going forward.

steps.title: Restore the host to production and verify controls
steps.desc: Return the host to service and confirm the fix and device-control policy are functioning.
steps.outcome: Host restored under verified controls.

steps.title: Review USB/removable-media policy org-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and evaluate whether broader USB device-control policy changes are warranted.
steps.outcome: Policy review completed.

ITID-33421.def: Unauthorized access to corporate data and systems arising from theft of a laptop or workstation lacking full-disk encryption, allowing the thief to read the disk contents or boot the device directly without credential-based protection.
ITID-33421.purpose: Captures unauthorized data/system access resulting from the physical theft of a laptop or workstation with no full-disk encryption.
scopeIncludes: Theft of an unencrypted corporate laptop/workstation from an office, vehicle, home, or in transit
Direct disk access via boot media or disk removal on a stolen unencrypted device
Data recovered from an unencrypted stolen device's storage
scopeExcludes: Theft of a device that was properly encrypted (see ITID-33422)
Theft of a mobile device with an active unlocked session/token (see ITID-33423)
ITID-33421.severity: High, since an unencrypted disk grants the thief unrestricted access to all locally stored data.
ITID-33421.priority: P1, given the near-certainty of data exposure and likely breach-notification obligations.
ITID-33421.escalation: Escalate immediately to security, legal/privacy, and asset management upon report of theft; assume data compromise pending confirmation of encryption status.
indicators: Theft report or loss report from an employee/security guard
MDM/asset-management system showing the device as non-compliant/unencrypted
Device check-in failure combined with a physical security incident report
vectors: Opportunistic theft from vehicles, offices, airports, or public spaces
Targeted theft of a specific individual's device
rootCauses: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault) not enforced fleet-wide
No asset tracking/MDM compliance verification for encryption status
Devices left unattended in insecure locations
controls: Mandatory full-disk encryption enforced via MDM/policy
Remote wipe capability for lost/stolen devices
Asset inventory tracking encryption compliance status
ITID-33421.detection: Weak from a technical standpoint (the compromise happens offline); relies on physical loss reporting and MDM compliance status rather than active detection.
ITID-33421.response: Remote wipe the device if possible, disable associated accounts/credentials stored on it, and initiate breach-assessment given the lack of encryption.
metrics: Number of stolen unencrypted devices reported per period
Fleet-wide full-disk encryption compliance percentage
ITID-33421.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33422 solely by encryption status; the theft event itself is the same, but lack of encryption removes the primary technical barrier to data access.

playbook.name: Stolen Unencrypted Laptop/Workstation Access
playbook.description: A laptop or workstation without full-disk encryption is stolen, exposing all locally stored data and cached credentials to the thief.

steps.title: Confirm the theft and verify the device's encryption status
steps.desc: Confirm the report of theft, and check the asset management/MDM record to verify whether full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault) was actually enabled on the device.
steps.guidance: Treat encryption status as unconfirmed until verified against the MDM record, not just policy assumption.
steps.outcome: Confirmed theft and definitive encryption status of the device.
steps.abort: If encryption is confirmed enabled and the recovery key was not compromised, this can be downgraded to a standard device-loss response rather than a data-breach investigation.

steps.title: Inventory data and cached credentials on the device
steps.desc: Determine what sensitive data, cached credentials, and stored sessions/tokens resided on the device at time of theft.
steps.guidance: Check for locally cached VPN/email credentials, browser-saved passwords, and locally stored files.
steps.outcome: Documented inventory of exposed data and credentials.

steps.title: Remote wipe the device and revoke its access
steps.desc: Trigger a remote wipe via MDM if the device is/was capable of receiving the command, and revoke its device trust/certificate from all systems.
steps.guidance: Attempt the wipe immediately even if the device may be offline — the command will execute upon its next network connection.
steps.outcome: Device wiped or trust revoked so it cannot access corporate resources.

steps.title: Reset all credentials cached on or accessible from the device
steps.desc: Force password resets and session/token revocation for every account that had cached credentials or active sessions on the stolen device.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials invalidated.

steps.title: File a police report and notify legal/compliance
steps.desc: File a formal police report for the theft and notify legal/compliance to assess breach-notification obligations given the lack of encryption.
steps.outcome: Report filed and legal/compliance engaged.

steps.title: Provision a replacement device and verify encryption enforcement
steps.desc: Issue a replacement device to the user, and verify full-disk encryption is enforced and enabled (with policy compliance checked via MDM) before deployment.
steps.outcome: User restored to productivity on a compliant, encrypted device.

steps.title: Enforce mandatory full-disk encryption fleet-wide via MDM compliance policy
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement an MDM compliance policy that blocks corporate resource access from any device not reporting full-disk encryption enabled.
steps.outcome: Compliance policy implemented and enforced.

ITID-33422.def: Unauthorized access to a stolen laptop or workstation that had full-disk encryption enabled, achieved because the disk-unlock or account credential was weak, guessable, reused, or separately compromised, defeating the encryption's practical protection.
ITID-33422.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to a stolen device that was encrypted, but where the unlock credential was weak, reused, or otherwise compromised.
scopeIncludes: Theft of an encrypted device followed by successful credential guessing/brute force of the unlock PIN/password
Theft of an encrypted device whose credential was independently compromised (e.g., reused password, phished)
Cold-boot or similar attacks against an encrypted device using a weak passphrase
scopeExcludes: Theft of a wholly unencrypted device (see ITID-33421)
Theft of a mobile device with an active session bypassing the need for unlock credentials at all (see ITID-33423)
ITID-33422.severity: Medium-High; encryption raises the bar but weak credentials substantially narrow the protection.
ITID-33422.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the credential is confirmed compromised or brute-forced successfully.
ITID-33422.escalation: Escalate to security upon theft report; escalate further to IR if evidence emerges the unlock credential was independently compromised.
indicators: Theft report for a device confirmed encrypted but using a weak/reused password
Subsequent account activity suggesting the device's stored credentials were used elsewhere
MDM logs showing repeated failed then successful unlock attempts post-theft (if device later reconnects)
vectors: Password guessing against a weak disk-unlock PIN/passphrase
Reuse of the device unlock credential elsewhere, later phished or breached
Credential written on/near the device (e.g., sticky note) at time of theft
rootCauses: Weak minimum complexity requirements for disk-unlock credentials
No enforced MFA/TPM-backed unlock in addition to password
Credential reuse practices not addressed by security awareness training
controls: Strong disk-unlock credential complexity requirements
TPM-backed encryption with pre-boot authentication
Remote wipe/lockout capability for lost devices
ITID-33422.detection: Weak; largely relies on physical loss reporting rather than technical detection, since offline brute forcing of an unlock credential is not observable remotely.
ITID-33422.response: Remote wipe/disable the device if possible, force reset of the compromised credential everywhere it was reused, and assess data exposure scope.
metrics: Number of stolen encrypted devices with weak-credential compromise confirmed
ITID-33422.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33421 by the device being properly encrypted, with the credential itself as the point of failure.

playbook.name: Stolen Encrypted Device with Compromised/Weak Unlock Credential
playbook.description: A full-disk-encrypted device is stolen, but its unlock PIN/password is weak or was otherwise compromised, allowing the thief to bypass the encryption protection.

steps.title: Confirm theft and assess unlock-credential strength/exposure
steps.desc: Confirm the theft report and determine whether the device's unlock PIN/password was weak (e.g., simple PIN), reused, or known to have been observed/compromised (e.g., shoulder-surfed, written down).
steps.guidance: Interview the user regarding PIN complexity and any known exposure.
steps.outcome: Documented assessment of unlock-credential risk.
steps.abort: If the unlock credential is strong and not known to be exposed, encryption is likely to hold — treat as lower urgency and proceed with standard device-loss handling.

steps.title: Determine what corporate access the unlock would enable
steps.desc: Inventory cached credentials, saved sessions, and locally stored data that would become accessible if the encryption is bypassed.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of exposure if the device is unlocked.

steps.title: Remote wipe the device and revoke device trust
steps.desc: Trigger an MDM remote wipe and revoke the device's certificate/trust relationship with corporate systems.
steps.outcome: Device access to corporate resources revoked.

steps.title: Reset credentials and sessions cached on the device
steps.desc: Force password resets and session revocation for all accounts with cached credentials on the device.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials invalidated.

steps.title: File a police report and assess breach-notification need with legal
steps.desc: File a theft report and consult legal/compliance on notification obligations given the weak/compromised unlock credential.
steps.outcome: Report filed; legal assessment documented.

steps.title: Provision replacement device with enforced strong unlock policy
steps.desc: Issue a replacement device with a mandatory minimum PIN/password complexity policy enforced via MDM.
steps.outcome: User restored to productivity under stronger unlock policy.

steps.title: Enforce strong unlock-credential complexity policy fleet-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and mandate a minimum PIN/password complexity (and lockout-after-attempts) policy across all managed devices.
steps.outcome: Policy implemented via MDM.

ITID-33423.def: Unauthorized access to corporate accounts and data arising from theft of a mobile device that was unlocked or in an active session at the time of theft, granting the thief immediate access to authenticated apps, tokens, and data without needing to defeat any lock or encryption.
ITID-33423.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from theft of a mobile device (phone/tablet) that was in an active, unlocked session with live app tokens at the time of theft.
scopeIncludes: Theft of an unlocked phone/tablet with active corporate email, chat, or app sessions
Theft immediately followed by unauthorized use of authenticated apps before remote lock/wipe is triggered
Access to push-notification-visible sensitive content on a stolen unlocked device's lock screen
scopeExcludes: Theft of a device that was locked, requiring credential compromise to access (see ITID-33422 for the encrypted-but-weak-credential case)
Theft of non-mobile hardware such as laptops/servers (see ITID-33421/ITID-33422/ITID-33424)
ITID-33423.severity: High, given immediate access to live, authenticated sessions with no barrier.
ITID-33423.priority: P1, given the time-critical nature — access is immediate and ongoing until remotely terminated.
ITID-33423.escalation: Escalate immediately to security and IAM for emergency remote wipe/session revocation upon any report of a stolen unlocked mobile device.
indicators: Theft report for a device that was unlocked/in-use at time of loss
Unusual app activity on corporate accounts immediately following a reported mobile device theft
MDM last-known-location/state showing the device as unlocked at time of loss
vectors: Opportunistic street/public-space theft of an in-use phone
Theft during device charging/unattended moments while unlocked
rootCauses: No automatic short-timeout screen lock enforced via MDM
No remote wipe/session revocation capability deployed
Sensitive content visible via lock-screen notifications
controls: Enforced short auto-lock timeout via MDM
Remote wipe and session-revocation capability for mobile devices
Lock-screen notification content restrictions
ITID-33423.detection: Moderate; app-level anomaly detection can flag suspicious activity immediately post-theft if correlated with the loss report in time.
ITID-33423.response: Trigger remote wipe/lock immediately, revoke all active sessions and tokens tied to the device, and monitor associated accounts for suspicious activity.
metrics: Mean time from theft report to remote wipe/session revocation
Number of stolen-unlocked-device incidents per period
ITID-33423.notes: Differentiated from other Stolen Hardware siblings by the defining trait of the device being actively unlocked/authenticated at time of theft.

playbook.name: Stolen Mobile Device with Active Session/Token Access
playbook.description: A stolen mobile device retains active, unlocked app sessions or stored tokens, giving the thief immediate access to corporate email, messaging, or business apps.

steps.title: Confirm theft and identify active sessions/tokens on the device
steps.desc: Confirm the theft report and query the MDM/app management console for which corporate apps had active, logged-in sessions or stored tokens on the device.
steps.guidance: Prioritize checking email, VPN, and any single-sign-on session persistence on the mobile OS.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of active app sessions/tokens exposed on the stolen device.

steps.title: Check for any unauthorized activity since the theft occurred
steps.desc: Review account activity logs for the affected sessions/accounts for any access occurring after the theft timestamp.
steps.outcome: Determined whether the thief has already used the active sessions.

steps.title: Remote wipe the device and revoke all active sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Trigger an MDM remote wipe (or selective corporate-data wipe for BYOD) and revoke all active sessions and OAuth tokens tied to the device across every corporate app.
steps.guidance: Ensure revocation includes mobile-specific push-notification and background-sync tokens, not just the interactive session.
steps.outcome: Device access and all its active sessions terminated.

steps.title: Force password reset for the affected user's accounts
steps.desc: Reset the user's primary credential as a defense-in-depth measure in case cached credentials (not just tokens) were also exposed.
steps.outcome: User's credential no longer usable by the thief.

steps.title: File a device-loss report and remove the device record
steps.desc: File the theft report and remove/deregister the device from MDM and any device-trust lists.
steps.outcome: Device fully deregistered from corporate systems.

steps.title: Provision a replacement device and re-establish sessions securely
steps.desc: Issue a replacement device and have the user re-authenticate to all corporate apps under fresh, verified sessions.
steps.outcome: User restored to productivity with clean, newly-authenticated sessions.

steps.title: Enforce shorter mobile session timeouts and app-level re-authentication
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement shorter session lifetimes and biometric/PIN re-authentication requirements within mobile apps to limit the exposure window of stolen unlocked devices.
steps.outcome: Session policy tightened via MDM/app configuration.

ITID-33424.def: Unauthorized access to corporate systems and data resulting from the physical theft of server, storage, or network infrastructure equipment (e.g., a rack-mounted server, switch, or NAS device) removed from a facility such as a data center, server room, or branch office.
ITID-33424.purpose: Captures unauthorized access enabled by the physical theft of server or network equipment from a corporate facility, rather than end-user endpoints.
scopeIncludes: Theft of a physical server, switch, router, firewall appliance, or storage array from a facility
Configuration or data extraction from stolen infrastructure equipment
Theft enabling network access via a stolen network device's stored credentials/configuration
scopeExcludes: Theft of end-user laptops/workstations or mobile devices (see ITID-33421/ITID-33422/ITID-33423)
ITID-33424.severity: Critical, given infrastructure equipment often stores credentials, keys, or configuration data enabling broader network compromise.
ITID-33424.priority: P1, given the potential for the theft to cascade into a wider network intrusion.
ITID-33424.escalation: Escalate immediately to security, IT infrastructure, and physical security teams; treat as a potential precursor to a broader network compromise.
indicators: Physical security/access-control logs showing unauthorized facility access followed by missing equipment
Network monitoring showing a device going offline unexpectedly with no maintenance record
Inventory/asset audit discrepancies for server room/data center equipment
vectors: Unauthorized physical entry to a server room or data center
Insider theft of infrastructure equipment
Theft during equipment transport/decommissioning
rootCauses: Insufficient physical access controls on server rooms/data centers
Equipment storing credentials/keys in plaintext or without hardware security modules
No inventory reconciliation process for infrastructure assets
controls: Strong physical access controls on server rooms/data centers (badge, biometric, camera)
Hardware security modules for key/credential storage on infrastructure devices
Immediate credential rotation and network segmentation review upon equipment theft
ITID-33424.detection: Moderate; physical access control logs and network monitoring can detect the theft event, but data exposure assessment on the stolen device itself is largely unobservable remotely.
ITID-33424.response: Rotate all credentials/keys the stolen equipment had access to, review network configuration for exposure, and conduct a physical security incident investigation.
metrics: Number of infrastructure equipment theft incidents
Time to rotate credentials/keys following theft
ITID-33424.notes: Differentiated from other Stolen Hardware siblings by targeting infrastructure/server equipment rather than end-user devices, with correspondingly higher blast radius.

playbook.name: Stolen Server/Network Equipment from Physical Facility
playbook.description: A server, switch, firewall, or other network equipment is physically stolen from a data center, wiring closet, or office facility.

steps.title: Confirm the theft and identify the exact equipment and data/access it held
steps.desc: Confirm the physical theft via facility security/CCTV review and asset inventory, and identify precisely what equipment was taken, including any stored data, credentials, or network access it provided.
steps.guidance: Check asset tags against the CMDB to confirm identity and configuration of the stolen equipment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed equipment identity, stored data/credentials, and network position.

steps.title: Assess how physical access to the facility/location was obtained
steps.desc: Investigate whether physical security controls (badge access, locks, cameras) were bypassed or failed, to understand root cause and residual risk.
steps.outcome: Documented physical security failure mode.

steps.title: Revoke network credentials/certificates associated with the stolen equipment
steps.desc: Immediately revoke any certificates, shared keys, or credentials stored on or associated with the stolen equipment so it cannot be used to gain network access if reconnected elsewhere.
steps.outcome: Stolen equipment cannot authenticate to the network even if powered on remotely.

steps.title: Segment/monitor the network segment the equipment served
steps.desc: Apply additional monitoring or temporary segmentation around the network segment previously served by the stolen equipment to detect any anomalous reconnection attempts.
steps.outcome: Enhanced visibility into the affected network segment.

steps.title: Remediate the physical security gap and file a police report
steps.desc: File a police report and fix the physical security failure identified (badge access, camera coverage, lock hardware).
steps.outcome: Physical security gap closed and report filed.

steps.title: Replace the equipment and rebuild with fresh credentials/keys
steps.desc: Deploy replacement equipment provisioned with newly-generated credentials and certificates, verified before returning to production.
steps.outcome: Service restored on trusted, freshly-provisioned hardware.

steps.title: Review physical security controls for all equipment locations
steps.desc: Document the incident and conduct a broader physical security review of all facilities housing network/server equipment.
steps.outcome: Physical security review completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33425.def: Unauthorized access resulting from theft of corporate hardware, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Stolen Hardware sibling.
ITID-33425.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for stolen-hardware unauthorized access cases that do not clearly fit unencrypted laptop, weak-credential encrypted device, active mobile session, or infrastructure equipment classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered stolen-hardware access patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33421 through ITID-33424 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33425.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33425.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33425.escalation: Escalate to security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed hardware theft with unclear access impact pending investigation
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: Asset tracking and loss reporting process
ITID-33425.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33425.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33425.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Stolen Hardware Access
playbook.description: Physically stolen hardware not otherwise classified is used or suspected of being used to gain unauthorized access to corporate data or systems.

steps.title: Confirm the theft and identify the device/equipment's access scope
steps.desc: Confirm the theft report and determine exactly what data, credentials, or network access the stolen hardware provided.
steps.outcome: Documented device identity and access scope.

steps.title: Check for any post-theft unauthorized activity
steps.desc: Review relevant logs for any unauthorized access attributable to the stolen device since the theft.
steps.outcome: Determined whether the device has already been misused.

steps.title: Revoke device credentials/trust and remote wipe if capable
steps.desc: Revoke any certificates/credentials associated with the device and trigger a remote wipe if the device supports it.
steps.outcome: Device access to corporate systems revoked.

steps.title: File a police report and close the physical security gap
steps.desc: File a theft report and remediate the physical security weakness that allowed the theft.
steps.outcome: Report filed and gap closed.

steps.title: Replace the device and restore affected user/service access
steps.desc: Provision a replacement and verify the affected user or service is restored to normal operation under fresh credentials.
steps.outcome: Access restored securely.

steps.title: Review physical asset security controls
steps.desc: Document the incident and evaluate whether broader physical security or asset-tracking improvements are needed.
steps.outcome: Review completed.

ITID-33431.def: Unauthorized or unmanaged access to corporate resources from a personally owned device that has not been enrolled in the organization's MDM/UEM platform, meaning no security baseline, compliance check, or remote-wipe capability applies to it.
ITID-33431.purpose: Captures corporate data/system access from a personal device that was never enrolled in mobile device management, bypassing baseline security controls.
scopeIncludes: Personal devices accessing corporate email/apps via basic ActiveSync or direct credentials with no MDM enrollment
Conditional access misconfiguration allowing unmanaged device access to sensitive resources
Contractors/third parties accessing systems from unmanaged personal devices
scopeExcludes: An enrolled but jailbroken/rooted device evading its compliance check (see ITID-33432)
A managed personal device compromised by malware (see ITID-33433)
ITID-33431.severity: Medium-High, since unmanaged devices carry no baseline security assurance (patching, encryption, screen lock).
ITID-33431.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the unmanaged device is found accessing highly sensitive data or systems.
ITID-33431.escalation: Escalate to IAM/identity for conditional access review; treat repeated unmanaged-device access as a policy gap requiring immediate technical enforcement.
indicators: Conditional access/compliance logs showing corporate resource access from non-compliant or unenrolled devices
Email/app access from device types never registered with MDM
Audit findings of BYOD policy exceptions never enforced technically
vectors: Direct use of corporate credentials on a personal device with no MDM enforcement gate
Legacy authentication protocols (e.g., basic auth/ActiveSync) bypassing modern conditional access
rootCauses: No conditional access policy requiring device compliance for resource access
Legacy authentication protocols left enabled
BYOD policy exists on paper but is not technically enforced
controls: Conditional access requiring MDM enrollment/compliance for resource access
Disabling legacy authentication protocols
BYOD enrollment enforcement at first access attempt
ITID-33431.detection: Strong; conditional access and identity provider logs clearly show device compliance state at time of access.
ITID-33431.response: Block or require enrollment before continued access, and audit what data was accessed from the unmanaged device.
metrics: Number of unmanaged-device access events blocked/detected
Percentage of corporate resource access from MDM-enrolled devices
ITID-33431.notes: Differentiated from siblings by focus on complete absence of MDM enrollment, rather than an enrolled device evading checks or being compromised.

playbook.name: Unmanaged/Non-MDM-Enrolled Personal Device Access
playbook.description: A personal device that was never enrolled in MDM connects to corporate resources, bypassing endpoint compliance and visibility controls.

steps.title: Identify the unmanaged device's access to corporate resources
steps.desc: Review conditional-access/IdP logs for logins from a device lacking an MDM-managed device identifier or compliance attestation.
steps.guidance: Look for a device that authenticated successfully but is absent from the MDM inventory.
steps.outcome: Confirmed identity of the unmanaged device, user, and resources accessed.
steps.abort: If the device is found to be enrolled and the log correlation was a lookup error, close as a false positive.
steps.tool: IdP conditional access logs / MDM inventory

steps.title: Determine what data was accessed from the unmanaged device
steps.desc: Review what corporate data or applications the device accessed while unmanaged.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of access/exposure.

steps.title: Block further access from unmanaged/non-compliant devices
steps.desc: Enforce a conditional-access policy requiring MDM enrollment and compliance attestation before granting access to corporate resources.
steps.outcome: The unmanaged device can no longer authenticate to corporate resources.

steps.title: Revoke any sessions established from the unmanaged device
steps.desc: Terminate active sessions/tokens issued to the device.
steps.outcome: No lingering session access remains.

steps.title: Enroll the device in MDM or block it permanently
steps.desc: Work with the user to either enroll the device in MDM with appropriate compliance policies, or permanently block it if it cannot/should not be enrolled (e.g., personal device policy violation).
steps.outcome: Device either compliant and managed, or permanently denied access.

steps.title: Verify conditional access policy enforcement
steps.desc: Confirm the conditional-access policy correctly blocks other unmanaged devices attempting access, via test.
steps.outcome: Policy verified effective.

steps.title: Audit for other unmanaged devices with active access
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit for any other unmanaged devices currently accessing corporate resources before the new policy was enforced.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33432.def: Unauthorized access risk arising from a personally owned, MDM-enrolled device that has been jailbroken (iOS) or rooted (Android) to remove operating-system security restrictions, thereby bypassing the compliance checks the MDM relies on to grant conditional access.
ITID-33432.purpose: Captures corporate data/system access from a BYOD device that has been jailbroken or rooted specifically to defeat its MDM compliance checks.
scopeIncludes: Jailbroken/rooted devices that pass or evade MDM jailbreak-detection checks
Use of jailbreak-detection bypass tooling to falsely report compliant status
Corporate data access from a device with root-level access available to any installed app or attacker
scopeExcludes: A fully unmanaged device never enrolled in MDM at all (see ITID-33431)
A managed, non-rooted device compromised by malware (see ITID-33433)
ITID-33432.severity: High, since root/jailbreak access undermines the sandboxing and integrity assumptions the entire BYOD security model depends on.
ITID-33432.priority: P1-P2 depending on what corporate data/systems the device can reach.
ITID-33432.escalation: Escalate to IAM/mobile security team immediately upon detection; revoke the device's access and require re-enrollment on a non-rooted device.
indicators: MDM jailbreak/root-detection alert for an enrolled device
Inconsistencies between device-reported compliance and independent verification
App-level attestation (e.g., SafetyNet/Play Integrity) failures for the device
vectors: User deliberately jailbreaking/rooting their own device for unrelated reasons, then retaining corporate access
Use of jailbreak-detection evasion tools to spoof compliance status to the MDM
rootCauses: MDM jailbreak/root detection not enforced or easily bypassed
No app-level attestation (e.g., Play Integrity/DeviceCheck) layered on top of MDM checks
BYOD policy not automatically revoking access on detected non-compliance
controls: MDM jailbreak/root detection with automatic access revocation
App-level integrity attestation for sensitive apps
Regular compliance policy review and evasion-technique updates
ITID-33432.detection: Moderate; jailbreak/root detection is available in most MDM/UEM platforms but can be evaded by sophisticated tooling, requiring layered attestation.
ITID-33432.response: Revoke access immediately upon detection, require the user to re-enroll on a compliant device, and review data accessed while non-compliant.
metrics: Number of jailbroken/rooted devices detected accessing corporate resources
Time from detection to access revocation
ITID-33432.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33431 by the device being enrolled but compromised at the OS-integrity level, actively evading compliance checks.

playbook.name: Jailbroken/Rooted BYOD Device Bypassing Compliance Check
playbook.description: A jailbroken or rooted personal device circumvents the MDM's jailbreak/root detection to appear compliant and retain corporate access.

steps.title: Confirm the jailbreak/root status and detection bypass
steps.desc: Investigate the reported or suspected device to confirm it is actually jailbroken/rooted and determine how it evaded the MDM's compliance check.
steps.guidance: Review MDM attestation logs and, if possible, obtain the device for direct inspection.
steps.outcome: Confirmed jailbreak/root status and bypass technique.
steps.abort: If the device is confirmed not jailbroken upon inspection, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine what corporate data/apps the device accessed while non-compliant
steps.desc: Review application and data-access logs for the device during the period it evaded detection.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of exposure.

steps.title: Revoke corporate access and wipe corporate data from the device
steps.desc: Trigger a selective (corporate-data-only) wipe via MDM and revoke the device's certificates/access tokens.
steps.outcome: Device no longer holds corporate data or access.

steps.title: Block the device and associated user session pending remediation
steps.desc: Add the device to a blocklist and force the user to re-authenticate from a compliant device.
steps.outcome: Device permanently barred from access until remediated.

steps.title: Patch or upgrade MDM jailbreak/root detection capability
steps.desc: Update the MDM agent/policy to close the specific detection-evasion technique identified, or move to a more robust attestation mechanism.
steps.outcome: Detection capability improved and validated against the bypass technique.

steps.title: Verify compliant re-enrollment or provide a managed alternative
steps.desc: Confirm the user can regain access only via a compliant device (re-flashed personal device or a corporate-issued alternative).
steps.outcome: User restored to access via a verified-compliant device.

steps.title: Audit BYOD fleet for the same detection-evasion technique
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit other enrolled BYOD devices for the same evasion technique before it is exploited further.
steps.outcome: Fleet audit completed.

ITID-33433.def: Unauthorized access to corporate resources originating from a personally owned device that was infected with malware through the user's personal activity (personal apps, browsing, side-loaded software), with the infection subsequently enabling access to corporate accounts, data, or systems reachable from that device.
ITID-33433.purpose: Captures cases where a BYOD device is compromised by malware from personal (non-corporate) use, and that compromise is then leveraged to access corporate resources.
scopeIncludes: Malware from a personal app/download harvesting corporate credentials or tokens stored on a BYOD device
Mobile malware capturing corporate email/app session data on an infected personal device
Corporate VPN/app access compromised via a device-resident personal-use infection
scopeExcludes: The unmanaged-device access case with no malware involved (see ITID-33431)
Jailbreak/root-specific compliance evasion with no malware infection identified (see ITID-33432)
ITID-33433.severity: High, since the malware may have full visibility into whatever corporate data/credentials reside on the device.
ITID-33433.priority: P1-P2 depending on scope of corporate access the infected device held.
ITID-33433.escalation: Escalate to IR and mobile security immediately upon confirmation; treat all corporate credentials/tokens accessible from the device as compromised.
indicators: Mobile threat defense (MTD) alert for malware on an enrolled BYOD device
Anomalous corporate account activity correlated with a known-infected personal device
App store/side-load telemetry showing installation of a known-malicious app
vectors: Malicious apps installed outside official app stores (side-loading)
Malicious ads or drive-by downloads during personal browsing on the device
Trojanized legitimate-looking personal apps
rootCauses: No mobile threat defense (MTD) solution deployed on BYOD devices
BYOD policy permitting side-loading/unrestricted app installation
No separation (containerization) between personal and corporate data on the device
controls: Mobile threat defense (MTD) integrated with MDM/conditional access
Containerization separating corporate apps/data from personal device content
App installation restrictions (blocking side-loading) for devices with corporate access
ITID-33433.detection: Moderate; dependent on MTD deployment, which is less universally adopted than endpoint EDR for traditional computers.
ITID-33433.response: Revoke device access, force credential/token resets for all corporate accounts reachable from the device, and require malware remediation or device replacement before re-enrollment.
metrics: Number of malware-compromised BYOD devices with corporate access
Percentage of BYOD fleet covered by MTD
ITID-33433.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the defining trait of a personal-use malware infection being the compromise vector for corporate access.

playbook.name: BYOD Device Compromised by Personal-Use Malware, Then Used for Corporate Access
playbook.description: A personal device is infected with malware through non-work-related use and the infection subsequently exposes corporate credentials or data accessed from that device.

steps.title: Confirm the malware infection and its access to the corporate work profile/app container
steps.desc: Review MDM/mobile threat defense (MTD) alerts confirming malware on the device, and determine whether the infection had access to the corporate work profile/container or only the personal partition.
steps.guidance: Check whether containerization (e.g., Android Work Profile, MDM app-wrapping) isolated corporate data from the infected personal side.
steps.outcome: Confirmed infection and whether corporate data/credentials were exposed to it.
steps.abort: If the corporate container was fully isolated and unaffected, this can be downgraded to a personal-device advisory rather than a corporate incident.

steps.title: Determine what corporate credentials/data were accessible to the malware
steps.desc: Identify what corporate app data, credentials, or tokens were present on the device and potentially exposed.
steps.outcome: Documented exposure scope.

steps.title: Selectively wipe corporate data and revoke access from the device
steps.desc: Trigger a selective corporate-data wipe via MDM and revoke the device's tokens/certificates.
steps.outcome: Corporate exposure via the infected device eliminated.

steps.title: Force credential reset for exposed corporate accounts
steps.desc: Reset any corporate credentials/tokens that were present on or accessible to the infected device.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Require malware remediation before re-enrollment
steps.desc: Require the user to fully clean/factory-reset the personal device (or have it professionally remediated) before it is permitted to re-enroll for corporate access.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed malware-free before regaining corporate access.

steps.title: Restore corporate access on the verified-clean device
steps.desc: Re-enroll the device (or a replacement) and confirm normal corporate access is restored.
steps.outcome: User restored to productivity securely.

steps.title: Deploy Mobile Threat Defense across the BYOD fleet
steps.desc: Document the incident and ensure Mobile Threat Defense and strict containerization are deployed to all BYOD enrollments to prevent personal-side infections from touching corporate data.
steps.outcome: MTD/containerization rollout tracked.

ITID-33434.def: Unauthorized exposure of corporate data occurring when a personally owned device's built-in or third-party personal cloud backup/sync service (e.g., iCloud, Google Photos/Drive, personal OneDrive) automatically captures and uploads corporate content — documents, screenshots, photos of whiteboards, or cached app data — to an account outside organizational control.
ITID-33434.purpose: Captures corporate data exposure caused by a BYOD device's personal cloud backup/sync service automatically capturing corporate data.
scopeIncludes: Corporate documents/screenshots auto-synced to a personal cloud backup account from a BYOD device
Photo/screenshot backup services capturing images of sensitive corporate material (whiteboards, documents)
App data backup to a personal cloud account inadvertently including corporate app content
scopeExcludes: Deliberate exfiltration of data by the device user (an insider-threat scenario, not a passive sync exposure)
Malware-driven data theft from the device (see ITID-33433)
ITID-33434.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of the data that was synced.
ITID-33434.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if regulated or highly sensitive data is confirmed to have synced to an uncontrolled personal account.
ITID-33434.escalation: Escalate to security and privacy/legal teams once confirmed; assess whether the exposure meets breach-notification thresholds.
indicators: DLP or CASB findings of corporate content present in a personal cloud storage account
User self-report of realizing a personal backup service captured corporate material
Audit of containerization/MAM logs showing corporate app data outside the managed container
vectors: Default personal cloud backup settings that capture all device content indiscriminately
Corporate apps not properly containerized, allowing OS-level backup services to include their data
Users manually saving/screenshotting corporate content into personal photo libraries
rootCauses: No mobile application management (MAM) containerization to prevent personal backup services from touching corporate app data
No policy or technical control restricting screenshots/copy-paste from corporate apps
Personal cloud backup services enabled by default with no corporate-data awareness
mitreTechniques: T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account
