steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy a preventive guardrail blocking public write ACLs/policies across all storage accounts/buckets in the organization.
steps.outcome: Guardrail implemented org-wide.

ITID-33723.def: Unauthorized access to sensitive files achieved because a network file share or drive is configured with permissions broader than necessary (e.g., granting Everyone/Domain Users read or write access), allowing users without a legitimate need to view or modify content they should not be able to reach.
ITID-33723.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from an on-premises or network file share/drive configured with overly broad permissions.
scopeIncludes: Network shares granting broad read/write access to 'Everyone' or 'Domain Users' groups
Shares containing HR, finance, or other sensitive data accessible to the general employee population
Internal lateral discovery of sensitive files via over-permissioned shares by a compromised low-privilege account
scopeExcludes: Anonymous/unauthenticated access to a share (see Open Directory Listings, ITID-33713)
Cloud storage or IAM permission misconfigurations (see ITID-33721/ITID-33722)
ITID-33723.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of the data accessible via the over-permissioned share.
ITID-33723.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if highly sensitive data (HR, financial, credentials) is found broadly accessible.
ITID-33723.escalation: Escalate to IT/data governance for permission remediation; escalate further if evidence of unauthorized access/exfiltration by a specific actor is found.
indicators: Data access governance/DLP tooling findings of overly broad share permissions on sensitive data
File access logs showing users outside the expected business function accessing a sensitive share
Permission audit revealing 'Everyone' or 'Domain Users' with access to sensitive folders
vectors: Compromised low-privilege account used to browse and access broadly permissioned shares containing sensitive data
Insider access to data outside their role's legitimate need due to lax permission scoping
rootCauses: No least-privilege file share permission model or periodic access review
Legacy or ad hoc share creation without security review
Data classification not applied to guide appropriate access restriction
controls: Least-privilege file share permission model with periodic access review
Data classification and access-governance tooling to flag overexposed sensitive data
Removal of broad 'Everyone'/'Domain Users' access grants on sensitive shares
ITID-33723.detection: Moderate; data access governance tooling can surface this, but many organizations lack full coverage of internal file share permission auditing.
ITID-33723.response: Restrict the share to least privilege, review who has accessed the sensitive content while overexposed, and reclassify/relocate data as needed.
metrics: Number of over-permissioned shares identified per audit cycle
Time to remediate upon discovery
detections: Data access governance / permission audit findings
ITID-33723.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33721/ITID-33722 by scope: on-premises/network file shares rather than cloud IAM or storage bucket permissions.

playbook.name: Overly Broad File Share/Network Drive Permissions Exploited
playbook.description: A network file share or drive is configured with permissions far broader than needed (e.g., Everyone/Domain Users full control), and is exploited for unauthorized data access.

steps.title: Identify the overly broad share permissions and unauthorized access
steps.desc: Review the share's ACL/permission configuration to confirm the overly broad grant, and check access logs for users accessing data beyond their legitimate need.
steps.outcome: Confirmed share, permission misconfiguration, and unauthorized access instances.
steps.tool: File server ACL audit / access logs

steps.title: Classify the sensitivity of data accessed
steps.desc: Determine the sensitivity of data on the share to assess breach-notification implications.
steps.outcome: Documented data classification.

steps.title: Restrict the share permissions to least-privilege groups
steps.desc: Reconfigure the share's ACL to grant access only to the specific groups/users who legitimately need it.
steps.outcome: Share no longer broadly accessible.

steps.title: Audit for other shares with the same over-broad permission pattern
steps.desc: Scan the file server/environment for other shares granting similarly broad access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope limited or additional shares remediated.

steps.title: Assess and remediate any unauthorized data exfiltration
steps.desc: If data was confirmed accessed inappropriately, assess for exfiltration and take appropriate remediation/notification action.
steps.outcome: Exfiltration scope documented and addressed.

steps.title: Verify least-privilege access and restore legitimate user access
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate users retain necessary access under the corrected permissions and unauthorized users no longer can access the share.
steps.outcome: Least-privilege access verified.

steps.title: Implement periodic file share permission reviews
steps.desc: Document the incident and establish a recurring audit process for file share/network drive permissions across the organization.
steps.outcome: Review process implemented.

ITID-33724.def: Unauthorized access to a database instance (e.g., MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Redis) that has been deployed with authentication disabled or not configured, and is network-accessible (often directly from the internet), allowing any party who discovers it to connect and read or modify its contents without credentials.
ITID-33724.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to a database instance that requires no authentication at all and is directly reachable, typically from the internet.
scopeIncludes: Internet-facing database instances with no authentication configured, discovered via scanning
Default installations left with authentication disabled out of the box
Ransom/wiper attacks against exposed, unauthenticated databases
scopeExcludes: A database with authentication enabled but using default credentials (see Default Admin Credentials, ITID-33612)
Overly broad IAM permissions on a managed cloud database service (see ITID-33721)
ITID-33724.severity: Critical, since this grants immediate, unauthenticated read/write access to potentially the entire dataset.
ITID-33724.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the severity and speed at which such exposures are typically discovered and exploited by opportunistic scanners.
ITID-33724.escalation: Escalate to database/infrastructure owners and IR immediately; treat as an active data-breach risk given the near-certainty of opportunistic scanning discovering such exposures within hours.
indicators: External attack-surface scan or CSPM finding of a database reachable without authentication
Unexpected connections or queries from unrecognized external IPs in database logs
Ransom note or data-wipe evidence characteristic of opportunistic unauthenticated-database attacks
vectors: Internet-wide scanning platforms (e.g., Shodan-style tools) identifying unauthenticated database instances
Default cloud marketplace database images deployed without enabling authentication
rootCauses: Database deployed with authentication disabled by default and never enabled
No network-level restriction (security group/firewall) limiting database access to trusted sources
No pre-deployment security review/hardening checklist for database instances
controls: Mandatory authentication enabled on all database instances as a hardening baseline
Network-level access restriction (security groups/firewalls) limiting database reachability
External attack-surface scanning and CSPM covering database exposure
ITID-33724.detection: Strong; unauthenticated database exposure is readily and reliably detectable via external scanning.
ITID-33724.response: Enable authentication and restrict network access immediately, assess for evidence of prior unauthorized access/exfiltration/ransom, and initiate breach-notification assessment.
metrics: Number of unauthenticated database exposures identified per scan cycle
Time to remediate upon discovery
detections: External attack-surface scanning for unauthenticated databases
ITID-33724.notes: Differentiated from Default Admin Credentials (ITID-33612) by the complete absence of any authentication mechanism, rather than a weak/default credential being present.

playbook.name: Database Instance with No Authentication Required (Publicly Accessible)
playbook.description: A database instance is exposed to the network (or internet) without any authentication required, allowing anyone to connect and query/modify data.

steps.title: Confirm unauthenticated access and assess exposure scope
steps.desc: Verify the database instance accepts connections without authentication and determine whether it is exposed to the internet or only internal network.
steps.guidance: Check binding configuration, network security group/firewall rules, and authentication settings.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure scope (internet-facing vs. internal) and authentication gap.

steps.title: Review database logs for unauthorized connections and data access
steps.desc: Check database connection and query logs for evidence of unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or destructive actions (a common pattern for exposed databases is ransom-note table replacement).
steps.outcome: Documented scope of unauthorized access/impact.

steps.title: Restrict network access to the database immediately
steps.desc: Apply firewall/security-group rules to block all external access, restricting connectivity to only authorized application servers.
steps.guidance: This is the most urgent action — do this before enabling authentication if immediate exposure exists.
steps.outcome: Database no longer reachable from unauthorized sources.

steps.title: Enable authentication and set strong credentials
steps.desc: Enable required authentication on the database and set strong, unique credentials.
steps.outcome: Database requires authentication for all connections.

steps.title: Assess data integrity and restore from backup if tampered
steps.desc: Verify data integrity; if data was deleted, encrypted for ransom, or tampered with, restore from the most recent clean backup.
steps.outcome: Data confirmed intact or restored.

steps.title: Verify secure configuration and restore application connectivity
steps.desc: Confirm the database is only reachable by authorized application servers with authentication enforced, and that dependent applications function correctly.
steps.outcome: Database and dependent applications restored securely.

steps.title: Implement automated scanning for unauthenticated/publicly exposed databases
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy continuous external-attack-surface scanning to detect exposed, unauthenticated database instances across the organization.
steps.outcome: Scanning program implemented.

ITID-33725.def: Unauthorized access achieved by exploiting an overly permissive access configuration, on a platform or in circumstances not yet classified into a more specific Unrestricted Access Permissions sibling.
ITID-33725.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for unrestricted-access-permission exploitation cases that do not clearly fit cloud IAM, publicly writable storage, file share, or unauthenticated database classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered unrestricted-permission exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific platform
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33721 through ITID-33724 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33725.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33725.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33725.escalation: Escalate to security engineering for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the platform is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed unrestricted-permission exploitation not yet attributable to a specific platform
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific platform
controls: CSPM and access governance tooling
ITID-33725.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33725.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the platform is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33725.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Unrestricted Access Permission Exploit
playbook.description: An overly permissive access control configuration is exploited for unauthorized access in a manner not otherwise classified.

steps.title: Identify the overly permissive configuration and how it was exploited
steps.desc: Review the relevant access control configuration to confirm the excess permission and identify how it was exploited for unauthorized access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed misconfiguration and exploitation details.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized access/impact
steps.desc: Review logs for the extent of data or system access obtained through the excess permission.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Restrict the permission/configuration to least privilege
steps.desc: Apply an emergency correction to the access control configuration to remove the excess permission.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access path closed.

steps.title: Remediate root cause and audit for similar misconfigurations
steps.desc: Fix the underlying process/configuration gap and check for similar misconfigurations elsewhere in the environment.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and similar issues found/remediated.

steps.title: Verify least-privilege access restored
steps.desc: Confirm the configuration now enforces least-privilege access and legitimate use cases still function.
steps.outcome: Least-privilege access verified.

steps.title: Implement periodic access control configuration reviews
steps.desc: Document the incident and establish periodic review of access control configurations across the environment.
steps.outcome: Review process implemented.

ITID-33731.def: Unauthorized access to sensitive data or functionality achieved by directly calling an API endpoint that requires no authentication token, key, or session, exposing data or actions to any party who discovers the endpoint URL/path.
ITID-33731.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to sensitive data via an API endpoint that has no authentication requirement at all.
scopeIncludes: Production API endpoints returning sensitive data with no authentication header/token check
Endpoints intended to be internal-only but reachable and callable without credentials
Data scraped in bulk from an unauthenticated API
scopeExcludes: An endpoint that requires authentication but is missing a specific authorization/role check (see Vertical Privilege Escalation, ITID-33222)
An internal/debug endpoint exposed to the public internet due to network/gateway misconfiguration where the endpoint itself may require auth internally but is reachable externally (see ITID-33732)
ITID-33731.severity: High-Critical depending on data sensitivity and volume accessible.
ITID-33731.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the low complexity and typically high impact of exploitation.
ITID-33731.escalation: Escalate to application security engineering immediately for emergency remediation; assess for evidence of scraping/mass access.
indicators: API gateway/WAF logs showing successful calls to a sensitive endpoint with no Authorization header present
External researcher or bug-bounty report of unauthenticated data access
Anomalous high-volume unauthenticated traffic to a specific API path
vectors: Direct discovery and invocation of an unauthenticated endpoint via client-side code review or API documentation leakage
Automated API endpoint discovery/fuzzing tools
rootCauses: Authentication middleware omitted on a new or refactored endpoint
Reliance on obscurity rather than enforced authentication
Insufficient API security testing prior to release
controls: Mandatory authentication enforced by default (deny-by-default API framework configuration)
API security testing (DAST/API fuzzing) in CI/CD covering all discovered endpoints
API gateway enforcing authentication at the edge for all routes
ITID-33731.detection: Moderate-Strong; API gateway logs can reveal unauthenticated access if baselined and monitored.
ITID-33731.response: Add the missing authentication requirement immediately, audit access logs for the exposure window, and notify affected parties if sensitive data was accessed.
metrics: Number of unauthenticated API endpoint findings
Time to remediate upon discovery
ITID-33731.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33222 (missing authorization) by the complete absence of any authentication requirement, not merely a missing role/permission check on an otherwise-authenticated endpoint.

playbook.name: Unauthenticated API Endpoint Exposing Sensitive Data
playbook.description: An API endpoint returns sensitive data without requiring any authentication, allowing anyone with the URL to retrieve it.

steps.title: Confirm the unauthenticated endpoint and the data it returns
steps.desc: Directly test the endpoint to confirm it returns sensitive data without any authentication header/token, and document exactly what data is exposed.
steps.guidance: Use a minimal, read-only test request; avoid bulk-pulling data during verification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed endpoint, missing auth requirement, and exposed data fields.
steps.abort: If the endpoint requires auth on retest (already fixed), close the finding.

steps.title: Review access logs for evidence of external enumeration/scraping
steps.desc: Check API gateway/access logs for requests to the endpoint from unrecognized external sources, especially in volume suggesting scraping.
steps.outcome: Documented history and scale of unauthorized access.

steps.title: Require authentication on the endpoint immediately
steps.desc: Add an authentication/authorization requirement to the endpoint, or take it offline if an immediate code fix cannot be deployed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint no longer returns data without valid authentication.

steps.title: Audit sibling endpoints for the same missing-auth pattern
steps.desc: Review other endpoints in the same route group/service for the same missing authentication requirement.
steps.outcome: No other endpoints found with the same gap, or all remediated.

steps.title: Verify enforcement and notify affected data subjects if required
steps.desc: Confirm the endpoint now enforces authentication and assess/execute any required breach notification based on data sensitivity and scale of exposure.
steps.outcome: Enforcement verified and notifications handled per policy.

steps.title: Require default-deny authentication for all new API endpoints
steps.desc: Document the incident and adopt a default-deny authentication pattern (or automated API security testing) so new endpoints cannot ship without an explicit auth requirement.
steps.outcome: Standard/testing gate implemented.

ITID-33732.def: Unauthorized access achieved by reaching an internal-only, debug, or administrative API endpoint from the public internet, where the endpoint's exposure is caused by a network, load-balancer, API gateway, or routing misconfiguration rather than an application-level authentication defect.
ITID-33732.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to an internal or debug API endpoint that was never intended for public exposure but is reachable from the public internet due to network/gateway misconfiguration.
scopeIncludes: Debug/diagnostic endpoints (e.g., actuator, swagger/admin UIs) unintentionally exposed externally
Internal microservice APIs reachable externally due to missing network segmentation or gateway route misconfiguration
Staging/pre-production API endpoints inadvertently left internet-reachable
scopeExcludes: An endpoint that is properly network-scoped but lacks authentication logic entirely (see ITID-33731)
A rate-limiting gap on a properly scoped and authenticated endpoint (see ITID-33733)
ITID-33732.severity: High-Critical, since debug/admin endpoints often expose configuration, stack traces, or administrative functions.
ITID-33732.priority: P1 upon confirmation, especially where the endpoint reveals internal configuration or credentials.
ITID-33732.escalation: Escalate to network/platform engineering and application security immediately; treat as a network architecture gap requiring both immediate blocking and root-cause routing review.
indicators: External scan discovering an internal-only path (e.g., /actuator, /admin, /debug) reachable from the internet
API gateway/load-balancer configuration audit revealing an unintended public route
Error pages or diagnostic output visible externally exposing internal architecture details
vectors: Internet-wide scanning identifying known debug/admin endpoint paths (e.g., Spring Boot Actuator, GraphQL introspection)
Misconfigured reverse proxy/API gateway routing rules exposing internal service paths externally
rootCauses: No network segmentation separating internal-only services from internet-facing infrastructure
API gateway/load-balancer route misconfiguration exposing internal paths
Debug/diagnostic features left enabled in production deployments
controls: Network segmentation isolating internal-only services from public-facing infrastructure
Disabling debug/diagnostic endpoints in production
API gateway route auditing as part of deployment review
ITID-33732.detection: Strong; external attack-surface scanning is well-suited to discovering unintentionally exposed internal paths.
ITID-33732.response: Block external reachability immediately, disable unneeded debug endpoints in production, and audit for evidence of exploitation.
metrics: Number of internal/debug endpoint exposures identified per scan cycle
Time to remediate upon discovery
detections: External attack-surface scanning for internal/debug paths
ITID-33732.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33731 by root cause: this leaf is a network/routing exposure of an endpoint that may otherwise be well-secured internally, rather than a missing application-level authentication check.

playbook.name: Internal/Debug API Endpoint Exposed to Public Internet
playbook.description: An internal-only or debug API endpoint (intended for internal testing/administration) is reachable from the public internet, exposing internal functionality or data.

steps.title: Confirm the endpoint is internet-reachable and assess exposed functionality
steps.desc: Verify the debug/internal endpoint is reachable from outside the corporate network and document what functionality or data it exposes (e.g., debug info, internal APIs, admin functions).
steps.guidance: Check network routing/firewall/load-balancer configuration to identify why the internal endpoint became internet-reachable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure and functional/data risk assessment.
steps.tool: External network scan / firewall config review

steps.title: Review access logs for external exploitation
steps.desc: Check logs for external access to the endpoint and any resulting information disclosure or unauthorized action.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of external access/impact.

steps.title: Block public access to the endpoint immediately
steps.desc: Apply a firewall/WAF/load-balancer rule to block external access to the endpoint, restoring it to internal-only reachability.
steps.outcome: Endpoint no longer reachable from the public internet.

steps.title: Fix the network/routing configuration that caused the exposure
steps.desc: Correct the root-cause network configuration (e.g., misconfigured ingress rule, missing network segmentation) rather than relying solely on a firewall patch.
steps.outcome: Root cause of exposure fixed and verified.

steps.title: Remove or disable debug functionality in production
steps.desc: If the endpoint is a debug endpoint, disable it entirely in production environments rather than merely restricting network access.
steps.outcome: Debug functionality unavailable in production.

steps.title: Verify exposure is fully remediated
steps.desc: Re-scan from an external vantage point to confirm the endpoint is no longer internet-reachable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no external reachability.

steps.title: Implement continuous external-attack-surface monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy continuous external attack-surface scanning to detect internal endpoints inadvertently exposed to the internet.
steps.outcome: Monitoring program implemented.

ITID-33733.def: Unauthorized access to bulk data achieved by exploiting an API endpoint's absence of rate limiting or throttling, allowing an adversary to make an abnormally high volume of requests and scrape data at scale that individual, low-volume requests would not have exposed as a meaningful risk.
ITID-33733.purpose: Captures unauthorized mass data access achieved by exploiting an API's lack of rate limiting to scrape data at high volume.
scopeIncludes: Automated scripts making high-frequency requests to enumerate/scrape data through a legitimate, authenticated or unauthenticated API endpoint
Data harvesting via sequential parameter iteration at high speed due to absent throttling
Competitive intelligence or bulk PII scraping via an under-throttled public API
scopeExcludes: The underlying authentication/authorization gap itself if the endpoint should not be accessible at all (see ITID-33731/ITID-33222)
A single or low-volume IDOR-style access to one other record (see ITID-33212)
ITID-33733.severity: Medium-High, escalating with the volume and sensitivity of data scraped.
ITID-33733.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if large-scale sensitive/PII data exposure is confirmed.
ITID-33733.escalation: Escalate to application security and, if PII/regulated data is involved, to privacy/legal; assess total volume of records exposed.
indicators: API request-volume anomalies far exceeding normal per-client/user baselines
Sequential or exhaustive parameter patterns in high-frequency request logs
Sudden spike in outbound data volume correlated with a single API consumer/IP
vectors: Automated scraping scripts/bots making rapid, sequential API calls
Distributed scraping across many source IPs to evade simple per-IP rate limits
rootCauses: No rate limiting or throttling implemented on API endpoints
No anomaly detection for abnormal per-client request volume
API design exposing bulk data via predictable, iterable parameters
controls: Rate limiting/throttling enforced on all API endpoints
Bot management/WAF detection of scraping patterns
Data minimization in API responses to reduce bulk-scrape value
ITID-33733.detection: Strong; volumetric anomaly detection on API traffic is a well-established and reliable technique.
ITID-33733.response: Implement/tighten rate limiting immediately, block the offending source(s), and assess the scope and sensitivity of data scraped.
metrics: Number of mass-scraping incidents detected
Records exposed per incident
ITID-33733.notes: Differentiated from siblings by focus on the rate-limiting gap enabling bulk/scale exploitation, rather than the underlying access-control gap itself.

playbook.name: API Missing Rate Limiting Exploited for Mass Data Scraping
playbook.description: An API lacking rate limiting is exploited to programmatically scrape large volumes of data at high speed.

steps.title: Confirm the scraping activity and identify the source(s)
steps.desc: Review API access logs for an abnormally high request volume from one or a small number of sources against the endpoint, confirming the lack of rate limiting allowed sustained mass extraction.
steps.guidance: Compare request volume/rate against normal usage baselines for the endpoint.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scraping source(s), volume, and data scraped.
steps.abort: If the volume is within normal bounds for a known legitimate integration, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Classify the sensitivity and scale of data scraped
steps.desc: Determine what data was scraped and its sensitivity to assess impact and notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Documented data classification and scale.

steps.title: Block the scraping source(s)
steps.desc: Block the identified IP(s)/API key(s)/account(s) at the WAF or API gateway.
steps.outcome: Scraping activity stops.

steps.title: Apply emergency rate limiting to the endpoint
steps.desc: Implement or tighten rate limiting on the affected endpoint as an immediate stopgap.
steps.outcome: Request volume constrained to reasonable levels.

steps.title: Implement permanent rate limiting and anti-scraping controls
steps.desc: Deploy durable rate limiting, pagination limits, and bot-detection/CAPTCHA controls on the endpoint and any similarly-exposed endpoints.
steps.outcome: Endpoint hardened against future mass-scraping attempts.

steps.title: Verify controls and restore normal legitimate API usage
steps.desc: Confirm rate limiting does not disrupt legitimate use cases and that scraping is now blocked via test.
steps.outcome: Controls verified effective without breaking legitimate usage.

steps.title: Establish rate-limiting as a mandatory API design standard
steps.desc: Document the incident and require rate limiting/anti-abuse controls as a mandatory part of the API design and review standard for all new endpoints.
steps.outcome: Standard updated and enforced.

ITID-33734.def: Unauthorized access via an exposed API, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Exposed APIs sibling.
ITID-33734.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for exposed-API unauthorized access cases that do not clearly fit unauthenticated endpoint, internal/debug exposure, or rate-limiting exploitation classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered exposed-API access patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33731, ITID-33732, or ITID-33733 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33734.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33734.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33734.escalation: Escalate to application security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed unauthorized API access not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: API gateway security controls
ITID-33734.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33734.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33734.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Exposed API
playbook.description: An API is exposed or misconfigured in a manner not otherwise classified, resulting in unauthorized access to functionality or data.

steps.title: Confirm the API exposure and identify the specific gap
steps.desc: Verify the reported exposure and identify the exact misconfiguration (missing auth, network exposure, missing rate limit, etc.).
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure and specific gap identified.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review logs for the extent of unauthorized access resulting from the exposure.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Restrict or disable the exposed API immediately
steps.desc: Apply an emergency gateway/firewall rule to restrict access or take the API offline pending a fix.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access no longer possible.

steps.title: Fix the root-cause misconfiguration
steps.desc: Remediate the specific gap identified (auth, network exposure, rate limiting, etc.) with a durable fix.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Verify the fix and restore legitimate API access
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate consumers can access the API normally and that the exposure is fully closed.
steps.outcome: API restored securely.

steps.title: Add API security review to the standard release process
steps.desc: Document the incident and require an API security review (auth, exposure, rate limiting) as part of the standard release checklist.
steps.outcome: Checklist updated.

ITID-33811.def: Unauthorized access achieved by forging or manipulating the source IP address of network traffic to match an entry on a system's IP allowlist, defeating an access control that relies on the client's apparent network origin as its sole or primary gate.
ITID-33811.purpose: Captures unauthorized access achieved by spoofing a source IP address to bypass an IP-based allowlist access control.
scopeIncludes: IP spoofing used to satisfy a firewall/application IP-allowlist check
Source address forgery combined with trust of an allowlisted partner/vendor IP range
Spoofing an internal IP range to bypass network-perimeter allowlist rules
scopeExcludes: IP spoofing used purely to hide the true source of an attack for attribution evasion, with no allowlist bypass involved (see ITID-33812)
IP spoofing combined with active exploitation of an established trust/session relationship (see ITID-33813)
ITID-33811.severity: High, since a successful bypass defeats a control the system was relying on as a primary gate.
ITID-33811.priority: P1-P2 depending on the sensitivity of the system protected by the allowlist.
ITID-33811.escalation: Escalate to network security immediately upon confirmation; review whether IP-based allowlisting is an appropriate sole control for the protected system.
indicators: Traffic matching an allowlisted IP but with anomalous TTL/packet characteristics inconsistent with the legitimate source
Asymmetric routing anomalies consistent with spoofed source addresses
Access from an allowlisted IP at a time/pattern inconsistent with the legitimate owner's known behavior
vectors: Source IP forgery on networks lacking egress/ingress filtering (BCP38) that would otherwise block spoofed packets
Exploitation of stateless firewall rules relying solely on source IP
rootCauses: Reliance on IP-based allowlisting as the sole access control with no additional authentication
Lack of ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) on networks enabling spoofed packets to transit
No mutual TLS or cryptographic authentication layered on top of network-level trust
controls: Layer authentication (mutual TLS, API keys, tokens) on top of any IP-based allowlist
Ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) to prevent spoofed packets from transiting networks
Anomaly detection on allowlisted-IP traffic patterns
ITID-33811.detection: Weak-to-moderate; IP spoofing is often difficult to detect directly without deep packet/route analysis or anomaly baselining on allowlisted sources.
ITID-33811.response: Layer additional authentication onto the allowlist control, investigate the scope of access gained, and review network filtering posture.
metrics: Number of IP-spoofing allowlist bypass incidents detected
Percentage of allowlist-protected systems with additional authentication layered
ITID-33811.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33812/ITID-33813 by the specific outcome of defeating an IP-allowlist access-control gate.

playbook.name: IP Spoofing to Bypass IP-Allowlist Access Control
playbook.description: An attacker forges the source IP address of packets to make them appear to originate from a trusted, allowlisted IP, bypassing an IP-based access control.

steps.title: Identify the spoofed traffic and the bypassed control
steps.desc: Review network flow/firewall logs for traffic claiming to originate from an allowlisted IP but exhibiting anomalies (asymmetric routing, TTL inconsistencies, or traffic from an interface/path inconsistent with the legitimate source), confirming spoofing bypassed the IP allowlist.
steps.guidance: Check TTL and TCP sequence anomalies, and whether the legitimate IP owner can corroborate they did not send the traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofing and the specific allowlist control bypassed.
steps.abort: If the traffic is corroborated as legitimate by the allowlisted party, this is not spoofing — reclassify.

steps.title: Determine what access/actions were obtained via the bypass
steps.desc: Review what resources or actions the spoofed traffic accessed once past the IP allowlist.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Block the spoofed traffic pattern and tighten ingress filtering
steps.desc: Apply ingress/egress filtering (e.g., BCP38-style anti-spoofing filtering) at the network edge to drop packets with implausible source IPs, and block the specific traffic pattern observed.
steps.outcome: Spoofed traffic no longer reaches the protected resource.

steps.title: Revoke any access/sessions established via the bypass
steps.desc: Terminate any sessions or access granted based on the spoofed IP's trusted status.
steps.outcome: No lingering unauthorized access remains.

steps.title: Replace IP-allowlist-only control with a stronger authentication factor
steps.desc: Since IP allowlisting alone is spoofable, add a cryptographic authentication factor (mutual TLS, signed requests, VPN with authenticated tunnel) rather than relying on source IP alone.
steps.guidance: This is the durable root-cause fix — IP allowlisting should be defense-in-depth, not the sole control.
steps.outcome: Access control no longer solely dependent on spoofable source IP.

steps.title: Verify the stronger control and restore legitimate access
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate traffic from the allowlisted party still functions correctly under the new authentication requirement, and that spoofed traffic is now rejected.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored; spoofing attempt verified blocked.

steps.title: Audit other systems relying solely on IP allowlisting
steps.desc: Document the incident and review other systems in the environment that rely solely on IP-based access control for the same spoofing weakness.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33812.def: Unauthorized activity in which an adversary forges the source IP address of network traffic specifically to evade source attribution, investigation, or IP-based blocking, without necessarily needing to defeat an allowlist-based access control.
ITID-33812.purpose: Captures IP spoofing used purely to conceal or falsify the true source of malicious traffic, evading attribution rather than bypassing an allowlist.
scopeIncludes: Source IP forgery used to complicate incident investigation and attribution
Reflection/amplification attack techniques relying on spoofed source addresses
Spoofing used to evade IP-based blocklisting/reputation-based blocking of known-bad sources
scopeExcludes: Spoofing specifically used to satisfy an IP allowlist and gain access to a restricted system (see ITID-33811)
Spoofing combined with active session/trust relationship exploitation (see ITID-33813)
ITID-33812.severity: Medium-High depending on what the spoofed traffic is used to accomplish (e.g., DDoS amplification vs. simple evasion).
ITID-33812.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if part of a larger attack campaign (e.g., DDoS).
ITID-33812.escalation: Escalate to network security/SOC upon detection; correlate with any concurrent attack activity the spoofing may be supporting.
indicators: Traffic with source IPs inconsistent with expected routing/AS path for that address
Reflection/amplification traffic patterns (e.g., DNS/NTP amplification) with spoofed sources
IP reputation-blocked traffic reappearing under a different, spoofed source
vectors: Spoofed-source DDoS reflection/amplification attacks
General evasion of IP-based blocklists by rotating/forging source addresses
rootCauses: Lack of ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) on networks allowing spoofed packets to transit
Sole reliance on IP-based blocking/reputation without behavioral or cryptographic verification
controls: Ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) to prevent spoofed packets from transiting networks
Behavioral/anomaly-based detection layered on top of IP reputation blocking
DDoS mitigation services with spoofed-traffic filtering capability
ITID-33812.detection: Weak-to-moderate; spoofed-source traffic is inherently difficult to attribute without upstream network cooperation and deep flow analysis.
ITID-33812.response: Engage upstream/ISP filtering where applicable, apply behavioral detection to compensate for defeated IP-based blocking, and document the evasion for threat intelligence.
metrics: Number of spoofed-source evasion incidents detected
ITID-33812.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33811 by purpose: attribution/evasion rather than defeating a specific allowlist access gate.

playbook.name: IP Spoofing for Source Attribution Evasion
playbook.description: An attacker spoofs source IP addresses during an attack (e.g., DoS, scanning) specifically to evade attribution and hinder investigation, rather than to bypass an access control.

steps.title: Identify the spoofed-source attack activity
steps.desc: Review network/firewall logs for attack traffic (e.g., flood, scan) exhibiting spoofed or randomized source IPs inconsistent with legitimate traffic patterns.
steps.guidance: Look for a very high diversity of source IPs each sending minimal traffic, or IPs from unallocated/reserved ranges.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofed-source attack pattern and targeted resource.

steps.title: Assess the attack's impact and any true-source indicators
steps.desc: Determine the operational impact of the attack and search for any non-spoofable indicators (e.g., TCP handshake completion, application-layer artifacts) that might reveal true attacker infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Documented impact and any available attribution leads.

steps.title: Apply anti-spoofing and traffic-scrubbing controls
steps.desc: Engage upstream ISP/DDoS scrubbing service or apply local anti-spoofing filtering to drop packets with implausible source IPs and mitigate the attack's impact.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic volume reduced/mitigated.

steps.title: Implement ingress/egress anti-spoofing filtering (BCP38) at network edges
steps.desc: Deploy source-address validation filtering at the network edge to prevent spoofed traffic from traversing in either direction.
steps.outcome: Spoofed traffic filtered at the edge going forward.

steps.title: Confirm service restoration and normal traffic patterns
steps.desc: Verify the targeted service/resource has returned to normal operation and traffic patterns are within baseline.
steps.outcome: Service confirmed restored.

steps.title: Establish a DDoS/spoofing response and mitigation retainer
steps.desc: Document the incident and evaluate whether a standing DDoS mitigation/scrubbing service retainer is warranted for faster future response.
steps.outcome: Retainer/service evaluated and, if warranted, put in place.

ITID-33813.def: Unauthorized access achieved by combining IP address spoofing with exploitation of an established session or network trust relationship — such as TCP session hijacking or exploiting a trusted host relationship (e.g., rlogin/rsh-style trust) — to actively assume another host's identity mid-communication rather than merely satisfying a static allowlist check.
ITID-33813.purpose: Captures IP spoofing combined with active exploitation of an existing session or trust relationship, going beyond simple allowlist bypass or attribution evasion.
scopeIncludes: TCP session hijacking combined with source IP spoofing to inject traffic into an established connection
Exploitation of host-based trust relationships (e.g., trusted-host authentication) via spoofed source addresses
Blind spoofing attacks predicting sequence numbers to inject into an active session
scopeExcludes: Simple allowlist bypass via spoofing with no active session/trust exploitation (see ITID-33811)
Spoofing used only for attribution evasion (see ITID-33812)
ITID-33813.severity: High-Critical, since this technique can hijack an already-authenticated, active communication session.
ITID-33813.priority: P1, given the direct compromise of an active trusted session.
ITID-33813.escalation: Escalate to network security and IR immediately; terminate the affected session/trust relationship and investigate scope of injected traffic.
indicators: Anomalous sequence-number or session-state behavior in an active TCP connection
Traffic appearing to originate from a trusted host but with inconsistent routing/timing characteristics
Unexpected commands/data injected into an established session
vectors: Blind IP spoofing with TCP sequence number prediction to hijack an active session
Exploitation of legacy trusted-host authentication mechanisms (e.g., .rhosts-style trust) via spoofed source IPs
rootCauses: Use of legacy protocols relying on host-based trust rather than cryptographic authentication
Predictable TCP sequence number generation on legacy systems
Lack of network-layer authentication (IPsec) protecting trusted host relationships
controls: Elimination of legacy trusted-host authentication protocols in favor of cryptographic authentication
IPsec or equivalent network-layer authentication for trusted relationships
TCP sequence-number randomization (standard on modern OS, verify on legacy systems)
ITID-33813.detection: Weak; this is a sophisticated, low-frequency technique requiring deep network traffic analysis to detect, and largely mitigated by modern OS defaults.
ITID-33813.response: Terminate the affected session, remove any legacy trust relationships exploited, and migrate to cryptographic authentication.
metrics: Number of session-hijack-via-spoofing incidents detected
Legacy trusted-host relationships remaining in the environment
ITID-33813.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33811/ITID-33812 by the additional active exploitation of a session or trust relationship, not merely a static credential-like allowlist check or passive attribution evasion.

playbook.name: IP Spoofing Combined with Session/Trust Relationship Abuse
playbook.description: An attacker spoofs a trusted source IP to exploit an existing trust relationship (e.g., host-based trust, rsh/rlogin-style, or application session binding) between systems.

steps.title: Identify the spoofed trust-relationship exploitation
steps.desc: Review logs for a trusted host-based or session-binding relationship being used from an unexpected source, with network-layer evidence of IP spoofing.
steps.guidance: Check for host-trust files (e.g., .rhosts-style trust) or IP-bound session tokens being exploited.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofing and the specific trust relationship abused.

steps.title: Determine what access/actions the trust relationship granted the attacker
steps.desc: Review what the attacker accomplished by exploiting the trust relationship.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke or disable the exploited trust relationship
steps.desc: Remove or disable the host-based trust configuration or IP-bound session mechanism that was exploited.
steps.outcome: Trust relationship no longer exploitable via spoofing.

steps.title: Apply anti-spoofing filtering at the network edge
steps.desc: Deploy ingress filtering to block spoofed source IPs from reaching the affected systems.
steps.outcome: Spoofed traffic blocked.

steps.title: Replace IP-based trust with cryptographic authentication
steps.desc: Redesign the trust relationship to use cryptographic authentication (SSH keys, mutual TLS, signed tokens) instead of relying on source IP identity.
steps.outcome: Trust relationship no longer dependent on spoofable network identity.

steps.title: Verify legitimate system communication under the new trust model
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate systems continue to communicate correctly under the new cryptographic trust mechanism.
steps.outcome: Legitimate functionality confirmed intact.

steps.title: Audit environment for other IP-based trust relationships
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit the environment for other legacy IP-based trust relationships that should be migrated to cryptographic authentication.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33814.def: Unauthorized activity involving forged source IP addresses, achieved or intended for a purpose not yet classified into a more specific IP Spoofing sibling.
ITID-33814.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for IP spoofing cases that do not clearly fit allowlist bypass, attribution evasion, or session/trust exploitation classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered IP spoofing patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific purpose/mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33811, ITID-33812, or ITID-33813 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33814.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33814.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33814.escalation: Escalate to network security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed IP spoofing activity not yet attributable to a specific purpose
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific purpose/mechanism
controls: Ingress/egress filtering (BCP38)
ITID-33814.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33814.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33814.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General IP Spoofing
playbook.description: An attacker forges source IP addresses in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access or evade detection.

steps.title: Identify the IP spoofing activity and its purpose
steps.desc: Review network/firewall logs to confirm IP spoofing occurred and determine its apparent purpose (access-control bypass, attribution evasion, trust abuse, or other).
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofing activity and apparent objective.

steps.title: Determine impact and scope
steps.desc: Assess what access, data, or service impact resulted from the spoofing activity.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Apply anti-spoofing filtering and block the observed pattern
steps.desc: Deploy ingress/egress anti-spoofing filtering at the network edge and block the specific traffic pattern observed.
steps.outcome: Spoofed traffic blocked.

steps.title: Remediate the underlying weakness exploited via spoofing
steps.desc: Fix the specific control (IP allowlist, trust relationship, etc.) that was vulnerable to spoofing-based bypass.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Verify controls and restore normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm the affected systems operate normally and the spoofing vector is closed.
steps.outcome: Systems restored under verified controls.

steps.title: Implement network-wide anti-spoofing filtering standards
steps.desc: Document the incident and establish anti-spoofing (BCP38-style) filtering as a standard control across all network edges.
steps.outcome: Standard implemented.

ITID-33821.def: Unauthorized network access achieved by cloning or forging the MAC address of a known-authorized device to bypass MAC-based network access control (NAC) or 802.1X authentication that relies (in whole or part) on the device's hardware address for admission.
ITID-33821.purpose: Captures unauthorized network access achieved by spoofing a MAC address to bypass network access control (NAC) or 802.1X port-based authentication.
scopeIncludes: Cloning an authorized device's MAC address to gain admission through MAC-filtering NAC
Bypassing 802.1X MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB) fallback mechanisms with a spoofed address
Connecting an unauthorized device to a network port after spoofing the MAC of a device previously authorized on that port
scopeExcludes: MAC spoofing used to impersonate a device specifically on Wi-Fi rather than wired NAC/802.1X (see ITID-33822)
MAC spoofing used for DHCP/IP reservation hijacking rather than network admission (see ITID-33823)
ITID-33821.severity: High, since successful NAC bypass grants network-level access equivalent to a trusted, managed device.
ITID-33821.priority: P1-P2 depending on the sensitivity of the network segment gained.
ITID-33821.escalation: Escalate to network security immediately upon confirmation; investigate concurrent presence of the legitimate device and the spoofing device (a MAC conflict is a strong indicator).
indicators: Simultaneous or overlapping network presence of the same MAC address from two different physical locations/ports
NAC/802.1X logs showing MAC Authentication Bypass admission for a device exhibiting anomalous behavior
Switch port MAC-flapping alerts indicating address reuse across ports
vectors: Cloning a known-good device's MAC address using readily available tools
Exploiting NAC deployments that fall back to weak MAC Authentication Bypass instead of full 802.1X
rootCauses: Reliance on MAC-based filtering/MAB as a primary or fallback access control
No 802.1X certificate-based authentication deployed for device admission
Lack of MAC address anomaly/conflict detection on the network
controls: 802.1X certificate-based device authentication rather than MAC-based filtering
MAC address conflict/duplicate detection and alerting
Network segmentation limiting the blast radius of a single admitted device
ITID-33821.detection: Moderate; MAC address conflict/duplication detection on switches can reveal this, but not all environments monitor for it.
ITID-33821.response: Disable the affected switch port/network access immediately, investigate the source of the spoofing, and migrate to certificate-based 802.1X if MAC filtering was the sole control.
metrics: Number of MAC-spoofing NAC bypass incidents detected
Percentage of network access points using certificate-based 802.1X vs. MAC filtering
ITID-33821.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33822 by network type: wired NAC/802.1X admission control rather than Wi-Fi device impersonation.

playbook.name: MAC Spoofing to Bypass Network Access Control (NAC/802.1X)
playbook.description: An attacker changes their device's MAC address to match an authorized/allowlisted device, bypassing NAC or 802.1X-based network admission control.

steps.title: Identify the MAC spoofing event via NAC/switch logs
steps.desc: Review NAC/802.1X and switch port logs for a MAC address appearing on multiple switch ports/locations simultaneously or in rapid succession (a classic spoofing indicator), or for authentication anomalies inconsistent with the legitimate device's known behavior.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference switch CAM table history and NAC authentication logs for the duplicate/conflicting MAC appearance.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofed MAC, rogue device's actual port/location, and the legitimate device it impersonated.
steps.abort: If the duplicate appearance is explained by legitimate device migration/VM movement, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine what network access/segment the spoofing device obtained
steps.desc: Identify what VLAN/network segment and resources the rogue device accessed by impersonating the authorized MAC.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of network access obtained.

steps.title: Disable the switch port/quarantine the rogue device
steps.desc: Immediately shut down or quarantine the switch port where the rogue/spoofing device is connected.
steps.outcome: Rogue device disconnected from the network.

steps.title: Investigate the legitimate device for compromise
steps.desc: Check the legitimate device whose MAC was spoofed for signs of compromise that may have leaked its MAC address (e.g., malware, physical access).
steps.outcome: Confirmed legitimate device status.

steps.title: Strengthen NAC to use certificate-based 802.1X authentication
steps.desc: Migrate from MAC-address-based allowlisting to certificate-based 802.1X authentication, which is not spoofable via a simple MAC address change.
steps.guidance: This is the durable root-cause fix — MAC filtering alone is inherently spoofable.
steps.outcome: Network admission control no longer solely dependent on MAC address.

steps.title: Verify legitimate devices retain access under the new authentication method
steps.desc: Confirm all legitimate devices can still authenticate and access the network under the certificate-based method.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access confirmed intact.

steps.title: Audit for other network segments relying solely on MAC-based NAC
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit other network segments/sites for reliance on MAC-address-only network access control.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33822.def: Unauthorized wireless network access achieved by cloning or forging the MAC address of a device already authorized on a Wi-Fi network's MAC-filtering access control list, allowing an adversary's device to be admitted in its place or alongside it.
ITID-33822.purpose: Captures unauthorized Wi-Fi network access achieved by spoofing the MAC address of an authorized wireless device.
scopeIncludes: Cloning an authorized device's MAC address to connect to a Wi-Fi network with MAC-address filtering
Impersonating a known device's MAC to blend in with expected wireless client inventory
Bypassing guest/corporate Wi-Fi MAC allowlists via address forgery
scopeExcludes: Wired network NAC/802.1X MAC bypass (see ITID-33821)
DHCP/IP reservation hijacking via MAC spoofing (see ITID-33823)
ITID-33822.severity: Medium-High, since MAC filtering alone is a weak Wi-Fi control and its bypass typically indicates an otherwise-inadequate wireless security posture.
ITID-33822.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the accessed wireless network reaches sensitive internal resources.
ITID-33822.escalation: Escalate to network security upon detection; if MAC filtering is the sole wireless access control, treat this as a systemic control-adequacy issue.
indicators: Duplicate MAC address observed connecting to the same or nearby wireless access points
Wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) alerts for MAC address conflicts
Anomalous device behavior/traffic inconsistent with the legitimate device's known usage pattern
vectors: Passive capture of an authorized device's MAC address via Wi-Fi sniffing, followed by cloning
Exploiting Wi-Fi networks relying solely on MAC filtering with no WPA2/3-Enterprise authentication
rootCauses: Wi-Fi network relying on MAC filtering instead of WPA2/3-Enterprise (802.1X) authentication
No wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) deployed to catch MAC conflicts
Lack of network segmentation isolating guest/BYOD wireless traffic
controls: WPA2/3-Enterprise (802.1X certificate or credential-based) wireless authentication in place of MAC filtering
Wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) for MAC conflict/rogue device detection
Network segmentation isolating wireless client traffic by trust level
ITID-33822.detection: Moderate; WIDS deployment enables detection, but many organizations lack wireless-specific intrusion detection.
ITID-33822.response: Disconnect the spoofing device, migrate away from MAC-filtering-only authentication, and investigate scope of wireless network access gained.
metrics: Number of Wi-Fi MAC-spoofing incidents detected
Percentage of wireless networks using WPA2/3-Enterprise vs. MAC filtering
detections: Wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) MAC conflict alerting
ITID-33822.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33821 by network type: Wi-Fi/wireless rather than wired NAC/802.1X.

playbook.name: MAC Spoofing to Impersonate an Authorized Device on Wi-Fi
playbook.description: An attacker spoofs the MAC address of an authorized device to associate with a Wi-Fi network that filters access by MAC allowlist.

steps.title: Identify duplicate/conflicting MAC association on the wireless network
steps.desc: Review wireless controller/AP logs for the same MAC address associating from multiple physical locations, devices, or signal characteristics simultaneously, or unusual deauth/reassociation patterns indicating spoofing.
steps.guidance: Compare RSSI/location data and device fingerprinting (OS/user-agent) between the legitimate and spoofing sessions if available.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofed device, its access point/location, and the legitimate device impersonated.
steps.abort: If the duplicate association is explained by device roaming/reconnect, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine what network access the spoofing device obtained
steps.desc: Identify what resources or segments the rogue device accessed via the Wi-Fi network.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of access.

steps.title: Deauthenticate and block the spoofed MAC/device
steps.desc: Force-deauthenticate the rogue session and block the MAC address at the wireless controller pending resolution.
steps.outcome: Rogue device disconnected from the wireless network.

steps.title: Migrate from MAC-filtering to WPA2/3-Enterprise (802.1X) authentication
steps.desc: Replace MAC-address allowlisting with certificate- or credential-based enterprise Wi-Fi authentication, which is not vulnerable to simple MAC spoofing.
steps.outcome: Wireless network access no longer solely dependent on spoofable MAC address.

steps.title: Verify legitimate devices retain wireless access under the new method
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate devices/users can still connect under the new authentication scheme.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access confirmed intact.

steps.title: Audit all wireless networks for MAC-filtering-only reliance
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit all wireless networks in the organization for reliance on MAC filtering as the sole access control.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33823.def: Unauthorized network access or disruption achieved by spoofing another device's MAC address specifically to claim its DHCP reservation or static IP assignment, allowing the adversary's device to receive an IP address, and any associated network privileges or routing treatment, intended for the legitimate device.
ITID-33823.purpose: Captures MAC spoofing used specifically to hijack a DHCP reservation or static IP assignment tied to another device's MAC address.
scopeIncludes: Spoofing a MAC address to obtain a DHCP-reserved IP address intended for another device
Claiming an IP address with elevated firewall/routing trust (e.g., a management VLAN reservation) via MAC spoofing
Denial-of-service to the legitimate device by claiming its reserved address first
scopeExcludes: MAC spoofing used purely for NAC/802.1X or Wi-Fi admission bypass with no DHCP/IP-reservation targeting (see ITID-33821/ITID-33822)
ITID-33823.severity: Medium-High, particularly when the hijacked IP reservation carries elevated network trust or routing privileges.
ITID-33823.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the hijacked reservation grants access to a sensitive network segment.
ITID-33823.escalation: Escalate to network engineering upon detection; review DHCP logs and reservation bindings for the affected segment.
indicators: DHCP server logs showing a reservation issued to an unexpected MAC-to-device pairing
IP address conflict alerts between the legitimate device and the spoofing device
Network access anomalies consistent with the spoofing device inheriting the legitimate device's reserved network privileges
vectors: Passive MAC address discovery followed by DHCP request spoofing to claim a reservation
Race-condition exploitation to obtain a reserved IP before the legitimate device boots/renews its lease
rootCauses: DHCP reservations relied upon as an implicit trust/privilege mechanism without additional authentication
No DHCP snooping or dynamic ARP inspection deployed on switches
Lack of monitoring for IP/MAC binding conflicts
controls: DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on network switches
Avoiding IP-reservation-based trust without additional device authentication
IP/MAC binding conflict monitoring and alerting
ITID-33823.detection: Moderate; DHCP snooping and IP conflict detection provide reasonable visibility where deployed.
ITID-33823.response: Revoke and reissue the affected DHCP reservation, isolate the spoofing device, and enable DHCP snooping/dynamic ARP inspection if not already active.
metrics: Number of DHCP/IP-reservation hijacking incidents detected
Percentage of switches with DHCP snooping enabled
detections: DHCP snooping / IP-MAC binding conflict alerting
ITID-33823.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33821/ITID-33822 by the specific target of the spoofing: a DHCP reservation/IP assignment rather than admission control itself.

playbook.name: MAC Spoofing for DHCP/IP Reservation Hijacking
playbook.description: An attacker spoofs a legitimate device's MAC address to obtain its reserved/static DHCP IP assignment, hijacking the network identity and any IP-based trust or access associated with it.

steps.title: Identify the DHCP reservation conflict/hijack
steps.desc: Review DHCP server logs for lease conflicts or the reserved IP being issued to an unexpected MAC address, and for the legitimate device subsequently failing to obtain its expected IP.
steps.guidance: Check DHCP lease history for the reservation and any conflict/decline events.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofed MAC, hijacked IP reservation, and the legitimate device affected.

steps.title: Determine what IP-based trust/access the hijacked reservation granted
steps.desc: Assess whether any firewall rules, application trust, or access controls were keyed to the hijacked IP address, and what the attacker accessed as a result.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Block the spoofing device and restore the legitimate reservation
steps.desc: Identify and block the rogue device's switch port/network access, then restore the DHCP reservation to the legitimate device.
steps.outcome: Legitimate device regains its intended IP; rogue device blocked.

steps.title: Implement DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection
steps.desc: Enable DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on network switches to prevent unauthorized DHCP responses and MAC/IP hijacking.
steps.outcome: DHCP/ARP-based hijacking technique blocked going forward.

steps.title: Replace IP-based trust with stronger authentication where feasible
steps.desc: Where systems relied on the hijacked IP for trust/access decisions, migrate them to stronger, non-network-identity-based authentication.
steps.outcome: Trust relationships no longer solely dependent on IP/MAC identity.

steps.title: Verify legitimate device connectivity and access restored
steps.desc: Confirm the legitimate device operates normally with its correct IP and access, and the hijacking vector is closed.
steps.outcome: Legitimate device restored and vector confirmed closed.

steps.title: Deploy DHCP snooping/ARP inspection network-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and extend DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection to all network segments, not just the affected one.
steps.outcome: Fleet-wide deployment tracked or completed.

ITID-33824.def: Unauthorized network activity involving a forged MAC address, achieved or intended for a purpose not yet classified into a more specific MAC Address Spoofing sibling.
ITID-33824.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for MAC address spoofing cases that do not clearly fit wired NAC bypass, Wi-Fi impersonation, or DHCP/IP hijacking classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered MAC spoofing patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific purpose/mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33821, ITID-33822, or ITID-33823 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33824.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33824.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33824.escalation: Escalate to network security for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed MAC spoofing activity not yet attributable to a specific purpose
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific purpose/mechanism
controls: Network access control monitoring
ITID-33824.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33824.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33824.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General MAC Address Spoofing
playbook.description: An attacker spoofs a device's MAC address in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized network access.

steps.title: Identify the MAC spoofing activity
steps.desc: Review network/NAC/wireless logs to confirm MAC spoofing occurred and identify the impersonated device and the rogue device's actual location/port.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofing activity and affected devices.
steps.tool: Network switch / NAC / wireless controller logs

steps.title: Determine scope of network access obtained
steps.desc: Assess what network segments/resources the spoofing device accessed.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Block/quarantine the spoofing device
steps.desc: Disable the switch port or wireless association for the rogue device.
steps.outcome: Rogue device disconnected.

steps.title: Strengthen network admission control beyond MAC-based filtering
steps.desc: Migrate the affected network access control to certificate- or credential-based authentication (802.1X) rather than relying on MAC address alone.
steps.outcome: Network access control no longer solely dependent on spoofable MAC address.

steps.title: Verify legitimate device access restored under the new control
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate devices retain access under the strengthened authentication method.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access confirmed intact.

steps.title: Audit network segments for MAC-based-only access control reliance
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit for other network segments relying solely on MAC-based access control.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33831.def: Unauthorized access achieved by crafting a fraudulent SAML assertion or exploiting a flaw in SAML signature verification (e.g., XML signature wrapping, accepting unsigned assertions, or algorithm confusion) to convince a service provider that an unauthenticated party is a legitimately authenticated user.
ITID-33831.purpose: Captures unauthorized access achieved by forging a SAML assertion or bypassing its signature verification.
scopeIncludes: XML signature wrapping attacks against SAML assertion processing
Exploitation of a service provider accepting unsigned or improperly validated SAML assertions
Algorithm confusion or weak-signature exploitation in SAML processing libraries
scopeExcludes: Forged SAML assertions created using a stolen IdP signing key/certificate, a distinct and more severe technique tracked as Golden SAML (see ITID-33834)
Exploiting a legitimate federation trust misconfiguration rather than the assertion/signature mechanism itself (see ITID-33832)
ITID-33831.severity: Critical, since a successful forgery grants full impersonation of any user to the relying service provider.
ITID-33831.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the severity of authentication bypass involved.
ITID-33831.escalation: Escalate to identity/federation engineering and IR immediately; treat as a critical authentication-bypass vulnerability requiring emergency patching of the SAML implementation.
indicators: SAML assertions with unexpected or missing signatures accepted by the service provider
Federation/SSO logs showing successful authentication with structurally anomalous SAML assertions
Security testing/penetration test findings of SAML signature validation weaknesses
vectors: XML signature wrapping (XSW) attacks against vulnerable SAML libraries
Exploiting misconfigured service providers that do not enforce assertion signature validation
rootCauses: SAML service provider implementation not strictly validating assertion signatures
Use of outdated or vulnerable SAML processing libraries
Insufficient security testing of the federation/SSO integration
mitreTechniques: T1606.002 Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
controls: Strict SAML assertion signature validation on all service providers
Use of up-to-date, well-vetted SAML processing libraries
Regular federation/SSO security testing including signature-wrapping test cases
ITID-33831.detection: Moderate; requires deep SAML assertion inspection capability, which is not always present in standard SSO logging.
ITID-33831.response: Patch the SAML validation flaw immediately, audit federation logs for exploitation attempts, and force re-authentication for potentially affected sessions.
metrics: Number of SAML forgery/signature-bypass incidents detected
Time to patch confirmed SAML validation vulnerabilities
detections: SAML assertion signature validation anomaly alerting
ITID-33831.notes: Differentiated from Golden SAML (ITID-33834) by the mechanism: exploiting a validation flaw or forging an assertion without a stolen signing key, rather than using a stolen key to sign fully valid-looking forged assertions.

playbook.name: SAML Assertion Forgery/Signature Bypass
playbook.description: An attacker forges or manipulates a SAML assertion (e.g., exploiting XML signature wrapping or a signature-validation flaw) to impersonate an identity to a relying party.

steps.title: Confirm the forged/manipulated SAML assertion and the exploited flaw
steps.desc: Review the identity provider and relying-party logs for an accepted SAML assertion with an invalid or manipulated signature, and identify the specific validation flaw (e.g., XML signature wrapping, algorithm confusion, missing signature check).
steps.guidance: Capture and analyze the raw SAML assertion/response for the forgery technique used.
steps.outcome: Confirmed forgery technique and the identity/account impersonated.
steps.abort: If the assertion is confirmed properly signed and valid, this is not a forgery — reclassify.

steps.title: Determine access obtained via the forged assertion
steps.desc: Review what the attacker accessed at the relying party using the forged identity.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke sessions established via the forged assertion
steps.desc: Terminate all sessions/tokens issued to the relying party based on the forged SAML assertion.
steps.outcome: Attacker's session access terminated.

steps.title: Disable the affected SSO integration if the flaw cannot be immediately patched
steps.desc: Temporarily disable SAML SSO for the affected relying party (falling back to a secure alternate authentication method) if the signature-validation flaw cannot be fixed immediately.
steps.outcome: No further forged assertions can be exploited.

steps.title: Patch the SAML signature-validation flaw
steps.desc: Fix or upgrade the SAML library/implementation to properly validate assertion signatures (correct XML canonicalization, reject wrapped/duplicate elements, enforce strict algorithm allowlisting).
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified to reject the previously successful forgery technique.

steps.title: Rotate the IdP signing certificate/key if compromise of the key is suspected
steps.desc: If there is any indication the signing key itself was compromised (rather than a pure validation bug), rotate the IdP's signing certificate.
steps.outcome: Signing key integrity assured.

steps.title: Re-enable SSO and verify signature validation enforcement
steps.desc: Restore the SSO integration and verify via test that manipulated/forged assertions are now rejected.
steps.outcome: SSO restored with verified signature enforcement.

steps.title: Audit all SSO/SAML integrations for the same signature-validation weakness
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit all other relying parties/SAML integrations in the environment for the same class of signature-validation flaw.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33832.def: Unauthorized access achieved by exploiting a misconfiguration in an identity federation trust relationship — such as an overly permissive trusted-issuer list, incorrect audience restriction, or a federation trust established with an unintended or compromised external tenant — allowing a party outside the intended trust boundary to authenticate as if from a trusted source.
ITID-33832.purpose: Captures unauthorized cross-tenant access achieved by exploiting a misconfigured identity federation trust relationship, rather than attacking the assertion mechanism itself.
scopeIncludes: Service provider accepting assertions from an unintended or overly broad set of trusted identity providers
Missing or incorrect audience (aud) restriction allowing a token issued for one application to be accepted by another
Federation trust with an external/partner tenant that is broader in scope than the business relationship requires
scopeExcludes: Exploiting the assertion signature/validation mechanism itself where the trust configuration is otherwise correct (see ITID-33831)
Use of a stolen IdP signing key to forge assertions within an otherwise correctly scoped trust (see ITID-33834, Golden SAML)
ITID-33832.severity: High-Critical, since federation trust misconfigurations can enable cross-tenant or cross-organization access at scale.
ITID-33832.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the potential for broad, systemic cross-tenant exposure.
ITID-33832.escalation: Escalate to identity/federation engineering and IR immediately; assess the full scope of tenants/applications reachable through the misconfigured trust.
indicators: Federation configuration audit revealing an overly broad trusted-issuer or audience list
Authentication logs showing tokens issued by an unexpected or partner IdP being accepted for a sensitive application
Cross-tenant access reports inconsistent with the intended business relationship scope
vectors: Exploiting an overly permissive trusted-issuer configuration to present tokens from an attacker-controlled or compromised partner IdP
Missing audience restriction allowing token reuse across unintended relying parties
rootCauses: Federation trust configured without strict issuer/audience validation
No periodic review of federation trust relationships against current business need
Overly broad multi-tenant federation setup for administrative convenience
mitreTechniques: T1606.002 Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
controls: Strict issuer and audience validation on all federation trust configurations
Periodic review and right-sizing of federation trust relationships
Least-privilege scoping of cross-tenant federation to only the necessary applications
