ITID-33832.detection: Moderate; requires federation configuration auditing tools and cross-tenant access monitoring, not universally deployed.
ITID-33832.response: Tighten the federation trust configuration immediately, audit all access gained through the misconfiguration, and review other trust relationships for similar gaps.
metrics: Number of federation trust misconfiguration findings/incidents
Time to remediate upon discovery
ITID-33832.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33831 by root cause: a trust/configuration gap rather than an assertion signature/validation defect.

playbook.name: Federation Trust Misconfiguration Exploited for Cross-Tenant Access
playbook.description: A misconfigured identity federation trust relationship (e.g., overly broad domain trust, missing tenant restriction) allows an identity from one tenant/organization to authenticate into another's resources.

steps.title: Confirm the federation misconfiguration and cross-tenant access
steps.desc: Review the federation trust configuration (issuer restrictions, allowed audiences, tenant claim validation) to confirm the misconfiguration, and identify which external identities gained cross-tenant access.
steps.guidance: Check for missing or overly permissive issuer/audience validation in the federation configuration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed misconfiguration and list of cross-tenant access instances.

steps.title: Determine what resources/data the cross-tenant access exposed
steps.desc: Review what the externally-federated identities accessed within the affected tenant.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Restrict the federation trust configuration immediately
steps.desc: Apply an emergency fix to the federation trust settings (tighten issuer/audience/tenant claim validation) or disable the trust relationship entirely if it cannot be immediately fixed.
steps.outcome: Cross-tenant access via the federation trust is blocked.

steps.title: Revoke sessions established via the misconfigured trust
steps.desc: Terminate any active sessions/tokens issued through the cross-tenant access path.
steps.outcome: No lingering unauthorized sessions remain.

steps.title: Rebuild the federation trust configuration with strict tenant scoping
steps.desc: Reconfigure the federation trust with strict issuer, audience, and tenant claim validation, and test explicitly against the previously exploitable cross-tenant scenario.
steps.outcome: Federation trust verified to enforce correct tenant isolation.

steps.title: Restore legitimate federated access and notify affected tenant(s)
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate, intended federated access continues to work and notify any affected tenant/customer of the cross-tenant exposure per policy.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored and notifications completed.

steps.title: Audit all federation trust relationships for tenant-scoping gaps
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit all other identity federation trust relationships for similar tenant-isolation gaps.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33833.def: Unauthorized access achieved by tampering with or exploiting weak validation of claims within an OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token or access token — such as role, group, or subject claims — causing the relying application to grant access or privilege inconsistent with the user's actual identity.
ITID-33833.purpose: Captures unauthorized access achieved by manipulating the claims within an OIDC (OpenID Connect) token to falsely elevate privilege or identity.
scopeIncludes: Modifying JWT claims (e.g., role, group, admin flags) where signature validation is weak, absent, or exploitable (e.g., 'none' algorithm acceptance)
Exploiting a relying application that trusts unsigned or client-supplied claims over verified token claims
Algorithm-confusion attacks (e.g., RS256-to-HS256 downgrade) enabling claim forgery
scopeExcludes: SAML-specific assertion forgery/signature bypass (see ITID-33831)
Federation trust misconfiguration allowing tokens from an unintended issuer, where the claims themselves are not tampered with (see ITID-33832)
ITID-33833.severity: Critical, since claims manipulation typically enables direct privilege escalation or identity impersonation.
ITID-33833.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the severity of authentication/authorization bypass involved.
ITID-33833.escalation: Escalate to identity/application security engineering and IR immediately; patch the token validation flaw as a critical vulnerability.
indicators: JWT validation logs/errors indicating algorithm mismatch or unexpected signing method acceptance
Application access logs showing privilege inconsistent with the user's actual IdP-issued role
Security testing findings of a relying application not validating token signatures/claims strictly
vectors: JWT 'alg: none' or algorithm-confusion attacks against poorly implemented token validation
Client-side token/claim tampering where the relying application trusts client-supplied values over verified token content
rootCauses: Token validation library/implementation not strictly enforcing expected signing algorithm
Relying application trusting claims without full cryptographic verification
Insufficient security testing of OIDC token handling logic
controls: Strict, allowlisted signing-algorithm enforcement in token validation logic
Use of well-vetted, up-to-date OIDC/JWT libraries
Regular security testing of token validation logic including algorithm-confusion test cases
ITID-33833.detection: Moderate; requires token-validation-specific logging and anomaly detection, which is not standard in most application logging.
ITID-33833.response: Patch the token validation flaw immediately, audit access granted under manipulated claims, and force re-authentication for affected sessions.
metrics: Number of OIDC claims-manipulation incidents detected
Time to patch confirmed token validation vulnerabilities
ITID-33833.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33831/ITID-33832 by protocol (OIDC/JWT rather than SAML) and mechanism (claims tampering rather than assertion forgery or trust misconfiguration).

playbook.name: OIDC Token Claims Manipulation
playbook.description: An attacker manipulates claims within an OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token or userinfo response (e.g., via an unsigned/weakly-verified token or a compromised claims-mapping rule) to impersonate a different identity or elevate privileges.

steps.title: Confirm the claims manipulation and identify the validation gap
steps.desc: Review relying-party logs and the OIDC token itself to confirm a claim (e.g., sub, email, role/group claim) was manipulated, and identify how validation failed to catch it (missing signature verification, trusting an unverified claim, alg=none acceptance).
steps.guidance: Decode and inspect the JWT header/payload/signature for anomalies such as alg:none or an unexpected signing key.
steps.outcome: Confirmed manipulation technique and impersonated/elevated identity.

steps.title: Determine access obtained via the manipulated claims
steps.desc: Review what the attacker accessed using the impersonated identity or elevated claim.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke sessions established via the manipulated token
steps.desc: Terminate all sessions/tokens issued based on the manipulated claims.
steps.outcome: Attacker's access terminated.

steps.title: Disable the vulnerable OIDC integration if not immediately patchable
steps.desc: Temporarily disable the affected OIDC login flow if the validation flaw cannot be patched immediately.
steps.outcome: No further exploitation of the flaw possible.

steps.title: Fix token signature/algorithm validation
steps.desc: Patch the relying party to strictly verify the ID token's signature using an allowlisted algorithm and the correct, pinned signing key, rejecting alg:none and unexpected keys.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified to reject the previously successful manipulation.

steps.title: Re-enable the integration and verify enforcement
steps.desc: Restore the OIDC login flow and confirm via test that manipulated tokens are now rejected.
steps.outcome: Integration restored with verified enforcement.

steps.title: Audit all OIDC relying-party integrations for the same validation gap
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit all other applications using OIDC for the same class of token-validation weakness.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33834.def: Unauthorized access achieved by stealing an identity provider's SAML token-signing private key/certificate (e.g., from AD FS) and using it to forge fully cryptographically valid SAML assertions impersonating any user — including highly privileged accounts — without any interaction with the actual identity provider at authentication time.
ITID-33834.purpose: Captures the Golden SAML attack, in which an adversary uses a stolen IdP token-signing certificate/key to forge fully valid SAML assertions for any user or privilege level.
scopeIncludes: Theft of an AD FS or equivalent IdP token-signing certificate followed by forged assertion generation
Forged assertions granting impersonation of any user, including privileged/administrative accounts, bypassing MFA entirely since no live authentication occurs
Persistent access maintained via the stolen signing key even after password resets across the environment
scopeExcludes: Signature validation bypass or assertion forgery that does not involve a stolen legitimate signing key (see ITID-33831)
Federation trust misconfiguration exploitation with no signing-key theft involved (see ITID-33832)
ITID-33834.severity: Critical, representing one of the most severe identity-spoofing techniques since it grants durable, MFA-bypassing impersonation of any identity.
ITID-33834.priority: P1, treated as a top-severity active intrusion requiring emergency, organization-wide remediation.
ITID-33834.escalation: Escalate immediately to executive security leadership, identity/federation engineering, and IR; this typically requires rotating the IdP signing certificate organization-wide and assuming full domain/tenant compromise.
indicators: SAML assertions with no corresponding real-time authentication event at the IdP
Assertions with unusual attribute combinations, lifetimes, or issuance patterns inconsistent with normal IdP behavior
Evidence of prior compromise of the AD FS server or equivalent IdP infrastructure hosting the signing key
vectors: Compromise of the AD FS server (or equivalent) to extract the token-signing certificate and private key
Extraction of the DKM (Distributed Key Manager) container in Active Directory used to decrypt the AD FS signing key
rootCauses: Insufficient hardening/monitoring of AD FS or equivalent IdP infrastructure
Token-signing certificates never rotated over long periods, extending the value of a stolen key
No hardware security module (HSM) protecting the signing key material
mitreTechniques: T1606.002 Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
controls: Hardware security module (HSM) protection for IdP token-signing keys
Rigorous hardening and monitoring of AD FS/IdP infrastructure as Tier-0 assets
Regular token-signing certificate rotation
ITID-33834.detection: Weak-to-moderate; Golden SAML is specifically designed to evade normal authentication logging since no real-time IdP interaction occurs, requiring specialized detection (e.g., anomalous assertion metadata analysis).
ITID-33834.response: Rotate the compromised signing certificate immediately across the environment, treat as a full identity infrastructure compromise, and conduct comprehensive forensic investigation of the IdP infrastructure.
metrics: Number of Golden SAML incidents detected
Time to rotate compromised signing certificates
ITID-33834.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33831/ITID-33832 by the specific, high-severity mechanism of stolen signing-key-based forgery, which produces cryptographically valid assertions indistinguishable from legitimate ones by signature alone.

playbook.name: Golden SAML Attack (Forged Assertions Using Stolen Signing Key)
playbook.description: An attacker steals the identity provider's SAML signing private key/certificate and uses it to forge fully-valid, arbitrary SAML assertions, impersonating any user to any relying party.

steps.title: Confirm signing-key compromise and identify forged assertion usage
steps.desc: Investigate the suspected compromise of the IdP's SAML signing private key (e.g., via ADFS server compromise) and search relying-party logs for logins with valid-signature assertions that do not correspond to a real IdP-issued login event.
steps.guidance: Golden SAML assertions will pass signature validation but often have no corresponding session/login record on the actual IdP — this discrepancy is the key detection signal.
steps.outcome: Confirmed signing key compromise and full list of relying parties/accounts accessed via forged assertions.
steps.tool: IdP server forensics / relying party logs

steps.title: Determine the full scope of impersonated identities and accessed resources
steps.desc: Because a stolen signing key allows impersonation of any user, exhaustively review all relying parties trusting the compromised IdP for anomalous access during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Complete scope of compromise across all trusting relying parties.

steps.title: Isolate the compromised IdP server and revoke the signing certificate
steps.desc: Immediately isolate the compromised identity provider server (e.g., ADFS) from the network and revoke the compromised SAML signing certificate at every relying party.
steps.guidance: This is a critical, high-priority action — every relying party trusting the old certificate remains vulnerable until it is revoked/rotated everywhere.
steps.outcome: Forged assertions signed with the stolen key are no longer accepted anywhere.
steps.tool: IdP server / relying party trust configuration

steps.title: Escalate to executive leadership and initiate full incident response
steps.desc: Escalate immediately to CISO/executive leadership and legal — a Golden SAML compromise typically warrants full incident response, external forensics, and regulatory/customer notification given the scope of potential impersonation.
steps.outcome: Full incident response engaged with appropriate stakeholders.

steps.title: Rebuild the IdP server and issue a new signing certificate
steps.desc: Rebuild the compromised IdP server from a known-good state (do not simply clean in place, given the severity), generate a new signing key/certificate, and re-establish trust with every relying party.
steps.outcome: New, uncompromised signing infrastructure in place and trusted by all relying parties.

steps.title: Investigate and remediate the initial compromise vector on the IdP server
steps.desc: Determine how the IdP server itself was compromised (the attacker needed admin access to extract the signing key) and remediate that root-cause vulnerability.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector to the IdP server closed.

steps.title: Restore SSO service and force credential resets for impersonated accounts
steps.desc: Restore SSO service on the rebuilt infrastructure, force credential/session resets for all accounts confirmed impersonated, and verify normal operation.
steps.outcome: SSO restored securely and affected accounts remediated.

steps.title: Harden IdP server security and implement signing-key protection (HSM)
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement hardware security module (HSM) protection for the signing key, plus tightened administrative access controls and monitoring on the IdP server, to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: HSM/hardening initiative implemented or tracked.

ITID-33835.def: Unauthorized access exploiting identity federation (SAML/OIDC/other) mechanisms, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Identity Federation Exploitation sibling.
ITID-33835.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for identity federation exploitation cases that do not clearly fit SAML forgery, trust misconfiguration, OIDC claims manipulation, or Golden SAML classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered federation exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33831 through ITID-33834 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33835.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification given the general severity of federation exploitation.
ITID-33835.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33835.escalation: Escalate to identity/federation engineering for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed federation-based unauthorized access not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: Identity federation security review process
ITID-33835.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33835.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33835.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Identity Federation Exploitation
playbook.description: An identity federation mechanism (SAML, OIDC, or similar) is exploited in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm the federation exploitation and identify the specific flaw
steps.desc: Review IdP/relying-party logs to confirm the exploitation and identify the specific federation flaw exploited (assertion/token validation, trust configuration, or key compromise).
steps.outcome: Confirmed exploitation and flaw type.

steps.title: Determine the scope of unauthorized access
steps.desc: Review what identities/resources were accessed via the exploitation.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke affected sessions and restrict the federation mechanism
steps.desc: Terminate sessions established via the exploitation and restrict or disable the affected federation flow pending a fix.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access via the flaw.

steps.title: Fix the root-cause federation flaw
steps.desc: Remediate the specific validation, configuration, or key-management flaw identified.
steps.outcome: Fix deployed and verified.

steps.title: Restore federated access and verify enforcement
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate federated access works correctly and the flaw is closed.
steps.outcome: Federation restored securely.

steps.title: Audit all federation integrations for similar weaknesses
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit other federation integrations in the environment for similar weaknesses.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33911.def: Unauthorized application access achieved by exploiting a security vulnerability in software that has reached end-of-life (EOL) status, meaning the vendor no longer issues patches, leaving any known or newly discovered vulnerability permanently unremediated at the source.
ITID-33911.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from exploitation of a known vulnerability in an end-of-life application for which no vendor patch is or will ever be available.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a publicly known CVE in an EOL application with no available vendor fix
Continued operational use of EOL software past its vendor-supported end date
Zero-day-equivalent risk from EOL software where even a hypothetical vendor fix will never be issued
scopeExcludes: A legacy application that is still vendor-supported but lacks modern authentication support (see ITID-33912)
A legacy application exploited via its underlying unsupported framework/runtime rather than the application itself being EOL (see ITID-33913)
ITID-33911.severity: High-Critical, since no patch path exists and the vulnerability window is effectively permanent absent replacement or compensating controls.
ITID-33911.priority: P1 upon active exploitation; P2 for confirmed EOL exposure pending exploitation evidence.
ITID-33911.escalation: Escalate to application/business owners and security leadership; treat unremediated EOL exposure as a standing risk requiring compensating controls or migration planning, and any active exploitation as an emergency.
indicators: Vulnerability scan findings flagging software as EOL with no available patch
Exploitation attempts targeting known CVEs in software confirmed to be past end-of-support date
Asset inventory showing continued production use of vendor-EOL software
vectors: Exploitation of publicly documented CVEs with public proof-of-concept code against unpatched EOL software
Automated scanning tools specifically targeting known-EOL software versions
rootCauses: Business dependency on EOL software with no migration plan or budget
No compensating controls (network isolation, WAF virtual patching) applied to known-EOL systems
Asset inventory not tracking software end-of-support dates
controls: Software end-of-life tracking integrated into asset/vulnerability management
Network isolation/segmentation for systems that cannot be patched or replaced
Virtual patching (WAF/IPS signatures) as a compensating control for known EOL vulnerabilities
ITID-33911.detection: Strong for identifying the exposure (vulnerability scanning readily flags EOL software); moderate for detecting active exploitation depending on logging maturity of the legacy system.
ITID-33911.response: Isolate or compensate for the vulnerable system immediately, prioritize migration/replacement, and monitor closely for exploitation given the permanent unpatched state.
metrics: Number of EOL applications in production with no compensating controls
Number of exploitation incidents against EOL software per period
ITID-33911.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33912/ITID-33913 by the defining trait of the software itself being fully end-of-life with no vendor patch path whatsoever.

playbook.name: End-of-Life (EOL) Application with No Available Patch Exploited
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a vulnerability in an application that has reached end-of-life and no longer receives vendor patches, gaining unauthorized access.

steps.title: Identify the exploited EOL application and confirm the vulnerability used
steps.desc: Confirm the application's EOL/unsupported status and identify the specific vulnerability/exploit technique used to gain access.
steps.guidance: Check vendor EOL announcements and CVE databases for known unpatched vulnerabilities affecting the version in use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed EOL status, vulnerability exploited, and unauthorized access gained.

steps.title: Determine scope of access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review logs for what the attacker accessed or did via the exploited application.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate the affected application/system from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the EOL application/host to prevent further exploitation or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access via the application.

steps.title: Apply a compensating control (WAF rule, virtual patch, network restriction)
steps.desc: Since no vendor patch exists, apply a compensating control such as a WAF rule blocking the specific exploit pattern, or restrict network access to the application to only essential sources.
steps.outcome: Exploitation vector mitigated pending a permanent fix.

steps.title: Migrate off the EOL application or upgrade to a supported version
steps.desc: Plan and execute migration to a supported, patchable version or replacement application, since no further patches will be issued for the EOL version.
steps.guidance: This is the only durable fix — compensating controls are a temporary bridge, not a resolution.
steps.outcome: Application migrated/upgraded to a supported state.

steps.title: Restore service on the remediated/replacement platform
steps.desc: Verify the replacement or upgraded application is functioning correctly and the original vulnerability is no longer present.
steps.outcome: Service restored on a secure, supported platform.

steps.title: Establish an EOL application inventory and retirement process
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement a formal process to track application end-of-life dates and force timely migration/decommissioning before support expires.
steps.outcome: EOL tracking/retirement process implemented.

ITID-33912.def: Unauthorized application access achieved because a legacy application, while still vendor-supported and patchable, only supports weak legacy authentication (e.g., static passwords with no MFA option, or no SSO/SAML integration), leaving it a comparatively weak link in an otherwise modern authentication environment.
ITID-33912.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to a legacy application that is still vendor-supported but lacks support for modern authentication mechanisms such as MFA or SSO.
scopeIncludes: Compromise of a legacy application's single-factor password authentication with no MFA option available
Legacy applications excluded from SSO/conditional access enforcement due to lack of modern protocol support
Credential-based attacks succeeding specifically because the application cannot enforce MFA
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of an EOL application with no available patch at all (see ITID-33911)
Exploitation via the application's underlying unsupported runtime/framework rather than its authentication model (see ITID-33913)
ITID-33912.severity: Medium-High, since the application itself may be secure aside from its weak authentication posture.
ITID-33912.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the application holds sensitive data and is internet-facing.
ITID-33912.escalation: Escalate to the application owner and IAM team; prioritize compensating controls (network restriction, privileged access workstation gating) given the inability to add native MFA.
indicators: Successful authentication to a legacy application immediately following a credential-stuffing or brute-force campaign, correlated with the app's lack of MFA
IAM inventory flagging the application as excluded from conditional access/SSO enforcement
Password-only authentication logs for the application with no corresponding MFA challenge
vectors: Credential stuffing or brute force succeeding specifically because MFA cannot be enforced on the legacy application
Phishing targeting the legacy application's credentials, which then bypass the MFA layer applied elsewhere
rootCauses: Legacy application architecture unable to support modern authentication protocols (SAML/OIDC/MFA)
No compensating access control (VPN, PAW, network restriction) layered around the legacy application
IAM/SSO rollout incomplete, leaving legacy applications as unintegrated exceptions
controls: Compensating access restriction (VPN-only access, jump host/PAW) for legacy applications lacking native MFA
Reverse-proxy-based MFA/SSO wrapping for legacy applications where technically feasible
Prioritized migration roadmap for legacy applications lacking modern authentication
ITID-33912.detection: Moderate; authentication logs for the legacy app are typically available, but lack the richer signal MFA-aware systems provide.
ITID-33912.response: Apply or tighten compensating network-level access controls immediately, force credential resets, and prioritize the application for MFA/SSO integration or replacement.
metrics: Number of legacy applications lacking MFA/SSO support
Incidents attributed to legacy authentication weakness
ITID-33912.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33911 by vendor-support status: this leaf assumes the application is still patchable, with the specific weakness being its authentication model.

playbook.name: Legacy Application Lacking Modern Authentication (No MFA/SSO Support) Exploited
playbook.description: An attacker gains unauthorized access to a legacy application that cannot support MFA or SSO, relying only on a single-factor password.

steps.title: Confirm the unauthorized access and the application's authentication limitation
steps.desc: Confirm the unauthorized login to the legacy application and verify that the application's architecture genuinely prevents MFA/SSO integration (versus simply not having it configured).
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized access and technical authentication limitation.
steps.abort: If MFA/SSO integration is actually possible but was just not configured, treat this as a configuration gap rather than an inherent legacy limitation, and prioritize enabling it.

steps.title: Determine scope of access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review what the attacker accessed via the single-factor-authenticated session.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Reset the compromised account's password and terminate its session
steps.desc: Force a password reset and terminate the active session for the compromised account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Apply a compensating access control (VPN/network restriction) in front of the legacy app
steps.desc: Restrict access to the legacy application to only a corporate VPN or trusted network segment, adding a layer of authentication in front of it.
steps.outcome: Application no longer reachable without passing an additional access control layer.

steps.title: Deploy a reverse-proxy/gateway MFA wrapper in front of the legacy application
steps.desc: Where the application itself cannot support MFA, deploy an identity-aware proxy or gateway that enforces MFA/SSO before allowing traffic through to the legacy application.
steps.guidance: This achieves modern authentication without requiring the legacy app itself to be re-architected.
steps.outcome: MFA/SSO effectively enforced for the legacy application via the proxy layer.

steps.title: Verify the proxy enforcement and restore legitimate user access
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate users can access the application only after passing MFA at the proxy layer.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored under enforced MFA.

steps.title: Prioritize migration or retirement of the legacy application
steps.desc: Document the incident and add the legacy application to a prioritized migration/retirement roadmap given its inherent authentication limitations.
steps.outcome: Migration/retirement item tracked.

ITID-33913.def: Unauthorized application access achieved by exploiting a vulnerability in the unsupported framework, programming language runtime, web server, or operating system underlying a legacy application, even where the application's own code may be actively maintained.
ITID-33913.purpose: Captures unauthorized access achieved by exploiting a legacy application's underlying unsupported framework, language runtime, or operating system, rather than the application's own code or authentication model.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of an unsupported/EOL web server, application server, or language runtime hosting an otherwise-maintained application
Exploitation of an unsupported operating system version underlying a legacy application
Container base images built on EOL OS/runtime versions never updated
scopeExcludes: The application itself being fully EOL with no vendor support at any layer (see ITID-33911)
The application's authentication model being the specific weakness, with the framework/runtime otherwise supported (see ITID-33912)
ITID-33913.severity: High-Critical, since the underlying platform vulnerability may grant remote code execution regardless of the application layer's own security posture.
ITID-33913.priority: P1 upon active exploitation; P2 for confirmed unsupported-runtime exposure pending exploitation evidence.
ITID-33913.escalation: Escalate to application/infrastructure owners and security engineering; prioritize runtime/framework upgrade or isolation given the application-layer team may not control or be aware of the underlying platform's support status.
indicators: Vulnerability scan findings identifying an EOL/unsupported framework, runtime, or OS underlying a production application
Exploitation attempts targeting known CVEs in the underlying platform rather than the application's own code
Container image scanning findings of EOL base images in production
vectors: Exploitation of known CVEs in an unsupported web/application server, language runtime, or OS
Automated scanning tools identifying and targeting known-vulnerable underlying platform versions
rootCauses: Application dependency management not tracking or upgrading the underlying framework/runtime/OS
Container base images not regularly rebuilt/patched
Organizational silo between application development ownership and infrastructure/platform patching responsibility
controls: Dependency and base-image scanning integrated into CI/CD to catch EOL frameworks/runtimes/OS versions
Regular rebuilding of container images from current, supported base images
Clear ownership assignment for underlying platform patching separate from application code ownership
ITID-33913.detection: Strong for identifying the exposure via vulnerability/dependency scanning; moderate for detecting active exploitation depending on platform-layer logging.
ITID-33913.response: Upgrade or isolate the vulnerable underlying platform immediately, and establish a process to prevent recurrence via dependency/base-image scanning.
metrics: Number of applications running on EOL/unsupported frameworks, runtimes, or OS versions
Time to remediate upon discovery
ITID-33913.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33911/ITID-33912 by locating the weakness at the underlying platform/runtime layer rather than the application's own code or authentication model.

playbook.name: Legacy Application Running on Unsupported Framework/Runtime Exploited
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a known vulnerability in an unsupported underlying framework or runtime (e.g., an old .NET/Java/PHP version) that a legacy application depends on, to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm the unsupported runtime and the exploited vulnerability
steps.desc: Confirm the application runs on an unsupported/EOL framework or runtime version and identify the specific known vulnerability exploited to gain access.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the runtime version against public CVE data and vendor EOL announcements.
steps.outcome: Confirmed runtime version, vulnerability, and unauthorized access gained.

steps.title: Determine scope of access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review logs for what the attacker accessed or executed via the exploited runtime vulnerability.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate the affected application/host from the network
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host running the vulnerable runtime to prevent further exploitation or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access via the vulnerability.

steps.title: Apply a virtual patch/WAF rule as a compensating control
steps.desc: Deploy a WAF rule or network-layer control blocking the specific exploit pattern, since the runtime itself cannot be patched further.
steps.outcome: Exploitation vector mitigated pending permanent remediation.

steps.title: Upgrade the application to a supported runtime/framework version
steps.desc: Plan and execute an upgrade of the underlying framework/runtime to a currently-supported, patchable version.
steps.guidance: This is the only durable fix — compensating controls are a temporary bridge.
steps.outcome: Application running on a supported, patched runtime.

steps.title: Restore service on the upgraded platform and verify the vulnerability is closed
steps.desc: Confirm the upgraded application functions correctly and the previously exploited vulnerability is no longer present.
steps.outcome: Service restored on a secure, supported platform.

steps.title: Establish runtime/framework version tracking and upgrade cadence
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement tracking of runtime/framework support lifecycles across the application portfolio, with a mandatory upgrade cadence before EOL.
steps.outcome: Tracking/upgrade process implemented.

ITID-33914.def: Unauthorized access exploiting a legacy application, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Exploiting Legacy Applications sibling.
ITID-33914.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for legacy application exploitation cases that do not clearly fit full end-of-life, weak-authentication, or unsupported-runtime classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered legacy application exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33911, ITID-33912, or ITID-33913 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33914.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33914.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33914.escalation: Escalate to application owners for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed legacy application exploitation not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: Legacy system risk management process
ITID-33914.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33914.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33914.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Legacy Application Exploit
playbook.description: A legacy application is exploited in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm the legacy application exploitation and identify the specific weakness
steps.desc: Confirm unauthorized access to the legacy application and identify the specific weakness exploited (unpatched vulnerability, weak authentication, unsupported dependency, etc.).
steps.outcome: Confirmed exploitation and weakness identified.

steps.title: Determine scope of access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review logs for the extent of unauthorized access or data exposure.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Isolate or restrict access to the affected application
steps.desc: Network-isolate the application/host or restrict access pending remediation.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access possible.

steps.title: Remediate the root-cause weakness or migrate off the legacy application
steps.desc: Fix the specific weakness identified, or if not fixable, plan migration off the legacy application.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed or migration initiated.

steps.title: Restore service and verify the weakness is closed
steps.desc: Confirm the application operates normally and the exploited weakness is remediated.
steps.outcome: Service restored securely.

steps.title: Establish a legacy application inventory and risk-review process
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement a periodic risk review process for legacy applications across the portfolio.
steps.outcome: Review process implemented.

ITID-33921.def: Unauthorized access to data hosted in a SaaS platform achieved by exploiting a user- or tenant-level sharing/permission misconfiguration — such as an overly broad 'anyone with the link' share, a public-facing folder, or an incorrectly scoped collaboration setting — rather than a flaw in the SaaS admin console or a malicious third-party integration.
ITID-33921.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to SaaS-hosted data resulting from a misconfigured sharing or permission setting within the SaaS platform itself.
scopeIncludes: Files/folders shared with 'anyone with the link' or public access when internal-only sharing was intended
Overly permissive default sharing settings applied at document/folder creation
External collaborator access retained long after the collaboration's legitimate purpose ended
scopeExcludes: Malicious third-party marketplace app/integration abuse (see ITID-33922)
SaaS tenant admin console misconfiguration (e.g., global security settings) rather than individual document/folder sharing (see ITID-33923)
ITID-33921.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of the shared content and its discoverability.
ITID-33921.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if highly sensitive data was publicly discoverable/indexed.
ITID-33921.escalation: Escalate to the data/SaaS platform owner for immediate access restriction; escalate further if evidence of external access/download by an unauthorized party is found.
indicators: CASB/DLP findings of files shared externally or publicly beyond policy
Search engine indexing of a publicly shared SaaS document
Sharing audit logs showing broad-access grants inconsistent with data sensitivity classification
vectors: Search engine discovery of publicly link-shared sensitive documents
Exploitation of an overly broad share by a former collaborator or unrelated third party who obtained the link
rootCauses: SaaS platform default sharing settings not restricted to internal-only by policy
No CASB/DLP monitoring for external/public sharing of sensitive content
No periodic review/expiration of external collaborator access
controls: Default-restrictive sharing settings enforced tenant-wide
CASB/DLP monitoring and alerting for external/public sharing of sensitive content
Periodic review and expiration of external sharing links/collaborator access
ITID-33921.detection: Strong; CASB and native SaaS sharing audit tools provide direct visibility into over-shared content.
ITID-33921.response: Restrict the sharing setting immediately, assess who accessed the content while overexposed, and notify affected parties if sensitive data was exposed.
metrics: Number of over-shared SaaS content items identified per audit cycle
Time to remediate upon discovery
ITID-33921.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33923 by scope: individual document/folder sharing settings rather than tenant-wide admin console configuration.

playbook.name: SaaS Platform Misconfigured Sharing/Permission Setting Exploited
playbook.description: A SaaS application's sharing or permission setting (e.g., 'anyone with the link', overly broad external sharing default) is misconfigured, exposing data to unauthorized parties.

steps.title: Confirm the misconfigured sharing setting and inventory exposed content
steps.desc: Review the SaaS platform's admin console/sharing audit report to confirm the misconfiguration and catalog what documents/data are exposed and to whom.
steps.guidance: Use the SaaS provider's external-sharing audit report (e.g., Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Box sharing reports) rather than manual spot-checks.
steps.outcome: Confirmed misconfiguration and full inventory of exposed content.

steps.title: Review access logs for evidence of unauthorized viewing/download
steps.desc: Check the SaaS platform's activity logs for external/unauthorized access to the exposed content.
steps.outcome: Documented access history.

steps.title: Correct the sharing setting and revoke unauthorized access links
steps.desc: Change the sharing configuration to restrict access appropriately and revoke/expire any public or overly-broad sharing links.
steps.outcome: Content no longer publicly/externally accessible.

steps.title: Audit for other content with the same sharing misconfiguration
steps.desc: Scan the tenant for other documents/data with the same overly-broad sharing setting.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope limited or additional exposures remediated.

steps.title: Tighten the tenant's default external-sharing policy
steps.desc: Change the tenant-wide default sharing policy to a more restrictive setting (e.g., internal-only by default, external sharing requires explicit approval).
steps.outcome: Default policy prevents recurrence of similarly broad sharing.

steps.title: Verify remediation and notify affected data owners if required
steps.desc: Confirm the exposure is closed and notify data owners/affected parties per policy if sensitive data was exposed.
steps.outcome: Remediation verified and notifications completed.

steps.title: Deploy continuous SaaS sharing-configuration monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy continuous CASB/SaaS security posture monitoring to detect risky sharing configurations proactively.
steps.outcome: Monitoring implemented.

ITID-33922.def: Unauthorized access to SaaS-hosted data achieved through a third-party marketplace application or integration that was installed/authorized within the SaaS platform and subsequently abused to read, modify, or exfiltrate data beyond its legitimate purpose.
ITID-33922.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from a malicious or overly permissive third-party marketplace application/integration connected to a SaaS platform.
scopeIncludes: Malicious marketplace apps installed by users granting broad data access to the SaaS platform
Legitimate third-party integrations later compromised and used to access connected SaaS data
Excessive-scope app installations approved without security review
scopeExcludes: OAuth token abuse targeting individual user account access (mailbox/session), tracked under the OAuth Token Abuse Tier-4 group (ITID-33141 series)
Misconfigured native sharing settings with no third-party app involved (see ITID-33921)
ITID-33922.severity: High, since marketplace app integrations often hold broad, standing API access to the SaaS platform's data.
ITID-33922.priority: P1-P2 depending on the scope of data the app can access.
ITID-33922.escalation: Escalate to IAM/SaaS platform admin immediately upon discovery of a malicious or compromised app; revoke org-wide and assess data accessed.
indicators: SaaS marketplace app audit revealing an app with excessive granted scope
API access logs showing an installed app accessing data beyond its stated function
Security advisory or threat intelligence flagging a known-malicious marketplace app
vectors: Malicious apps published to a SaaS marketplace disguised as productivity tools
Compromise of a legitimate third-party vendor's integration credentials
Users installing apps with broad data-access scopes without security review
rootCauses: No admin approval workflow for marketplace app installation
No periodic review of installed third-party app inventory and granted scopes
SaaS platform marketplace vetting relied upon as the sole security control
controls: Admin approval workflow for marketplace app installation
Periodic review and right-sizing of installed third-party app scopes
SaaS security posture management (SSPM) tooling covering third-party app risk
ITID-33922.detection: Moderate; requires SSPM or dedicated third-party app governance tooling, which is not universally deployed.
ITID-33922.response: Revoke the app's access org-wide, audit data accessed under its scope, and notify affected users/data owners.
metrics: Number of malicious/risky marketplace apps identified and revoked
Percentage of installed apps under active security review
ITID-33922.notes: Scope decision: individual-user OAuth consent-phishing and token abuse against a specific mailbox/account is tracked under the OAuth Token Abuse Tier-4 group (ITID-33141 series); this leaf covers platform-level marketplace app risk affecting the broader SaaS tenant.

playbook.name: SaaS Third-Party Marketplace App/Integration Exploited for Data Access
playbook.description: A third-party application installed from a SaaS platform's marketplace (e.g., Slack app, Google Workspace add-on) is exploited or found malicious, exposing tenant data it had been granted access to.

steps.title: Identify the marketplace app and its granted permissions/scopes
steps.desc: Review the SaaS platform's installed-app/integration list to identify the app in question, when it was installed, by whom, and what scopes/permissions it holds.
steps.outcome: Confirmed app identity, installer, and granted scopes.

steps.title: Review the app's actual data access/API activity
steps.desc: Review API/audit logs for what data the app actually accessed and whether that access pattern is abusive or unexpected relative to its stated function.
steps.outcome: Confirmed evidence of exploitation or malicious behavior, or ruled out.
steps.abort: If the app's activity is fully consistent with its legitimate function and scope, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Uninstall/revoke the third-party app's access tenant-wide
steps.desc: Remove the app's installation and revoke its OAuth tokens/API access across the entire tenant.
steps.outcome: App no longer has any access to tenant data.

steps.title: Rotate any credentials/data exposed to the app
steps.desc: Rotate any credentials or sensitive data the app had access to during its installation period.
steps.outcome: Exposure window closed with no reusable secrets remaining.

steps.title: Implement marketplace app approval/allowlisting policy
steps.desc: Require admin review and approval before any third-party marketplace app can be installed tenant-wide, closing the gap that allowed unreviewed installation.
steps.outcome: Approval workflow implemented.

steps.title: Verify tenant data integrity and evaluate a vetted replacement if needed
steps.desc: Confirm no lingering access remains and, if the app provided a legitimate function, help the business find/approve a vetted replacement.
steps.outcome: Business function restored securely if needed.

steps.title: Audit all existing marketplace app installations tenant-wide
steps.desc: Document the incident and audit all currently-installed third-party marketplace apps for excessive scope or suspicious behavior.
steps.outcome: Audit completed and findings remediated.

ITID-33923.def: Unauthorized access to a SaaS platform's data or functionality achieved by exploiting a tenant-wide administrative console misconfiguration — such as an overly permissive global security policy, a disabled security feature, or an incorrectly scoped administrative role — affecting the entire tenant rather than a single document or a specific third-party integration.
ITID-33923.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from a misconfiguration in a SaaS platform's tenant-wide administrative console settings, rather than individual document sharing or third-party app abuse.
scopeIncludes: Global sharing/security policy misconfigured to allow broader access than intended across the entire tenant
SaaS admin console security features (e.g., conditional access, DLP, MFA enforcement) left disabled or improperly scoped
Overly broad tenant administrative role grants to non-admin users
scopeExcludes: An individual document/folder sharing setting misconfigured at the user level (see ITID-33921)
A malicious or over-scoped third-party marketplace app (see ITID-33922)
ITID-33923.severity: High-Critical, since tenant-wide misconfigurations affect the entire organization's SaaS footprint rather than a single item.
ITID-33923.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the tenant-wide blast radius.
ITID-33923.escalation: Escalate to SaaS platform administrators and security engineering immediately; assess org-wide impact of the misconfigured setting.
indicators: SSPM/CSPM findings of tenant-wide SaaS security settings deviating from baseline
Security configuration audit revealing disabled MFA enforcement, DLP, or conditional access at the tenant level
Multiple users/documents affected by the same underlying tenant-wide setting
vectors: Exploitation of a tenant-wide security feature left disabled during initial SaaS platform setup
Abuse of an overly broad administrative role grant to access tenant-wide settings and data
rootCauses: No SaaS security posture management (SSPM) baseline/drift detection for tenant configuration
SaaS platform deployed with default (often permissive) settings never hardened
Administrative role grants not reviewed or right-sized periodically
controls: SaaS security posture management (SSPM) with configuration baseline and drift detection
Formal SaaS tenant hardening checklist at deployment
Periodic administrative role review and right-sizing
ITID-33923.detection: Strong; SSPM tooling provides direct, continuous visibility into tenant-wide configuration drift.
ITID-33923.response: Correct the tenant-wide misconfiguration immediately, audit for data accessed while exposed, and add the setting to the hardening baseline to prevent recurrence.
metrics: Number of tenant-wide SaaS misconfigurations identified per scan cycle
Time to remediate upon discovery
ITID-33923.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33921 by scope: tenant-wide administrative configuration rather than an individual document/folder sharing setting.

playbook.name: SaaS Admin Console Misconfiguration Exploited
playbook.description: A misconfiguration in a SaaS platform's tenant administration console (e.g., overly permissive admin role assignment, disabled security feature) is exploited to gain unauthorized administrative access or capability.

steps.title: Identify the admin console misconfiguration and how it was exploited
steps.desc: Review the tenant's admin role assignments and security settings to confirm the misconfiguration (e.g., excess users with Global Admin, disabled conditional access, MFA not enforced for admins) and how it was exploited.
steps.outcome: Confirmed misconfiguration and exploitation method.
steps.tool: SaaS admin console / secure score tool

steps.title: Determine what administrative actions were taken during exploitation
steps.desc: Review admin audit logs for changes made using the exploited administrative access.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of administrative actions taken.

steps.title: Revoke the exploited admin access and reset affected admin credentials
steps.desc: Remove unauthorized administrative role assignments and force credential/session reset for the affected admin account(s).
steps.outcome: Unauthorized administrative access terminated.

steps.title: Revert unauthorized administrative changes
steps.desc: Identify and revert any tenant configuration changes made using the exploited access (e.g., disabled security features, new admin accounts created).
steps.outcome: Tenant configuration restored to a known-good state.

steps.title: Fix the root-cause misconfiguration and enforce least-privilege admin roles
steps.desc: Correct the specific misconfiguration and apply least-privilege, role-based administrative access with MFA enforced for all admin accounts.
steps.outcome: Tenant hardened against recurrence.

steps.title: Verify tenant security posture and restore normal administration
steps.desc: Confirm the tenant's security configuration meets baseline standards and normal administrative operations resume securely.
steps.outcome: Tenant restored under verified hardened configuration.

steps.title: Implement continuous SaaS security posture monitoring for admin settings
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy continuous monitoring (e.g., secure score, SSPM tooling) for tenant admin configuration drift.
steps.outcome: Monitoring implemented.

ITID-33924.def: Unauthorized access to a SaaS platform's data or functionality, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific SaaS Application Exploitation sibling.
ITID-33924.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for SaaS application exploitation cases that do not clearly fit sharing misconfiguration, third-party marketplace abuse, or tenant admin console misconfiguration classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered SaaS exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific mechanism used
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33921, ITID-33922, or ITID-33923 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33924.severity: Assess per incident; default High pending clarification.
ITID-33924.priority: P1-P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33924.escalation: Escalate to SaaS platform administrators for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed SaaS-related unauthorized access not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific mechanism
controls: SaaS security posture management (SSPM)
ITID-33924.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33924.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
ITID-33924.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SaaS Application Exploitation
playbook.description: A SaaS application is exploited in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access to tenant data or functionality.

steps.title: Confirm the SaaS exploitation and identify the specific gap
steps.desc: Review SaaS admin console and activity logs to confirm the exploitation and identify the specific gap exploited (sharing, integration, admin config, or other).
steps.outcome: Confirmed exploitation and specific gap.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized access/data exposure
steps.desc: Review logs for the extent of unauthorized access resulting from the exploitation.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Revoke the exploited access path
steps.desc: Revoke the specific access, session, or integration that enabled the exploitation.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Fix the root-cause SaaS configuration gap
steps.desc: Remediate the specific gap identified with a durable configuration or policy fix.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Verify remediation and restore legitimate access
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate users retain necessary access and the exploited gap is closed.
steps.outcome: Access restored securely.

steps.title: Implement SaaS security posture management (SSPM) monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy or expand SSPM tooling to catch similar SaaS misconfigurations proactively.
steps.outcome: Monitoring implemented.

ITID-33931.def: Unauthorized access to corporate data occurring because employees stored or shared it via a cloud storage or file-sharing service that was never sanctioned, reviewed, or secured by IT/security, placing the data outside all corporate access controls, monitoring, and DLP coverage.
ITID-33931.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to corporate data placed in an unsanctioned cloud storage or file-sharing service outside IT/security's visibility and control.
scopeIncludes: Corporate files uploaded to a personal or unsanctioned cloud storage service (e.g., a personal Dropbox/Google Drive account) later found compromised or misconfigured
Team use of an unapproved file-sharing tool for business collaboration outside IT visibility
Data breach of the unsanctioned service exposing corporate data stored there
scopeExcludes: Unsanctioned SaaS productivity/business tools not primarily used for file storage (see ITID-33932)
Personal email/messaging accounts used for business data (see ITID-33933)
ITID-33931.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of data placed in the unsanctioned service.
ITID-33931.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the unsanctioned service is confirmed breached or the data is highly sensitive.
ITID-33931.escalation: Escalate to security and data governance upon discovery; assess exposure scope and migrate data to a sanctioned, monitored platform.
indicators: CASB discovery of unsanctioned cloud storage service usage carrying corporate data
Breach notification from an unsanctioned third-party service naming a corporate user/data
DLP findings of corporate data being uploaded to unrecognized cloud storage domains
vectors: Compromise of the unsanctioned service itself (outside corporate control) exposing stored corporate data
Employees bypassing sanctioned tools due to convenience or unmet business needs
rootCauses: No CASB/shadow IT discovery program to identify unsanctioned cloud service usage
Sanctioned tools not meeting a genuine business need, driving shadow IT adoption
No DLP policy blocking corporate data upload to unrecognized cloud domains
mitreTechniques: T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account
controls: CASB/shadow IT discovery and governance program
DLP policies blocking or flagging corporate data uploads to unsanctioned cloud domains
Regular review of sanctioned tool adequacy to reduce shadow IT drivers
ITID-33931.detection: Moderate; CASB shadow IT discovery tooling provides good visibility where deployed, but coverage gaps exist for services accessed outside monitored networks.
ITID-33931.response: Migrate the data to a sanctioned platform, assess exposure if the unsanctioned service was breached, and address the underlying business need driving shadow IT use.
metrics: Number of unsanctioned cloud storage services discovered carrying corporate data
Volume of corporate data identified in shadow IT services
sops: Shadow IT Discovery and Governance SOP
ITID-33931.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33932/ITID-33933 by service type: cloud storage/file-sharing specifically, rather than general SaaS tools or personal email/messaging.

playbook.name: Unsanctioned Cloud Storage/File-Sharing Service Exploited
playbook.description: An employee uses an unapproved, unmanaged cloud storage/file-sharing service to handle corporate data, and that service is subsequently compromised or misconfigured, exposing the data.

steps.title: Identify the unsanctioned service and what corporate data it holds
steps.desc: Confirm via CASB/DLP shadow-IT discovery which unsanctioned service is in use, by whom, and what corporate data was uploaded to it.
steps.guidance: CASB shadow-IT discovery reports are typically the fastest path to identifying the service and usage volume.
steps.outcome: Confirmed service, users, and data inventory.

steps.title: Determine the nature and scope of the exposure/compromise
steps.desc: Investigate what happened to the data on the unsanctioned service (breach of the service itself, misconfigured public sharing, etc.) and the scope of exposure.
steps.outcome: Documented nature and scope of exposure.

steps.title: Block access to the unsanctioned service and retrieve/remove corporate data
steps.desc: Block the service at the web proxy/CASB and work with the user to retrieve and delete the corporate data from the unsanctioned account.
steps.outcome: Corporate data removed from the unsanctioned service and further use blocked.

steps.title: Provide an approved, managed alternative for the legitimate business need
steps.desc: Identify the underlying business need that drove use of the shadow-IT service and provision an approved, managed alternative.
steps.outcome: Users have a sanctioned tool meeting their legitimate need.

steps.title: Assess breach-notification obligations and confirm remediation
steps.desc: Consult legal/compliance on notification obligations given the data exposure and confirm the unsanctioned service is no longer in use for corporate data.
steps.outcome: Notifications handled per policy and remediation confirmed.

steps.title: Expand CASB shadow-IT monitoring and communicate approved-tool guidance
steps.desc: Document the incident and expand continuous shadow-IT discovery monitoring plus communicate clear guidance on approved data-handling tools.
steps.outcome: Monitoring expanded and guidance communicated.

ITID-33932.def: Unauthorized access to or exposure of corporate data occurring because a team or individual adopted a SaaS tool (e.g., a project management, communication, or productivity application) for business use without security review, leaving the tool's security configuration, data handling, and vendor risk entirely unassessed.
ITID-33932.purpose: Captures unauthorized access resulting from an unsanctioned SaaS tool used for business purposes that was never reviewed by security.
scopeIncludes: Business use of an unreviewed SaaS productivity/collaboration tool storing or processing corporate data
Security incidents at the unreviewed vendor exposing corporate data processed through the tool
Team adoption of a SaaS tool bypassing procurement/security review processes
scopeExcludes: Unsanctioned cloud storage/file-sharing services specifically (see ITID-33931)
Personal email/messaging accounts used for business data (see ITID-33933)
ITID-33932.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of data processed by the unreviewed tool and the vendor's own security posture.
ITID-33932.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the tool is confirmed to have suffered a security incident or handles highly sensitive data.
ITID-33932.escalation: Escalate to security/procurement for retroactive vendor risk assessment; migrate to a sanctioned alternative if material risk is identified.
indicators: CASB/shadow IT discovery identifying an unreviewed SaaS tool in active business use
Vendor breach notification naming the organization as an affected customer for a tool never through security review
Expense report or procurement audit revealing SaaS subscriptions with no security sign-off
vectors: Compromise of the unreviewed vendor's own infrastructure, exposing customer (corporate) data
Weak security controls at the unreviewed vendor (e.g., no MFA, weak encryption) exploited by an external attacker
rootCauses: No enforced SaaS procurement/security review gate before tool adoption
Business units adopting tools independently of centralized IT/security oversight
No ongoing shadow IT discovery to catch unreviewed tools already in use
controls: Mandatory security review gate in SaaS procurement process
CASB/shadow IT discovery program to identify tools already in use without review
Vendor risk assessment program covering third-party SaaS security posture
ITID-33932.detection: Moderate; dependent on shadow IT discovery tooling and procurement process visibility.
ITID-33932.response: Conduct retroactive vendor risk assessment, migrate to a sanctioned alternative if risk is unacceptable, and tighten the procurement review gate.
metrics: Number of unreviewed SaaS tools discovered in active use
Percentage of SaaS adoptions passing through formal security review
sops: Shadow IT Discovery and Governance SOP
ITID-33932.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33931 by tool type: general SaaS business tools rather than cloud storage/file-sharing specifically.

playbook.name: Unsanctioned SaaS Tool Never Reviewed by Security Exploited
playbook.description: A department adopts a SaaS tool without security review, and a vulnerability or misconfiguration in that tool is subsequently exploited to access corporate data processed by it.

steps.title: Identify the unreviewed SaaS tool and what corporate data/process it handles
steps.desc: Confirm via CASB discovery or business unit interview which unreviewed SaaS tool is in use, its business purpose, and what corporate data flows through it.
steps.outcome: Confirmed tool, business owner, and data flow.

steps.title: Investigate the vulnerability/exploitation and resulting exposure
steps.desc: Determine what vulnerability or misconfiguration in the tool was exploited and the scope of data exposed.
steps.outcome: Documented exploitation details and exposure scope.

steps.title: Restrict or suspend use of the tool pending security review
steps.desc: Block or restrict access to the tool via CASB/web proxy and instruct the business unit to pause use pending a security review.
steps.outcome: No further data exposure via the tool during review.

steps.title: Conduct a retroactive security review of the tool
steps.desc: Perform the vendor/security review that should have occurred before adoption, and either approve the tool with required controls or find an approved alternative.
steps.outcome: Tool either approved with appropriate controls or replaced.

steps.title: Restore business function under an approved, secured tool
steps.desc: Confirm the business unit's function is restored using either the remediated original tool or an approved alternative.
steps.outcome: Business function restored securely.

steps.title: Enforce a mandatory pre-adoption security review process for new SaaS tools
steps.desc: Document the incident and establish/reinforce a mandatory security review gate before any new SaaS tool can be adopted for handling corporate data.
steps.outcome: Review process implemented and communicated.

ITID-33933.def: Unauthorized access to corporate data occurring because an employee conducted business communication or stored business data using a personal email or messaging account outside corporate control, and that personal account was subsequently compromised, exposing the business data it contained.
ITID-33933.purpose: Captures unauthorized exposure resulting from an employee using a personal email or messaging account for business data, which is then compromised.
scopeIncludes: Business emails/documents forwarded to or conducted via a personal email account later breached
Business conversations conducted on personal messaging apps (e.g., personal WhatsApp/Telegram) later compromised
Personal account credential compromise exposing forwarded business correspondence or attachments
scopeExcludes: Use of an unsanctioned cloud storage/file-sharing service (see ITID-33931)
Use of an unsanctioned general SaaS business tool (see ITID-33932)
ITID-33933.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity and volume of business data conducted through the personal account.
ITID-33933.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if sensitive business data (financials, credentials, customer data) was present in the compromised personal account.
ITID-33933.escalation: Escalate to security and, if relevant, HR/legal upon discovery; assess what business data was exposed via the compromised personal account.
indicators: Employee report of a personal account compromise that also contained business correspondence
Evidence in phishing/BEC investigations that business communication routed through a personal account
Data loss prevention findings of business data being forwarded to personal email addresses
vectors: Phishing or credential-stuffing compromise of the employee's personal email/messaging account
Employee habitually forwarding work email/documents to a personal account for convenience
rootCauses: No policy or technical control preventing forwarding of business data to personal accounts
Insufficient user awareness of the risk of conducting business via personal accounts
Business need (e.g., mobile access) not adequately met by sanctioned tools, driving personal-account use
mitreTechniques: T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account
controls: DLP policy blocking/flagging auto-forwarding of business email to personal domains
User awareness training on the risks of conducting business via personal accounts
Ensuring sanctioned mobile-access tools adequately meet legitimate business needs
ITID-33933.detection: Weak-to-moderate; largely relies on the employee's self-report or DLP forwarding-rule detection, since the compromise occurs entirely outside corporate visibility.
ITID-33933.response: Assess what business data was exposed, notify affected parties if sensitive data was involved, and reinforce policy against business use of personal accounts.
metrics: Number of incidents involving business data exposed via a personal account compromise
DLP-flagged auto-forwarding rule incidents to personal domains
sops: Shadow IT Discovery and Governance SOP
detections: DLP auto-forwarding to personal domain alerting
ITID-33933.notes: Differentiated from ITID-33931/ITID-33932 by the specific vector: personal email/messaging account compromise, rather than an unsanctioned cloud storage or SaaS business tool.

playbook.name: Personal Email/Messaging Account Used for Business Data, Then Compromised
playbook.description: An employee uses a personal email or messaging account to handle business data, and that personal account is subsequently compromised, exposing the business data.

steps.title: Confirm the personal account compromise and what business data it held
steps.desc: Confirm the personal email/messaging account was compromised (via user report or breach notification) and determine what business data/communications were stored in or forwarded to it.
steps.guidance: Interview the user regarding the extent of business use of the personal account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed compromise and inventory of exposed business data.

steps.title: Determine if the personal account had any residual access to corporate systems
steps.desc: Check whether the personal account was ever used to receive password resets, MFA codes, or other corporate-account recovery information that could enable further compromise.
steps.outcome: Documented any corporate-account exposure risk stemming from the personal account compromise.

steps.title: Reset any corporate credentials linked to or recoverable via the personal account
steps.desc: Force reset of any corporate account credentials that used the personal account for recovery, and remove the personal account as a recovery method.
steps.outcome: Corporate accounts no longer exposed via the compromised personal account.

steps.title: Assist the user in securing/regaining control of the personal account
steps.desc: Provide guidance or support to help the employee recover and secure their personal account.
steps.outcome: Personal account secured (best-effort, outside corporate control).

steps.title: Enforce policy prohibiting personal account use for business data
steps.desc: Reinforce and technically enforce (where possible, e.g., DLP blocking business data sent to personal email domains) the policy against using personal accounts for business communications/data.
steps.outcome: Policy reinforced and technical control applied where feasible.

steps.title: Assess breach-notification obligations for the exposed business data
steps.desc: Consult legal/compliance to determine notification obligations based on the sensitivity of the business data exposed via the personal account.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations assessed and handled.

steps.title: Reinforce acceptable-use training and DLP coverage for personal accounts
steps.desc: Document the incident and reinforce acceptable-use training plus expand DLP coverage to detect business data being sent to personal email/messaging domains.
steps.outcome: Training and DLP coverage updated.

ITID-33934.def: Unauthorized access or data exposure arising from use of an unsanctioned technology outside IT/security's visibility, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Shadow IT Exploits sibling.
ITID-33934.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for shadow IT exploitation cases that do not clearly fit unsanctioned cloud storage, unreviewed SaaS tool, or personal email/messaging classification.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered shadow IT exploitation patterns pending triage
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish the specific unsanctioned tool/service category
scopeExcludes: Any case classifiable into ITID-33931, ITID-33932, or ITID-33933 once evidence is sufficient
ITID-33934.severity: Assess per incident; default Medium-High pending clarification.
ITID-33934.priority: P2 pending triage; reclassify and adjust once root cause is determined.
ITID-33934.escalation: Escalate to security/shadow IT governance for triage; reclassify to a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Any confirmed shadow IT related exposure not yet attributable to a specific tool category
vectors: Varies — placeholder pending classification
rootCauses: Insufficient initial telemetry to determine the specific tool category
controls: Shadow IT discovery and governance program
ITID-33934.detection: Varies; this bucket exists because initial detection lacks fidelity to classify further.
ITID-33934.response: Triage promptly and reclassify into a specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents logged here pending reclassification
sops: Shadow IT Discovery and Governance SOP
ITID-33934.notes: Intake/catch-all leaf, not a terminal classification.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Shadow IT Exploit
playbook.description: An unsanctioned, unreviewed IT tool or service is exploited in a manner not otherwise classified to gain unauthorized access to corporate data.

steps.title: Identify the shadow-IT tool/service and how it was exploited
steps.desc: Confirm via CASB discovery or user report which unsanctioned tool is involved and how it was exploited to expose corporate data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed tool and exploitation details.

steps.title: Determine scope of corporate data exposure
steps.desc: Review what corporate data was exposed via the unsanctioned tool.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Block or restrict the unsanctioned tool and remove corporate data
steps.desc: Block access to the tool and work to remove/retrieve corporate data stored within it.
steps.outcome: No further exposure via the tool.

steps.title: Provide an approved alternative and enforce shadow-IT policy
steps.desc: Identify the legitimate business need and provide an approved, reviewed alternative, and reinforce policy against unsanctioned tool adoption.
steps.outcome: Legitimate need met securely; policy reinforced.

steps.title: Confirm remediation and assess notification obligations
steps.desc: Confirm the exposure is remediated and consult legal/compliance on any required notifications.
steps.outcome: Remediation confirmed and notifications handled if required.

steps.title: Expand shadow-IT discovery and governance program
steps.desc: Document the incident and expand the organization's shadow-IT discovery and governance program to reduce recurrence.
steps.outcome: Program expanded.

ITID-34111.def: Exfiltration of data from a compromised device to an attacker-controlled server over an encrypted (typically TLS/HTTPS) command-and-control channel that mimics legitimate web traffic patterns, ports, and often legitimate-looking domains or CDN fronting to avoid standing out to network defenders.
ITID-34111.purpose: Captures data theft carried out over a malware C2 channel that is deliberately dressed up as ordinary encrypted web traffic so it blends into the noise of normal outbound HTTPS.
scopeIncludes: Malware pushing stolen data out over its existing HTTPS-based C2 beacon
Use of domain fronting or a CDN to hide the true destination of exfiltrated data
Exfiltration piggybacking on a standard TLS session that also carries C2 tasking traffic
scopeExcludes: Exfiltration via a named third-party SaaS API such as a chat app webhook (see Encrypted Messaging App API Abuse)
Exfiltration over a bespoke, non-standard encrypted tunneling protocol built by the attacker (see Custom Encrypted Tunneling Protocol)
DNS-based tunneling (a distinct sibling group)
ITID-34111.severity: High. This indicates a fully established C2 foothold with active data loss, not just reconnaissance.
