ITID-34111.priority: P1 for confirmed data-bearing beacons on sensitive hosts; P2 while volume/content is still being scoped.
ITID-34111.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR/SOC leadership and notify data owners once the destination and approximate volume are known; loop in legal/privacy if regulated data is suspected.
indicators: TLS beacon to a rare or newly-registered domain with regular interval/jitter pattern
Outbound data volume asymmetry (upload >> download) on an otherwise low-traffic host
JA3/JA3S fingerprint mismatch against the claimed browser/user agent
SNI/domain-fronting mismatch between TLS SNI and HTTP Host header
vectors: Malware implant with a hardcoded or DGA-resolved HTTPS C2 endpoint
Living-off-the-land use of curl/PowerShell/Invoke-WebRequest to POST data to attacker infrastructure
CDN or domain-fronting abuse to disguise true C2 destination
rootCauses: No TLS inspection/decryption on egress for endpoint traffic
Absence of network-level anomaly detection (beaconing/volume baselines)
Overly permissive outbound firewall rules to all HTTPS destinations
mitreTechniques: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: TLS interception/inspection at egress
Network beaconing/anomaly detection (NDR)
Egress allow-listing by destination category
DLP/CASB inspection of decrypted outbound traffic
ITID-34111.detection: Strong when TLS inspection or NDR beaconing analytics are deployed; weak to none in pure metadata-only network monitoring where payload volume is the only visible signal.
ITID-34111.response: Isolate the host, capture full packet/flow data for the session, identify the C2 destination and block it network-wide, and determine what data left before containment.
metrics: Mean time to detect beaconing exfil
Volume of data confirmed exfiltrated per incident
Percentage of egress traffic covered by TLS inspection
ITID-34111.notes: Scoped strictly to standard encrypted web-protocol C2 channels; named SaaS API abuse and custom/proprietary tunneling protocols are split into sibling ITIDs so investigators pick the leaf matching the actual channel mechanism.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Encrypted C2 Channel Disguised as Normal HTTPS Traffic
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration over an encrypted command-and-control channel that mimics legitimate HTTPS traffic (e.g. domain fronting, JA3/TLS fingerprint mismatch, beaconing to a look-alike domain).

steps.title: Confirm the beaconing/C2 pattern in network traffic
steps.desc: Review proxy, firewall, and TLS inspection/JA3 logs for the affected host for periodic beaconing, TLS certificate mismatches, SNI/Host header mismatches, or connections to a domain with no legitimate business purpose.
steps.guidance: Compare observed JA3/JA3S fingerprints and certificate issuers against known-good baselines for the claimed destination.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 channel with destination IP/domain and beacon interval identified.
steps.abort: If traffic matches an approved third-party service and no other indicators are present, downgrade and route to standard change review.

steps.title: Determine what data left via the channel
steps.desc: Correlate outbound byte counts and timing on the C2 connection against endpoint file-access and process logs to estimate what was staged and sent.
steps.outcome: Estimated scope of exfiltrated data and affected systems.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host from the network
steps.desc: Move the host to a quarantine VLAN or apply EDR network isolation to stop further outbound traffic while preserving the host for forensics.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; C2 traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination and associated fronting domains
steps.desc: Add the confirmed destination IP/domain and any related fronting infrastructure to firewall, proxy, and DNS blocklists organization-wide.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked for all hosts.

steps.title: Search for the same C2 indicators across the fleet
steps.desc: Sweep proxy and EDR telemetry organization-wide for the same JA3 fingerprint, destination, or beacon pattern on other hosts.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed as single host or additional infected hosts identified and contained.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Identify and remove the malware or agent generating the C2 traffic along with any persistence (scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys).
steps.outcome: Host confirmed free of the implant.

steps.title: Determine and close the initial access vector
steps.desc: Identify how the implant was delivered (phishing, exploit, supply chain) and remediate the underlying weakness.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Rebuild and restore the host, then monitor closely
steps.desc: Reimage the host from known-good media, restore data from clean backups, and place it under heightened network monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored to service with no recurrence of C2 traffic.

steps.title: Document the incident and improve detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the C2 technique, indicators of compromise, and detection gaps; update TLS inspection or JA3-based detection rules if the channel evaded existing controls.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and detection improvements tracked.

ITID-34112.def: Data theft in which stolen data is sent from a compromised device to an attacker-controlled channel/bot hosted on a legitimate, widely-trusted SaaS messaging platform, using that platform's own API/webhook mechanism as both the transport and the destination.
ITID-34112.purpose: Captures exfiltration that abuses a legitimate, named third-party messaging or collaboration platform's API (Telegram bots, Discord webhooks, Slack incoming webhooks) as the covert transport.
scopeIncludes: Malware posting stolen files/credentials to a Telegram bot via the Telegram Bot API
Beaconing/exfil to a Discord webhook URL
Use of a Slack incoming webhook or bot token to relay stolen data
scopeExcludes: Generic encrypted HTTPS C2 not tied to a named consumer SaaS platform (see Encrypted C2 Channel Disguised as Normal HTTPS Traffic)
Legitimate corporate cloud storage/file-sync abuse (see Cloud Storage Uploads group)
ITID-34112.severity: High, since these platforms are rarely blocked and confirm an active, likely automated exfil pipeline.
ITID-34112.priority: P1 once a live bot/webhook token receiving data is identified; P2 during initial triage.
ITID-34112.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; involve threat intel to see if the bot/channel is a known commodity malware family's exfil infrastructure.
indicators: Outbound connections to api.telegram.org, discord.com/api/webhooks, or hooks.slack.com from unexpected processes
Process making repeated small POST requests to a chat-platform API endpoint
Presence of a hardcoded bot token or webhook URL in malware strings/memory
vectors: Commodity infostealer malware configured with a Telegram/Discord exfil channel
Malicious script using a webhook URL as a drop-off point for scraped credentials or files
rootCauses: Consumer messaging/collaboration domains not blocked or monitored at the network egress layer
Lack of process-to-destination correlation in EDR telemetry
controls: Category-based web/egress filtering of consumer messaging platforms from server/workstation subnets
EDR process-network correlation alerting
Threat-intel indicator blocking for known bot/webhook infrastructure
ITID-34112.detection: Good where EDR correlates process identity with destination domain; weak in pure firewall-log environments since traffic is legitimate TLS to a trusted domain.
ITID-34112.response: Block the specific bot token/webhook and the platform API domain if policy allows, identify all hosts that communicated with it, and scope data sent via chat history/API logs if obtainable.
metrics: Count of detections involving SaaS-platform API abuse per quarter
Time to identify and revoke abused bot/webhook credentials
detections: EDR process-to-destination correlation for chat-platform APIs
ITID-34112.notes: Distinguished from generic HTTPS C2 by the use of a specifically named, legitimate SaaS messaging API as the channel; this is the differentiator that keeps it from overlapping with ITID-34111.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Encrypted Messaging App API (Telegram/Discord/Slack Webhook Abuse)
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where malware or an insider abuses a messaging platform's bot/webhook API (e.g. Telegram Bot API, Discord webhook) as a covert, encrypted exfiltration channel.

steps.title: Confirm outbound traffic to the messaging platform API
steps.desc: Review proxy/firewall logs for connections to Telegram, Discord, or Slack API endpoints from hosts with no legitimate business use of that platform, and correlate with process execution on the host.
steps.guidance: Identify the specific bot token or webhook URL if visible in traffic or host artifacts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed abuse of the messaging API as an exfiltration channel, with bot/webhook identifier captured.
steps.abort: If the platform is an approved business tool for that user, treat as a policy question rather than an incident.

steps.title: Estimate data sent via the channel
steps.desc: Review outbound payload sizes and message/file-send timestamps to estimate volume and type of data transferred through the bot or webhook.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate of exfiltrated data.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating traffic to the bot/webhook endpoint.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; exfiltration channel stopped.

steps.title: Revoke the bot token/webhook and block the platform endpoint if needed
steps.desc: Request the messaging platform (or the internal admin of the workspace/bot) revoke the specific bot token or webhook; if the platform itself is not needed for business use, block its API domains at the proxy.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with IT to avoid disrupting legitimate use of the platform elsewhere in the organization.
steps.outcome: Bot/webhook access revoked; channel no longer usable.

steps.title: Remove the malware or script using the API
steps.desc: Locate and remove the malware, script, or unauthorized application making the API calls, along with any persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean of the exfiltration tool.

steps.title: Sweep for the same technique on other hosts
steps.desc: Search proxy logs fleet-wide for connections to the same bot token, webhook URL, or API pattern.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; additional affected hosts remediated if found.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor outbound API traffic
steps.desc: Restore the host to a known-good state and monitor proxy logs for renewed attempts to reach messaging platform APIs.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and assess proxy category coverage
steps.desc: Record the technique and evaluate whether messaging/collaboration API categories need proxy visibility or blocking policy changes.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34113.def: Exfiltration over a custom-built encrypted tunnel or protocol (proprietary encryption, non-standard port/framing, or an encrypted wrapper around another protocol) designed specifically to evade signature- and protocol-based network detection.
ITID-34113.purpose: Captures the more sophisticated case where an attacker builds and uses a bespoke, non-standard encrypted tunneling protocol rather than piggybacking on standard HTTPS or a named SaaS API.
scopeIncludes: Custom encryption layered over TCP/UDP on a non-standard port
Attacker-built VPN-like tunneling tool used purely for exfil
Protocol tunneling that wraps exfil traffic inside another allowed protocol (e.g., encrypted payload inside ICMP or a custom SSH-tunneled channel)
scopeExcludes: Standard TLS/HTTPS C2 exfil (see Encrypted C2 Channel Disguised as Normal HTTPS Traffic)
Use of a named public SaaS API as the channel (see Encrypted Messaging App API Abuse)
DNS-based tunneling (a distinct sibling group under Network-Based Exfiltration)
ITID-34113.severity: High to Critical — custom tooling generally signals a more capable, targeted adversary.
ITID-34113.priority: P1 on confirmation; treat as a targeted-actor indicator warranting broader threat-hunt scope.
ITID-34113.escalation: Escalate to IR leadership and threat intel immediately; a custom protocol strongly suggests advanced/targeted actor involvement rather than commodity malware.
indicators: Non-standard port usage with high-entropy payload not matching any known protocol signature
Persistent long-lived connection with encrypted, unclassifiable traffic pattern
Protocol anomalies flagged by deep packet inspection unable to identify the application layer
vectors: Custom malware implant with proprietary C2/exfil protocol
Protocol tunneling tool used to smuggle exfil traffic inside an allowed protocol
rootCauses: Network monitoring reliant solely on known-protocol signatures
Insufficient anomaly-based (vs. signature-based) network detection
Overly broad outbound port/protocol allow rules
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: Anomaly-based NDR/deep packet inspection
Default-deny egress with strict port/protocol allow-listing
Full packet capture retention for forensic replay
ITID-34113.detection: Limited to anomaly-based network detection; signature-based tools will typically miss this entirely, which is the core investigative challenge.
ITID-34113.response: Full packet capture and forensic protocol analysis are typically required to characterize the channel; isolate affected hosts and hunt for the same protocol fingerprint elsewhere on the network.
metrics: Time to characterize an unknown protocol
Number of hosts found using the same custom channel during hunt
ITID-34113.notes: Reserved for genuinely custom/proprietary protocols; if the traffic is standard TLS or a recognizable public SaaS API, route to ITID-34111 or ITID-34112 instead.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Custom Encrypted Tunneling Protocol
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration over a custom or non-standard encrypted tunneling protocol built by the threat actor, not matching known commodity C2 or VPN tooling.

steps.title: Characterize the unknown protocol traffic
steps.desc: Capture and analyze packet captures for the connection to determine port, handshake pattern, and traffic shape; confirm it does not match a known legitimate protocol or approved encrypted service.
steps.guidance: Use protocol analysis tooling and, where safe, static/dynamic analysis of any binary generating the traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed custom tunnel with source host, destination, and traffic characteristics documented.
steps.abort: If the traffic is later matched to an approved internal tool, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate data volume and duration
steps.desc: Review historical flow data (NetFlow/packet captures) to determine when the tunnel began and estimate the volume of data transferred.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the custom tunnel traffic.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; tunnel traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination and associated infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the destination IP/port and any related infrastructure identified through passive DNS or threat intelligence pivoting at the firewall.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Reverse-engineer and remove the tunneling client
steps.desc: Identify the binary or script implementing the custom protocol, determine its persistence mechanism, and remove it from the host.
steps.guidance: Preserve a sample for malware analysis and threat intelligence sharing before removal.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean; sample preserved for analysis.

steps.title: Sweep the environment for the same custom protocol signature
steps.desc: Develop a network or host-based signature from the analyzed traffic/binary and sweep other systems for matches.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional hosts remediated.

steps.title: Rebuild the host and monitor for reappearance
steps.desc: Reimage the affected host and monitor closely for reappearance of the custom protocol traffic pattern.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the technique and update detection signatures
steps.desc: Record the custom protocol's characteristics and add detection signatures to network monitoring tooling.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection signature deployed.

ITID-34114.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred over an encrypted network channel, where the specific mechanism (standard HTTPS C2, SaaS API abuse, or custom protocol) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34114.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for encrypted-channel network exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the exact encrypted channel type is confirmed
Cases where evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the sibling encrypted-channel ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific channel mechanism has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34111, ITID-34112, or ITID-34113
Unencrypted or plaintext exfiltration channels
ITID-34114.severity: Set provisionally based on volume/sensitivity of data suspected; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34114.priority: P2 pending triage; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
ITID-34114.escalation: Escalate as for any active exfiltration pending; do not let unclassified status delay containment actions.
indicators: Encrypted outbound traffic anomaly without a confirmed protocol/destination classification
Alert fired from a broad DLP or NDR rule not tied to a specific technique
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient telemetry to fingerprint the channel at detection time
controls: General network egress monitoring
DLP alerting on encrypted-channel anomalies
ITID-34114.detection: Variable; this bucket exists precisely because coverage/classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34114.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified encrypted-channel exfil incidents
ITID-34114.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification into a specific sibling ITID.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Encrypted Channel Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration over an encrypted network channel that does not fit a more specific encrypted-channel category (C2-as-HTTPS, messaging API abuse, or custom tunneling protocol).

steps.title: Confirm the encrypted exfiltration channel
steps.desc: Review network traffic logs (proxy, firewall, NetFlow) for the affected host to identify the encrypted connection carrying the suspected exfiltration and classify its type as specifically as possible.
steps.guidance: If the channel can be matched to a more specific category during investigation, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration channel with destination and traffic characteristics documented.
steps.abort: If no exfiltration is confirmed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate data volume and scope
steps.desc: Correlate outbound traffic volume with endpoint file-access logs to estimate what data was affected and over what time period.
steps.outcome: Scope and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the encrypted exfiltration traffic.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination at the network perimeter
steps.desc: Add the destination IP/domain to firewall and proxy blocklists.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify and remove the exfiltration mechanism
steps.desc: Determine whether the channel was driven by malware, a misused legitimate tool, or manual user action, and remove or disable it accordingly.
steps.outcome: Exfiltration mechanism neutralized.

steps.title: Sweep for the same channel or indicators on other hosts
steps.desc: Search network and endpoint telemetry fleet-wide for the same encrypted-channel destination or indicators to confirm whether other hosts are affected.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Restore the host to a known-good state and monitor network traffic for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification and reference the appropriate specific playbook for future occurrences.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34121.def: Exfiltration in which data is chunked and encoded into DNS TXT record queries or responses exchanged with an attacker-controlled authoritative DNS server, exploiting the fact that DNS is almost universally allowed to egress.
ITID-34121.purpose: Captures DNS-tunneling exfiltration that specifically encodes stolen data inside DNS TXT record responses/queries.
scopeIncludes: Malware/tooling encoding stolen data as TXT record query strings sent to attacker-controlled DNS infrastructure
Use of TXT record responses to relay data or commands as part of the same tunnel
scopeExcludes: Exfiltration encoded purely in subdomain labels of A/AAAA queries (see DNS Subdomain Label Encoding Exfiltration)
Use of a named commodity DNS tunneling tool where the record type is incidental to the tool's design (see Commodity Tunneling Tool)
ITID-34121.severity: High — successful DNS tunneling indicates other egress controls have already failed or been bypassed.
ITID-34121.priority: P1 on confirmation of active data-bearing TXT tunnel traffic.
ITID-34121.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and network engineering immediately to sinkhole or block the resolving domain.
indicators: High volume of TXT record queries to a single domain from one host
Base32/Base64-like encoded strings in TXT query names or response content
DNS query volume/size far exceeding normal resolution patterns for that host
vectors: Malware implant using TXT-record-based tunneling for low-and-slow exfil
Custom exfil script chunking a file into successive TXT queries
rootCauses: No DNS query logging or analytics beyond basic resolution
DNS traffic not restricted to approved recursive resolvers
No entropy/volume-based DNS anomaly detection
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: DNS query logging and analytics (volume, entropy, record-type baselining)
Restriction of DNS egress to approved internal resolvers only
DNS sinkholing for known malicious domains
ITID-34121.detection: Good where DNS analytics tooling with entropy/volume baselining is deployed; poor in environments only logging resolution results.
ITID-34121.response: Sinkhole or block the malicious domain at the resolver, isolate the source host, and estimate exfiltrated volume from the DNS query log.
metrics: Percentage of DNS egress restricted to approved resolvers
Time to detect and sinkhole a tunneling domain
detections: DNS TXT record volume/entropy anomaly alerting
ITID-34121.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs by encoding mechanism (TXT record content) rather than subdomain labels or a specific named tool.

playbook.name: Response: DNS TXT Record-Based Exfiltration Encoding
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where data is encoded into DNS TXT record queries/responses to a domain controlled by the threat actor.

steps.title: Confirm the TXT record exfiltration pattern
steps.desc: Review DNS query logs for the affected host for a high volume of TXT record requests to a single unusual domain, and inspect query names for base32/base64-style encoded content.
steps.guidance: Decode sample queries where feasible to confirm they carry structured data rather than legitimate TXT lookups (e.g. SPF/DKIM checks).
steps.outcome: Confirmed TXT-based tunneling activity with destination domain identified.
steps.abort: If the TXT queries match legitimate mail authentication lookups, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate volume and duration of the exfiltration
steps.desc: Review historical DNS logs to determine how long the TXT-based channel has been active and estimate data volume transferred based on query count and encoded payload size.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the TXT record queries.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; tunneling traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination domain at the DNS/firewall level
steps.desc: Add the tunneling domain and its authoritative name servers to the DNS sinkhole/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify and remove the tunneling tool/malware from the host
steps.desc: Locate and remove the client generating the TXT-encoded queries and any dropper/persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Check for the same tool on other hosts
steps.desc: Sweep the environment for the same tool signature or DNS query pattern on other endpoints.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope limited to the one host, or additional hosts found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor DNS traffic
steps.desc: Rebuild or restore the host from a known-good state and monitor DNS traffic closely for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and assess DNS-monitoring coverage
steps.desc: Record the TXT-encoding technique and recommend improved DNS anomaly detection (query-volume and entropy alerting) if this evaded existing monitoring.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34122.def: Exfiltration where data is broken into chunks and encoded directly into the subdomain portion of DNS queries (e.g., <encoded-chunk>.attacker-domain.com) resolved as standard A/AAAA lookups, using the query itself — rather than any response content — as the covert channel.
ITID-34122.purpose: Captures DNS-tunneling exfiltration that encodes stolen data into the subdomain labels of standard A/AAAA queries rather than TXT records.
scopeIncludes: Data chunked and Base32/hex-encoded into successive subdomain labels queried against attacker-controlled authoritative DNS
Use of wildcard DNS records at attacker infrastructure to accept arbitrary encoded subdomains
scopeExcludes: Exfiltration via TXT record content (see DNS TXT Record-Based Exfiltration Encoding)
Use of an identifiable commodity DNS tunneling tool as the mechanism of record (see Commodity Tunneling Tool)
ITID-34122.severity: High — indicates a deliberate, low-and-slow exfil technique built to evade content inspection.
ITID-34122.priority: P1 on confirmation of sustained encoded-subdomain query patterns tied to data loss.
ITID-34122.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and network engineering to block/sinkhole the parent domain and identify all affected hosts.
indicators: Abnormally long, high-entropy subdomain labels queried repeatedly against one parent domain
Sustained, sequential-looking subdomain query patterns suggesting chunked data transfer
Queries to a domain with no legitimate business purpose registered recently
vectors: Malware/script encoding stolen data into DNS query subdomains for exfil
Wildcard-DNS-backed attacker infrastructure accepting arbitrary encoded queries
rootCauses: No entropy or length-based analysis of DNS query names
DNS logging limited to top-level domain rather than full query string
No baseline for normal per-host DNS query volume/pattern
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: Full DNS query-string logging with entropy/length analytics
DNS sinkholing for identified malicious parent domains
Restriction of DNS egress to approved internal resolvers
ITID-34122.detection: Good with dedicated DNS security analytics; largely invisible to tools that only log resolved IPs.
ITID-34122.response: Block/sinkhole the parent domain, isolate the source host, and reconstruct approximate data volume from the query log where retained.
metrics: Number of encoded-subdomain tunneling incidents detected per quarter
Coverage percentage of hosts with full DNS query logging
ITID-34122.notes: Differentiated from ITID-34121 by encoding location (query subdomain vs. TXT record content); both may co-occur in a single campaign, in which case log under whichever mechanism carried the bulk of the exfiltrated data.

playbook.name: Response: DNS Subdomain Label Encoding Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where data is encoded into subdomain labels of DNS A/AAAA queries (e.g. long, high-entropy, or sequential subdomain strings) sent to an attacker-controlled authoritative domain.

steps.title: Confirm the subdomain encoding pattern
steps.desc: Review DNS query logs for the affected host for abnormally long or high-entropy subdomain labels queried in sequence against a single parent domain.
steps.guidance: Reassemble a sample of subdomain labels in query order to confirm they decode to structured data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed subdomain-encoded tunneling with destination domain identified.
steps.abort: If the pattern matches a legitimate CDN or load-balancer naming scheme, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate volume and duration of the exfiltration
steps.desc: Review historical DNS logs to determine how long the tunnel has been active and estimate data volume based on query count and label length.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the subdomain-encoded queries.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; tunneling traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the parent domain at the DNS/firewall level
steps.desc: Add the parent domain used for subdomain encoding to the DNS sinkhole/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify and remove the tunneling tool/malware from the host
steps.desc: Locate and remove the client generating the encoded subdomain queries and any dropper/persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Check for the same tool on other hosts
steps.desc: Sweep the environment for the same tool signature or subdomain query pattern on other endpoints.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope limited to the one host, or additional hosts found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor DNS traffic
steps.desc: Rebuild or restore the host from a known-good state and monitor DNS query patterns closely for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and assess DNS-monitoring coverage
steps.desc: Record the subdomain-encoding technique and recommend entropy/length-based DNS anomaly detection if this evaded existing monitoring.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34123.def: Exfiltration of data over DNS using an identifiable, publicly-available DNS tunneling utility (e.g., iodine, dnscat2, DNSCat, Heyoka) whose known protocol signature, handshake, or client fingerprint is directly attributable to that tool.
ITID-34123.purpose: Captures DNS tunneling exfiltration carried out using a recognizable, named commodity tunneling tool rather than bespoke encoding.
scopeIncludes: Traffic matching the known protocol signature of a public DNS tunneling tool
Presence of the tool's binary/artifact on the source host confirming its use for the tunnel
scopeExcludes: Bespoke or hand-built DNS encoding schemes not matching a known public tool (see TXT Record-Based or Subdomain Label Encoding ITIDs)
ITID-34123.severity: High, though generally slightly lower sophistication signal than fully custom encoding since the tool is a known commodity artifact.
ITID-34123.priority: P1 on confirmation of active tunnel traffic; P2 during initial artifact discovery.
ITID-34123.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; check threat-intel for known campaigns associated with the specific tool identified.
indicators: Network signature/IDS match for a known DNS tunneling tool's protocol
Presence of the tool's executable, config, or command history on the host
Known default ports, record-type patterns, or handshake sequences specific to the tool
vectors: Attacker deploying a public/commodity DNS tunneling utility post-compromise for exfil
Red-team or unauthorized use of legitimate tunneling software for data exfil
rootCauses: IDS/IPS signatures for known tunneling tools not enabled or up to date
Endpoint allow-listing not blocking known tunneling tool binaries
No behavioral detection layered behind signature-based tools
controls: IDS/IPS signatures for known DNS tunneling tools
Endpoint application control/allow-listing
DNS sinkholing
ITID-34123.detection: Strong where up-to-date IDS/IPS signatures for the specific tool are in place; otherwise falls back to the same generic DNS anomaly detection as sibling ITIDs.
ITID-34123.response: Remove the tool artifact from the host, block the tunnel destination, and hunt for the same tool signature elsewhere in the environment.
metrics: Count of known-tool DNS tunneling detections per quarter
Signature coverage rate for known tunneling tools
detections: IDS/IPS signature match for named DNS tunneling tools
ITID-34123.notes: Use this leaf only when the specific tool is identified; if the encoding scheme is custom/unattributed, use ITID-34121 or ITID-34122 based on encoding location instead.

playbook.name: Response: DNS Tunneling Using a Commodity Tunneling Tool
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration via a known commodity DNS tunneling tool encoding data in DNS queries.

steps.title: Confirm the DNS tunneling pattern
steps.desc: Review DNS query logs for the affected host for high-volume queries to a single unusual domain, abnormal subdomain entropy, or TXT record request patterns.
steps.outcome: Confirmed tunneling activity with the destination domain identified.

steps.title: Estimate volume and duration of the exfiltration
steps.desc: Review historical DNS logs to determine how long the tunnel has been active and estimate data volume transferred.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the tunneling traffic.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; tunneling traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination domain at the DNS/firewall level
steps.desc: Add the tunneling domain to the DNS sinkhole/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify and remove the tunneling tool/malware from the host
steps.desc: Locate and remove the tunneling client and any dropper/persistence mechanism that installed it.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Check for the same tool on other hosts
steps.desc: Sweep the environment for the same tool signature/indicators on other endpoints.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope limited to the one host, or additional hosts found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Rebuild or restore the host from a known-good state and monitor DNS traffic closely for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and assess DNS-monitoring coverage
steps.desc: Record the technique and recommend improved DNS anomaly detection if this evaded existing monitoring.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34124.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via DNS tunneling, where the specific technique (TXT record encoding, subdomain label encoding, or named commodity tool) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34124.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for DNS tunneling exfiltration that cannot yet be classified by encoding mechanism or tool.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification of suspected DNS tunneling before the mechanism is confirmed
Cases with insufficient DNS logging to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific mechanism has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34121, ITID-34122, or ITID-34123
ITID-34124.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34124.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34124.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic DNS volume/pattern anomaly alert not yet attributed to a specific encoding scheme or tool
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient DNS query logging detail to fingerprint the tunneling mechanism
controls: General DNS anomaly monitoring
DNS sinkholing capability
ITID-34124.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34124.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified DNS tunneling incidents
ITID-34124.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General DNS Tunneling Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration via DNS tunneling that does not fit a more specific DNS tunneling category (TXT record encoding, subdomain label encoding, or a known commodity tool).

steps.title: Confirm the DNS tunneling activity and characterize the technique
steps.desc: Review DNS query logs for the affected host for anomalous query volume, record types, or naming patterns to a single domain, and attempt to classify the specific encoding technique used.
steps.guidance: If the technique can be matched to a more specific category during investigation, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed DNS tunneling activity with destination domain identified.
steps.abort: If no tunneling is confirmed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate volume and duration of the exfiltration
steps.desc: Review historical DNS logs to determine how long the tunnel has been active and estimate data volume transferred.
steps.outcome: Timeline and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host generating the tunneling traffic.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; tunneling traffic stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination domain at the DNS/firewall level
steps.desc: Add the tunneling domain to the DNS sinkhole/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify and remove the tunneling mechanism
steps.desc: Locate and remove the client, script, or malware generating the tunneling traffic and any persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Sweep for the same DNS tunneling indicators on other hosts
steps.desc: Search DNS logs fleet-wide for the same destination domain or query pattern to confirm whether other hosts are affected.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor DNS traffic
steps.desc: Rebuild or restore the host from a known-good state and monitor DNS traffic closely for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification for future reference.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34131.def: Data theft in which files are transferred from a compromised device to an external FTP or SFTP server under the attacker's control, using standard file-transfer protocols rather than web or email channels.
ITID-34131.purpose: Captures exfiltration where stolen data is uploaded directly to an FTP or SFTP server that the attacker owns and controls.
scopeIncludes: Malware or script uploading stolen files via FTP/SFTP to an external, attacker-owned server
Use of hardcoded attacker FTP/SFTP credentials embedded in malware
scopeExcludes: Exfil disguised as a legitimate scheduled backup job (see Exfiltration Disguised as Legitimate Scheduled Backup FTP Transfer)
Use of a compromised internal FTP server as a staging point before external transfer (see Compromised Internal FTP Server as Staging Point)
ITID-34131.severity: High — confirms both compromise and completed or in-progress data transfer to attacker infrastructure.
ITID-34131.priority: P1 on confirmation of an active or completed transfer to an attacker-controlled FTP/SFTP endpoint.
ITID-34131.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; block the destination IP/domain and identify the full set of files transferred.
indicators: Outbound FTP/SFTP connection to an external IP with no known business relationship
Large or unusual file uploads over FTP from a host that does not normally use FTP
FTP credentials found hardcoded in malware or scripts
vectors: Malware implant with built-in FTP/SFTP exfil functionality
Manual attacker use of an FTP client post-compromise to upload staged data
rootCauses: Outbound FTP/SFTP not blocked or monitored at the network egress layer
No allow-listing of approved external file-transfer destinations
Lack of DLP inspection on FTP/SFTP protocol traffic
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: Egress blocking/allow-listing for FTP/SFTP destinations
DLP inspection of file-transfer protocol traffic
Network flow monitoring for anomalous FTP/SFTP sessions
ITID-34131.detection: Good where network flow monitoring and DLP cover FTP/SFTP; weak in environments treating this protocol as low-priority/legacy and under-monitoring it.
ITID-34131.response: Block the destination, isolate the source host, and identify and inventory the exact files transferred from FTP session logs where available.
metrics: Volume and count of files exfiltrated via external FTP/SFTP per incident
Percentage of egress FTP/SFTP traffic monitored by DLP
detections: Network flow anomaly detection for FTP/SFTP egress
ITID-34131.notes: Scoped to a straightforward external attacker-owned FTP/SFTP destination; disguised-as-backup and internal-staging variants are split into sibling ITIDs to preserve the differentiating detection angle each requires.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled FTP/SFTP Server
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where a compromised host uploads data to an FTP or SFTP server controlled by the threat actor.

steps.title: Confirm the FTP/SFTP connection to the attacker-controlled server
steps.desc: Review firewall/proxy logs and endpoint process activity for outbound FTP/SFTP connections to an external server with no legitimate business relationship, and correlate with file-access timestamps.
steps.guidance: Check threat intelligence for the destination IP/hostname.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration channel with destination server identified.
steps.abort: If the server is a known legitimate vendor endpoint, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine what data was uploaded
steps.desc: Correlate file-access and staging activity on the host with FTP/SFTP session logs to identify the files and volume transferred.
steps.outcome: Scope of exfiltrated data established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host that established the FTP/SFTP connection.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; connection terminated.

steps.title: Block the destination server
steps.desc: Block the destination IP and associated FTP/SFTP ports at the firewall for all hosts.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Remove the malware or script driving the transfer
steps.desc: Identify and remove any malware, script, or scheduled task that initiated the FTP/SFTP upload, along with its persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Sweep for the same indicators on other hosts
steps.desc: Search network and endpoint logs fleet-wide for connections to the same destination or the same malware/script indicators.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor outbound FTP/SFTP traffic
steps.desc: Restore the host to a known-good state and monitor for renewed outbound FTP/SFTP connections.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review egress FTP/SFTP policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether outbound FTP/SFTP should be restricted or more closely monitored at the network perimeter.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34132.def: Data theft in which the attacker times, names, or configures the FTP/SFTP transfer to mimic a legitimate scheduled backup job (matching normal backup windows, filenames, or destinations) specifically to avoid drawing scrutiny from staff or monitoring tuned to expect such traffic.
ITID-34132.purpose: Captures exfiltration deliberately disguised to resemble a routine, scheduled backup FTP transfer so it blends into expected recurring traffic.
scopeIncludes: Attacker scheduling exfil transfers to run during known legitimate backup windows
Renaming or restructuring exfil archives/filenames to match backup-job naming conventions
Abuse of an existing legitimate backup job's credentials or destination configuration to redirect a copy of data to attacker infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Straightforward exfiltration to an attacker FTP server with no disguise attempt (see Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled FTP/SFTP Server)
Compromise of an internal FTP server used purely as a staging hop (see Compromised Internal FTP Server as Staging Point)
ITID-34132.severity: High — the deliberate camouflage indicates a more deliberate, harder-to-detect adversary.
ITID-34132.priority: P1 on confirmation; treat as a strong indicator of insider knowledge of backup schedules or prior reconnaissance.
ITID-34132.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and backup/infrastructure teams to verify legitimate backup jobs were not themselves tampered with.
indicators: A backup-named job transferring to an unexpected or new destination
Backup job configuration modified recently without a corresponding change ticket
Transfer timing exactly matching backup windows but destination IP not matching approved backup infrastructure
vectors: Attacker modifying an existing backup job's destination to add or redirect to attacker infrastructure
Attacker creating a new scheduled task disguised with backup-like naming
rootCauses: No change-control/alerting on modifications to backup job configuration
Backup traffic exempted from DLP/monitoring by default because it is assumed trusted
Lack of destination validation for scheduled backup transfers
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: Change-control and alerting on backup job/config modifications
Destination validation/allow-listing for scheduled backup transfers
DLP inspection extended to backup-classified traffic rather than exempting it
ITID-34132.detection: Weak by design — the technique specifically targets the blind spot where backup traffic is trusted and excluded from monitoring; requires configuration-change monitoring to close.
ITID-34132.response: Validate all backup job configurations for unauthorized changes, restore legitimate configuration, block the rogue destination, and scope data transferred under the disguised job.
metrics: Number of unauthorized backup-job configuration changes detected per quarter
detections: Destination allow-list violation alerting for backup traffic
ITID-34132.notes: The differentiator from ITID-34131 is the deliberate camouflage-as-backup element; without evidence of that disguise intent, classify under the plain attacker-controlled-FTP leaf instead.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration Disguised as Legitimate Scheduled Backup FTP Transfer
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where the threat actor abuses or mimics an existing scheduled backup FTP/SFTP job to disguise the transfer as routine business traffic.

steps.title: Compare the transfer against the legitimate backup schedule and destination
steps.desc: Review the scheduled backup job's configured destination, timing, and file set, and compare against the actual transfer observed to identify discrepancies (wrong destination, unscheduled run time, unexpected file selection).
steps.guidance: Check for recently modified backup job configuration, credentials, or destination settings.
steps.outcome: Confirmed that the transfer deviates from the legitimate backup job, with the unauthorized destination identified.
steps.abort: If the transfer matches the documented backup job exactly, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine how the backup job was altered or impersonated
steps.desc: Review change history and access logs for the backup job configuration and the service account credentials used to run it, to determine whether it was reconfigured or its credentials reused by an attacker-controlled process.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the disguise established (config tampering vs. credential reuse vs. mimicked process name/schedule).

steps.title: Disable or isolate the affected backup job and host
steps.desc: Pause the compromised scheduled job and isolate the host or service running it to prevent further transfers.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized transfer stopped.

steps.title: Block the unauthorized destination and rotate backup credentials
steps.desc: Block the unauthorized destination at the firewall and rotate any service account credentials used by the backup job.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked and credentials rotated.

steps.title: Restore the legitimate backup job configuration
steps.desc: Revert the backup job configuration to its known-good state and remove any attacker-added scripts or tasks.
steps.outcome: Backup job confirmed restored to authorized configuration.

steps.title: Audit other scheduled jobs for similar tampering
steps.desc: Review other scheduled backup and automated transfer jobs for similar configuration tampering or credential reuse.
steps.outcome: Other scheduled jobs confirmed unaffected or remediated.

steps.title: Re-enable the backup job and verify normal operation
steps.desc: Re-enable the backup job with rotated credentials and monitor its next scheduled runs to confirm it transfers only to the authorized destination.
steps.outcome: Backup job confirmed operating normally with no unauthorized transfers.

steps.title: Document the incident and harden backup job change control
steps.desc: Record the incident and recommend change-control alerting for backup job configuration changes and destination allowlisting.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34133.def: Exfiltration technique in which the adversary first stages stolen data on a compromised internal (on-premises) FTP server — using it as an internal collection/aggregation point — before a subsequent transfer moves the aggregated data out of the organization's network.
ITID-34133.purpose: Captures cases where an attacker compromises an internal, legitimate FTP server and uses it purely as a staging point before moving data onward, rather than uploading straight to external attacker infrastructure.
scopeIncludes: Attacker aggregating stolen files from multiple internal hosts onto a compromised internal FTP server
Internal FTP server repurposed as a staging hop ahead of a later external exfil step
scopeExcludes: Direct upload from an endpoint to an external attacker-controlled FTP/SFTP server (see Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled FTP/SFTP Server)
The subsequent external transfer step itself, which should be logged under whichever external-exfil ITID matches its channel
ITID-34133.severity: High — indicates lateral movement and internal infrastructure compromise in addition to data staging.
ITID-34133.priority: P1 given the internal server compromise represents both a data-loss and infrastructure-integrity incident.
ITID-34133.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and the server/infrastructure team owning the compromised FTP host immediately.
indicators: Unusual inbound file transfers from multiple internal hosts converging on one FTP server
New or unauthorized accounts/credentials created on the FTP server
Unexpected growth in disk usage on the FTP server tied to unrecognized file types/names
vectors: Compromise of internal FTP server credentials or exploitation of a server vulnerability
Lateral movement from an initially compromised endpoint to the internal FTP server
rootCauses: Internal FTP server not hardened, patched, or segmented from general endpoint networks
No monitoring of internal file-transfer server activity for anomalous aggregation patterns
Excessive internal network access allowing arbitrary hosts to reach the FTP server
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: Network segmentation isolating internal file-transfer servers
Monitoring/alerting on internal FTP server activity anomalies
Regular patching/hardening of internal FTP infrastructure
ITID-34133.detection: Moderate — requires internal server-side logging and network segmentation visibility rather than perimeter monitoring alone.
ITID-34133.response: Isolate and forensically image the compromised internal FTP server, identify all data staged on it, trace both the inbound aggregation and any onward external transfer, and remediate the server.
metrics: Number of internal servers found compromised and used for staging per year
Time to detect anomalous internal file aggregation
ITID-34133.notes: This leaf covers only the internal staging step; log the onward external transfer separately under the matching external-exfil ITID to avoid double-counting a single incident's data volume across two leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Compromised Internal FTP Server as Staging Point
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where an internal FTP server has been compromised and used as an intermediate staging point before data is moved externally.

steps.title: Confirm compromise of the internal FTP server and identify staged data
steps.desc: Review the internal FTP server's logs, file system, and recent uploads/downloads to confirm unauthorized access and identify what data was staged there.
steps.guidance: Check for anomalous accounts, newly created directories, or archive files inconsistent with the server's normal use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed compromise with the staged data set identified.

steps.title: Trace onward transfer from the staging server
steps.desc: Review the FTP server's outbound connection logs to identify whether and where staged data was subsequently transferred externally.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether data left the environment, and to where.

steps.title: Isolate the compromised FTP server
steps.desc: Network-isolate the FTP server to prevent further staging or onward transfer while preserving it for forensics.
steps.outcome: Server isolated; no further data movement.

steps.title: Disable compromised accounts and block onward destinations
steps.desc: Disable any compromised or unauthorized FTP accounts and block identified external destinations at the firewall.
steps.outcome: Attacker access removed; onward transfer path blocked.

steps.title: Remove attacker access and staged data
steps.desc: Remove any backdoors, unauthorized accounts, or persistence mechanisms from the FTP server, and securely remove staged data after evidence collection.
steps.outcome: Server confirmed clean of attacker access.

steps.title: Determine and close the initial compromise vector
steps.desc: Identify how the FTP server was initially compromised (e.g. weak credentials, unpatched vulnerability, lateral movement) and remediate.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector closed.

steps.title: Rebuild and restore the FTP server, then monitor
steps.desc: Rebuild the server from a known-good baseline, restore legitimate configuration, and monitor closely for renewed unauthorized activity.
steps.outcome: Server restored to service with no recurrence.

steps.title: Document the incident and review internal server hardening
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether internal FTP servers require stronger access controls, monitoring, or decommissioning in favor of managed file transfer.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34134.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred over FTP/SFTP, where the specific pattern (direct external upload, backup disguise, or internal staging) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34134.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for covert FTP/SFTP exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific FTP/SFTP exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34131, ITID-34132, or ITID-34133
ITID-34134.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34134.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34134.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic FTP/SFTP anomaly alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
mitreTechniques: T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol
controls: General FTP/SFTP egress monitoring
ITID-34134.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34134.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified FTP/SFTP exfil incidents
ITID-34134.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Covert FTP/SFTP Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration via FTP/SFTP that does not fit a more specific category (attacker-controlled server, disguised backup job, or compromised internal staging server).

steps.title: Confirm the FTP/SFTP exfiltration activity
steps.desc: Review network and server logs to confirm unauthorized FTP/SFTP transfer activity and attempt to classify the specific pattern (attacker-controlled destination, disguised legitimate job, or compromised internal server).
steps.guidance: If the pattern matches a more specific category, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration activity with source, destination, and data scope identified.
steps.abort: If no exfiltration is confirmed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate volume and scope of exfiltrated data
steps.desc: Review transfer logs and file-access history to determine what data was moved and the affected systems.
steps.outcome: Scope and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host or server
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host or server involved in the transfer.
steps.outcome: Transfer activity stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination and disable compromised credentials
steps.desc: Block the destination at the firewall and disable any compromised accounts or credentials used for the transfer.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked; compromised access removed.

steps.title: Remove the exfiltration mechanism
steps.desc: Identify and remove any malware, script, or unauthorized process responsible for the transfer.
steps.outcome: System confirmed clean.

steps.title: Sweep for the same indicators on other hosts
steps.desc: Search network and endpoint logs fleet-wide for connections to the same destination or the same malware/script indicators.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore affected systems and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Restore the affected host/server to a known-good state and monitor outbound FTP/SFTP traffic closely.
steps.outcome: System restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification for future reference.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34141.def: Data theft in which files are uploaded from a compromised or malicious process to an external cloud storage service (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, MEGA, etc.) account that is owned and controlled by the attacker, rather than by the organization or a legitimate employee.
ITID-34141.purpose: Captures exfiltration where stolen data is uploaded to a personal or attacker-registered cloud storage account not sanctioned by the organization.
scopeIncludes: Malware uploading stolen files to an attacker-registered cloud storage account via its public API
Use of a throwaway/burner cloud storage account as an exfil drop point
scopeExcludes: An employee's abuse of their own sanctioned corporate cloud storage account (see Insider Using Legitimate Account)
Unintentional uploads via a local sync client folder (see Cloud Sync Client Auto-Upload Abuse)
ITID-34141.severity: High — confirms both compromise and completed or in-progress transfer to attacker-controlled cloud storage.
ITID-34141.priority: P1 on confirmation of an active or completed transfer to an identified attacker-controlled cloud storage account.
ITID-34141.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; request the cloud provider's abuse/legal team assist with account takedown and, if possible, evidence preservation.
indicators: API calls to a cloud storage service's upload endpoint from an unexpected process or host
Outbound connections to cloud storage domains with no corresponding sanctioned corporate account
Large or bursty upload volume to a consumer cloud storage service from a server or workstation
vectors: Malware with built-in cloud storage API exfil module (e.g., using OAuth tokens or API keys for Dropbox/Drive)
Attacker manually uploading staged/archived data via a browser session to a personal cloud account
rootCauses: No CASB or cloud-access monitoring distinguishing sanctioned vs. unsanctioned cloud storage accounts
Overly permissive egress allowing all cloud storage domains without account-level control
No DLP inspection of uploads to cloud storage services
controls: CASB enforcement distinguishing sanctioned vs. unsanctioned cloud storage tenants
DLP inspection of uploads to cloud storage services
Egress restriction to approved corporate cloud storage tenants only
ITID-34141.detection: Strong where a CASB with tenant-restriction/DLP is deployed; weak where cloud storage domains are broadly allowed without tenant-level control.
ITID-34141.response: Block the attacker's cloud storage account/domain, identify and inventory the files uploaded, and request provider takedown/preservation where possible.
metrics: Volume of data exfiltrated to unsanctioned cloud storage per incident
Percentage of cloud storage egress restricted to sanctioned tenants
ITID-34141.notes: The differentiator from ITID-34142 is account ownership: this leaf is for attacker-owned/unsanctioned accounts; legitimate corporate accounts misused by an insider go to the sibling leaf instead.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled Cloud Storage Account (Dropbox/Google Drive/OneDrive)
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where malware or an external actor uploads data to a cloud storage account not owned or sanctioned by the organization.

steps.title: Confirm the upload to an unsanctioned cloud storage account
steps.desc: Review proxy/CASB logs for uploads to consumer cloud storage services from the affected host, and confirm the destination account is not a corporate-sanctioned tenant.
steps.guidance: Check CASB tenant/account identifiers to distinguish sanctioned corporate tenants from personal or unknown accounts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unsanctioned-account exfiltration with destination account and uploaded files identified.
steps.abort: If the account is confirmed as a sanctioned corporate tenant, route to the sanctioned-account insider playbook instead.

steps.title: Determine whether this is malware-driven or manual external-actor activity
steps.desc: Correlate the upload with endpoint process activity and prior indicators of compromise to determine whether the upload was performed by malware or by an external actor operating on the compromised host/account.
steps.outcome: Root cause classified as malware-driven or manual attacker action.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host performing the upload.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; upload activity stopped.

steps.title: Block the cloud storage destination
steps.desc: Block the specific unsanctioned account/domain endpoint at the CASB/proxy, or block the consumer cloud storage category entirely if policy permits.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked organization-wide.

steps.title: Remove the malware or unauthorized process driving the upload
steps.desc: Identify and remove any malware or unauthorized application performing the upload, along with its persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Sweep for the same destination account on other hosts
steps.desc: Search CASB/proxy logs fleet-wide for uploads to the same unsanctioned cloud storage account to determine whether other hosts are affected.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor cloud upload activity
steps.desc: Restore the host to a known-good state and monitor CASB/proxy logs for renewed attempts to reach consumer cloud storage services.
steps.outcome: Host restored; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review cloud storage access policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether unsanctioned cloud storage categories need broader blocking via CASB policy.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34142.def: Data theft in which an authorized employee uses their valid, organization-sanctioned cloud storage account (e.g., corporate OneDrive/Google Workspace Drive) to upload, share externally, or download sensitive data beyond their legitimate business need, exploiting the fact that the account itself is trusted infrastructure.
ITID-34142.purpose: Captures exfiltration where an insider uses their own legitimate, sanctioned corporate cloud storage account to move data out, rather than an external attacker-owned account.
scopeIncludes: Sharing a corporate cloud storage file/folder externally to a personal or third-party email address
Bulk downloading or copying data into a personal folder within the sanctioned corporate tenant ahead of external transfer
Changing sharing permissions on corporate cloud content to make it externally accessible
scopeExcludes: Upload to an external, attacker-owned/unsanctioned cloud account (see Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled Cloud Storage Account)

Motivation/behavioral investigation of the insider's intent (see the ITID-13111–13114 Insider Threats/Risk domain for the motivational and HR-investigation angle) — this leaf covers only the technical mechanism
ITID-34142.severity: Medium-High, scaling with data sensitivity and volume; higher if external sharing settings were deliberately altered to bypass controls.
ITID-34142.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for large volumes of highly sensitive data or a departing employee.
ITID-34142.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal in parallel with SOC/IR; coordinate with the insider-threat program for motivation-side investigation.
indicators: External sharing permission added to sensitive corporate cloud files
Abnormal bulk download/copy activity from corporate cloud storage by one user
Cloud audit log showing sharing link creation to a non-corporate domain
vectors: Employee changing a file/folder's sharing setting to 'anyone with the link' or a personal email
Employee bulk-downloading data from corporate cloud storage prior to resignation
rootCauses: No DLP policy governing external sharing from corporate cloud storage
Overly permissive default sharing settings in the cloud storage tenant
No anomaly detection on bulk download/sharing behavior by user
controls: DLP policy enforcement on external sharing from corporate cloud storage
User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) for bulk download/sharing anomalies
Restrictive default external-sharing tenant settings
ITID-34142.detection: Good where the cloud tenant's native audit logs and DLP/CASB policies are enabled and monitored; weak where external sharing is unrestricted and unlogged.
ITID-34142.response: Revoke external sharing links immediately, preserve cloud audit logs, and hand off to the insider-threat program for motive/intent investigation per the ITID-13111–13114 domain.
metrics: Count of unauthorized external-sharing events detected per quarter
Volume of data exposed via improper sharing permissions
ITID-34142.notes: Scope decision: this leaf owns the technical exfil mechanism (legitimate account, cloud sharing/upload) only; motive, intent, and HR-side investigation route to ITID-13111–13114 (Insider Theft of ... Records) to avoid duplicating that domain's content here.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Abuse of Sanctioned Corporate Cloud Storage (Insider Using Legitimate Account)
playbook.description: For suspected or confirmed data exfiltration where an insider uses their own legitimate, sanctioned corporate cloud storage account to move data outside authorized channels (e.g. sharing to a personal account, bulk external sharing, unusual upload volume). Requires HR/Legal-coordinated handling given the potential for disciplinary or legal action.

steps.title: Review sanctioned cloud storage audit logs for anomalous activity
steps.desc: Review the corporate cloud storage tenant's audit logs for the user's account for unusual upload volume, bulk downloads, external sharing events, or sync to unmanaged devices.
steps.guidance: Establish a baseline of the user's normal activity before concluding the volume/pattern is anomalous.
steps.outcome: Anomalous activity pattern confirmed and quantified with specific files/folders and timestamps.
steps.abort: If activity is consistent with the user's normal job function, close as a false positive.
steps.tool: Cloud storage admin audit logs / CASB

steps.title: Engage HR and Legal before further investigative action
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal of the suspected insider activity and obtain guidance on evidence handling and any personnel action before proceeding further, given the potential for disciplinary or legal proceedings.
steps.guidance: Do not confront the employee or take account action until HR/Legal have weighed in.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal engaged and investigative plan agreed.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Export and preserve relevant audit logs, file access records, and sharing activity with a documented chain of custody before any account restriction is applied, in case the evidence is needed for disciplinary or legal action.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.
steps.tool: Cloud storage admin console / evidence management

steps.title: Restrict external sharing on the account per HR/Legal direction
steps.desc: Once authorized by HR/Legal, revoke external sharing links and restrict the account's external sharing capability to stop further data leaving the environment.
steps.outcome: External sharing capability revoked.

steps.title: Identify and revoke any external recipients' continued access
steps.desc: Identify external parties who received shared data and revoke their access where technically possible.
steps.outcome: External access revoked where feasible.

steps.title: Review other sharing activity by the same account
steps.desc: Review the account's broader sharing and upload history in the sanctioned tenant to determine whether this was an isolated event or part of a wider pattern.
steps.outcome: Full scope of the account's sharing activity established.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action and monitor the account
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal (e.g. account suspension, role change, termination process) and monitor the account closely for the duration of the process.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied per HR/Legal direction; account activity monitored.

steps.title: Document the case and review DLP/insider-risk monitoring for sanctioned cloud storage
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal, and evaluate whether DLP or insider-risk monitoring policies for sanctioned cloud storage need strengthening.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34143.def: Data loss in which files are moved to a folder monitored by an installed cloud-sync client (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive desktop app) — whether by malware, a script, or an insider dragging files in — causing them to be automatically and silently uploaded to the cloud without any explicit upload/share action being taken.
ITID-34143.purpose: Captures exfiltration that occurs through a local cloud-sync client's automatic upload behavior, rather than a deliberate manual upload or share action.
scopeIncludes: Malware placing stolen files into a locally-synced cloud folder to trigger automatic upload
An insider moving/copying sensitive files into their personal sync-client folder for automatic offsite upload
Sync client configured to sync a broader set of local directories than intended, unintentionally uploading sensitive data
scopeExcludes: Direct API-based upload to an attacker-controlled account with no local sync client involved (see Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled Cloud Storage Account)
Deliberate use of sharing permissions in a sanctioned account without a sync client (see Insider Using Legitimate Account)
ITID-34143.severity: Medium-High — the automatic nature can mean large or unnoticed volumes before detection.
ITID-34143.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if sensitive data volume is large or the sync destination is an unsanctioned personal account.
ITID-34143.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and, where the account is personal/unsanctioned, to Insider Threat/HR as well.
indicators: Cloud sync client process uploading unusually large volumes shortly after new files appear locally
Sync client configured/linked to a personal rather than corporate account on a corporate device
File-system events showing files copied into a monitored sync folder immediately before upload traffic spikes
vectors: Malware drops stolen files into a sync-monitored folder to exfiltrate via the legitimate client
Employee installs a personal cloud sync client on a corporate device and points it at sensitive shared drives
rootCauses: No policy/technical control preventing installation of personal cloud sync clients on corporate devices
Sync-client scope not restricted, allowing broad folders to be monitored for auto-upload
No DLP visibility into sync-client upload traffic
controls: Application allow-listing to block unauthorized personal cloud sync clients on corporate devices
DLP/CASB inspection of sync-client upload traffic
Restriction of sync-client folder scope via corporate policy/MDM
ITID-34143.detection: Moderate — requires endpoint application control visibility plus network/CASB monitoring of sync-client traffic to fully cover.
ITID-34143.response: Disconnect/uninstall the unauthorized sync client, identify all files uploaded via its history, and revoke access to the cloud account where possible.
metrics: Number of unauthorized personal sync clients detected on corporate endpoints
Volume of data auto-uploaded via unsanctioned sync clients per quarter
detections: Endpoint application control alerting for unauthorized sync clients
ITID-34143.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by the automatic/passive nature of the upload trigger (folder sync) rather than a deliberate manual API call or sharing action.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltration via Cloud Sync Client Auto-Upload Abuse
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration where a cloud storage sync client (e.g. Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive desktop app) is configured or abused to automatically upload sensitive files from a monitored folder to an external or personal account.

steps.title: Identify the sync client and configured sync folders/account
steps.desc: Review the endpoint's installed sync clients and their configuration to identify which folders are being synced and to which account (personal vs. sanctioned corporate tenant).
steps.guidance: Check sync client logs and configuration files for account identifiers and sync folder paths.
steps.outcome: Confirmed sync destination and scope of synced folders.
steps.abort: If the sync targets a sanctioned corporate tenant per policy, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine when sensitive files entered the synced folder
steps.desc: Review file system and access logs to determine when sensitive files were placed into or moved into the auto-syncing folder, and by whom or what process.
steps.outcome: Timeline established for when exfiltration began.

steps.title: Disable the sync client or block its network access
steps.desc: Pause or uninstall the unauthorized sync client, or block its network access at the host/proxy level to stop further uploads.
steps.outcome: Sync uploads stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination cloud account/domain
steps.desc: Block the specific unsanctioned account or domain at the CASB/proxy if it is not a sanctioned tenant.
steps.outcome: Destination blocked.

steps.title: Remove the unauthorized sync configuration
steps.desc: Remove the unauthorized sync client or reconfigure it to remove sensitive folders from the sync scope, per endpoint management policy.
steps.outcome: Sync configuration confirmed remediated.

steps.title: Sweep for the same sync client configuration on other endpoints
steps.desc: Check endpoint management inventory for other hosts running the same unauthorized sync client configuration or syncing sensitive folders.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected endpoints remediated.

steps.title: Restore endpoint configuration and monitor for renewed sync activity
