steps.desc: Confirm the endpoint's sync client configuration complies with policy and monitor for any renewed unauthorized sync activity.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and review sync client allowlisting policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether endpoint policy should restrict which sync clients can be installed or which folders can be synced.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34144.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via cloud storage upload, where the specific pattern (attacker-owned account, insider abuse of a sanctioned account, or sync-client auto-upload) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34144.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for cloud storage upload exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific cloud storage exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34141, ITID-34142, or ITID-34143
ITID-34144.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34144.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34144.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic cloud storage upload anomaly alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
controls: General CASB/cloud storage upload monitoring
ITID-34144.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34144.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified cloud storage exfil incidents
detections: General cloud storage exfiltration anomaly alerting
ITID-34144.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Cloud Storage Upload Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed data exfiltration via cloud storage upload that does not fit a more specific category (attacker-controlled account, sanctioned-account insider abuse, or sync client auto-upload).

steps.title: Confirm the cloud storage upload and classify sanctioned vs. unsanctioned use
steps.desc: Review CASB/proxy logs for the upload activity and determine whether the destination account is a sanctioned corporate tenant (pointing to likely insider misuse) or an unsanctioned/personal account (pointing to likely malware or external actor activity).
steps.guidance: If the pattern matches a more specific category, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration activity with destination account type and uploaded data identified.
steps.abort: If no exfiltration is confirmed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate scope and volume of uploaded data
steps.desc: Review upload logs and file-access history to determine what data was uploaded and the affected systems or accounts.
steps.outcome: Scope and volume estimate established.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host or restrict the affected account
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host or restrict the account involved in the upload, as appropriate to the classification.
steps.outcome: Upload activity stopped.

steps.title: Block the destination or revoke sharing access
steps.desc: Block the destination account/domain at the CASB/proxy, or revoke external sharing access if the sanctioned tenant was misused.
steps.outcome: Destination access blocked or revoked.

steps.title: Remove the exfiltration mechanism
steps.desc: Remove any malware, unauthorized sync configuration, or process responsible for the upload.
steps.outcome: System confirmed clean.

steps.title: Sweep for the same destination or mechanism on other hosts
steps.desc: Search CASB/proxy and endpoint logs fleet-wide for the same destination account or upload mechanism.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected hosts remediated.

steps.title: Restore affected systems and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Restore the affected host/account to a known-good state and monitor cloud storage activity closely.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the incident and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification for future reference.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34211.def: An authorized user sends, forwards, or auto-forwards sensitive organizational data from their internal corporate email account to a personal (non-corporate) email address they control, using their own legitimate mailbox access.
ITID-34211.purpose: Captures the specific technical mechanism of an insider forwarding sensitive data from their corporate mailbox to their own personal email account.
scopeIncludes: A single or repeated manual forward/send of sensitive attachments or content to a personal Gmail/Yahoo/etc. address
Insider setting up a one-time or persistent forward specifically targeting their own personal account
scopeExcludes: Forwarding/emailing data to another internal colleague's mailbox for later retrieval (see Insider Emailing Data to an Uninvolved Internal Colleague)
Motivation, intent, and behavioral investigation of the insider (see the ITID-13111–13114 Insider Threats/Risk domain) — this leaf covers only the technical send mechanism
A persistent mail-rule-based auto-forward configured on a compromised (not self-owned) account (see the Compromised Email Accounts group)
ITID-34211.severity: Medium-High, scaling with data sensitivity and volume; higher for regulated data categories (PII, financial, IP).
ITID-34211.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for large volumes of highly sensitive data or where the individual has since departed.
ITID-34211.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal in parallel with SOC/IR upon confirmation.
indicators: Outbound email logs showing sensitive attachments sent to a known personal email domain (gmail.com, etc.)
DLP alert on sensitive content pattern match in an outbound message to an external personal address
Repeated forwarding pattern to the same personal address over time
vectors: Manual forward/send of an email or attachment to a personal address
Copy-paste of sensitive content into a new message addressed to a personal account
rootCauses: No outbound DLP policy scanning for sensitive content sent to personal webmail domains
No user-behavior baseline flagging first-time sends to a personal address
Overly broad email permissions allowing bulk attachment sends without approval
controls: Outbound DLP scanning for sensitive content to personal webmail domains
Block-list/warn-list for known personal webmail domains on outbound mail
User behavior analytics for first-time or anomalous external sends
ITID-34211.detection: Strong where outbound DLP with content inspection is deployed and tuned to personal webmail domains; weak without content-aware DLP.
ITID-34211.response: Preserve outbound mail logs and DLP evidence, notify Insider Threat/HR, and determine full scope of data sent before any further action (e.g., account suspension) that could alert the individual.
metrics: Count of DLP blocks/alerts for personal-webmail sends per quarter
Volume of sensitive data sent to personal accounts per incident
detections: Outbound DLP content-match alerting for personal webmail domains
ITID-34211.notes: Scope decision: this leaf and its siblings (ITID-34211–34213) own only the technical send mechanism; motive, intent, and case-management investigation route to ITID-13111–13114 (Insider Theft of ... Records) to avoid duplicating that domain's content here.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Self-Forwarding Sensitive Data to Personal Email
playbook.description: For an insider identified as forwarding company data to their own personal email account, typically for convenience or in preparation to leave.

steps.title: Confirm forwarding activity and data sensitivity
steps.desc: Review mail server/DLP logs to identify all messages the user sent or forwarded to their own personal address, and classify the sensitivity of the attached/embedded data.
steps.guidance: Check both manual forwards and any auto-forward rules the user may have set on their own account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of messages, dates, and data classification sent to the personal address.

steps.title: Establish business justification and intent
steps.desc: Check whether the user has a documented business reason (e.g. remote work exception) for the transfer, and review any prior DLP alerts or policy violations for this user.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether this appears to be policy violation, negligence, or deliberate exfiltration.
steps.abort: If a valid, pre-approved business exception exists, document and close as a false positive.

steps.title: Notify HR per insider-data-handling policy
steps.desc: Loop in HR (and Legal if the data is regulated or high-sensitivity) before taking any account action that could tip off the employee.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and directing next steps on employee notification and account action.

steps.title: Restrict further self-forwarding capability
steps.desc: Apply a mail rule or DLP policy blocking outbound mail from this user to their known personal address, per HR/Legal direction and timing.
steps.outcome: Further self-forwarding blocked without alerting the user prematurely.

steps.title: Determine feasibility of remote deletion
steps.desc: Assess whether the personal email provider or account is in any way recoverable/company-managed (e.g. a personal Office 365 tenant under a different agreement).
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether remote remediation of the received data is possible.
steps.abort: If sent to a fully personal, non-company-managed address, remote remediation is typically not possible; proceed to Legal for external options.

steps.title: Assess data exposure and determine disciplinary/legal action
steps.desc: Work with HR/Legal to assess business impact and appropriate response, ranging from a policy reminder to formal disciplinary action.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and resolution path (disciplinary, legal, or educational) agreed with HR/Legal.

steps.title: Confirm no residual access to the personal account/device
steps.desc: Verify the personal email account or synced device is not still receiving company mail once containment is lifted, and re-issue a written policy acknowledgment to the employee if they remain employed.
steps.outcome: No further leakage and policy acknowledgment on file.

steps.title: Document the case and review self-forward DLP coverage
steps.desc: Record the timeline and evaluate whether DLP rules should be tightened to alert on outbound mail to personal domains for sensitive data classes.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with HR/Legal sign-off and any DLP tuning tracked.

ITID-34212.def: An authorized user emails sensitive organizational data to a co-worker's internal mailbox where that co-worker has no legitimate business need for the data, with the intent of retrieving or re-accessing it later — often as a way to move data to a mailbox less likely to be scrutinized, or ahead of the sender's own access being revoked.
ITID-34212.purpose: Captures the technical mechanism of an insider emailing sensitive data to another internal colleague's mailbox who is not part of the legitimate business process, to launder the data through an internal hop before later retrieval.
scopeIncludes: Data sent to a colleague's internal mailbox with no business justification, followed by later retrieval or forwarding by the original sender or an accomplice
Use of a colleague's mailbox as an intermediate 'drop point' ahead of the sender's planned departure
scopeExcludes: Sending data directly to the insider's own personal email account (see Insider Self-Forwarding Sensitive Data to Personal Email)
Motivation and behavioral investigation of the insider (see ITID-13111–13114 Insider Threats/Risk domain) — this leaf covers only the technical mechanism
Collaboration where the receiving colleague is a knowing, active accomplice coordinating with an external attacker (see the ITID-13511–13513 Insider Collaboration with External Attacker leaves)
ITID-34212.severity: Medium-High, scaling with data sensitivity and whether the receiving colleague appears complicit versus unaware.
ITID-34212.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if evidence suggests coordinated intent between sender and recipient.
ITID-34212.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal; assess whether the recipient colleague requires separate investigation for complicity.
indicators: Internal email logs showing sensitive data sent to a colleague with no functional/business relationship to that data
Recipient colleague subsequently forwarding or downloading the same data externally
Pattern of internal transfers shortly before the sender's resignation or termination
vectors: Direct internal email transfer of sensitive attachments/content to an uninvolved colleague
Use of internal shared mailboxes or distribution lists as an indirect data parking mechanism
rootCauses: No internal DLP monitoring for sensitive data moving between mailboxes with no functional relationship
Lack of least-privilege review flagging unusual internal data flows
No correlation between HR departure timelines and internal data movement patterns
controls: Internal DLP monitoring for anomalous mailbox-to-mailbox sensitive data transfers
HR departure/notice-period correlation with data movement monitoring
Least-privilege access reviews on sensitive data repositories
ITID-34212.detection: Moderate — internal-to-internal transfers are generally less monitored than external sends, making this a harder detection surface than ITID-34211.
ITID-34212.response: Preserve internal mail logs for both sender and recipient, investigate the recipient's role, and coordinate with Insider Threat/HR before any account action.
metrics: Count of internal DLP alerts for unusual mailbox-to-mailbox sensitive transfers per quarter
ITID-34212.notes: Scope decision: this leaf covers the technical laundering-via-internal-mailbox mechanism only; motive and case management route to ITID-13111–13114, and any evidence of active recipient complicity with an external actor routes to ITID-13511–13513 instead.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Emailing Data to an Uninvolved Internal Colleague for Later Retrieval
playbook.description: For an insider identified as emailing sensitive data to a colleague uninvolved in the relevant work, apparently staging it for later personal retrieval or off-site collection.

steps.title: Confirm the recipient has no legitimate business need for the data
steps.desc: Review the recipient's role and confirm with their manager whether they had a legitimate reason to receive the data.
steps.guidance: Do not tip off either the sender or the recipient while confirming.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the transfer was outside normal business need.
steps.abort: If the recipient had a legitimate need, document and close as a false positive.

steps.title: Determine whether the recipient mailbox was subsequently accessed externally
steps.desc: Check whether the recipient's mailbox was later accessed via personal device, webmail from an unusual location, or forwarded onward.
steps.outcome: Determined whether the staged data has already moved further, and to where.

steps.title: Notify HR and Legal before further action
steps.desc: Given the coordinated, multi-person nature of this activity, involve HR and Legal early to guide interviews and any account restrictions.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and directing next steps.

steps.title: Preserve both mailboxes and restrict onward movement
steps.desc: Export/preserve both the sender's and recipient's mailboxes, and apply holds or forwarding restrictions per HR/Legal direction.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and further movement of the staged data prevented.

steps.title: Remove the staged data from the recipient mailbox once evidence is secured
steps.desc: After forensic preservation, coordinate with HR/Legal on removing or quarantining the staged copies.
steps.outcome: Staged data no longer accessible to either party pending investigation outcome.

steps.title: Assess intent and determine disciplinary/legal action for both parties
steps.desc: Work with HR/Legal to determine whether the recipient was a knowing participant and what action is warranted for each individual.
steps.outcome: Resolution path agreed for both employees.

steps.title: Confirm both mailboxes are restored to normal monitored state
steps.desc: Once investigation concludes, lift any temporary holds and confirm both accounts return to standard monitoring.
steps.outcome: Both accounts back to normal operating state under standard monitoring.

steps.title: Document the case and review internal-transfer monitoring
steps.desc: Record findings and evaluate whether DLP should flag sensitive-data transfers to colleagues outside a project's normal distribution list.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with HR/Legal sign-off.

ITID-34213.def: An authorized user, in the period shortly before a known resignation, termination, or role change, sends an unusually large volume or breadth of sensitive organizational data via email (to a personal account, a colleague, or otherwise) compared to their normal baseline activity.
ITID-34213.purpose: Captures the technical mechanism of a departing employee bulk-emailing organizational data to themselves or others in the window immediately before their exit.
scopeIncludes: A spike in outbound email volume/attachment count in the days or weeks before a confirmed departure date
Bulk collection-and-send activity (e.g., emailing entire project archives, contact lists, or client files) tied to a known exit event
scopeExcludes: A single self-forward with no departure-timing correlation (see Insider Self-Forwarding Sensitive Data to Personal Email)
Motivation and behavioral investigation of the departing insider (see ITID-13111–13114 Insider Threats/Risk domain) — this leaf covers only the technical bulk-send pattern
ITID-34213.severity: High, given the volume and the closing window for investigation before account deactivation.
ITID-34213.priority: P1 — departure timing narrows the response window significantly and should trigger expedited handling.
ITID-34213.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal immediately; coordinate account access review with IT before the standard offboarding deactivation if not yet executed.
indicators: Outbound email volume/attachment-size spike correlated with an HR-recorded resignation or termination date
Bulk export/email of entire folders, project archives, or contact/client lists shortly before exit
Activity occurring outside the employee's normal working pattern in their final days
vectors: Bulk manual forwarding of multiple emails/attachments to a personal account ahead of departure
Mass export-then-email of files from shared drives or CRM systems in the final days of employment
rootCauses: No automated pre-departure monitoring tied to HR exit/resignation triggers
Standard offboarding process not tightening monitoring or access ahead of the last working day
No volume-based anomaly detection on outbound email activity
controls: HR-triggered heightened monitoring during notice/exit periods
Volume-based outbound email anomaly detection
Pre-emptive access review/tightening ahead of confirmed departure dates
ITID-34213.detection: Good where HR exit data feeds into security monitoring (departure-aware UEBA); weak where security and HR offboarding processes are not integrated.
ITID-34213.response: Immediately review and, if not already scheduled, expedite account access restriction; preserve all outbound mail evidence and conduct a full data-scope investigation before the employee's final day where feasible.
metrics: Percentage of departures with HR-to-security exit monitoring triggered
Volume of data flagged as bulk-sent during exit windows per quarter
ITID-34213.notes: Scope decision: this leaf covers the technical bulk-send-before-exit pattern only; motive and case management route to ITID-13111–13114 to avoid duplicating that domain's content here.

playbook.name: Response: Departing Employee Bulk-Emailing Data Before Exit
playbook.description: For a departing employee identified as having emailed a large volume of company data to a personal account before their exit.

steps.title: Confirm the scope of emailed data
steps.desc: Review mail server/DLP logs for all outbound messages from the employee's account to personal addresses during the relevant window.
steps.guidance: Widen the window to cover the weeks leading up to resignation notice, not just the final days.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of what was sent, when, and to which destination address.

steps.title: Loop in HR and Legal before further action
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal given the personnel and potential IP/trade-secret implications.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and directing next steps.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with proper chain of custody
steps.desc: Image the employee's mailbox and device before any account action that could alert them or lose data.
steps.outcome: Forensically sound evidence preserved.

steps.title: Restrict account access per HR/Legal direction
steps.desc: Suspend mail-sending and file-access privileges, timed per HR/Legal guidance.
steps.outcome: Further exfiltration prevented.

steps.title: Assess whether the recipient address is recoverable/revocable
steps.desc: Determine if the personal email provider or a corporate-controlled destination allows remote deletion.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether remote remediation of the sent data is possible.
steps.abort: If sent to a personal, non-company-managed address, remote remediation typically isn't possible — proceed to Legal for external options.

steps.title: Assess data-loss/IP exposure with Legal and business stakeholders
steps.desc: Determine business impact and whether legal action (cease-and-desist, injunction) is warranted.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and next legal steps determined.

steps.title: Finalize offboarding and revoke all remaining access
steps.desc: Ensure standard offboarding (device return, full account deprovisioning) proceeds and confirm no lingering access remains once the investigation permits it.
steps.outcome: Employee fully offboarded with no residual access.

steps.title: Document the case and review offboarding/DLP controls
steps.desc: Record the timeline and assess whether earlier DLP alerting or offboarding-timing changes would have caught this sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with HR/Legal sign-off.

ITID-34214.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via an insider's own internal email account, where the specific pattern (self-forwarding, internal-colleague laundering, or departure-driven bulk send) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34214.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for internal email account exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific internal-email exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34211, ITID-34212, or ITID-34213
ITID-34214.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34214.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34214.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic internal email DLP alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
controls: General outbound email DLP monitoring
ITID-34214.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34214.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified internal email exfil incidents
detections: General outbound email exfiltration anomaly alerting
ITID-34214.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Internal Email Account Exfiltration
playbook.description: For internal-email-account-based exfiltration activity that does not fit a more specific sub-category — use as a general starting checklist and escalate to a specific playbook once the pattern is clear.

steps.title: Characterize the exfiltration activity
steps.desc: Review mail server/DLP logs to determine what data was sent, to whom, when, and by which account, to identify whether this matches a known specific pattern (self-forwarding, colleague-staging, departing employee).
steps.outcome: Activity characterized well enough to either proceed here or redirect to a more specific playbook.

steps.title: Assess data sensitivity and employment context
steps.desc: Classify the sensitivity of the data involved and check the employee's status (active, under notice, recently disciplined).
steps.outcome: Risk level established.

steps.title: Notify HR and Legal
steps.desc: Loop in HR (and Legal for sensitive/regulated data) before taking account action.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and directing next steps.

steps.title: Restrict further outbound transfer as directed
steps.desc: Apply mail restrictions or account holds per HR/Legal guidance.
steps.outcome: Further exfiltration prevented.

steps.title: Assess remediation options for the exfiltrated data
steps.desc: Determine if any of the destination locations are recoverable or subject to deletion requests.
steps.outcome: Confirmed remediation options, if any.

steps.title: Determine appropriate resolution with HR/Legal
steps.desc: Agree on disciplinary, legal, or educational resolution based on findings.
steps.outcome: Resolution path agreed.

steps.title: Confirm the account/mailbox is returned to normal monitored state
steps.desc: Lift any temporary restrictions once resolution is complete and confirm normal monitoring resumes.
steps.outcome: Account returned to standard operating state.

steps.title: Document and reclassify for future reference
steps.desc: Record the case, and if it matches a more specific pattern, note it for future classification consistency.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34221.def: Following compromise of a legitimate user's email account (via phishing, credential stuffing, etc.), the attacker configures a mailbox rule (client-side or server-side) that silently forwards or BCCs some or all incoming/outgoing mail to an attacker-controlled address, providing ongoing, low-effort exfiltration.
ITID-34221.purpose: Captures an attacker configuring a persistent, silent auto-forwarding rule on a compromised (not self-owned) email account to continuously exfiltrate mail without further manual action.
scopeIncludes: Server-side or client-side inbox rules created by an attacker post-account-compromise to forward mail externally
Hidden/disguised forwarding rules (e.g., named to look benign, or excluded from the mailbox rule UI) set up after account takeover
scopeExcludes: An insider deliberately configuring their own forwarding rule on their own account (a distinct sibling group under the ITID-346xx Insider Email Forwarding Rule Exfiltration leaves, not this compromised-account group)
A one-off manual send of stolen data from the compromised mailbox with no persistent rule (see Attacker Manually Sending Stolen Data from Compromised Mailbox)
ITID-34221.severity: High — persistent forwarding rules provide ongoing exposure until discovered and removed, not just a single data-loss event.
ITID-34221.priority: P1 on confirmation, given the ongoing/compounding nature of the exposure.
ITID-34221.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; force password reset, revoke sessions, and audit all mailbox rules on the affected account and any others accessed by the same attacker.
indicators: Newly created inbox/mail-flow rule forwarding to an external, unrecognized address
Mailbox audit log showing rule creation from an unfamiliar IP/location around the time of suspected compromise
Rule configured to delete or hide forwarded copies from the mailbox to avoid detection by the legitimate user
vectors: Attacker uses stolen credentials or an OAuth token from a phishing attack to log into the mailbox and create a forwarding rule
Business Email Compromise (BEC) actor sets up forwarding as part of a broader fraud scheme
rootCauses: No monitoring/alerting on creation of new mail-forwarding rules
Lack of MFA allowing credential-based account takeover in the first place
Mail-flow rules not regularly audited for unauthorized external forwarding
mitreTechniques: T1114.003 Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
controls: Alerting on creation/modification of mailbox forwarding rules
MFA enforcement on all email accounts
Periodic audit of all active mail-flow/forwarding rules tenant-wide
ITID-34221.detection: Strong where mailbox audit logging and forwarding-rule alerting are enabled (native in most modern email platforms); weak if audit logging is not turned on.
ITID-34221.response: Remove the forwarding rule, reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens, and review all mail sent/received during the rule's active period to scope data loss.
metrics: Count of malicious forwarding rules detected and removed per quarter
Mean time to detect an unauthorized forwarding rule
ITID-34221.notes: Scope decision: this leaf is specifically for attacker-created rules on a compromised account; an insider's self-configured forwarding rule on their own legitimate account is a distinct, separately-tracked leaf group (ITID-346xx) and is out of scope here to avoid overlap.

playbook.name: Response: Auto-Forwarding Rule Configured for Silent Data Exfiltration
playbook.description: For a compromised mailbox with a hidden auto-forwarding rule silently sending incoming/outgoing mail to an attacker-controlled address.

steps.title: Enumerate all mailbox rules for the affected account
steps.desc: Pull the full list of inbox rules (including hidden/server-side rules not visible in the client UI) and identify the malicious forwarding rule and its destination.
steps.guidance: Attacker rules are often named innocuously or use hidden rule flags — check via admin PowerShell/API, not just the mail client.
steps.outcome: Malicious rule and destination address identified.
steps.tool: Mail admin console / mailbox rule audit

steps.title: Determine the compromise vector and account access history
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs for the account to find the initial compromise (phishing, credential stuffing, token theft) and how long the rule has been active.
steps.outcome: Compromise timeline and vector established.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions and OAuth/refresh tokens for the account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access to the mailbox terminated.

steps.title: Remove the malicious forwarding rule and audit for others
steps.desc: Delete the identified rule and audit all mailboxes in the tenant for similarly-patterned hidden forwarding rules.
steps.outcome: Malicious rule removed and no similar rules remain elsewhere.
steps.tool: Mail admin console / bulk rule audit script

steps.title: Enforce MFA and conditional access on the account
steps.desc: Ensure MFA is enrolled and enforced, and apply conditional access policies to prevent re-compromise.
steps.outcome: Account hardened against repeat compromise.

steps.title: Determine what data was exposed via the forwarded mail
steps.desc: Review the volume and sensitivity of mail forwarded during the rule's active window to scope the data-exposure impact.
steps.outcome: Data exposure scoped for notification/impact assessment.

steps.title: Assess breach-notification obligations with Legal
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal on whether the exposed data triggers regulatory or contractual notification requirements.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations determined and actioned if required.

steps.title: Document and review forwarding-rule alerting
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm alerting exists for newly created external-forwarding rules tenant-wide.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and alerting gap closed if found.

ITID-34222.def: Following compromise of a legitimate user's email account, the attacker manually searches the mailbox for valuable data (financial documents, credentials, sensitive attachments) and sends it directly to an external address they control, as a discrete, one-time action rather than an ongoing rule-based mechanism.
ITID-34222.purpose: Captures an attacker manually locating and sending stolen data from a compromised mailbox as a one-off action, rather than establishing a persistent automated forwarding mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Attacker logging into a compromised webmail/mail client session and manually forwarding or composing a message with stolen attachments to their own address
One-off searches within the compromised mailbox (e.g., for 'invoice', 'wire transfer', 'password') followed by a manual send of found content
scopeExcludes: A persistent auto-forwarding rule configured for ongoing exfiltration (see Auto-Forwarding Rule Configured for Silent Data Exfiltration)
Use of the draft folder to avoid a traceable sent-item record (see Compromised Mailbox Used to Exfiltrate via Draft Folder)
ITID-34222.severity: Medium-High, generally somewhat lower ongoing risk than a persistent rule since it is a bounded, one-time event, but still confirms full mailbox compromise and data loss.
ITID-34222.priority: P1 on confirmation of the compromise and data sent; treat urgently given likely concurrent BEC/fraud risk.
ITID-34222.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; force password reset/session revocation and review sent items for the full scope of what was sent.
indicators: Sent-items folder containing outbound messages the legitimate user did not send, often around a login from an unfamiliar location/device
Search activity within the mailbox for financial or credential-related keywords shortly before an anomalous send
Login anomaly (impossible travel, new device) immediately preceding the send
vectors: Credential-phished or credential-stuffed account accessed directly by the attacker to manually search and exfiltrate
Session hijacking via stolen cookies/tokens used to access webmail and manually send data
rootCauses: Lack of MFA enabling straightforward credential-based takeover
No login anomaly detection (impossible travel, new device/location alerts)
No monitoring of sent-item anomalies
controls: MFA enforcement on all email accounts
Login anomaly/impossible-travel detection
Sent-item and mailbox-access audit log monitoring
ITID-34222.detection: Moderate — relies on login-anomaly detection and sent-item review, which many organizations do not actively monitor in real time.
ITID-34222.response: Reset credentials, revoke sessions, review sent items and mailbox access logs to determine exactly what was searched for and sent, and notify affected data owners.
metrics: Count of confirmed manual-exfil-from-compromised-mailbox incidents per quarter
ITID-34222.notes: Differentiated from ITID-34221 by the one-off manual nature of the send versus a persistent automated rule; both may occur in the same incident, in which case log the rule under ITID-34221 and reference this leaf for the manual component.

playbook.name: Response: Attacker Manually Sending Stolen Data from Compromised Mailbox
playbook.description: For a compromised mailbox where the attacker manually composed and sent messages containing stolen data, rather than using an auto-forward rule.

steps.title: Identify the sent messages and their content
steps.desc: Review the Sent Items folder and mail gateway logs for messages the legitimate user did not send, noting recipients, attachments, and content.
steps.outcome: Full list of attacker-sent messages and data disclosed.

steps.title: Determine the compromise vector and access timeline
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs to establish how and when the account was compromised.
steps.outcome: Compromise timeline and vector established.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions and OAuth/refresh tokens for the account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Audit for forwarding rules and mailbox delegation changes
steps.desc: Check for any forwarding rules, delegate access, or mailbox permission changes the attacker may have also added.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no additional persistence mechanisms remain.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and conditional access on the account
steps.desc: Ensure MFA is enrolled and enforced, and apply conditional access policies to prevent re-compromise.
steps.outcome: Account hardened against repeat compromise.

steps.title: Notify recipients and scope data-exposure impact
steps.desc: Where the data disclosed is sensitive/regulated, coordinate with Legal on recipient notification and breach-reporting obligations.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and notification obligations addressed.

steps.title: Restore normal mailbox operation
steps.desc: Confirm the account is functioning normally for the legitimate user and no further attacker artifacts remain.
steps.outcome: Mailbox confirmed clean and restored to the legitimate user.

steps.title: Document and review anomalous-send detection
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether behavioral send-pattern alerting would have caught this sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34223.def: An attacker who has compromised a mailbox composes or saves stolen data as an unsent draft message, which another party with access to the same account (a co-conspirator, or the attacker returning later) reads directly from the Drafts folder, deliberately avoiding the Sent/Inbox trail that a normal send-and-receive exchange would create.
ITID-34223.purpose: Captures the specific evasion technique of an attacker using a compromised mailbox's Drafts folder to stage or relay stolen data without ever sending a traceable message.
scopeIncludes: Stolen data saved as a draft and never sent, later retrieved by the attacker or an accomplice with access to the same mailbox
Multiple co-conspirators sharing one compromised mailbox's credentials to exchange data purely via drafts
scopeExcludes: A traditional send of stolen data to an external address (see Attacker Manually Sending Stolen Data from Compromised Mailbox)
A persistent forwarding rule (see Auto-Forwarding Rule Configured for Silent Data Exfiltration)
ITID-34223.severity: High — the technique's specific purpose is evading standard mail-flow-based detection, indicating a more sophisticated/careful adversary.
ITID-34223.priority: P1 on confirmation; treat as a strong indicator of premeditated, detection-aware tradecraft.
ITID-34223.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR immediately; forensically preserve the Drafts folder and full mailbox audit trail before any remediation that might alter it.
indicators: Draft messages present containing sensitive data that the legitimate user did not create
Mailbox access logs showing logins from multiple distinct locations/devices with no corresponding sent mail
Drafts folder modification timestamps inconsistent with the legitimate user's known activity pattern
vectors: Credential-compromised mailbox shared covertly between two or more collaborating threat actors
Attacker using the draft-folder technique specifically because outbound mail-flow monitoring is known to be strong
rootCauses: Mail-flow-based DLP/monitoring that only inspects sent/received messages, missing drafts entirely
No mailbox access-pattern anomaly detection covering non-send activity
Lack of MFA enabling the initial credential compromise
controls: Mailbox audit logging extended to cover Drafts folder access/modification, not just sent mail
MFA enforcement on all email accounts
Access-pattern anomaly detection covering login/location diversity on a single account
ITID-34223.detection: Weak by design — most mail-flow DLP tooling inspects only sent/received traffic and will not see draft-based exchange; requires mailbox-level audit logging to close the gap.
ITID-34223.response: Preserve the Drafts folder and full access logs forensically, reset credentials, and identify every account/session that accessed the mailbox during the compromise window.
metrics: Count of draft-folder-based exfiltration techniques identified per year
ITID-34223.notes: Reserved specifically for the draft-folder evasion technique; if data was actually sent/forwarded, classify under ITID-34221 or ITID-34222 instead.

playbook.name: Response: Compromised Mailbox Used to Exfiltrate via Draft Folder (Never-Sent Message Technique)
playbook.description: For a compromised mailbox where the attacker staged or exfiltrated data using draft messages that were never sent, evading normal sent-mail monitoring.

steps.title: Check the Drafts folder for attacker-created content
steps.desc: Specifically inspect the mailbox's Drafts folder (and any subfolders) for messages the legitimate user did not create, since this technique evades Sent Items and outbound mail-gateway monitoring entirely.
steps.guidance: This is the single most important identification step for this technique — normal DLP/sent-mail review will miss it because no message is ever transmitted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence/absence of attacker-authored draft content and what data it contains.

steps.title: Determine whether drafts were accessed via a shared/linked account
steps.desc: Check sign-in logs for access to the mailbox from unrecognized locations/devices around the time the drafts were created or modified, which may indicate the attacker is reading the drafts from a separate compromised or attacker-owned account with shared access.
steps.outcome: Access pattern and likely second-party access point identified.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions and OAuth/refresh tokens for the account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Preserve and remove the draft content
steps.desc: Export the draft messages for evidence before deleting them, and check for any shared-mailbox or delegate access enabling the second party to read drafts.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and exfiltration channel closed.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and review delegate/shared-mailbox permissions
steps.desc: Ensure MFA is enforced and audit/remove any unnecessary delegate access or shared-mailbox permissions on the account.
steps.outcome: Account hardened and unauthorized access paths closed.

steps.title: Scope data exposure from staged draft content
steps.desc: Assess what sensitive data was staged in drafts to determine breach-notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Impact scoped.

steps.title: Assess breach-notification obligations with Legal
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal on whether the staged data triggers regulatory or contractual notification requirements, even though it was never transmitted.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations determined.

steps.title: Document and add draft-folder monitoring to DLP scope
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate adding draft-folder change monitoring to DLP/mailbox-audit tooling, since this vector is otherwise invisible to standard controls.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and monitoring gap addressed.

ITID-34224.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a compromised email account, where the specific mechanism (auto-forwarding rule, manual send, or draft-folder technique) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34224.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for compromised email account exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific compromised-mailbox exfil mechanism is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific mechanism has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34221, ITID-34222, or ITID-34223
ITID-34224.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34224.priority: P1 pending triage given account compromise is already confirmed; refine once mechanism is known.
ITID-34224.escalation: Escalate as for confirmed account takeover; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic account-compromise indicator (anomalous login, MFA bypass) without a confirmed exfil mechanism yet identified
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration mechanism
controls: General mailbox compromise/account-takeover monitoring
ITID-34224.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34224.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as confirmed account compromise in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified compromised-mailbox exfil incidents
ITID-34224.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Compromised Email Account Exfiltration
playbook.description: For compromised-mailbox exfiltration activity that does not fit a more specific sub-category — use as a general starting checklist and escalate to a specific playbook once the pattern is clear.

steps.title: Confirm compromise and characterize the exfiltration method
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs, mailbox rules, Sent Items, and Drafts to determine how the account was compromised and which exfiltration mechanism (forwarding rule, manual send, drafts) was used.
steps.outcome: Compromise and exfiltration method characterized well enough to redirect to a specific playbook or proceed here.
steps.tool: Identity provider logs / mail admin console

steps.title: Scope data exposure
steps.desc: Determine what data was accessed or transmitted during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Data exposure scoped.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions and OAuth/refresh tokens for the account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Audit and remove any persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Check for forwarding rules, delegate access, and OAuth app grants added during the compromise, and remove them.
steps.outcome: All attacker persistence removed.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and conditional access
steps.desc: Ensure MFA is enrolled and enforced, and apply conditional access to prevent re-compromise.
steps.outcome: Account hardened.

steps.title: Assess notification and breach-reporting obligations
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal on any required disclosure based on the data exposed.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations addressed.

steps.title: Restore normal account operation
steps.desc: Confirm the account is functioning normally for the legitimate user and no attacker artifacts remain.
steps.outcome: Account confirmed clean and restored.

steps.title: Document and reclassify for future reference
steps.desc: Record the case, and note the specific technique used for future classification consistency.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34231.def: Exfiltration in which a large volume of sensitive data is sent in one outbound email as a single large attachment (a database export, archive, or large document), typically large enough to be conspicuous by size alone.
ITID-34231.purpose: Captures the simplest and most direct pattern of email-based bulk exfiltration: a single, large attachment sent in one message.
scopeIncludes: A single outbound email with one unusually large attachment containing sensitive data
Attachment size itself being the primary signal distinguishing this from routine business correspondence
scopeExcludes: The same total data volume deliberately split across multiple smaller attachments/messages to stay under a size threshold (see Multiple Split/Segmented Attachments)
Data hidden inside a compressed or password-protected archive specifically to defeat content inspection (see Compressed/Password-Protected Archive Attachment)
ITID-34231.severity: Medium-High, scaling directly with attachment size and data sensitivity.
ITID-34231.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for very large volumes or highly sensitive/regulated data categories.
ITID-34231.escalation: Escalate to data owner and, where an insider is suspected, to Insider Threat/HR; escalate to legal/privacy if regulated data is confirmed.
indicators: Outbound email attachment size far exceeding the sender's or department's historical norm
DLP size-threshold or content-pattern alert triggered on an outbound message
Recipient domain with no known business relationship to the sender
vectors: Manual attachment of a bulk data export/report to an outbound email
Malware or script automating attachment and send of collected data via the mail client/API
rootCauses: No DLP size-threshold or content-inspection policy on outbound attachments
Overly permissive attachment size limits with no review workflow for large sends
No baseline of normal attachment-size patterns per user/department
controls: DLP size-threshold and content-inspection policy on outbound email attachments
Approval workflow for unusually large outbound attachments
User behavior baselining for attachment size/frequency
ITID-34231.detection: Strong where DLP with size and content-pattern rules is deployed on the mail gateway; weak without any outbound attachment inspection.
ITID-34231.response: Quarantine/recall the message where possible, identify the recipient and content sent, and determine intent (insider vs. compromised account) before further action.
metrics: Count of DLP size-threshold blocks/alerts per quarter
Average size of flagged outbound attachments
ITID-34231.notes: The differentiator from sibling ITIDs is the absence of any splitting or archive-obfuscation technique; this is the straightforward, unobfuscated bulk-attachment case.

playbook.name: Response: Bulk Data Exfiltration via Single Large Attachment
playbook.description: For a single unusually large email attachment identified as containing bulk exfiltrated data.

steps.title: Identify and inspect the large attachment
steps.desc: Pull the message and attachment from mail gateway logs/quarantine, confirm the file type and contents, and identify the sender, recipient, and timing.
steps.outcome: Attachment content and data classification confirmed.
steps.tool: Mail gateway / email security gateway quarantine

steps.title: Determine whether this was sent by a compromised account or an insider
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs and the sender's recent activity to determine if the account is compromised or if this is insider-driven.
steps.guidance: If insider-driven, escalate to HR/Legal per insider-data-handling policy.
steps.outcome: Root cause (compromise vs. insider) established.

steps.title: Block/quarantine the message if not already delivered
steps.desc: If the message is still in transit or quarantined, block delivery; if already delivered, assess remote-wipe/recall options.
steps.outcome: Further delivery or access to the attachment prevented where possible.

steps.title: Contain the account or notify HR/Legal as appropriate
steps.desc: If compromised, reset credentials and revoke sessions; if insider-driven, notify HR/Legal before further account action.
steps.outcome: Root cause contained appropriately.

steps.title: Tune size-based DLP thresholds if this attachment evaded detection
steps.desc: Review why the attachment was not flagged (if applicable) and adjust DLP size/content thresholds.
steps.outcome: DLP gap closed.

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess the sensitivity of the data sent and coordinate with Legal on any required disclosure.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Confirm remediation is complete
steps.desc: Verify the account/mailbox is restored to normal operation and any remote-wipe or recall action has taken effect where applicable.
steps.outcome: Remediation confirmed complete.

steps.title: Document the case and review attachment-size DLP policy
steps.desc: Record findings and confirm DLP thresholds are appropriately tuned to catch bulk single-file transfers.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and policy reviewed.

ITID-34232.def: Exfiltration in which a large data set is deliberately broken into multiple smaller attachments and/or sent across several separate emails, each individually small enough to fall below a size-based DLP or mail-gateway inspection threshold, defeating detection that relies purely on single-message size.
ITID-34232.purpose: Captures the specific evasion technique of splitting a large data set across multiple smaller attachments or messages to stay under a size-based DLP threshold.
scopeIncludes: A single file split into multiple parts (e.g., .zip.001, .zip.002) sent across successive emails
Multiple distinct smaller files sent in a rapid succession of messages to the same recipient, collectively constituting a large bulk transfer
scopeExcludes: A single large attachment sent without any splitting technique (see Bulk Data Exfiltration via Single Large Attachment)
Compression/password-protection used as the primary evasion mechanism rather than splitting (see Compressed/Password-Protected Archive Attachment)
ITID-34232.severity: High — the deliberate splitting behavior indicates awareness of and intent to evade existing DLP controls.
ITID-34232.priority: P1 on confirmation, given the demonstrated intent to defeat detection.
ITID-34232.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and SOC/IR immediately upon pattern confirmation.
indicators: Multiple emails to the same external/internal recipient in a short window, each with a similarly-sized attachment just under the DLP threshold
Sequentially-named file parts (e.g., part1, part2) across separate messages
Sudden change in a user's sending pattern to many small messages instead of their historical norm
vectors: Manual splitting of a large file into parts before sending across multiple emails
Scripted/automated splitting and sending to evade a known size threshold
rootCauses: DLP policy relying solely on single-message size thresholds without aggregate/time-windowed analysis
No correlation of multiple outbound messages to the same recipient over a short time window
Users' awareness of the exact DLP size threshold, often from internal documentation or trial-and-error
controls: DLP aggregate/time-windowed analysis of multiple small outbound sends to the same recipient
Alerting on sequential file-part naming patterns
Periodic review/adjustment of DLP thresholds to close known gaps
ITID-34232.detection: Weak against pure size-threshold DLP by design; requires aggregate/pattern-based analysis across multiple messages to detect reliably.
ITID-34232.response: Correlate and reassemble the full set of related messages/attachments to determine true total data volume, then proceed as for any confirmed bulk exfiltration.
metrics: Count of detected split-attachment evasion attempts per quarter
DLP aggregate-analysis coverage percentage
ITID-34232.notes: Differentiated from ITID-34231 specifically by the deliberate splitting/segmentation intended to evade size-based controls; treat detection of this pattern as a signal to review DLP threshold configuration.

playbook.name: Response: Data Exfiltration via Multiple Split/Segmented Attachments (Evading Size-Based DLP)
playbook.description: For exfiltration carried out by splitting a large dataset across multiple smaller attachments/messages, each under size-based DLP thresholds.

steps.title: Correlate the split messages into a single exfiltration event
steps.desc: Review mail gateway logs for a series of similarly-named or sequentially-numbered attachments sent by the same account to the same recipient over a short window, and reassemble the total volume transferred.
steps.guidance: Look for naming patterns like part1/part2, .001/.002, or identical filenames sent repeatedly in quick succession.
steps.outcome: Full set of split messages identified and total data volume/content established.

steps.title: Determine whether this is a compromised account or insider activity
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs and recent account behavior to establish root cause; the deliberate splitting pattern suggests intentional DLP evasion.
steps.guidance: If insider-driven, escalate to HR/Legal per insider-data-handling policy given the deliberate evasion.
steps.outcome: Root cause established.

steps.title: Block further segments and quarantine already-sent messages where possible
steps.desc: Prevent any remaining segments from being delivered, and assess recall/remote-wipe options for delivered ones.
steps.outcome: Further transfer of remaining segments prevented.

steps.title: Contain the account or notify HR/Legal as appropriate
steps.desc: If compromised, reset credentials and revoke sessions; if insider-driven, notify HR/Legal before further account action.
steps.outcome: Root cause contained appropriately.

steps.title: Implement content-aggregation DLP detection
steps.desc: Work with the DLP/security team to add detection logic that aggregates related attachments across a time window rather than evaluating each message in isolation.
steps.outcome: Split-attachment evasion technique no longer bypasses DLP.

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess the sensitivity of the reassembled dataset and coordinate with Legal on any required disclosure.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Confirm remediation is complete
steps.desc: Verify the account is restored to normal operation and no remaining segments are pending delivery.
steps.outcome: Remediation confirmed complete.

steps.title: Document the case and the DLP evasion technique used
steps.desc: Record findings, including the specific splitting pattern, to inform future detection rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with technique documented for detection engineering.

ITID-34233.def: Exfiltration in which sensitive data is packaged into a compressed archive (ZIP, RAR, 7z) that is additionally password-protected or encrypted before being attached to an outbound email, specifically to prevent DLP or mail-gateway content-inspection engines from reading inside the archive to identify sensitive content.
ITID-34233.purpose: Captures the specific evasion technique of hiding exfiltrated data inside a compressed and/or password-protected archive to defeat content-inspection DLP.
scopeIncludes: A password-protected or encrypted ZIP/RAR/7z archive attached to an outbound email containing sensitive data
Use of steganographic or obfuscated file renaming in combination with archiving to further evade inspection
scopeExcludes: An unprotected, non-compressed single large attachment (see Bulk Data Exfiltration via Single Large Attachment)
Splitting data across multiple messages as the primary evasion technique rather than archive protection (see Multiple Split/Segmented Attachments)
ITID-34233.severity: High — password protection specifically defeats content-based DLP, indicating deliberate, informed evasion intent.
ITID-34233.priority: P1 on confirmation, given the demonstrated intent to defeat detection controls.
ITID-34233.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and SOC/IR immediately upon pattern confirmation; request the password from the sender's device/session if legally and procedurally appropriate during investigation.
indicators: Outbound email with a password-protected or encrypted archive attachment that DLP cannot inspect
Password for the archive sent separately (e.g., in a follow-up message, chat, or verbally) to enable recipient access
Archive file type/extension mismatch or renamed extension attempting to disguise the true file type
vectors: Manual creation of a password-protected archive before attaching to an outbound email
Automated/scripted archiving-and-encryption as part of a malware exfil routine
rootCauses: DLP/mail-gateway content inspection unable to open password-protected or encrypted archives
No policy blocking or quarantining unidentifiable/encrypted attachments by default
No monitoring correlating an encrypted-attachment send with a separately-sent password
controls: Default quarantine/hold policy for password-protected or unidentifiable archive attachments pending review
Correlation alerting between encrypted-attachment sends and password-sharing messages
Sandboxed detonation/attempted-password analysis for suspicious archives
ITID-34233.detection: Weak against content-based DLP by design; effective detection depends on policy-based handling of encrypted/unidentifiable attachments rather than content inspection.
ITID-34233.response: Quarantine the message where possible, attempt legitimate access to verify contents during investigation, and treat as confirmed bulk exfiltration once contents are established.
metrics: Count of encrypted/password-protected attachment detections per quarter
Percentage of such attachments successfully reviewed vs. unresolved
ITID-34233.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs specifically by the use of compression plus password-protection/encryption as the evasion mechanism, rather than raw size or message-splitting.

playbook.name: Response: Data Exfiltration via Compressed/Password-Protected Archive Attachment
playbook.description: For exfiltration carried out using a compressed and/or password-protected archive attachment, which also evades content-inspection DLP that cannot see inside the archive.

steps.title: Identify the archive and attempt to determine its contents
steps.desc: Pull the message and archive attachment from mail gateway logs/quarantine. If unencrypted, extract and inspect contents; if password-protected, note that content-based DLP could not scan it.
steps.guidance: Correlate with any separately-sent password (often sent via a different channel like chat or a follow-up email) to attempt extraction for evidentiary purposes.
steps.outcome: Archive contents identified where possible, or confirmed as an unscannable DLP blind spot.
steps.tool: Mail gateway / email security gateway quarantine

steps.title: Determine whether this was sent by a compromised account or an insider
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs and the sender's recent activity to determine if the account is compromised or if this is insider-driven; deliberate password-protection suggests intent to evade detection.
steps.guidance: If insider-driven, escalate to HR/Legal per insider-data-handling policy.
steps.outcome: Root cause established.

steps.title: Block/quarantine the message if not already delivered
steps.desc: If the message is still in transit or quarantined, block delivery; if already delivered, assess remote-wipe/recall options.
steps.outcome: Further delivery or access to the attachment prevented where possible.

steps.title: Contain the account or notify HR/Legal as appropriate
steps.desc: If compromised, reset credentials and revoke sessions; if insider-driven, notify HR/Legal before further account action.
steps.outcome: Root cause contained appropriately.

steps.title: Review and tighten policy on password-protected attachments
steps.desc: Work with the DLP/security team to add default-block or mandatory-inspection policies for password-protected archives leaving the organization.
steps.outcome: Archive-based DLP evasion technique addressed going forward.
steps.tool: DLP / email security gateway policy console

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Where contents could be determined, assess sensitivity and coordinate with Legal on any required disclosure.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.
steps.abort: If the archive contents could never be determined, document the blind spot and proceed on a worst-case assumption with Legal.

steps.title: Confirm remediation is complete
steps.desc: Verify the account is restored to normal operation and controls block similar future transfers.
steps.outcome: Remediation confirmed complete.

steps.title: Document the case and the archive-based evasion technique used
steps.desc: Record findings, including the DLP blind spot presented by encrypted archives, to inform future detection investment.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with technique documented for detection engineering.

ITID-34234.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a large email attachment, where the specific pattern (single large attachment, split/segmented attachments, or compressed/password-protected archive) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34234.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for large-attachment email exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific large-attachment exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34231, ITID-34232, or ITID-34233
ITID-34234.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34234.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34234.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic outbound attachment DLP alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
controls: General outbound attachment DLP monitoring
ITID-34234.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34234.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified large-attachment exfil incidents
detections: General outbound attachment exfiltration anomaly alerting
ITID-34234.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Large Attachment Exfiltration
playbook.description: For large-attachment-based exfiltration activity that does not fit a more specific sub-category — use as a general starting checklist and escalate to a specific playbook once the pattern is clear.

steps.title: Characterize the attachment-based exfiltration
steps.desc: Review mail gateway logs to determine the attachment type, size, sender, recipient, and whether it matches a known pattern (single large file, split segments, compressed archive).
steps.outcome: Activity characterized well enough to redirect to a specific playbook or proceed here.
steps.tool: Mail gateway / email security gateway logs

steps.title: Determine whether this was sent by a compromised account or an insider
steps.desc: Review sign-in logs and recent account behavior to establish root cause.
steps.outcome: Root cause established.

steps.title: Block/quarantine further transfer where possible
steps.desc: Prevent further delivery and assess recall/remote-wipe options for anything already delivered.
steps.outcome: Further transfer prevented.

steps.title: Contain the account or notify HR/Legal as appropriate
steps.desc: If compromised, reset credentials and revoke sessions; if insider-driven, notify HR/Legal before further account action.
steps.outcome: Root cause contained appropriately.

steps.title: Review DLP thresholds and rules relevant to the technique observed
steps.desc: Tune DLP size, content, or archive-handling rules based on what evaded detection.
steps.outcome: DLP gap addressed.

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess sensitivity of the data sent and coordinate with Legal on any required disclosure.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Confirm remediation is complete
steps.desc: Verify the account is restored to normal operation.
steps.outcome: Remediation confirmed complete.

steps.title: Document and reclassify for future reference
steps.desc: Record the case, and note the specific technique used for future classification consistency.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34311.def: An authorized user connects a personally-owned USB storage device (drive, external HDD/SSD) to an organizational endpoint and copies sensitive data onto it, physically removing the data from organizational control without using any network-based channel.
ITID-34311.purpose: Captures the technical mechanism of an insider copying sensitive organizational data onto a personal USB storage device for removal from the premises/network.
scopeIncludes: File copy operations from a corporate endpoint to a personal USB drive detected via endpoint DLP/USB control logging
Insertion of an unrecognized/unregistered USB storage device followed by large file-copy activity
scopeExcludes: Use of an encrypted or password-protected USB device specifically to evade DLP content inspection (see Encrypted/Password-Protected USB Drive Used to Evade DLP Detection)
A USB device physically disguised as another object to avoid visual/physical detection (see USB Device Disguised as Ordinary Object)
Motivation and behavioral investigation of the insider (see the ITID-13111–13114 Insider Threats/Risk domain) — this leaf covers only the technical mechanism
ITID-34311.severity: Medium-High, scaling with data sensitivity and volume copied.
ITID-34311.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for large volumes of highly sensitive data or a departing employee.
ITID-34311.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal in parallel with SOC/IR upon confirmation.
indicators: Endpoint DLP/USB control log showing large file-copy volume to an unregistered removable device
USB device serial number not matching any organization-issued asset
File-copy activity occurring outside normal working hours or shortly before a known departure
vectors: Direct drag-and-drop or command-line copy of sensitive files to an inserted USB drive
Bulk export of a database or file share directly onto removable media
rootCauses: No USB device control policy restricting removable media to organization-issued, encrypted devices
Endpoint DLP not configured to inspect/block copy operations to removable storage
USB ports not disabled or restricted on endpoints handling highly sensitive data
controls: USB device control policy restricting removable media to approved, encrypted, organization-issued devices
Endpoint DLP inspection/blocking of copy operations to removable storage
USB port disablement on endpoints handling highly sensitive data
ITID-34311.detection: Good where endpoint DLP/USB control tooling with device allow-listing and copy-volume logging is deployed; weak without any removable-media control.
ITID-34311.response: Preserve endpoint DLP logs, identify the device and files copied, and recover or account for the physical device where possible.
metrics: Count of unauthorized removable-media copy events detected per quarter
Percentage of endpoints with USB device control enforced
ITID-34311.notes: Scope decision: this leaf and its siblings own only the technical physical-removal mechanism; motive, intent, and case-management investigation route to ITID-13111–13114 to avoid duplicating that domain's content here.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Copying Data to Personal USB Drive
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where an employee copies sensitive files to a personally owned USB drive.

steps.title: Confirm the USB write event and identify files copied
steps.desc: Review DLP/USB device-control logs and endpoint file-access history to confirm the write event to a removable drive and identify which files were copied.
steps.guidance: Correlate device serial number/vendor ID against the device-control policy's known/registered device list.
steps.outcome: Confirmed USB copy event with file list and device identifier established.
steps.abort: If the device is a company-issued, policy-compliant drive used for authorized business purposes, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Review the device-control policy applied to the user/host
steps.desc: Confirm whether USB write access should have been blocked or alerted under the current device-control policy, and identify any policy gap that allowed the transfer.
steps.outcome: Policy gap identified, if any.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Preserve DLP logs, file lists, and device identifiers with a documented chain of custody before any personnel action, given potential disciplinary or legal use.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Engage HR/Legal and, if authorized, recover the physical device
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal, and if authorized, coordinate recovery of the physical USB drive from the employee for forensic imaging.
steps.guidance: Do not attempt device recovery without HR/Legal and, where applicable, physical security involvement.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal engaged; device recovery coordinated if authorized.

steps.title: Forensically image the recovered device
steps.desc: If the device is recovered, create a forensic image and analyze its contents to confirm what data it holds and whether it was further distributed.
steps.outcome: Forensic image obtained and analyzed.
steps.abort: If the device cannot be recovered, document the attempt and proceed with available log evidence.

steps.title: Verify no residual copies remain on the endpoint
steps.desc: Scan the endpoint's local storage, browser history, and application caches for residual copies of the exfiltrated files not captured on the removed device.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed free of residual copies, or copies identified and removed.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action and tighten device-control policy
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal and close any device-control policy gap identified during investigation.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied; policy gap closed.

steps.title: Document the case and review USB device-control coverage
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal and evaluate whether device-control policy needs broader enforcement (e.g. block-by-default with exceptions).
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34312.def: An insider or attacker copies sensitive data onto a USB storage device that is hardware- or software-encrypted (or otherwise password-protected at the volume level), specifically preventing endpoint DLP or forensic tooling from inspecting the content of what was copied, whether in real time or after the fact.
ITID-34312.purpose: Captures the specific evasion technique of using an encrypted or password-protected USB drive to prevent DLP content inspection from identifying what data was copied.
scopeIncludes: Use of a self-encrypting USB drive (hardware keypad or software-locked) to copy sensitive data
Creation of an encrypted container/volume on a standard USB drive before copying data into it
scopeExcludes: Use of an unencrypted, standard USB drive with no evasion technique (see Insider Copying Data to Personal USB Drive)
A device physically disguised as another object as the primary evasion mechanism (see USB Device Disguised as Ordinary Object)
ITID-34312.severity: High — encryption specifically defeats content-based DLP and forensic recovery, indicating deliberate, informed evasion intent.
ITID-34312.priority: P1 on confirmation, given the demonstrated intent to defeat detection and forensic recovery.
ITID-34312.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal immediately; involve digital forensics to assess whether the device or its contents can be recovered/accessed.
indicators: Endpoint DLP/USB control log detecting an encrypted volume or self-encrypting drive connected and used for large file copy
Device model/vendor identified as a known hardware-encrypted USB product
File-copy activity where DLP content inspection reports 'unreadable/encrypted' rather than a content match
vectors: Insider purchasing/bringing a hardware-encrypted USB drive specifically to evade known DLP controls
Creation of a software-encrypted container (e.g., VeraCrypt volume) on a standard USB drive before copying data
rootCauses: USB device control policy not distinguishing or blocking encrypted/unrecognized volume types
No policy prohibiting personally-owned encrypted storage devices on corporate endpoints
Lack of alerting when DLP content inspection is unable to read a removable-media transfer
controls: USB device control policy restricting removable media to approved, organization-issued (non-personal) encrypted devices only
Alerting when DLP content inspection cannot read a removable-media transfer (encrypted/unknown format)
Policy prohibiting personally-owned encrypted storage on corporate endpoints
ITID-34312.detection: Weak against content-based DLP by design; detection depends on device-type/volume-format alerting rather than content inspection.
ITID-34312.response: Recover the physical device where possible, engage digital forensics to attempt access, and treat as confirmed high-sensitivity data loss pending content verification.
metrics: Count of encrypted/unreadable removable-media transfer alerts per quarter
ITID-34312.notes: Differentiated from ITID-34311 specifically by the deliberate use of encryption/password-protection as the evasion mechanism.

playbook.name: Response: Encrypted/Password-Protected USB Drive Used to Evade DLP Detection
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where an employee uses an encrypted or password-protected USB drive specifically to prevent DLP content inspection of the files being copied.

steps.title: Confirm the encrypted device write event and inspect available metadata
steps.desc: Review DLP/USB device-control logs for a write event to an encrypted or password-protected device where content inspection failed or was blocked, and review file metadata (names, sizes, counts) that remained visible despite encryption.
