steps.guidance: Note that content-level DLP inspection may be unavailable for encrypted volumes; rely on file system metadata and user activity context.
steps.outcome: Confirmed encrypted-device transfer event with available metadata documented.
steps.abort: If the device is a company-issued, policy-compliant encrypted drive used for authorized purposes, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Review the device-control policy for encrypted/unmanaged device handling
steps.desc: Determine whether the device-control policy should have blocked unmanaged encrypted devices outright, and identify the policy gap.
steps.outcome: Policy gap identified.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Preserve all available logs and metadata with a documented chain of custody before any personnel action, given potential disciplinary or legal use.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Engage HR/Legal and, if authorized, recover the physical device
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal, and if authorized, coordinate recovery of the physical device, potentially with the employee's decryption cooperation or through legal process.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal engaged; device recovery coordinated if authorized.

steps.title: Attempt forensic access to the recovered device
steps.desc: If recovered and access can be obtained (with cooperation or legal authority), forensically image and analyze the device's contents.
steps.outcome: Forensic image obtained and analyzed where access is possible.
steps.abort: If the device cannot be accessed, document the limitation and proceed with available metadata and log evidence.

steps.title: Verify no residual copies remain on the endpoint
steps.desc: Scan the endpoint's local storage, browser history, and application caches for residual copies of the files not captured on the encrypted device.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed free of residual copies, or copies identified and removed.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action and block unmanaged encrypted devices
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal and update device-control policy to block or require enrollment of encrypted removable devices.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied; policy updated.

steps.title: Document the case and review DLP coverage for encrypted removable media
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal and evaluate detection strategies for encrypted-device use, since content inspection is inherently limited.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34313.def: An insider or attacker uses a USB storage device deliberately built or modified to physically resemble an innocuous object (a pen, watch, charging cable, or novelty item) specifically to evade visual inspection by physical security or casual observation during removal of stolen data from the premises.
ITID-34313.purpose: Captures the specific evasion technique of using a USB storage device physically disguised as an unrelated everyday object to avoid visual detection during removal from the premises.
scopeIncludes: Use of a covert/novelty-form-factor USB storage device to copy and remove data
Modification of an everyday object to conceal a USB storage component
scopeExcludes: Use of a standard-form-factor USB drive, encrypted or not, with no physical disguise element (see the other two USB sibling ITIDs)
A malicious peripheral implant left connected to attack infrastructure rather than carried out by a person (see the Hardware Implants group)
ITID-34313.severity: High — the deliberate physical disguise indicates premeditation and specific intent to defeat physical security controls.
ITID-34313.priority: P1 on confirmation; treat as a strong indicator of premeditated theft.
ITID-34313.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR, legal, and physical security immediately upon confirmation or credible suspicion.
indicators: Endpoint DLP/USB control log identifying a device with a vendor ID/descriptor inconsistent with its outward appearance
Physical security review or search recovering a disguised storage device
Witness or camera evidence of an unusual object being used at a workstation
vectors: Insider bringing a covert-form-factor USB device specifically to defeat casual physical inspection
Use of the device at an endpoint with weaker physical oversight (e.g., after hours, in an isolated area)
rootCauses: No physical security screening/inspection process for devices at sensitive facility exits
USB device control policy not flagging device descriptor/vendor-ID anomalies
Insufficient endpoint physical security in areas handling highly sensitive data
controls: USB device control policy alerting on device descriptor/vendor-ID anomalies regardless of physical form factor
Physical security screening at exits from sensitive facilities
Endpoint-level restriction to organization-issued devices only, identifiable by asset tag/serial
ITID-34313.detection: Weak against purely visual physical security; effective detection depends on endpoint-level USB device fingerprinting rather than appearance-based screening.
ITID-34313.response: Recover the device through physical security/HR process where possible, preserve endpoint DLP logs, and determine full scope of data copied.
metrics: Count of disguised-device incidents identified per year
ITID-34313.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs by the physical-concealment element of the device itself, independent of whether its contents are also encrypted.

playbook.name: Response: USB Device Disguised as Ordinary Object for Covert Removal
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where a USB storage device is disguised as an everyday object (e.g. pen, charger, cable) specifically to defeat visual inspection or physical security checks on the way out of the facility.

steps.title: Confirm the device connection and disguise via endpoint and security logs
steps.desc: Review DLP/USB device-control logs to confirm a removable storage device connected to the host, and cross-reference device vendor/product ID against known disguised-device signatures where available.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with physical security if the disguised device was observed or seized at an exit checkpoint.
steps.outcome: Confirmed device connection event with files copied identified.

steps.title: Review physical security camera footage around the connection time
steps.desc: Coordinate with physical security to review camera footage covering the employee's workspace and facility exits around the time of the device connection to corroborate use and removal of the device.
steps.outcome: Physical corroboration obtained where available.
steps.abort: If footage is unavailable, proceed with log-based evidence alone.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Preserve DLP logs, file lists, and any camera footage with a documented chain of custody before personnel action, given potential disciplinary or legal use.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Engage HR/Legal and physical security to recover the device
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal, and coordinate with physical security to recover the disguised device from the employee if it has not already been seized.
steps.guidance: Do not attempt recovery without HR/Legal and physical security involvement given the deliberate concealment.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal/physical security engaged; device recovery coordinated.

steps.title: Forensically image the recovered device
steps.desc: If the device is recovered, create a forensic image and analyze its contents to confirm the scope of data taken.
steps.outcome: Forensic image obtained and analyzed.
steps.abort: If the device cannot be recovered, document the attempt and proceed with available log evidence.

steps.title: Verify no residual copies remain on the endpoint
steps.desc: Scan the endpoint's local storage and application caches for residual copies of the files not captured on the disguised device.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed free of residual copies, or copies identified and removed.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action and tighten physical/device-control screening
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal, and coordinate with physical security on whether exit screening or device-control policy needs adjustment to catch disguised devices.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied; screening/policy gap addressed.

steps.title: Document the case and review physical exit-screening procedures
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal and physical security, and evaluate whether exit-screening or device-control detection needs improvement for disguised devices.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34314.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a USB storage device, where the specific pattern (standard device, encrypted/password-protected device, or physically disguised device) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34314.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for USB device exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific USB exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34311, ITID-34312, or ITID-34313
ITID-34314.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34314.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34314.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic USB/removable-media DLP alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
controls: General USB device control monitoring
ITID-34314.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34314.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified USB exfil incidents
ITID-34314.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General USB Device Data Transfer Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration via USB device transfer that does not fit a more specific category (personal drive copying, encrypted device evasion, or disguised device).

steps.title: Confirm the USB transfer event and classify the device type
steps.desc: Review DLP/USB device-control logs to confirm the write event, identify the device, and attempt to classify it against more specific categories (personal drive, encrypted/evasive device, or disguised device).
steps.guidance: If the pattern matches a more specific category, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed USB transfer event with device and file scope identified.
steps.abort: If the device is a company-issued, policy-compliant drive used for authorized purposes, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Review device-control policy coverage
steps.desc: Determine whether the device-control policy should have blocked or alerted on this transfer, and identify any gap.
steps.outcome: Policy gap identified, if any.

steps.title: Preserve evidence and engage HR/Legal as warranted
steps.desc: Preserve logs and file lists with documented chain of custody; engage HR/Legal if insider involvement is suspected before further account or personnel action.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved; HR/Legal engaged if warranted.

steps.title: Recover the physical device where authorized
steps.desc: If authorized, recover the physical device for forensic imaging.
steps.outcome: Device recovered where possible.
steps.abort: If recovery is not possible or not authorized, proceed with available log evidence.

steps.title: Forensically analyze the recovered device if available
steps.desc: Image and analyze the device to confirm scope of data taken.
steps.outcome: Forensic analysis completed where device is available.

steps.title: Verify no residual copies remain on the endpoint
steps.desc: Scan the endpoint's local storage for residual copies of the transferred files not captured on the removable device.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed free of residual copies, or copies identified and removed.

steps.title: Apply appropriate action and close policy gaps
steps.desc: Apply personnel action per HR/Legal direction if applicable, and close any device-control policy gap identified.
steps.outcome: Action applied; policy gap closed.

steps.title: Document the case and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification for future reference.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34321.def: An insider connects a personal smartphone or tablet to an organizational endpoint (via USB cable, or a direct wireless protocol such as Bluetooth or AirDrop) and copies sensitive files directly onto the mobile device's local storage.
ITID-34321.purpose: Captures data copied directly from an organizational endpoint onto a personal mobile device via a physical cable connection or a direct wireless transfer protocol.
scopeIncludes: USB cable-based file transfer from a corporate endpoint to a personal phone/tablet (e.g., MTP file transfer mode)
Bluetooth or AirDrop-based direct file transfer to a personal mobile device
scopeExcludes: Photographing or screen-recording on-screen content rather than transferring the underlying file (see Screenshot/Photo of Screen Content Using Personal Mobile Device)
Using the mobile device purely as a network relay/hotspot rather than a storage destination (see Mobile Device Used as Wi-Fi Hotspot to Bypass Network DLP Controls)
ITID-34321.severity: Medium-High, scaling with data sensitivity and volume transferred.
ITID-34321.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for large volumes of highly sensitive data.
ITID-34321.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and legal in parallel with SOC/IR upon confirmation.
indicators: Endpoint DLP/MDM log showing a personal mobile device connected in file-transfer mode with subsequent large file copy
Bluetooth/AirDrop file-transfer event logged to an unrecognized/personal device
Mobile Device Management (MDM) policy violation alert for connection of a non-enrolled device
vectors: Direct USB cable connection with the phone set to file-transfer (MTP) mode rather than charge-only
Bluetooth or AirDrop file send initiated from the corporate endpoint to a nearby personal device
rootCauses: Endpoint configuration allowing USB file-transfer mode rather than restricting to charge-only for unrecognized devices
Bluetooth/AirDrop not disabled or restricted on endpoints handling sensitive data
No MDM enrollment requirement blocking non-enrolled personal devices from pairing
controls: Endpoint policy restricting USB connections to charge-only for non-enrolled devices
Bluetooth/AirDrop/wireless-transfer restriction on endpoints handling sensitive data
MDM enrollment enforcement for any device permitted to pair/transfer files
ITID-34321.detection: Good where endpoint DLP/MDM logs USB mode changes and wireless pairing events; weak where mobile-device connections are not monitored at all.
ITID-34321.response: Preserve endpoint logs, identify the device and files transferred, and where feasible obtain and image the personal device through the appropriate HR/legal process.
metrics: Count of unauthorized mobile-device file-transfer events detected per quarter
ITID-34321.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs by the file-transfer (data copy) nature of the connection, as opposed to screen capture or network-hotspot use.

playbook.name: Response: Data Copied to Personal Mobile Device via Cable/Wireless Transfer
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where an employee transfers sensitive files to a personal mobile device via USB cable, Bluetooth, or local wireless transfer.

steps.title: Confirm the mobile device connection and transfer event
steps.desc: Review endpoint logs (MDM, DLP, or OS-level device connection logs) for the connection of an unmanaged personal mobile device and correlate with file-access activity around that time.
steps.guidance: Check whether the device appears in the organization's MDM as a managed device; an unmanaged device connecting to a corporate endpoint is a stronger indicator.
steps.outcome: Confirmed transfer event with device identified and file scope estimated.
steps.abort: If the device is enrolled/managed and the transfer is consistent with authorized business use, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Review the device-control policy for mobile device connections
steps.desc: Determine whether endpoint policy should have blocked or alerted on unmanaged mobile device connections, and identify any gap.
steps.outcome: Policy gap identified, if any.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Preserve logs and file lists with a documented chain of custody before any personnel action, given potential disciplinary use.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Engage HR/Legal and, if authorized, request the mobile device for review
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal, and if authorized, request access to or imaging of the personal device per policy and applicable law.
steps.guidance: Personal device access typically requires explicit policy basis, consent, or legal process; follow Legal's direction closely.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal engaged; device access coordinated if authorized.

steps.title: Remote-wipe corporate data from the device if MDM-enrolled
steps.desc: If the device is enrolled in MDM with a corporate profile, selectively wipe corporate data/apps from the device.
steps.outcome: Corporate data removed from the device where technically possible.
steps.abort: If the device is not enrolled, document the limitation.

steps.title: Check MDM enrollment status and enforce policy going forward
steps.desc: Confirm whether the personal device could later be brought into scope of MDM management, or ensure endpoint policy blocks similar unmanaged-device connections going forward.
steps.outcome: MDM/endpoint policy confirmed enforced against the same bypass.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action and tighten mobile device policy
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal and close any policy gap around personal mobile device connections.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied; policy gap closed.

steps.title: Document the case and review mobile device connection controls
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal and evaluate whether endpoint policy should restrict USB/Bluetooth data transfer to unmanaged mobile devices.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34322.def: An insider uses a personal smartphone or tablet's camera to photograph or video-record sensitive information displayed on a corporate screen, extracting data through a purely optical/analog channel that leaves no digital copy or network trace on organizational systems.
ITID-34322.purpose: Captures data theft carried out by photographing or screen-recording sensitive on-screen content using a personal mobile device, bypassing all digital DLP controls entirely.
scopeIncludes: Photographing screens displaying sensitive data (documents, dashboards, credentials) using a personal phone camera
Video-recording a screen over time to capture scrolling or multi-page content
scopeExcludes: Direct digital file transfer to a mobile device via cable or wireless protocol (see Data Copied to Personal Mobile Device via Cable/Wireless Transfer)
ITID-34322.severity: Medium-High; severity is hard to bound precisely since there is no digital trace, so assume full exposure of what was visible on screen.
ITID-34322.priority: P2, escalating to P1 where the visible content included highly sensitive or regulated data, or the behavior was repeated/systematic.
ITID-34322.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR, legal, and physical security immediately upon observation or credible report.
indicators: Physical security camera or witness observation of an employee photographing a screen
Employee's phone found (via authorized device review) to contain photos of sensitive on-screen content
Unusual employee behavior such as consistently angling a screen or positioning a phone near a monitor
vectors: Insider using their phone camera during normal work hours to capture sensitive dashboards, documents, or credentials
Insider systematically photographing content across multiple sessions to build a complete dataset
rootCauses: No policy or physical control (e.g., privacy screens, no-phone zones) restricting personal device use near sensitive displays
Lack of workplace monitoring/camera coverage in areas where highly sensitive data is regularly displayed
No employee awareness training on this exfiltration vector specifically
controls: Policy restricting personal device/camera use in areas displaying highly sensitive data
Privacy screens on monitors displaying sensitive information
Physical security camera coverage of high-sensitivity work areas
ITID-34322.detection: Very weak from a technical control standpoint — this is fundamentally an analog channel; detection relies almost entirely on physical observation, camera surveillance, or after-the-fact device review.
ITID-34322.response: Rely on physical security/witness evidence and, where legally permitted, authorized review of the employee's device; treat as full exposure of the visible content and notify affected data owners.
metrics: Count of observed/reported screen-photography incidents per year
detections: Physical security camera monitoring of sensitive work areas
ITID-34322.notes: This is the leaf in its sibling group with essentially no technical detection surface; response depends almost entirely on physical/behavioral controls rather than logging.

playbook.name: Response: Screenshot/Photo of Screen Content Using Personal Mobile Device
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where an employee uses a personal mobile device's camera to photograph sensitive screen content, bypassing technical DLP controls entirely.

steps.title: Corroborate the photography event through observation or camera footage
steps.desc: Gather witness accounts, manager reports, or facility camera footage that shows the employee photographing a screen, since this technique leaves no direct technical log trail.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with physical security for camera review covering the employee's workspace.
steps.outcome: Corroborating evidence of the photography event obtained where available.
steps.abort: If no corroborating evidence can be obtained, document as an unconfirmed report and monitor for recurrence.
steps.tool: Facility security camera system / witness statements

steps.title: Identify what sensitive content was on screen at the time
steps.desc: Review the employee's application/file access logs and screen session activity to determine what sensitive data was likely visible and photographed.
steps.outcome: Best-estimate scope of data exposed established.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with documented chain of custody
steps.desc: Preserve camera footage, witness statements, and activity logs with a documented chain of custody before any personnel action.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Engage HR/Legal for personnel handling
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal given the potential disciplinary or legal implications; determine whether a request to review the personal device's photos is appropriate and legally supportable.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal engaged with a determined course of action.

steps.title: Assess and limit further exposure of the same content
steps.desc: Determine whether the same sensitive content remains displayable to the employee and apply access restrictions if the investigation is ongoing.
steps.outcome: Access to the sensitive content limited pending investigation outcome.

steps.title: Assess whether privacy screens or display controls are warranted
steps.desc: Evaluate whether the affected workstation or role requires additional physical controls (privacy screen, restricted-camera zone) given the confirmed camera-capture technique.
steps.outcome: Additional physical controls applied where warranted.

steps.title: Apply HR/Legal-directed personnel action
steps.desc: Implement the personnel action determined by HR/Legal based on investigation findings.
steps.outcome: Personnel action applied per HR/Legal direction.

steps.title: Document the case and assess controls against camera-based capture
steps.desc: Record the incident with HR/Legal and evaluate mitigations such as privacy screens, restricted-camera zones, or watermarking for highly sensitive display content, since this vector defeats technical DLP.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34323.def: An insider connects a corporate endpoint to a personal mobile device's Wi-Fi or Bluetooth hotspot (tethering over the device's own cellular data connection), routing outbound traffic — including exfiltrated data — outside the organization's monitored network path, defeating network-based DLP and egress monitoring.
ITID-34323.purpose: Captures the use of a personal mobile device as a Wi-Fi or cellular hotspot to bypass organizational network egress controls, DLP, and monitoring entirely.
scopeIncludes: Corporate laptop connected to a personal phone's mobile hotspot to upload data via a channel outside corporate network monitoring
Use of USB tethering to a personal device's cellular connection for the same purpose
scopeExcludes: Direct file copy onto the mobile device's local storage (see Data Copied to Personal Mobile Device via Cable/Wireless Transfer)
Photographing screen content rather than routing network traffic through the device (see Screenshot/Photo of Screen Content Using Personal Mobile Device)
ITID-34323.severity: High — bypassing the corporate network entirely defeats essentially all network-based detection and DLP controls simultaneously.
ITID-34323.priority: P1 on confirmation, given the complete bypass of network-based monitoring.
ITID-34323.escalation: Escalate to Insider Threat/HR and SOC/IR immediately upon detection.
indicators: Endpoint network configuration showing connection to an unrecognized/personal-hotspot SSID or tethered interface
Endpoint DLP/agent telemetry showing large file activity followed by a network interface change to a non-corporate network
MDM/endpoint policy violation alert for connection to an unmanaged network
vectors: Employee disconnects from corporate Wi-Fi/VPN and connects to their own phone's hotspot before uploading data via a browser or app
Employee uses USB tethering to route traffic through their phone's cellular connection, bypassing corporate egress controls entirely
rootCauses: Endpoint policy does not restrict or alert on connection to non-corporate/unmanaged networks
No requirement that sensitive-data-handling endpoints operate only on corporate-managed networks with always-on VPN
Endpoint DLP has no visibility/enforcement capability once off the corporate network
controls: Endpoint policy blocking or alerting on connection to unmanaged/non-corporate networks
Always-on VPN with split-tunneling disabled for endpoints handling sensitive data
Endpoint DLP/agent enforcement that persists regardless of network connection
ITID-34323.detection: Weak for network-perimeter tooling by design (traffic never traverses the monitored network); detection depends on endpoint-resident agents that can see network-interface changes and enforce policy independent of network path.
ITID-34323.response: Review endpoint agent telemetry for the network-change event and preceding file activity, and treat as confirmed exfiltration pending device/data review.
metrics: Count of detected unmanaged-network/hotspot bypass events per quarter
Percentage of endpoints with always-on VPN/split-tunnel-disabled enforcement
ITID-34323.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs by the mobile device's role as a network conduit/bypass rather than a storage or optical capture destination.

playbook.name: Response: Mobile Device Used as Wi-Fi Hotspot to Bypass Network DLP Controls
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration where an employee tethers a corporate endpoint to a personal mobile device's Wi-Fi/cellular hotspot to route traffic around corporate network monitoring and DLP controls.

steps.title: Confirm the hotspot connection and loss of network visibility
steps.desc: Review endpoint network interface logs and EDR telemetry for connection to an unrecognized Wi-Fi SSID or tethered network consistent with a mobile hotspot, and identify the gap in DLP/network monitoring coverage during that period.
steps.guidance: Endpoint-based DLP/EDR telemetry may still be available even without network-level visibility; prioritize host-based logs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hotspot use with the time window of reduced network visibility identified.
steps.abort: If the hotspot connection is for an approved remote-work scenario with no policy violation, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Reconstruct data activity from host-based telemetry
steps.desc: Use endpoint DLP and file-access logs (which remain available even when network-level monitoring is bypassed) to reconstruct what files were accessed or transferred during the hotspot session.
steps.outcome: Best-available scope of data activity established from host telemetry.

steps.title: Disable tethering/hotspot connectivity per device policy
steps.desc: Apply or enforce endpoint policy to block connections to mobile hotspot/tethered networks from managed devices.
steps.outcome: Hotspot connectivity blocked going forward.

steps.title: Preserve evidence and engage HR/Legal if insider intent is suspected
steps.desc: Preserve host-based evidence with chain of custody and engage HR/Legal if the use of a hotspot appears deliberate rather than incidental (e.g. for connectivity reasons).
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved; HR/Legal engaged if warranted.

steps.title: Remediate the endpoint policy gap allowing the bypass
steps.desc: Update endpoint firewall/network policy so that DLP and monitoring agents enforce controls regardless of network path, closing the bypass.
steps.outcome: Bypass path closed; DLP enforcement confirmed network-independent where feasible.

steps.title: Sweep for the same hotspot bypass technique on other endpoints
steps.desc: Review endpoint network interface logs fleet-wide for other hosts connecting to mobile hotspot/tethered networks to determine if this is an isolated case or a broader pattern.
steps.outcome: Scope confirmed; any additional affected endpoints remediated.

steps.title: Apply appropriate personnel action and monitor the endpoint
steps.desc: Apply personnel action per HR/Legal direction if applicable, and monitor the endpoint for renewed hotspot use.
steps.outcome: Action applied; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the case and strengthen host-based DLP independence from network path
steps.desc: Record the incident and evaluate whether DLP/monitoring controls need to be less dependent on corporate network egress to catch this bypass technique in the future.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34324.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a personal mobile device, where the specific pattern (direct file transfer, screen photography, or network-bypass hotspot use) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34324.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for mobile device exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific mobile-device exfil pattern is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific pattern has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34321, ITID-34322, or ITID-34323
ITID-34324.severity: Set provisionally based on suspected volume/sensitivity; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34324.priority: P2 pending triage; do not delay containment while classification is in progress.
ITID-34324.escalation: Escalate as for active exfiltration pending; escalate priority as evidence narrows the mechanism.
indicators: Generic mobile-device policy violation alert not yet attributed to a specific pattern
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient logging detail to fingerprint the exfiltration pattern
controls: General mobile-device policy monitoring
ITID-34324.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34324.response: Investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID as soon as possible; treat as active exfiltration in the interim.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified mobile-device exfil incidents
ITID-34324.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; every incident logged here should be actively worked toward reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Mobile Device Exfiltration
playbook.description: For confirmed or suspected data exfiltration via a personal mobile device that does not fit a more specific category (cable/wireless transfer, screen photography, or hotspot bypass).

steps.title: Confirm the mobile device involvement and classify the technique
steps.desc: Review available endpoint, DLP, and physical security evidence to confirm a personal mobile device was involved in the suspected exfiltration and attempt to classify the specific method used.
steps.guidance: If the method matches a more specific category, transition to that playbook.
steps.outcome: Confirmed mobile device involvement with method and scope identified as far as possible.
steps.abort: If no exfiltration is confirmed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Estimate scope of data affected
steps.desc: Review available logs and physical evidence to estimate what data was accessed or transferred.
steps.outcome: Best-available scope estimate established.

steps.title: Preserve evidence and engage HR/Legal as warranted
steps.desc: Preserve available logs and evidence with a documented chain of custody; engage HR/Legal if insider involvement is suspected.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved; HR/Legal engaged if warranted.

steps.title: Restrict the relevant access or connectivity path
steps.desc: Restrict the endpoint's ability to connect to unmanaged mobile devices or apply account restrictions as appropriate.
steps.outcome: Exfiltration path restricted.

steps.title: Remediate any identified policy or technical gap
steps.desc: Close the technical or policy gap that allowed the mobile-device-based exfiltration to occur.
steps.outcome: Gap remediated.

steps.title: Verify no residual exposure remains
steps.desc: Confirm no residual technical or policy gap remains that would allow the same mobile-device-based exfiltration method to recur.
steps.outcome: Residual exposure confirmed closed.

steps.title: Apply appropriate personnel action and monitor
steps.desc: Apply personnel action per HR/Legal direction if applicable, and monitor for recurrence.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document the case and reclassify if a specific pattern emerges
steps.desc: Record findings and, if the technique is later identified as a specific known pattern, update the incident classification for future reference.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

ITID-34331.def: A physical hardware device (inline network tap, port mirror device, or covert packet-capture implant) is installed on organizational network cabling or infrastructure — typically requiring physical facility access — to passively capture and later retrieve or transmit intercepted network traffic containing sensitive data.
ITID-34331.purpose: Captures a physical network tap or packet-capture device covertly installed on organizational network infrastructure to passively intercept and exfiltrate data in transit.
scopeIncludes: A physical inline tap or mirroring device discovered connected to network cabling/switch ports
A covert packet-capture device with local storage retrieved and analyzed for stolen data
scopeExcludes: A wireless rogue access point or cellular modem used for exfiltration (see Covert Wireless Exfiltration Implant)
A malicious USB peripheral such as a rogue Raspberry Pi or O.MG cable (see Malicious Peripheral Device Implant)
ITID-34331.severity: Critical — physical implants indicate a highly capable, likely well-resourced adversary with facility access and long-dwell intent.
ITID-34331.priority: P1 immediately upon discovery, regardless of whether active data loss is yet confirmed.
ITID-34331.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, physical security, and executive leadership immediately; treat as a targeted, sophisticated threat actor incident.
indicators: Unrecognized physical device found connected inline on network cabling or a switch port
Unexplained switch port mirroring configuration or unauthorized span port activity
Physical security review/audit discrepancy in server room or wiring closet asset inventory
vectors: Adversary with physical facility access installing an inline tap on a network segment carrying sensitive traffic
Insider or social-engineered third party (e.g., posing as a contractor) planting the device during a facility visit
rootCauses: Insufficient physical security controls over network closets, server rooms, and cabling
No regular physical inventory/audit of network infrastructure and connected devices
Lack of network access control (802.1X) on switch ports preventing rogue device connection
controls: Physical access control and monitoring for network closets/server rooms
Regular physical audit of network infrastructure against an authorized asset inventory
802.1X network access control preventing unauthorized device connection to switch ports
ITID-34331.detection: Weak from purely digital monitoring; effective detection depends on physical security audit, port-security/802.1X enforcement, and periodic infrastructure inventory checks.
ITID-34331.response: Physically remove and forensically preserve the device, audit all network segments for similar implants, and assess the full scope/duration of traffic exposure.
metrics: Count of physical infrastructure audits completed per year
Number of unauthorized devices found during audits
ITID-34331.notes: Differentiated from sibling hardware-implant ITIDs by the wired, in-line packet-capture nature of the device rather than a wireless transmitter or USB peripheral.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue Network Tap/Packet Capture Implant
playbook.description: For a confirmed or suspected physical hardware implant (inline network tap or covert packet capture device) discovered on organizational network infrastructure, capturing traffic for later exfiltration. Typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical facility access.

steps.title: Confirm the physical implant and document its installation point
steps.desc: Physically inspect and photograph the suspected device in place, document its exact location (rack, port, cable run), and confirm it is an unauthorized inline tap or capture device not on the approved asset inventory.
steps.guidance: Do not immediately remove or power off the device without first coordinating with the investigation team, to preserve evidentiary value and assess whether monitored removal is preferable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized physical implant with location and installation method documented.
steps.abort: If the device is found to be an approved monitoring tap on the asset inventory, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Assess what traffic/segments the implant had visibility into
steps.desc: Determine which network segments, VLANs, or traffic flows the implant's placement gave it access to, to scope potentially exposed data.
steps.outcome: Scope of exposed network traffic established.

steps.title: Coordinate a broader facility sweep given likely sophisticated/targeted actor involvement
steps.desc: Given that a physical hardware implant typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical access, coordinate with physical security to sweep other facility areas, wiring closets, and comparable infrastructure for additional implants, and consider engaging broader incident response/threat intelligence resources.
steps.outcome: Facility sweep completed; broader investigation scoped appropriately.

steps.title: Coordinate physical security response before disturbing the device
steps.desc: Engage physical security to secure the area, review access logs/badge records, and pull camera footage for the location and time window before the device is disturbed.
steps.outcome: Physical security engaged; access and camera evidence preserved.
steps.tool: Physical security / badge access system / camera system

steps.title: Remove the implant under controlled, documented conditions
steps.desc: Remove the device following a documented evidence-handling process, photographing each step, and restore normal cabling/configuration.
steps.outcome: Implant removed and evidence preserved.

steps.title: Audit affected network infrastructure for further tampering
steps.desc: Inspect surrounding network equipment, cabling, and configurations for additional tampering, rogue devices, or unauthorized configuration changes.
steps.outcome: Infrastructure confirmed clean or additional tampering identified and remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and increase physical monitoring
steps.desc: Restore the network segment to normal operation and increase physical security monitoring (camera coverage, access restrictions) for the affected area.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored; enhanced physical monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document the incident and review facility access controls
steps.desc: Record the incident, coordinate with physical security and threat intelligence on attribution where possible, and review facility access controls for network infrastructure areas (locked racks, badge zones, visitor escort policy).
steps.outcome: Finding logged; physical access control recommendations tracked.

ITID-34332.def: A physical wireless device — a rogue Wi-Fi access point, a cellular (3G/4G/5G) modem, or similar radio-based implant — is covertly installed on organizational premises, either connected to the internal network or independently powered, to create an exfiltration path that bypasses wired network monitoring and egress controls entirely.
ITID-34332.purpose: Captures a covert wireless device (rogue access point or cellular modem) physically planted on-premises to provide an out-of-band exfiltration channel independent of the organization's monitored network.
scopeIncludes: A rogue Wi-Fi access point discovered broadcasting from within or near organizational premises, bridged to the internal network
A standalone cellular modem/implant discovered connected to internal systems, providing an independent out-of-band exfil path
scopeExcludes: A wired inline network tap or packet-capture device (see Rogue Network Tap/Packet Capture Implant)
A malicious USB peripheral implant such as a rogue Raspberry Pi or O.MG cable (see Malicious Peripheral Device Implant)
ITID-34332.severity: Critical — an independent, cellular-connected implant can operate entirely outside network monitoring, representing a near-total blind spot.
ITID-34332.priority: P1 immediately upon discovery, regardless of whether active data loss is yet confirmed.
ITID-34332.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, physical security, and executive leadership immediately; treat as a targeted, sophisticated threat actor incident.
indicators: Wireless survey detecting an unrecognized SSID broadcasting from within or near a facility
Unrecognized device found physically connected to internal network infrastructure with no corresponding asset record
RF/cellular signal detected from an area with no authorized wireless equipment
vectors: Adversary or insider physically planting a small Wi-Fi/cellular device connected to an internal switch port or workstation
Device disguised within or behind existing legitimate equipment (e.g., inside a power strip or under a desk) to avoid casual discovery
rootCauses: No regular wireless spectrum/rogue-AP survey of facility premises
Insufficient physical security controls allowing covert device placement
No port-security/802.1X enforcement preventing an unauthorized device from bridging onto the internal network
controls: Regular rogue-access-point/wireless spectrum surveys of facility premises
Physical access control and monitoring for areas where such a device could be planted
802.1X network access control preventing unauthorized bridging devices
ITID-34332.detection: Weak from purely digital/network monitoring, especially for cellular-connected implants; effective detection depends on wireless spectrum surveys and physical security audits.
ITID-34332.response: Physically remove and forensically preserve the device, sweep the facility for additional implants, and assess the full scope/duration of exposure.
metrics: Count of wireless spectrum surveys completed per year
Number of rogue devices identified during surveys
ITID-34332.notes: Differentiated from ITID-34331 by the wireless/out-of-band nature of the channel, which can bypass wired network monitoring entirely — a materially different detection challenge.

playbook.name: Response: Covert Wireless Exfiltration Implant (Rogue Access Point/Cellular Modem Planted On-Premises)
playbook.description: For a confirmed or suspected physical hardware implant providing covert wireless connectivity (rogue Wi-Fi access point or cellular modem) planted on-premises to exfiltrate data outside normal network monitoring. Typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical facility access.

steps.title: Confirm the rogue wireless device and its physical location
steps.desc: Use wireless spectrum scanning/rogue AP detection tools to locate the device's physical signal source, and physically confirm and photograph the device once located.
steps.guidance: Do not immediately remove or power off the device without first coordinating with the investigation team.
steps.outcome: Confirmed rogue wireless implant with physical location documented.
steps.abort: If the device is an approved guest AP or IoT device on the asset inventory, close as a false positive.
steps.tool: Wireless spectrum analyzer / rogue AP detection / physical inspection

steps.title: Assess what network access or traffic the implant could reach
steps.desc: Determine whether the device is bridged to the internal network (posing a broader access risk) or standalone with cellular backhaul (used purely to relay exfiltrated data), and scope accordingly.
steps.outcome: Scope of network exposure or exfiltration capability established.

steps.title: Coordinate a broader facility sweep given likely sophisticated/targeted actor involvement
steps.desc: Given that a physical hardware implant typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical access, coordinate with physical security to sweep other facility areas for additional implants and engage broader incident response resources.
steps.outcome: Facility sweep completed; broader investigation scoped appropriately.

steps.title: Coordinate physical security response before disturbing the device
steps.desc: Engage physical security to secure the area and pull badge access/camera footage for the location and relevant time window before the device is disturbed.
steps.outcome: Physical security engaged; access and camera evidence preserved.
steps.tool: Physical security / badge access system / camera system

steps.title: Remove the implant under controlled, documented conditions
steps.desc: Remove the device following a documented evidence-handling process, photographing each step.
steps.outcome: Implant removed and evidence preserved.

steps.title: Audit the network for any bridging or configuration changes enabling the implant
steps.desc: Inspect network switch ports, wireless controller configurations, and firewall rules for evidence of how the implant obtained connectivity, and remediate.
steps.outcome: Enabling access confirmed removed or closed.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and increase physical/wireless monitoring
steps.desc: Restore normal operations and deploy or increase ongoing rogue-AP/wireless spectrum monitoring for the facility.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored; enhanced wireless monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document the incident and review facility access controls
steps.desc: Record the incident, coordinate with physical security and threat intelligence on attribution where possible, and review facility access controls and wireless monitoring coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34333.def: A malicious peripheral device — such as a small single-board computer (e.g., a disguised Raspberry Pi) connected to an internal port, or a keystroke-injection/exfiltration cable (e.g., an O.MG Cable) substituted for a legitimate charging or peripheral cable — is planted at a workstation to provide the attacker with covert local access, keystroke capture, or a network implant for data theft.
ITID-34333.purpose: Captures a malicious USB-form-factor peripheral (a covert single-board computer or a cable with embedded attack hardware) planted or substituted at a workstation to provide covert access or exfiltration capability.
scopeIncludes: A covert single-board computer (e.g., Raspberry Pi) found connected to an internal network port or workstation, configured for remote access or data capture
A modified cable (charging/USB/keyboard) containing embedded attack hardware substituted for a legitimate one, used for keystroke injection or exfiltration
scopeExcludes: A wired inline network tap purpose-built for passive packet capture (see Rogue Network Tap/Packet Capture Implant)
A standalone wireless access point or cellular modem implant (see Covert Wireless Exfiltration Implant)
ITID-34333.severity: Critical — this class of implant typically provides active remote access in addition to data capture, not just passive interception.
ITID-34333.priority: P1 immediately upon discovery, regardless of whether active data loss is yet confirmed.
ITID-34333.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, physical security, and executive leadership immediately; treat as a targeted, sophisticated threat actor incident.
indicators: Unrecognized small computing device found connected to a workstation or network port
A charging/USB cable that behaves unexpectedly (e.g., enumerates as a keyboard/HID device) when inspected
Asset inventory discrepancy where a cable or peripheral does not match the organization's approved equipment
vectors: Attacker or insider swapping a legitimate charging cable for a malicious lookalike at a target's desk
Attacker planting a disguised single-board computer inside or behind legitimate equipment during a facility visit
rootCauses: No policy or technical control restricting peripherals/cables to organization-issued, asset-tagged equipment
USB device control not configured to flag anomalous HID enumeration behavior
Insufficient physical security allowing unsupervised access to individual workstations
controls: USB/peripheral device control policy restricted to organization-issued, asset-tagged equipment
Endpoint alerting on anomalous HID device enumeration behavior
Physical security controls limiting unsupervised access to individual workstations
ITID-34333.detection: Weak from network monitoring alone; effective detection depends on endpoint HID-anomaly alerting, physical asset inventory checks, and employee awareness of peripheral substitution.
ITID-34333.response: Physically remove and forensically preserve the device, image the affected workstation, and assess what was captured or accessed via the implant.
metrics: Count of malicious peripheral implants identified per year
detections: Endpoint anomalous HID device enumeration alerting
ITID-34333.notes: Differentiated from sibling ITIDs by the peripheral/endpoint-level (rather than network-infrastructure-level) point of compromise, and by typically combining active access capability with data capture.

playbook.name: Response: Malicious Peripheral Device Implant (Rogue Raspberry Pi/O.MG Cable)
playbook.description: For a confirmed or suspected malicious peripheral device implant (e.g. a rogue single-board computer plugged into internal infrastructure, or a weaponized USB cable such as an O.MG cable providing keystroke injection/remote access) planted to enable data exfiltration. Typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical facility or workstation access.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious peripheral and document its placement
steps.desc: Physically inspect the suspected device (unusual small computer, cable, or dongle) and confirm it does not match an approved asset; photograph and document exactly where and how it was connected.
steps.guidance: Be aware some weaponized cables are visually near-identical to legitimate cables; inspect connectors and check EDR for unusual HID (keyboard/mouse) device enumeration events as corroboration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious peripheral with placement documented.
steps.abort: If the device is confirmed as an approved IT asset, close as a false positive.
steps.tool: Physical inspection / EDR device enumeration logs

steps.title: Assess what activity the implant performed on the host/network
steps.desc: Review EDR and network logs for the affected host to determine what commands were executed, what network access the implant used, and what data may have been accessed as a result.
steps.outcome: Scope of implant activity and potential data exposure established.

steps.title: Coordinate a broader facility/workstation sweep given likely sophisticated/targeted actor involvement
steps.desc: Given that a physical implant typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical access, coordinate with physical security to sweep comparable workstations and areas for additional implants and engage broader incident response resources.
steps.outcome: Sweep completed; broader investigation scoped appropriately.

steps.title: Coordinate physical security response before disturbing the device
steps.desc: Engage physical security to secure the area and pull badge access/camera footage for the location and relevant time window before the device is disturbed.
steps.outcome: Physical security engaged; access and camera evidence preserved.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host and remove the implant under documented conditions
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host the implant was connected to, then remove the device following a documented evidence-handling process, photographing each step.
steps.outcome: Host isolated; implant removed and evidence preserved.

steps.title: Rebuild the affected host and audit for further compromise
steps.desc: Reimage the host that was connected to the implant and audit for any malware, credential theft, or persistence mechanisms introduced via the device.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore the host and increase physical/USB security controls
steps.desc: Restore the host to service and implement or reinforce controls such as USB port restrictions, HID device allowlisting, and physical port locks.
steps.outcome: Host restored; enhanced physical/USB controls in place.

steps.title: Document the incident and review facility/workstation access controls
steps.desc: Record the incident, coordinate with physical security and threat intelligence on attribution where possible, and review physical access controls for workstations and peripheral security policy.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34334.def: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a covertly planted physical hardware device, where the specific type (network tap, wireless implant, or malicious peripheral) has not yet been determined at time of logging.
ITID-34334.purpose: Catch-all intake bucket for hardware implant exfiltration that cannot yet be classified into a specific mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage classification before the specific hardware implant type is confirmed
Cases with insufficient evidence to distinguish between sibling ITIDs
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific implant type has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-34331, ITID-34332, or ITID-34333
ITID-34334.severity: Critical by default given the class of threat; re-assess once reclassified.
ITID-34334.priority: P1 immediately upon discovery, regardless of classification status.
ITID-34334.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, physical security, and executive leadership immediately upon any discovery.
indicators: An unrecognized physical device discovered on premises or network infrastructure with type not yet determined
vectors: Unknown at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient physical/network forensic detail at time of discovery to fingerprint the implant type
controls: General physical security and infrastructure audit controls
ITID-34334.detection: Variable; exists because classification is incomplete at time of intake.
ITID-34334.response: Physically secure and forensically preserve the device immediately, then investigate to reclassify into the correct sibling ITID.
metrics: Count and average time-to-reclassify of unclassified hardware implant incidents
ITID-34334.notes: Intake/overflow leaf only; given the criticality of this threat class, do not delay containment/forensic preservation pending reclassification.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Hardware Implant Exfiltration
playbook.description: For a confirmed or suspected physical hardware implant used for data exfiltration that does not fit a more specific category (network tap, wireless implant, or malicious peripheral). Typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical facility access.

steps.title: Confirm the physical implant and classify its type
steps.desc: Physically inspect and document the suspected device, confirm it is unauthorized, and attempt to classify it against more specific categories (network tap, wireless implant, malicious peripheral).
steps.guidance: If the device matches a more specific category, transition to that playbook. Do not disturb the device before coordinating with the investigation team.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized physical implant with type and location documented.
steps.abort: If the device is confirmed as an approved asset, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Coordinate a broader facility sweep given likely sophisticated/targeted actor involvement
steps.desc: Given that a physical hardware implant typically indicates a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical access, coordinate with physical security to sweep other areas for additional implants and engage broader incident response resources.
steps.outcome: Facility sweep completed; broader investigation scoped appropriately.

steps.title: Coordinate physical security response before disturbing the device
steps.desc: Engage physical security to secure the area and pull badge access/camera footage before the device is disturbed.
steps.outcome: Physical security engaged; access and camera evidence preserved.

steps.title: Remove the implant under controlled, documented conditions
steps.desc: Remove the device following a documented evidence-handling process, photographing each step.
steps.outcome: Implant removed and evidence preserved.

steps.title: Audit affected systems/infrastructure for further tampering
steps.desc: Inspect surrounding systems, cabling, and configurations for additional tampering or unauthorized changes.
steps.outcome: Systems confirmed clean or additional tampering remediated.

steps.title: Sweep for additional implants given likely sophisticated/targeted actor involvement
steps.desc: Coordinate a broader sweep of comparable systems and facility areas for additional hardware implants, since physical implants typically indicate a sophisticated, targeted threat actor with physical access.
steps.outcome: Sweep completed; scope confirmed or additional implants found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and increase physical monitoring
steps.desc: Restore normal operations and increase physical security monitoring for the affected area.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored; enhanced physical monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document the incident and review facility access controls
steps.desc: Record the incident, coordinate with physical security and threat intelligence on attribution where possible, and review facility access controls.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendations tracked.

ITID-34411.def: An attacker exploits a SQL injection vulnerability in a web application's input handling to craft queries that extract large volumes of data directly from the backend database, bypassing the application's intended access controls and business logic entirely.
ITID-34411.purpose: Captures the classic web application attack of using SQL injection to bulk-extract records directly from a backend database via a vulnerable application input.
scopeIncludes: Classic, blind, or time-based SQL injection used to dump database tables/records
Automated SQLi tooling (e.g., sqlmap) used to enumerate and exfiltrate database contents
scopeExcludes: Server-Side Request Forgery used to reach internal data sources (see Server-Side Request Forgery Used to Exfiltrate Internal Data)
Bulk scraping via an authorization-logic flaw rather than an injection flaw (see Insecure Direct Object Reference Used for Bulk Record Scraping)
ITID-34411.severity: Critical — direct database access typically exposes the full dataset, not just individual records.
ITID-34411.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation of successful data extraction.
ITID-34411.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, application owners, and legal/privacy immediately given the typical breadth of data exposed.
indicators: WAF/application logs showing SQL injection payload patterns in request parameters
Abnormal, high-volume database query patterns originating from the application's own service account
Database audit logs showing queries structurally inconsistent with the application's normal query patterns
vectors: Unsanitized user input passed directly into a SQL query, exploited manually or via automated tooling
Blind/time-based SQL injection used where direct output is not visible, exfiltrating data bit-by-bit
rootCauses: Lack of parameterized queries/prepared statements in application code
No Web Application Firewall (WAF) or inadequate WAF rule coverage for injection patterns
Excessive database privileges granted to the application's service account beyond what is functionally required
controls: Parameterized queries/prepared statements enforced in application code
WAF with SQL injection detection rules
Least-privilege database service account permissions
Secure code review/SAST scanning for injection vulnerabilities pre-deployment
ITID-34411.detection: Good where WAF and database audit logging are both deployed and correlated; weaker for blind/time-based injection that produces low, slow query volumes.
ITID-34411.response: Patch the vulnerable input handling immediately, identify the full scope of data queried/extracted from database audit logs, and rotate any exposed credentials or secrets.
metrics: Count of confirmed SQL injection exploitation incidents per year
Time from vulnerability introduction to detection/patch (where determinable)
detections: Database audit log anomalous query volume alerting
ITID-34411.notes: Differentiated from sibling web-application ITIDs by the specific exploitation class (injection into the query layer) rather than server-side request forgery or authorization-logic (IDOR) flaws.

playbook.name: Response: SQL Injection Used to Bulk-Extract Database Records
playbook.description: For an application-layer SQL injection vulnerability exploited to bulk-extract records from a backend database.

steps.title: Confirm the injection point and extracted data scope
steps.desc: Review WAF and application/database logs to identify the vulnerable endpoint/parameter, the injection payloads used, and the tables/records accessed.
steps.guidance: Look for classic indicators: UNION SELECT patterns, error-based enumeration, or abnormal query volume/response sizes from a single source.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable endpoint identified and scope of extracted data established.

steps.title: Identify the source and determine if exploitation is ongoing
steps.desc: Determine the source IP(s)/account(s) used and whether the injection attempts are still active.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the attack is ongoing or historical.

steps.title: Block the malicious source at the WAF/gateway
steps.desc: Add a WAF rule or IP/account block to stop further injection attempts immediately.
steps.outcome: Active exploitation stopped.

steps.title: Apply a virtual patch or input-validation rule at the WAF layer
steps.desc: Deploy a targeted WAF rule to block the injection pattern for the vulnerable parameter while the code fix is prepared.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable endpoint protected pending a permanent code fix.

steps.title: Patch the underlying vulnerability in application code
steps.desc: Work with the application team to fix the vulnerable query (parameterized queries/prepared statements) and deploy the fix.
steps.outcome: Root-cause vulnerability remediated.

steps.title: Scan for similar vulnerabilities elsewhere in the application
steps.desc: Run static/dynamic analysis across the application for similar unparameterized query patterns.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other instances of the same vulnerability class remain.

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess the sensitivity of the extracted records and coordinate with Legal on breach-notification requirements.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Document the case and review secure-coding/testing practices
steps.desc: Record findings and confirm SQLi testing is included in the SDLC/pen-test scope going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and process gap addressed.

ITID-34412.def: An attacker exploits a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability to make the vulnerable server-side application issue requests to internal-only endpoints (internal APIs, cloud metadata services, internal admin panels), exfiltrating the response content back to the attacker through the application's own output.
ITID-34412.purpose: Captures the use of Server-Side Request Forgery to coerce a web application into fetching and exposing internal data or resources the attacker could not otherwise reach directly.
scopeIncludes: SSRF used to reach cloud instance metadata services and extract credentials/tokens
SSRF used to reach an internal-only API or data service not otherwise internet-accessible, with the response relayed back to the attacker
scopeExcludes: SQL injection used to extract data directly from a database (see SQL Injection Used to Bulk-Extract Database Records)
Authorization-logic (IDOR) exploitation to scrape records the attacker can access directly (see Insecure Direct Object Reference Used for Bulk Record Scraping)
ITID-34412.severity: Critical, particularly when cloud metadata/credential endpoints are reached, as this often enables further compromise beyond the immediate data exposure.
ITID-34412.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation, given the potential for credential exposure enabling broader compromise.
ITID-34412.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR and cloud/infrastructure teams immediately; rotate any credentials potentially exposed via metadata service access.
indicators: Application logs showing outbound requests to internal-only IP ranges or the cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) initiated by user-supplied input
WAF/application logs showing URL parameters containing internal hostnames, IPs, or metadata service paths
Unusual response sizes/content from an endpoint that should return only application-specific data
vectors: User-supplied URL parameter passed unvalidated to a server-side fetch/request function
Exploitation of an image/file-fetching feature to target internal endpoints instead of external resources
rootCauses: No input validation/allow-listing on server-side request destinations
Cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) not configured to require session tokens (IMDSv2 or equivalent)
Lack of network segmentation preventing the application server from reaching sensitive internal endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
controls: Input validation/allow-listing on server-side request destinations
Enforcement of IMDSv2 (or equivalent token-required metadata service) on cloud instances
Network segmentation limiting application-server reach to only required internal endpoints
ITID-34412.detection: Moderate — requires application-layer logging of outbound server-side requests plus awareness of internal/metadata IP ranges to catch reliably; often missed by perimeter-focused monitoring alone.
ITID-34412.response: Patch the SSRF vulnerability, rotate any credentials/tokens potentially exposed via metadata or internal endpoint access, and determine the full scope of internal resources reached.
metrics: Count of confirmed SSRF exploitation incidents per year
Percentage of cloud instances enforcing IMDSv2/equivalent
ITID-34412.notes: Differentiated from sibling web-application ITIDs by the SSRF exploitation mechanism, which uniquely enables reaching internal-only resources the attacker cannot otherwise directly access.

playbook.name: Response: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Used to Exfiltrate Internal Data
playbook.description: For an SSRF vulnerability exploited to have the application server request and disclose internal data (e.g. cloud metadata, internal APIs) to the attacker.

steps.title: Confirm the SSRF vector and internal resources reached
steps.desc: Review WAF and application logs to identify the vulnerable parameter accepting attacker-controlled URLs, and what internal endpoints (cloud metadata service, internal APIs, admin interfaces) were reached.
steps.guidance: Cloud instance metadata endpoints are a high-priority check — SSRF is commonly used to steal instance credentials from them.
steps.outcome: SSRF vector and internal resources accessed identified.

steps.title: Determine if credentials or secrets were exposed via the SSRF path
steps.desc: Check whether cloud instance credentials, internal API tokens, or other secrets were retrieved through the SSRF.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether secrets were exposed, which drives urgency of containment.

steps.title: Block the malicious source and vulnerable request pattern
steps.desc: Block the source at the WAF/gateway and apply a rule restricting outbound requests from the vulnerable parameter.
steps.outcome: Active exploitation stopped.

steps.title: Rotate any exposed credentials/secrets immediately
steps.desc: If instance credentials or tokens were retrieved via SSRF, rotate them immediately and review their usage for misuse.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials invalidated before further misuse.

steps.title: Patch the SSRF vulnerability and restrict outbound server requests
steps.desc: Fix the vulnerable code (URL allow-listing, disabling redirects, blocking internal IP ranges) and apply network-level egress restrictions from the application tier to metadata/internal services.
steps.outcome: Root-cause vulnerability remediated and defense-in-depth network control applied.
steps.tool: Application code repository / network security groups

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess what internal data/secrets were disclosed and coordinate with Legal on notification requirements.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Verify no lateral movement occurred using exposed credentials
steps.desc: Review activity logs for the rotated credentials/tokens to confirm they were not used for further access before rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope is contained to the SSRF disclosure itself, or further compromise identified and escalated.

steps.title: Document the case and review SSRF defenses across the estate
steps.desc: Record findings and confirm SSRF protections (metadata service hardening, egress filtering) are applied consistently across other applications.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and broader hardening tracked.

ITID-34413.def: An attacker exploits an authorization-logic flaw in which the application fails to verify that a requesting user is authorized to access a specific record, allowing systematic enumeration of predictable or sequential object identifiers (record IDs, account numbers) to scrape large volumes of other users' data through an otherwise legitimate-looking, authenticated application feature.
ITID-34413.purpose: Captures bulk record scraping enabled by an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) flaw, where an attacker enumerates predictable identifiers to access records belonging to other users at scale.
scopeIncludes: Automated enumeration of sequential/predictable record IDs via an API or web endpoint lacking per-object authorization checks
Bulk scraping of another user's records by manipulating an ID parameter in an otherwise legitimate request
scopeExcludes: Data extraction via injection into the query/database layer (see SQL Injection Used to Bulk-Extract Database Records)
Use of SSRF to reach internal-only resources rather than exploiting an authorization flaw on user-facing records (see Server-Side Request Forgery Used to Exfiltrate Internal Data)
ITID-34413.severity: High to Critical, scaling with the number of records accessible and the sensitivity of the data exposed per record.
ITID-34413.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation of active bulk enumeration or scraping.
ITID-34413.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR, application owners, and legal/privacy immediately given the typical scale of a successful IDOR-based scrape.
indicators: Application/API logs showing a single account making sequential requests across a wide range of object IDs
Abnormally high request rate for a per-record endpoint from one authenticated session
Access to record IDs falling outside any range the requesting user should legitimately own or have been issued
vectors: Automated script iterating through sequential or predictable IDs against a vulnerable endpoint
Manual parameter tampering discovered during reconnaissance, then automated for bulk extraction
rootCauses: Missing or incomplete per-object authorization checks (relying on ID obscurity rather than explicit access control)
Use of sequential, predictable identifiers instead of non-guessable identifiers (e.g., UUIDs) for sensitive records
No rate limiting or anomaly detection on per-record API/endpoint access patterns
controls: Explicit per-object authorization checks on every record-access endpoint
Use of non-guessable identifiers for sensitive record access
API rate limiting and anomaly detection on per-user record-access volume
ITID-34413.detection: Moderate — requires API/application-layer request-pattern monitoring capable of spotting sequential-ID enumeration by a single account; often missed by traditional network or WAF signature-based tools since each individual request looks legitimate.
ITID-34413.response: Patch the authorization flaw immediately, identify the full range of record IDs accessed by the offending account/session, and notify affected data subjects/owners as required.
metrics: Count of confirmed IDOR-based bulk scraping incidents per year
Number of records exposed per incident
ITID-34413.notes: Differentiated from sibling web-application ITIDs by the authorization-logic (rather than injection or SSRF) nature of the flaw; the attacker typically uses fully legitimate, authenticated requests with only the object identifier manipulated.

playbook.name: Response: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) Used for Bulk Record Scraping
playbook.description: For an IDOR vulnerability exploited by iterating predictable object identifiers to scrape records the requester was not authorized to access.

steps.title: Confirm the IDOR pattern and scope of records accessed
steps.desc: Review application/API logs for sequential or enumerated identifier requests from a single account/source, and determine which records were exposed relative to the requester's actual authorization.
steps.guidance: Look for rapid, sequential ID requests (e.g. /records/1001, /records/1002...) far exceeding the user's normal single-record access pattern.
steps.outcome: Scope of over-accessed records established.

steps.title: Determine whether the source account is legitimate but abusing access, or externally controlled
steps.desc: Establish whether this is an authenticated legitimate user scraping beyond their authorization (insider) or an attacker using a compromised/valid session.
steps.guidance: If insider-driven, escalate to HR/Legal per insider-data-handling policy.
steps.outcome: Root cause established.

steps.title: Block the source and/or suspend the abusing account
steps.desc: Rate-limit or block the source at the API gateway/WAF, and suspend the account if abuse is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Further scraping stopped.

steps.title: Apply a temporary authorization check or rate limit at the gateway
steps.desc: Deploy a stop-gap object-ownership check or aggressive rate limit on the affected endpoint while the code fix is prepared.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable endpoint protected pending a permanent fix.

steps.title: Patch the missing authorization check in application code
steps.desc: Fix the endpoint to enforce object-level authorization (verify the requester owns/is entitled to the requested record) and deploy the fix.
steps.outcome: Root-cause vulnerability remediated.

steps.title: Scan for similar IDOR patterns on other endpoints
steps.desc: Review other endpoints using sequential/predictable identifiers for the same missing-authorization pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other instances of the same vulnerability class remain.

steps.title: Scope data exposure and notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess the sensitivity of the scraped records and coordinate with Legal on breach-notification requirements.
steps.outcome: Impact assessed and obligations addressed.

steps.title: Document the case and review authorization-testing practices
steps.desc: Record findings and confirm object-level authorization testing is included in the SDLC/pen-test scope going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and process gap addressed.
